verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Now draw some out and take it to the master of the feast." So they took it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now draw some out. No prayer, no touch, no word over the water. This is the moment of the sign, and John refuses to describe it: no gesture, no shimmer on the surface. Somewhere in that sentence the water became wine, silently, by his will, and the text does not say where. That is characteristic of this Gospel. John is far more interested in what a sign means than in how it looked.

The master of the feast. The head steward was probably a trusted guest or senior servant put in charge of the celebration, responsible for the food and drink, whose job was to know what was being served and to stop anything unsuitable reaching the guests.

So they took it. More obedience, and a real risk. They are to walk up to the steward, in front of the party, and hand him a cup of what they drew out of a washing jar a moment ago. If nothing has happened, they are presenting the master of ceremonies with hand-washing water at a wedding. They had watched the water go in. Nobody had told them anything had changed. All they had was a sentence from a guest, and a woman’s instruction to do whatever he said.

The proof comes after. They do not taste it first. There is no version of this story in which the servants get to verify the wine in the kitchen and then decide whether to carry it out. That is not a defect in the arrangement. It is what trust is, and every other arrangement is something else wearing trust’s clothes.

Does faith mean acting without any evidence at all? No. The servants were not leaping in the dark; they had a word from Jesus and the testimony of someone who knew him. Christian faith rests on solid grounds: the eyewitness record of his life, death and resurrection, the fulfilled Scriptures, the changed lives around us. What faith does not have is a guarantee in advance of how each step of obedience will turn out. We trust the person, and then we act, and the confirmation often comes after. That is not irrational. It is how every relationship of trust works.

For worship. He never touched the water. The Word who spoke the world into being needs no ceremony to change water into wine; he wills it, and it is so. And out of sheer kindness he chooses to work through the hands of servants who trust him, and to let us carry what he has made new.
verseByVerse.note: The master of the feast was the guest put in charge of the celebration.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the master of the feast tasted the water now become wine, and did not know where it came from (though the servants who had drawn the water knew), the master of the feast called the bridegroom and said to him, 'Everyone serves the good wine first, and when people have drunk freely, then the poor wine. But you have kept the good wine until now.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The servants knew. The water had truly become wine. The steward tastes it and cannot account for it. The bridegroom gets the credit and has no idea what for. The guests drink it and never learn anything happened. The only people in the building who understand are the ones who carried the jars. The knowledge went not to the man with the office, nor to the one being honoured, but to the servants, who obeyed a strange instruction and therefore found out (7:17).

Where from? The word is pothen, where from, and it is going to follow Jesus through the whole book. The crowd in Jerusalem will say they know where this man comes from and that settles it (7:27). A blind man will tell the authorities that the remarkable thing is precisely that they do not know where he comes from (9:29–30). And at the very end, Pilate, out of his depth in his own judgment hall, will ask him straight out, where are you from? and get no answer at all (19:9). The first person in this Gospel to taste what Jesus has done and be unable to account for it is a wine steward at a party, and he will not be the last.

The bridegroom praised by mistake. The steward, having no idea where the wine came from, calls over the man he assumes is responsible and congratulates him. The bridegroom is being praised for the one thing at his own wedding he had nothing whatever to do with. And within a chapter John the Baptist will use that exact word about Jesus: the one who has the bride is the bridegroom (3:29). The real bridegroom is standing in that room. The compliment is being paid to the wrong man, by a man who does not know what he is saying, which keeps happening in this Gospel and will happen most famously when a high priest explains that it is better for one man to die for the people (11:49–52).

The good wine until now. The world front-loads: the advertisement is better than the product, the holiday is finest in the brochure, youth is spent early, and almost every pleasure is arranged so that the best comes first and what follows is a slow negotiation with decline. God works the other way round. The old covenant was good, but the new is better (Hebrews 8:6). Israel got the shadow first and the substance later. And Scripture ends not simply with a garden restored but with a city, and a wedding, and the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9).

What it does not mean. The best wine last is not an assurance that your circumstances will improve, and it must not be handed to someone as though it were. Plenty of Christian lives get harder rather than easier; health goes, work narrows, the people you love are buried one at a time, and there is no verse anywhere that guarantees the second half will be more comfortable than the first. What is promised is not a better stretch of road. It is a better end, and an end that is not the end.

Where Christians differ: wine and alcohol. Some Christians argue that biblical wine was unfermented grape juice, and that Christians should abstain completely. This commentary’s view: the wine Jesus made was real wine, as the master’s comment shows. Scripture praises wine as God’s gift (Psalm 104:15) while forbidding drunkenness (Ephesians 5:18; Proverbs 23:29–35). Christians are free to drink in moderation, and free to abstain; they must never get drunk, and must be willing to abstain out of love for weaker brothers (Romans 14:21). Abstinence is a wise choice for many, but not a command.

Not a killjoy. The steward’s remark about guests who have drunk freely makes no sense of grape juice. But nothing here licenses excess, and nothing shames the Christian who abstains, whether from conviction or from hard experience of what drink has done in a family. What the sign does say is that the God who came among us was not a killjoy. His first miracle was not a rebuke but a wedding present, and an extravagant one.

What if alcohol has been a problem for me or my family? Then abstaining is not legalism but wisdom, and often love. Freedom to drink is not an obligation to drink, and Paul says it is good not to drink wine if it makes a brother stumble (Romans 14:21); the brother may be you. If drink has a hold on you, the gospel offers forgiveness and real help: confess it honestly to God and to a trusted Christian, get practical support, and remove it from your home. And if a parent’s or spouse’s drinking has wounded you, this passage does not ask you to celebrate wine. It shows you a Lord who brings joy without ruin, and who can heal what drink has broken.

On a Tuesday. If you have begun to suspect that your best days are behind you, that the years when you felt most alive and most in love with God are in the past, say the steward’s sentence over your life. On any account but this one that instinct would be correct. For anyone in Christ the arrangement has been reversed.

For worship. The good wine kept until now is not only a vintage; it is the Son himself. Long ago God spoke by the prophets, at many times and in many ways, and he kept his best until these last days, when he spoke to us by his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2). The Father did not open the finest he had first. He opened it in the fullness of time (Galatians 4:4), and the one who made the wine at Cana would give his own blood for the new covenant. Every cup of grace since has come from that store, and it has not run dry. Glory to the God who kept the best until now.

parallels.desc: a feast of well-aged wine
the mountains shall drip sweet wine

verseByVerse.quote: "This, the first of his signs, Jesus did at Cana in Galilee, and manifested his glory. And his disciples believed in him. After this he went down to Capernaum, with his mother and his brothers and his disciples, and they stayed there for a few days."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first of his signs. John calls Jesus’ miracles signs (sēmeia), pointers to who he is: not just displays of power, but signs that reveal his identity. That is a deliberate choice, and you can prove it by what he never says. Matthew, Mark and Luke commonly describe the miracles as dynameis, acts of power, mighty works. John does not use that word for them at all. He uses the word for a signpost.

A signpost, not a show. The difference is the whole of his method. A mighty work invites you to be impressed by the one who did it. A signpost is not for admiring. It has no interest in itself; its entire value lies in pointing away from where it stands to somewhere you have not got to yet, and a traveller who stops at a signpost and praises the carpentry has missed the point. That is precisely what will go wrong with the crowds in chapter 6, who eat the loaves and want to make him king and are told they came looking for him not because they saw signs but because they ate their fill of the loaves (6:26).

Seven signs. John records seven signs before the resurrection: water into wine (2:1–11), the official’s son (4:46–54), the paralysed man (5:1–15), the five thousand (6:1–15), walking on water (6:16–21), the man born blind (9:1–41), and Lazarus (11:1–44). Each reveals something of who Jesus is. The counting is debated at the edges, but the pattern is not, and he tells you at the close exactly what he was doing (20:30–31). And note that he calls this the first, and the Greek word is the one he opened the Gospel with. In the beginning was the Word. This was the beginning of his signs. The book is quietly starting again.

And manifested his glory. His divine glory (1:14), hidden in his humanity, shone through. Fourteen verses into chapter 1 John had written, we have seen his glory, and here is the first instalment. The sign shows that Jesus is the Creator, who turns water into wine every year through the vine and now does it in a moment; that he brings the abundance of the messianic age; and that the old order of purification gives way to the new wine of the kingdom. Glory is the shining out of who God is: his worth and beauty made visible. When Moses asked to see God’s glory, God answered by making his goodness pass before him and proclaiming his name, merciful and gracious (Exodus 33:18–19; 34:6). At Cana that same goodness is seen in a man’s kindness to a bridegroom in trouble.

The glory in clay cups. The glory of God, the thing that filled the tent until Moses could not go in, that drove the priests out of Solomon’s temple so that they could not stand to minister (1 Kings 8:11), that Isaiah saw for one moment and cried out that he was undone, was in a back room in Cana, quietly seeing to it that a young couple were not humiliated on their wedding day. Nothing shook. Nobody fell down. The steward went on doing his job and the bridegroom accepted a compliment he had not earned, and the glory of the eternal God went round that room in cups.

His disciples believed. That is the purpose of the signs (20:30–31), and it ought to stop you, because they already had (1:41–49). Andrew had said, we have found the Messiah; Nathanael had said, you are the Son of God. Their faith deepened. Faith is not a switch thrown once; it grows, is tested, and grows again. The same men will be terrified in a boat and scattered on the night of his arrest, and one will refuse to believe the resurrection without touching the wounds. If your faith is larger or smaller than it was five years ago, that is not instability. It is the ordinary condition of everyone in this chapter.

Should I look for signs and miracles today? Look for what the signs were for. They were written down so that you may believe (20:31); the record of them is God’s chosen means of bringing you to faith now, and Jesus pronounced a blessing on those who have not seen and yet have believed (20:29). God still answers prayer, and he can heal and provide in ways that astonish us; we should ask him freely. But the apostolic signs belonged to the founding of the church, and we do not need fresh wonders to confirm a gospel already confirmed. That is the view called cessationism, held because the New Testament ties such signs to the apostles’ own witness (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4). Many faithful Christians, in Pentecostal and charismatic churches among others, believe these gifts continue, and we honour them as brothers; all of us agree that every sign points to Christ. A faith that keeps demanding new signs has missed the one they all point to. You have the signs, in writing, and the Lord himself.

His mother and his brothers. This is the first mention of his brothers in this Gospel, and John will tell us plainly where they stood: for not even his brothers believed in him (7:5). So the group walking that road includes men who grew up in the same house as the Son of God, are travelling with him now, and did not believe.

Who were the brothers who went down to Capernaum? The natural reading is that they were sons of Mary and Joseph, born after Jesus, and so his half-brothers; Matthew names them (Matthew 13:55–56), and Paul met James the Lord’s brother (Galatians 1:19). Roman Catholic and Orthodox Christians, holding that Mary remained a virgin, take them as cousins or as Joseph’s sons by an earlier marriage. But Scripture never says so, and the plain reading is the more likely.

For the one praying for family. This is for you if you have been praying a long time for someone in your family. Familiarity did not convert them. A flawless life lived in front of them for three decades did not convert them, and neither did this wedding. And yet James is later found leading the church in Jerusalem, called a pillar by Paul, and writing a letter that is in your Bible (Acts 15:13; Galatians 2:9). What changed them was not more exposure. It was the resurrection: Paul records that the risen Christ appeared to James (1 Corinthians 15:7), and what thirty years under one roof had not done, the risen Lord did. Keep praying.

On a Tuesday. After the first sign John records a few quiet days in a fishing town with nothing to report. Remember that the next time an ordinary fortnight follows a Sunday when God seemed close. Most of the Christian life is Capernaum for a few days. Do not take the quiet as absence; do the next faithful thing, and let your faith grow there.
verseByVerse.note: John calls Jesus’ miracles “signs” — pointers to who he is. Capernaum was a fishing town on the lake shore.

parallels.desc: these are written so that you may believe

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–25 — The Temple Cleansing and the New Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At Passover Jesus finds the temple court full of traders and money-changers and drives them out: his Father’s house is not a place of business. Asked for a sign, he speaks of a temple destroyed and raised in three days, and John explains that he meant his body. Many at the feast believe because of his signs, but Jesus does not entrust himself to them, for he knows what is in every heart.
verseByVerse.theology:
The temple cleansing is the Lord coming suddenly to his temple (Malachi 3:1). The zeal that consumes him is the Son’s passion for his Father’s honour, and my Father’s house is the claim that gives him authority there.

The temple thread runs the length of Scripture and this passage is its hinge. In 1:14 the Word dwelt among us; here John says the temple is a body (v. 21); and the Bible ends with a city with no temple at all, for its temple is the Lord God and the Lamb (Revelation 21:22).

Verse 22 shows how understanding arrives. The disciples heard the saying and grasped nothing for three years; the resurrection made it plain, as Jesus promised the Spirit would (14:26). And they believed Scripture and Jesus’ word together, as one kind of word.

Verses 23–25 must not be used to unsettle the wrong reader. They describe faith produced by spectacle and not yet tested, like the crowd who turn back in chapter 6 (6:66). Anxiety about whether one’s faith is real is not a symptom of this condition; the people described were untroubled. And Jesus withholding himself is not Jesus withdrawing: the next thing he does is explain the new birth to Nicodemus.
verseByVerse.examples:
The buying and selling were not wicked in themselves, but they had filled the one court where the nations could pray. The searching question is not about churches selling things but whether anything in the ordinary life of a congregation, its assumptions, its vocabulary, the things everyone knows and nobody explains, makes it hard for an outsider to get near God. Nobody in Jerusalem had decided to exclude the nations. They had simply needed the space.

The anger of this scene needs handling in both directions. It is not at odds with meekness: anger is what love does when what it loves is being damaged, and he stops to make the whip himself, a decision, not a loss of temper. But it is no warrant for aggression on God’s behalf: it is aimed at the dishonouring of God and the exclusion of the powerless, never at a slight to himself (1 Peter 2:23), and it is the Son acting with the owner’s authority in his own house.

The chapter break hides a joint. Verse 25 says he knew what was in man, and the next sentence introduces a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus: the statement and its illustration, side by side.

verseByVerse.quote: The Passover of the Jews was at hand, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. In the temple he found those who were selling oxen and sheep and pigeons, and the money-changers sitting there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Passover of the Jews was at hand. John mentions three Passovers (2:13; 6:4; 11:55), which is the main reason Jesus’ public ministry is usually reckoned at about three years. And Jesus went up to Jerusalem: the Lord has come to his temple, exactly as Malachi said he would (Malachi 3:1), and the first thing he does there is turn over the furniture.

In the flow. John sets two scenes side by side at the start of Jesus’ work, and they belong together. At Cana he turned the water of purification into the wine of the feast; in Jerusalem he confronts the temple, the centre of the whole system of sacrifice. In both, the old order is not thrown away but fulfilled in him, and verse 21 will say it outright: the true temple is his body. This scene also opens the conflict with the Jerusalem leaders that runs through the whole Gospel and ends at the cross.

In the temple. The trading happened in the outer court, the Court of the Gentiles: animals for sacrifice, sold on the spot to pilgrims. And he found them: he is not told about it; he arrives and looks.

A trade with a rationale. The trade was not obviously a racket. An animal for sacrifice had to be without blemish and certified as such, and a lamb carried a hundred miles had a poor chance of passing inspection. Buying one on site, already approved, was far more practical. It grew up because people needed it.

The money-changers. Every adult male Jew owed an annual half-shekel temple tax, and it had to be paid in a particular currency. Money-changers exchanged pilgrims’ everyday coins for the Tyrian shekel used to pay the temple tax, taking a commission; it was required because of the reliability of its silver, even though it carried the image of a pagan god. The trade was probably controlled by, and profitable to, the high-priestly families; later Jewish writings remember them for exactly that.

Rot by convenience. The problem was not that somebody had smuggled something wicked into the temple. It was that a set of reasonable arrangements, each defensible on its own terms, had together turned worship into a transaction, gradually, with nobody deciding it. Institutions do not usually rot by scandal. They rot by convenience. And the heart likes the arrangement. A God who can be dealt with at a counter asks for your money but not for you; pay the fee, perform the rite, and you are free to go. That is religion as a way of keeping God at a safe distance, and it is the opposite of what the temple was built for.

The court of the nations. Now the location, which most readers have never been told. The temple’s courts grew more restricted as you went in: the Court of the Women, then the court for Israelite men, then the priests’ court. The outermost and largest was the Court of the Gentiles, the only place in the building where a non-Jew could come and pray. Beyond it a barrier carried notices warning any foreigner who passed that he would have himself to blame for his death; inscribed stones from it have been dug up. The market was in that court. The one place on earth where a Gentile could come near the God of Israel had been given over to livestock pens and currency tables in festival week.

A house of prayer for all the nations. That is why, in Mark’s account of the later cleansing, the sentence Jesus cries out is from Isaiah and includes the clause we usually leave off: my house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations (Isaiah 56:7; Mark 11:17). The offence is not merely commerce in a holy place. It is that the arrangements of the religious had made it impossible for the outsider to pray.

Is it wrong for churches to sell things or handle money? Not in itself. Churches need money to pay ministers, care for the poor and support missionaries, and Scripture commands generous giving (2 Corinthians 9:7). A bookstall or a collection is not a temple market. The question is whether money and convenience have begun to shape worship and push people out: whether the gospel is ever made to look like something you buy, whether the poor feel unwelcome, whether leaders profit from the flock (1 Peter 5:2). Watch the purpose, not merely the transaction.

On a Tuesday. The easy application of this passage is about churches selling things, and it is about somebody else. The harder question is the Court of the Gentiles one: is there anything about the way your church operates, its vocabulary, its arrangements, the things everyone knows and nobody explains, that would make it hard for an outsider to get near God? Nobody in Jerusalem had decided to exclude the nations. They had simply needed the space. Christ made room for you when you were far off; make room for one such person this Sunday.
verseByVerse.note: The trading happened in the outer court. Money-changers exchanged coins into the currency accepted for the temple tax. John places this cleansing early; the other Gospels record one in the last week.

verseByVerse.quote: And making a whip of cords, he drove them all out of the temple, with the sheep and oxen. And he poured out the coins of the money-changers and overturned their tables. And he told those who sold the pigeons, "Take these things away; do not make my Father's house a house of trade."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Making a whip of cords. This passage is either enjoyed too much or quietly regretted, and a great deal has been done in the world with the sentence Jesus made a whip. Begin with what the text says, since the Greek is more restrained than the paintings. He made it of cords, improvised perhaps from rushes or ropes lying about a place full of tethered livestock; not an implement he brought. It was most likely for driving the animals, not for beating people.

He drove them all out. With righteous anger. And the phrase is followed immediately by with the sheep and oxen, which many read as specifying who the all were. It is grammatically possible to read it as including the traders, and honest to say the point cannot be settled from the words alone. What the text does make plain is that it reports no one being struck. There is no injury reported, no blood, no arrest, and the authorities who arrive a moment later do not accuse him of assault; they ask him for his credentials. Whatever happened, it was not a brawl.

The coins and the cages. Look at how the action is graded. The animals are driven out. The coins are poured across the stone floor and the tables turned over. But the pigeon-sellers, whose birds were caged, are told to take them away. He does not tip over their cages, and one likely reason is that pigeons were the offering of the poor, the sacrifice for those who could not afford a lamb (Leviticus 5:7), and released birds do not come back. Even in the middle of it, he will not wreck what the poorest worshippers depended on.

Is this consistent with the gentle Jesus? It is, and the way to see it is to ask what anger actually is. Anger is what love does when what it loves is being damaged. A man who can watch his own child be harmed and feel nothing is not gentle; he is absent. The reason this scene sits so oddly with us is that we have quietly redefined gentleness as the absence of strong feeling, when in Scripture meekness is strength brought under command. Everything here is under command. He does not snatch up a weapon; he stops and makes a whip of cords. Whatever this was, it was not a loss of temper; it was a decision. The Lamb of God has a holy wrath (Revelation 6:16), and it is the same love that weeps over Jerusalem.

What it does not mean. This passage has been used to justify a great deal that has nothing to do with it. It is not a warrant for Christians to be aggressive on God’s behalf, still less to use violence. It is not cover for the man whose temper is a standing problem in his household and who has learned to call it righteous anger. Two things separate this from that, and they are not subtle. First, every scrap of it is aimed at the abuse of God’s honour and the exclusion of the powerless, and none of it at a slight to himself; when the injuries were personal he did not open his mouth (Isaiah 53:7; 1 Peter 2:23). Second, this is the Son acting in his own house with the authority of the owner, which is precisely the authority the temple officials at once demand that he prove. If your anger is regularly about your own treatment, this passage is not about you.

Then is anger always wrong for me? No. Be angry and do not sin, Paul writes (Ephesians 4:26). Anger at real evil, at cruelty, injustice, abuse, the dishonouring of God, can be right, and indifference to such things is not a virtue. But our anger is rarely pure, so Scripture surrounds it with fences: be slow to anger (James 1:19–20), do not let the sun go down on it, never take revenge (Romans 12:19), and do not let it harden into bitterness. Ask whose honour your anger is defending. Then bring it to God, act through right channels, and leave vengeance to him.

My Father’s house. Not the house of God, not our Father’s house, but my Father’s house: Jesus claims a unique relationship with God. It is the phrase Luke records him using at twelve, in this same building, to parents who had searched for him for three days: did you not know that I must be in my Father’s house? (Luke 2:49). That is what licenses the whip. He is not a reformer with strong views about temple administration. He is the Son, standing in his own family’s house, dealing with what has been done to it. And he names what it has become: a house of trade, perhaps echoing Zechariah 14:21, where on the day of the LORD there will no longer be a trader in the house of the LORD of hosts. That day has come. And it should sober us as well as thrill us. The one who came to Cana as a guest comes to the temple as its owner, and the God who is lavish at a wedding is the God who will not be trifled with in his own house. Malachi, who promised that the Lord would come suddenly to his temple, asked in the next breath who could endure the day of his coming (Malachi 3:1–2).

One cleansing or two? John places a cleansing at the start of Jesus’ ministry; the other Gospels place one at the end (Mark 11:15–17). Some think John moved it to the beginning for theological reasons. But the details and wording differ, and it is quite possible that Jesus did it twice, at the beginning and end of his ministry.

Weighing the two answers. Two cleansings is not the strained solution it sounds. The abuse was structural and profitable and would have resumed soon after any one-off protest, and the details differ: here a whip of cords and my Father’s house; in the other Gospels, Isaiah and Jeremiah, a house of prayer and a den of robbers. The other answer is that John, who tells us plainly that he is selecting (20:30–31), has set this true episode at the front as a doorway into everything that follows; ancient writers were free to order true events for meaning, and that is not invention. Either way the point of the scene is untouched.

On a Tuesday. Ask what has been allowed to clutter your own worship: the phone in the pew, the mind running through the week’s accounts during the prayers, the habit of treating church as a service you consume. The Son who cleared his Father’s house has made you part of it, so ask him to clear it out, even if the clearing is uncomfortable.

For worship. In this chapter the Son holds the whip. Before the Gospel ends, Pilate takes Jesus and has him flogged (19:1), and the one who drove the traders from his Father’s house stands silent under the lash. He cleared the temple with cords, and he was scourged to make a defiled people into a clean house for God. The zeal that would not let his Father be cheapened is the same love that let himself be beaten for those who had cheapened him. Holy is the Son of the house, and gentle, and both all the way down.

parallels.desc: no longer a trader in the house of the LORD
my Father’s house

verseByVerse.quote: "His disciples remembered that it was written, 'Zeal for your house will consume me.' So the Jews said to him, 'What sign do you show us for doing these things?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
His disciples remembered. The verb comes twice in this chapter, and the two are not the same. Here the Scripture surfaces while the coins are still rolling. Later they will remember his saying about the temple of his body, and it will take three years and a resurrection to do it (v. 22).

Zeal for your house will consume me. Psalm 69:9, a psalm of the righteous sufferer often applied to Jesus in the New Testament (15:25; 19:28–29; Romans 15:3). Consume means devour, eat me up. And notice the tense. In the psalm the zeal has consumed the psalmist, a thing already done. What the disciples remember is will consume me. So the sentence that comes to them as they watch him overturn the tables is not merely, look how zealous he is. It is a prediction. This will eat him. The temple authorities are the ones who will finally move against him, and his zeal for his Father’s house will carry him to his death.

Psalm 69 at the cross. Psalm 69 will not leave this Gospel alone. It is the long complaint of a righteous man hated without cause, and John will reach for it again at the cross when they lift up the sour wine (19:28–29). The zeal and the vinegar come out of the same psalm.

What is zeal, and why do I not seem to have it? What is being described here is not a temperament. Some people are naturally intense and some are not, and the intense ones are not thereby more godly; a great deal of what passes for zeal in religious life is simply a strong personality with a subject. What the disciples saw was not energy. It was a man who could not be indifferent to his Father’s honour because he loved his Father, and the zeal was the shape the love took when the honour was being damaged. So the question to ask is not, am I zealous enough? No one has ever answered that helpfully. Ask instead what it takes to move you. Everybody has something. Find the last thing that genuinely stirred you, that you could not simply let pass, and you have located what you love. And if it is not God’s honour, ask him to grow your love for him, and the zeal will follow.

What sign do you show us for doing these things? By what authority? Prove it with a miracle. The prophets sometimes did symbolic acts; let him prove he is a prophet. And there is an irony in it that only grows as the book goes on: what sign do you show us? is asked in a Gospel built entirely out of signs, by men who, as a body, will be shown sign after sign and refuse to believe.

Querying the credentials. But look carefully at what they are and are not disputing. In John’s account nobody says the market should stay. Nobody defends the money tables or argues that the Court of the Gentiles was the right place for livestock. What is challenged is his standing to do anything about it: not you are wrong, but who authorised you? The safest way to avoid a charge is to query the credentials of whoever brought it.

On a Tuesday. Jesus’ zeal for his Father’s honour cost him his life, and it was spent for you, so you have no standing to protect. When you are rightly challenged about something wrong in you, resist the urge to query the credentials of the one who said it. Ask first whether it is true.

For worship. The same verse of Psalm 69 goes on: the reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen on me, and Paul says that was Christ (Romans 15:3). Every insult ever flung at God, every sneer at his holiness and his law, he took on himself. He was so jealous for his Father’s name that he let the abuse aimed at heaven land on his own head, and in being consumed he became the house where God and sinners meet. Praise the Son whose zeal for God was our salvation.

parallels.desc: zeal for your house has consumed me

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered them, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." The Jews then said, "It has taken forty-six years to build this temple, and will you raise it up in three days?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Destroy this temple. The sign he offers: his resurrection. Destroy is a command, meaning if you destroy: go on, then; do it. You will destroy it; I will raise it. It is a challenge thrown at men who have just asked for his credentials, and it has the form of a dare that both parties know is not really a dare. They will not lay a finger on Herod’s stonework. They will, in about three years, do precisely what he has invited them to do to the temple he actually meant. “Raise up” (egeirō) is the word for resurrection.

How testimony gets bent. Mark records that the words were twisted at his trial into a threat (Mark 14:58): witnesses are produced who say: we heard him say, I will destroy this temple that is made with hands. And as he hangs on the cross, those who pass by jeer: you who would destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days (Mark 15:29). Compare the pronouns. He said you destroy. They reported I will destroy. The pronoun was moved, and the sentence changed from a prophecy about what they would do to him into a threat about what he would do to them. Little was invented. Something was shifted, and that was enough to hang a capital charge on.

Forty-six years. Herod the Great began rebuilding around 20 BC; forty-six years later puts this at about AD 27, and this one exasperated remark is a main peg for the chronology of Jesus’ ministry. There is a bitterness in it they could not have known. The work went on until about AD 63, and in AD 70 the Romans burned the temple and pulled it down. They were holding up to the Son of God a building that would stand complete for about seven years.

And will you raise it up in three days? They take him literally, and mock. It is the first appearance of a pattern that runs through this whole Gospel. They hear a claim about masonry and answer with a building schedule. In the next chapter a teacher of Israel will hear born again and ask whether a grown man can enter his mother’s womb a second time (3:4). A woman at a well will hear living water and point out that he has nothing to draw with (4:11). A crowd will hear bread from heaven and ask for a permanent supply (6:34). Every time, the misunderstanding takes the same form: the words are taken at the flattest possible level, and the flat reading is the one that keeps the hearer from having to deal with him. The natural mind cannot perceive the things of the Spirit without new birth (1 Corinthians 2:14).

Why did Jesus speak in riddles? Not to hide the truth from honest seekers, but to draw them in and to expose hearts. A saying like this one sticks in the memory and opens up later, which is exactly what happened to the disciples (v. 22). It also sifts the hearers: those who want to understand him keep asking, while those who have already decided against him take the flattest reading and walk away. Jesus never plays games with people who truly want him. When Nicodemus asks, he explains at length. When the disciples ask, he tells them plainly. If something he says puzzles you, do what they did: stay near, keep reading, and ask.
verseByVerse.note: Herod the Great began rebuilding the temple around 20 BC; forty-six years brings us to about AD 27. The work went on for decades more.

parallels.desc: the charge at his trial

verseByVerse.quote: But he was speaking about the temple of his body. When therefore he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this, and they believed the Scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The temple of his body. John’s explanation, and the key. The thread runs the length of the Bible and this verse is the knot in the middle of it. In chapter 1 John wrote that the Word dwelt among us (1:14), the language of the tabernacle, the tent where the glory came down. Here the tabernacle has become the temple, the fixed house where God could be met, and John says the address is a body. Not a building that contains the presence, but a person in whom God is present. Through his death and resurrection Jesus himself becomes the meeting place of God and humanity (4:21–24). Here is the change it makes. In the old temple a worshipper met God by coming to a place, through a priest, with a sacrifice. Now we meet God by coming to a person. When you pray in Jesus’ name and trust his sacrifice, you come as near to God as any high priest behind the curtain, for through him we have access in one Spirit to the Father (Ephesians 2:18).

No temple in the city. It ends where you would expect once you have seen the direction. At the very close of the Bible, John is shown the city that is the end of everything, and he records what was missing from it: I saw no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb (Revelation 21:22). There is no building at the end. There was never going to be.

We are his temple too. And his people, united to him, become God’s temple (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:21–22). The living stones are built on the living cornerstone (1 Peter 2:4–5). Where Christ’s people gather in his name, God dwells; and each believer’s body is a temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19).

Then does it matter where or how we worship? Where, much less than before. Jesus will tell the Samaritan woman that the hour is coming when true worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, not on this mountain or in Jerusalem (4:21–24). No building is holy ground in itself, and you can meet God in a kitchen as truly as in a cathedral. How, very much. We come to God only through Christ, the true temple, and we must worship him as he has revealed himself, not as we invent. And because the church is his temple, gathering with his people is not optional decoration; it is where he has promised to dwell (Hebrews 10:25; Matthew 18:20).

After he was raised. They did not understand it at the time. They heard the words with their own ears, they were the inner circle, and it meant nothing to them for the best part of three years. Then an event occurred that made the old sentence clear, and the memory came back with its meaning attached. That is what he had promised: the Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you (14:26). This verse is that promise working, recorded by a man who was on the receiving end of it.

For anyone in the middle of something they cannot read. There is a great deal of pressure on Christians to understand what God is doing while he is doing it: to have an account of the illness, the redundancy, the years that went nowhere, the prayer that was not answered. That pressure does not come from this book. The men closest to Jesus, watching the most important events in human history at a distance of a few feet, understood almost none of it until afterwards, and were not disqualified for it. What was asked of them was not comprehension. It was staying near enough to remember.

Scripture and his word. One verb, two things believed, and no distinction drawn between them. A sentence he said in a courtyard is placed alongside the Hebrew Scriptures as the same kind of word. John simply writes it down, and it is one of the highest claims in the chapter: Jesus’ word has the authority of Scripture.

Which Scripture? John does not name one. Passages such as Psalm 16:10, you will not abandon my soul to Sheol, and Isaiah 53 were among those the apostles later preached, and Jesus himself opened all the Scriptures to them after he rose (Luke 24:27). Their faith was in the whole Old Testament witness to his death and resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).

parallels.desc: they remembered his words

verseByVerse.quote: Now when he was in Jerusalem at the Passover Feast, many believed in his name when they saw the signs that he was doing. But Jesus on his part did not entrust himself to them, because he knew all people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many believed. Faith produced by spectacle: real, but shallow. Nothing has yet been asked of these people or cost them anything; they have been carried along by a movement that is going well. John is not saying their belief is fake. He is saying it is untested, and that Jesus, who sees the whole of a person, knows exactly what it is worth. Some who believed would later turn away (6:66; 8:31, 59).

Did not entrust himself. A play on words that English cannot carry. They believed (episteusan) in him, but he did not believe (episteuen), entrust himself, to them. It is the same verb both times. They put their trust in him; he did not put himself in their trust. The effect in Greek is like a door swinging shut on its own hinge: he did not treat their excitement as a commitment, or open his heart and purposes to them as he would to friends (15:15).

What happens to it. He also shows us what happens to this kind of faith. In chapter 6 a crowd of the same kind is fed on a hillside and follows him across a lake, and then he says something they find intolerable, and John records the outcome in one of the saddest verses in the book: after this many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him (6:66). That is this kind of faith, four chapters later, meeting the first thing it did not like.

Because he knew all people. This is not cynicism but knowledge. Jesus knows the difference between excitement about evidence and the faith that perseveres through suffering and offence. Not all who follow the miracle-worker will follow the crucified one, and many want his blessings without himself.

How do I know my faith is not like theirs? This is a frightening sentence, and it should be handled slowly, because it unsettles people who are already unsettled. If you are troubled by these verses, if you have read them and gone cold and started auditing your own conversion, see that the people being described here were not troubled at all. They were delighted. Nobody in that Passover crowd was lying awake wondering whether their faith would hold, because nothing had yet happened to make them wonder. Anxiety about the reality of your faith is not a symptom of the condition described here. It is nearly always a symptom of caring whether it is real, which is the one thing this crowd conspicuously did not do. Look away from your faith to its object: true faith rests on Christ himself, not on the excitement of signs, and he keeps those who are his (10:28–29).

Same words, different outcome. John uses exactly the same phrase of these people that he used in the prologue of the saved: believed in his name (1:12). He does not have a separate vocabulary for false faith. The words are identical, and the difference does not lie in the words. It lies in what the faith turns out to do when the wine runs out. So the question is not, and never was, whether your believing began with the right feeling. Nothing in Scripture asks you to establish that. What it asks is whether you are still holding on to Christ. And those whom God has truly given faith he will keep to the end (Philippians 1:6).

Withholding, not withdrawing. There is a further comfort hidden in the sentence. He did not entrust himself to them, but he did not send them away either. He goes on speaking, and the very next thing that happens in this Gospel is that one member of the Jerusalem religious establishment comes to him at night with a compliment about signs, and gets the longest and tenderest explanation of the new birth anywhere in the Bible. Jesus withholding himself is not Jesus withdrawing. It is a refusal to be naive, and it is the opposite of a dismissal.

parallels.desc: I the LORD search the heart

verseByVerse.quote: and needed no one to bear witness about man, for he himself knew what was in man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one to bear witness. Two things finish the chapter. First, the word that keeps appearing where you would least expect it. This is a Gospel obsessed with witness: John the Baptist is called to bear witness, the works bear witness, the Father bears witness, the Scriptures bear witness, and by chapter 5 Jesus will lay out a whole case with the witnesses named one after another. And here, in the middle of it, John records the one subject on which he needed no one to bear witness. Everything about himself he was content to have testified to by others. About human beings he required no evidence, because he already had it all.

He himself knew what was in man. He knows the human heart perfectly, as only God does (1 Samuel 16:7; Jeremiah 17:9–10; Psalm 139:1–4). He knew Nathanael (1:47–48), and will know the Samaritan woman’s past (4:18), and Judas’ betrayal (6:64).

The chapter break in the wrong place. Verse 25 ends with the word man, anthrōpos, and the next sentence John wrote, before anyone had invented chapter numbers, begins: now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus. He knew what was in man, and here comes one. Nicodemus is the illustration of the sentence just made, set against it like a caption and a photograph: a good, learned, genuinely searching member of the ruling council who has understood nothing, and who will be told that what he needs is not more instruction but to be born. His first words to Jesus, that no one can do these signs unless God is with him, are the sign-based faith of the Passover crowd in the mouth of one of the best-qualified men in Jerusalem.

A comfort and a warning. That Christ knows what is in a man is either the worst news or the best, and most of us hold both on different days. It is the worst because there is no version of your life in which you present the edited copy. Not the account you give your friends, nor the one you give yourself at three in the morning: he has read the actual contents, and we cannot deceive him with shallow profession.

Full-knowledge love. And it is the best news for the same reason, once you know what he did after reading it. The man who knew what was in man went to Jerusalem anyway, into the hands of people whose contents he had read in full, and died for them. If he had loved us on the strength of a favourable report, the love would be worth nothing, because the report would have been wrong. There was no report. He looked. The cross is not love in ignorance of human sin; it is love offered in full knowledge of it.

If he knows my heart, why should I confess? Because confession is not giving him information; it is agreeing with him. When you confess, you stop hiding and start walking in the light with him (1 John 1:7–9). He already knows; what changes is you. Confession breaks the power of secrecy, humbles pride, and opens you to receive the forgiveness he has promised. It is the difference between a child whose father knows what he did and a child who comes and says so. The father’s knowledge is the same. The relationship is not.

On a Tuesday. A short question: is there anything you are hoping God has not noticed? Name it, silently, now. The naming told him nothing, and the chapter that follows this sentence is the one containing the words for God so loved the world. Be honest with him today about what he already knows, and receive what he offers.

parallels.desc: you alone know the hearts of all

2.title: The First Sign: Water into Wine
2.text: <sup>1</sup>On the third day there was a wedding at Cana in Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there.<sup>2</sup>Jesus also was invited to the wedding with his disciples.<sup>3</sup>When the wine ran out, the mother of Jesus said to him, “They have no wine.”<sup>4</sup>And Jesus said to her, “Woman, what does this have to do with me? My hour has not yet come.”<sup>5</sup>His mother said to the servants, “Do whatever he tells you.”<sup>6</sup>Now there were six stone water jars there for the Jewish rites of purification, each holding twenty or thirty gallons.<sup>7</sup>Jesus said to the servants, “Fill the jars with water.” And they filled them up to the brim.<sup>8</sup>And he said to them, “Now draw some out and take it to the master of the feast.” So they took it.<sup>9</sup>When the master of the feast tasted the water now become wine, and did not know where it came from (though the servants who had drawn the water knew), the master of the feast called the bridegroom<sup>10</sup>and said to him, “Everyone serves the good wine first, and when people have drunk freely, then the poor wine. But you have kept the good wine until now.”<sup>11</sup>This, the first of his signs, Jesus did at Cana in Galilee, and manifested his glory. And his disciples believed in him.<sup>12</sup>After this he went down to Capernaum, with his mother and his brothers and his disciples, and they stayed there for a few days.<sup>13</sup>The Passover of the Jews was at hand, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.<sup>14</sup>In the temple he found those who were selling oxen and sheep and pigeons, and the money-changers sitting there.<sup>15</sup>And making a whip of cords, he drove them all out of the temple, with the sheep and oxen. And he poured out the coins of the money-changers and overturned their tables.<sup>16</sup>And he told those who sold the pigeons, “Take these things away; do not make my Father’s house a house of trade.”<sup>17</sup>His disciples remembered that it was written, “Zeal for your house will consume me.”<sup>18</sup>So the Jews said to him, “What sign do you show us for doing these things?”<sup>19</sup>Jesus answered them, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.”<sup>20</sup>The Jews then said, “It has taken forty-six years to build this temple, and will you raise it up in three days?”<sup>21</sup>But he was speaking about the temple of his body.<sup>22</sup>When therefore he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this, and they believed the Scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken.<sup>23</sup>Now when he was in Jerusalem at the Passover Feast, many believed in his name when they saw the signs that he was doing.<sup>24</sup>But Jesus on his part did not entrust himself to them, because he knew all people<sup>25</sup>and needed no one to bear witness about man, for he himself knew what was in man.
2.overview:
Two scenes open Jesus’ public ministry, one in a village home and one in the temple, and both announce that something new has come. At a wedding in Cana Jesus turns the water standing in stone jars for Jewish purification into an overflowing supply of the best wine. It is the first of the signs John records: he reveals his glory, and his disciples believe. The prophets pictured the messianic age as a feast overflowing with wine (Isaiah 25:6; Amos 9:13), and the water of the old rites gives way to the wine of the kingdom.

At Passover in Jerusalem Jesus drives the traders from the temple court, and when he is asked for a sign he points to the temple of his body, destroyed and raised in three days. The meeting place of God and people is now Jesus himself. Many in Jerusalem believe because of his signs, but he does not entrust himself to them, for he knows what is in every heart.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — Nicodemus and the New Birth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nicodemus visits Jesus by night and is told that without a birth from above no one can see God’s kingdom. Jesus explains the birth of water and the Spirit, rebukes Israel’s teacher for not understanding, and points to the Son of Man who must be lifted up like the bronze serpent. The reason is God’s love for the world in the gift of his Son, who came to save, not to condemn; and the light that has come divides those who come to it from those who love the darkness.
verseByVerse.theology:
The new birth is the work of the Spirit, who blows where he wills: no one can produce, control or predict it, and the Spirit gives it to those whom the Father has given to the Son. The lifting up of the Son of Man is the means by which eternal life comes to those who look in faith. God’s motive is love for a world set against him; his means is the gift of his Son; his purpose is salvation, not condemnation. And the light that has come shows each person’s verdict by whether he comes to it or runs from it.

The chapter rules out religious effort as a way in, not because effort is insincere but because it is the wrong kind of thing. Like produces like, and flesh, human nature working with its own resources, even at its best, cannot give birth to spirit. What it needs is not improvement but a new life from above.
verseByVerse.examples:
Born again, or born from above, is one of the fullest descriptions of salvation in the New Testament: it names the kind of change (rebirth, not reform), its source (God), and its necessity (without it the kingdom cannot be seen).

Nicodemus is not finished at the end of this conversation. He appears twice more, each time further into the open: speaking up in the council (7:50–51), and after the crucifixion bringing about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes to bury Jesus (19:39). The man who came at night buried him by day.

The bronze serpent was a strange remedy: an image of the very thing that was killing them, and the only thing asked of a dying man was that he look. Israel later burned incense to it, and Hezekiah broke it in pieces (2 Kings 18:4). Even the instrument of mercy becomes an idol if the look lands on it rather than passing through it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews. This man came to Jesus by night and said to him, "Rabbi, we know that you are a teacher come from God, for no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. John 3 is the chapter of the new birth and of the best-known verse in the Bible. Nicodemus, a respected Pharisee and teacher, comes to Jesus by night, and Jesus tells him that no one can see or enter God’s kingdom unless he is born again, from above, of water and the Spirit: a new life that only God can give. Then Jesus points to the cross: as Moses lifted up the bronze serpent, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, so that whoever believes in him may have eternal life. For God so loved the world that he gave his only Son. The chapter ends with John the Baptist’s final testimony: Jesus is the bridegroom, the one from above, into whose hands the Father has given all things, and he must increase.

The link. Do not let the chapter number suggest a new subject. John has just said that Jesus knew what was in man (2:25), and the next sentence begins: now there was a man of the Pharisees. Same word, back to back, with nothing between them in the original. Having told us that Jesus reads the human heart, John opens one up to show what the reading looks like.

A man of the Pharisees. A Pharisee: devout, learned, moral, strict in keeping the law, one of the movement that took God’s law with total seriousness in the details of an ordinary week. John has not chosen a tax collector or a man with an obvious hole in his life. If a man could be got into the kingdom by conviction, learning, discipline or religious office, this man is already inside. The point of Nicodemus is not that he is a hypocrite. It is that he is the best we have.

A ruler of the Jews. Nicodemus was a member of the Sanhedrin, the ruling council of seventy-one men who governed the religious life of the nation. And in a few verses Jesus will call him the teacher of Israel, with the definite article, as though he held a recognised position rather than merely a good reputation.

By night. Perhaps for fear of being seen (12:42; 19:38): a member of the council calling on an unlicensed Galilean preacher who had just overturned the temple tables would not want to be seen doing it in daylight. Perhaps for a quiet talk, since later Jewish writings commend study of the law at night. But John rarely mentions night without meaning more. This is the Gospel in which the light shines in the darkness, people love the darkness, and the blackest moment of the story is marked with the words: and it was night (13:30). Nicodemus came out of the darkness toward the light, and where he goes from there is the whole of his story.

Three appearances. This is the first of three appearances, each further out into the open. Here he comes at night with a compliment. In chapter 7, when the authorities are moving against Jesus, Nicodemus speaks up, not bravely, but he speaks: does our law judge a man without first giving him a hearing? (7:50–51). He is answered with a sneer (7:52). And after everything, when most of the twelve have scattered and there is nothing left to gain, he comes to a Roman execution site to help bury the body, bringing about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes (19:39), a quantity fit for a king, in front of anyone who cared to look. He seems to have become a believer. Whatever happened in the conversation that follows did not finish that evening, and it does not seem to have failed.

A teacher come from God. Respectful, and true as far as it goes. The we suggests colleagues who think this and have not come. He may be speaking for a group, and he will leave having been told something no group can do for him. A teacher come from God leaves Nicodemus a student, a position he understands and can occupy with dignity. What he is about to hear is that he does not need a better teacher. He needs to be born.

More than he knew. Nicodemus has said more than he understands. Jesus has indeed come from God, but not as prophets and rabbis come, raised up from among men. He is the one who descended from heaven (v. 13), the Word who was with God and was God (1:1), the one who comes from above and is above all (v. 31). The teacher of Israel has come by night to consult a promising colleague, and the man across from him is the one of whom every Scripture he has studied bears witness (5:39). He came to an expert; he has come to the subject of the whole Bible.

Unless God is with him. Every clause of that is true. It is also precisely the position of the Passover crowd who believed because they saw signs, and to whom Jesus did not entrust himself (2:23–24). Nicodemus is that crowd with a doctorate.

Is it wrong to come to Jesus secretly or hesitantly? It is not where anyone should stay, but it is where many begin, and Jesus did not turn Nicodemus away. He received a frightened, half-convinced man at night and gave him his fullest teaching on the new birth. If you are exploring the faith quietly, or a believer still afraid of what others will think, come anyway; he welcomes honest seekers. But do not stay in the dark. Nicodemus’ story moves toward the open, and so should yours. Jesus warns that whoever is ashamed of him and his words, of him he will be ashamed (Luke 9:26). Ask him for courage for the next step into the light.
verseByVerse.note: Nicodemus was a member of the Sanhedrin, the ruling council. Coming by night may have been for secrecy or simply for quiet conversation.

parallels.desc: Nicodemus speaks up in the council
he brings spices for Jesus’ burial

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered him, "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truly, truly. Nicodemus had not asked a question. Jesus does not answer the compliment; he answers the need, cutting through politeness to the question of the heart. And he opens with the doubled amen that in this Gospel only he uses: a solemn statement on his own authority, not thus says the LORD but I say to you.

Unless one is born again. The ESV notes that “again” (Greek anōthen) can also be rendered “from above”. The word can mean a second time, and it can mean from above, and both are intended: a second birth, and a birth from God. Nicodemus hears only the first, which is not stupidity; it is the natural reach of a mind with no category for what is being said. A second natural birth would change nothing; flesh would still produce flesh (v. 6). What he needs is a birth of a different order, whose source is not the womb but the Spirit: not improvement, but a new life given by God.

What does born again mean? It means that God the Holy Spirit gives a spiritually dead person new life, so that he is made alive to God, given a new heart that loves him, and enabled to repent and believe (Ezekiel 36:26; Ephesians 2:4–5). Theologians call it regeneration. It is not turning over a new leaf, having an emotional experience, or joining a particular kind of church. It is something God does in a person, as invisible as conception and as real as birth, and its effects show in a changed life: faith in Christ, love for God and his people, hatred of sin (1 John 5:1; 3:14). Every true Christian is born again; there is no other kind.

He cannot see. Without the new birth a person is blind to the kingdom, every person, even the most religious. And the verb changes when Jesus repeats himself: here it is see the kingdom; in verse 5 it is enter it. Without this birth a man does not merely fail to get in; he cannot make out what he is failing to get into. The kingdom is not a locked room he is standing outside of, rattling the handle. It is a country he cannot perceive. That is why the argument never works from the outside: you cannot persuade someone toward a thing they are unable to see.

The kingdom, twice. The kingdom of God is the headline of Jesus’ preaching in Matthew, Mark and Luke, the subject of many of the parables. In John the phrase appears only here and in verse 5. The great theme of the other three Gospels surfaces once, in a night-time conversation with one man, and is used to tell him that he cannot get in as he is.

The King across the room. And the King is sitting opposite him. Nicodemus cannot see the kingdom, and its King is a few feet away, speaking to him. The birth from above is announced by the one who is himself from above (v. 31), and it brings people to him: to all who received him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God, born not of the will of the flesh but of God (1:12–13). The new birth is not a door beside Christ. It is God opening blind eyes to see the King, so that they receive him and believe in his name.

The wrong category. Nicodemus has spent his life on a project of improvement, and by any measure available it has succeeded. He is not being told that the project was fraudulent, or that he did it badly, or that he needs to try harder at it. He is being told it was the wrong category of thing altogether. You cannot educate your way into a family. You cannot be promoted into a bloodline. A man may study a language for forty years and speak it beautifully and still not be French. Grace is not the improvement of nature but its renewal, not the assistance of a willing heart but the giving of a new one.

On a Tuesday. Ask what would have to change for God to be more pleased with you than he is today. If the honest answer is a list, pray more, lose the temper less, be more generous, sort out the thing nobody knows about, then the answer is being given in the wrong currency, and this verse is aimed at exactly that instinct. Every item on that list may be worth doing. Not one of them is a birth. Bring the list to God, and ask him first for what only he can give.

For worship. The God who said, let light shine out of darkness, has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). That is what seeing the kingdom is: not a vision of a place but the sight of a face. No one climbed into his family; we were born into it from above, by the will of God, while we were still blind. Every eye that now sees the King was opened by the hand that made the first light. Glory to the Father of lights, who gives sight to the born-blind.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “again” (Greek anōthen) can also be rendered “from above.” Nicodemus hears one sense; Jesus means both.

parallels.desc: born of God
born again to a living hope

verseByVerse.quote: Nicodemus said to him, "How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother's womb and be born?" Jesus answered, "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother’s womb and be born? Nicodemus takes it literally, or perhaps means: how can someone my age change completely? A whole life of religious habit cannot be undone. His question is not absurd; it is the honest bewilderment of natural reason confronting something only God can do. And his own picture answers it: a person cannot cause his own birth. That is the point.

Water and the Spirit. Together they recall Ezekiel’s promise of cleansing and a new heart (Ezekiel 36:25–27). Water: cleansing from sin. Spirit: new life. One birth, with two aspects. Without it a man cannot enter the kingdom, not merely see it. What Jesus presses on Nicodemus is not a rite he has missed but a work of God he cannot perform on himself, and the teacher of Israel should have known it (v. 10).

Ezekiel 36 seen, not only cited. Israel is in exile. The temple is rubble, the land is lost, the name of God has been dragged through the mud of the nations by the very people who carried it, and into that, God says: I will sprinkle clean water on you. I will give you a new heart. I will remove the heart of stone. I will put my Spirit within you. Count the verbs: God is doing all of them. There is not one instruction in the passage. God is not telling a defeated people what to do about their condition; he is telling them what he intends to do about it, while they are in no position to contribute anything at all. The water and the Spirit were promised together, in that order, six hundred years earlier, to people who had proved beyond argument that they could not fix themselves. Nicodemus is being told that the promise has arrived, and that he is one of the people it was made about. And the one telling him is the man on whom the Baptist saw the Spirit come down and remain, he who baptizes with the Holy Spirit (1:33). The God who promised to put his Spirit within his people has come in person to keep his word.

Where Christians differ: “born of water”. Roman Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and some Anglican teaching take the water to be baptism, and teach that baptism is the means of regeneration (baptismal regeneration). Others take water to mean physical birth, the water of the womb; others take it as John’s baptism of repentance. This commentary’s view: the best reading, in context, is Ezekiel 36: water and Spirit describe one spiritual birth, the cleansing and renewing work of the Spirit. Nicodemus could not have understood a reference to Christian baptism, not yet instituted, and Jesus expected him to understand (v. 10). Baptism is the sign of this new birth, not its cause. The thief on the cross entered paradise without baptism (Luke 23:43).

Then what is baptism for? Baptism is the sign Christ commanded for those who have been born again and believe (Matthew 28:19; Acts 2:38, 41). It pictures what the Spirit has done: washing from sin, burial with Christ and rising to new life (Romans 6:3–4). It is the believer’s public confession of faith and the church’s welcome into its fellowship. So it matters greatly and should not be neglected, but it is not a switch that produces new life. This Gospel says again and again that it is believing that gives life (1:12; 3:15; 20:31). This commentary holds, with the 1689 London Baptist Confession (29.1–2), that baptism belongs to those who profess faith, because in the New Testament it follows hearing and believing (Acts 2:41; 8:12). It honours paedobaptist brothers and sisters, who baptise the infants of believers as the covenant sign that replaced circumcision, and who agree that baptism does not of itself regenerate.

On a Tuesday. If you are older and think it is too late for real change, remember that Nicodemus spoke as if he were old, and the promise was for him. You cannot make yourself born again, so ask God today for the cleansing and new life only his Spirit can give.
verseByVerse.note: Water and Spirit together recall Ezekiel’s promise of cleansing and a new heart.

parallels.desc: I will sprinkle clean water on you and put my Spirit within you
the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit

verseByVerse.quote: "That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Flesh is flesh. Flesh here means human nature, mortal and fallen, working with its own resources. Like produces like. An apple tree does not, with any amount of encouragement, produce a pear. Human beings by nature can only produce more human nature, and religion, morality and effort, however good, are still flesh.

What it does not mean. The sentence is not an insult aimed at the body. Flesh here does not mean the physical as opposed to the spiritual; this is the Gospel that has just said the Word became flesh and meant it as the highest news in the world. It means everything a person is by birth, including the best of it. The intelligence. The moral seriousness. The religious instinct. The genuine longing after God that had a member of the Sanhedrin walking through Jerusalem after dark to find one. All of that is real, and none of it is spirit, and no quantity of it turns into spirit. If the flesh could produce even a little of the life of God, the correct advice to Nicodemus would be to produce more of it, and a great deal of religion gives exactly that advice.

Spirit is spirit. Only the Spirit can produce spiritual life. New birth is not the improvement of the old nature but the creation of a new one (2 Corinthians 5:17), and we do not cooperate in our own birth: the initiative and the power belong to the Spirit. This does not mean that a Christian stops being an ordinary human being with a body and a personality, but that there is now in him a life that comes from God and is alive to God. He can pray as a child to a Father, love what God loves and grieve over what grieves him, because the Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God (Romans 8:15–16).

Spirit and life in his words. Jesus will say it again in this Gospel and tie it to himself: it is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is no help at all; the words he has spoken are spirit and life (6:63). The Spirit does not give birth in a vacuum. He brings the dead to life through the words of Christ, and gives them life in Christ, who is himself the life (14:6). What the flesh could never produce, the Son speaks into being, as he once called into a tomb and a dead man came out (11:43–44).

For the one who has tried and failed. There is a hard comfort in this for anyone who has spent years trying and getting nowhere. The reason the effort did not work is not that it was insufficient. It is that effort was never the mechanism. Stop trying to manufacture spiritual life, and ask the Spirit to give it.

For the one raised in a Christian home. There is a warning on the other side, for the reader raised inside all this. Nothing transmits. Not the family, not the church, not the years of sitting under good teaching, not the vocabulary you can use fluently. Flesh gives birth to flesh in a minister’s house as reliably as anywhere else. Your parents’ faith cannot be inherited; it must be given to you as it was given to them. If that worries you, take heart: a real love for Christ, however small, a grief over sin, a wish to be his, is not something flesh produces. It is a sign that the gift has come.

Does this mean nothing good can come from an unbeliever? Not in the ordinary sense. Unbelievers can be honest, generous, brave and kind, and we should thank God for it; it is his common grace restraining sin and blessing the world (Matthew 5:45). But none of it is spiritual life, and none of it can make a person right with God or produce love for him. The flesh can build hospitals and write symphonies. It cannot give birth to a child of God. That is why the gospel is not advice for decent people to try harder, but news for dead people that God gives life.

verseByVerse.quote: "Do not marvel that I said to you, 'You must be born again.' The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You must be born again. The you is plural: all of you, all Israel, everyone. Through Nicodemus Jesus addresses the whole religious establishment, and past them everyone who has assumed that being properly brought up, taught and serious would be enough. Must: no exceptions.

The wind blows. The ESV notes that the same Greek word (pneuma) means both “wind” and “spirit”. English cannot carry it: this is not merely an illustration but a pun, and the pun is the argument. There are not two words compared but one word used twice. Hebrew is the same: ruach is wind, the breath in a man’s nostrils and the Spirit of God at once. Jesus speaks of wind and of the Spirit in the same breath, and lets Nicodemus feel the join: no one controls, commands or predicts either.

You hear its sound. Wind is not vague. It takes roofs off and puts ships on rocks. What it is not is manageable: nobody schedules it or makes it come, and you never see it, only what it does to everything else. That is the answer to the question Nicodemus has been circling. He wants to know how. Teachers deal in method, which can be taught and transmitted. Jesus gives him weather: not because the new birth is vague, but because it has no technique attached.

So it is. The new birth cannot be manufactured or explained by human methods; it comes where the Spirit wills (1:13), and its effects can be seen in a changed life. This is a foundation of the Reformed doctrine of effectual calling and irresistible grace: the Spirit gives new birth sovereignly, as he wills. Effectual calling means that when God calls a person by his Spirit through the gospel, the call does not merely invite; it brings him, giving the very life that answers (6:44; Romans 8:30). Irresistible does not mean that anyone is dragged in against his will. It means the Spirit so renews the will that the person comes freely and gladly, wanting Christ for the first time.

The breath of the risen Lord. This Gospel does not leave the wind anonymous. On the evening of the resurrection the risen Jesus stood among his frightened disciples, breathed on them, and said, Receive the Holy Spirit (20:22). The sovereign Spirit who blows where he wills is the Spirit the Son sends from the Father (15:26), and the Son gives life to whom he will (5:21). The wind that brings the new birth comes from the one who died and rose, and its first work is always to turn a dead heart toward him (16:14).

So is there nothing I can do? There is no technique that produces the new birth, but that does not leave you idle. Wind is unmanageable and sailors are not therefore idle: they cannot make it blow, and they can put up a sail, and it makes all the difference whether they have. Reading Scripture, hearing it preached, praying, keeping company with God’s people: none of these produces the wind. All of them are sails, the means through which God ordinarily gives new life (Romans 10:17; 1 Peter 1:23). And it does not mean nobody can know whether they have been born again; John wrote a whole letter to settle that question (1 John 5:13). If you want God, ask him; the wanting is itself the breeze.

On a Tuesday. Pray today, by name, for someone you love who is not yet born again. You cannot make the wind blow, but you can ask the one who sends it.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the same Greek word (pneuma) means both “wind” and “spirit.”

parallels.desc: you do not know the way the spirit comes
come from the four winds, O breath

verseByVerse.quote: "Nicodemus said to him, 'How can these things be?' Jesus answered him, 'Are you the teacher of Israel and yet you do not understand these things?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
How can these things be? Nicodemus’ last words in this conversation, and then he fades from view. His second how is deeper than his first: not mocking incredulity but genuine confusion.

Are you the teacher of Israel. The article is the sting. Jesus does not say a teacher; he says the teacher, a recognised authority, the man other teachers consulted.

And yet you do not understand these things? The Old Testament had promised the new birth: a new heart and a new spirit (Ezekiel 36:25–27; 11:19), the circumcision of the heart (Deuteronomy 30:6), the new covenant written on hearts, so that no one would need to say, know the LORD, because they all would (Jeremiah 31:33–34), and the valley of dry bones brought to life by the Spirit (Ezekiel 37). All of them say the same thing: Israel’s problem is not information and the solution will not be effort. God will have to operate. He should have known. A man who had spent a lifetime in those texts had every piece of the puzzle on the table in front of him.

Why he missed it. So the failure is not a gap in his reading. He knows the verses.
