What he has never done is apply them to himself, because the promise of a new heart is only good news to a man who has concluded that his own heart is the problem, and Nicodemus has spent his life being told, accurately, that his conduct is exemplary. Learning without the Spirit leaves even the greatest teachers blind.

How the new heart comes. Nicodemus asks how, and within a few sentences Jesus answers with the cross (vv. 14–15). The texts Nicodemus knew promised a new covenant, a new heart, God’s law written within. That covenant would be made in blood, and Jesus is its mediator, whose death redeems those who are called (Hebrews 9:15). The how of the new birth is not a technique. It is a Person, lifted up for sinners.

I know my Bible well but feel nothing. What should I do? This is a real condition and it deserves to be named rather than scolded. A person can hold correct positions on every disputed doctrine, follow an argument through Romans, spot a bad sermon inside two minutes, and have the whole apparatus running on nothing. The knowledge is not the problem; Jesus does not tell Nicodemus to read less. But the same equipment that lets a man handle Scripture well can also let him handle it at arm’s length, as a subject rather than as a summons. So read it differently: slowly, prayerfully, asking not what it says but what it says to you, and confessing what it shows you. Ask the Spirit to give you a heart that is moved (Psalm 119:18). And look to Christ, not to your feelings; warmth follows sight of him.

The tone of the rebuke. Before this turns into an attack on learning, note the tone. Jesus asks a question. He does not end the conversation, and goes on talking, giving this bewildered official more sustained teaching on the new birth than anyone else in the Gospels receives. The rebuke is real and it is not a rejection. It is what it looks like when the light shines on somebody it intends to keep.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus calls him “the teacher of Israel” — a recognised authority who should have known the prophets’ promises.

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, truly, I say to you, we speak of what we know, and bear witness to what we have seen, but you do not receive our testimony. If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how can you believe if I tell you heavenly things?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
We speak of what we know. The plural is odd. It may include his disciples, or John the Baptist and the other witnesses, or the Father with the Son, or it may be Jesus speaking with the authority of heaven. What is certain is that this is eyewitness testimony: he speaks of what he has seen.

You do not receive. The ESV notes that “you” in these verses is plural: Jesus is now addressing Nicodemus’ group, or Israel’s teachers, the whole body Nicodemus came representing. He does not say Nicodemus cannot understand; he says he does not receive. The obstacle is not intellectual ability; this is one of the best-equipped minds in the country. Testimony is not the sort of thing you solve. It is the sort of thing you either take from the witness or refuse, and refusing it is not a failure of comprehension but a decision about a person.

Earthly things. The new birth, which happens on earth, in people’s lives, illustrated by earthly things like birth and wind. Earthly things does not mean trivial things. It means the things that happen down here: a birth, a wind over a field, water and Spirit at work in a man in Jerusalem.

How can you believe if I tell you heavenly things? Truths about heaven itself, God’s plan, the Son’s relationship to the Father, which only one from heaven could reveal (v. 13): a descent from heaven, a lifting up, a Son given, the love of God for the world. If the visible end of it cannot be received, the far end has no chance.

In the flow. These verses prepare the next ones. The heavenly things Jesus is about to speak of are the Son who came down from heaven and the Son of Man who must be lifted up (vv. 13–15), and they are the real answer to Nicodemus’ how.

Should I settle the hard questions before I trust Christ? Not necessarily, and Jesus’ order here is wise. People often want to begin with the furthest questions: predestination and free will, those who never heard, the timetable of the last days, why there is suffering. They are real questions and should not be sneered at, and Scripture says much about them. But look at the order Jesus insists on. He will not take a man to the mysteries of heaven who has not yet dealt with the mystery standing in the room, which is that he needs to be born and cannot arrange it. Settle the plain things first: your need, and Christ’s sufficiency for it. Many hard questions look different from inside the family.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “you” in these verses is plural: Jesus is addressing Nicodemus’s whole circle.

verseByVerse.quote: "No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man. And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up."
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one has ascended. No human being has gone up to heaven to bring back knowledge of God (Deuteronomy 30:12; Proverbs 30:4). Jesus grounds his heavenly authority in his heavenly origin: he can speak of heavenly things because he has come from heaven. No mystic, no prophet, no visionary has this. He is from above (v. 31).

But were not Enoch and Elijah taken up to heaven? They were taken (Genesis 5:24; 2 Kings 2:11), but they did not go up and come back to tell what they had seen. Jesus’ point, in the context of verses 11–12, is that no one has ascended to bring down knowledge of heavenly things; only the one who came from heaven can speak of it.

The Son of Man. The ESV notes that some manuscripts add “who is in heaven”. The KJV and NKJV include the phrase; many of the earliest manuscripts lack it, so most modern Bibles put it in a footnote. If those words are original, they point to the Son’s unbroken communion with the Father even while on earth (1:18).

As Moses lifted up the serpent. Numbers 21:4–9. Near the end of forty years Israel complained about the food, the route, God and Moses in one breath (Numbers 21:5). God sent poisonous snakes and people began to die all through the camp. When they repented and cried out, God’s answer was not what anyone would design. He did not remove the snakes. He told Moses to make a bronze serpent and set it on a pole where the whole camp could see it, and anyone bitten who looked at it lived: not by medicine or effort, but by looking in faith at what God provided.

A strange remedy. Consider how much seems wrong with that remedy. It is an image, made at the command of the God who had forbidden images for worship. It is an image of the very thing that was killing them, raised in the middle of the camp like a standard. And it requires the dying man to do nothing at all: no offering, no journey. A man face down in the sand with poison in him has one thing left that he can do, and it is to turn his head.

The serpent’s afterlife. The bronze snake had an afterlife. Israel kept it. Centuries later Hezekiah found them burning incense to it, called it Nehushtan, and broke it in pieces (2 Kings 18:4). Even the instrument of God’s mercy will be turned into an idol if it is kept long enough. The look was never meant to land on the bronze.

So must the Son of Man. “Must” (dei): divine necessity. Not may, not will choose to. Given what God had determined to do about sin, and given what sin is, there was no other route. The cross is not a tragedy that overtook a good plan; it is the plan, and it was the plan before there was a wilderness or a serpent or a nation to be bitten (Acts 2:23; 1 Peter 1:19–20).

Lifted up. The word (hypsōthēnai) is used of the cross in three passages of John (here, 8:28 and 12:32–34), and it has a double meaning: raised physically off the ground, and exalted to honour. John explains it in his own voice: he said this to show by what kind of death he was going to die (12:33). Lifted up on the cross, and lifted up in glory. The cross is his glory and his throne. He is never more visibly the King than when he is nailed up under a placard announcing it.

What hung on the pole. As the serpent, a symbol of the curse, was lifted up, so Jesus, made a curse for us (Galatians 3:13), was lifted up on the cross. To be made a curse means that he took the place of the condemned: the sentence God’s law pronounces on lawbreakers fell on him, so that it would not fall on those who trust him (Deuteronomy 21:23; Galatians 3:10–13). Centuries after the wilderness the Son of Man hung on a Roman cross outside the city, and what hung there was our sin. Not his own; he had none. All of it, laid on one body, in daylight, where the whole camp could see (2 Corinthians 5:21). And those who look to him in faith will live.

What does it mean to look to Christ? To look is to trust: to turn away from every other hope and rest your whole weight on Christ crucified for you. It is not a feeling you must work up or a degree of understanding you must reach. The dying Israelite did not need to understand bronze or theology; he needed to believe God’s word and turn his eyes. So it is for you. Look to Christ when you first come to him, and keep looking: when guilt accuses, when temptation bites, when death comes near. Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth (Isaiah 45:22).

On a Tuesday. If you feel that your sin is the thing killing you, you are not being melodramatic; it is what the passage says is happening. The instruction to you is not to fight the snake, or to explain how you came to be bitten, or to demonstrate improvement first, or to feel the right degree of horror. It is to look. That is the whole of it, and it was deliberately made the one thing a dying man can still manage. Today, when the old guilt bites, look again at the cross.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add “who is in heaven.” In John, “lifted up” means both the cross and his exaltation.

parallels.desc: the bronze serpent on a pole
he said this to show by what kind of death he was going to die

verseByVerse.quote: "that whoever believes in him may have eternal life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever believes in him. As the Israelites looked at the serpent, we look to Christ in faith. Whoever means anyone: not whoever understands, for Nicodemus is proof that understanding is not the entrance, and not whoever qualifies. The dying Israelite did not have to comprehend the bronze; he had to trust that the God who told him to look meant it. The KJV adds should not perish here, borrowed from verse 16; the earliest manuscripts do not have it, so most modern Bibles omit it.

May have eternal life. The first appearance in the Gospel of the phrase that will become its whole purpose, and it arrives attached to a snake on a pole. Eternal life (zōē aiōnios) is the life of the age to come, given now and lasting for ever. Aiōnios does mean unending, and the endlessness is not to be dropped. But the noun matters more: zōē, the word from 1:4, the life that was in the Word from the beginning. Eternal life is not chiefly a very long time. It is a kind of life, his kind, shared out: this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent (17:3). Not a location or a reward scheme, but knowing a person.

It begins now. The tense is the thing to hold on to. May have is present. Not will receive at death, not will be awarded at the judgment. This Gospel will keep saying it in the present tense until there is no way to miss it: whoever believes has eternal life (6:47); whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life; he does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life (5:24). Passed. Already. It begins now, at the new birth, and continues for ever. For anyone in Christ, death is not the doorway into eternal life but an interruption in the middle of it.

Where do Jesus’ words end? The ESV notes that some interpreters end Jesus’ words at verse 15, with verses 16–21 as John’s comment. Ancient Greek had no quotation marks. Either way, the words are true. In a red-letter edition the next verse may be printed in red or in black depending on which publisher you happen to be holding. There are reasons for thinking John is now reflecting: the tense shifts to the past, God’s giving of his Son is spoken of as a completed thing, and the phrase only Son is one John uses in his own voice elsewhere (1:14, 18; 1 John 4:9). Others reply that nothing signals a change of speaker. Nothing whatever hangs on it. If John wrote it, it is the Spirit-carried testimony of the apostle who leaned on Jesus’ chest, and it is Scripture. If Jesus said it, it is Scripture. The words are not more true in red ink.

Does eternal life mean I will float in the clouds for ever? No. Eternal life is the life of the age to come, and Scripture pictures that age not as a ghostly existence but as resurrection life in a renewed creation: new heavens and a new earth, where God dwells with his people (Revelation 21:1–4). Believers who die go at once to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23), and they will be raised bodily when he returns (5:28–29; 1 Corinthians 15:42–44). At the centre of it all is not a place but a person: we will see him and know him and enjoy him for ever. That knowing begins today.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some interpreters end Jesus’ words at verse 15 and read verses 16–21 as John’s comment.

verseByVerse.quote: "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life. For God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but in order that the world might be saved through him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The best-known verse in the Bible. Martin Luther is often credited with calling John 3:16 the gospel in miniature. Its problem is familiarity. It is on placards at football matches and the bottom of paper cups, and a verse can be worn out the way a coin is worn: still legal tender, with the face rubbed off. So take the words apart slowly, as though they had not been heard before.

In the flow. The verse opens with For, and it explains what has just been said. The Son of Man must be lifted up (v. 14), and behind that must stands not a grim fate but the Father’s love. The serpent on the pole showed how sinners are saved; this verse shows why. And it sets up verses 17–21, which ask what happens when the gift meets the world: some believe and are not condemned, and others love the darkness.

For God so loved the world. The ESV notes that verse 16 can also be rendered: For this is how God loved the world. So (houtōs) means in this way, more than so much. The sentence is not measuring the love and pronouncing it enormous; it points at something and says, that is how: by giving his Son. The degree comes flooding back the moment the manner is stated, which is why the traditional reading is not wrong in its instinct. But the size of the love is not asserted. It is demonstrated, and left standing.

The world. This is the word that has been quietly sentimentalised. In John, the world is humanity in rebellion against God (1:10): the world that did not know him, that cannot receive the Spirit (14:17), that hates Christ and will hate his people (7:7; 15:18–19). That is the object of the love. Not a world that was lovable and therefore loved; a world that was hostile and loved anyway. Take the sentimental reading and the verse says God cared about a rather nice planet. Take John’s own vocabulary and it says God set his love on the very thing that was set against him. The wonder is not that the world is big, but that it is bad. God loved those who hated him.

That he gave his only Son. Gave: in the incarnation, and supremely on the cross. Not only sent, though he did send. To give a thing is to part with it, and the weight of the verse rests on the fact that the Giver did not keep what he gave. His only Son (monogenē): unique, beloved, and not created (1:14, 18). The KJV’s only begotten renders the same word; most scholars now take it to mean one of a kind, and both renderings confess a Son who is uniquely and eternally the Father’s. The Father had one Son, eternally his, his delight before there was a world, and put him into the hands of a race that did not know him or receive him. Abraham was told to take his son, his only son Isaac, whom he loved (Genesis 22:2), and at the last moment his hand was stopped and a ram was provided. On Golgotha no hand stopped the Father’s. He did not spare his own Son (Romans 8:32), because this time the Son was the Lamb.

Should not perish. Perish (apolētai) means be destroyed, be lost for ever, and it is stated without softening. This is not a verse about improving lives. It is a rescue verse, and rescue implies something to be rescued from.

Does perish mean simply ceasing to exist? No. Some have taught that the lost are finally annihilated, but Scripture speaks of the wicked going away into eternal punishment as the righteous go into eternal life, with the same word for both (Matthew 25:46), and of a destruction that is everlasting and conscious, away from the presence of the Lord (2 Thessalonians 1:9; Revelation 14:11). To perish is to be lost: ruined, cut off from God, under his wrath for ever (v. 36). That is a terrible truth, and it is told here not to frighten us for its own sake but to show the size of the rescue. God gave his Son so that we need not perish.

Not to condemn. The purpose of his first coming was salvation, not judgment (12:47), and salvation through him alone (14:6; Acts 4:12). This needs a guard, because it is often used to cancel the rest of the paragraph. It is a statement of purpose, not a denial that judgment exists, as the next sentence proves by saying that whoever does not believe is condemned already. The two sit together without strain. A lifeboat does not go out to drown anybody. That the drowning is real is why it was launched.

Where Christians differ: God’s love and the extent of the atonement. Some take this verse to prove that Christ died equally for every individual, making salvation possible for all: this is the Arminian view, which holds that God’s choosing rests on faith he foresees, and many faithful Christians hold it or something near it. This commentary’s view: the verse teaches God’s love for a rebellious world, the gift of his Son, and the promise of life to everyone who believes. It is the foundation of the free offer of the gospel to all people: anyone who believes will be saved. It does not say Christ died in the same way for every individual. Elsewhere John shows that Christ lays down his life for his sheep (10:11, 15), and that those who believe are those the Father gives him (6:37, 44). Both truths stand: the gospel is offered to all, and those who believe are saved by a Saviour whose death secured their salvation. Reformed theology calls this definite (or particular) atonement: Christ died to save, and surely saves, those the Father gave him. Believers who read these verses differently are brothers to be heard, and all agree that whoever believes will not perish.

Is it not cruel for a father to send his son to die? Only if the Son were an unwilling third party. But he is not a victim the Father sacrifices to spare himself. Father and Son are one God, and the Son goes willingly: no one takes his life from him; he lays it down of his own accord (10:18). Nor does the Father give up something he cares little for. He gives what he loves most (Romans 8:32). The cross is not God making someone else pay so that he need not. It is God himself, in the person of his Son, bearing the judgment his own holiness requires, because he would rather suffer than lose us.

Can I tell anyone that God loves them? Yes, and you should, with care. God’s goodness and kindness extend to every person he has made (Psalm 145:9; Matthew 5:44–45), and his offer in the gospel is sincere to all: he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but would rather they turn and live (Ezekiel 33:11). So you may say to anyone: God so loved the world that he gave his Son, and if you believe in him you will not perish; come to him, and he will not turn you away (6:37). What you should not do is tell someone that God loves them in a way that makes no claim on them, or that they are safe without Christ. The love of John 3:16 is a love that calls rebels to believe.

On a Tuesday. Say the verse about yourself, out loud, with your own name where the world stands. It was not written to be agreed with as a general truth. It was written to be believed by somebody. Then think of one person who needs to hear it, and pray for a chance to tell them.

For worship. The Father gave the Son, and the Son gave himself. Paul, who had once hated his name, wrote it in the first person: the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me (Galatians 2:20). The love of John 3:16 is wide enough for the world and personal enough to have a single name on it. In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins (1 John 4:10): the sacrifice that turned his own just anger away from us by bearing it. Glory to the Father who gave, and to the Son who was given.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that verse 16 can also be rendered “For this is how God loved the world” — the stress is on the manner of his love.

parallels.desc: your son, your only son

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever believes in him is not condemned, but whoever does not believe is condemned already, because he has not believed in the name of the only Son of God. And this is the judgment: the light has come into the world, and people loved the darkness rather than the light because their works were evil."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not condemned. No condemnation, now or ever (5:24; Romans 8:1). The verdict is settled.

Condemned already. Everything turns on one word, and it is the word that frightens people: already. It is more merciful than it sounds. The point is not that unbelief is their only sin, but that they are already under condemnation for their sin, and by refusing Christ, they refuse the only rescue. They remain where they are (v. 36). The verse is not saying that a sentence is passed on people the moment they hear about Christ and decline. It is saying the sentence was passed long before, and that the arrival of Christ is not what put anyone in danger. He walked into a situation that was already lost. Nobody was standing in neutral territory waiting to see how they felt about him.

A rescue, not an examination. That means the gospel is not an examination that a person might fail. It is a rescue that a person might refuse, and those are entirely different things, though they feel similar from the inside. In the first, Christ increases the risk. In the second, he is the only reason the risk has an exit. That is why not believing in the name of the only Son of God is the final sin: it refuses the only cure.

How strong must my faith be? This verse does real damage in the hands of the wrong reader. There are people who read condemned already and immediately begin auditing themselves for whether they have believed hard enough or sincerely enough to have crossed the line. Read the sentence again. The condemnation attaches to one thing only: not believing in the name of the only Son of God. It is not measuring the quality of anyone’s faith. It is distinguishing between those who have come to him and those who have not. A weak hand on a strong rope is not the same as no hand at all, and this verse is about which rope, not about the strength of the grip. Weak faith in a strong Saviour saves.

This is the judgment. Judgment (krisis) is the verdict, the dividing line, and verse 19 defines it in a way no one would write. Not a throne, not a book opened, not a sentence pronounced, but a person arriving. The light is Jesus (1:9), and the judgment is what people do when he comes.

Loved the darkness. The real reason for unbelief is not lack of evidence but love of sin. People do not reject Jesus because they cannot believe, but because they will not give up the darkness. So the judgment is not only something done at the end. It is something disclosed now: God’s verdict is the publication of a preference that was already operating, which is why the last day can be perfectly just without anybody being surprised by it. The verb matters. Not tolerated the darkness, not drifted into it. Loved it. This is not a verdict on every honest questioner; Nicodemus came with questions and Jesus welcomed him. It names the root of the world’s refusal, and each of us can recognise it in himself.

Because their works were evil. This locates the real difficulty exactly where Nicodemus has been told it is. If unbelief were an information problem it could be solved by teaching, and he of all people would already be safe. It is a problem of the affections. And affections are not argued into place; they have to be born.

What of those who have never heard of Christ? This verse describes everyone apart from him: no one is saved another way (14:6; Acts 4:12). Those who never hear are not condemned for rejecting a message they never received, but for their sins against the light they had (Romans 1:20; 2:12). That is why Paul asks how they are to believe in him of whom they have never heard (Romans 10:14). The answer is not speculation but mission. And we may trust that the Judge of all the earth will do what is right (Genesis 18:25), including with infants who die before they can hear: the Reformed confessions teach that elect infants dying in infancy are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where he pleases (the Westminster Confession 10.3; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 10.3). Parents who have lost a little one may rest their grief with that Judge, whose tenderness to children Jesus showed when he took them in his arms and blessed them (Mark 10:16).

parallels.desc: no condemnation

verseByVerse.quote: "For everyone who does wicked things hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works should be exposed. But whoever does what is true comes to the light, so that it may be clearly seen that his works have been carried out in God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hates the light. Light exposes, and the wicked avoid it as thieves avoid daylight. Exposed (elenchthē) means convicted, shown for what one is. The instinct is universal and needs no teaching: a child who has broken something goes quiet and moves toward the door. The edited version we give at dinner parties, the tone of an email that is covering for something, the friendships kept carefully shallow, are sophisticated developments of the same reflex: stay where the lighting is favourable.

Avoidance feels like busyness. This is where the verse becomes uncomfortable, because avoidance of the light is not usually experienced as avoidance. It is experienced as being busy: as not having time to pray, or finding a book of the Bible dull, or preferring to read about the faith rather than sit still before God. The man in this verse is not shaking his fist. He simply does not come. Not every dry season is avoidance, though: tiredness, grief and depression can make prayer heavy for people who love the light dearly. The mark of this verse is unwillingness, not difficulty, and anyone grieved by his own coldness is already turned toward the lamp.

Whoever does what is true. The phrase means lives honestly, sincerely, by God’s truth: literally, whoever does the truth. In Scripture truth is not merely a property of statements. It is something a person can do, or fail to do; it means integrity, faithfulness, being in reality the thing one appears to be. Such a person is not afraid of the light. So the two groups are not the clever and the stupid, or the religious and the irreligious. They are those who will come out into the open and those who will not.

Carried out in God. His works were done by God’s grace and in union with him, and the light shows it. Perhaps an encouragement to Nicodemus, who had come by night: come into the light.

Exposed and not ashamed. The next chapter shows what coming to this light looks like. A Samaritan woman with five husbands behind her meets Jesus at a well, and he tells her the whole of it. She does not run from him. She runs into her town saying, come, see a man who told me all that I ever did (4:29). Being known by him did not destroy her; it set her free to bring others. That is the light this verse describes: not a searchlight hunting criminals, but the face of the Saviour, who exposes in order to heal and names sin in order to forgive it.

What it does not mean. This pair of verses can be read as saying that good people come to Christ and bad people avoid him, which would undo the whole chapter. Read the last clause again: his works have been carried out in God. Whatever is found in the light was put there by the one holding the lamp. Nobody in this passage brings his own goodness to the light for inspection and passes. Even what the light finds in God’s children is never flawless; it is accepted because the Son obeyed perfectly in their place, and his obedience is counted as theirs (Romans 5:19). The new birth stands behind every honest thing a person does, which is why coming into the light is not the terror it looks like from outside. This is not a system of salvation by works, but a description of the direction of genuine faith.

How do I come into the light in practice? By refusing to hide from God or from his people. Begin with honest confession to God, naming what you have done rather than speaking of it vaguely (1 John 1:9). Read Scripture in a way that lets it search you, not only inform you (Hebrews 4:12). Where there is a sin that has a grip on you, tell a mature, trusted Christian, and let them pray with you and ask you about it (James 5:16). Put right what can be put right. None of this earns forgiveness; Christ has done that. It is simply what it looks like to live as a forgiven person who no longer needs the dark.

For worship. He was exposed for us. At the cross the soldiers divided his garments and cast lots for his tunic (19:23–24), and the Light of the world hung stripped in the open, under every eye, bearing the shame our hiding had earned. Because he was laid bare, the worst the light can find in his people has already been answered for. He clothes with his own righteousness those who come out of the dark (Isaiah 61:10). The Lord was uncovered in the light so that we could stand in it clothed.

parallels.desc: expose the works of darkness

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–36 — John's Final Testimony: The Bridegroom's Friend
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus and his disciples baptise in the Judean countryside while John, still free, baptises at Aenon near Salim. When John’s disciples complain that everyone is going to Jesus, John answers that a person receives only what heaven gives: he is the friend of the bridegroom, whose joy is complete when he hears the groom’s voice, and Jesus must increase while he decreases. The closing verses give the reason: the one from heaven is above all, speaks the words of God, has the Spirit without measure, and holds all things in his hand, so that to believe in him is life and to refuse him is to remain under God’s wrath.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Baptist’s last words in this Gospel (if the closing verses are his) sum up its theology: Jesus comes from above, speaks the words of God, gives the Spirit without measure, and holds in his hands both eternal life and God’s wrath. There is no middle ground. The Baptist who began by pointing to the Lamb of God ends by declaring the eternal stakes of the decision about him.

Both verbs in verse 30 carry the same must that Jesus used of the Son of Man being lifted up (v. 14): the rise of one and the waning of the other are a single arrangement of God. Verse 36 sets believes against does not obey, so the unbelief in view is not doubt politely held but the refusal of a person who has a right to be obeyed. And the wrath remains: it does not arrive but stays where it already was. That is also where the mercy lies, because what remains can be lifted, and this chapter has already said how.
verseByVerse.examples:
He must increase, but I must decrease is the mark of all genuine ministry: a minister who builds his own kingdom rather than Christ’s has misunderstood the calling. The friend of the bridegroom is not diminished but fulfilled when the bridegroom claims his bride, and the bride is not the audience at the wedding; she is the one being married.

The words were not sentimental. Within months John was in Herod’s prison, sending to ask whether Jesus was the one who was to come (Matthew 11:2–3), and he was executed without trial; yet Jesus’ verdict, given while he was in that cell, was that among those born of women none was greater (Matthew 11:11). So this is the passage for anyone being replaced. The decrease is bearable, and even a completed joy, only because of who fills the space.

verseByVerse.quote: After this Jesus and his disciples went into the Judean countryside, and he remained there with them and was baptizing. John also was baptizing at Aenon near Salim, because water was plentiful there, and people were coming and being baptized.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Into the Judean countryside. An early Judean ministry, recorded only in John. Jesus has left Jerusalem, the temple, the council, the centre, where he had the attention of a member of the Sanhedrin and could have built on it. He goes to the fields instead, where the water is, and works there.

In the flow. John sets one last scene of the Baptist beside Jesus, and it is no change of subject. Nicodemus was told that new birth comes from above; the Baptist will say that the one who comes from above is above all (v. 31). The chapter that began with a teacher who did not understand ends with a witness who does, and both are measured against the same Son.

Baptizing. John later clarifies that Jesus himself did not baptise, but his disciples did (4:2). There is a fitness in that. The Baptist had said that the one coming after him would baptize with the Holy Spirit (1:33). The disciples handled the water, the sign; the Lord kept for himself the giving of what it signifies, the new birth by the Spirit he had just described to Nicodemus.

At Aenon near Salim. The location of Aenon (springs) near Salim is uncertain, perhaps in the Jordan valley, or in Samaria.

Water was plentiful. Plenty of water suggests immersion. Baptists note this; it is not conclusive. It is first a logistical remark: it tells us why a preacher pitched at that particular spot, with enough water for the crowds who came.

Two ministries, no rivalry. What matters more is the picture of two ministries at once, in the same region, without either man treating the other as competition. The text records no meeting, no division of territory and no comment from either about the other. That is not indifference; John will speak of Jesus in a moment with more warmth than anyone in the Gospel. It is that neither experienced the other’s work as a problem to be managed. The only people in this passage worried about the arrangement are the followers, which is how it usually goes.

How should I think about other churches in my town? As fellow workers, where they preach the same gospel. Christ has one church, gathered in many congregations, and the success of a faithful church down the road is a gain for the kingdom, not a loss for yours. Name them in your prayers, speak well of them, and rejoice when people are converted there. That does not mean every difference is unimportant; where the gospel itself is denied, love must speak plainly. But most of our rivalries are not about the gospel at all. They are about numbers, style and pride, and those are not worth one moment of the Spirit’s grief.
verseByVerse.note: The location of Aenon (“springs”) near Salim is uncertain.

verseByVerse.quote: (for John had not yet been put in prison)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not yet put in prison. The other Gospels begin Jesus’ Galilean ministry after John’s arrest (Mark 1:14). John explains that this Judean ministry came earlier, overlapping with John’s.

An eyewitness filling the gap. The bracket reads like someone who knows the sequence and takes the trouble to steady readers coming from the other accounts, which fits this Gospel’s own claim to rest on an eyewitness (21:24).

A shadow across the parenthesis. Not yet put in prison: the reader is told in passing how this ends. The man about to say he must increase, but I must decrease is a few months from a cell and, as the other Gospels record, not long from an executioner. He spoke those words not from a settled retirement but on a downward slope, as a man who could feel the gradient and did not yet know where it went.

Forerunner to the end. John went before Jesus in birth, in preaching and in baptising, and he went before him in suffering too. Matthew records Jesus saying that Elijah had already come and they did to him whatever they pleased, and that so also the Son of Man would suffer at their hands; and the disciples understood that he spoke of John the Baptist (Matthew 17:12–13). The prison and the sword were part of the road John was preparing. The King who followed him would be arrested and bound (18:12), condemned without justice and put to death, and would go further into the dark than John ever went: under the wrath of God for sinners.

Do the Gospels contradict each other on the order of events? No. They complement one another. Each Gospel writer selected and arranged true events for his purpose, and John, probably writing last, often fills in what the others pass over: an early Judean ministry, several visits to Jerusalem, long conversations. Here he even flags the seam for us. Apparent differences in order usually arise because one writer groups events by theme while another follows the calendar more closely. Not every question of order has a certain answer, and believers can say so honestly while trusting that the accounts are true. Reading the four together does not weaken our confidence in them; it gives us a fuller, stereoscopic picture of one Lord, from four angles, resting on eyewitness testimony.
verseByVerse.note: The other Gospels begin Jesus’ Galilean ministry after John’s arrest; John fills in an earlier period.

verseByVerse.quote: Now a discussion arose between some of John's disciples and a Jew over purification. And they came to John and said to him, "Rabbi, he who was with you across the Jordan, to whom you bore witness — look, he is baptizing, and all are going to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A discussion arose … over purification. Perhaps about the value of John’s baptism compared with Jesus’, or with Jewish ritual washings. The argument that produces the New Testament’s great statement about humility began as a dispute about ceremonial washing: whose water counted, which rite was valid. This Gospel has been circling the question since chapter 2, when six stone jars for the Jewish rites of purification stood at a wedding and were filled with something else entirely. The answer to the dispute is not a better rite but a person, the Son who would himself make purification for sins and then sit down at the right hand of the Majesty on high (Hebrews 1:3).

He who was with you. They do not name Jesus. A hint of resentment: the one you helped is now taking your followers. Every word of it is the language of a threatened camp. He who was with you puts Jesus in a subordinate position, the junior figure who used to be part of John’s operation. To whom you bore witness implies he owes his standing to their master, and is now trading on a reference.

All are going to him. Jealousy: John’s disciples are upset that Jesus is more popular. And all is not true, since John is still baptising crowds big enough to need springs. All is what anxiety says, the arithmetic of a man watching numbers move the wrong way; nobody at peace about a comparison needs to reach for a total. And look, the smallest word in the sentence, gives it away. They are not informing him. They are directing his attention, as one does when a person is failing to be as alarmed as the situation warrants.

Loyal and wrong. The saddest thing in the verse is that they are being loyal. They are defending their master, out of real affection. That is how the ugliest instincts in church life often present themselves: not as jealousy but as concern, about standards, about where things are heading, about a church down the road that seems to be doing rather well. They are measuring one ministry against another, which is the only arithmetic left to someone who has lost sight of who Jesus is. John is measuring nothing, because he settled the question at the Jordan.

How do I deal with jealousy of other Christians? Name it honestly as sin, not as concern, and confess it to God. Then fight it with truth. Remember that their gifts and fruit were given from heaven (v. 27), so envying them is a complaint against God. Remember that you are one body, so their gain is yours (1 Corinthians 12:26). Thank God for them specifically, out loud, and pray for their further blessing; envy rarely survives sincere intercession. And look again at Christ, because jealousy grows where we have stopped being satisfied in him.

verseByVerse.quote: John answered, "A person cannot receive even one thing unless it is given him from heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not even one thing. Everything comes from God: John’s ministry, Jesus’ ministry, every gift, every success. The sentence is absolute, and the temptation is to hear it as modesty and move on. Not most things. Not the important things. Not one (1 Corinthians 4:7).

It cuts both ways. Applied to the case in hand it cuts in two directions at once. If Jesus is drawing the crowds, heaven gave him the crowds, so envying him is a complaint against God. If John’s numbers are falling, heaven arranged that too, so the decline is an allocation to be accepted. And if John ever had a crowd, that was given as well, which removes any basis for regarding it as his to lose. Envy always requires a sense of ownership: the assumption that a thing was mine, or ought to have been. Take away the ownership and there is nothing for envy to attach to. A man cannot be robbed of what he was only ever handed. The same truth cuts against taking credit: the intelligence, the temperament, even the capacity to work hard, were all given.

The Gift from heaven. The greatest thing ever received from heaven was a few miles from where John spoke. God gave his only Son, and Jesus calls himself the true bread from heaven, which his Father gives (6:32). Even the Son, as the one sent, lives as one who receives from the Father: the works he does, the words he speaks, the life he has in himself (5:26), and all things given into his hand (v. 35). If the Son himself delights to receive, no servant of his has anything that was not handed to him.

If everything is given, does my effort not matter? It matters greatly, and it too is given. Paul says he worked harder than any of the apostles, and in the same breath, though it was not I, but the grace of God that is with me (1 Corinthians 15:10). God gives gifts so that we will use them diligently, and he holds us accountable for what we do with them (Matthew 25:14–30). The point of this verse is not that we should be passive, but that we should be humble and content: working hard with what we have been given, without pride when it prospers or envy when others prosper more.

For worship. Even the receiving is given. No one can come to me, Jesus says, unless it is granted him by the Father (6:65). The Father gave the Son from heaven, and then gave the empty hands that take him, the eyes that see him, and the faith that holds on. From the first breath of the new birth to the last day of perseverance, nothing in a Christian’s salvation came from below. We have nothing we did not receive, and so nothing to boast of except the Giver, and he is endlessly generous.

parallels.desc: what do you have that you did not receive?

verseByVerse.quote: "You yourselves bear me witness, that I said, 'I am not the Christ, but I have been sent before him.' The one who has the bride is the bridegroom. The friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom's voice. Therefore this joy of mine is now complete."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am not the Christ. John has been saying it since chapter 1 (1:20, 23), to delegations and to disciples, and it has never once sounded like a disappointment. The reason he can watch the crowd leave without panic is that he never mistook himself for the reason they came.

The bridegroom. In the Old Testament, God is the bridegroom of his people (Isaiah 54:5; 62:5; Hosea 2:19–20). Jesus is the bridegroom; his people are the bride (Mark 2:19–20; Ephesians 5:25–32; Revelation 19:7; 21:2). John is quietly applying to Jesus the role that belongs to the LORD himself.

The friend of the bridegroom. In Jewish custom the friend of the bridegroom often helped arrange the wedding and brought the bride to the groom, like a best man. He stood beside the groom and served the wedding; in a real sense it was his project. His joy was to see the marriage happen, not to take the bride for himself, and the moment the bridegroom’s voice was heard, his work was over.

Rejoices greatly. Perhaps the bridegroom’s shout of joy on receiving his bride. The Greek doubles the joy: he rejoices with joy. This is not resignation dressed up, nor a spectator’s pleasure. It is the gladness of somebody whose own work has just succeeded, and whose success takes the form of being no longer required.

This joy of mine. People going to Jesus is the fulfilment of John’s whole life. The tense is a perfect, a thing brought to fullness and standing full, at the very moment the crowds transfer. He is not managing a loss. He is at the height of his life.

The bride is not the audience. The metaphor has a quiet largeness. If Jesus is the bridegroom, there is a bride, and she is not an afterthought or an audience. The people being baptised in that river, and the ones who would follow for two thousand years, are not the crowd at the wedding. They are the one being married.

What does it mean that the church is Christ’s bride? It means that Christ loves his people with the faithful, exclusive, self-giving love of a husband, and has bound himself to them by covenant for ever. He gave himself up for her, to make her holy and present her to himself in splendour (Ephesians 5:25–27). It means the church belongs to him, not to its leaders; ministers are at most the friends of the bridegroom. And it means our story ends with a wedding: the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:7–9). If you are in Christ, you are not merely a guest at that feast. You are part of the bride.

On a Tuesday. If you teach, lead, parent or befriend people in the faith, ask whose voice they are learning to love: yours, or the bridegroom’s? Your task is to bring them to him and step back. The next time someone you have helped grows close to Christ in a way that no longer needs you, let it complete your joy rather than diminish it.
verseByVerse.note: The friend of the bridegroom arranged the wedding and brought bride and groom together — his joy was the groom’s joy.

parallels.desc: as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride

verseByVerse.quote: "He must increase, but I must decrease."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He must increase. These are, on most readings, the last recorded words of John the Baptist in this Gospel (some think he speaks on to verse 36), and they are worth reading as a final statement rather than a devotional maxim. Must (dei) is divine necessity, the same word Jesus used of the Son of Man who must be lifted up on the cross (v. 14). Jesus must grow in prominence, in followers, in glory, and the rise of one and the shrinking of the other are a single arrangement, not John’s to negotiate.

But I must decrease. Not reluctantly, but gladly: a classic statement of humility, and the motto of every true servant of Christ. Think of the moon: it has no light of its own, its business is to shine when the sun is not up, and its fading is not a tragedy but the arrival of morning.

What I must decrease came to. He said it, and then it happened, and not gently. Within months Herod arrested him for telling the truth about a marriage. From a fortress cell he sent messengers to ask Jesus whether he was the one who was to come, or whether they should look for another (Matthew 11:2–3), which is not the question of a man serenely fulfilled. And he was beheaded without trial, to keep a promise made in front of dinner guests. He was describing, without knowing it, the rest of his life.

The greatest, wobbling. And Jesus’ verdict on him was delivered while he was in that cell, doubting: among those born of women there has arisen no one greater than John the Baptist (Matthew 11:11). The greatest of those born of women, on the assessment of the only person qualified to make it, is the one who arranged his entire existence around becoming unnecessary, who seems to have wobbled at the end, and was called the greatest anyway.

Does decreasing mean I must think nothing of myself? No. John did not despise himself; he knew exactly who he was, the voice, the friend of the bridegroom, and he did that work with courage. Decreasing is not self-hatred or false modesty. It is the gladness of seeing Christ honoured more than yourself, and the willingness to be forgotten if he is remembered. The decrease is bearable, and in fact a completed joy, solely because of who is filling the space. Nobody in Scripture is ever asked to shrink for the sake of shrinking. You are asked to make room for him, and in him you will find yourself more truly than you ever could by holding on (Matthew 16:25).

On a Tuesday. This is the verse for anyone being replaced: by the younger colleague who is plainly better at it, the role handed on, the children who no longer ring, the body doing less than it did. The world has no account of these except loss. Make John’s words your prayer today: Lord, may you increase, and may I decrease; and remember that the one who must increase went lower for you than any slope can take you.

verseByVerse.quote: "He who comes from above is above all. He who is of the earth belongs to the earth and speaks in an earthly way. He who comes from heaven is above all. He bears witness to what he has seen and heard, yet no one receives his testimony."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who is speaking? Verses 31–36 may be John the Baptist’s words continuing, or the Gospel writer’s reflection; the Greek has no quotation marks, and the same uncertainty arises earlier in this chapter about where Jesus’ words to Nicodemus end. John moves from reporting a voice to adding his own without announcement, because in his mind the two are saying the same thing. Either way the words explain why Jesus must increase, and their authority is unaffected.

Above all. Jesus, from heaven, is supreme over all. The first half of the verse states the principle underneath everything in this chapter. Origin decides authority.

He who is of the earth. John the Baptist, and every human teacher. Even the greatest prophets speak as earthly men, with limited knowledge. If it is the Baptist speaking, he is describing himself: the man Jesus would call the greatest born of women filing himself under earth without complaint. He is not being falsely modest. He is being accurate about the one distinction that matters, which is not between a great man and a small one but between everyone born here and the one who came from somewhere else. That is why Nicodemus at the start of this chapter and the Baptist at the end of it are in the same category. The best teacher in Israel and the last of the prophets are both of the earth. Only one person in the passage came down.

What he has seen and heard. Jesus speaks from direct knowledge of heaven (v. 11), as no other teacher can.

No one receives. A general rejection (1:11), not literally no one, as the next verse shows. It is not a statistic but a lament. The testimony is perfect; the evidence was never the problem.

If Jesus is above all, how should I weigh other voices? Every other voice is of the earth, however wise, and must be tested by his. That includes teachers you admire, traditions you love, experts, your own feelings, and the spirit of the age. Many of them say true and useful things, and we should listen with humility. But when they contradict what Christ has said in his word, he wins, every time (Galatians 1:8). That is what sola Scriptura means in practice: not that only the Bible is useful, but that only the Bible, as the word of the one from above, has the final say.

parallels.desc: you are from below, I am from above

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever receives his testimony sets his seal to this, that God is true."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sets his seal. Some do receive it. To set one’s seal to something is to certify it as true. A seal pressed into wax or clay by a signet ring was the ancient equivalent of a signature on a contract: this is mine, I stand behind it, and it can be produced against me later. Setting a seal was not an opinion. It was a commitment.

That God is true. To believe Jesus’ testimony is to affirm that God is truthful, since Jesus speaks God’s words (v. 34). So faith, in this verse, is not first a feeling or even first a benefit received. It is a signature. To believe Christ is to put one’s name to the claim that God tells the truth, and to do it in advance of much of the evidence, since a great deal of what God has said has not happened yet. And to refuse it is to call God a liar (1 John 5:10). If God has testified about his Son and a man declines the testimony, there is no third position available. Which quietly disposes of the idea that unbelief is always a modest, humble posture. It is a verdict, and it is a verdict about somebody’s character. That does not make every doubter dishonest; it means the question is finally personal: whether God can be trusted.

The Son the Father sealed. The image has a deeper layer in this Gospel. Jesus says of himself that on him God the Father has set his seal (6:27): the Father has certified the Son, by the Spirit who came down and remained on him at the Jordan (1:32–33), by the works he gave him to do, and finally by raising him. So the believer’s seal is a countersignature. God has already signed his name to his Son, and faith adds its own underneath, agreeing that what the Father says about Jesus is true. And a seal works both ways: believers are themselves sealed with the promised Holy Spirit (Ephesians 1:13). The one who signs his name to God’s truthfulness discovers that God has already signed his name to him.

What if I believe but still have doubts? Then you are like many in Scripture: the father who cried, I believe; help my unbelief (Mark 9:24), the psalmists who asked how long, John the Baptist in his cell. Doubt is not the opposite of faith; unbelief is. Faith is trusting God’s word while questions remain. So bring your doubts to God honestly, take them to his word, talk to mature believers, and keep doing what faith does: praying, gathering, obeying. Your seal is not on the strength of your feelings but on the truthfulness of God, and he does not change when you waver (2 Timothy 2:13).

On a Tuesday. Think of a promise of God that your circumstances currently contradict: that he works all things for good, that he will never leave, that the light is not overcome. Ask which of the two you are treating as the fixed point. Faith is not the absence of the contradiction. It is putting your name to the promise while the contradiction is still standing, and God does not change while you waver.
verseByVerse.note: To set one’s seal to something is to certify it as true.

parallels.desc: let God be true

verseByVerse.quote: "For he whom God has sent utters the words of God, for he gives the Spirit without measure. The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The words of God. Jesus’ words are God’s words (7:16; 12:49–50; 14:10). Not in the partial, occasional manner of the prophets, but fully.

Without measure. Prophets received the Spirit in measure, for particular tasks. The Greek does not supply the subject. It can mean the Father gives the Spirit to the Son without measure, which fits what the Baptist saw at the Jordan when the Spirit came down and remained on him (1:32–33; Isaiah 11:2). Or it can mean the Son gives the Spirit without measure, as the Baptist announced at the beginning: this is he who baptizes with the Holy Spirit (1:33). Both are true, and the order between them is the point. The Spirit rests on the Son without limit, and out of that fullness the Son gives, so that what reaches the believer is not a diluted portion.

The Father loves the Son. The eternal love within the Trinity (5:20; 17:24). Before there was anything made, or anyone to save, or a world to be given up for, that was already the case, and it is the oldest fact in existence. Everything in this chapter runs downstream of it. The Son was given because the Father loves the world; all things were put into his hand because the Father loves the Son and would deny him nothing.

All things into his hand. All authority (13:3; Matthew 28:18). Everything is in his hands, including salvation and judgment. The handing over of all things is not an administrative arrangement. It is what love does: the Father withholds nothing from the Son because he loves him. And hold on to the phrase for later in this Gospel. All things into his hand: the same hand out of which, in chapter 10, Jesus will say no one is able to snatch his sheep (10:28–29). What has been put into that hand includes people, and nothing has ever been taken out of it.

Can I be sure I am safe in his hand? If you belong to Christ, yes. The Father has given all things into the Son’s hand, including those who come to him, and Jesus says of them: I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand (10:28). Your security does not rest on the strength of your grip but on his. You will still stumble and doubt, but the one who holds you is the one who loves the Father and does his will, and it is the Father’s will that he should lose nothing of all that he has been given (6:39). That is not a licence to drift. It is the ground on which a trembling believer can stand.

For worship. The love that holds the universe together is not a policy God adopted toward creatures. It is what passed between the Father and the Son before there were any creatures, and in the upper room, with the cross a few hours away, the Son asked that this very love might be in his people: that the love with which you have loved me may be in them, and I in them (17:26). The oldest love there is has been opened, and there is room inside. Glory to the Father, the Son and the Spirit, one God in eternal love.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever does not obey the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Has eternal life. The chapter that began with new birth ends with the sharpest possible alternative: eternal life or the abiding wrath of God.

Whoever does not obey the Son. Unbelief is disobedience. Faith in Christ is obedience to God’s command (1 John 3:23). Note the pairing, which is deliberately asymmetrical: not believes against does not believe, which is what we would expect, but believes against does not obey. The word (apeitheō) means refuses to be persuaded, will not comply. John is not smuggling works into salvation. He is saying that the unbelief in question is not an intellectual position politely held but a refusal of a person who has a right to be obeyed. It is closer to insubordination than to doubt.

The wrath of God remains. Wrath (orgē) is God’s settled, holy opposition to sin, and this is its only appearance in John’s Gospel. Not that God becomes angry when someone rejects Christ, but that all people are already under his wrath because of sin (Ephesians 2:3), and it remains on those who refuse the only one who can remove it. We hear wrath and picture something arriving. Nothing arrives. The wrath remains, as the condition already in place: the same truth as condemned already (v. 18), said with a different verb. Christ bore God’s wrath for those who believe (Romans 5:9; 1 Thessalonians 1:10).

The abiding word. The verb here is menō, the abiding word, and this Gospel has used it before. Its first appearance was in chapter 1, when the Baptist watched the Spirit come down and remain on Jesus (1:32–33). Its echo will run all the way to chapter 15 and the vine: abide in me, and I in you. And here is the same verb describing what settles on a man who will not have the Son. Something abides on everyone. On Christ, the Spirit rests and does not lift. On those who are his, he himself abides. And on the one who refuses him, the wrath he was born under simply stays where it was, because nothing has happened to move it.

How can a God of love have wrath? Because his love is holy. Wrath in God is not a mood that flares and fades; it is his steady, just opposition to evil, the right response of perfect goodness to what destroys his creatures and defies his glory. A God who felt nothing about cruelty, abuse and lies would not be loving; he would be indifferent. And the cross shows the two together: God’s love provided what his justice required, when Christ bore the wrath we deserved as our substitute (Romans 3:25–26; 1 John 4:10). The same chapter that speaks of wrath speaks of a love that gave its only Son. The love is the way out of the wrath.

What it does not mean. This verse frightens people, and some of them are the wrong people. It is not addressed to the Christian who has bad days, or doubts, or a faith that feels thinner than he wishes. The one described here is not struggling with the Son; he is declining him. And the whole sentence turns on a present-tense contrast, has eternal life against remains, which means the two conditions are the two states people are in this evening. If wrath remains rather than arrives, then it can be lifted rather than merely postponed, and this chapter has already said how. It was lifted the way the poison was lifted in the desert: not by the dying man’s exertion but by his looking at something raised up on his behalf.

For worship. In the garden, as they came to arrest him, Jesus said to Peter, shall I not drink the cup that the Father has given me? (18:11). It was the cup of the wrath that remains on the unbelieving, and he drank it to the bottom, so that for those who believe in the Son not a drop is left. The chapter that began with a man coming in the dark ends with the wrath of God, and between them stand the Son given and the Son lifted up. Worthy is the Lamb who drank the cup so that it would never be ours.

parallels.desc: the wrath of God is revealed

3.title: You Must Be Born Again
3.text: <sup>1</sup>Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews.<sup>2</sup>This man came to Jesus by night and said to him, “Rabbi, we know that you are a teacher come from God, for no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him.”<sup>3</sup>Jesus answered him, “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God.”<sup>4</sup>Nicodemus said to him, “How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother’s womb and be born?”<sup>5</sup>Jesus answered, “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.<sup>6</sup>That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit.<sup>7</sup>Do not marvel that I said to you, ’You must be born again.’<sup>8</sup>The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit.”<sup>9</sup>Nicodemus said to him, “How can these things be?”<sup>10</sup>Jesus answered him, “Are you the teacher of Israel and yet you do not understand these things?<sup>11</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, we speak of what we know, and bear witness to what we have seen, but you do not receive our testimony.<sup>12</sup>If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how can you believe if I tell you heavenly things?<sup>13</sup>No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man.<sup>14</sup>And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up,<sup>15</sup>that whoever believes in him may have eternal life.<sup>16</sup>“For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life.<sup>17</sup>For God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but in order that the world might be saved through him.<sup>18</sup>Whoever believes in him is not condemned, but whoever does not believe is condemned already, because he has not believed in the name of the only Son of God.<sup>19</sup>And this is the judgment: the light has come into the world, and people loved the darkness rather than the light because their works were evil.<sup>20</sup>For everyone who does wicked things hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works should be exposed.<sup>21</sup>But whoever does what is true comes to the light, so that it may be clearly seen that his works have been carried out in God.”<sup>22</sup>After this Jesus and his disciples went into the Judean countryside, and he remained there with them and was baptizing.<sup>23</sup>John also was baptizing at Aenon near Salim, because water was plentiful there, and people were coming and being baptized<sup>24</sup>(for John had not yet been put in prison).<sup>25</sup>Now a discussion arose between some of John’s disciples and a Jew over purification.<sup>26</sup>And they came to John and said to him, “Rabbi, he who was with you across the Jordan, to whom you bore witness—look, he is baptizing, and all are going to him.”<sup>27</sup>John answered, “A person cannot receive even one thing unless it is given him from heaven.<sup>28</sup>You yourselves bear me witness, that I said, ’I am not the Christ, but I have been sent before him.’<sup>29</sup>The one who has the bride is the bridegroom. The friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom’s voice. Therefore this joy of mine is now complete.<sup>30</sup>He must increase, but I must decrease.”<sup>31</sup>He who comes from above is above all. He who is of the earth belongs to the earth and speaks in an earthly way. He who comes from heaven is above all.<sup>32</sup>He bears witness to what he has seen and heard, yet no one receives his testimony.<sup>33</sup>Whoever receives his testimony sets his seal to this, that God is true.<sup>34</sup>For he whom God has sent utters the words of God, for he gives the Spirit without measure.<sup>35</sup>The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand.<sup>36</sup>Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever does not obey the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him.
3.overview:
Nicodemus, a Pharisee on the ruling council, comes to Jesus at night with a compliment, and Jesus answers that no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again, or born from above (the Greek word means both). This birth is of water and the Spirit, the cleansing and new heart God promised through Ezekiel, and it is as free and unmanageable as the wind. The Son of Man must be lifted up as Moses lifted up the bronze serpent, so that whoever believes may have eternal life, because God so loved the world that he gave his only Son.

Those who refuse him are condemned already, because they love the darkness. In the second half of the chapter John the Baptist, told that everyone is going to Jesus, rejoices like the bridegroom’s friend. The chapter ends with the choice that runs through the whole Gospel: eternal life for whoever believes in the Son, and God’s wrath remaining on whoever will not obey him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–42 — The Woman at the Well
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the road through Samaria Jesus rests at noon by Jacob’s well and asks a Samaritan woman for a drink. He offers her living water that becomes a spring of eternal life, then brings up her husbands, answers her question about the right mountain for worship, and tells her that he is the Messiah. She leaves her jar and brings her town, while Jesus tells his puzzled disciples that his food is to do his Father’s will and that the fields are already ripe for harvest. Many Samaritans believe, and confess him as the Saviour of the world.
verseByVerse.theology:
The living water Jesus offers is not a religious programme or a moral reform; it is the life that is in himself. He does not merely point to the source of life; he is the source. John himself explains the image later: the rivers of living water are the Spirit (7:38–39). So the gift at the well is the same new birth from above that Nicodemus could not grasp one chapter earlier, now pictured as a spring, which turns the one who drinks into a source.

Worship in spirit and truth is not sincerity set against ritual. It is worship enabled by God’s own Spirit and shaped by the truth, who in this Gospel is a person (14:6); so both halves are gifts, not techniques, and both are what the new covenant makes possible. And the decisive clause is that the Father is seeking such worshippers (v. 23). Worship is usually thought of as a search conducted from our end; here God is the one out looking, which is exactly what the chapter has been narrating since verse 4.
verseByVerse.examples:
Jesus begins with an ordinary need (water), moves to her deeper need (living water), brings her actual life into the conversation, and leads her to the question of worship and the identity of the Messiah. He does not condemn; he shows her the truth and stays on her side while he does it.

The five husbands need more care than they often get. John never calls this woman immoral, and a woman could not ordinarily divorce in that world, so five marriages may mean five times widowed or five times sent away. We are not told, and it matters to say so, because women have sat through sermons on this chapter and been handed a shame the passage never assigns.

Her testimony was poor by our usual standards: one fact, about herself, and a hesitant question. And the town came out. What travels is not the completeness of the account but the evidence that something has happened to the person giving it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus learned that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John (although Jesus himself did not baptize, but only his disciples),
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. John 4 sets two people side by side who could hardly be further apart. In chapter 3 Jesus spoke with Nicodemus: a man, a Jew, a respected teacher of Israel, who came by night. In chapter 4 he speaks with a Samaritan woman: a woman, an outsider, with a broken history, met at noon. Both need exactly the same gift, and only one of them goes home and tells a town. The chapter then returns to Cana, where a royal official takes Jesus at his bare word and finds his son alive. The thread through all of it is this: the Son of God crosses every barrier to find his worshippers, and the faith he looks for is faith that believes his word.

The setting. Jesus has been in Judea with his disciples, and his ministry is growing faster than John the Baptist’s (3:22–30). He now travels north to Galilee through Samaria, the hostile country that lay between, and the whole first half of the chapter happens at a single well outside the town of Sychar, under the shadow of Mount Gerizim.

The Pharisees had heard. Read this straight on from the end of chapter 3 and it stops being a bare travel note. Just before, John’s disciples came to him upset and said that all are going to Jesus. Now the same report reaches the Pharisees, who had already sent men to investigate John (1:24), and John words it with care: the Pharisees heard, and Jesus learned that they had heard. The same piece of news travels to two different sets of ears, and the reactions could not be further apart. In one camp it produces a jealousy their master refuses to share. In the other it produces surveillance.

Making and baptising more disciples than John. The news itself was numbers. Not doctrine, not a healing, not a claim he had made: a count of disciples. The reason given for the Pharisees’ attention is that Jesus was growing faster than the competition. When religious authorities begin measuring ministries by headcount, they have already confused the kingdom of God with an institution in rivalry with others. And John the Baptist had already given the only right response to the same figures: he must increase, but I must decrease (3:30).

Jesus himself did not baptise. The narrator comes back to tighten what he wrote at 3:22. There is no record anywhere in the New Testament of Jesus baptising a single person with his own hands. It removes, at a stroke, any possibility of a class of Christians who could say they had been baptised by Jesus personally. Paul saw the same danger at Corinth and was relieved to have baptised almost nobody, precisely so no one could form a party around the man who did it (1 Corinthians 1:13–17). Whatever divides the church, it was never going to be a hierarchy of who had the better officiant.

Why did he leave? Not in fear. This is a man who had recently cleared the temple courts in front of these same authorities. He goes because a collision now would be premature, and everything in this Gospel runs on an hour that has not yet come (2:4; 7:30). There is a kind of courage that consists of walking away from a fight you could win, at a moment of your own choosing, because the fight is not the point.

Does it matter who baptises me? No. The power of baptism does not lie in the minister, however gifted or famous, but in Christ, who commanded it, and in the faith of the one who is baptised into him. Jesus deliberately left the water to his disciples so that no one would treasure a baptism for the hand that gave it. If you were baptised as a believer by an ordinary pastor in an ordinary church, you were baptised into exactly the same name as those who were baptised by Peter or by the disciples on the Jordan. Thank God for the man who baptised you, but do not boast in him.

verseByVerse.quote: he left Judea and departed again for Galilee. And he had to pass through Samaria.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He had to pass through Samaria. Samaria lay between Judea and Galilee. It is often said that strict Jews travelled round it, down the Jordan valley through Perea and up again, to avoid contact with Samaritans, though Josephus says Galilean pilgrims usually took the direct route, which took about three days. So the road through Samaria was the quicker one, not the only one. When John writes that Jesus had to go this way, he is almost certainly saying more than a fact about maps.

The word of divine necessity. The word is edei, it was necessary, and this Gospel keeps using it for things that are settled in heaven. You must be born again (3:7). So must the Son of Man be lifted up (3:14). And now: he had to go through Samaria. The necessity that put him on that road is the same necessity that put him on the cross. There was a woman, and a town, that the Father had prepared to hear him.

The whole chapter is an appointment. A woman is going to walk out to a well at the hottest hour of the day, on an errand she has run a thousand times, and find that the shortest route between Judea and Galilee has been redrawn in heaven so that a tired man would be sitting on the wall when she arrived.

Who were the Samaritans? Their neighbours called them half-breeds and heretics, which is how enemies describe each other rather than a neutral account. When Assyria destroyed the northern kingdom in 722 BC it deported the leading families and resettled foreigners in the land, and the population that resulted was mixed in blood and in religion (2 Kings 17:24–41). By Jesus’ day they held to the five books of Moses and nothing else, no prophets and no psalms, and they worshipped on Mount Gerizim rather than in Jerusalem. The hostility had recent history in it: in the late second century BC the Jewish ruler John Hyrcanus marched north and destroyed the Samaritan temple on Gerizim. Its ruins stood on the mountain above the well.

Does every detour in my life have a purpose like this? This verse does not promise that every closed door has a well and a waiting woman behind it, or that you will be told the reason. It does say that the God who arranges routes is not confined to the ones that look sensible, and that at least once in history the pointless-looking detour was the whole plan. Scripture says more broadly that God works all things together for good for those who love him (Romans 8:28). So hold your detours with open hands. You may never see the reason this side of glory, but you are not on the road by accident.

For worship. The Son did not drift into Samaria. He was sent there by the same love that sent him into the world. Long before the woman left her house that morning, the Father had set her name on his Son’s road, and the Son walked it gladly, though his own people avoided it. That is the God we worship: not one who waits behind a wall for the clean and the qualified, but one who must go through Samaria, because he will not leave his sheep in enemy country.
verseByVerse.note: Samaria lay between Judea and Galilee. Many Jews travelled round it by the Jordan valley; the direct route went through it.

parallels.desc: Philip preaches in Samaria

verseByVerse.quote: So he came to a town of Samaria called Sychar, near the field that Jacob had given to his son Joseph. Jacob's well was there; so Jesus, wearied as he was from his journey, was sitting beside the well. It was about the sixth hour.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A town of Samaria called Sychar. Probably near ancient Shechem, at the foot of Mount Gerizim, close to the modern city of Nablus.

Jacob’s field. The geography is thick with covenant memory, and John names Jacob twice in two verses. This is the field Jacob bought outside Shechem when he came back from Paddan-aram, one of the only pieces of the promised land a patriarch ever owned outright (Genesis 33:18–20). It is the plot he willed to Joseph (Genesis 48:22), and it is where Joseph’s bones were finally buried after being carried out of Egypt and round the wilderness for forty years (Joshua 24:32). It is where Israel stood and swore that they would serve the LORD (Joshua 24), and where the kingdom tore in half a few generations later (1 Kings 12). There is hardly a square yard of ground in Israel more layered with promise, oath-taking and failure, and it is in Samaria, in enemy country.
