Jacob’s well was there. Jacob’s well is still shown near Shechem at the foot of Gerizim, one of the most certainly identified sites in the Gospels. It goes down more than a hundred feet through rock. Somebody had to lower a vessel all that way and haul it up, day after day, for as long as the family lasted.

Wearied. The verb means worn out by labour, the exhaustion that comes from work rather than lack of sleep. He is truly human: tired here, thirsty in verse 7, and hungry, as the disciples’ errand implies (v. 8). The Word made flesh (1:14) gets tired. This is the Gospel that opened by saying all things were made through him (1:3). Four chapters in, he is too worn out to walk on and has to sit down. The two facts are placed in the same book by the same author without any sense that they need reconciling, and any account of Christ that finds one of them embarrassing has stopped reading somewhere. The one who made the stars sat down because his legs ached.

Beside the well. Literally on the well, on the low stone wall around its mouth. A Jewish traveller has sat down on the wall of a Samaritan well with nothing to draw with.

The sixth hour. Noon, by Jewish reckoning: the sun overhead, the worst part of the day to be walking and the worst part of the day to be fetching water. Women usually drew water in the cool of the morning or evening, and together. A woman coming alone at noon was probably avoiding the others, though John does not say so, and we should hold that guess lightly.

From this well to the cross. There is a line running from this well to the end of the book. The man sitting here with no bucket is about to offer a stranger water that ends thirst for ever. Fifteen chapters later he will hang on a cross, and almost the last thing he says before it is finished is I thirst (19:28). He ended thirsty. That is how the offer was paid for.

Was Jesus really tired, if he was God? Yes. The eternal Son took to himself a true body and a reasonable soul (the Westminster Shorter Catechism, Q. 22), with the common weaknesses of our nature, yet without sin (the Westminster Confession 8.2; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 8.2), and in that nature he truly grew weary, hungry and thirsty. His divine nature did not become tired, and it was not turned into something less than God; but the person who sat on the well was the Son of God, and his weariness was his own. This is not a weakness in the gospel. It is its glory. A Saviour who only seemed human could not stand in our place, and he could not sympathise with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15).

On a Tuesday. A word to the reader who is simply tired. Not spiritually dry: tired, the kind where the body has stopped cooperating and the day still has eight hours in it. There is no rebuke here and no instruction to push through. The Son of God sat down on a wall in the heat because he could not go on, and the most important conversation in the chapter happened while he was in that condition. Being exhausted is not a lapse in discipleship, and God is not obliged to wait until you are at your best. Sit down if you must, and let him use you there.
verseByVerse.note: Jacob’s well is still shown near Shechem (modern Nablus) at the foot of Mount Gerizim. The ESV notes that the sixth hour was about noon — the heat of the day.

parallels.desc: Jacob buys land at Shechem
Joseph buried there

verseByVerse.quote: A woman from Samaria came to draw water. Jesus said to her, "Give me a drink."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A woman from Samaria. Alone, at noon, and unnamed. John never tells us her name, and she becomes one of the most remembered people in the Bible.

Give me a drink. Count what is wrong with this scene by the standards of the day, because the list is longer than we feel it. He is a man, alone, speaking to a woman, alone, in an isolated place. Rabbinic caution about this was severe; there were teachers who held that a man should not greet a woman in public. He is a Jew asking a Samaritan for water, which raises a question of ritual cleanness that she will name herself, since the vessel is hers and strict Jews regarded Samaritan vessels as unclean. And he is asking a favour of somebody with nothing, which is not how benefactors behave. He breaks three barriers, sex, race and religion, in four words, and offers no explanation for any of it.

He begins by asking. The first thing the Son of God says to this woman is a request for help. For the length of one sentence he hands her the position of the one who has something the other needs. She is not approached as a case, or a project, or a problem to be addressed. She is approached as the person by the well with the rope.

It was not a technique. A favour asked in order to open a conversation is a manoeuvre, and people can smell it. He was genuinely thirsty. He had walked since morning and had nothing to draw with. The request was true, and being true, it did what no strategy could have done.

What he did not open with. Not her history, which he already knew in full. Not her theology, which was defective. Not her nationality. Every one of those comes up later in the conversation, and not one of them is the doorway.

How do I start a conversation about Christ without it feeling artificial? Begin where Jesus began: with honesty and ordinary common ground. Nearly all our discomfort comes from arriving as the one with all the answers, which sets up a transaction where one party is deficient and both know it. This conversation starts from the other end. The most common ground between two human beings is not that one is right; it is that both need things. Be genuinely interested in the person, accept their help when you need it, and let real questions come. Do not hide that you are a Christian, and do not force the subject; pray for the moment and take it when it comes, as Jesus does in verse 10.

On a Tuesday. Who is on the other side of a line from you: the neighbour of another religion, the colleague whose politics you dislike, the person whose life is visibly in a mess? Ask one of them for something today, a recommendation, an opinion, a bit of help, and mean it.
verseByVerse.note: A Jewish teacher would not normally speak with a woman in public, still less a Samaritan.

parallels.desc: meetings at a well

verseByVerse.quote: (For his disciples had gone away into the city to buy food.) The Samaritan woman said to him, "How is it that you, a Jew, ask for a drink from me, a woman of Samaria?" (For Jews have no dealings with Samaritans.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples had gone. So Jesus was alone, and the conversation private. That absence is providential. And there is a small sign in the bracket: a party of Jewish men buying food in a Samaritan town is already looser about boundaries than the custom.

How is it that you, a Jew, ask for a drink from me, a woman of Samaria? Her reply is not a rebuff and it is not bitterness. It is astonishment, and it is worth hearing the arithmetic in it: you, a Jew; me, a woman of Samaria. She names both barriers in one breath, in the order that puts the greatest distance between them. She has spent her life on the wrong side of a line she did not draw, and here is somebody standing on the other side of it asking for a drink.

No dealings. John explains the situation twice in two verses, in two brackets, because he is writing for readers who would not otherwise follow. The verb may be narrower than the English: some understand it as do not use vessels in common with Samaritans, which would fit the scene exactly. A Samaritan woman was regarded by strict opinion as unclean, and so was anything she handled. If that is the sense, her surprise is precise: not that a Jew has spoken to her, but that he proposes to drink from her jar. Hatred ran deep on both sides; Samaritan villagers would later refuse to receive Jesus because he was going to Jerusalem, and James and John wanted to call down fire on them (Luke 9:52–54).

The crack through which grace enters. Contempt she could have handled. Contempt is familiar, and there are ways of standing that absorb it. What she has no defence against is a Jewish man asking her for a favour. The wall she had braced herself against did not arrive, the bracing is doing nothing, and she is off balance and talking. Many people outside the faith already know what they expect from Christians; they have an idea of the disapproval and have arranged themselves against it. The single most disarming thing available is not a better argument. It is the disapproval failing to turn up.

Does this mean Christ does not care about truth, only about kindness? No. In a few verses he will tell her plainly that the Samaritans worship what they do not know (v. 22). He crosses the barrier of contempt, not the barrier of truth. What he refuses is the hatred, the ritual separation and the assumption that she is beneath him. What he never gives up is the truth about God and about her life. The church needs both: no wall of contempt around itself, and no blurring of the gospel. Love that hides the truth is not love, and truth spoken with contempt is rarely heard.

For worship. Christ is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility (Ephesians 2:14). It began here, at a well, with a cup. The hostility of centuries between Jew and Samaritan, and between every people and every other, met a man who would not keep it. He went to the cross to make one new people out of enemies, and every church where former enemies share the Lord’s Table is a monument to what he began beside Jacob’s well.
verseByVerse.note: Samaritans were a mixed people descended from Israelites and settlers brought in by Assyria; Jews and Samaritans had centuries of hostility. The ESV notes that the last sentence may mean Jews did not share vessels with Samaritans.

parallels.desc: the settling of Samaria

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered her, "If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that is saying to you, 'Give me a drink,' you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you knew the gift of God. God’s gift: eternal life, the Spirit, Christ himself (3:16; Romans 6:23). A gift is free. It cannot be earned, bartered or bought.

Who it is. Two ignorances are named here. She does not know what is on offer, and she does not know who is offering it. The second is the one that matters, because a gift is only as good as the giver is able, and she is looking at a tired man with no bucket. The theme of the whole conversation is who Jesus is.

You would have asked him. That is all. Not you would have qualified, or made amends first, or got the mountain question right. The only thing standing between this woman and living water, on Jesus’ own account, is that it had not occurred to her to ask, and it had not occurred to her because she did not know who she was talking to. Her difficulty is not that she is unworthy; her history is about to be laid out and it changes nothing. It is not that she is a Samaritan; that barrier has already been crossed. Ignorance, not unworthiness, is what keeps her poor. And he does not lecture her about it. He tells her, in stages, until she asks.

Living water. The roles reverse: the one asking for water is the one who gives it. Living water (hudōr zōn) had an ordinary meaning before it had a spiritual one. It meant running water, a spring or a stream, as opposed to the still, stored water of a cistern or a well. It was the better water, the kind everyone preferred. So she hears a claim about plumbing: this stranger with no rope is offering fresh spring water in place of Jacob’s standing well. She is not being dull. She hears the plain sense of the word, exactly as Nicodemus heard the plain sense of born again.

What is the living water? In the Old Testament God himself is the fountain of living waters, whom his people forsook for broken cisterns (Jeremiah 2:13; 17:13). Living water pictures the life and the Spirit that God pours out on his people (Isaiah 44:3; 55:1; Ezekiel 47; Zechariah 14:8). And John tells us in so many words what Jesus means: standing in the temple at the feast, Jesus promises rivers of living water to whoever believes, and John adds that he said this about the Spirit (7:37–39). The gift at the well is nothing less than the Spirit of God dwelling in a person, the same new birth from above that Nicodemus could not grasp, now pictured as a spring. For you, it means that God himself comes to live in you, and from the inside he gives you a new love for him, an understanding of his word and the power to turn from sin (Ezekiel 36:27; Galatians 5:22–23). And Jesus gives the Spirit; he is the fountain.

Then why do so few people ask? Because they do not know the gift or the giver. Many people who stay away from Christ are not refusing living water; they think they are refusing a set of rules, a dull institution or a moral lecture. That is why Christian witness must keep pointing to who Jesus is and what he gives. When people truly see him, the asking follows.
verseByVerse.note: “Living water” normally meant fresh, flowing water from a spring, as opposed to still water in a cistern.

parallels.desc: the fountain of living waters

verseByVerse.quote: The woman said to him, "Sir, you have nothing to draw water with, and the well is deep. Where do you get that living water? Are you greater than our father Jacob? He gave us the well and drank from it himself, as did his sons and his livestock."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nothing to draw water with. Travellers carried a leather bucket and a rope; Jesus had none, and the well is deep. Her objections are perfectly sensible, the objections of a competent person stating the facts to a man who appears not to have noticed them. She takes him literally, as Nicodemus did (3:4).

Our father Jacob. The possessive is the interesting word. The Samaritans traced themselves to Joseph and claimed the patriarchs as their own, which Jews disputed. In one phrase she has half crossed the boundary she raised two verses earlier: whatever else divides them, they have the same forefather, and she is standing on his land.

Are you greater than our father Jacob? An ironic question, expecting the answer no. The answer is yes. Jacob gave a well; Jesus gives living water. Jacob dreamed of a ladder between heaven and earth; Jesus is the ladder (1:51). John loves this kind of irony. It is exactly the shape of the question the crowd will ask about Abraham in chapter 8, to which Jesus answers that before Abraham was, I am (8:53–58). The Gospel keeps putting the true answer in the mouths of people who mean it as an impossibility. Jacob dug a hole, and it was a good hole, and his descendants were still drawing from it nearly two thousand years later. The man she is talking to made the water.

Her literalism is the staircase. He does not correct her about the bucket, and he does not answer the question about Jacob for another fourteen verses, when he answers it far more fully than she asked. He takes the practical difficulty she has raised and uses it as the next step up.

What do I do with objections that seem to miss the point? Take them seriously, as Jesus does. A question that sounds naive or off-target is very often the real question, held at the only end the person can currently reach. Do not mock it or brush past it. Answer honestly what can be answered, and then use it, as Jesus does, to lift the conversation toward who he is. Patient, respectful answers to plain questions have led more people to Christ than clever arguments.
verseByVerse.note: The well is deep — said to be over 100 feet.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "Everyone who drinks of this water will be thirsty again."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thirsty again. It is a strange thing to say to a woman with a jar in her hand, mild in sound and total in reach. It is not a complaint about Jacob’s water; it is a statement about the mechanism, not the quality.

It is simply true. Every good thing available to a human being works on the same cycle: it satisfies, the satisfaction wears off, and the need returns at full strength and slightly sooner than last time. The meal, the holiday, the promotion, the applause, the relationship. None of them fails. They all work exactly as advertised, and then they stop working, and the stopping is not a fault in them. The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing (Ecclesiastes 1:8). Human beings have a thirst no earthly thing can quench, because we were made for God.

Thirst is not the sin. Say it plainly to the reader who keeps going back to the same well and hates himself for it, whether the well is a bottle, a screen, a person he should have stopped calling, or the approval of someone whose opinion he cannot get out from under. The verse does not rebuke the thirst. Thirst is a design feature; the ache is not evidence that something has gone wrong with you. What the verse says is that the well you keep returning to has never once promised what you keep arriving with. It gives what it has. It gives it every time. And the interval between drinks gets shorter, which is the mechanism of every addiction there has ever been.

He does not despise the well. He asked for a drink from it six verses ago. There is nothing in this chapter against ordinary water, ordinary marriage, ordinary bread. The problem was never that people love good things too much. It is that they ask of them what they were never built to carry.

If I am a Christian, should earthly pleasures stop satisfying me? They should satisfy you more truly, not less, because you no longer need them to be God. A Christian can enjoy a meal, a friendship or a holiday as a gift from the Father, give thanks, and let it go when it ends, because his soul is not hanging on it. What changes is not that the gifts taste of nothing, but that their running out is no longer a disaster. The danger comes when we start asking a gift to do what only the Giver can do.

On a Tuesday. You need no spiritual vocabulary for this. Take the thing you were most sure would settle you, the thing you honestly believed five or ten years ago would mean you had arrived. Suppose you got it. Did the wanting stop, or did it change address? That is not cynicism about good gifts. It is evidence, gathered from your own life, about what kind of creature you are. Name the well you keep going back to, and bring that thirst to Christ.

For worship. God did not make us small enough to be filled by the world. He made us for himself, as Augustine confessed, and nothing less than himself will ever fill us. When we had forsaken the fountain and dug cisterns that hold no water, he did not leave us with our broken jars. He came himself to the well, sat down beside the old water that always runs out, and offered us the fountain again. Every ache that returns after the last drink is a signpost, and the Son of God stands where it points, holding out himself.

verseByVerse.quote: "'but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again. The water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life.' The woman said to him, 'Sir, give me this water, so that I will not be thirsty or have to come here to draw water.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Never be thirsty. Never: a strong double negative in the Greek, never, ever. It is not a mild reassurance. It is a door closing on the whole cycle of drinking and thirsting again. The deepest thirst of the soul, for God himself, is satisfied for ever.

A spring of water. Then the image changes in a way that should stop the reader, because it stops being about drinking at all. He does not say the water will keep her topped up, or that she may come back whenever she runs low. He says the water he gives becomes in him a spring. The one who drinks becomes a source. That is the difference between a well and a spring. A well is a hole where water is stored; it has to be gone to, lowered into, hauled out of, and it is finite. A spring is water arriving from underneath, under its own pressure. The picture is not of a reservoir carefully managed. It is of something that will not stay down.

Welling up. The word (hallomenou) means leaping, springing up; it is used of the lame man leaping in the temple (Acts 3:8). This is the life of the Holy Spirit within the believer (7:38–39), an inner source of life that never runs dry, rising toward its goal: eternal life.

In the flow. Verses 13 and 14 answer her question of verse 12: instead of simply saying yes, he compares the two waters, and the comparison is the answer. Her request in verse 15 then sets up the sharp turn of verse 16: she has asked for the water, and now he must show her how thirsty she really is.

Sir, give me this water. She asks, but still misunderstands. She wants to be spared the daily trip to the well, and perhaps the shame of coming alone at noon. She has heard an offer she does not understand and asked for it anyway, which is more than Nicodemus managed with a far better education. Her theology is wrong and her hand is out. In this Gospel that combination does considerably better than the reverse.

He does not correct her yet. Jesus could have said: you have misheard me; let me define my terms. He lets her ask for the right thing for the wrong reason and goes on. That is worth remembering for anyone tempted to withhold the gospel until a person’s motives are sorted out. No one’s motives are ever wholly sorted out; people come to Christ with a tangle of reasons, and he has never yet sent one of them away to think it over.

Why, then, do believers still thirst for God? The Psalms are full of it: as a deer pants for flowing streams, so pants my soul for you, O God (Psalm 42:1). The thirst that ends is the thirst of emptiness, the restless search for something to fill the soul. The Christian has found the spring; it is in him. But a spring is drawn on every day, and Jesus goes on inviting his own: if anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink (7:37). The longing believers feel is not the old emptiness. It is the appetite of those who have tasted and want more, and it will be fully satisfied when we see him face to face (Revelation 7:16–17).

What if I feel dry, not like a spring at all? Feelings rise and fall; the spring is not your feelings but the Spirit himself, and he does not leave the believer (14:16). Dry seasons come to all God’s children, through tiredness, sorrow, sin or simply God’s wise testing. In them, keep to the means by which the Spirit refreshes his people: his word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper, the fellowship of the church. Confess any sin you know of. And keep asking. The promise does not depend on how full you feel today, but on the faithfulness of the one who gave it.

On a Tuesday. If you belong to Christ, the source is already inside you. Begin the day not by hauling up your own resources but by asking the Spirit to rise in you: for patience with the children, for words at work, for joy in a dull task. Then let it overflow to someone else.

parallels.desc: like a spring of water whose waters do not fail

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "Go, call your husband, and come here." The woman answered him, "I have no husband." Jesus said to her, "You are right in saying, 'I have no husband';"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Go, call your husband. The turn is so abrupt that it is worth asking why he makes it. They have been talking about water and eternal life; she has just asked for the gift. Instead of giving it, he says: go and fetch your husband. It is not a change of subject. It is the point at which the conversation stops being about a subject at all. Everything up to here could be had in the abstract: thirst in general, life in general, a gift available to whoever wants one. The moment he mentions her husband, the conversation acquires a particular person with a particular history, and it can no longer be conducted at a safe distance. She cannot receive living water without facing her thirst, and her sin. Jesus goes straight to the wound.

Where the difficulty lies. It is not hard to be interested in Christianity. Many people read about it, find it beautiful, and are never once cornered by it, because the whole thing is conducted in the third person. The sentence that changes the temperature is never a doctrine. It is always something like go, call your husband: a request that cannot be answered without bringing one’s actual life into the room.

I have no husband. Four words that are entirely true and are being used to hide something. It is not a lie. It is an accurate sentence deployed as a wall, a half-truth to close the subject.

You are right. He does not knock the wall down. He agrees with it, and then, in the next breath, says the thing the wall was built to keep out. He takes her words and hands them back with the rest of the sentence attached. He begins with what she got right. Most exposure in human hands leads with the discrepancy; this leads with the accuracy and lets the discrepancy follow. The difference in effect is enormous. It is the difference between a person being caught out and a person being told the truth by somebody who is plainly on their side.

Why does Christ bring up my sin if salvation is a free gift? Because the gift is for sinners, and no one drinks who will not admit they are thirsty. Jesus does not raise her history to make her earn the water, but so that she will know he is offering it to her, the real woman, and not to an idealised version of her. A gospel that never touches your actual life cannot save your actual life. Repentance is not a price paid for grace; it is the hand opening to receive it. When Christ puts his finger on something, it is because he means to heal it.

On a Tuesday. Is there a question you are keeping Christ from asking, a subject you steer around in prayer the way she steered around her household? Name it to him today; he raises it only to heal it. And when you have to speak truth to someone else, begin, as he did, with what is true in what they have said.

verseByVerse.quote: "for you have had five husbands, and the one you now have is not your husband. What you have said is true."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You have had five husbands. Jesus knows everything about her (2:25). He had never met her and he knows every year, every name, every ending. Whether through death or divorce, she has had five marriages. In that culture a woman could not ordinarily divorce her husband, while a husband could dismiss a wife for very little. So five marriages behind her may mean five times widowed, or five times sent away, or some mixture: a life of things done to her at least as much as things done by her, perhaps rejected over and over. Some rabbinic opinion, recorded in later writings, held that a woman should not marry more than two or three times.

Not your husband. She was living with a man without marriage. This is the one irregularity Jesus names outright, and it is a real one: the present arrangement is not a marriage in God’s sight. That may be why she came to the well alone at noon.

How much do we actually know? It is worth being honest about how much the text supplies, because a great deal has been built on very little. John never calls this woman immoral, and Jesus never tells her, as he tells the man at the pool, to sin no more (5:14). The town listens to her and comes out at her word (vv. 29–30, 39), which is not how a town treats a woman it has entirely cast out. There are women who have sat through sermons on this chapter and heard themselves described, divorced not by their choosing, widowed young, or long ago abandoned, and been handed a shame the passage never assigns. What the passage does assign is this: Jesus knew every year of her history before she said a word, asked her for a drink anyway, gave her the plainest statement of his identity in the Gospels, and sent her back to tell her town who he was.

Are the five husbands a symbol? Some have read them as an allegory: Assyria resettled Samaria with people from five foreign cities, each bringing their own gods (2 Kings 17:24–31), so the five husbands stand for false worships and the sixth for corrupt Samaritan religion. It is ingenious, but John gives no hint of it, the numbers do not work cleanly, and above all it dissolves a real woman into a symbol, which is the very thing this passage refuses to do to her. She is not a diagram of Samaria. She is somebody with five marriages behind her and a man in the house now, standing in the heat with a jar.

What you have said is true. Jesus exposes her, but without contempt. He does not condemn or lecture. He simply tells the truth, and in telling it shows her that he knows her completely and is still speaking to her. That is total knowledge joined to total gentleness. The gentleness is not softness about sin. The one speaking is the holy God in human flesh, whose eyes are too pure to look on evil (Habakkuk 1:13), and the wonder is that holiness so pure came close enough to ask her for a cup.

What if I am living in a situation like hers? Then hear both halves of this verse. Christ knows your situation completely, and he does not pretend it is right: living together outside marriage is not what God designed, and he calls you out of it, into marriage or into chastity. But he says it while offering you living water, not while slamming a door. Come to him as you are; he will not send you away. Talk honestly with a pastor about the steps to take. And if your story is one of being left, widowed or divorced against your will, know that this verse does not lay at your feet a shame that belongs to others.

For worship. Five marriages had ended, and the man in the house now had not married her. Then, at a well, the kind of place where Abraham’s servant found a bride for Isaac and Jacob first met Rachel, she met the Bridegroom whom John the Baptist had just named (3:29), and he came to give, not to take. He knew the whole history before she spoke, and it did not alter the offer by a drop. The Lord who searches the heart is the Lord who died for what he finds there: no one else knows us so completely and loves us still.

parallels.desc: he knew what was in man

verseByVerse.quote: The woman said to him, "Sir, I perceive that you are a prophet. Our fathers worshiped on this mountain, but you say that in Jerusalem is the place where people ought to worship."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A prophet. Only a prophet could know such things. Her understanding is growing: from a Jew (v. 9), to sir (v. 11), to a prophet, and soon to the Christ (v. 29).

This mountain. It is Mount Gerizim, which rose directly above the well; she could have pointed at it as she spoke. Its history is layered. It is where Israel was told to stand to pronounce the blessings when they entered the land (Deuteronomy 11:29; 27:12), and the Samaritans’ whole case rested on that; their own copy of the law of Moses even named Gerizim as the place for the altar. And on its summit lay the rubble of their temple, torn down by John Hyrcanus. So the disagreement she raises is not a seminar topic. It is a ruin she can see from where she is standing, and the people who made it are the people this man belongs to.

But you say Jerusalem. The great dispute between Jews and Samaritans. Is she changing the subject to avoid her sin? Both readings are available, and the honest thing is to hold them together, because the same words can be spoken by two very different people.

It may be deflection. It has all the marks. A man has just named the most painful arrangement in her life, and within one sentence she is discussing comparative religion. Anyone who has tried to talk to a friend about something real knows the manoeuvre: the sudden availability of a large, interesting, impersonal question at exactly the moment the small personal one became unbearable. Religion is uncommonly good for this. There is always a doctrine to argue about, and arguing is a great deal easier than being known.

It may be entirely genuine. Here is a woman whose life has gone wrong in the place where people look hardest for happiness, standing in front of somebody who has just proved he can see. If she has ever wanted to know where God can be found, where a sinner should go to offer sacrifice and find forgiveness, this may be the only chance she will ever get, and she takes it with the first question that comes.

Jesus does not force a verdict. He answers the question. He does not say, we were talking about your husband. He takes what she asks and gives her the fullest teaching on worship in the Gospels, which is what he would do if it were sincere, and is also the only thing that would ever have helped if it were not. And he is about to tell her that the argument is over, and that neither side won it.

What should I do when someone turns a personal conversation into a religious debate? Answer the question briefly and honestly, as Jesus does, and then bring it back to the person and to Christ. Do not get drawn into a long argument about church history, other religions or the hypocrisy of Christians while the real matter waits. You might say: that is a fair question, and here is a short answer; but can I ask what you make of Jesus himself? Most debates of this kind are not won by winning them.

On a Tuesday. When you are the one changing the subject, when God puts his finger on something and you find yourself suddenly fascinated by an interesting theological question, notice it. Stop, and go back to what he was saying to you.
verseByVerse.note: “This mountain” is Mount Gerizim, where the Samaritans worshipped; a Samaritan temple had stood there until the Jews destroyed it more than a century before.

parallels.desc: the blessing on Mount Gerizim
the place the LORD will choose

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "Woman, believe me, the hour is coming when neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem will you worship the Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woman, believe me. A solemn and respectful address, the same he used to his mother at Cana and will use to her from the cross (2:4; 19:26). In English it lands cold; in that setting it is formal and courteous, and he speaks to a Samaritan at a well in exactly the register in which he speaks to his own mother. And believe me is a direct request for trust, as one person to another, before he says the thing that will cost her her side of the argument.

The hour is coming. The new age Jesus is bringing through his death and resurrection. In John the hour is always tied to his glorification (12:23; 17:1) and to the gift of the Spirit.

Neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem. The scale of this is easy to miss because it is so calmly put. Neither mountain. Not your mountain is wrong and ours is right, which was the whole content of the dispute, and half of which he is about to say. Neither. The argument is not going to be settled. It is going to be made obsolete. Jesus himself is the new temple (2:19–21), and after his resurrection God can be worshipped anywhere, through him. Within about forty years the Jerusalem temple would be rubble too, in AD 70, as the one on Gerizim already was.

The Father. The first time in this conversation he uses the name. She asked where people ought to worship; he answers by telling her who it is that is worshipped, and the name he chooses is the family one. Worship in the new age is the worship of children.

In the flow. Jesus’ answer to the question of verse 20 starts here, and verses 21 to 24 move in three steps: neither mountain (v. 21); salvation from the Jews and an hour that has already come (vv. 22–23); and the reason, that God is spirit (v. 24). All of it drives toward verse 26, where the one who brings that hour names himself. In the Gospel as a whole it belongs to a larger thread: Jesus fulfils and replaces the temple (2:19–21), and then the great feasts of Israel in chapters 5 to 10.

The end of holy places. What is dismantled here is older than the Samaritan question: the assumption, held by most religions and sitting deep in human instinct, that God is more available in some places than others. That there is a spot, the spot has to be reached, and getting there is most of the work. It survives in people who would deny holding it: the sense that prayer counts more in a church building than in a car, that the same words weigh more before six in the morning than at eleven at night, the low-grade grief of coming home from a place where God seemed close. This verse says the mountain has been closed, and that everyone who cannot get to the holy place, the housebound, the shift worker, the mother of small children, the prisoner, has not been kept away from anything at all.

Does this mean church buildings and gathering on Sunday do not matter? Gathering matters; the place does not. Christ abolished holy geography, not the holy assembly. Believers are commanded not to neglect meeting together (Hebrews 10:25), and the gathered church is where the word is preached and the Supper shared. But the building is a roof, not a temple. God is not more present in the sanctuary than in your kitchen; he is present with his people, wherever they meet in Christ’s name. Love your church’s gathering because God’s people are there, not because the bricks are holy.

Is this not what people mean by spiritual but not religious? Only half. Jesus does abolish the holy place, but he does not make worship private or shaped by taste. In the next breath he says the Samaritans worship what they do not know, that salvation is from the Jews, and that the Father must be worshipped in truth (vv. 22–24), and in this Gospel the truth is Jesus himself (14:6). He removed the location, not the object or the way. A spirituality that builds its own picture of God has not left the mountain behind; it has built a new one inside the self, and it is just as unable to bring a sinner to the Father.

parallels.desc: in every place incense will be offered to my name

verseByVerse.quote: "You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, for salvation is from the Jews. But the hour is coming, and is now here, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for the Father is seeking such people to worship him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You worship what you do not know. One clause in these verses keeps the passage from being turned into a mere lesson in tolerance, and it should not be softened. Everything else here is so generous, the barriers down, the mountain abolished, a Samaritan woman taught by Jesus himself about worship, that it is tempting to conclude Jesus is indifferent to the disagreement. He is not. The Samaritans had cut themselves off from the prophets and writings and kept only the five books of Moses, and the result was real impoverishment: a God known in outline, a knowledge incomplete and distorted.

Salvation is from the Jews. He puts himself unmistakably on one side. He does not call Samaritan religion a different route up the same mountain. He calls it worshipping what they do not know. Jesus does not pretend all religions are equal. God revealed himself to Israel, and the Messiah came from Israel according to the flesh (Romans 9:4–5). Salvation is from the Jews, and Jesus himself is a Jew. He does not flatter her; he tells her the truth.

From, not for. The same sentence takes away any possibility of boasting. Salvation is from the Jews. The privilege was never a possession; it was a channel. Israel was the well the water came through, and a well does not congratulate itself on the water. The Jew hearing this is told his heritage is genuine and, in the same breath, where it was always headed.

And is now here. Here the chapter turns. He has already said the hour is coming (v. 21); only now does he add that it is here. Something has already begun. The new worship is not entirely future. It is beginning at this well, in this conversation, with this woman, in the presence of Jesus.

In spirit and truth. In spirit: not tied to a place, but from the heart, by the Holy Spirit, who gives new birth (3:5). In truth: according to God’s true revelation of himself, now fully given in Jesus, who is the truth (14:6). Not Samaritan worship, which lacked truth, nor merely Jewish worship tied to a temple, but worship through Christ, by the Spirit.

The Father is seeking. A wonderful statement, and every word of it is the wrong way up by ordinary religious instinct. Worship is what we do to find God; here God is the one out looking. She came to this well to fetch water and found somebody already sitting there who had come by a road his countrymen avoided. That is not an illustration of the verse; it is the verse, happening while it is spoken. Not that God needs our worship (Acts 17:25); he seeks us for our good and his glory.

Is it narrow to say other religions do not know God? It is honest, and it is what Jesus says. Many religions contain true things about right and wrong, and every person has some knowledge of God from creation and conscience (Romans 1:19–20). But saving knowledge of God comes only through his own revelation, given to Israel and fulfilled in Christ, and no one comes to the Father except through him (14:6). To say otherwise would not be kind; it would be leaving people at a dry well. And see the spirit in which Jesus says it: sitting with a Samaritan, asking for her help, offering her the gift. Truth about other faiths should always come with that kind of love.

What if I do not feel like much of a worshipper? Take heart from the last clause. You may have spent years with a low sense that the singing does not move you, that your prayers are dutiful, that others plainly have something you do not. This verse does not tell you to try harder to find God. It says the Father is out looking for worshippers. The search that matters is the one conducted from his end, and it has a far better record than ours. True worship is not measured by the strength of your feelings, but by whether you come to the Father through the Son, trusting what he has revealed.
verseByVerse.note: The Samaritans accepted only the five books of Moses.

parallels.desc: out of Zion shall go the law

verseByVerse.quote: "God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is spirit. One of the great definitions of God in John’s writings, with God is light (1 John 1:5) and God is love (1 John 4:8). Three words, and they need unpacking rather than admiring, because everyone nods at them and few could explain them to a child.

What it does not say. It does not say God is a spirit, one item in a category of ghostly beings; the point is not to classify him. It does not mean God is vague, an atmosphere, a force, or an impersonal energy behind things. The God described here talks, seeks, loves, sends, and is called Father in the same breath.

What it does say. God has no body and is not located. He is invisible, everywhere present, not confined to a mountain or a temple (1 Kings 8:27; Acts 17:24–25). He cannot be run out of or run to. He does not occupy a spot that another spot lacks. A statue can be stolen, a temple burned, a mountain captured, and Gerizim had been. None of that touches him, because he was never on it.

Must worship in spirit and truth. Must: it is necessary, because worship must match the nature of the one worshipped. If God were a local deity, worship would be a matter of arriving. Since he is not, worship is a matter of being a certain kind of person in his presence, and every person is already in his presence all the time, which is what makes this comforting and uncomfortable at once.

Not sincerity against ritual. The phrase is often misread as heartfelt against formal. That is not quite it. Spirit here is the Holy Spirit, the one Jesus described to Nicodemus as the agent of the new birth and has just pictured as a spring inside a person. Truth is not mere sincerity either; in this Gospel truth is a person before it is a quality: I am the way, and the truth, and the life (14:6). So worship in spirit and truth means worship enabled by God’s own Spirit and shaped by God’s own revelation in his Son. Both halves are gifts. Neither is a technique. And it cuts both ways. It rules out worship that is correct and dead, the right words in the right order with nobody home. And it rules out worship that is warm and invented, deeply felt and directed at a God assembled from preference. Truth without Spirit is a corpse. Spirit without truth is a mood.

Where Christians differ: how should we worship? Some traditions emphasise elaborate liturgy, ritual and visual symbols; others, free and spontaneous worship. Lutherans and Anglicans have generally held that churches may use what Scripture does not forbid; Reformed churches, that they should use only what it commands. This commentary’s view: Reformed churches have drawn from this verse, among others, what is called the regulative principle: worship should be shaped by what God has revealed in his word, not by human invention, and offered from the heart by the Spirit. External forms matter less than the heart, but worship must be true to Scripture: the reading and preaching of the word, prayer, singing, the sacraments. Held charitably toward brothers who differ in practice.

What does this mean for how a church worships? It removes sacred places, not the gathered church (Hebrews 10:25). In truth means worship shaped by what God has revealed in Scripture; the Reformed tradition has expressed this as the principle that worship should include only what God commands (the Westminster Confession 21.1; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 22.1). In spirit means worship from the heart, by the Spirit’s work. Neither rules out order or form, a planned service or a written prayer; both rule out empty ritual on one side and worship invented to please ourselves on the other.

If God is spirit, how could Jesus be God in a body? God in his own being is spirit and has no body. In the incarnation the eternal Son did not turn into matter or stop being spirit; he took a true human body and soul into union with himself (1:14). So the invisible God is seen in Jesus (1:18; 14:9). This is not a contradiction of God is spirit but the wonder of it: the God who cannot be confined to a mountain chose to dwell among us in the flesh, so that we might know him and worship him in truth.

On a Tuesday. Ask, plainly, what is left of your worship when the service is dull, the preacher is poor, the room is cold, and nothing at all is being generated for you. That residue is the part that was in spirit and truth; the rest was the building. Then ask the Spirit, who makes true worshippers, to make your worship heartfelt and true to God’s word.

verseByVerse.quote: "The woman said to him, 'I know that Messiah is coming (he who is called Christ). When he comes, he will tell us all things.' Jesus said to her, 'I who speak to you am he.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
I know that Messiah is coming. The Samaritans did not use the word Messiah as Jerusalem did. Having only the five books of Moses, they had no royal prophecies of David’s line. What they looked for came out of Deuteronomy 18:15–18: a prophet like Moses into whose mouth God would put his words. Later Samaritan writings call him the Taheb, the one who returns or the restorer.

He will tell us all things. That is what they chiefly expected: not a king who would reign, but a teacher who would settle everything, including the argument about the mountain. Which makes her sentence quietly poignant. She has been told something enormous about worship, and her response is essentially: one day somebody will come who can sort this out. Perhaps she is postponing the matter. Perhaps she is wondering. Either way she defers it all to a figure in the future, standing three feet from him.

I who speak to you am he. Literally, I am, the one speaking to you (egō eimi). It is a perfectly normal way of saying that is me, and it is also the beginning of the most loaded formula in this Gospel. Jesus will use I am of himself again and again (6:20; 8:58), and it echoes the name God gave Moses at the bush (Exodus 3:14), until in chapter 8 the crowd picks up stones.

To her, first. Hold the whole scene together, because it is an improbable arrangement of facts. He has been in Jerusalem for a feast. He has spoken with a member of the ruling council by night and told him a great deal without ever saying this. His disciples have been with him for months and are at this moment in town buying lunch. And the first time in John that Jesus himself plainly says he is the Messiah, he says it to a Samaritan woman with a broken past, alone, in the heat, with none of the disciples there. Not to the Sanhedrin. Not to Nicodemus.

Why does Jesus say so openly here what he hides elsewhere? The Samaritans expected a Messiah who would be a teacher and restorer, not a king leading a revolt. In Galilee and Judea the title would have brought crowds wanting to make him king by force (6:15). In Samaria his open claim carried less political danger, and it could be said plainly.

For worship. A whole people had waited for a prophet like Moses who would one day tell them all things, and the waiting was answered in one sentence to one woman at a well. The voice that once spoke from a burning bush, where Moses hid his face, spoke now from the wall of a well, and she did not need to hide hers. The one she had been waiting for had been waiting for her.
verseByVerse.note: The Samaritans expected a coming prophet like Moses. Jesus’ “I who speak to you am he” is literally “I am, the one speaking to you.”

verseByVerse.quote: Just then his disciples came back. They marveled that he was talking with a woman, but no one said, "What do you seek?" or, "Why are you talking with her?" So the woman left her water jar and went away into town.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They marveled. Not even that she was a Samaritan; simply a woman. Rabbis were expected to avoid talking with women in public, and some rabbinic sayings warned against it. Their surprise is the instinct of every religious person who has quietly ranked people into those worth Christ’s time and those who are not. Grace upsets the ranking, because none of us earned his time either (Romans 5:8).

The questions nobody asked. John records something that did not happen, and the wording is exact. The first is the question Jesus himself asked at the beginning of this Gospel when two men followed him: what are you seeking? (1:38). The disciples have the question available to them and do not use it, not on him and not on themselves. Whether that is reverence or awkwardness John does not say, and it is probably both. They have learned that he does things they would not have advised, and they have not yet learned to ask why.

A familiar silence. There is a way of following Christ for years while never bringing him the question that is actually there: the prayer that was not answered, the person he did not heal, the passage that troubles rather than comforts. It is possible to mistake that for reverence. This Gospel is full of people who asked him poor questions and got somewhere; it has far fewer examples of people who asked nothing. Bring your honest questions to him in prayer and to his word. He is not offended by them.

She left her water jar. A small, vivid detail. She had walked out to that well for one reason, in the heat, carrying an empty vessel, and she went back to town without it. She came for water and forgot it, because she had found living water. It is not a symbol she intended. She simply left it, the way people leave things when something has happened that makes the errand irrelevant. And there is a practical edge to it: she would have to come back for it. Whatever happened to her did not remove the daily walk, the hundred feet of rope, or the heat. It removed whatever reason she had for coming alone.

Does this show that women may teach men in the church? Her witness was an invitation, come, see a man, and her neighbours then came to Christ himself and believed because of his word (vv. 39–42). Every believer, man or woman, is to bear witness to Christ like this. The authoritative teaching of the gathered church is a different thing, which Paul reserves for qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12). This commentary holds that view because Paul grounds it in creation rather than local custom (1 Timothy 2:13), though many faithful Christians read the passage differently and deserve a respectful hearing. On any view, Christ honoured this woman’s witness, and a town came to him through it.

verseByVerse.quote: and said to the people, "Come, see a man who told me all that I ever did. Can this be the Christ?" They went out of the town and were coming to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Come, see. The woman who came to the well alone now runs to the people, with the words of Jesus and Philip on her lips (1:39, 46). She becomes an evangelist, and she evangelises her own community.

All that I ever did. Look at what her testimony consists of, because it is a remarkably poor piece of evangelism by any standard we would apply. She has one fact, and it is about herself. She overstates it, all that I ever did, when he had named her marriages and the man in her house. She cannot explain the living water, she has no doctrine of the incarnation, her view of the mountain was the Samaritan one, and he had just set it aside. And the town came out. She does not hide her past. The very thing that made her ashamed becomes her testimony. What is missing is telling: there is no and he did not despise me. She does not need to say the second half, because it is the tone of the whole sentence. Being completely known had turned out not to be the disaster she would have predicted. That is the entire content of her testimony.

Can this be the Christ? The Greek frames it as a tentative question, something nearer to this could not be the Christ, could it? She does not preach; she invites them to decide for themselves. The tentativeness may be the strength of it. A woman marching back into town with a finished doctrine would be easy to dismiss. A woman asking a question she plainly cannot answer herself, in evident agitation, having left her water jar, is harder to walk past. People argue with a conclusion. They find it harder to argue with somebody who has obviously been changed.

They were coming to him. Her testimony worked. She did not attempt to close the argument. She got people into the same field as the man, and stood out of the way.

What if I do not know enough to witness? Then you are in exactly her position, and look what God did with it. You do not need a theology degree. You need to know what Christ has done for you and where people can find him. Tell the truth about your own life, invite people to come and see, to read a Gospel, to come to church, to meet him in his word, and let him do the rest. Keep learning, of course, so that you can give a reason for your hope (1 Peter 3:15). But do not wait until you know everything. She knew one sentence, and a town came out.

On a Tuesday. Write down in one sentence what Jesus has done for you, the plainest, truest sentence you can. Then ask God for one person to say it to this week, and an invitation to add: come and see.

verseByVerse.quote: Meanwhile the disciples were urging him, saying, "Rabbi, eat." But he said to them, "I have food to eat that you do not know about."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the flow. Verses 31 to 38 fill the gap between verse 30 and verse 39: the woman has gone into town, and the people are on their way out. While the harvest is walking toward them, Jesus teaches the disciples what it is. The woman has learned that he gives life; now the disciples are to learn that giving it is what feeds him.

Rabbi, eat. They had brought food. The comedy of the scene is not accidental. A town is walking out across the fields toward Jesus because of something that happened while the disciples were shopping, and the disciples’ whole contribution to the moment is to press him about lunch.

They are being kind. He had been too tired to walk; they had gone to fetch food; they are now trying to get him to eat it. This is thoughtfulness, and it is completely blind. The largest thing that had happened all day was standing in front of them, and they were looking at a man who had not eaten. That is a fair description of a great deal of church life. The failure is rarely a failure to care. It is that the caring runs entirely along the practical grain, the rota, the building, the meal, and the thing God is doing in the room goes unremarked because nobody was looking for it there.

Food you do not know about. As with the water (v. 10), Jesus speaks of a spiritual reality and is misunderstood. It is the second time in this chapter, and the third since Nicodemus heard born again. She said water, and he answered with water that was not water. Now they say eat, and he answers with food they know nothing about. He does not reject the material thing; he takes the ordinary object already in the conversation and uses it as a handle on something the hearer has no other way of reaching. It is not evasion and it is not mysticism. It is the only way to speak about a realm people have never seen in words made for the one they have, and it is why almost everyone in this Gospel misunderstands him at first. He pays that cost in nearly every conversation, and never once sounds impatient.

Is it wrong to care about practical things in church? Not at all. Someone has to buy the bread, and the disciples were right to look after their tired Master. Practical service is honoured throughout Scripture (Acts 6:1–6). The danger is only that the practical becomes the whole of what we see. Do the rota and the catering gladly, as service to Christ, but lift your eyes while you do it. Ask, in every meeting and every task: what is God doing here, and with whom?

parallels.desc: man shall not live by bread alone

verseByVerse.quote: So the disciples said to one another, "Has anyone brought him something to eat?" Jesus said to them, "My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Has anyone brought him something to eat? Literal again. It is the most human sentence in the chapter. They are not mocking; they have concluded, reasonably, that somebody must have got there first with a basket, and they are working out the logistics.

My food. His answer redefines what has been sustaining him for the last hour. Not that he did not need food; he did, he was too tired to walk. But there is something that works in him the way food works, and he names it. His deepest satisfaction and sustenance is doing the Father’s will (Deuteronomy 8:3; Matthew 4:4). Talking to this woman had refreshed him more than food. And it is worth pressing this: the Father’s will is described as food, which is to say it feeds rather than costs. That is not how obedience usually feels. We tend to think of doing God’s will as expenditure, drawn from a limited account that has to be topped up later by rest or pleasure. Jesus describes it as intake. Much of what drives us runs the other way: we work in order to be fed, by approval, by success, by the feeling of being needed, and when the praise stops we go hungry. Jesus was fed by the Father’s will itself, so no crowd could fill him up and no rejection could empty him.

To accomplish his work. Accomplish (teleiōsō) means to complete, to finish. It is the work the Father gave him to do (5:36; 17:4), and it belongs to the same family of words as his cry from the cross: it is finished (tetelestai, 19:30). What he is doing at this well and what he does at Calvary are, on his own account, one work with a beginning and an end, and he is nourished by both.

Does this mean I am doing ministry wrongly if it exhausts me? No. The verse has sometimes been used to flog tired people, and it should not be. The man who said this had sat down earlier that day because he could not go on; both facts are in the same chapter on the same afternoon. Weariness in God’s work is normal and honourable, and rest is God’s gift, not a failure (Mark 6:31). What the verse says is that some work, whatever it takes out of the body, puts something back into the soul, and that this is the mark of work done for the Father rather than merely about him.

On a Tuesday. Compare two things you do for God: one that leaves you flat, and one that tires you and yet you would not give up. Both may be duties, and both may be right. But the difference is worth examining, because it is often the difference between a task you took on to be useful and a task the Father actually gave you. The first is a job. The second, in the vocabulary of this verse, is dinner.

For worship. The Son delighted to do his Father’s will. It was his meat and drink all the way to the cross, where he finished the work the Father gave him and cried, It is finished. There was never a moment when his obedience was grudging, and it is that perfect, glad obedience that is counted to all who trust him: God credits it to their account as if it were their own, and accepts them for its sake (Romans 5:19; 2 Corinthians 5:21). And because he finished the work, our obedience can be food too: not a wage we pay, but the joy of children doing the will of a Father who has already given us everything in his Son.

parallels.desc: having accomplished the work

verseByVerse.quote: "Do you not say, 'There are yet four months, then comes the harvest'? Look, I tell you, lift up your eyes, and see that the fields are white for harvest. Already the one who reaps is receiving wages and gathering fruit for eternal life, so that sower and reaper may rejoice together."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four months. Grain was sown in late autumn or winter and harvested in spring, and the saying may have been a proverb for the wait. Whether a saying or the actual state of the crops, the point is that harvest is the one thing in farming that cannot be hurried. Everything else can be worked at; harvest arrives when it arrives, and until then a farmer’s whole discipline is waiting. Jesus takes the one agricultural certainty about delay and cancels it.

White for harvest. Picture what he is looking at. A woman has run back to a town, and the town is coming out across open country toward the well, a straggle of people in the middle of the day, perhaps in the white robes many wore, moving through the fields (v. 30). Ripe grain turns pale, white-gold. He is not offering an image. He is pointing. The harvest of people is ready now, not in four months, walking toward you while you are asking about lunch.

Already receiving wages. The reward of gospel work is not entirely deferred; it is being handed over during the work. And the fruit is gathered for eternal life: people saved for ever. This harvest does not rot, when everything else a person spends a life gathering has a shelf life measured in decades at best.

Sower and reaper. The generous clause. In ordinary farming the reaper gets the visible result. Here it is arranged so that neither can celebrate without the other. Somebody prayed for years and saw nothing; somebody else said one sentence at the right moment and saw a town come out. In this economy those two are paid at the same table, and the joy is shared.

Does this mean everyone around me is about to believe? No. Jesus is speaking of what God was doing that day in Sychar, and elsewhere he says the labourers are few and that many will reject the word. But the verse warns us that our estimate of readiness is nearly always four months behind the actual state of the field. God has his elect in every place (Acts 18:10), and the Spirit is often at work where we see nothing. The elect are those whom God chose in Christ before the world began, and whom he will surely bring to himself (Ephesians 1:4; John 6:37). So sow widely, pray boldly, and do not write anyone off. The last people anyone expected were already on their way.
verseByVerse.note: Crops were sown in winter and harvested in spring; “four months” was roughly the gap between sowing and harvest, and the saying may have been proverbial.

parallels.desc: the ploughman shall overtake the reaper

verseByVerse.quote: "For here the saying holds true, 'One sows and another reaps.' I sent you to reap that for which you did not labor. Others have labored, and you have entered into their labor."
verseByVerse.commentary:
One sows and another reaps. A proverb, and here it holds true in a direction nobody expects: the disciples will reap a harvest prepared by others.

In the flow. These verses complete the harvest saying, and verse 39 shows it happening: a town believes because of a woman’s word, and the disciples did none of the sowing. In the Gospel as a whole it prepares them for the mission on which Jesus will send them as the Father sent him (20:21).

Others have labored. Who were the others? Samaria has a history, and Jesus is standing in the middle of it. Some of it is very old: Jacob dug the well the disciples are standing beside, Joseph’s bones are buried in the field, Moses sent Israel to that mountain to hear the blessings, and the prophets laboured for centuries. Some of it is recent: John the Baptist had been preaching not far away. And some is a matter of hours: Jesus himself, and a woman who had just gone back to her town and did all the sowing there was time for. The disciples arrive with the shopping and walk into a harvest that centuries of history and one conversation had prepared. And in Acts, Philip, and then Peter and John, would reap in Samaria what Jesus sowed here (Acts 8:4–25).

Somebody always got tired first. The word for laboured is the same root as wearied in verse 6. Every harvest anyone reaps was preceded by exhaustion the reaper did not feel and often never hears about.

Entered into their labor. Every gospel worker builds on others’ work. There is no room for pride (1 Corinthians 3:6–9). Nothing you are reaping is yours. The building was paid for by people who are dead. The doctrine you preach was fought for by people who were burned for it. The person ready to believe in front of you was worked on for years by somebody whose name you will never learn, quite possibly a grandmother who prayed, saw nothing, and died thinking she had failed.

What about the sower who never sees fruit? This is the verse for the discouraged sower: the parent who has prayed for a child for thirty years, the Sunday school teacher who watched most of a generation drift, the missionary who left with almost nothing to report. There is no promise that the sower sees it. There is a promise, one verse earlier, that when it is finally seen, he rejoices with the reaper. God does not forget any seed sown in faith; your labour in the Lord is not in vain (1 Corinthians 15:58). Keep sowing.

On a Tuesday. Name three people who sowed the gospel in you. If any are still alive, write to one of them this week and thank them. And sow faithfully today, even if others reap.

parallels.desc: cities you did not build
I planted, Apollos watered

verseByVerse.quote: Many Samaritans from that town believed in him because of the woman's testimony, "He told me all that I ever did." So when the Samaritans came to him, they asked him to stay with them, and he stayed there two days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because of the woman’s testimony. John repeats her sentence rather than summarising it, so we know exactly what carried, and it was not a doctrine of the atonement or the two natures of Christ. A town heard a woman say that he knew everything about her, and walked out across the fields to see whether it might be true of them too. What makes the gospel travel is not first the completeness of the account but the evidence that something has happened to the person giving it. Everyone in that town had known the earlier version of her.

They asked him to stay. Stay (meinai) is John’s great word abide. Samaritans asking a Jew to stay: barriers broken. And it is a larger step than believing. It is one thing to be persuaded about a man; it is another to want him in the house for two days.

Two days. A Jewish rabbi accepted the hospitality of a Samaritan town, which means he ate their food, off their plates, under their roofs, for two days. Every one of those actions carried a ritual cost in the eyes of the men he had left in Jerusalem. He had spent the morning refusing to be governed by the boundary, and now he spends two days living on the wrong side of it. Nothing in the text treats this as remarkable, and that says a great deal.

Is the later giving of the Spirit in Samaria a pattern for us? In Acts the Samaritans receive the Spirit only after the apostles come. That was a later group, and a special moment in the spread of the church, when God showed that Samaritans were fully included in the one church of the apostles (Acts 8:14–17). These Samaritans in John truly believed, knowing Jesus as the Saviour of the world. Neither passage sets up a two-stage pattern for all believers. Everyone who truly believes in Christ has the Spirit (Romans 8:9).

On a Tuesday. Ask Christ to stay: in your home, your evenings, your plans. Faith that keeps Christ at the town gate is not yet the faith of Sychar.

parallels.desc: Samaria receives the word

verseByVerse.quote: And many more believed because of his word. They said to the woman, "It is no longer because of what you said that we believe, for we have heard for ourselves, and we know that this is indeed the Savior of the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because of his word. Testimony brings people to Jesus; his word brings them to faith.

No longer because of what you said. Not an insult. They are describing the only journey that ever ends anywhere, from someone else’s account to first-hand knowledge, and telling her, in effect, that her errand worked. A witness who is still needed after two days has not finished the job. They have heard for themselves: a personal encounter with Christ through his word, second-hand faith become first-hand.

Saviour of the world. The summit of the episode. Not only the Jewish Messiah, but the Saviour of all peoples, including Samaritans. A saviour rescues from something, and John has already named it: from the judgment that rests on everyone who does not believe, into eternal life (3:16–18, 36). The title appears in the New Testament only here and in John’s first letter (1 John 4:14). And the title had a ring in the first century: inscriptions across the empire honoured emperors as saviour and benefactor. Readers who knew that would hear a title fit for Rome given to a Jewish teacher in a Samaritan village, by Samaritans, outsiders to Israel’s hopes. Outsiders understood what insiders missed. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read the Christ, the Saviour of the world; the earliest lack the Christ, so most modern Bibles omit it.

The ironies stacked in the sentence. The people who confess him as Saviour of the world are the people a Jew would not share a cup with. They reach it in two days. The teacher of Israel in the previous chapter, with the Scriptures and the training and every advantage, could not follow a sentence about birth. And the confession comes in the one chapter where Jesus has said that salvation is from the Jews, so the outsiders are not correcting him. They are the first evidence that he was right.

Does Savior of the world mean that everyone will be saved? No. It means that Jesus is not the Saviour of Jews only but of Samaritans and Gentiles too, of all who believe, as these Samaritans did. John uses the same title in his letter (1 John 4:14), and Paul calls God the Saviour of all people, especially of those who believe (1 Timothy 4:10). The title speaks of the scope of the offer and the reach of his rule, not of universal salvation.

What if my faith is still borrowed? That is where this whole town started, and where most people start: a parent, a minister, a book. It is a good place to begin and a poor place to remain, because a second-hand faith is only as durable as the person it leans on, and people move away, disappoint and die. The remedy is the one the Samaritans found: hear him for yourself. Read the Gospels as his own words to you, pray to him directly, and sit under the preaching of his word asking him, not the preacher, to speak.

For worship. Caesar claimed the title and is dust; Christ bears it and reigns for ever. One day a great multitude no one can number will stand before his throne and cry that salvation belongs to our God and to the Lamb, and among them will be a town from Samaria and a woman whose name we never learned.

parallels.desc: the Father has sent his Son to be the Savior of the world

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 43–54 — The Official's Son: The Second Sign
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After two days Jesus goes on to Galilee, where the people welcome him because of what they saw him do in Jerusalem. At Cana a royal official from Capernaum begs him to come and heal his dying son. Jesus speaks of a faith that must see signs, then tells the man to go: his son will live. The man believes and goes, his servants meet him with the news, and the timing shows that the fever left at the hour Jesus spoke. He and his household believe. This is the second sign at Cana.
verseByVerse.theology:
The second sign shows faith that believes the word of Jesus before any visible confirmation. In this Gospel faith grows from believing because of signs, to believing his word, to believing in the crucified and risen Lord himself, and each stage is a step deeper into trust in his person.

The two Cana signs are numbered (2:11; 4:54) and the counting then stops, so the numbering ties these two together and frames everything between them: a member of the ruling council who could not follow the plainest thing, and a Samaritan woman who understood enough to fetch a town. At the wedding Jesus was present and gave instructions to servants standing there; here he is twenty miles away and only speaks. That is the position of every reader after the ascension: no touch, no visible presence, only his word, and John wrote it down so that people who were never in the room might believe (20:30–31).
verseByVerse.examples:
The official believed before he saw. Everything he came for, Jesus coming down to the house, was refused, and he went home with five words about a child who had been at the point of death when he left. That is the pattern of mature faith: not the absence of evidence, but trust in the word of the one who cannot lie, before the confirming experience comes.

His prayer was not eloquent: one sentence, repeated under pressure. It was answered at once and generously, and nothing suggests Jesus was waiting for a better-formed request. His assumption that Jesus had to be in the room is what people ask when they love somebody and are frightened, and the answer he received was not smaller than he asked. It was the same answer, delivered without the twenty miles.

verseByVerse.quote: After the two days he departed for Galilee. (For Jesus himself had testified that a prophet has no honor in his own hometown.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
No honour in his own country. There is a genuine puzzle in this bracket. The proverb says a prophet has no honour in his own country, and John then reports that Jesus went to Galilee, where the Galileans welcomed him. The reason given seems to contradict what follows.

Two solutions. The first is that his own country here means Judea, the land of his birth, and Jerusalem, where he has just been rejected: the temple authorities demanding his credentials, the Pharisees counting his disciples. On this reading the sentence explains why he left Judea. The prophet has no honour where he properly belongs, so he goes north. It also fits John’s habit of using his own for the people who should have received him and did not (1:11). The second is that the welcome in Galilee was no honour at all, and John says as much in the next verse: they welcomed him having seen what he did in Jerusalem. That is enthusiasm for a performer. A prophet is not honoured by a crowd that has come for the signs; he is merely popular, which is a different and less durable thing. The first is the more likely, since John has just shown Jesus rejected in Jerusalem and Galilee does in fact welcome him. Either way the verse does the same work. It casts a shadow over the applause before the applause arrives, so that the reader does not mistake the noise in Galilee for something better than the silence in Judea.

Being liked and being believed. They are not the same, and the first can be a considerable obstacle to the second. A church well thought of in its town, a Christian whom colleagues find pleasant company: neither is a bad thing, and neither is evidence of anything at all. The Galileans were delighted with him, and chapter 6 will show how long that lasted.

Should I expect rejection from those closest to me? Often, yes, and it should not surprise you. Jesus’ own brothers did not believe in him for a long time (7:5), and he warned that a person’s enemies may be those of his own household (Matthew 10:36). Familiarity can breed a kind of deafness: they knew you before, and find it hard to take seriously what has changed. Keep living faithfully and lovingly among them, speak when there is opportunity, and pray. Jesus’ brothers were in the upper room after the resurrection (Acts 1:14).

verseByVerse.quote: So when he came to Galilee, the Galileans welcomed him, having seen all that he had done in Jerusalem at the feast. For they too had gone to the feast.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Galileans welcomed him. Because of his signs in Jerusalem at the feast (2:23), not because of who he was. This is the sign-faith John introduced at 2:23–25: real as a beginning, insufficient as a foundation.

Set the two receptions side by side. John has arranged them to be compared, and the comparison is uncomfortable. The Samaritans had no signs; no healing or wonder is recorded in that village. They had a woman with a complicated history, one sentence about being known, and two days of listening to him, and they arrived at the Saviour of the world, believing because of his word (v. 41). The Galileans had everything else. They were his own people. They had been up to Jerusalem and seen the signs with their own eyes. They welcomed him warmly. And what they had was an appetite, which he names in a moment and which chapter 6 will test to destruction: after the bread and the fish, many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him (6:66).

What separates them. The difference is not information and it is not privilege. Both groups met the same person; one had far more evidence. What separates them is what they were looking for when they came. Spiritual sight is not proportional to religious advantage.

Warm approval with nothing underneath. This is for ourselves rather than for somebody else, because the Galileans are much the easier group to belong to. They were not sceptics or opponents. They were fans. They were pleased he had come, spoke well of him, and turned out when he was in the area. The most dangerous position in this chapter is not hostility. It is warm approval with nothing underneath it. If that question troubles you, take heart: fans do not lose sleep over whether they truly love him.
