The concern is itself a sign of life, and the remedy is not anxious self-examination but looking again at Christ.

Is it wrong to come to Jesus because of what he can do for me? It is not wrong to begin there; most of us did, and Jesus welcomed the sick, the hungry and the desperate. The problem is staying there. Faith that wants only his gifts will leave when the gifts seem to stop. Saving faith comes to rest on Christ himself, as Lord and Saviour, and trusts him even when he gives nothing visible. If you came for help, keep coming, and ask him to show you himself, until you would want him even with nothing else.

verseByVerse.quote: So he came again to Cana in Galilee, where he had made the water wine. And at Capernaum there was an official whose son was ill. When this man heard that Jesus had come from Judea to Galilee, he went to him and asked him to come down and heal his son, for he was at the point of death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cana again. The site of the first sign. This will be the second (v. 54), and John is building a frame.

In the flow. John brings the story back to where Jesus’ signs began (2:1), and sets a Jewish nobleman beside the Samaritan woman. She was not looking for Jesus at all, and he found her; this man comes looking for Jesus with an urgent request, and will be given only a word. Both stories press the question that runs through the whole chapter: will a person believe Jesus because of his word?

An official. A royal official (basilikos), probably in the service of Herod Antipas, who ruled Galilee. That places him among the leading men of the region: a court appointment, a household, servants, standing. Capernaum lies on the lakeshore; Cana is up in the hills, about twenty miles away, some thirty kilometres. In that country twenty miles is a hard day’s walk, and it is a climb.

He went to him. Take the measure of what this man does, because the distance is the point. A courtier left a dying child, travelled all day into the hills on the strength of a report that a travelling teacher had returned to the district, and begged him to come. Nothing about it is dignified, and men in his position spent a good deal of energy on dignity. What he had was a boy at the point of death, and every door his rank could open had already been opened. When a man of standing goes personally rather than sending a servant, the ordinary machinery of his life has stopped working. Wealth and position could not save his son.

Come down. The assumption is in the verb: come down. He needs Jesus present. Everything he has seen work in the world, physicians, officials, favours, requires the person to be in the room. He believes Jesus can heal, but thinks Jesus must be there. He is not lacking faith; he is exercising the only kind he has.

Is this the same as the centurion’s servant in Matthew and Luke? Probably not (Matthew 8:5–13; Luke 7:1–10). Here it is a royal official’s son, at Cana, and the man asks Jesus to come down; there it is a Gentile centurion’s servant, at Capernaum, and the centurion says he is not worthy to have Jesus come under his roof. The likeness is in the healing from a distance, which Jesus did more than once.

Is it wrong to ask God to come and be present in my crisis? Not at all. Many people pray exactly like this: Lord, be in the room at the operation, come to my son. It is what a person asks when they love somebody and are frightened, and the psalms are full of such prayers. What this story does is not rebuke the request but enlarge it. The answer, when it comes, is not smaller than he asked. It is the same answer, delivered without the twenty miles. Christ is not limited by where he is, and by his Spirit he is present with his people everywhere.

On a Tuesday. Bring your desperate needs to Jesus, as this father did. Do not send a servant, so to speak, by offering a quick and distant prayer about something that is breaking your heart. Go yourself: take time, name the person, plead with him.
verseByVerse.note: The official was probably in the service of Herod Antipas. Capernaum lay down by the lake, about 20 miles from Cana.

parallels.desc: a similar healing of a centurion’s servant

verseByVerse.quote: So Jesus said to him, "Unless you see signs and wonders you will not believe."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Unless you see signs. The you is plural, and that single grammatical fact changes the temperature of the verse. Jesus is not turning on a frantic father. He is speaking over his head to the Galileans in general (v. 45), the ones who saw the signs at the feast and came out to see whether there would be more. Faith that depends on miracles is weak faith. They want signs; the Samaritans believed his word. The father is standing in the middle of a diagnosis that is not mainly about him.

What was it for? It is a hard thing to have said in one’s hearing when one’s child is dying, and it is worth asking why Jesus said it. The clue is what happens next. Jesus does not, in the end, give this man a sign he can see. He gives him a sentence. The point of verse 48 is that the man is about to be asked to do what the crowd will not: take a word and go, with nothing in his hands. The apparent rebuke sets up the test, and Jesus is testing the official’s faith: will he believe without seeing? The father passes within two verses.

Then are miracles bad for faith? No. John records Jesus’ signs precisely so that we may believe (20:30–31), and Jesus appeals to his works as evidence (10:38; 14:11). Signs are good when they point us to Christ and lead us to trust his word. The weakness Jesus exposes is a faith that will believe only if it keeps seeing: faith in the spectacle rather than in the one who performs it. The signs were given once for all and are written down for us. We do not need fresh ones to believe; we need to believe what has been written.

On a Tuesday. There is relief here for anyone who has prayed badly under pressure. When something is genuinely at stake, the words go, the composure goes, and what is left is a single sentence repeated. This chapter records such a prayer word for word, and records that it was answered at once and generously. Nothing suggests Jesus was waiting for a better-formed request.
verseByVerse.note: The “you” here is plural — Jesus speaks to the Galileans in general.

verseByVerse.quote: The official said to him, "Sir, come down before my child dies." Jesus said to him, "Go; your son will live." The man believed the word that Jesus spoke to him and went on his way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before my child dies. It is not an argument at all. He does not defend his motives, or protest that his faith is better than that, or engage with the theology of signs. He has one thing to say and says it again. And note the word for his son. Not the formal word of verse 47. The Greek here is a diminutive, paidion: my little boy. The rank has fallen off the man entirely.

Go; your son will live. Five words, striking for what they leave out. No journey, no touch, no prayer. No condition attached, no instruction to believe, no if you have faith. Not even a gesture in the direction of Capernaum. The man asked him to come down, and Jesus declines to come down and answers anyway: just a word, from twenty miles away.

The man believed the word. He had travelled all day into the hills for one thing: to bring this man back down to the house. He is being sent home without him. Everything he came for has been refused, and what he has instead is a sentence from somebody he has only just met, about a child who was at the point of death when he left. This is the faith Jesus looks for: believing his word, without a sign.

He went on his way. He did not wait for proof. That is the miracle in this verse, and it happens before the other one is known about. He had no evidence of any kind. There was no way to send word ahead or to hear anything until he arrived, and the arriving would take the rest of that day and into the next. The whole journey home was made on the strength of five words, and every hour of it the alternative explanation was available to him: that he had been fobbed off, that he should have insisted, that a real healer would have come. This is what it looks like when a promise is the only thing in a person’s hands. Not the absence of fear, for there is no reason to think he was calm, but the willingness to act as though the word were true while everything visible is unchanged and the clock is running.

Does this mean that a parent with enough faith can secure healing for a sick child? No. This was a particular word from Jesus to this man: your son will live. We have no such word about every illness, and the faith he commends is trust in what Christ has said, not confidence that he will do what we ask. A parent whose child was not healed did not fail to believe enough. Jesus wept at the grave of a friend he loved (11:35), and his promise to his people is not that no child will die, but that whoever believes in him, though he die, yet shall he live (11:25).

What has Christ actually promised me, then? Far more than one healing. He has promised that whoever comes to him he will never cast out (6:37), that he will never leave nor forsake his people (Hebrews 13:5), that nothing can separate them from God’s love (Romans 8:38–39), that he will raise them on the last day (6:40), and that he is preparing a place for them (14:2–3). These are words as certain as the one spoken at Cana. Faith takes them and walks home on them, often long before the evidence arrives.

Is the official’s faith just wishful thinking? No. Wishful thinking trusts a feeling; this man trusted a person and a sentence, and the sentence could be checked, which is exactly what he did the next day when he asked the hour (v. 52). Faith in the Bible is not believing without reasons. It is resting on someone who has shown himself trustworthy, and staying on his word while the evidence is not yet in. Its strength lies in its object: a weak faith in a reliable Christ saves, and a strong faith in the wrong thing does not.

For worship. His word is enough. The Word who was in the beginning speaks, and it is done; he commands, and it stands fast. A father turned his back on the healer he had come to fetch and went home with nothing but a sentence, and the sentence was worth more than the visit. Every promise of Christ is made of the same stuff: the grass withers and the flower fades, but the word that sent a man down the hill from Cana stands for ever. His promise is as good as his presence.

parallels.desc: he sent out his word and healed them

verseByVerse.quote: As he was going down, his servants met him and told him that his son was recovering.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His servants met him. He is on the road to Capernaum, the next day (v. 52), and they have not waited at the house. Somebody in that household was so relieved that they set off up the road to shorten the wait by a few hours.

Recovering. Literally, was living: the very word Jesus had used. His word had come true. What they bring is not, at this stage, a miracle. It is the ordinary best news a household can send: the boy is better, the fever has turned. Nothing in their message suggests anything supernatural. They think they are reporting a recovery.

How God’s answers usually arrive. Not with a label on them. The relief comes, the door opens, the feared thing does not happen, and from outside it looks exactly like an ordinary good outcome of the kind that sometimes occurs. The father is about to ask one question that will turn a recovery into a revelation, and it is not a spiritual question. It is a matter of fact: when?

How can I tell whether something was an answer to prayer or just coincidence? Often you cannot prove it, and you do not need to. Scripture teaches that God governs all things, including the ordinary course of events (Matthew 10:29–30), so the recovery that looks natural is still his gift. But it is worth doing what this father did: go back and check. Note what you prayed for and when, and notice what happened. Over time a pattern of God’s faithfulness becomes plain. Give thanks for every mercy without needing to label it a miracle; all good gifts come from above (James 1:17).

verseByVerse.quote: So he asked them the hour when he began to get better, and they said to him, "Yesterday at the seventh hour the fever left him." The father knew that was the hour when Jesus had said to him, "Your son will live." And he himself believed, and all his household.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He asked them the hour. He wanted to confirm, and the servants’ answer settles it: yesterday at the seventh hour the fever left him. The ESV notes that the seventh hour was about 1 p.m. And one word in the servants’ answer is easy to read past: yesterday. Jesus spoke at about one in the afternoon, and Capernaum is some twenty miles away, more than an afternoon’s walk. Unless yesterday simply means after sunset, when a Jewish day began, the father spent a night on the way before he met the servants. Many have seen a quiet sign of faith in that: a man still frightened for his son would hardly have stopped. It is a likely reading rather than a certain one, but it fits what John has just told us: he believed the word and went.

That was the hour. Then the arithmetic lands. The hour the fever broke is the hour the words were spoken, twenty miles away, in a village in the hills. Nothing had touched the boy and nothing had been sent. There had been a sentence, a father walking down a road with nothing in his hands, and a fever going out of a child at that moment. Not coincidence.

He himself believed. John notes that he believed a second time. The first time (v. 50) was trust in a promise about his son. This time no object is named; he simply believed, which in this Gospel is the word for what a person does about Christ himself rather than about a request. His faith had grown from faith in a healer, to faith in his word, to full faith in Jesus.

All his household. His whole family and servants believed, the first household conversion in John (compare Acts 16:15, 34). That is not a formula and it is not a guarantee. But consider what they had to go on: a man who came home, a boy who was well, and a father who could tell them the hour.

What if my household has not believed? Then this verse must not be used to reproach you. Plenty of faithful people have households that have not followed, and Jesus himself warned that families would be divided over him (Luke 12:51–53). Salvation is God’s gift, and each person must believe for himself. What this verse does give is hope and a pattern: pray for your whole household by name, live the faith visibly before them, and tell them plainly what Christ has done. God delights to save families, and he is not finished with yours.

Does the household believing support baptising whole households, including infants? Here the household believed; John says so. That is the pattern this commentary takes throughout the New Testament: those who were baptised, or counted as believers, were those who heard and believed (Acts 16:32–34; 18:8). Our paedobaptist brothers, who baptise the infants of believers, read the household passages differently and see in them the covenant inclusion of children, and they hold that view with deep conviction and care for their children’s souls. We honour them as brothers. But this verse, at least, describes a household of believers.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the seventh hour was about 1 p.m.

parallels.desc: he believed, with his entire household

verseByVerse.quote: This was now the second sign that Jesus did when he had come from Judea to Galilee.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second sign. John counts, and the counting is deliberate. He has told us that the water made wine was the first sign (2:11), and now the second, and then he stops counting; the numbering never resumes. Its purpose seems to be to tie these two together, and they are tied at both ends: both at Cana, both after a journey north into Galilee, both ending in belief (2:11; 4:53).

A frame around the chapters. Everything between the two signs sits inside the frame. Between Cana and Cana there is a night visit from a member of the ruling council who cannot understand the plainest thing, and a midday conversation with a Samaritan woman who understands enough to fetch a town. The man with everything missed it, the woman with nothing did not, and the section closes with a royal official, probably of Herod’s court, believing on a word alone.

What changes between the first sign and the second. The first revealed his glory at a wedding; the second, his power over sickness and death at a distance. At the wedding he was present, the water was in front of him, and he gave an instruction to servants standing there. Here he is twenty miles away and does nothing but speak. The first sign needed his hands on the situation. The second needed only his voice, and the voice worked across a day’s journey as if the journey were not there. Both show that his word has creative power.

Why does this matter for me? Because this is the position of everyone who follows Christ after the ascension. We are the man on the road home: no touch, no visible presence, no sign before our eyes, only his word and a distance and the walking. The signs escalate so that the last one in this frame can be a word alone. And John says at the end of his Gospel that he wrote these signs down so that people who were never in the room might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life in his name (20:30–31). That is, so that there could go on being men and women walking home on nothing but his sentence, and finding that the fever had gone at the hour it was spoken.

For worship. Each of Jesus’ signs reveals who he is: the Lord of creation who turned water into wine, the Lord of life who drives out death with a word. The glory that shone at the wedding shone again in a sickroom he never entered. And the same voice that spoke at Cana will one day speak at every grave, and all who are in the tombs will hear it and come out. Blessed be the Word made flesh, whose word is life, and whose glory is full of grace and truth.

parallels.desc: the first sign

4.title: The Woman at the Well
4.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when Jesus learned that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John<sup>2</sup>(although Jesus himself did not baptize, but only his disciples),<sup>3</sup>he left Judea and departed again for Galilee.<sup>4</sup>And he had to pass through Samaria.<sup>5</sup>So he came to a town of Samaria called Sychar, near the field that Jacob had given to his son Joseph.<sup>6</sup>Jacob’s well was there; so Jesus, wearied as he was from his journey, was sitting beside the well. It was about the sixth hour.<sup>7</sup>A woman from Samaria came to draw water. Jesus said to her, “Give me a drink.”<sup>8</sup>(For his disciples had gone away into the city to buy food.)<sup>9</sup>The Samaritan woman said to him, “How is it that you, a Jew, ask for a drink from me, a woman of Samaria?” (For Jews have no dealings with Samaritans.)<sup>10</sup>Jesus answered her, “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that is saying to you, ’Give me a drink,’ you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.”<sup>11</sup>The woman said to him, “Sir, you have nothing to draw water with, and the well is deep. Where do you get that living water?<sup>12</sup>Are you greater than our father Jacob? He gave us the well and drank from it himself, as did his sons and his livestock.”<sup>13</sup>Jesus said to her, “Everyone who drinks of this water will be thirsty again,<sup>14</sup>but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again. The water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life.”<sup>15</sup>The woman said to him, “Sir, give me this water, so that I will not be thirsty or have to come here to draw water.”<sup>16</sup>Jesus said to her, “Go, call your husband, and come here.”<sup>17</sup>The woman answered him, “I have no husband.” Jesus said to her, “You are right in saying, ’I have no husband’;<sup>18</sup>for you have had five husbands, and the one you now have is not your husband. What you have said is true.”<sup>19</sup>The woman said to him, “Sir, I perceive that you are a prophet.<sup>20</sup>Our fathers worshiped on this mountain, but you say that in Jerusalem is the place where people ought to worship.”<sup>21</sup>Jesus said to her, “Woman, believe me, the hour is coming when neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem will you worship the Father.<sup>22</sup>You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, for salvation is from the Jews.<sup>23</sup>But the hour is coming, and is now here, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for the Father is seeking such people to worship him.<sup>24</sup>God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth.”<sup>25</sup>The woman said to him, “I know that Messiah is coming (he who is called Christ). When he comes, he will tell us all things.”<sup>26</sup>Jesus said to her, “I who speak to you am he.”<sup>27</sup>Just then his disciples came back. They marveled that he was talking with a woman, but no one said, “What do you seek?” or, “Why are you talking with her?”<sup>28</sup>So the woman left her water jar and went away into town and said to the people,<sup>29</sup>“Come, see a man who told me all that I ever did. Can this be the Christ?”<sup>30</sup>They went out of the town and were coming to him.<sup>31</sup>Meanwhile the disciples were urging him, saying, “Rabbi, eat.”<sup>32</sup>But he said to them, “I have food to eat that you do not know about.”<sup>33</sup>So the disciples said to one another, “Has anyone brought him something to eat?”<sup>34</sup>Jesus said to them, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work.<sup>35</sup>Do you not say, ’There are yet four months, then comes the harvest’? Look, I tell you, lift up your eyes, and see that the fields are white for harvest.<sup>36</sup>Already the one who reaps is receiving wages and gathering fruit for eternal life, so that sower and reaper may rejoice together.<sup>37</sup>For here the saying holds true, ’One sows and another reaps.’<sup>38</sup>I sent you to reap that for which you did not labor. Others have labored, and you have entered into their labor.”<sup>39</sup>Many Samaritans from that town believed in him because of the woman’s testimony, “He told me all that I ever did.”<sup>40</sup>So when the Samaritans came to him, they asked him to stay with them, and he stayed there two days.<sup>41</sup>And many more believed because of his word.<sup>42</sup>They said to the woman, “It is no longer because of what you said that we believe, for we have heard for ourselves, and we know that this is indeed the Savior of the world.”<sup>43</sup>After the two days he departed for Galilee.<sup>44</sup>(For Jesus himself had testified that a prophet has no honor in his own hometown.)<sup>45</sup>So when he came to Galilee, the Galileans welcomed him, having seen all that he had done in Jerusalem at the feast. For they too had gone to the feast.<sup>46</sup>So he came again to Cana in Galilee, where he had made the water wine. And at Capernaum there was an official whose son was ill.<sup>47</sup>When this man heard that Jesus had come from Judea to Galilee, he went to him and asked him to come down and heal his son, for he was at the point of death.<sup>48</sup>So Jesus said to him, “Unless you see signs and wonders you will not believe.”<sup>49</sup>The official said to him, “Sir, come down before my child dies.”<sup>50</sup>Jesus said to him, “Go; your son will live.” The man believed the word that Jesus spoke to him and went on his way.<sup>51</sup>As he was going down, his servants met him and told him that his son was recovering.<sup>52</sup>So he asked them the hour when he began to get better, and they said to him, “Yesterday at the seventh hour the fever left him.”<sup>53</sup>The father knew that was the hour when Jesus had said to him, “Your son will live.” And he himself believed, and all his household.<sup>54</sup>This was now the second sign that Jesus did when he had come from Judea to Galilee.
4.overview:
Chapter 3 showed Jesus with a respected Jewish teacher at night; chapter 4 shows him with an unnamed Samaritan woman at noon. Tired and thirsty at Jacob’s well, he asks her for a drink, crossing the barriers of race, sex and religion at once, and offers her living water, a spring of eternal life within. He gently brings her history into the light, answers her question about where to worship with the news that the Father now seeks worshippers in spirit and truth, and tells her plainly that he is the Messiah.

She leaves her water jar and brings her town, and many Samaritans believe, first through her word and then through his, and confess him as the Saviour of the world. Back in Cana a royal official begs Jesus to come and heal his dying son; Jesus only speaks, the man believes and goes, and the fever leaves at that very hour. Together the stories show the gospel crossing every boundary, and faith growing from hearing about him to trusting his word.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — The Healing at the Pool of Bethesda
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A healing at the pool of Bethesda, given to a man who did not ask and did not know who healed him, becomes a dispute about the Sabbath, and the dispute becomes the first plot against Jesus’ life. His answer, that his Father is working and so is he, is heard rightly as a claim to be equal with God.
verseByVerse.theology:
The opposition shows what Jesus was claiming. When he defends his Sabbath work by appeal to his Father’s, the leaders understand him to claim equality with God, and he does not correct them; the discourse that follows explains the claim rather than withdrawing it. Teachers of the day already agreed that God keeps working on the seventh day, giving life and judging, and Jesus goes on to claim exactly those two works (vv. 21–22).

Those who wanted him dead were not offended by his ethics; they understood him to be saying that God was his own Father in a way true of no one else.
verseByVerse.examples:
The healing shows how grace comes: the man did not ask, did not know who Jesus was, and showed no faith before he was healed.

Jesus’ question, whether he wants to be healed, speaks to anyone who long ago stopped asking God for something, and invites us to bring it to him plainly. And the mat carried through the city is a reminder that grace received is meant to be seen, not left discreetly at the pool.

verseByVerse.quote: After this there was a feast of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. Now there is in Jerusalem by the Sheep Gate a pool, in Aramaic called Bethesda, which has five roofed colonnades.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. John 5 is a turning point. A Sabbath healing, given unasked to a man with no recorded faith, leads to the first plot against Jesus’ life, because the leaders rightly hear him making himself equal with God. A man who could do nothing was made whole; the best-taught men in the nation had every witness and would not come.

A feast of the Jews. Unnamed; perhaps Pentecost, Tabernacles or Purim. John normally names the feasts, so we cannot date the chapter precisely.

By the Sheep Gate. The Sheep Gate was in the north wall, near the temple (Nehemiah 3:1), and its name suggests it was where sheep for sacrifice were brought in. The healing happens beside the gate of the sacrificial lambs, in the presence of the Lamb of God.

A pool, in Aramaic called Bethesda. The ESV notes other spellings in the manuscripts (Bethzatha, Bethsaida). Bethesda may mean house of mercy: a colonnade full of blind, lame and paralysed people waiting for water that mostly did not come. That was either the bitterest name in Jerusalem or a prophecy, and on this morning it turned out to be the second.

Which has five roofed colonnades. For a long time this description was treated as proof that the writer did not know Jerusalem: four sides need four porticoes, and no such structure was known. Then it was dug up. Excavations near the Church of St Anne uncovered a double pool north of the temple, with colonnades on the four outer sides and a fifth across the partition between them, though details of the layout are still debated. The writer knew the city in a detail that was later lost. That does not prove the miracle, and it should not be overstated, but it removes a confident objection. And has is present tense, which may suggest John wrote before AD 70, or may simply describe the scene vividly.

Does archaeology prove the Bible true? It cannot prove the miracles or the gospel; those rest on the testimony of God in his word, received by faith through the Spirit. But archaeology has again and again confirmed the Bible’s places, names and details, and has often embarrassed confident critics, as it did here. That matters. Christianity is not a set of timeless ideas detached from history; it stands or falls on real events in real places. When the details John mentions in passing turn out to be accurate, it is a reasonable confirmation that he is telling the truth about the larger things as well.
verseByVerse.note: The Sheep Gate was in the north wall, near the temple. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read Bethsaida. Archaeologists have uncovered twin pools there with colonnades on four sides and one across the middle.

parallels.desc: the Sheep Gate

verseByVerse.quote: In these lay a multitude of invalids — blind, lame, and paralyzed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A multitude of invalids. Paralysed is literally withered. They are the very conditions Isaiah promised would be reversed when God came: then shall the lame man leap like a deer (Isaiah 35:5–6), and the ones Jesus listed for the Baptist: the blind see, the lame walk (Matthew 11:4–5). The colonnade is the exact address at which the messianic promise was due to be paid, full of people for whom it had not been.

He walks into it. The Son of God, in a city full of holy places, spent part of a feast day where untreated suffering was most concentrated. Where suffering gathers, he does not withdraw.

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts, followed by the KJV and NKJV, add the end of verse 3 (waiting for the moving of the water) and verse 4, about an angel who stirred the water, so that the first person to step in was healed. It is missing from the earliest and best manuscripts and was probably added to explain verse 7, reflecting popular belief. That is why the verse numbers jump from 3 to 5. Some think the pool was fed by an intermittent spring that bubbled up, which people believed had healing power. Nothing is lost: the man trusted the water and its legend; Jesus ignored the water entirely and healed with a word.

Does a missing verse mean the Bible is unreliable? No. We have thousands of manuscripts of the New Testament, far more and far earlier than for any other ancient book, and comparing them lets scholars see clearly where a later copyist added a note. Modern Bibles are open about these places, as the ESV is here. No doctrine of the faith depends on a disputed verse. The very fact that we can identify such additions shows how well God has preserved his word.

A mercy for the quickest. Whatever was true about that water, the belief around it had a cruel shape: whoever gets in first is healed. It was a mercy available to the quickest, the people who needed it least, and closed to the man who had been there longest. Jesus does not touch the water, carry the man to it or make him first. He heals him where he lies, and the whole apparatus of stirring and racing becomes irrelevant. That is the difference between a mercy you have to qualify for and a mercy that comes to where you are.

On a Tuesday. Every town has its colonnade: the care home, the hospital ward, the street where people sleep. The people there are not a problem to be managed but the very ones Jesus walked towards, and his servants find, often to their surprise, that he is already there.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 4, about an angel stirring the water and the first one in being healed — a popular belief explaining why the sick waited there.

verseByVerse.quote: One man was there who had been an invalid for thirty-eight years. When Jesus saw him lying there and knew that he had already been there a long time, he said to him, "Do you want to be healed?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
An invalid for thirty-eight years. It is longer than many people lived then. If he was struck down at twenty, he is nearly sixty, and he has spent his whole adult life on a mat beside a pool, watching other people get well. The number may echo Israel’s thirty-eight years in the wilderness (Deuteronomy 2:14), but John does not say so, and the link is better held loosely.

When Jesus saw him. Out of the multitude, Jesus chose this one; the man did not ask. Why this man? John does not explain. Grace is sovereign: God gives his kindness freely, as he chooses, not as a wage for anything he finds in us (Romans 9:16). And Jesus knew that he had already been there a long time, without being told (2:25).

Do you want to be healed? The strangest thing Jesus says in the chapter. To a man who has lain beside a healing pool for thirty-eight years it sounds almost like an insult. Of course he wants it. And yet Jesus does not ask this of everyone he heals, so it is meant for this man and this history. Something happens to a want that has been disappointed for thirty-eight years. It does not stay a clean, sharp thing. It goes quiet, gets managed, and turns into a routine: the same spot, the same hours, the same near misses, until the waiting is the life. That is not weakness of character; it is what happens to human beings, and it happens fast. Perhaps he had given up hope, or grown used to his condition and the life of a beggar. Healing would mean new responsibilities. So the question is not cruel. It is the most respectful thing in the passage. Jesus wakes him to desire. He asks a man who has not been asked anything in decades what he actually wants.

What if I have stopped hoping for something? This question is for you too: the marriage that has been like this for years, the child who does not call, the sin confessed so often the confessing has gone hollow, the prayer abandoned around the fifth year of praying it. The question is not a rebuke for having stopped hoping. It is an invitation to say aloud what would be different if God moved, which is harder than it looks. God may answer as you ask, or differently, or in his own time; but he invites you to bring the desire to him honestly rather than bury it. Hope in God is never foolish, even when hope in the circumstance has worn thin.
verseByVerse.note: Thirty-eight years may echo Israel’s thirty-eight years of wandering before entering the land (Deut 2:14), though John does not draw the link.

parallels.desc: thirty-eight years until that generation perished

verseByVerse.quote: The sick man answered him, "Sir, I have no one to put me into the pool when the water is stirred up, and while I am going another steps down before me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sir, I have no one. The loneliest words in the chapter. What he names as his problem is not his legs. It is that in thirty-eight years, in a colonnade full of people, at the season of a feast, nobody had stayed close enough to put him in the water. The Greek is bare: a man I do not have. The paralytic in Mark had four friends (Mark 2:3); this man had none. He is surrounded by people and alone, a common kind of alone.

Another steps down before me. He has tried, more times than he could count, and every time someone quicker got in first. Thirty-eight years of nearly.

He does not answer the question. Asked whether he wants to be well, he describes the system and his place at the bottom of it. Not one word is untrue and not one word is an answer: thirty-eight years has converted hope into an explanation. He does not know who is speaking to him (v. 13); his hope is in the water. He is talking to the answer while explaining why there isn’t one.

Why does Jesus heal someone who showed no faith? Because grace does not wait for us to be ready. This healing is a picture of how God saves: not because we reached the water first, or had the right friends, or even knew who he was, but because Christ came to us and spoke. Faith is the hand that receives Christ, and God gives that hand too (Ephesians 2:8). In this man’s case the healing came first and the knowing later. That should encourage you to pray for people who seem to have no faith at all. Christ can begin where there is nothing.

For worship. When there was no man to help, the Son of Man came, the friend of the friendless, the one who stays when everyone else has stepped down before us. He was himself forsaken by all his friends, so that no one who trusts him need ever say again, I have no one.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to him, "Get up, take up your bed, and walk." And at once the man was healed, and he took up his bed and walked. Now that day was the Sabbath.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Get up, take up your bed, and walk. Three commands, all impossible, given before there is any evidence that he can obey. Take up your bed: the word is krabattos, a poor man’s mat, the pallet a beggar rolls under his arm. His word gives the power to obey. No pool, no stirring, no help needed.

At once. After thirty-eight years, instantly, with no touch and no prayer: grace arriving unrequested at a man who had given up asking, which is why Bethesda has so often been read as a picture of the gospel.

The mat. A healed man walking away is a private mercy. A healed man carrying his bed through the city is a public claim, the evidence held up in both arms. Jesus tells him to carry the mat, on the Sabbath, in Jerusalem, at a feast, past the authorities. That is deliberate, and the rest of the chapter follows from it.

Now that day was the Sabbath. John withholds it until after the healing, so that the reader feels the joy first and the objection second. Jesus knew what day it was, and his answer in verse 17 shows he chose it.

Must Christians, then, keep the Sabbath? Christians differ here, and both views are held by faithful believers. Many Reformed Christians, following the Westminster Confession, hold that the fourth commandment still binds, the day of rest now kept on the Lord’s Day, the first day of the week, and kept with joy as a day for worship and works of mercy (Westminster 21.7–8). (The 1689 London Baptist Confession says the same, 22.7–8.) Others read the Sabbath as fulfilled in Christ, the true rest (Hebrews 4:9–10), so that no day binds the conscience (Colossians 2:16–17; Romans 14:5–6), while still gathering gladly on the first day, the day of resurrection. This commentary’s view: the second fits the New Testament best: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, and the Lord’s Day is a gift, gladly set apart for worship, fellowship and rest, not the fourth commandment moved to Sunday, and no one may bind another’s conscience over it. The first view is held by many godly brothers and deserves respect. Both agree with what this passage plainly teaches: the day was never meant to forbid mercy, and Jesus is Lord of it.

On a Tuesday. It is possible to be genuinely helped by Christ and entirely discreet about it, to leave the mat at the pool. He told this man to pick it up. Is there some evidence of his grace in your life that you have kept out of sight?

For worship. He speaks, and the dead legs stand; he commands, and the thing commanded is done. The word that called the world out of nothing called a withered man off his mat. And he chose the Sabbath, the day of God’s rest, to give a man the first true rest he had known in thirty-eight years.
verseByVerse.note: The bed was a light mat. Carrying a load on the Sabbath was forbidden by tradition, drawing on the prophets.

parallels.desc: a similar command to a paralytic
bear no burden on the Sabbath

verseByVerse.quote: So the Jews said to the man who had been healed, "It is the Sabbath, and it is not lawful for you to take up your bed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the Jews said. In John, the Jews often means the Jewish religious authorities in Jerusalem, not the Jewish people as a whole. Jesus, his disciples and the healed man were all Jews.

Not lawful. The Mishnah, written down around AD 200 but preserving older tradition, lists carrying an object from one domain to another among the thirty-nine kinds of forbidden work (Mishnah Shabbat 7:2).

Be fair to them first. They were not inventing a rule out of nothing. The prophets had been explicit: take care, and do not bear a burden on the Sabbath day or bring it in by the gates of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 17:21–22). Jeremiah names the city and the gates. He was forbidding the traffic of trade on God’s day, loads carried in to be bought and sold (Nehemiah 13:15–19 shows the same abuse); a healed man carrying his own mat home was never what he had in view. These men are standing in that city, watching a man carry a load, and they have a text. So this is not a case of religious people making things up. It is something more uncomfortable and far more common: people applying a real command of God, in a situation it was never written for, and being badly wrong while sounding entirely correct.

The lens and the subject. The arithmetic of the sentence condemns them. A man who has been paralysed for thirty-eight years is walking through Jerusalem carrying his own bed, and the whole content of their response is a citation. Not one question about how, not one word to him about what has happened. They see the mat, the mat is against the rules, and the man holding it is invisible. It is what happens when a system of rules becomes the lens rather than the subject. A miracle walks past and is processed as an infringement. And there is a reason the heart prefers the rule. Rules you can keep give you a sense of control and of standing before God: you know where you are, and you know you are doing well. A grace that comes unasked to a man who had kept nothing threatens that whole arrangement, because it says that God’s best gift is not earned, and so cannot be earned by us either.

Lord of the day they were guarding. The Sabbath these men were defending was God’s sign of the rest he would give his people, and the giver of that rest had just given it. The one load the man lifts that day is the proof that his real burden has been taken away. The men at the gate see the fourth commandment broken; they are looking at what it pointed to, walking past them on two healed legs.

Does this mean rules do not matter? No. God’s commands are good, and Jesus never broke the law of God. What he exposed was a way of handling God’s law that loses sight of its purpose: love for God and neighbour (Matthew 22:37–40). The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath (Mark 2:27). The problem was not that they cared about obedience, but that they cared about their reading of a rule more than about the man in front of them and the God who had just healed him. Keep God’s commands; but never let your system of applying them blind you to his mercy.

On a Tuesday. Think of the last time something happened in a Christian setting outside your expectations: a convert with a chaotic life, someone doing good work with theology you would want to correct. What was your first movement? Discernment is a duty. But these men’s first movement was a rule, and the second, joy at what God had done, never came.
verseByVerse.note: In John, “the Jews” often means the Jewish religious authorities.

verseByVerse.quote: But he answered them, "The man who healed me, that man said to me, 'Take up your bed, and walk.'" They asked him, "Who is the man who said to you, 'Take up your bed and walk'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man who healed me. His logic is sound: someone with the power to end thirty-eight years of paralysis with a word plainly has standing to say what may be carried and when. That is not an evasion but an argument. What he lacks is a name.

Who is the man who said to you? Read the two sentences side by side and see what each party seizes on. He says: the man who healed me. They say: the man who said to you. They repeat his sentence with the healing surgically removed. Not who healed you, but who told you to break the rule. They are not interested in the miracle, only the offence. That is an editorial decision made in real time, the exact operation by which an inconvenient fact stops being part of a discussion.

The right question for the wrong reason. Yet who is the man? is the question this whole Gospel exists to answer. They ask it to identify a suspect. But they ask it.

Be gentle with the healed man. He has had his legs for perhaps an hour, does not know who healed him, and is questioned by the most powerful men in the city about an infringement he committed on instructions. People are often hard on him for later naming Jesus to the authorities, and some of it may be fair. But not everyone is at his best in that position.

What do I say when I am challenged about my faith and do not know much yet? Say what you know, as this man did. You may not be able to answer every question, but you can say what has happened to you and who did it. The man born blind in chapter 9 said: one thing I do know, that though I was blind, now I see (9:25). That is enough to begin with. Then go and learn more, so that next time you can say more. And do not be ashamed to say, I do not know the answer to that yet, but I will find out.

For worship. Who is the man? His enemies asked it to name a suspect, and every page of this Gospel answers it: the Word made flesh, the Lamb of God, the Lord who heals. At the last they answered it themselves without knowing, with a title fixed above his head on a cross: Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews (19:19).

verseByVerse.quote: Now the man who had been healed did not know who it was, for Jesus had withdrawn, as there was a crowd in the place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus had withdrawn. Healed without knowing his healer: grace before knowledge. He was gone before anything could gather around the miracle, as he will be again (6:15), the opposite of what anyone building a following would do.

Set him beside the man born blind. The contrast is deliberate. That man is interrogated by the same authorities and grows sharper with every round, is thrown out of the synagogue, and then, found by Jesus, worships (9:38). This man is asked one question and produces a name. One received his sight, lost his standing and gained Christ. This one received his legs and told the authorities who had done it.

Answered prayer is not conversion. The healing did not, as far as we are told, save him. Every physical mercy in the Gospels is real, and none of them is automatically anything more. A marriage restored, a diagnosis reversed, a job that came in time: each may be a genuine gift from God and leave the recipient where they were.

Can someone receive God’s blessings and still not be saved? Yes, sadly. God is kind to all; he sends rain on the just and the unjust (Matthew 5:45), and many received healing from Jesus without following him (Luke 17:17–18). Blessings are meant to lead us to repentance (Romans 2:4), but they do not save by themselves. Only faith in Christ unites us to him. So do not measure your standing with God by your circumstances, good or bad. Ask instead: do I know him, trust him and follow him?

verseByVerse.quote: "Afterward Jesus found him in the temple and said to him, 'See, you are well! Sin no more, that nothing worse may happen to you.' The man went away and told the Jews that it was Jesus who had healed him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus found him. The man had gone to the temple, perhaps to give thanks, walking where for years he could only have been carried. And the finding is deliberate: Jesus had slipped away, and now he goes looking for a man who does not know his face. The healing was the beginning of the errand, not the end. He comes back for people: for the blind man after he is thrown out (9:35), and for Peter on a beach after the denials (21:15).

See, you are well! Jesus does not say all illness is punishment for sin (9:3), but warns this man that sin has worse consequences than paralysis: eternal judgement. And the order matters: the mercy came first, unasked, and the command follows it. He is not told to stop sinning so that he may be helped; he has been helped, and now he must turn from sin.

Am I ill because of something I did? Many readers carry that question quietly for years. John himself settles the general question four chapters on. The disciples see a man born blind and ask who sinned, this man or his parents, and Jesus rejects the premise: neither (9:3). Illness is not a scoreboard. In a world under the curse, bodies fail, and the failure is not a message decoded from the sufferer’s record. Job’s friends built a theology on the opposite assumption, and God told them they had not spoken rightly of him (Job 42:7). Sometimes a particular sin does bring particular harm, and then repentance is the path. But you must not assume your suffering is punishment. If you are in Christ, the punishment for your sin was borne at the cross, and whatever you suffer now comes from a Father’s hand.

So what is Jesus saying here? Not that this man’s thirty-eight years were a sentence served, but the thing any of us most needs to hear on the far side of a mercy: there is something worse than thirty-eight years on a mat. He has given the man his legs; now he warns him about his soul, in the temple, where the man has rightly come. Taken at that level the warning stops sounding cruel and becomes kind. Sin is worth abandoning not because it made you ill, but because judgement is real, and the body you have just got back will not last for ever either.

He told the Jews. Why? Perhaps naively, perhaps to protect himself, perhaps as testimony; John does not say, and it is wise not to judge him harshly. But the effect is plain: from then on the authorities pursued Jesus (v. 16).
verseByVerse.note: Jesus does not say all illness is punishment for sin, but warns that sin leads to worse than illness.

parallels.desc: go, and from now on sin no more

verseByVerse.quote: And this was why the Jews were persecuting Jesus, because he was doing these things on the Sabbath. But Jesus answered them, "My Father is working until now, and I am working."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Persecuting Jesus. The tense means they kept on persecuting, and the cause was a pattern, not one incident. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add here that they sought to kill him; the earliest do not, and John says it in verse 18 anyway.

My Father is working until now. A staggering claim, and sharper than it looks, because it lands inside a debate the rabbis were already having. God rested on the seventh day (Genesis 2:2–3), but Jewish teachers, as rabbinic writings later record, knew that God does not down tools on the seventh day: children are born and people die on the Sabbath, and giving life and judging the dead were the standard examples of divine work that never stops. One recorded answer was that God is exempt: the whole universe is his house, so he may work in his own home on his own day. Jesus takes that exact exemption and applies it to himself. Not God is allowed, therefore mercy is allowed, which would be an argument about ethics; he puts himself on the same side of the line as the one who is exempt, because he does God’s work. And he spends the next dozen verses on those two works: giving life and executing judgement. And my Father: not our Father. A unique relationship.

The rest of God and the work of God. The rest God took on the seventh day was rest from making, not from holding. There has not been an hour when God was not sustaining the universe.

Who actually kept the Sabbath that day? Consider what happened. A man who had not stood for thirty-eight years stood. He had spent every seventh day of nearly four decades lying on a mat beside a pool, and on this one he walked home. If any human being in Jerusalem entered into rest that day, it was him. The one accused of breaking the Sabbath is the only person in the story who gave anyone a Sabbath, and the men defending the day spent it drawing up charges. The day was made as a mercy, a weekly memorial of a God who finished his work. To turn it into an instrument for keeping a healed man from carrying his bedding is not strictness. It is a misreading of what the day was for.

Is God really working all the time, even in the boring parts of my life? Yes. My Father is working until now. God does not take weekends off from caring for his creation or his children. He is at work in the dull Tuesday as much as in the dramatic answer to prayer, upholding all things by the word of his power (Hebrews 1:3), working all things for the good of those who love him (Romans 8:28), and completing the good work he began in you (Philippians 1:6). You may not see it. But you are never in a moment that God has left unattended.
verseByVerse.note: Jewish teachers recognised that God keeps working on the Sabbath, sustaining the world; Jesus claims the same right.

parallels.desc: lord even of the Sabbath

verseByVerse.quote: This was why the Jews were seeking all the more to kill him, because not only was he breaking the Sabbath, but he was even calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seeking all the more to kill him. The first time John mentions the plot, and the thread runs on through the Gospel (7:1, 19; 8:37; 11:53). He healed a man who had been on the ground for thirty-eight years, and they began to plan his death.

His own Father. His own (idion): personally, in a way no one else could. Jews called God Father collectively, the Father of the nation. To speak of God as one’s own Father, in a way that made his working and God’s working the same working, was a different kind of sentence altogether.

Making himself equal with God. They understood him perfectly. John reports it flatly as what was happening: the narrator agrees with their reading of the words, not with what they did about it. Either Jesus was a blasphemer, or he is God. He does not deny it; the discourse that follows explains it.

The people who understood him best. This closes off one of the most popular ways of handling Jesus: the idea that he was a teacher of ethics whose followers later inflated him into something divine. The people who wanted him dead were the ones who understood him best. They were not offended by his ethics; nobody organises an execution over the golden rule. They killed him for who he said he was, and this verse is where the machinery starts moving. A sceptic may reply that John wrote late and put the claim in Jesus’ mouth. But the earliest Gospel tells the same story: Mark has the scribes call him a blasphemer for forgiving sins, which only God can do (Mark 2:7), and the high priest condemn him for blasphemy at his trial (Mark 14:61–64).

Two charges, neither right as they put it. He was not breaking the Sabbath, only their reading of it; he never once broke the law of God. And he was not making himself equal with God: he was stating what was already the case, a larger claim altogether.

In the flow. The whole chapter turns on verse 18: everything after it is Jesus’ answer to this one charge, and he does not retract it but unfolds it. John opened by saying that the Word was God (1:1) and will close with Thomas saying, my Lord and my God (20:28); here, halfway between, the enemies of Jesus state the same truth as an accusation.

If Jesus is equal with God, why does he pray to the Father and obey him? Because within the one God there are three persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, equal in power and glory, and distinct in their relations (Westminster Confession 2.3; 1689 London Baptist Confession 2.3). The Son is fully God, and he is also the Son: from all eternity he shares one life, one will and one love with the Father. And in the work of salvation, becoming man, he took the form of a servant, humbled himself, and became obedient to death (Philippians 2:6–8). So his prayers and obedience do not make him less than God. They show us God the Son living out, in our nature, the love and unity he has always shared with the Father.

For worship. The charge sheet, when it was finally drawn up, said that he made himself the Son of God (19:7). It was the only accusation ever brought against him that was true, and true in a sense the prosecution never suspected, since he had not made himself anything. He claimed equality with God and died for the claim, and the empty tomb was the Father’s verdict that every word of it was true.

parallels.desc: you, being a man, make yourself God

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–47 — The Son's Authority: Witness and Judgment
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus answers the charge. The Son acts in perfect union with the Father; he gives life and will judge, so that all may honour him as they honour the Father. Whoever hears and believes has already passed from death to life, and at the last day all the dead will hear his voice. Then he calls four witnesses, and the trial turns on the accusers.
verseByVerse.theology:
The discourse claims for the Son the two works that belong to God alone, giving life and judging, and the honour that belongs to God alone. No one can honour God while declining Christ. The four witnesses are not offered as proofs that force belief; their rejection shows the state of the rejecting heart.

The Son has life in himself as the Father does (v. 26): not life on loan, as every creature has it, but his own, with nothing behind it that could fail. That the Father granted it describes the eternal relation of Father and Son, not an event in time. And verse 29 does not teach salvation by works, since verse 24 gives life to whoever hears and believes: the good and evil done are the evidence of a life that had or had not crossed from death to life.
verseByVerse.examples:
The claims of this discourse leave no middle ground: a man who says he will raise the dead and judge the world is either deluded or who he says he is. And the judgment of the last day is already being decided in each person’s response to him now (vv. 24, 28–29).

The chapter also names three ways of being religious without coming to Christ: enjoying a faithful preacher for a while without following where he points (v. 35); studying Scripture as if life were found in the text rather than in the one it points to (v. 39); and living for the approval of one’s own circle rather than the glory that comes from the only God (v. 44).

verseByVerse.quote: "So Jesus said to them, 'Truly, truly, I say to you, the Son can do nothing of his own accord, but only what he sees the Father doing. For whatever the Father does, that the Son does likewise. For the Father loves the Son and shows him all that he himself is doing. And greater works than these will he show him, so that you may marvel.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nothing of his own accord. Not weakness, but unity. Jesus answers the charge of verse 18 not by denying it but by explaining it: the Son never acts independently of the Father. It sounds like a limitation, but it is the strongest claim in the paragraph. Anyone can act independently of God; every one of us does it hourly, and that is what sin is. Only one person can say that he never has, and that everything he does is what he sees the Father doing, continuously and without deviation, which no prophet ever said.

The workshop. There may well be a picture underneath this. In that world a trade passed from father to son by watching: a boy stood in his father’s shop and learned by seeing it done. The claim is both homely and enormous. Then look at what is made in this workshop: raising the dead and judging the world, which are on no human trade’s list.

For whatever the Father does, that the Son does likewise. Whatever: everything, not approximately but exactly. Only one who is God can do everything God does.

The Father loves the Son. The verb here is philei; in 3:35 the same love is agapa, and John uses the two interchangeably. What matters is what that love does: it shows, and withholds nothing, and the reason given is love rather than policy. And the Father will show him greater works than healing a paralysed man: giving life and judging (vv. 21–22).

Where Christians differ: the Son and the Father. Arians (named after a fourth-century teacher who held that the Son was the first and highest creature) and today Jehovah’s Witnesses read “the Son can do nothing of his own accord” as proof that the Son is inferior to the Father. This commentary’s view: the passage teaches that the Son is equal with the Father in nature and power (he does whatever the Father does, gives life, judges, receives equal honour), while distinct in person and relationship (the Father sends; the Son is sent and obeys). This is the doctrine of the Trinity: one God, three persons, equal in power and glory, distinct in relations (Westminster Shorter Catechism 6).

How can I explain the Trinity simply? Start with what the Bible says, not with an illustration. There is one God (Deuteronomy 6:4). The Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God. The three are not the same person: the Father sends the Son, the Son prays to the Father, the Spirit is sent by both. So God is one in being and three in persons. Most illustrations, water and ice and steam, or one man as father, son and husband, end up teaching an old error, that God is one person wearing three masks. It is better to say plainly: this is beyond us, and it is what God has shown us about himself, and it is the most beautiful truth there is, because it means God has always been love.

On a Tuesday. You cannot do what the Son does, but in him his Father is your Father, and his Spirit is in you. Before the main decisions of today, stop and ask: what is my Father doing here? Do your work as a child learning in your Father’s workshop.

verseByVerse.quote: "For as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he will. For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Father raises the dead. In the Old Testament, only God gives life to the dead (Deuteronomy 32:39; 1 Samuel 2:6; 2 Kings 5:7).

So also the Son. Having claimed to work as his Father works, Jesus now names those two divine works and claims both, a precise argument his hearers understood. To whom he will: by his sovereign choice, spiritual life now (v. 24) and resurrection life at the last day (v. 29). Christians differ over whether that choice rests on faith God foresees (the debate is set out at 6:37); all agree that no one is saved by merit.

To whom he will. Not to whoever qualifies, not to whoever arrives first at the stirring of the water, which is what had kept the man on the mat on the ground. The first half of this chapter demonstrates that clause. Jesus walked into a colonnade of sick people, healed one, and left, and John offers no account of why that man. A Christ who healed everyone at the pool would be easier to admire and would tell us nothing about how mercy actually comes to anyone. What we have is a man who was not first in the queue, had nobody, and got up and walked, because the Son gives life to whom he will.

All judgment to the Son. The final judgement, which belongs to God alone (Genesis 18:25), is given to the Son (Acts 17:31). Every human being will be judged, and the one who judges is the one who was crucified. The bench is not occupied by a stranger to the case.

But Jesus also says he did not come to judge the world. How do these fit? He says it in 3:17 and 12:47, and in 8:15 he says, I judge no one. These fit together. He came the first time to save, not to condemn; the condemnation already rests on those who reject him (3:18). At the end, all judgement is committed to him, and he will judge (v. 27). And in 8:15 he means that he does not judge as they do, by outward appearance, by the standards of the flesh.

If the Son gives life to whom he will, is it unfair to those he passes by? No one has a claim on God’s mercy; if we did, it would not be mercy. All of us are sinners deserving judgement, and God would be perfectly just to leave us all to it. That he chooses to save any is pure grace, and that he saves a great multitude is amazing grace (Romans 9:14–16). And the same Christ who gives life to whom he will freely invites all: whoever comes to me I will never cast out (6:37). No one who wants to come is turned away. If you want Christ, that wanting is itself the sign that he is giving you life.

On a Tuesday. If you are praying for someone who seems far from God, take heart: the Son gives life to whom he will, and no one is too far gone for his voice.

parallels.desc: I kill and I make alive

verseByVerse.quote: "that all may honor the Son, just as they honor the Father. Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Just as they honor the Father. The phrase just as fixes the measure and leaves no room to negotiate. Not honour him more than any other teacher: honour him the same kind, the same degree, the same worship. God will not give his glory to another (Isaiah 42:8). If the Son is to be honoured just as the Father, the Son is God.

The Father wants his Son honoured. It would be natural to assume that any honour paid to the Son is a detour from the Father. The verse says the reverse: the Father has given life and judgement to the Son precisely so that all may honour the Son. Withholding it is not modesty on God’s behalf.

Whoever does not honor the Son. This closes every exit. There is no arrangement in which a person keeps God and declines Christ (1 John 2:23). That makes Christianity permanently awkward in polite company, and it is better stated than hedged. Many people believe in God, admire Jesus as a moral teacher, and regard his divinity as a later addition. This verse says that arrangement does not exist, not because Christians are narrow, but because the Son himself refuses to be admired at a discount.

Is it right to pray to Jesus and sing to him, or only to the Father? It is right to do both. Ordinarily Christians pray to the Father through the Son by the Spirit, since through Christ we have access in one Spirit to the Father (Ephesians 2:18). But Stephen prayed to the Lord Jesus as he died (Acts 7:59), the first Christians called on the name of the Lord Jesus (1 Corinthians 1:2), and all heaven sings to the Lamb (Revelation 5:12–13). Since the Son is to be honoured just as the Father is, worship offered to him is not misdirected. It is exactly what the Father wants.

On a Tuesday. Listen to how you speak about Jesus when you are not in church: with colleagues, with family, in an argument. It is easy to slide into speaking of him as a figure of great importance rather than a person to be worshipped. Speak of him today as your Lord.

For worship. The Father has decreed that every knee shall bow to the Son, and to the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:10–11). Honour given to the Son is never stolen from the Father. There is no praise of Christ that needs holding back in case it overshoots. The man who stood bound before a council and was mocked by soldiers is owed the worship of the universe, and one day he will have it.

parallels.desc: no one who denies the Son has the Father

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life. He does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life. Truly, truly, I say to you, an hour is coming, and is now here, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Has eternal life. Hearing and believing is the way life is received, and the tense is present: already.

He does not come into judgment. No condemnation (3:18; Romans 8:1). This is the strongest assurance in the chapter: not will be acquitted at the judgement, but will not come into it. The verdict was settled at the cross, where Christ took the condemnation in the believer’s place (Romans 8:3).

Passed from death to life. Perfect tense: has crossed over, and remains on the other side, from spiritual death (Ephesians 2:1) to eternal life. Not is crossing; not will cross when the accounts are settled. The believer is not a candidate for life awaiting a verdict. He is a person who has already emigrated.

An hour is coming, and is now here. Already happening. These dead are not in graves: they are people walking around Jerusalem, spiritually dead and unaware of it, and some are about to hear a voice and start living. In verse 28 he will not add and is now here, and that hour will involve tombs. Two kinds of rising, one spiritual and now, one bodily and still ahead. The same voice does both.

The dead will hear. As Lazarus would hear his voice and come out of the tomb (11:43), so the spiritually dead hear his voice in the gospel and are made alive (Ephesians 2:4–5). This is regeneration, the new birth of 3:3–8: God giving spiritual life to someone dead toward him, so that he now hears, believes and loves what he once ignored. The dead do not cooperate in being raised.

But Paul says we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ. How can believers not come into judgement? Both are true (2 Corinthians 5:10). The believer does not come into judgement in the sense of condemnation (Romans 8:1); that verdict has been given. But his life and work will be reviewed for reward, and some will suffer loss though they themselves are saved (1 Corinthians 3:12–15).

What if I am frightened of the last day? Then hear this verse as Jesus meant it. There is a way of holding the faith in which the whole thing is provisional: a hope that the balance will come out right in the end, with a private suspicion that it may not. This verse forecloses it. If you have heard Christ’s word and believe the Father who sent him, the passing has happened. You will stand before Christ, but as one already acquitted, with your sins carried away by him. What remains for you is not a hearing but a homecoming. Your assurance does not rest on the strength of your feelings, but on the word of the Judge himself.

On a Tuesday. When you share the gospel with someone, remember whose voice gives life. Your task is to speak his word faithfully; his task is to raise the dead.

parallels.desc: dead in trespasses, made alive

verseByVerse.quote: "For as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself. And he has given him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Life in himself. God is self-existent. He depends on nothing; life is his by nature. It is the highest thing said about God in the chapter, and it sounds like philosophy, so put it plainly. Everything that lives has life on loan. A tree has it from the soil and the light, an animal from what it eats, a man from his food and breath and the fact that his heart has not yet stopped, and every one of those supplies can be cut, which is why everything that lives also dies. To have life in himself means to be the one exception: to hold life not as a supply but as his own being, underived, with nothing behind it that could fail. Theologians call this aseity, from the Latin a se, from himself, and it belongs to God alone.

Granted to the Son. The Son too has life in himself: not borrowed, but his own (1:4). At first hearing this sounds like a contradiction, since a life that is granted would seem by definition not to be underived. The church thought long about this and arrived at the right place. Granted does not mean the Son once lacked it. It is not an event in time. The eternal Son receives life eternally from the Father, as the Son eternally comes from the Father (eternal generation). Eternal generation means simply this: the Father has always been the Father and the Son has always been the Son. There was never a time when the Son was not (1:1–2), and his being the Son is not a beginning but an eternal relationship. He is not a creature who was topped up. He is the Son, and what the Father is, the Son is. And as incarnate, he has it in his human nature too, to give to others.

Because he is the Son of Man. Not, as the argument might lead us to expect, because he is the Son of God. In the Greek there is no article, a son of man, which may stress his true humanity as well as recall Daniel 7:13–14, where one like a son of man receives an everlasting dominion. As a man, he can judge humanity fairly, having lived as one of us (Hebrews 4:15). The one who will judge the human race was tired at a well, wept at a grave, and knows from the inside what it costs to be one of the accused.

What difference does it make that God has life in himself? All the difference in the world. Because God depends on nothing, he cannot be worn out, run out or used up. He does not need you, and so his love for you is pure gift, not a deal. And because the Son has life in himself, the life he gives is not a borrowed supply that might run dry. It is his own inexhaustible life. Whoever is joined to him by faith is joined to the one source of life that can never fail, which is why Jesus can promise, because I live, you also will live (14:19).

For worship. The one who holds life in himself took a body that could be killed. Nothing in him required feeding or resting, and he consented to both, and then to the loss of the whole of it. He gave his life away, took it up again, and now gives it to whoever hears his voice.

parallels.desc: one like a son of man given dominion

verseByVerse.quote: "Do not marvel at this, for an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out, those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not marvel at this. The spiritually dead hearing his voice and living is the smaller of the two things. Wait until the graves. This time he says only that an hour is coming, not that it is now here: it is the last day.

All who are in the tombs. The bodily resurrection of all the dead, righteous and wicked: everyone who has ever been buried, in every unmarked place, in the sea and under the ash. And the summons is a voice, the voice of the man who stood in a Jerusalem colonnade and told someone to pick up a mat.

Life and judgment. Both are raised in the body: the one to eternal life, the other to condemnation.

What it does not mean. Not salvation by good works. In John, the “good” is above all believing in Jesus (6:29), and life comes to whoever hears his word and believes (v. 24). The good and the evil are evidence, not currency: the visible form of a life that had already crossed from death to life, or had not (Ephesians 2:8–10; James 2:17–18). Nobody is raised to life because their file was satisfactory, but this Gospel will not let faith be a word said once with nothing following.

One resurrection or two? This verse speaks of one hour in which all who are in the tombs come out, the righteous and the wicked together (compare Daniel 12:2; Acts 24:15). Premillennial Christians (who expect Christ to return before a thousand-year reign on earth) read Revelation 20 as teaching two bodily resurrections a thousand years apart, the first for believers and the second for the rest. The more likely reading is the one this verse gives: a single general resurrection at Christ’s return, with Revelation’s first resurrection referring to the new life believers already share with Christ. This is the amillennial view, which takes the thousand years as a picture of the present age between Christ’s two comings. Many faithful Christians read Revelation 20 otherwise, and the hope they share is the same: Christ will return, raise the dead and judge the world.

How can a loving God raise anyone to judgement? Because he is holy as well as loving, and the two are not rivals. A judge who shrugged at cruelty, betrayal and the abuse of the weak would not be loving; he would be indifferent, and every victim would know it. God takes evil seriously because he takes people seriously. And the verse shows how seriously he takes mercy too: the Judge who will speak at the graves is the one who came first to be judged in our place (v. 24). His offer is real and free, and no one who comes to him will be raised to judgement. Those who come to him will find the Judge is their Saviour.

What will the resurrection body be like? It will be your own body, raised, not a different one, just as Jesus’ risen body bore the marks of the nails (20:27). For believers it will be raised imperishable, glorious and powerful, fitted for the new creation (1 Corinthians 15:42–44), like Christ’s glorious body (Philippians 3:21). The unbelieving dead will also be raised bodily, to face judgement and conscious, eternal punishment (Matthew 25:46). This is why the body matters in the Christian life: what you do with it now is done with something God intends to raise.

On a Tuesday. Ask what your life would look like to someone who watched it for a year without hearing you say anything about God. Verse 29 is asking whether the crossing has left any tracks. If you see little, do not despair: the tracks are often plainer to others than to ourselves, and life is received by hearing and believing (v. 24), not by the size of the tracks.

parallels.desc: some to everlasting life, some to shame

verseByVerse.quote: "I can do nothing on my own. As I hear, I judge, and my judgment is just, because I seek not my own will but the will of him who sent me. If I alone bear witness about myself, my testimony is not true."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As I hear, I judge. The Son never acts apart from the Father (v. 19), and so his judgement is perfectly just, because it is the Father’s.

Not my own will. Perfect submission (4:34; 6:38). That is the qualification for a judge: not superior intelligence but the total absence of self-interest.

If I alone bear witness. The law required two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15). Jesus accepts the rule, and now calls his witnesses. The vocabulary of witness has run through this Gospel since the Baptist (1:7–8); now the case is formally opened. Not true here means not legally admissible, rather than factually false.

But in 8:14 Jesus says his testimony about himself is true. Is that a contradiction? No; each answers a different question. Here he meets them on their own ground: you require corroboration, and you shall have it, and here are the witnesses. In chapter 8 he is answering a challenge to his knowledge, and his point is that he alone knows where he came from and where he is going, so his testimony, whatever a court makes of it, is accurate. One statement is about legal standing; the other is about truthfulness. He does not need corroboration to be right. He offers it because they need it to be persuaded.
