He builds a case. He is under no obligation to argue, yet the Son who claims to raise the dead builds a case like a defendant, because the men in front of him will move only on evidence, and he will give them evidence rather than stand on his dignity.

On a Tuesday. Only one man has ever sought the Father’s will and never his own, and his perfect obedience is counted to all who trust him (Romans 5:19). With nothing left to defend, you can be honest about your motives: before you form an opinion of someone today, ask what you stand to gain from it. A judgement with self-interest in it is already bent.
verseByVerse.note: The law required two or three witnesses; a man’s testimony about himself did not count as valid evidence.

verseByVerse.quote: "There is another who bears witness about me, and I know that the testimony that he bears about me is true."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The other witness. Some take the other witness to be John the Baptist (v. 33), but it is most likely the Father, since verse 37 says the Father who sent me has himself borne witness about me. Both point the same way: John spoke because the Father sent him (1:6, 33).

The testimony is true. The Father cannot lie. He is not producing witnesses because he is uncertain. He knows; the case is being built for the benefit of people who do not.

The witnesses. Jesus now calls four witnesses, as in a trial: John the Baptist (vv. 33–35), his works (v. 36), the Father (vv. 37–38), and the Scriptures, including Moses (vv. 39–47).

There is another. He is standing alone in a hostile room: the disciples are not mentioned in this chapter, and the healed man has just identified him to the authorities. The corroboration comes from outside the building, from the one who sent him, and it does not depend on a single person present being persuaded.

How should I argue for the faith with someone who wants proof? From knowledge, not anxiety. Evidence is offered in Scripture constantly and without embarrassment; this Gospel is a marshalling of evidence, and says so at the end (20:30–31). So give reasons gladly: the eyewitness testimony, the empty tomb, fulfilled prophecy, the changed lives. But there is a way of arguing for Christ that has fear underneath it, and it communicates the fear rather than the case. Jesus never once sounds worried about the verdict. The truth does not depend on your winning the argument. Speak calmly, honestly and kindly, and leave the persuading to God.

On a Tuesday. If you have to hold a position alone today, in a family, at work, in a church that has gone somewhere you cannot follow, remember this sentence. It is not an encouragement to be stubborn, but a statement about where the verdict actually comes from.
verseByVerse.note: The other witness is probably the Father (v. 37), though some take it as John the Baptist (v. 33).

verseByVerse.quote: "You sent to John, and he has borne witness to the truth. Not that the testimony that I receive is from man, but I say these things so that you may be saved."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You sent to John. The delegation of 1:19. They cannot dispute his standing, because they investigated him themselves, and John told them, on the record, who he was. Jesus is producing the transcript of their own enquiry.

He has borne witness. He testified that Jesus is the Lamb of God and Son of God (1:29, 34). The tense matters: the testimony stands, still doing its work in a hearing he is not present at. He must increase, but I must decrease (3:30), and by now the decreasing has gone a long way. He is not in the room. His witness is.

Not from man. He sets it aside in the same breath, and it would be a poor foundation if he rested on it, since the greatest man born of women is still a man.

So that you may be saved. He mentions John for their sake, because they respected him. Under investigation by men already trying to work out how to kill him (v. 18), he says the reason he is bothering is not to secure an acquittal but to secure them: a man on trial for his life, telling the court his defence is being offered for their benefit.

Does my witness matter if I never see results? Yes. Faithful testimony goes on working after the person who gave it can no longer give it: in rooms they never entered, in arguments they did not know were happening, long after they have been forgotten by everyone but God. John was probably in prison, perhaps already dead, when Jesus cited him. Your words to a child, a friend or a colleague may be called as evidence by the Spirit years from now. Speak truly, and leave the timing to God.

On a Tuesday. Even Jesus’ hard words are spoken so that people may be saved. When you have to say something hard to someone this week, check your motive first. Are you speaking so that they may be saved, or so that you may be right?

verseByVerse.quote: "He was a burning and shining lamp, and you were willing to rejoice for a while in his light."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A burning and shining lamp. A lamp, not the light itself (1:8). The word is lychnos, the ordinary oil lamp you carry into a room after dark. Burning: with zeal; shining: giving light. A lamp actually alight, which is more than can be said for much religious furniture, but still the thing you use until morning. And the tense is past: by now John was probably in prison.

For a while. Literally, for an hour. The whole country went out to the Jordan (Matthew 3:5), and it lasted about as long as such things last. They did not follow where he pointed: enthusiasm without repentance. The lamp had been admired and put out, and here stands the daylight it was lit for, and they are trying to work out how to kill him.

Reaction is not response. There is a way of consuming preaching as an experience: hearing a man who is genuinely alight, feeling something, discussing it warmly, and being at the end of the season exactly where you started. The enjoyment is not fraudulent, which is what makes it dangerous. It feels like a response, and it is a reaction.

Is it wrong to have a favourite preacher? Not in itself. God gives gifts to his church, and it is right to thank him for preachers who help you. But the Corinthians turned admiration into parties, I follow Paul, I follow Apollos, and Paul rebuked them (1 Corinthians 3:4–7). The test of a good preacher is that, like John, he is a finger aimed at Christ, and the test of a good hearer is that he follows where the finger points. If you would stop going to church when your favourite preacher leaves, it may be the lamp you love and not the light.

For worship. Christ is the light; every faithful preacher is only a lamp lit by him, burning for a while and then put out. The lamps pass, but the light of the world shines on, and the city to come has no need of sun or moon, for the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb.

parallels.desc: I have prepared a lamp for my anointed

verseByVerse.quote: "But the testimony that I have is greater than that of John. For the works that the Father has given me to accomplish, the very works that I am doing, bear witness about me that the Father has sent me. And the Father who sent me has himself borne witness about me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Greater than that of John. First, the works that the Father has given him to accomplish, culminating in the cross (17:4; 19:30). Not works he chose as demonstrations, but works handed to him as an assignment, to be finished, the verb of 4:34. The healing at the pool was not an improvisation. It was an item on a schedule, and so was every other sign in this book, and so was the last one.

The works bear witness. The works show who he is (10:25, 37–38; 14:11), and they outrank the Baptist for a simple reason. John’s testimony was a man’s word, and men have been wrong. A man who had been on the ground for most of his life is walking through Jerusalem carrying his bed, and the fact does not depend on anyone’s credibility. Either it happened or it did not.

The Father has borne witness. Perfect tense: a lasting testimony. When did it happen? He does not say here, and the Gospel offers several answers: the Spirit descending and remaining at the Jordan, which the Baptist saw and reported (1:32–34); the Scriptures, which he is about to name; and most simply the works themselves, since it is the Father who gives them.

A cumulative case. Each witness on its own could be argued with. Together they make a strong case, and in this room the problem was not a shortage of evidence, which is why the next verse turns from the evidence to the men.

Where can I see Jesus’ works today? In the written record first, given for this very purpose (20:31). But also in what he goes on doing by his Spirit through his church: sinners converted, drunkards made sober, enemies reconciled, the dying unafraid, the gospel spreading through every nation as he said it would. These are not new revelations, and they do not replace Scripture; but they are the living fruit of the finished work, and they bear witness too. Look for them, and tell others what you have seen.

parallels.desc: the Father’s voice at the baptism

verseByVerse.quote: "His voice you have never heard, his form you have never seen, and you do not have his word abiding in you, for you do not believe the one whom he has sent."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Never heard, never seen. Here the discourse turns, and it should be felt as an insult before it is understood as a diagnosis. He is telling the most religiously accomplished men in the nation, whose lives were organised around the word of God, that they have never heard God’s voice, never seen his form, and do not have his word living in them. At Sinai, Israel heard God’s voice and saw no form (Deuteronomy 4:12); his likeness is now visible in Jesus (14:9).

But Israel heard God’s voice at Sinai, and Moses saw his glory. What does Jesus mean? Jesus is not denying that; he is saying that these hearers have not truly heard or seen, since his word does not abide in them (v. 38). And no one has seen the Father as he is (1:18; Exodus 33:20); the appearances of God in the Old Testament were real but partial, and many believe they were appearances of the Son himself.

His word abiding in you. The phrase looks ahead to the vine (15:4, 7). What these men lack is not information about God, which they had in quantity, but God’s word taking up residence. It is possible to have the whole text and none of the tenancy.

You do not believe. The proof: when the Word of God stood in front of them they did not recognise him. The Father’s self-disclosure runs through the Son, so a relationship with God that bypasses Jesus is not a different route to the same place.

The trial has changed sides. It opened with Jesus in the dock; now the men who convened the hearing are being examined. And the finding against them is not that they weighed the evidence wrongly. The evidence was never the problem.

Why do good arguments sometimes change nothing? Because the difficulty is not always in the evidence. Anyone who has argued about the faith with someone they love knows the experience of watching a good case land on nothing. It is tempting to conclude that a better argument would have done it. Sometimes that is true, and the argument is worth improving. But this verse says there is a condition in which no quantity of evidence will be enough, because the problem lies in the heart. Knowing that keeps a person praying for someone, and not merely preparing for the next conversation. Only God can open the heart (Acts 16:14).

parallels.desc: you heard the sound of words, but saw no form

verseByVerse.quote: "You search the Scriptures because you think that in them you have eternal life; and it is they that bear witness about me, yet you refuse to come to me that you may have life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You search the Scriptures. They studied the Old Testament with great diligence; later Jewish tradition remembers scribes counting its letters. They were serious Bible students.

Command or statement? It can be read as a command, Search the Scriptures, as the King James Version has it, and searching is rightly commended elsewhere (Acts 17:11). But the context favours a statement: they were searching, and missing the one the Scriptures spoke of.

In them. A saying attributed to Hillel runs: the more study of the law, the more life (Mishnah Avot 2:7). The sentence turns on a preposition they got wrong: in them. The life was understood to be located in the text, obtainable by handling it. Jesus does not deny that the Scriptures give life. He denies the address.

They bear witness about me. The purpose of Scripture is to point to Christ (Luke 24:27, 44). The Scriptures are the fourth witness in his case, and no one calls a witness so that the court may admire the witness.

You refuse to come. Life is not in the Bible itself, but in the one to whom it points. The problem was their will: not you cannot, not you have not understood, but you refuse. Men bent over scrolls for a lifetime, tracing every promise of the one who was to come, and he stands in the room, having just healed a man in front of them. The distance between the text and the person was a few feet, and they would not cross it.

How does you refuse to come fit with No one can come to me unless the Father draws him? The inability is not that people want to come and are prevented, but that their wills are bound by love of themselves and their own glory (v. 44). They cannot because they will not, and that is why they are responsible. Only the Father’s drawing changes the will (6:44).

Am I in danger of reading the Bible like this? This is aimed at people who read their Bibles, so it is better felt than pointed at someone else. A person can conduct a serious study of Scripture as a closed system: to enjoy tracing themes, resolving difficulties, the satisfaction of a passage finally coming clear, and for the whole exercise to end in itself. The pleasure is real; it feels like devotion; and it can go on for years without once arriving at a person. The remedy is not to study less but to study prayerfully, asking at every passage: what does this show me of Christ, and how will I come to him because of it?

On a Tuesday. After the last passage you studied, did you end up knowing something, or wanting him? Both can be good. Only one is what the text was for.

verseByVerse.quote: "I do not receive glory from people. But I know that you do not have the love of God within you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I do not receive glory from people. He seeks his Father’s glory (7:18; 8:50). He has no stake in their good opinion, so his assessment of them is not coloured by what he needs from them, and a man who wants nothing from you is the only one who can tell you the truth about yourself.

The love of God within you. Love for God, or God’s love: the Greek permits both, and in this Gospel the two are never far apart. Despite their religiousness, they did not love God; if they did, they would love the one he sent (8:42). They are not mainly failing a logical test but a love test. To have the love of God within you is for God himself to have become your joy, so that you are glad when he is honoured and grieved when he is not (Matthew 22:37), the one thing no amount of religious activity can counterfeit.

Why this sentence is frightening. It is frightening precisely because these men would have passed every other test. Attendance, orthodoxy, knowledge of the text, moral seriousness, faithful keeping of the feasts: all in order. What was missing does not show up on any of those instruments. And it explains the whole chapter. They had watched a man paralysed for decades get up and walk, and their first and only response was a rule about carrying. Nothing in them leapt. A person who loves God is not able to watch God do something and feel only procedural concern; the loving gets in the way. Their reaction was not a failure of information. It was the accurate reading of an instrument that registered nothing because there was nothing to register.

What if I fear this describes me? Then take an honest comfort from it. The men in this passage were entirely untroubled by the question. The very anxiety a verse like this produces in you is a form of caring, and caring is not what is being diagnosed here. And the remedy, if it is needed, is not to work up an affection. Love for God is not manufactured by an effort of will. It is what happens when a person actually sees him, which is precisely what Jesus spent this chapter offering. We love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). Look at his love for you in Christ, and ask the Spirit to pour God’s love into your heart (Romans 5:5).

verseByVerse.quote: "I have come in my Father's name, and you do not receive me. If another comes in his own name, you will receive him. How can you believe, when you receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
In my Father’s name. He comes with his Father’s authority, representing him, and he is rejected: his own people did not receive him (1:11).

Another in his own name. False messiahs who came on their own authority were often welcomed; in AD 132 Simon bar Kokhba led a disastrous revolt, and Rabbi Akiba is said to have hailed him as Messiah. The man who arrives sent, pointing away from himself, requires submission to someone the follower did not choose; the man whose warrant is himself flatters the follower’s judgement.

Glory from one another. The root of their unbelief: love of human praise (12:42–43). Glory here means reputation, the opinion others hold of you. So the sentence describes a closed economy. These men held a currency they issued to each other: standing, deference, the seat at the front, the title in the street, the respect of colleagues who were the only people qualified to grant it. And that currency had a fatal property. It could only be earned from the people inside the system, which means it could only be kept by not leaving. Belief in Jesus would have cost every one of them everything the system paid. A man cannot pursue two kinds of honour issued by different authorities that exclude each other. He will take the one he is nearer to.

And do not seek the glory that comes from the only God? God’s approval is the only honour that matters. The way out is in the same verse. He does not tell them to want no approval at all. He tells them they are seeking it from a bankrupt issuer. The glory that comes from the only God is real, and Christ will one day say to his servants, well done.

Is it wrong to care what people think of me? Not entirely: a good name is valued (Proverbs 22:1), but people’s opinion must not decide what you will say and do about Christ (Proverbs 29:25), and in Christ God’s approval is already yours. (See Luke 16:14 for the fuller answer.)

On a Tuesday. Think of the decisions you would make differently if nobody you respected ever found out: what you would say in a meeting, which opinion you would voice, whether you would mention Christ in a particular room. That gap is the size of the account you hold in the currency of verse 44. But in Christ the only God has already given you his approval, and it is not withdrawn when you fail.

parallels.desc: Theudas and Judas the Galilean

verseByVerse.quote: "Do not think that I will accuse you to the Father. There is one who accuses you: Moses, on whom you have set your hope. For if you believed Moses, you would believe me; for he wrote of me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will not accuse you. The reversal is complete. They convened this hearing and have been the prosecution throughout. Now the defendant says he will not prosecute. For one second it sounds like mercy, and then the sentence finishes.

One who accuses you. Moses, the giver of the law they trusted, the name that gave them standing, will be their prosecutor. The law they thought would save them will condemn them (Romans 3:19–20).

He wrote of me. Moses wrote of Christ: the seed of the woman (Genesis 3:15), the offspring of Abraham (Genesis 22:18), the Passover lamb (Exodus 12), the bronze serpent (Numbers 21:9; John 3:14), the prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15–18). And the claim is larger than a few predictions: the whole body of his writing was about him, the tabernacle and the glory that filled it, the priest who went in with blood once a year, the rock that gave water, each written by a man who saw only part of what he was describing.

What Moses was for. So the disagreement in this room is not between a Jewish teacher and a Christian innovation, but about what Moses was for. Jesus does not set Moses aside as a preliminary stage. He claims him as his own witness and tells the men holding the scrolls that they have misread the author they built their lives on.

Did Moses really write the first five books? Jesus treats it as settled that Moses wrote (compare Mark 12:26; Luke 24:27, 44), and he means the books of the law. That need not mean Moses wrote every line: the account of his death (Deuteronomy 34) was plainly added by another hand, and many believing scholars allow for some later editing; but Jesus treats the law as Moses’ own testimony. Where did Moses write of him? Beyond the pictures already named, in the ruler from Judah (Genesis 49:10), and above all in the prophet like Moses: the LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me (Deuteronomy 18:15).

parallels.desc: a witness against you

verseByVerse.quote: "But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words? They claimed to honour Moses, but did not truly believe what he wrote. If they will not believe the written Scriptures they revere, they will not believe Jesus’ spoken words. Faith in Scripture and faith in Christ stand or fall together. Jesus places his own words alongside Scripture. The chapter ends on a question, and it is left unanswered, which is the point, since the answer would have to come from the men it was asked of. The logic is simple. Moses wrote of Christ. They do not believe Christ. Therefore they do not, in any sense that matters, believe Moses, whatever they think they are doing when they read him.

The problem is not the medium. People who will not be persuaded by Scripture are not waiting for a better delivery. They had the writings, the works, the Baptist, the Father’s testimony, and the man himself, available for questions.

Stand back and see the whole chapter. It opened with a man who could not get himself to the water, who had nobody, and he was made whole. It closes with the most scripturally literate men in the nation, who had every witness heaven could produce, and would not come. Between the two lies the sentence that explains both: the Son gives life to whom he will.

Should I trust the Old Testament as much as the words of Jesus? Yes. Jesus puts Moses’ writings and his own words side by side, and treats doubting one as the road to doubting the other. He believed the Old Testament to be the word of God, quoted it as settling arguments, and said Scripture cannot be broken (10:35). The whole Bible is one book with one Author and one subject. The Old Testament is not a lesser Bible to be outgrown; it is the testimony to Christ that Jesus himself used. Read both Testaments with the same trust, because the Lord you love trusted both.

5.title: The Son Has Life in Himself
5.text: <sup>1</sup>After this there was a feast of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.<sup>2</sup>Now there is in Jerusalem by the Sheep Gate a pool, in Aramaic called Bethesda, which has five roofed colonnades.<sup>3</sup>In these lay a multitude of invalids—blind, lame, and paralyzed.<sup>5</sup>One man was there who had been an invalid for thirty-eight years.<sup>6</sup>When Jesus saw him lying there and knew that he had already been there a long time, he said to him, “Do you want to be healed?”<sup>7</sup>The sick man answered him, “Sir, I have no one to put me into the pool when the water is stirred up, and while I am going another steps down before me.”<sup>8</sup>Jesus said to him, “Get up, take up your bed, and walk.”<sup>9</sup>And at once the man was healed, and he took up his bed and walked. Now that day was the Sabbath.<sup>10</sup>So the Jews said to the man who had been healed, “It is the Sabbath, and it is not lawful for you to take up your bed.”<sup>11</sup>But he answered them, “The man who healed me, that man said to me, ’Take up your bed, and walk.’”<sup>12</sup>They asked him, “Who is the man who said to you, ’Take up your bed and walk’?”<sup>13</sup>Now the man who had been healed did not know who it was, for Jesus had withdrawn, as there was a crowd in the place.<sup>14</sup>Afterward Jesus found him in the temple and said to him, “See, you are well! Sin no more, that nothing worse may happen to you.”<sup>15</sup>The man went away and told the Jews that it was Jesus who had healed him.<sup>16</sup>And this was why the Jews were persecuting Jesus, because he was doing these things on the Sabbath.<sup>17</sup>But Jesus answered them, “My Father is working until now, and I am working.”<sup>18</sup>This was why the Jews were seeking all the more to kill him, because not only was he breaking the Sabbath, but he was even calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God.<sup>19</sup>So Jesus said to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, the Son can do nothing of his own accord, but only what he sees the Father doing. For whatever the Father does, that the Son does likewise.<sup>20</sup>For the Father loves the Son and shows him all that he himself is doing. And greater works than these will he show him, so that you may marvel.<sup>21</sup>For as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he will.<sup>22</sup>For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son,<sup>23</sup>that all may honor the Son, just as they honor the Father. Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him.<sup>24</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life. He does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life.<sup>25</sup>“Truly, truly, I say to you, an hour is coming, and is now here, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live.<sup>26</sup>For as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself.<sup>27</sup>And he has given him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man.<sup>28</sup>Do not marvel at this, for an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice<sup>29</sup>and come out, those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment.<sup>30</sup>“I can do nothing on my own. As I hear, I judge, and my judgment is just, because I seek not my own will but the will of him who sent me.<sup>31</sup>If I alone bear witness about myself, my testimony is not true.<sup>32</sup>There is another who bears witness about me, and I know that the testimony that he bears about me is true.<sup>33</sup>You sent to John, and he has borne witness to the truth.<sup>34</sup>Not that the testimony that I receive is from man, but I say these things so that you may be saved.<sup>35</sup>He was a burning and shining lamp, and you were willing to rejoice for a while in his light.<sup>36</sup>But the testimony that I have is greater than that of John. For the works that the Father has given me to accomplish, the very works that I am doing, bear witness about me that the Father has sent me.<sup>37</sup>And the Father who sent me has himself borne witness about me. His voice you have never heard, his form you have never seen,<sup>38</sup>and you do not have his word abiding in you, for you do not believe the one whom he has sent.<sup>39</sup>You search the Scriptures because you think that in them you have eternal life; and it is they that bear witness about me,<sup>40</sup>yet you refuse to come to me that you may have life.<sup>41</sup>I do not receive glory from people.<sup>42</sup>But I know that you do not have the love of God within you.<sup>43</sup>I have come in my Father’s name, and you do not receive me. If another comes in his own name, you will receive him.<sup>44</sup>How can you believe, when you receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?<sup>45</sup>Do not think that I will accuse you to the Father. There is one who accuses you: Moses, on whom you have set your hope.<sup>46</sup>For if you believed Moses, you would believe me; for he wrote of me.<sup>47</sup>But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?”
5.overview:
The third sign takes place in Jerusalem at the pool of Bethesda. Jesus heals a man who has been an invalid for thirty-eight years, unasked, and tells him to carry his mat on the Sabbath. The authorities object, and when Jesus answers that his Father is working and so is he, they understand him exactly: he is making himself equal with God, and they now seek to kill him.

His reply (vv. 19–47) is one of the fullest statements in the Gospels of who he is. The Son does what the Father does, gives life to whom he will, holds all judgment, and is to be honoured as the Father is. Then, as in a courtroom, he calls his witnesses: John the Baptist, his works, the Father and the Scriptures. The men who searched the Scriptures most carefully would not come to the one they spoke of.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — Feeding the Five Thousand and Walking on Water
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The feeding on the hillside and the crossing of the lake at night form a pair: Jesus provides more than enough from a boy’s lunch and refuses a forced crown, then comes to his disciples over the dark water and tells them who he is.
verseByVerse.theology: Together the two signs show Jesus as Lord of provision and Lord of the sea. His words on the water, “It is I” (v. 20), are the words behind the divine name, and they lead into the first of the great I am sayings later in the chapter. The crowd that wants to crown him misreads the sign: they want the bread without the one who gives it.
verseByVerse.examples: Philip’s sum was correct; his mistake was to answer a question about where with a calculation of how much. And walking on the sea is the most revealing of the nature miracles: in the Old Testament the sea is the realm only God commands (Job 9:8; Psalm 77:19).

verseByVerse.quote: After this Jesus went away to the other side of the Sea of Galilee, which is the Sea of Tiberias. And a large crowd was following him, because they saw the signs that he was doing on the sick.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. John 6 is the chapter of the bread. Near Passover Jesus feeds five thousand, refuses a crown, walks on the sea, and next day explains the sign: he himself is the true bread from heaven, of which the manna was a shadow, his flesh given for the life of the world and received by faith. The crowd thins to a handful, and Peter confesses: Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life.

The only miracle in all four Gospels. Apart from the resurrection, the feeding of the five thousand is the only miracle of Jesus recorded in all four Gospels.

The Sea of Tiberias. Another name for the Sea of Galilee, after the city Herod Antipas built on its western shore around AD 20 and named after the emperor Tiberius.

In the flow. Jesus had just told the leaders in Jerusalem that Moses wrote of him (5:46). Chapter 6 is full of Moses: Passover, a mountain, bread in the wilderness, a crossing of the sea, a grumbling people and a demand for manna. At every point Jesus is shown to be not the one who passes on bread from heaven, but the bread himself. It begins with the largest crowd of his ministry and ends with a handful, and shows that the signs alone do not make disciples.

Because they saw the signs. They followed for the miracles, not for who he was (v. 26), which is a reasonable thing to want and is not yet faith. Between this crowd and the emptying synagogue at the end of the chapter lies no scandal and no change of policy, only a sermon. The crowd shrinks because he explains himself.

Signs point to the one who gives them. In this Gospel a sign is never an end in itself (20:30–31). The healings were the old promises coming true (Isaiah 35:5–6). So the crowd was right to follow the signs and wrong to stop at them: every healing was a finger pointing at the healer, and this chapter is the day he tells them what the finger was pointing at.

He fed them anyway. They were following for the wrong reason, and he fed them anyway. He did not begin by correcting their motives; he began by giving them lunch. The rebuke comes the next morning.

Is it wrong if I first came to Christ for what I needed from him? No; almost nobody arrives for adequate reasons. People come because something hurts, a marriage is failing, a child is ill, or the fear of dying has become concrete, and every one of those is a version of wanting the loaves. It is where practically everyone starts, and this chapter does not despise it. Jesus received the crowd and fed them. What he will not do is leave anyone there. The question is not why you first came, but whether you are now coming to him for himself.
verseByVerse.note: The Sea of Tiberias is another name for the Sea of Galilee, from the city Herod Antipas built on its western shore and named after the emperor Tiberius.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus went up on the mountain, and there he sat down with his disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus went up on the mountain. The hills east of the lake, and an echo of Moses going up the mountain (Exodus 19; 24).

He sat down with his disciples. The posture of a teacher (Matthew 5:1). But what follows on this mountain is a meal. That is the order the chapter runs on: the bread first and the explanation second, and the crowd delighted by the first is offended by the second. It is possible to enjoy what Christ does and find what he says intolerable.

Withdrawal at both ends. He goes up the mountain before the crowd arrives, and goes up again by himself after they have gone (v. 15), Mark tells us for prayer (Mark 6:46).

Greater than Moses on the mountain. Moses went up to receive what God gave and came down to pass it on; he was faithful as a servant in God’s house (Hebrews 3:5). Jesus goes up and sits, the posture of one with authority of his own, and what follows will come from his own hands. John said it on his first page: the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ (1:17). Moses could only tell Israel where the manna came from. This teacher will feed them himself, and then tell them that he is the bread.

How can I find time to be alone with God when life is so full? Jesus’ days were fuller than yours, with crowds pressing on him and needs everywhere, and he still withdrew. It was not a luxury for him but a habit. Begin small and regular: a set time, a set place, a Bible and a few minutes of prayer, even if it is in the car before work or after the children are asleep. Protect it as you would a meeting with someone you love. The aim is not a perfect routine but real fellowship with the Father, which feeds everything else you do.

For worship. When God came down on Sinai, the mountain was fenced and the people begged not to hear his voice again (Exodus 19:12; 20:19). On a Galilean hill the same Lord sat down in the grass with fishermen around him. His people have not come to a mountain that burns but to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant (Hebrews 12:18–24).

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Passover, the feast of the Jews, was at hand. Lifting up his eyes, then, and seeing that a large crowd was coming toward him, Jesus said to Philip, "Where are we to buy bread, so that these people may eat?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the Passover was at hand. The second of the three Passovers John mentions (2:13; 11:55), and it colours the whole chapter: the feast of unleavened bread and a lamb killed, and behind it the memory of bread that came down morning by morning for forty years. At the next Passover Jesus would give his flesh for the life of the world (v. 51), dying as the Passover lamb (19:36).

A large crowd coming. Jesus sees the need, and he moves first. Nobody requests a meal; in Matthew and Mark the disciples even suggest sending everyone away.

Jesus said to Philip. Philip was from Bethsaida, nearby (1:44); he might be expected to know where food could be bought. Jesus asks the local man.

Where are we to buy bread, so that these people may eat? An echo of Moses: Where am I to get meat to give to all this people? (Numbers 11:13). And note the pronoun: we. He does not say they. He includes Philip in a responsibility Philip has not accepted and could not discharge. That is how the test is set: not by asking Philip to do the impossible, but by quietly making the crowd’s hunger his problem too.

Does Jesus expect me to meet needs I cannot possibly meet? He expects you to care about them and to bring them to him. He does not expect you to supply what only he can. The pronoun we means Philip is included in the work, not left to do it alone. When you see a need too big for you, the hungry, the lonely, the lost, do not look away and do not despair. Bring it to Christ in prayer, offer what you have, and do the part he gives you. He knows what he will do.
verseByVerse.note: This is the second Passover John mentions; the Passover setting prepares for Jesus’ words about bread and his flesh and blood.

verseByVerse.quote: He said this to test him, for he himself knew what he would do. Philip answered him, "Two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be enough for each of them to get a little."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said this to test him. To stretch Philip’s faith. Would he look to his own resources, or to Jesus?

He himself knew. John’s bracket is one of the kindest in the Gospel. The test was not an audition he could fail at the cost of the crowd’s dinner. It was a question asked by someone who had already decided, so that the man being asked might find out what was in him.

Two hundred denarii. The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage; two hundred denarii was about eight months’ wages. Philip calculated, and despaired. He looked at the problem, not at Jesus. His answer deserves to be heard fairly: the sum is correct. His problem is not his arithmetic. It is that he was asked where and answered how much. The question was about a source; he replied with a budget. A man who converts every question about God’s provision into a question about available resources will always arrive at the same answer, and it will always be right, and always beside the point.

Why does God test us if he already knows what is in us? Not to inform himself, but to show us, and to strengthen us. The tests God sets are not entrance examinations with the result pending. He knows what he will do. The examination exists so that the person taking it discovers where his own arithmetic runs out, which is knowledge he needs and cannot get any other way. Testing also proves and refines faith, as gold is refined by fire (1 Peter 1:6–7). And God never tests in order to make his children fall (James 1:13); he tests in order to make them stand.

On a Tuesday. Is there a situation you have been treating as a budget problem rather than a question about God? Do the sums, by all means; then ask where the bread will come from.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage; two hundred denarii was most of a year’s wages.

parallels.desc: where am I to get meat?

verseByVerse.quote: One of his disciples, Andrew, Simon Peter's brother, said to him, "There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish, but what are they for so many?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Five barley loaves. Only John mentions the boy and the barley. Barley loaves were the cheap bread of the poor: a child’s packed lunch of the plainest kind. The fish were probably small dried or pickled fish.

The Elisha story underneath. An echo of Elisha (2 Kings 4:42–44): twenty barley loaves, a servant who objected, how can I set this before a hundred men?, a command to give, and food left over. Andrew’s sentence is almost the servant’s, and any Jew who knew his Scriptures would have felt it. What differs is the scale, and the source. Elisha fed a hundred from twenty loaves; here it is five thousand from five. And Elisha spoke as a messenger, for thus says the LORD, they shall eat and have some left (2 Kings 4:43). Jesus quotes no one. He gives thanks, and the bread multiplies in his own hands. The prophet passed on the word of God; this man is the Word, and the bread is his to give.

But what are they for so many? Andrew is again bringing someone to Jesus, as he brought his brother (1:41) and will bring the Greeks (12:22). Andrew brought what there was, even though it seemed useless. That is all Jesus asks. Look at what Andrew actually does, because he is easy to patronise for the second half of his sentence. He is the only person in the passage who has gone and looked. Philip did the sum; Andrew went through the crowd and found out what was actually there. And he brings it, knowing it is absurd, saying so out loud, and bringing it anyway. That is not weak faith. It is the posture the chapter requires: hands out, holding something insufficient, with no idea what will happen.

What if what I have to offer seems ridiculously small? Then you are in good company: a boy with five cheap loaves. Jesus does not ask for enough; he asks for what you have. Your few hours, your small gift, your weak prayers, your stumbling words to a friend: put them in his hands and let him decide what they are for. The miracle did not begin with abundance but with an offering. Nothing in the Gospels suggests Jesus wanted the disciples to feel confident. He wanted the loaves.
verseByVerse.note: Barley loaves were the cheap bread of the poor.

parallels.desc: Elisha feeds a hundred men with twenty barley loaves

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said, "Have the people sit down." Now there was much grass in the place. So the men sat down, about five thousand in number. Jesus then took the loaves, and when he had given thanks, he distributed them to those who were seated. So also the fish, as much as they wanted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Have the people sit down. The word means recline, as guests do at a banquet. About five thousand men sat, and with women and children many more (Matthew 14:21).

Much grass. Grass in Galilee means spring, at Passover, and it turns a hillside into a dining room: green pastures (Psalm 23:2). Mark says Jesus had compassion on them because they were like sheep without a shepherd (Mark 6:34). Four chapters later Jesus will say, I am the good shepherd.

And when he had given thanks. Eucharistēsas, the word the church would take for its central meal. John mentions only thanksgiving, not breaking, perhaps pointing to the Lord’s Supper, which he does not otherwise describe. He probably said a blessing like the one Jewish households still say before eating, whose core is recorded in the Mishnah (Berakhot 6:1): blessed are you, Lord our God, king of the universe, who brings forth bread from the earth. It is one of the most ordinary sentences in Jewish life. He says it over five loaves in front of five thousand people, and it turns out to be true in a way it had never been before.

He distributed them. The other Gospels tell us the disciples carried the food to the crowd; some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV and NKJV, add it here, but the earliest copies of John do not. John keeps every eye on Jesus: the bread came from his hands, the picture the chapter will explain when he says the bread he gives is his flesh (v. 51).

As much as they wanted. Not a small piece each, which is what Philip had calculated could not be managed, but every person eating until they stopped wanting more.

Should Christians still give thanks before meals? Yes, and this verse is one reason why. Jesus gave thanks before he gave the bread, and Paul says that everything created by God is good and is made holy by the word of God and prayer (1 Timothy 4:4–5). A short prayer at the table is not a superstition or a formality. It is a confession that every meal comes from the Father’s hand, and it keeps us from eating like the crowd, who enjoyed the bread and never looked up at the giver.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had eaten their fill, he told his disciples, "Gather up the leftover fragments, that nothing may be lost." So they gathered them up and filled twelve baskets with fragments from the five barley loaves left by those who had eaten.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That nothing may be lost. Only John records this command. God’s abundance is not wasteful.

Extravagance and care. The man who made the meal could make another, and the first thing he says after five thousand have eaten is: pick up the bits. Extravagance and carefulness are not opposites in him. He minds.

The word lost. The verb is apollymi, to be destroyed or lost, and it runs through the rest of the chapter and out into the Gospel. In a few verses Jesus will say the Father’s will is that he should lose nothing of all the Father has given him (v. 39). In chapter 18, when the soldiers come, John says this fulfilled the word: of those whom you gave me I have lost not one (18:9). So the barley crusts in the grass are the first instalment of a promise about people. The one who sends men round a hillside so that a scrap of a poor child’s lunch is not wasted is the one who will not lose a single person the Father has given him.

Twelve baskets. More left over than at the start; perhaps one for each apostle, and perhaps a hint of the twelve tribes. The arithmetic of the kingdom: what is handed over comes back larger.

What if I feel like a scrap, not worth keeping? Then this verse was written for you. Jesus sent his disciples to gather fragments, crumbs that anyone else would have let lie in the grass, so that nothing would be lost. If he cares for crusts, he cares far more for the people the Father has given him. Your worth to him does not depend on how whole or impressive you feel, but on his love and his promise. He does not lose what is his.

verseByVerse.quote: When the people saw the sign that he had done, they said, "This is indeed the Prophet who is to come into the world!" Perceiving then that they were about to come and take him by force to make him king, Jesus withdrew again to the mountain by himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Prophet. The prophet like Moses whom Moses promised (Deuteronomy 18:15). They had identified the man correctly and misunderstood him entirely. Being right about who Jesus is and wrong about what he is for sent five thousand people up a hill with a crown.

To make him king. A political Messiah, to lead a revolt against Rome, at the feast of liberation. The verb is violent: harpazein, to seize, used of a wolf carrying off a sheep (10:12). He is in real danger here, not from the authorities but from an adoring mob who have decided what he is for.

Jesus withdrew again. He refused. His kingdom is not of this world (18:36). It is the temptation Satan offered in the wilderness (Matthew 4:8–10): a crown without a cross. And what he refuses is not the kingship. He is the King, and he will say so to Pilate. He refuses a kingship on their terms: a bread-king, installed by acclaim, who solves the food problem and then the Roman problem and never goes near a cross. The largest crowd of his ministry wanted to crown him, and he walked away from them up a hill in the dark to talk with his Father.

Is it wrong to want Jesus to solve my problems? It is not wrong to bring him your problems; he invites it. It is wrong to try to make him king on your terms, a Saviour who exists to deliver your agenda. The crowd wanted bread and political freedom and no cross. Jesus will give far more than they asked, but in his way: through his death, by his Spirit, for eternity. When he does not do what you want, it is not because he cannot, but because he is King, and his plans are better.

For worship. He would not be crowned by a crowd, because he had come to be crowned with thorns. He refused the throne of bread so that he could take the throne of the cross, and from there the throne of heaven.
verseByVerse.note: “The Prophet” is the prophet like Moses whom Moses promised. Many hoped for a Messiah who would lead a revolt against Rome.

parallels.desc: my kingdom is not of this world

verseByVerse.quote: When evening came, his disciples went down to the sea, got into a boat, and started across the sea to Capernaum. It was now dark, and Jesus had not yet come to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His disciples went down to the sea. Mark says Jesus made them go (Mark 6:45), perhaps to remove them from the crowd’s political excitement.

It was now dark. In John, darkness often carries more than the time of day (3:2; 13:30). The weather on the lake is real, not an allegory, but a reader of this Gospel cannot hear that it was dark and Jesus had not yet come without remembering its first page: the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it (1:5). Later Jesus will say, I am the light of the world; whoever follows me will not walk in darkness (8:12). So John lets the night on the lake say what his whole Gospel says: the disciples’ darkness is measured by his absence, and it will end, not at sunrise, but when he reaches them.

Jesus had not yet come. Two facts sit side by side, and the Gospel does not soften either. They are exactly where they should be, doing exactly what they were told. And it is dark, and he is not there. John does not write that Jesus had not come and therefore it was dark, as though the absence caused the darkness.

Not yet. The last words make it bearable. John writes decades later and knows how the night ended. He puts the yet in deliberately, and it is the only comfort in the sentence: not that the darkness is short, or that it means something, but that his absence has a term on it.

From the best day to the worst night. They are coming down off the best day of their lives, five thousand fed and a crowd trying to crown their master, and that evening they are alone on black water. Anyone who has had a high Sunday followed by a Monday will recognise the geography.

Why does God sometimes seem absent when I am trying to obey him? Because seeming absent is not the same as being absent. The disciples were in the boat by his command, and he had gone up the mountain to pray (Mark 6:46–48), and he saw them in the dark. Scripture is honest that believers pass through seasons when God feels far away (Psalm 13:1; 88). In them, keep rowing in the direction he sent you, keep to his word and prayer, and remember the yet. He has not forgotten you, and he will come.

verseByVerse.quote: The sea became rough because a strong wind was blowing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sea became rough. One sentence, with no dramatics. The lake sits about seven hundred feet below sea level in a bowl of hills, and cold air spilling down the ravines produces squalls with little warning. This is not a supernatural assault. It is the weather, and the men rowing into it were professionals.

Sometimes the wind is simply the wind. It does not say the storm came because they had done wrong, or to teach them a lesson. Much harm is done by assuming every hardship in a Christian life is a message. In a world under the curse things break and boats get caught out on lakes, and being in the middle of obeying God when it happens is not evidence of anything.

The wind he made. All things were made through the Word (1:3), the wind that night among them. It was never beyond his reach or notice, and in a few minutes he would walk on top of the water it was stirring.

Is every hardship in my life a sign that God is displeased with me? No. God does discipline his children in love (Hebrews 12:6), and sometimes trouble is the fruit of our own sin. But many hardships are simply part of life in a fallen world, and God uses them for our good without their being punishments (Romans 8:28). The disciples were in the storm because they obeyed. So do not torment yourself trying to decode every trial. Confess any sin you know of, trust your Father’s love, and look for the Lord who comes across the water.
verseByVerse.note: The Sea of Galilee lies low and ringed by hills; sudden strong winds are common.

verseByVerse.quote: When they had rowed about three or four miles, they saw Jesus walking on the sea and coming near the boat, and they were frightened. But he said to them, "It is I; do not be afraid."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three or four miles. The ESV notes that the distance is literally twenty-five or thirty stadia: roughly halfway across. Mark says the wind was against them (Mark 6:48).

Walking on the sea. In the Old Testament, God alone treads on the waves of the sea (Job 9:8; Psalm 77:19). The sea pictures chaos. Jesus walks on it as its master. And Mark, describing this night, says he meant to pass by them (Mark 6:48), which sounds like indifference until you know that passing by is the language of God showing himself, as he passed by Moses in the cleft of the rock (Exodus 33:22) and Elijah at the cave (1 Kings 19:11). It is a man doing, in front of witnesses, the specific thing the Old Testament says God does.

And they were frightened. Their terror was the right response, and John records it without embarrassment. When the holy God draws near, the right first response of sinful creatures is fear (Isaiah 6:5). The comfort that follows means something only because the fear was real.

It is I. Literally I am (egō eimi), the divine name (Exodus 3:14; Isaiah 43:10–11). It is an ordinary way of saying it is me, and translators are right to render it so. It is also the two words behind the burning bush, on which this Gospel will build seven declarations, spoken by a man standing on a lake in a gale.

Do not be afraid. God’s word to his people throughout Scripture (Isaiah 43:1–2). They are not told there is nothing to fear. They are told who it is, and the reason to stop being afraid is that the one on the water is the one whose sea it is.

Did Jesus really walk on water, or is this a story with a spiritual meaning? He really did. John presents it as something that happened, seen by the disciples, on a particular night, at a measured distance from shore. The spiritual meaning depends on the event: it shows who Jesus is precisely because he did what only God does. If the Word made flesh could make bread out of five loaves and raise the dead, walking on the water he created is no difficulty. To make it a mere symbol is to lose the very thing it reveals.

On a Tuesday. Name the thing you are most afraid of this week. Then say to yourself the words he said on the lake, and notice that he does not promise the thing will not happen. He tells you who is coming toward you across it.

For worship. The voice that said It is I over the black water of Galilee is the voice that will say I am he in a garden at night, and armed men will draw back and fall to the ground (18:5–6). The same words flatten those who come against him and quieten those he comes to save. A man walked across the top of a storm to reach a boatload of tired men, none of whom had asked him to come, and the first thing he said was not a rebuke but his name. He needs no introduction but that name, and he makes it his people’s peace.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the distance is literally twenty-five or thirty stadia. “It is I” can also be heard as the divine name, “I am.”

verseByVerse.quote: Then they were glad to take him into the boat, and immediately the boat was at the land to which they were going.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Glad to take him. Or they wanted to take him: either way, fear has turned to gladness.

Immediately at the land. Perhaps a further miracle. Psalm 107 describes men at sea whose courage melts; they cry to the LORD, he makes the storm be still, and he brings them to their desired haven (Psalm 107:23–30). John does not quote the psalm, but a reader who knows it will hear it.

The shape, not the mechanics. They had rowed for hours and covered half a lake. He steps in, and the journey is over. Everything they had achieved by straining was real and was not enough; what finished it was his presence in the boat.

Does this mean my troubles will disappear if I have enough faith? No, and the passage itself guards against that. This crossing had a storm, hours of useless rowing and real fear, and none of it was cancelled afterwards. The rowing still happened. What the verse says is that the arrival did not finally depend on it. Christ does not promise that faith will make difficulties evaporate. He promises to be with his people in them, and to bring them home at last.

parallels.desc: he brought them to their desired haven

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–71 — The Bread of Life Discourse
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the synagogue at Capernaum Jesus explains the sign: he is the bread of life, given in death and received by faith. The discourse thins the crowd to a handful, and Peter’s confession closes the chapter, with the warning that one of the Twelve will betray him.
verseByVerse.theology: The key to the eating language is Jesus’ own explanation: it is the Spirit who gives life, and the flesh is no help at all (v. 63). To eat his flesh and drink his blood is not physical eating but receiving his atoning death by faith, and the Lord’s Supper is a visible form of that same feeding. Alongside it the chapter sets the sovereignty of grace: no one comes unless the Father draws him, all whom the Father gives will come, and all who come will be raised on the last day. Grace and the call to believe are held together throughout.
verseByVerse.examples: The departure of many disciples (v. 66) shows that following Jesus for his gifts is not the same as believing in him. Peter’s answer is the model for anyone facing a hard saying: when you cannot fully understand what Jesus says, you stay because of who he is, and because no one else has the words of eternal life.

verseByVerse.quote: On the next day the crowd that remained on the other side of the sea saw that there had been only one boat there, and that Jesus had not entered the boat with his disciples, but that his disciples had gone away alone. Other boats from Tiberias came near the place where they had eaten the bread after the Lord had given thanks.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd saw that there had been only one boat. They had counted the boats: he cannot have crossed the lake. Then they cross it themselves and find him on the other side, and instead of stopping where they stood they open with a question about his timetable. It is possible to be extremely observant about Jesus and entirely incurious.

Other boats from Tiberias. Perhaps blown across by the storm.

After the Lord had given thanks. John’s own aside calls Jesus the Lord, a title he rarely uses of him during the ministry, and stresses the thanksgiving, writing to churches that gave thanks over bread every week.

The Lord who gave thanks. In this Gospel the Lord is what Mary Magdalene calls the risen Jesus (20:18) and what Thomas confesses (20:28). The man who bowed his head over five loaves and thanked his Father, as any son of Israel would, is the Lord whom the church worships. He gave thanks as a man, and he receives thanks as God.

Can I be interested in Jesus without really knowing him? Very easily, and this crowd shows how. They paid close attention to where he was, worked out the clues, and travelled to find him, and every bit of it was directed at the surface. Many people today read about Jesus, discuss him, even admire him, without ever asking the question his actions force: who is this, that he does what only God does? The cure is to stop treating him as a puzzle and come to him as a person, asking him to show you himself.

verseByVerse.quote: So when the crowd saw that Jesus was not there, nor his disciples, they themselves got into the boats and went to Capernaum, seeking Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seeking Jesus. Diligently, but for the wrong reason (v. 26). Give them their due: it is several miles across that lake. The seeking is strenuous and costly, and Jesus is about to tell them it was aimed at the wrong thing.

Effort is not evidence. It is possible to work hard at religion, to travel, give, attend and serve, in pursuit of something other than God. The energy proves the wanting; it says nothing about what is wanted.

To his own address. They find him at Capernaum, the town of the synagogue (v. 59), and the search is still a failure, because finding Jesus and receiving him are two different things (1:11).

He let himself be found. The one who slipped away from a crown the night before is standing in the open the next morning, ready to be questioned by the same people. He does not hide from those who seek him for poor reasons, because he has come to give himself and means them to hear it.

How do I know if I am seeking Jesus for the right reasons? Ask what you would do if the benefits were removed. Suppose the specific blessing you associate with your faith were gone: the community, the sense of purpose, the moral order it gives your life, the hope of things going well. Suppose only Christ were left. Would you still cross the lake? No one answers that perfectly, and it is not asked to produce despair. Mixed motives are normal; even the apostles had them. The question is which way you are moving: toward wanting him more than his gifts. Ask him to make it so.

verseByVerse.quote: When they found him on the other side of the sea, they said to him, "Rabbi, when did you come here?" Jesus answered them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, you are seeking me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate your fill of the loaves."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rabbi, when did you come here? Curiosity. He does not answer the question they asked. They want to know when he arrived; he tells them why they came.

Not because you saw signs. They had not seen it in the sense the word carries in this Gospel. A sign is a signpost, and they had eaten the signpost. The bread on the grass was saying that the one who gave it is himself the bread of life (v. 35).

You ate your fill. They want what he gives, not who he is. The verb (echortasthēte) once belonged to the feeding of animals, but by this time simply meant to eat your fill (compare Matthew 5:6). He had given them the meal himself, and lavishly. But being filled up was the whole of what had happened to them.

The danger of every good gift. Nobody decides to want the gift more than the giver. It happens by the ordinary working of appetite, and a person can live for years on that circuit without once looking at where the bread came from.

Does Jesus mind that I pray for practical things? No. He taught us to pray, give us this day our daily bread (Matthew 6:11), and he fed this crowd gladly. The problem is not asking for bread, but wanting only bread. Pray for your needs, freely and specifically. Then let every answered prayer turn your eyes upward, to the Father who gave it and the Son who is himself the bread of life. A prayer life that is all requests and no worship has begun to eat the signpost.

For worship. He had fed them with his own hands, and now he spoke hard words to them with the same love. A lesser benefactor would have kept the loaves coming. He wanted them to have him. His bread and his rebuke come from one heart, and the rebuke is the larger gift.

verseByVerse.quote: "Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give to you. For on him God the Father has set his seal."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The food that perishes. Physical food is necessary, but temporary (Isaiah 55:2). Perishes is the same verb as the fragments, that nothing may be lost; the loaves of the day before were already going stale. Most of what we labour for is not wrong in itself. The trouble comes when we ask it to bear more than bread can bear: a career asked to give us our worth, a family asked to give us our meaning, comfort asked to give us peace. Bread asked to be God always goes stale in the hand.

The food that endures. They are to work for it, yet it is a gift. The working is not the purchasing: a man may labour hard to get to where something is being given out without having earned it. What is forbidden is not effort but effort aimed at the wrong provision.

The Father has set his seal. A seal marked ownership and guaranteed authenticity. The Father has stamped his Son as a supplier stamps a consignment, at the baptism and through the signs. The question is whether they will accept the certificate of the only authority competent to issue it.

Does this mean I should not work hard at my job? No. Scripture commands honest work and says that if anyone will not work, neither should he eat (2 Thessalonians 3:10). Jesus is not condemning daily labour but warning against making it the goal of your life. Work hard for your bread, as service to Christ (Colossians 3:23). But do not work for bread as if it were what you were made for. Give your deepest energy, your hope and your heart to the food that endures, and you will find even your daily work changed by it.
verseByVerse.note: A seal marked ownership and guaranteed authenticity.

parallels.desc: why do you labour for that which does not satisfy?

verseByVerse.quote: "Then they said to him, 'What must we do, to be doing the works of God?' Jesus answered them, 'This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
What must we do, to be doing the works of God? They take “work” literally: tell us what to do, what deeds, what rules, to earn this food. Watch the plural become singular, because the whole exchange is in it. They ask about the works, plural: a programme, a list. Give us the list. There is real sincerity in it, because a list can be worked at, progress can be measured, and a person can know where he stands.

This is the work of God. Not works (plural), but one work: believe. Faith is not a work that earns salvation; it is the receiving of a gift. And it is “the work of God” in a double sense: the work God requires, and the work God does in us (v. 44, 65; Philippians 1:29). Salvation is not by doing but by believing in Jesus.

The easiest and the hardest answer. Easiest, because a man on his deathbed with no strength for a list can do it. Hardest, because it offers nothing to measure. A list lets a person keep control of the transaction; faith hands it over. They asked for a list, and God answered with a Person.

Him whom he has sent. Faith is not a technique or a mood; it is believing in him whom God has sent, standing in front of them as he says it. Faith saves because of the one it rests on. A weak faith in a strong Saviour saves, because the strength is his.

If faith is not a work, why does Jesus call it the work of God? Because he is answering their question in their own words, and then turning it inside out. They asked what work they must do; he says the only work is to believe, which is to stop working for acceptance and receive it. Faith is not something we contribute that earns a reward. It is the empty hand that takes Christ. And even that hand is God’s gift (Ephesians 2:8–9). So we are saved by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone, and the good works that follow are the fruit of salvation, never its price.

On a Tuesday. If a sermon that ends without steps to take leaves you mildly frustrated, that instinct is the one in this verse. Before you do anything for God today, rest in what he has done for you.

verseByVerse.quote: So they said to him, "Then what sign do you do, that we may see and believe you? What work do you perform? Our fathers ate the manna in the wilderness; as it is written, 'He gave them bread from heaven to eat.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then what sign do you do, that we may see and believe you? They want more, perhaps a sign as great as Moses’ manna, which lasted forty years. Yesterday afternoon they ate bread that came out of nothing, with twelve baskets over, and this morning they ask what sign he will do, as though the account were empty. Gratitude has a shorter life than anyone expects, and it is not cured by the size of the mercy: the generation that walked out of Egypt through a parted sea was complaining about the food within about a month (Exodus 16:1–3).

That we may see and believe you. They are proposing terms: produce the evidence, and belief will follow, with themselves as assessors. Jesus never accepts that arrangement from anyone (20:29).

Our fathers ate the manna. Exodus 16. Some Jewish writings from around the end of the first century expected that the manna would fall again in the days of the Messiah (2 Baruch 29:8). Moses, they imply, gave bread daily for forty years; one hillside meal was a single afternoon. They are negotiating for a supply.

Bread from heaven. Psalm 78:24; Exodus 16:4. They quote Scripture correctly and use it as a weapon against the man in front of them. Jesus will take the sentence apart word by word and show they have misread its subject (5:46).

The sign they wanted was talking to them. The manna was always a picture of him. Jesus will not give them a bigger miracle. He will give them the explanation of every miracle: himself, come down from the Father.

Why doesn’t God give more signs to convince unbelievers? Because more signs do not produce faith in an unwilling heart. This crowd had just eaten a miracle and wanted another. In one of Jesus’ parables Abraham says that if people do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead (Luke 16:31). God has given sufficient evidence: the signs written in the Gospels, the resurrection, and his word. What the unbeliever needs is not more light outside but new sight within, and that is the Spirit’s work. So pray for unbelievers, and keep showing them Christ.

parallels.desc: he gave them the grain of heaven
bread from heaven

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus then said to them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, it was not Moses who gave you the bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven. For the bread of God is he who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not Moses. He corrects their quotation in two places, both in the grammar. First the subject: God said, I am about to rain bread from heaven for you (Exodus 16:4). The manna was never Moses’ to give; he woke up to it on the ground like everybody else.

The true bread. “True” (alēthinon): the real thing, of which the manna was a shadow. The second correction is the tense. They said God gave: past, finished. He says the Father gives: it is happening in the room.

He who comes down from heaven. Or “that which comes down”. Up to this point every hearer has assumed they are discussing a substance, and the substance has become a person (3:13).

The manna was always too small a picture. It kept a nation alive for forty years. It also had to be gathered again the next day, went rotten if hoarded, and did not keep the generation that ate it from dying in the desert.

Life to the world. Not only to Israel. It is the first time in this Gospel that the bread is given a scope, spoken in an argument with hostile men as the purpose of the bread.

How is the manna a picture of Christ? In several ways. (Christians call such an Old Testament picture a type.) It came down from heaven, as he did. It was given freely, by grace, to people who could not feed themselves in the wilderness. It had to be received and eaten, not merely looked at. It was enough for all who gathered it (Exodus 16:18). And Paul calls Israel’s food in the wilderness spiritual food (1 Corinthians 10:3). But Christ surpasses the type: the manna sustained a life that ended; he gives life that never ends.

On a Tuesday. Your soul needs daily bread as much as your body does. Before you check your phone tomorrow morning, gather your manna: a passage of Scripture, read slowly, with a prayer that Christ would feed you by it.

For worship. The bread of God is heaven’s own Son. The manna cost heaven nothing. This bread cost the Father his Son and the Son his life (3:16), and the Spirit makes it our food.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, "Sir, give us this bread always." Jesus said to them, "I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sir, give us this bread always. Like the Samaritan woman (4:15), they still think of physical bread. They are asking for the right thing and still mean the wrong one.

I am the bread of life. This is the first of Jesus’ seven “I am” sayings in John: the bread of life (6:35), the light of the world (8:12), the door (10:7), the good shepherd (10:11), the resurrection and the life (11:25), the way, the truth and the life (14:6), the true vine (15:1). “I am” (egō eimi) echoes the divine name. Jesus does not just give bread; he is the bread.

In the flow. Verse 35 is the centre on which the whole chapter turns: the sign, the night on the sea and the demand for manna lead here, and the coming (vv. 37–40), the drawing (vv. 44–46) and the eating (vv. 51–58) unfold it. If a reader holds on to one sentence of John 6, it should be this one.

Bread first. Most of the seven take something ordinary and say: I am the thing itself, and every example you have met was the picture. And bread comes first, not light, which would be grander: the plainest, most daily thing in the world, said to people who had eaten the day before, in a district where a bad harvest meant a funeral.

Shall not hunger. Coming to Jesus is like eating; believing in him is like drinking (4:14). Coming and believing are the same thing. This is how this Gospel always speaks of faith: not an inward opinion but a movement toward a person.

The search is over. Every human being is running an experiment on what will finally satisfy, and has found the answers temporary. He is not offering to improve the supply. He is saying the appetite ends in him.

What does it mean to feed on Christ day by day? It means to keep coming to him and keep believing in him, drawing your life from him as you draw strength from food. In practice: hear and read his word, because his words are spirit and life (v. 63); pray to him; trust his death for you afresh when you are guilty; come to his table; rest on his promises when you are afraid. Faith is not a single meal but a daily diet. You do not eat once and live for ever on the memory; you go back to the table.

On a Tuesday. Pay attention to your hungers today: for approval, comfort, distraction, control. Each time you feel one, take it to Christ in a short prayer, and ask him to be what that hunger is really looking for.
verseByVerse.note: This is the first of Jesus’ seven “I am” sayings in John.

parallels.desc: come, buy and eat

verseByVerse.quote: "But I said to you that you have seen me and yet do not believe."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You have seen me. Seeing is not believing; unbelief is not a lack of evidence. Not you have seen my works, though they had: you have seen me. They have had him in front of them for a whole day, with a meal in between. The disciples could say, we have seen his glory (1:14). This crowd had looked at the same face and seen a man who might keep the bread coming.

If only we had been there. Being present was not enough. The people who watched him make bread out of nothing are the people he describes as unbelieving. That takes something else, and Jesus names it next: the Father’s giving and drawing (vv. 37, 44).

Would I believe more easily if God gave me more evidence? Probably not, and this verse is why. The crowd had more evidence than you will ever have, and it did not produce faith. That is not because evidence is worthless, but because the problem lies deeper than the mind. Faith comes by hearing the word of Christ, opened to the heart by the Spirit (Romans 10:17). If you struggle to believe, do not wait for a sign. Go to the Gospels, read what he said and did, and ask the Father to give you eyes to see. That is a prayer he delights to answer.

On a Tuesday. Pray for those who have seen and heard and still don’t believe. Only God can open their eyes. Choose one person you have been trying to convince, and this week spend more time praying for them than arguing with them.

verseByVerse.quote: "All that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will never cast out. For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
All that the Father gives me. The Father has given a people to the Son (17:2, 6, 9, 24). They are given before they come. “All” of them will come: not might, but will. None will be missing. This is unconditional election and effectual calling: the Father chooses a people, gives them to the Son, and draws them so that they certainly come (v. 44). Unconditional means the choice rests on God’s free love, not on anything he foresaw in them (Ephesians 1:4–5); effectual means the call does what it says, and brings them.

He is not counting the room. There is not a word here about the strength of anyone’s grip. Speaking to a crowd that came for bread and will shortly be abandoned by many of his disciples, he says not that his ministry has failed but that everyone the Father has given him will arrive.

Whoever comes to me. “Never” (ou mē): the strongest negative in Greek. A wonderful assurance for anyone who comes to Christ, however unworthy. You do not need to wonder whether you are chosen before you come; if you come, he will receive you.

Never cast out. The verb is physical, used of the man born blind put out of the synagogue (9:34) and of the traders driven from the temple (2:15). There is no version of the story in which someone who came to him is put outside afterwards. And the promise does not depend on how a person came, from conviction or desperation or sheer exhaustion, nor on what they have done since. The only condition is whoever comes, stated so broadly that no one can be excluded by a technicality.

Not to do my own will. Jesus’ mission is to do the Father’s will, which is to save all the Father has given him. He did that will perfectly, as no one else ever has, and his obedience is counted to those who come to him (Romans 5:19), so their welcome never rests on how well they have done it themselves.

Where Christians differ: election. Arminians (a broad family that includes many Methodists, Pentecostals and others) teach that God chooses those he foresees will freely believe. Many faithful Christians hold this view, and they too confess that salvation is all of grace. This commentary’s view: the text puts the Father’s giving first, and the coming second, as its result: all that the Father gives will come. God’s choice is the cause of faith, not its result (also 6:44, 65; 10:26; Ephesians 1:4–5; Acts 13:48). Yet human responsibility is real: everyone who comes is welcomed, and those who refuse are responsible (5:40). Both truths are taught together, and we hold them together.
