How do I know if I am one of those the Father has given? By coming. You will never find your name by searching the secret counsel of God; it is not written where you can read it. But it is written where you can see its effect: whoever comes to Christ was given by the Father, and whoever comes will never be cast out. So do not ask first, am I chosen?, and wait for an answer before coming. Come to Christ now, as you are, trusting him. That coming is the evidence of the Father’s giving, and the promise of the Son’s welcome stands over you.

On a Tuesday. Ask yourself what you are secretly afraid would get you thrown out: not sin in general, but the particular thing. Now read verse 37 again and notice that it has no exceptions clause, and that the man who said it knew everything about you before you came and made the promise anyway.

verseByVerse.quote: "And this is the will of him who sent me, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the will of him who sent me. He is quoting his job description, stated as the Father’s will. So if a single person given to Christ were finally lost, it would mean the Son had failed to do what the Father sent him to do, and that can never be (5:19).

Lose nothing. “All that he has given me” is neuter in Greek (pan ho), the whole company of the given seen as one gift. “Lose” (apollymi) is the word of the fragments in v. 12. The Shepherd who would not lose a crust of barley bread will not lose one of his people. This is the perseverance of the saints: everyone God truly saves he keeps believing to the end, grounded not in the strength of the believer but in the will of the Father and the faithfulness of the Son (10:28–29; 17:12; 18:9).

Raise it up. Salvation is not complete until the body is raised. The phrase “raise up on the last day” comes four times in this chapter (vv. 39, 40, 44, 54). Anyone can be kept safe until they die, and everyone dies; what is promised is that the keeping extends through the grave and out the other side.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that someone who makes a profession and then abandons Christ for ever was one of the given (see 1 John 2:19). Nor does it mean believers can live carelessly: those whom Christ keeps, he keeps believing and following (10:27).

Where Christians differ: can a true believer be lost? Many Arminians teach that a genuine believer may finally fall away. This commentary’s view: this verse rules it out, since the Father’s will would fail; the warnings are one of the means by which Christ keeps his own. (See Romans 8:38 for the fuller answer.)

What about the warning passages, like John 15:6 and Hebrews 6? Some Christians hold that Christ keeps only those who go on abiding in him, and that a believer may abandon faith and be lost (compare 15:6; Hebrews 6:4–6). But here the promise is not conditioned on our holding on: those the Father has given, Christ will not lose, but will raise up. He warns his sheep so that they will not wander, and the warning itself is one of the ways his hand holds them.

What if I fall into serious sin? Have I lost my salvation? If you belong to Christ, no. Peter denied him three times, and was restored (21:15–19). David fell into adultery and murder, and repented (Psalm 51). A true believer may fall grievously and for a time, bringing God’s fatherly displeasure and much grief on himself (Westminster Confession 17.3; 1689 London Baptist Confession 17.3); but he will not fall finally, because Christ will not lose him. The proof that you belong to him is that you cannot rest in the sin: you are grieved, you return, you confess. Run back to him now. The door he promised never to shut is still open.

For worship. He does not say he will do his best. He says the Father has willed it and he will do it: lose nothing, raise it up. He will stand on the last day with every one of his people, saying, behold, I and the children God has given me (Hebrews 2:13).

verseByVerse.quote: "For this is the will of my Father, that everyone who looks on the Son and believes in him should have eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The will of my Father. The same will, now seen from the human side. Verse 39 spoke of what the Father gives; v. 40 speaks of what people do.

Everyone who looks on the Son. “Looks” (theōreō) means to gaze, to look with attention. The crowd had seen him without believing (v. 36); this is seeing that leads to faith. “Everyone” is wide open: there is no one who looks and believes who is shut out.

Looking is the one thing required. It sends the reader back to the bronze serpent, where the dying were told to look and live (3:14–15), and forward to the cross: they will look on him whom they have pierced (19:37). Looking is the one thing a person with nothing left can still do.

Now and then. Present possession and future completion: eternal life now, resurrection then.

The pastoral order. Held next to verse 44, these verses produce a tension that has divided the church, yet Jesus spoke them four verses apart with no sense of conflict. No one is kept out by the doctrine of election. The door has everyone written over it. What the drawing explains is not who may come but why anyone does, a question asked afterwards, looking back, by people already inside.

Can I freely offer the gospel to everyone if God has chosen only some? Yes, and you must. Jesus himself does both in the same breath. The offer is sincere: whoever looks and believes will live, and God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 33:11). You do not know who the elect are, and you are not asked to find out. You are asked to say to everyone: look to the Son and live. Election is not a reason to hold back the invitation; it is the guarantee that the invitation will not fall on deaf ears everywhere.

On a Tuesday. Today, when you feel guilty or afraid, do not look inward first. Look at the Son, lifted up on the cross for you, and believe. Then tell someone else to look.

verseByVerse.quote: So the Jews grumbled about him, because he said, "I am the bread that came down from heaven." They said, "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How does he now say, 'I have come down from heaven'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Jews grumbled. “Grumbled” (gongyzō) is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for Israel grumbling in the wilderness, where the manna was given (Exodus 16:2, 7–8). They are acting out their fathers’ story while they talk about their fathers’ bread. “The Jews” here means people in the Galilean synagogue opposing Jesus. What offends them is his claim to heavenly origin.

Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? They know where he comes from, they think. They know his family. Ironically, they know only half the truth. John’s readers know he came from the Father (1:14), and many would know he was born of a virgin. Familiarity breeds contempt (compare Mark 6:3). And their objection is unanswerable on its own terms. They are not making anything up. They could probably have named the street. There is no way, from inside that information, to get to the conclusion that the man came down from heaven.

How does he now say, I have come down from heaven? Their objection is the incarnation itself: how can an ordinary man claim to come from heaven? This is still the stumbling block. God did not arrive in a form that made the conclusion easy. He came as somebody’s son, in a known family, from a town people could point to, and the very facts that make the story checkable are the facts that make it seem incredible.

How can Jesus have a human mother and come down from heaven? Because he is one person with two natures. As the eternal Son he came from the Father; as man he was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the virgin Mary (Luke 1:35). Joseph was his legal father, not his natural father. The crowd saw only the human side and thought it ruled out the divine. But the incarnation means that the one who came down from heaven really did grow up in Nazareth, and that the carpenter’s son really is the Word who was with God in the beginning.

On a Tuesday. The obstacle in this verse is familiarity, the settled sense that one already knows all there is to know about him, which feels like being well informed. Read a Gospel this week as if for the first time, and stop wherever the man of Nazareth does what only one from heaven could do.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered them, "Do not grumble among yourselves. No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him. And I will raise him up on the last day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not grumble among yourselves. Jesus doesn’t argue with their objection about his family. He goes to the root: why they cannot believe.

No one can come to me. “Can” (dynatai) is about ability, not permission. Fallen human beings, left to themselves, are unable to come to Christ (3:3; 8:43; Romans 8:7–8). The historic name for this is the bondage of the will: the will is not destroyed or forced but bound, so that it chooses freely and always chooses against God until it is set free.

Unless the Father who sent me draws him. “Draws” (helkō) is used of drawing a net full of fish to land (21:6, 11) and of drawing a sword (18:10). It is an effective pull, not a gentle suggestion. God’s drawing does not force anyone against their will; it changes the will, so that the sinner comes gladly, as v. 45 explains: the Father teaches, and the taught come.

I will raise him up. The one who is drawn is the one who is raised: drawn, comes, raised, and none drop out on the way. The whole work is in divine hands from the first pull to the last day.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that people who want to come to Christ are turned away because they are not drawn. Anyone who wants to come has already been drawn. Nor does it excuse unbelief: people do not come because they will not (5:40), and they are responsible for it.

Where Christians differ: is the Father’s drawing resistible? Arminians (Christians who hold that God’s saving grace can be resisted) teach that God draws everyone (citing 12:32) with a grace that can be resisted, so that some who are drawn do not come. Many earnest believers read it so, and both sides agree that whoever comes owes it to grace. This commentary’s view: in this verse the one who is drawn is the one who is raised up on the last day. If drawing could be resisted, the verse would promise resurrection to people who never come. The drawing is effectual. In 12:32 Jesus says he will draw “all people,” meaning all kinds of people, Gentiles as well as Jews (the Greeks of 12:20 have just asked to see him), not every single person. This is effectual calling: the Spirit’s work by which God persuades and enables us to embrace Jesus Christ, freely offered in the gospel.

Does this make us puppets? No. A puppet has no will; the sinner has a will, and uses it freely, and that is exactly the problem: left to himself he freely prefers his own way to Christ (3:19). God’s drawing does not switch the will off. It sets it free, so that for the first time the person wants Christ and comes gladly. No one in heaven will say, I was dragged here against my will. Everyone there will say, he opened my eyes, and I came running.

What this doctrine is for. It is regularly used as a weapon, and it is not one. Nobody has been given the list, and Jesus is pleading with the very room he describes. It is an explanation offered to people who already believe, and it answers one question: why me, when it did not land on the man beside me who had the same information? The only answer the chapter permits is that somebody came and got me. That removes the last possibility of taking credit, and with it the fear that a faith I produced could be one I might fail to keep.

If no one can come unless drawn, why should I evangelise? Because the Father draws through means, and the chief means is the gospel spoken. The Father teaches (v. 45), and he teaches through the word preached and shared: faith comes from hearing (Romans 10:14–17). The doctrine of drawing does not make your witness pointless; it makes it hopeful. You are not trying to talk dead people into life by your own power. You are speaking the words that the Father uses to raise the dead. Speak boldly, pray earnestly, and expect him to draw.

For worship. No one ever wandered into the kingdom by accident or fought his way in. At the end of this Gospel the disciples haul a net to the shore where the risen Jesus stands with breakfast ready, and for all the fish the net is not torn (21:6–11). So the Father draws: every one he pulls is brought to his Son, and none is lost on the way.

parallels.desc: I will draw all people to myself

verseByVerse.quote: "It is written in the Prophets, 'And they will all be taught by God.' Everyone who has heard and learned from the Father comes to me — not that anyone has seen the Father except he who is from God; he has seen the Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is written in the Prophets. The quotation is from Isaiah 54:13, a promise about the restored people of God in the new covenant age (compare Jeremiah 31:33–34).

All taught by God. “All” means all God’s people: in the new age, God himself teaches every one of them, not just prophets and priests.

Heard and learned. This explains what drawing is: the Father draws by teaching, opening the mind and heart to hear and learn, and everyone who learns comes. Drawing is inward teaching, which always succeeds, the same as the new birth (3:3–8) and the opening of Lydia’s heart (Acts 16:14).

He who is from God. Being taught by the Father does not mean having visions of God (1:18). The Father teaches by pointing to the Son, who speaks of the Father as one who has seen him, and so every lesson in the Father’s school ends at the same place.

How does God teach me today? Through his word, by his Spirit. He does not normally speak in private voices or visions, and verse 46 warns against expecting to see the Father directly. Christians differ over whether God still gives private words today; this commentary holds that, since the apostles, Scripture is his complete and sufficient word, while gladly respecting believers who expect more, and both agree that nothing heard elsewhere may add to it or contradict it. He teaches as the Scriptures are read and preached, the Spirit opening your mind to understand and your heart to love what you hear (Luke 24:45; 1 Corinthians 2:12). So the way to be taught by God is to put yourself under his word, with prayer, and in the fellowship of his church. Every true insight into Christ you have ever had was a lesson from the Father.

parallels.desc: all your children shall be taught by the LORD

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes has eternal life. I am the bread of life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truly, truly, I say to you. The doubled amen is peculiar to this Gospel. The word normally endorses someone else’s statement; he puts it at the front of his own, endorsing his words in advance with the formula used for the words of God, and here to introduce the simplest sentence in the chapter.

Whoever believes has eternal life. Not whoever believes and does, but whoever believes. And has, now. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV and NKJV, read believes on me; the earliest have simply believes, with the same meaning. The sentence says nothing about how much is believed, or how well, or with what feelings, and nothing about understanding, in a chapter where hardly anyone understands anything.

I am the bread of life. The great “I am” saying is repeated (v. 35): a preacher who has been interrupted, argued with and grumbled at, going back to the point.

I worry whether I am really one of the elect. What should I do? Stop auditing the secret counsel of God and look at the promise in front of you. There is a way of hearing the strong doctrine of the previous verses, the drawing, the giving, the Father’s will, and then trying to inspect oneself for evidence of a decision made before the world began. That way lies misery, and it is not what those verses are for. The instruction never changes and it is not complicated: whoever believes has eternal life. If you are trusting Christ, however weakly, the promise is yours. Assurance grows as you look at him, not at yourself (Westminster Confession 18.2; 1689 London Baptist Confession 18.2).

On a Tuesday. If you believe, you have eternal life today. Live from that, not towards it: obey God not to gain life but because you already have it, by the Spirit who gives it (v. 63). Do one thing today that you would do only if you were sure you were safe in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died. This is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that one may eat of it and not die."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they died. The crowd had held up the manna as the great sign (v. 31). It kept people alive for a day. The whole generation that ate it died in the wilderness, many in unbelief (Numbers 14:29; 1 Corinthians 10:5), the part of the story they were not quoting.

The best of our arrangements. So the manna is not the standard Jesus has to match. Medicine, food, safety, all the ordinary mercies, are real, and every one of them extends a life rather than saves it. The best possible outcome of all our arrangements is a longer wait.

Eat of it and not die. Not that he will escape the death of the body, but that death will not be the end (11:25–26). Not eat and live longer: not die.

But Christians still die. What does not die mean? It means that the death that is final, separation from God for ever, will never touch you. Your body will die, unless Christ returns first, and this Gospel will soon show Jesus weeping at a friend’s tomb (11:35). But for the believer death is no longer the end of the sentence. At death the soul goes immediately to be with Christ (Philippians 1:23; Westminster Confession 32.1; 1689 London Baptist Confession 31.1), and at the last day the body will be raised. The manna could not stop a single funeral. This bread does not stop them either. It stops them being the last word.

parallels.desc: your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness

verseByVerse.quote: "I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. And the bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The living bread. Living bread: bread that is alive, and gives life. A new form of the claim.

He will live forever. Eating is a picture of believing (compare v. 35 with v. 47). As food becomes part of you and keeps you alive, so receiving Christ by faith unites you to him and gives you life.

The bread is my flesh. Here the discourse turns. “I will give”: future, looking to the cross. “For” (hyper) means on behalf of, and in sayings like this one, in the place of (10:11, 15; 11:51–52). “My flesh”: his real human body (1:14), given up in death. To feed on Christ is to trust in his sacrifice.

The bread is a dying man. The whole discourse has been walking toward this. The preposition is the one Caiaphas will use, that one man should die for the people (11:50). The bread is not spiritual sustenance in general but a specific man, on a specific afternoon, dying in the place of others, and anyone can be fed by him only because he was broken first.

For the life of the world. “The world” in John is humanity in its rebellion against God, Gentiles as well as Jews (11:51–52).

Where Christians differ: does this mean Christ died for everyone alike? Some take “for the life of the world” to mean that Christ died equally for every human being. This commentary’s view: in John, Christ lays down his life “for the sheep” (10:11, 15), for those the Father has given him (17:9, 19). “The world” here stresses the extent of his people, from every nation, and the greatness of the gift, not that every individual is saved. His death actually gives life, and it gives it to everyone who feeds on him. This is definite atonement: the death that truly secures life for all who are his. Many faithful Christians believe Christ died in the same way for every person, and they preach the same free offer; the difference is over what the cross was designed to accomplish, and both sides glory in it.

Can I tell anyone that Christ died for sinners like them? Yes. The death of Christ is of infinite worth, sufficient for the whole world, and the gospel offers it freely to everyone without exception: whoever eats of this bread will live for ever. You may say to any person, Christ died for sinners, and if you come to him, you will find that he died for you, and his death will not fail you. Definite atonement does not narrow the offer; it guarantees that the cross actually saves, rather than merely making salvation possible.

On a Tuesday. When guilt rises today, do not argue with it from your record; answer it from his cross. Every time you trust his death for you, you are feeding on him.

verseByVerse.quote: The Jews then disputed among themselves, saying, "How can this man give us his flesh to eat?" So Jesus said to them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Jews then disputed among themselves. “Disputed” (machomai) means fought. The grumbling has become open argument; the room has split.

How can this man give us his flesh to eat? They take him literally and crudely, as Nicodemus took the new birth (3:4) and the woman took living water (4:11). The misunderstanding is part of John’s method: it leads to deeper teaching.

Unless you eat. Jesus does not soften it; he adds the blood. Flesh and blood separated speak of a violent death: the body broken and the blood poured out. To eat his flesh and drink his blood is to receive his death as your life, by faith, depending on it entirely.

How appalling this sounded. The prohibition on blood was absolute (Genesis 9:4): whoever eats any blood, God would set his face against him and cut him off from his people (Leviticus 17:10). The blood was the life, and the life belonged to God. He names the one thing their law forbade on pain of being cut off, in a synagogue, and says it is necessary.

You have no life in you. Without union with Christ crucified, there is only death, for the respectable too: a person may be busy, moral and religious and still be dead in trespasses and sins (Ephesians 2:1). Life in this Gospel is knowing God (17:3).

What it does not mean. It does not mean literal eating of Jesus’ physical body. The crowd thought that, and Jesus corrects it in v. 63: the flesh is no help at all; his words are spirit. Nor does it mean that everyone who takes the Lord’s Supper has eternal life, or that no one who has not taken it can be saved. The thief on the cross never took it, and was with Christ that day.

Where Christians differ: John 6 and the Lord’s Supper. Roman Catholics read these verses as teaching transubstantiation, the bread and wine becoming Christ’s actual body and blood; Lutherans see Christ’s body present in, with and under the elements; some see here only a symbol of faith. This commentary’s view: the Supper had not yet been instituted, and Jesus speaks to the crowd of something they must do now, on pain of having no life. Feeding on Christ is believing in him (vv. 35, 40, 47). John 6 is about faith, not first about the sacrament. Yet the same feeding is what happens at the Supper: there, as Calvin taught, believers by the Spirit truly feed on Christ’s body and blood, not by a change in the bread, but by being lifted up in faith to the living Christ, who nourishes them with himself. The Supper is a visible, sealing form of what John 6 describes.

Why does Jesus use such shocking language? Because nothing less would describe what he offers. He is speaking of a union with a dying man so complete that the nearest picture is taking him into yourself and living on him. The picture offends precisely because the reality is so total. Faith is not admiring Christ from a distance or agreeing with his teaching; it is depending on his death as your only life, as completely as your body depends on food. A few verses later he will tell his disciples that his words are spirit and life. He is not being obscure for effect. He is saying the only thing that is true.

For worship. The law kept the blood for the altar, given to make atonement (Leviticus 17:11). What no Israelite was ever allowed to take, the Son of God gives: his own life, poured out in death, received by faith, so that sinners condemned to die might live by his.
verseByVerse.note: Drinking blood was forbidden by the law, which made these words shocking.

parallels.desc: the life is in the blood

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever feeds on my flesh. The verb changes from the usual word for eat to trōgō, to chew or munch. Some take it as deliberately vivid; others note it simply serves as the present tense of eating in later Greek. Either way, the present tense matters: the ongoing feeding of a life of faith.

Has eternal life. The positive promise of v. 53: has eternal life now.

The last day. Compare v. 40: whoever looks on the Son and believes has eternal life and will be raised. The parallel shows that feeding means believing. This is the last of the four appearances of the refrain.

Does the realism of this language support the Roman Catholic view? The reading deserves to be stated at its strongest. Rome points out that the crowd plainly took Jesus literally, and that instead of correcting them he pressed harder, moving to the more vivid word feeds on; that he says his flesh is true food and his blood true drink; and that when disciples walked away he did not call them back to say he had meant a figure. That is a serious argument and it deserves a serious answer, which the passage itself supplies nine verses later. When his own disciples say the saying is hard, Jesus tells them what it was: it is the Spirit who gives life, the flesh is no help at all; the words he has spoken are spirit and life (v. 63). That is the clarification, given exactly where a reader would want it, and it points away from physical eating. The parallel he offers is that whoever feeds on him abides in him, and abiding is John’s word for a relationship held by faith, not by digestion. And Jesus is speaking a year before the Last Supper, to a crowd who had no sacrament to think of. Whatever this chapter describes, it is how a person receives a crucified Saviour, which is by believing in him, as he said outright in verse 35.

Then is the Lord’s Supper only a memorial? No. None of this makes the Supper a bare reminder or an optional extra. The Reformed churches have taught that Christ is truly given to his people at his table and truly received, really and spiritually, by faith, through the Spirit, so that the feeding is no mere metaphor even though his flesh is not chewed (1689 London Baptist Confession 30.7; Westminster 29.7). The disagreement with Rome is not about whether Christ gives himself to us there. It is about how, and about whether the once-for-all sacrifice can be offered again. It cannot (Hebrews 10:10–14). So come to the table expecting to meet him: not in the bread, but by the Spirit, through faith, the risen Christ feeding you with himself.

On a Tuesday. Next time you come to the Lord’s Supper, prepare for it the day before: confess your sins, give thanks for the cross, and come hungry.

parallels.desc: a participation in the blood of Christ

verseByVerse.quote: "For my flesh is true food, and my blood is true drink. Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
True food. “True” (alēthēs): real, as the true light (1:9) and the true bread (v. 32): not genuine as opposed to fake, but the real thing of which every other example is a copy.

Abides in me. “Abides” (menō), remains, dwells: one of John’s great words (15:4–10; 1 John 2:24, 27). Feeding leads to union with Christ.

Both ways. The Spirit came down on Jesus and remained (1:32), and the word will carry chapter 15. But here for the first time the abiding runs both ways: in me, and I in him. Ordinary bread goes into the man and is changed into him. Here the one fed ends up inside the food: two persons who come to be in each other.

What does union with Christ mean in everyday life? It means that everything Christ is and has done is yours, and that your life is now bound up with his. His death counts as your death to sin, his righteousness is credited to you, his Spirit lives in you, and his resurrection guarantees yours (Romans 6:4–11; Galatians 2:20). So you are never alone, never facing temptation in your own strength, never praying to a distant God. When you work, suffer, love or die, you do it in him. Learn to say, with Paul, it is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me.

parallels.desc: abide in me

verseByVerse.quote: "As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever feeds on me, he also will live because of me. This is the bread that came down from heaven, not like the bread the fathers ate, and died. Whoever feeds on this bread will live forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The living Father. The Son’s life comes from the Father (5:26), the living one, the fountain of life, who has never had life handed to him.

Because of me. “Feeds on me”: now not flesh and blood but simply “me,” the person of Christ received. The believer lives because of Christ as Christ lives because of the Father: not the same in kind, since one is eternal and the other a gift to a creature, but running along the same line out of the same source.

Not like the bread the fathers ate. The discourse ends where it began, with the manna (vv. 31–32). The manna was a substance, and substances sustain and then stop. What is offered here is a place in a chain that begins in the life of God and has no end.

Hard to want. He has said it four ways in twenty verses. The disciples will call it a hard saying, and they are right, though not for their reason. It is not hard to follow. It is hard to want.

Does live forever just mean existing for ever? No. Everyone will exist for ever, the lost as well as the saved (5:29). Eternal life is not mere endless existence but a quality of life: knowing the Father and the Son (17:3), sharing in the very life of God, with joy, holiness and love that never fade. It begins now, when you first believe, and it will be complete in the resurrection, in a new creation without sin or death. That is the life that flows from the Father through the Son into all who feed on him.

parallels.desc: Christ who lives in me

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said these things in the synagogue, as he taught at Capernaum. When many of his disciples heard it, they said, "This is a hard saying; who can listen to it?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the synagogue. The whole discourse was given in the synagogue at Capernaum, Jesus’ base in Galilee. The remains of a later white limestone synagogue stand there on the dark basalt foundations of an earlier one, possibly the one Jesus taught in, which a Gentile centurion had built (Luke 7:5).

Many of his disciples. Not the Twelve, but a wider circle of followers; being called a disciple did not mean being a true believer (v. 64). Not the Jews, who have grumbled since verse 41, but people who had travelled with him and called him teacher. The crowd’s objection was hostility; this is desertion forming in the ranks.

This is a hard saying. “Hard” (sklēros) means harsh, offensive, used of a stiff wind or a harsh master. It was not hard to understand; it was hard to accept. They are saying they cannot stomach it.

Who can listen to it? “Listen” here means accept, obey. They will not take it. Not who can understand it, but who can go on sitting here while this is said. They are already halfway out of the building.

Two kinds of objection. There is genuine intellectual difficulty, and it deserves patient work. And there is the objection where the thing is understood perfectly well and found intolerable. This is the second kind, and Jesus’ reply does not soften the content; it points them to his ascension and to the Spirit.

Truth that will not bend. The hardness does not belong to a careless preacher. The man in the synagogue is the Word made flesh (1:14), and when he speaks, God is speaking. That is why he cannot make the saying easier. To soften it would be to say something less true about himself, and he will not lie about who he is or what he has come to do, not even to keep the people who have followed him longest. What makes the saying hard is that it is about a cross: a Messiah whose flesh is given and whose blood is poured out, and a salvation that leaves the sinner nothing to bring but hunger.

What should I do with a teaching of Jesus I find hard to accept? First, make sure it is what he actually teaches, read in its context, and not a distortion. Then ask honestly whether your difficulty is that you do not understand it, or that you do not like it. If the first, study and ask for help. If the second, bring the struggle to Christ himself, as you would to a friend whose judgement you trust more than your own. Many believers have found that the sayings they once resisted became the ones they love most. Faith does not mean pretending something is easy; it means trusting the one who said it.
verseByVerse.note: The remains of a later synagogue at Capernaum stand on the foundations of an earlier one, perhaps the one where Jesus taught.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus, knowing in himself that his disciples were grumbling about this, said to them, "Do you take offense at this? Then what if you were to see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Knowing in himself. Jesus knows what is in people (2:24–25); nobody reported it. The knowledge that read the woman at the well is now turned on his own followers as they are quietly deciding to leave. He watched them go before they went.

Do you take offense at this? “Offense” (skandalizō): to trip, to stumble. The cross is the great stumbling block (1 Corinthians 1:23).

Then what if you were to see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before? The sentence is left unfinished in Greek. Two readings are possible. It could mean: if this offends you, how much more will his ascent, the full revelation of his heavenly origin, overwhelm you? Or: when you see him ascend, you will understand that he truly came from heaven, and that his words about his flesh were not about literal eating. In John, his going up includes the cross, resurrection and ascension together (3:13–14; 12:32–34). Either way, the ascension proves his claim that he came down from heaven (vv. 38, 42), and it shows that his flesh would not stay on earth to be literally eaten.

Both readings hold. Either way, where he was before carries the weight. It is the very thing the objectors in verse 42 denied, and he answers by referring, without argument, to the place he came from and is going back to.

Why does the ascension matter to me? Because the one who ascended is now reigning, praying and preparing. He sits at the Father’s right hand as King over all things for the good of his church (Ephesians 1:20–23). He always lives to intercede for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). He has sent the Spirit (16:7). He is preparing a place for you, and will come again (14:2–3). The ascension means you have a friend at the very centre of all power, wearing your nature, and your life is hidden with him there (Colossians 3:1–3).

verseByVerse.quote: "It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is no help at all. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life. But there are some of you who do not believe." (For Jesus knew from the beginning who those were who did not believe, and who it was who would betray him.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is the Spirit who gives life. Life comes from the Holy Spirit, as in the new birth (3:5–8). This is the key to the chapter, where Jesus tells his own disciples what the previous twenty verses were about.

The flesh is no help at all. “Flesh” here means human nature on its own, apart from the Spirit, not Jesus’ own flesh given for the world (v. 51). He has just told them to eat his flesh, and now says flesh is no help at all. That is not a contradiction but a signal, placed where a hearer needs it: the category they have been reasoning in, the physical and literal, is the wrong one.

Spirit and life. Not describe spirit and life: are. The saying they have just called intolerable is itself what carries the life, so the way to eat him is to receive what he has said. That is why the eating is believing, the explanation the speaker gives before anyone had a doctrine to defend.

Some of you who do not believe. Said not to the crowd or the authorities but to the people standing closest, some of whom he is telling to their faces that they do not believe.

From the beginning. John’s comment, probably meaning from the start of his ministry. Jesus chose the Twelve knowing what Judas would do (v. 70; 13:18). It is the first mention of the betrayal in this Gospel.

Did Jesus’ knowing make Judas betray him? No. Foreknowledge is not the same as compulsion. John does not say Judas was made to do it; he says Jesus knew. God’s eternal purpose does include even the sins of men, so that the cross came by his definite plan and foreknowledge (Acts 2:23), yet God is not the author of sin, and Judas acted freely and wickedly, and was fully responsible (Westminster Confession 3.1; 5.4; 1689 London Baptist Confession 3.1; 5.4). And the terrible thing about this sentence is not what it does to Judas’s freedom but what it shows of Christ’s patience. He kept a man beside him for years, giving him everything he gave the others, knowing.

On a Tuesday. Without the Spirit, even the Bible is read and not heard. Before you open Scripture today, pray in one sentence: Holy Spirit, make these words life to me.

For worship. On the evening of his resurrection Jesus breathed on his disciples and said, Receive the Holy Spirit (20:22). His words are not ink but breath: the dead hear the voice of the Son of God and live (5:25). He knew every unbelieving heart in the room, and spoke life into it anyway.
verseByVerse.note: “Flesh” here means human nature on its own, apart from the Spirit.

parallels.desc: the Spirit gives life

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "This is why I told you that no one can come to me unless it is granted him by the Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is why I told you. He is quoting himself (v. 44): the doctrine is restated at the very moment it is being demonstrated.

Granted by the Father. “Granted” (dedomenon), given as a gift (Ephesians 2:8; Philippians 1:29). Three times in this chapter: the Father gives (v. 37), draws (v. 44), grants (v. 65). Unbelief is human refusal; faith is God’s gift. Drawing stressed the power required; granting stresses that it was a present.

No room for pride. Whatever separates those who stay from those leaving, it is not insight, loyalty or a better grasp of the argument: it was granted them.

The comfort in it. If staying were a matter of resolve, every Christian would be one bad season away from the door, and anyone who knows his own resolve would find that terrifying. This verse takes the whole question off that ground. The eleven did not out-endure the others. They were given something, and the giving did not depend on their performance that evening or any evening afterward. Within a year every one of them would run away and one would deny knowing him. They came back, because the one who received them kept them. While I was with them, he would pray, I kept them in your name, and not one of them has been lost except the son of destruction (17:12). That is the part the doctrine explains and self-confidence cannot.

Are those to whom coming is not granted still responsible? Yes. The inability is not like a prison door shut on someone trying to get out; it is a will that does not want to come (5:40). No one is turned away who comes, and no one stays away against his will. God’s gift is mercy, owed to no one; its absence is justice, not cruelty.

On a Tuesday. The person you find hardest to be patient with looks different once you remember that your faith was granted, not earned.

verseByVerse.quote: After this many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him. So Jesus said to the twelve, "Do you want to go away as well?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many turned back. The turning point of Jesus’ Galilean ministry. The day before, a crowd wanted to make him king (v. 15). “Turned back” literally means went away to the things behind. They had followed for bread and a political Messiah. This is not true believers falling away, but false disciples being revealed (v. 64; 1 John 2:19).

And nothing happened. There was no scandal and no miracle that went wrong. He preached a sermon, and the sermon emptied the room. This is where the faith based on signs at 2:24 and the Galilean welcome of 4:45 were always going to come.

No longer walked with him. A physical description: they stopped travelling in the same direction. Falling away often looks less like a decision than like a road no longer taken.

So Jesus said to the twelve. The first mention of “the twelve” in John.

Do you want to go away as well? The question is framed in Greek to expect a no. Jesus doesn’t beg them to stay or soften his teaching. He tests them, and invites a confession. He does not chase the crowd or send anyone after them. He turns to the twelve, his closest circle, and offers them the door. It is a real question, asked by a man who has just watched a room empty and has nothing left to hold anyone with except himself.

Were these disciples true believers who lost their salvation? Some read them so. But John has already shown that following and believing in a shallow way is not the same as being born again (2:23–25), and Jesus says plainly that some of them did not believe (v. 64). The more likely reading is that they had followed without being given saving faith. As John writes later, they went out from us, but they were not of us (1 John 2:19).

What if someone I love has walked away from Christ? Then this chapter is for you. It happened to Jesus, in his own town, in numbers, on the strength of his own preaching, and it was not evidence that anything had gone wrong in him. It is not necessarily evidence that you failed either. Keep loving them, keep the door open, and keep praying: some who seem to have walked away are wandering believers whom the Shepherd will bring back, like Peter. And the Father who draws can still draw. Leave the final judgement with God, who knows those who are his (2 Timothy 2:19).

For worship. The message was himself, and he would not be less than he is to be more popular. He stood in an emptying synagogue and did not flinch, and the same faithfulness took him to a garden at night, where he said of his friends, let these men go (18:8).

verseByVerse.quote: Simon Peter answered him, "Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simon Peter answered him. Peter speaks for the Twelve, as he does in the other Gospels (Matthew 16:16).

Lord, to whom shall we go? A confession made in a hard hour. Peter doesn’t claim to understand everything Jesus has said. But he knows there is no alternative. There is no one else to go to. His answer is not a compliment, and not a declaration of loyalty. It is a question, and the question is the point. Nothing suggests the twelve understood the discourse any better than the people walking out; they had heard the same sermon. What Peter says is that there is nowhere else: having been where they have been, the alternatives have stopped being alternatives.

Stronger than enthusiasm. A faith held in bewilderment is not a poor one. There is a holding on that survives precisely because it no longer depends on full comprehension: not I understand and therefore I stay, but I have nowhere else to take this, and the words that give life are here.

You have the words of eternal life. Peter has heard v. 63 and believed it. He has just heard the words called a hard saying by men leaving over it, and he calls the same words life. The difference is not that Peter found the saying easier. It is what he concluded about the speaker.

In the flow. John 5 ended with men who had every witness and would not come (5:40); John 6 ends with a few who have not understood everything and will not leave. The difference is the one the chapter has explained: the Father gives, draws and grants (vv. 37, 44, 65).

What should I do when I have doubts? Do what Peter did: take them to Jesus, not away from him. Doubt is not the same as unbelief; it is often faith struggling. Be honest with God about your questions (the psalms are full of honest complaint), and ask, where else would I go? Every alternative, unbelief, other religions, self-made spirituality, has its own hard sayings, and none offers what Christ does: words of eternal life from one who rose from the dead. Stay close to his word and his people, talk to a mature Christian, and keep coming. Many of the strongest believers have walked through seasons when all they could say was Peter’s question.

parallels.desc: all the words of this Life

verseByVerse.quote: "and we have believed, and have come to know, that you are the Holy One of God." Jesus answered them, "Did I not choose you, the twelve? And yet one of you is a devil."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And we have believed, and have come to know. Both verbs are in the perfect tense: a settled conviction. And the order is the one this Gospel keeps insisting on: believing first, knowing second. The servants filled the jars before they saw the wine; the official walked home before he had news; and these men believed and then came to know.

That you are the Holy One of God. Set apart, the one consecrated and sent by the Father (10:36). Holy is the word God uses of himself (Leviticus 11:44): this man stands wholly on God’s side of that line, pure where we are stained (compare Luke 5:8). Textual note: later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read “the Christ, the Son of the living God,” borrowed from Matthew 16:16; the earliest and best read “the Holy One of God,” and the ESV rightly follows them. The title was cried by a demon in a synagogue in this same town (Mark 1:24); Peter now says as a confession of faith what the demons said under duress. The words can be perfectly orthodox and mean two different things depending on who says them and why.

Did I not choose you, the twelve? Jesus’ reply both encourages and warns. He chose them, not they him (15:16). Peter has just said the finest thing anyone says in the chapter, on behalf of all of them, at the lowest point of the ministry so far, and the reply must have been very hard to hear. He will not let the confession stand as a headcount. Eleven of them meant it. He does not correct the substance of what Peter said; he corrects the assumed arithmetic behind the we.

One of you is a devil. “Devil” (diabolos): an adversary. Not that Judas was a demon, but that he was the devil’s tool (13:2, 27). The choice of Judas was a choice to be an apostle, not the electing love that saves (17:12). It is said of a man who at that moment had done nothing publicly wrong and had also just stayed.

Can a church contain people who are not truly Christians? Yes. The visible church, those who profess faith and gather for worship, has always included some who are not truly born again, as the Twelve included Judas, and as Simon the magician was baptised while still bound by sin (Acts 8:13, 20–23). Only God sees the heart perfectly. That is why churches must preach the gospel to their own members as well as to outsiders, practise loving discipline, and why every believer should examine himself (2 Corinthians 13:5). But it is not a reason for suspicion of everyone. Love believes all things, and we leave the final sorting to Christ.

parallels.desc: Peter’s confession

verseByVerse.quote: He spoke of Judas the son of Simon Iscariot, for he, one of the twelve, was going to betray him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He spoke of Judas the son of Simon Iscariot. “Iscariot” is often taken to mean man of Kerioth, a town in Judea (Joshua 15:25), so Judas was probably the only Judean among the Twelve. Nobody in the room worked out who was meant; at the last supper they will still be asking. John names him here for readers who know how it ends.

One of the twelve. The betrayer was an insider. Jesus knew, and kept him close, and washed his feet (13:5, 26). Judas’ betrayal fulfilled Scripture (13:18; Psalm 41:9), yet he was fully responsible for it (Mark 14:21).

Judas stayed. The crowd leaves, the wider circle leaves, and Judas stays. He heard the hard saying and did not walk out. He stood there when Peter said, to whom shall we go?, and by every visible measure he was one who held on. He remained among the twelve for about another year, was trusted with the money, and had his feet washed by the man he sold. What the verse says without softening is that nearness guarantees nothing. Three years at close quarters with the Son of God, inside the smallest circle, did not produce faith in one man of twelve. The chapter has told us what does: no one can come unless it is granted him by the Father.

Could I be a Judas without knowing it? If you are asking the question in fear, almost certainly not. Consider what the Gospel shows of Judas: until after the betrayal he is never once recorded as troubled about his own state. Anxiety about your own heart, sorrow over sin, longing to love Christ more: these are not the marks being described. The mark of Judas is a man entirely at ease while he loves something more than Christ (12:6). So examine yourself honestly, confess what you find, and then look away from yourself to the Saviour who never casts out anyone who comes. Fear that drives you to Christ is grace, not a sign of reprobation (God’s passing someone by).

For worship. He knew which of the twelve would sell him, and he kept him close. Such is the patience of the Son of God with sinners. The chapter ends where it began, with bread. Five thousand ate it and were hungry again the next morning. One of the twelve ate from the very hands that made it, and starved. But all who come to the living bread are fed for ever.
verseByVerse.note: “Iscariot” is often taken to mean “man of Kerioth,” a town in Judea, but that is uncertain.

6.title: The Bread of Life
6.text: <sup>1</sup>After this Jesus went away to the other side of the Sea of Galilee, which is the Sea of Tiberias.<sup>2</sup>And a large crowd was following him, because they saw the signs that he was doing on the sick.<sup>3</sup>Jesus went up on the mountain, and there he sat down with his disciples.<sup>4</sup>Now the Passover, the feast of the Jews, was at hand.<sup>5</sup>Lifting up his eyes, then, and seeing that a large crowd was coming toward him, Jesus said to Philip, “Where are we to buy bread, so that these people may eat?”<sup>6</sup>He said this to test him, for he himself knew what he would do.<sup>7</sup>Philip answered him, “Two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be enough for each of them to get a little.”<sup>8</sup>One of his disciples, Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, said to him,<sup>9</sup>“There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish, but what are they for so many?”<sup>10</sup>Jesus said, “Have the people sit down.” Now there was much grass in the place. So the men sat down, about five thousand in number.<sup>11</sup>Jesus then took the loaves, and when he had given thanks, he distributed them to those who were seated. So also the fish, as much as they wanted.<sup>12</sup>And when they had eaten their fill, he told his disciples, “Gather up the leftover fragments, that nothing may be lost.”<sup>13</sup>So they gathered them up and filled twelve baskets with fragments from the five barley loaves left by those who had eaten.<sup>14</sup>When the people saw the sign that he had done, they said, “This is indeed the Prophet who is to come into the world!”<sup>15</sup>Perceiving then that they were about to come and take him by force to make him king, Jesus withdrew again to the mountain by himself.<sup>16</sup>When evening came, his disciples went down to the sea,<sup>17</sup>got into a boat, and started across the sea to Capernaum. It was now dark, and Jesus had not yet come to them.<sup>18</sup>The sea became rough because a strong wind was blowing.<sup>19</sup>When they had rowed about three or four miles, they saw Jesus walking on the sea and coming near the boat, and they were frightened.<sup>20</sup>But he said to them, “It is I; do not be afraid.”<sup>21</sup>Then they were glad to take him into the boat, and immediately the boat was at the land to which they were going.<sup>22</sup>On the next day the crowd that remained on the other side of the sea saw that there had been only one boat there, and that Jesus had not entered the boat with his disciples, but that his disciples had gone away alone.<sup>23</sup>Other boats from Tiberias came near the place where they had eaten the bread after the Lord had given thanks.<sup>24</sup>So when the crowd saw that Jesus was not there, nor his disciples, they themselves got into the boats and went to Capernaum, seeking Jesus.<sup>25</sup>When they found him on the other side of the sea, they said to him, “Rabbi, when did you come here?”<sup>26</sup>Jesus answered them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, you are seeking me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate your fill of the loaves.<sup>27</sup>Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give to you. For on him God the Father has set his seal.”<sup>28</sup>Then they said to him, “What must we do, to be doing the works of God?”<sup>29</sup>Jesus answered them, “This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent.”<sup>30</sup>So they said to him, “Then what sign do you do, that we may see and believe you? What work do you perform?<sup>31</sup>Our fathers ate the manna in the wilderness; as it is written, ’He gave them bread from heaven to eat.’”<sup>32</sup>Jesus then said to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, it was not Moses who gave you the bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven.<sup>33</sup>For the bread of God is he who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world.”<sup>34</sup>They said to him, “Sir, give us this bread always.”<sup>35</sup>Jesus said to them, “I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst.<sup>36</sup>But I said to you that you have seen me and yet do not believe.<sup>37</sup>All that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will never cast out.<sup>38</sup>For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me.<sup>39</sup>And this is the will of him who sent me, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day.<sup>40</sup>For this is the will of my Father, that everyone who looks on the Son and believes in him should have eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day.”<sup>41</sup>So the Jews grumbled about him, because he said, “I am the bread that came down from heaven.”<sup>42</sup>They said, “Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How does he now say, ’I have come down from heaven’?”<sup>43</sup>Jesus answered them, “Do not grumble among yourselves.<sup>44</sup>No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him. And I will raise him up on the last day.<sup>45</sup>It is written in the Prophets, ’And they will all be taught by God.’ Everyone who has heard and learned from the Father comes to me—<sup>46</sup>not that anyone has seen the Father except he who is from God; he has seen the Father.<sup>47</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes has eternal life.<sup>48</sup>I am the bread of life.<sup>49</sup>Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died.<sup>50</sup>This is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that one may eat of it and not die.<sup>51</sup>I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. And the bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh.”<sup>52</sup>The Jews then disputed among themselves, saying, “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?”<sup>53</sup>So Jesus said to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you.<sup>54</sup>Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day.<sup>55</sup>For my flesh is true food, and my blood is true drink.<sup>56</sup>Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him.<sup>57</sup>As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever feeds on me, he also will live because of me.<sup>58</sup>This is the bread that came down from heaven, not like the bread the fathers ate, and died. Whoever feeds on this bread will live forever.”<sup>59</sup>Jesus said these things in the synagogue, as he taught at Capernaum.<sup>60</sup>When many of his disciples heard it, they said, “This is a hard saying; who can listen to it?”<sup>61</sup>But Jesus, knowing in himself that his disciples were grumbling about this, said to them, “Do you take offense at this?<sup>62</sup>Then what if you were to see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?<sup>63</sup>It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is no help at all. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life.<sup>64</sup>But there are some of you who do not believe.” (For Jesus knew from the beginning who those were who did not believe, and who it was who would betray him.)<sup>65</sup>And he said, “This is why I told you that no one can come to me unless it is granted him by the Father.”<sup>66</sup>After this many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him.<sup>67</sup>So Jesus said to the twelve, “Do you want to go away as well?”<sup>68</sup>Simon Peter answered him, “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life,<sup>69</sup>and we have believed, and have come to know, that you are the Holy One of God.”<sup>70</sup>Jesus answered them, “Did I not choose you, the twelve? And yet one of you is a devil.”<sup>71</sup>He spoke of Judas the son of Simon Iscariot, for he, one of the twelve, was going to betray him.
6.overview:
John sets the feeding of the five thousand near Passover and lets it open into one of Jesus’ longest discourses. After the meal the crowd tries to make him king by force, and he withdraws; that night he comes to his disciples across the stormy lake with words that echo the divine name.

Next day, in the synagogue at Capernaum, he explains the sign. He himself is the true bread from heaven, of which the manna was a picture. All whom the Father gives him will come, none who come will be cast out, and he will raise them up on the last day. The bread is his flesh, given in death for the life of the world and received by faith. Many disciples leave; Peter says there is no one else to go to, though even among the Twelve is one who will betray him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter moves in three stages: Jesus’ refusal to go up on his brothers’ terms (vv. 1–13), his teaching in the temple in the middle of the feast (vv. 14–36), and his invitation on the last day, followed by the failed arrest and the council’s quarrel (vv. 37–52). Behind it all stands the hour of his death, which has not yet come.
verseByVerse.theology: The controversy in John 7 turns on where Jesus comes from and by whose authority he speaks. Asked how he knows the Scriptures without a rabbi, he answers that his teaching is not his own but the Father’s, and that anyone who wants to do God’s will will recognise it. The two questions, where he is from and who gave him authority, are really one: who sent him?
verseByVerse.examples: The Feast of Booths looked back to the wilderness and forward to the day when living waters would flow from Jerusalem (Zechariah 14:8). Jesus stands up at its climax and says that the river flows from him. The officers sent to arrest him came back saying that no one ever spoke like this man (v. 46).

verseByVerse.quote: After this Jesus went about in Galilee. He would not go about in Judea, because the Jews were seeking to kill him. Now the Jews' Feast of Booths was at hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. John 7 and 8 take place at one feast in Jerusalem, and the question running through both is: who is Jesus, and where does he come from? The setting is chosen with care: a week in which the nation camped in shelters of branches to remember God living among them in a tent, poured out water at the altar to remember the rock in the desert, and lit great lamps in the temple court. Into the middle of that week walks the one all three were pointing to.

After this. “After this” covers about six months, from Passover (6:4) in spring to the Feast of Booths in autumn. The hillside crowd of chapter 6 has melted away and many disciples have stopped walking with him (6:66). John records nothing of the summer; what he wants us to see is the next confrontation.

Seeking to kill him. Since the Sabbath healing in Jerusalem (5:18), the authorities had wanted him dead, and everything in this chapter happens with that sentence standing over it. His hour has not yet come (v. 30), and he will not die before the time the Father has set. Yet he is no coward: in the spring he will walk into Jerusalem in the open, knowing what waits for him. He is refusing to die at a time of other people’s choosing. He moves when the Father says, and his moves are never reactions.

The Feast of Booths. The Feast of Booths, or Tabernacles (skēnopēgia, pitching of tents), was the third of the great pilgrim festivals, along with Passover and Pentecost (Deuteronomy 16:16). It came in September or October, at the end of the harvest, and lasted seven days, with an eighth day of solemn assembly (Leviticus 23:33–43). Families built shelters of branches on courtyards and flat roofs and slept in them for the week, remembering the wilderness years when they had nothing and God provided everything. It was the most joyful feast of the year.

The water and the light. By Jesus’ day two ceremonies had been added. Every morning a priest carried water up from the Pool of Siloam and poured it out at the altar, with prayers for rain and songs of joy (Isaiah 12:3). And at night great lamps were lit in the Court of the Women, lighting up all Jerusalem; the sources say there was not a courtyard in the city that did not glow with their light. Jesus will say “come to me and drink” (v. 37) and “I am the light of the world” (8:12) against this background. He is standing in front of the ceremony and saying that it was about him. Zechariah 14, with its living waters flowing from Jerusalem, belonged to this feast: it names Booths as the festival all the nations will one day keep (Zechariah 14:16).

Was Jesus wrong to avoid danger? Should he not have trusted the Father? No. Trusting God has never meant walking carelessly into harm. Jesus refused to throw himself from the temple to prove that God would catch him (Matthew 4:5–7), and here he refuses to throw himself into the hands of men who had already decided to kill him. Paul did the same when he was let down over the wall of Damascus in a basket (Acts 9:25). The question is not whether we take sensible steps to stay safe, but why. Fear says, I must save my life at any cost. Faith says, my life is in the Father’s hands, so I will neither waste it nor cling to it. When the hour came, the same Jesus who avoided Judea set his face to go to Jerusalem, and nothing could turn him back.
verseByVerse.note: The Feast of Booths (Tabernacles) was the joyful autumn harvest festival. For a week people lived in shelters made of branches, remembering Israel’s years in the wilderness.

parallels.desc: the Feast of Booths

verseByVerse.quote: So his brothers said to him, "Leave here and go to Judea, that your disciples also may see the works you are doing. For no one works in secret if he seeks to be known openly. If you do these things, show yourself to the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So his brothers said to him. His brothers were James, Joses, Judas and Simon (Mark 6:3), and Mark mentions sisters as well. Roman Catholic teaching takes them as cousins, and Eastern Orthodox teaching as Joseph’s sons by an earlier marriage, to preserve Mary’s perpetual virginity; but the natural reading is that they were Mary’s later sons (Matthew 1:25; Luke 2:7), and they appear again and again with Mary as her family (Mark 3:31; Acts 1:14).

Your disciples. “Your disciples” may mean the followers in Judea, or those who had turned away (6:66). The phrase is spoken at arm’s length: your disciples, not ours.

No one works in secret. They think like the world: if you want to be famous, go public. Read it as advice rather than villainy; any modern adviser would say the same. That is exactly what is wrong with it. His kingdom does not advance by staged displays for the largest possible audience.

Show yourself to the world. “If” reveals their doubt: they don’t deny the miracles, but they don’t trust him. It is the temptation Satan put to him (Matthew 4:5–7). And there is a terrible irony in the words: he will show himself to the world. In this Gospel that is what the cross is: the lifting up, the public display, the moment when he is shown to everybody, written over in three languages for every passer-by to read (19:20). His brothers have named the right event and the wrong method, and they have no idea that the showing they are urging on him will happen at Passover and will kill him.

Does it matter whether Mary had other children? It is not the centre of the gospel, but the plainest sense of the Gospels is that Jesus grew up in a crowded house with brothers and sisters, and Mary is honoured as the mother of our Lord without needing a perpetual virginity. (See Mark 6:3 for the fuller answer.)

On a Tuesday. Be wary of advice that measures faithfulness by publicity. The pressure is everywhere now: grow the following, post the result, build the brand, be seen. Some visibility is simply the cost of telling people the truth, and nobody should hide a light under a basket. But ask of any plan, in your church or your own heart: is this aimed at making Christ known, or at making me known? The two can look identical from the outside for a long time.
verseByVerse.note: His brothers were James, Joses, Judas and Simon.

verseByVerse.quote: For not even his brothers believed in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not even his brothers. John explains their advice (compare Mark 3:21), in an aside that is among the most useful in the New Testament for a particular kind of grief. These men had lived in the same small house with him for most of their lives, watched him work, eat, sleep and pray, and they did not believe. If moral excellence at close range were enough to produce faith, these four men would have been the first converts in history. Familiarity is the enemy of awe: they knew Jesus the man too well to recognise Jesus the Lord.

But that is not the end of the story. After the resurrection, Jesus appeared to James (1 Corinthians 15:7), and the brothers were among the believers praying in the upper room (Acts 1:14). James later led the church in Jerusalem (Acts 15:13; Galatians 2:9) and is generally held to have written the letter of James, as Judas (Jude) is held to have written the letter of Jude. The scandal of unbelief can be overcome, but only by resurrection: the same power that raised Jesus from the grave raised James from his unbelief.

The case was not closed. Take the person you have most nearly given up on. If this chapter had been the last word about James, every reasonable observer would have concluded the case was closed: a lifetime of evidence, no result. It was about six months from being reopened, and nothing in the meantime looked like progress. The worst week of all, the week his brother was crucified, was the week that, as far as we can tell, led to James’ conversion.

My family has watched my life for years and still does not believe. Have I failed them? Not necessarily. The most compelling life ever lived was on display in one household for thirty years and did not persuade the people in it. Unbelief is not proof that your witness was poor, and it is not proof that the case for Christ is weak. Faith is not produced by example alone; it is the gift of God, who opens blind eyes when he chooses (6:44). Your example still matters: live in a way that makes the gospel credible, apologise when you fail, keep loving them. But the burden of converting them was never yours to carry. Keep praying, keep loving, and leave the timing with the one who went to see James.

On a Tuesday. Write down the name of the relative you have quietly stopped praying for, and bring that name back to God today. And if you grew up around Christianity, take the warning: it is possible to have grown up in the very house and still not believe.

For worship. For thirty years the eternal Son let his brothers judge him ordinary, and he never forced their faith. When it came, it came as worship. James, who could have signed himself the brother of the Lord, wrote instead a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ (James 1:1); Jude called himself a servant of Jesus Christ, and only then a brother of James (Jude 1). The brothers who once told him to show himself to the world spent their lives showing him to it. He is patient with the people closest to him, and his patience wins.
verseByVerse.note: James later led the church in Jerusalem, and the brothers were among the believers after the resurrection.

parallels.desc: with Mary and his brothers
he appeared to James

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them, "My time has not yet come, but your time is always here. The world cannot hate you, but it hates me because I testify about it that its works are evil."
verseByVerse.commentary:
My time has not yet come. “Time” here is kairos, the right moment for a thing. John’s usual word is the hour (hōra), the fixed appointment of his death and glorification, which turns up at Cana (2:4) and in verse 30 and finally arrives in chapter 12 (12:23). Jesus lives by the Father’s timetable, not his brothers’.

But your time is always here. For them any time is fine: they have no mission to fulfil, no appointment they are waiting on, and they are not under threat. He does not mean it as a compliment.

The world cannot hate you. “The world” in John is humanity organised in rebellion against God. It cannot hate them, because they belong to it. Not does not: cannot. They fit; they speak its language and want what it wants. He is telling his brothers that their safety is a symptom. Later he tells his disciples the same truth from the other side: if you were of the world, the world would love you as its own (15:19).

Its works are evil. Light shows up the darkness (3:19–20). People don’t object to Jesus as a teacher of kindness; they object when he says their works are evil. The world tolerates many kinds of religion and moral teaching; it cannot tolerate the claim that its basic direction is sinful and that only grace can save it. The cross is the world’s answer to that testimony.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that being disliked is proof of faithfulness. Many Christians are disliked for being rude, ignorant, harsh or politically obnoxious, and that hostility has nothing to do with Christ. The verse names the cause exactly: the world hates him because he testifies that its works are evil. The offence is having the truth told about oneself by someone who loves you enough to tell it. So the test is narrow: not, am I disliked? but, is there anything in my life that would make the world uncomfortable if it were paying attention? A faith with no friction at all may simply be a private faith. It may also be one that has quietly stopped saying the thing that causes friction; and the one who bore the world’s hatred for us gives his Spirit for both courage and love.

Is it not arrogant for Jesus to call the world’s works evil? That charge would stick only if he spoke from a safe height and exempted himself and his friends. He did neither. He says it to the devout and the careless alike, to his own brothers in this verse and to the leaders of the temple in the same chapter, and he says it as the one who has come to carry that evil away. A doctor who tells you the truth about the tumour is not arrogant; the one who hides it to keep you comfortable is cruel. And this doctor pays for the cure himself, with his own life. A teacher who never names evil can never save anyone from it.

But does God not love the world (3:16)? How can the world be the enemy? Both are true, and John holds them together. The world is humanity in rebellion against God, and God loves it anyway, not because it is lovable but because he is love. He loved it enough to send his Son into it, knowing it would hate him. So when Jesus says the world hates him, he is not describing a world God has given up on; he is describing the world he came to save. Christians are called to the same double stance: not loving the world’s rebellion (1 John 2:15), and loving the people caught in it enough to tell them the truth.

parallels.desc: if the world hates you

verseByVerse.quote: "You go up to the feast. I am not going up to this feast, for my time has not yet fully come." After saying this, he remained in Galilee.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You go up to the feast. Jerusalem stands high in the hills, so one always went up to it; the pilgrim psalms are the Songs of Ascents (Psalms 120–134).

I am not going up to this feast. Yet he does go (v. 10); the charge of lying is answered below. Some see a play on “go up”: the same verb is used of his ascending to the Father (20:17). He will not “go up” in that sense, to glory, at this feast.

A charge worth answering. The sentence has been used for centuries to accuse Jesus of lying. The third-century critic Porphyry pressed exactly this point. It answers well, because the whole exchange is about a manner of going, not a matter of geography. His brothers were not offering him a lift to Jerusalem; they were urging a campaign: show yourself to the world (v. 4), go up publicly, with the crowds, and stake your claim. That is the going up he refuses. And John himself supplies the distinction in the very next sentence: when Jesus did go, he went not publicly but in private (v. 10). The man who would shortly refuse to come down from a cross was not a man who trimmed his words to make an afternoon easier.

For my time has not yet fully come. “Fully come” (peplērōtai, been fulfilled). He is not managing his image with a convenient untruth; he is declining a schedule that was not his Father’s.

Textual note. Many manuscripts, including two of the earliest papyri, read “I am not yet going up,” and the KJV and NKJV follow them. Other early manuscripts read “I am not going up,” and most modern Bibles judge this the original, since a scribe was more likely to add “yet” to ease the problem than to remove it. So the honest course is to answer the harder text rather than shelter behind the easier, and as we have seen, the harder text needs no shelter.

If manuscripts differ, can I trust my Bible? Yes. We have far more early copies of the New Testament than of any other ancient book, and comparing them lets scholars see clearly where a copyist slipped or smoothed. The great majority of differences are spelling, word order or small words like this “yet”, and none of them touches any teaching of the faith. This very note shows it: the reading that looks harder is kept precisely because it is harder, which shows that the copyists were not freely inventing but were anxious about every word. Your Bible’s footnotes are not a sign that the text is shaky. They are a sign that it has been handled with great care.

He remained in Galilee. The remaining is not passivity but restraint: the hour has been set from eternity and cannot be rushed by family pressure or popular demand.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add “yet” — “I am not yet going up.”

verseByVerse.quote: But after his brothers had gone up to the feast, then he also went up, not publicly but in private. The Jews were looking for him at the feast, and saying, "Where is he?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not publicly but in private. The Son of God goes up to his own people’s feast in a stream of pilgrims, unrecognised. And the secrecy is temporary: he goes up hidden in verse 10 and is teaching in the temple courts by verse 14. What he refused was his brothers’ method: the arrival, the entourage, the staged display. Days later he does the most public thing available to a man in Jerusalem, and does it alone.

Looking for him. Two searches run through the chapter: the authorities are looking for him in order to end him, and the crowd because they cannot stop talking about him. He walks through the middle of both.

Where is he? “Where” is a key word in John 7 and 8: where he comes from, and where he is going (vv. 27, 34–35; 8:14, 21). And the question has a coldness to it. They will not use his name. It is the tone of people discussing somebody they have already decided about. Yet beneath the surface it is the deepest question there is: where is God? The answer John gives across twenty-one chapters is that he is here, in this man, at this feast.

The man they cannot find is the tent. The word for the feast comes from the same root as the verb he used in the prologue: the Word became flesh and dwelt, literally pitched his tent, among us (1:14). The whole city is sleeping under branches to remember the time God travelled with them in a tent, and the man they are looking for is the tent.

Is it ever right for a Christian to be secret? Sometimes discretion is wisdom, and Jesus himself shows it here. Believers in hostile countries meet quietly; a Christian may wisely choose not to announce every plan to people who mean him harm (Matthew 10:16–17). But there is a difference between discretion about our movements and silence about our Lord. Jesus hid his journey for a few days; he never hid who he was. If we are hiding our faith because we are ashamed of Christ, that is not wisdom but fear (Mark 8:38). Prudence protects the mission. Cowardice abandons it.

verseByVerse.quote: And there was much muttering about him among the people. While some said, "He is a good man," others said, "No, he is leading the people astray." Yet for fear of the Jews no one spoke openly of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
