Much muttering. “Muttering” is the same word as “grumbled” in 6:41 (gongysmos), here meaning whispered debate. It is the wilderness word for Israel’s grumbling in the desert, used here of admirers and accusers alike.

Some said, “He is a good man.” A compliment that falls far short (see below). It is the kindly verdict, and the one most people still reach for.

Others said, “No, he is leading the people astray.” “Leading astray” (planaō) was a serious charge: the false prophet who leads Israel away from God was to be put to death (Deuteronomy 13:1–5). Later Jewish writings describe Jesus as one who practised sorcery and led Israel astray: this is the formal accusation on which he will be executed. The one thing nobody in this verse says is that he might be telling the truth about himself.

For fear of the Jews. Fear of the leaders silences everyone, and it is not the opposition who are silent. It is the people who think well of him who say nothing. The phrase becomes one of John’s refrains: it is why the blind man’s parents will not answer a straight question (9:22), why Joseph of Arimathea kept his discipleship quiet (19:38). Jesus himself will name the root: they loved the glory that comes from man more than the glory that comes from God (12:43).

Why can’t Jesus simply be a good man and a great teacher? Because of what he taught. A good man does not claim to be equal with God, to forgive sins against other people, to be the bread from heaven, or to be the one by whom everyone will be judged. If those claims are false, he is either deceived about himself on a scale no sane good man could be, or he is deceiving others, which is exactly the charge in this verse. The verdicts that take him seriously are that he was deceived, that he was a deceiver, or that he is the Lord. Some reply that the large claims were put in his mouth by the later church; but the earliest sources we have, Mark and the letters of Paul, written within a few decades, already present him forgiving sins and claiming to be the coming judge (Mark 2:5–10; 14:62), and already worship him as Lord (Philippians 2:9–11), so the question cannot be dodged that way. The good teacher who claims nothing is a figure people invented later to avoid having to decide.

Does John’s phrase “the Jews” make his Gospel anti-Jewish? No. John was a Jew, Jesus was a Jew, every disciple and nearly every believer in this Gospel is a Jew, and Jesus says salvation is from the Jews (4:22). In passages like this, “the Jews” plainly means the religious authorities in Jerusalem who opposed him, as the sentence itself shows: the Jewish crowd is afraid of the Jews. The Gospel never gives any warrant for hatred of the Jewish people. Christians who have used it that way have sinned grievously, and contempt for Jews is a denial of the Christ who was born a son of David and wept over Jerusalem.

On a Tuesday. Recall a recent conversation in which the subject came near enough that you could have said something about him, and you did not. What held you back was probably not persecution but the half-second of awkwardness, the sense of becoming the person who brings that up. The pressure here was far heavier than ours; the mechanism is the same. He was not ashamed to die openly for you, and his Spirit gives the words: next time, say one true sentence about him.

parallels.desc: a prophet who leads you astray
that impostor

verseByVerse.quote: About the middle of the feast Jesus went up into the temple and began teaching. The Jews therefore marveled, saying, "How is it that this man has learning, when he has never studied?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
About the middle of the feast. Around the fourth day of the seven. The timing is deliberate: he let the festival fill up until the crowds were at their largest, and then walked into the busiest place in Jerusalem and began to teach.

Into the temple. Now he appears openly, in the temple courts where rabbis taught. Malachi had promised that the Lord whom you seek would suddenly come to his temple (Malachi 3:1). In the middle of a feast, without announcement, he does, and before long he is exposing the hearts of the men who ran it (v. 19).

How is it that this man has learning, when he has never studied? “Learning” is literally “letters” (grammata), meaning knowledge of the Scriptures and their interpretation. It is not a claim that he was illiterate; Luke shows him handed a scroll in the synagogue and finding his place in it (Luke 4:16–17). “Never studied” means he had not been trained under a recognised rabbi, the way Paul was trained under Gamaliel (Acts 22:3). A teacher was expected to cite his teachers: Rabbi So-and-so said, in the name of Rabbi So-and-so. That is how authority worked, and it is not a foolish system; it is how a community protects itself from anyone who turns up with a private revelation. Jesus quoted no rabbi, and yet he knew the Scriptures more deeply than any of them. They are not sneering, quite. They are trying to account for something that does not fit their categories. The same surprise is expressed about the apostles (Acts 4:13).

Does this mean training does not matter for preachers? No. The system was not wrong to ask where he had studied, and that question has saved the church from a great deal of nonsense. Paul was highly trained, and Scripture requires that elders be able to teach and hold firm to sound doctrine (Titus 1:9; 2 Timothy 2:15). Jesus is unique: his teacher was the Father, which no one else can claim. For everyone else, study is the ordinary way God makes faithful teachers. But the final test is not a certificate. It is whether a teacher’s words agree with Scripture and point to Christ. A trained man can be wrong, and an untrained believer can be right, and both must be weighed by the Word.

For worship. Christ needed no teacher but the Father. The rabbis looked for a chain of teachers behind him and found none, because the chain ended in him: he is the Word who was with God in the beginning, and every true teacher who has ever opened the Scriptures has been borrowing from him. In him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3), and he gives them freely to fishermen.
verseByVerse.note: “Never studied” means he had not been trained under a recognised rabbi.

parallels.desc: uneducated, common men

verseByVerse.quote: So Jesus answered them, "My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me. If anyone's will is to do God's will, he will know whether the teaching is from God or whether I am speaking on my own authority."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not mine. Jesus answers their question. He did have a teacher: the Father (5:19; 8:28; 12:49). The Son’s school was eternal communion with the Father, a far greater authority than any rabbinic lineage.

If anyone’s will is to do God’s will. “Will” (thelē) means wants, wills, desires. The condition for knowing the truth is not first intellectual, but moral and spiritual: a will set on doing what God wants. This answers a question honest people ask: how could I know whether this is true? He offers no argument or sign: willingness first, knowledge second. If a person insists on staying uncommitted while he weighs the evidence, that stance, however honest, keeps him from the one kind of evidence that matters most here.

He will know. The problem with unbelief is not lack of evidence but an unwilling heart (5:40; 8:43–47). That can sound like a cheat, but it is not. Some things can be known while remaining uninvolved, like the boiling point of water; others are only knowable from inside. Nobody has ever learned whether a person is trustworthy by studying them at a distance; you find out by trusting them. To claim that God is known in the second way is not special pleading. It is a claim about what sort of being God is: not an object to be examined but a Lord to be obeyed. And the promise is wide: not if anyone is clever or educated. The condition is a disposition, not an achievement, and it is open to the least equipped person in the room.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that we can come to faith by our own good will, as if some people are naturally willing. John has just said no one can come unless the Father draws (6:44). The willing heart is itself God’s work. Whoever is of God hears the words of God (8:47). The verse describes how the Father’s drawing works: he gives a heart that wants to obey, and that heart recognises the Son’s teaching as God’s. But it does mean that the person who genuinely wants God’s will will never be left in the dark.

I want to believe, but I still have doubts. Does that mean my will is not set on God? No. Doubt is not the same as unwillingness. Many true believers carry questions for years, and Scripture is full of them (Psalm 73; Mark 9:24). What this verse describes is the person who keeps God at arm’s length so as not to have to obey him. If you want God’s will, even weakly, and you are grieved by your doubts rather than comfortable with them, that wanting is itself his work in you. Bring your questions to him, keep reading his word, and keep obeying what you already know. Light comes along the road of obedience, often more slowly than we would like, but it comes.

On a Tuesday. Take the one thing you already suspect God wants of you: not a doctrine you are unsure of, but the plain duty you have been avoiding, the apology, the confession, the habit. Do that, in the strength of the Spirit who gave you the wanting. Sometimes the doubt was standing on top of the disobedience, and cannot survive its removal. You will not obey perfectly; the Son did his Father’s will perfectly for you, his obedience is counted as yours, and your halting obedience is accepted in him.

verseByVerse.quote: "The one who speaks on his own authority seeks his own glory; but the one who seeks the glory of him who sent him is true, and in him there is no falsehood. Has not Moses given you the law? Yet none of you keeps the law. Why do you seek to kill me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seeks his own glory. A test for any teacher: whose glory does he seek? Not eloquence or success, but the direction his ambition points: who is bigger at the end of the sermon?

No falsehood. Jesus seeks only the Father’s glory, and that is the proof of his truthfulness. “Falsehood” here is adikia, unrighteousness. He is not merely claiming to be accurate; he is claiming that there is nothing crooked in him at all, no bent motive under the straight sentence. It is either true or insufferable, and in him it is simply true.

Has not Moses given you the law? Yet none of you keeps the law. Jesus turns to the attack. They pride themselves on Moses, but they don’t keep his law. The change of register is abrupt. He has been reasoning; now he accuses.

Why do you seek to kill me? The proof: the law forbids murder, and they are planning one. They accuse Jesus of breaking the Sabbath, while they are planning to break the sixth commandment. It is the first time in the chapter that anybody says it out loud. John told the reader at verse 1, but no one in the courts has admitted it, and Jesus puts it in the middle of an argument about Moses, the most pointed place it could go. The charge is not exaggeration. Within months they will do precisely that, and it will be arranged by the men standing in front of him. He is reading their diary aloud.

In the flow. Verse 19 turns the question back on his hearers and leads into verses 21–24, where he defends the Sabbath healing of chapter 5 from their own law: the accused becomes the judge.

How can I tell whether a preacher is seeking his own glory? Watch over time, not over a single sermon, because the test works over years rather than sentences. A man seeking Christ’s glory will make Christ large and himself small in his preaching; he will open the text rather than use it as a launch pad for himself. He will be accountable to others and will not build a ministry that cannot survive without him. He will be glad when someone else is preferred, slow to defend his own reputation, and quick to admit when he is wrong. Be wary of the teacher whose stories are mostly about himself, who cannot take correction, or whose church seems to exist to display him. And turn the test on yourself: when you serve, whose name do you most want remembered?

For worship. There has only ever been one teacher in whom there was no falsehood at all. Every word he spoke aimed at his Father’s glory, and the Father answered by glorifying him (17:1). The men who held Moses in their hands and murder in their hearts stood before the only man who ever kept the law perfectly, and he kept it for them, all the way to the cross they were planning for him.

verseByVerse.quote: The crowd answered, "You have a demon! Who is seeking to kill you?" Jesus answered them, "I did one work, and you all marvel at it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You have a demon. “Have a demon” was a way of saying mad (10:20); the same charge returns in 8:48, 52. On the crowd’s part this is not so much hostility as alarm. Pilgrims who know nothing of the leaders’ plot hear a teacher say people are trying to murder him and conclude he is unwell. It is the ordinary fate of anyone who names what the room has agreed not to see, and the cheapest response available. In this case the man was entirely correct.

Who is seeking to kill you? They don’t know. The leaders do (v. 25). It is worth keeping the two groups apart in this chapter, because John does. The crowd here is the festival pilgrims: ignorant, volatile and mostly well disposed. “The Jews”, in John’s shorthand, generally means the Jerusalem leadership, the men in verse 1 who had already decided. When the crowd asks who is seeking to kill him, they are telling the truth; they do not know. The reader has been told in the chapter’s first sentence, and so watches the exchange knowing what nobody in it knows.

One work. The “one work” is the healing at the pool on the Sabbath (5:1–9), which started the plot to kill him. “Marvel” here means they are disturbed and shocked by it, not admiring. His reply goes straight past the insult. And count how long ago that was: chapter 5 was at an unnamed feast, chapter 6 at Passover, and this is Tabernacles. Many months on, they are still on it. The word one points not at the scale of the offence but at the arithmetic of the grievance. A single act of kindness to a man who had been ill for thirty-eight years has produced a settled determination to kill the one who did it, and the grievance has outlasted the memory of everything else he has done.

How should I respond when people think my faith is foolish or unhinged? Much as Jesus did: without panic and without retaliation. He did not argue about whether he was mad; he went straight back to the real issue. When people call your faith foolish, do not take the bait of defending your sanity or your intelligence. Gently bring the conversation back to Christ himself: what he did, what he said, why it matters. Paul was told he was out of his mind and answered with courtesy and the truth (Acts 26:24–25). And remember that if they said it of the Master, they will say it of his servants (15:20). It is not a sign you have failed. It may be a sign you have been clear.

On a Tuesday. Most of us carry a grievance like this somewhere: one act, by one person, still held against them months or years later, while everything else they have done is forgotten. Grudges grow in the dark. Brought to the God who has dropped every charge against you, they can be seen for the size they really are, and let go.
verseByVerse.note: The “one work” is the healing at the pool on the Sabbath.

verseByVerse.quote: "Moses gave you circumcision (not that it is from Moses, but from the fathers), and you circumcise a man on the Sabbath."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses gave you circumcision. Jesus argues from their own law, in a standard rabbinic form his opponents would have recognised instantly.

Not that it is from Moses, but from the fathers. Circumcision was given to Abraham (Genesis 17:10–12), centuries before Moses, and the law confirmed it (Leviticus 12:3). The obligation they allow to override the Sabbath is older than the Sabbath laws of Sinai. He is showing them that they already know how to rank two commandments when they seem to collide.

You circumcise a man. The law said a boy must be circumcised on the eighth day. If the eighth day fell on a Sabbath, circumcision went ahead, even though it was work. The rabbis agreed, and the Mishnah says everything needed for circumcision may be done on the Sabbath. Jesus is not proposing a novelty; he is taking their own ruling and asking why it stops where it does.

What kind of thing wins. Circumcision overrides the Sabbath because it marks a child as belonging to God. The principle they have already granted is not administrative but merciful. When a rule and a person’s standing before God seem to collide, the person wins. Jesus is about to apply that to a man who had been on a mat for thirty-eight years, and it is their principle, not his.

Does this mean God’s commandments can be broken when they clash? No. God’s law does not contradict itself; the problem lies in how men had applied it. The Sabbath was never meant to forbid works of necessity and mercy, and even the confessions that keep Sunday as the Christian Sabbath, the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, say so plainly, permitting works of necessity and mercy (Westminster 21.8; 1689 22.8). Jesus is not setting one command against another. He is showing that the command, rightly understood, always had room for love. When we feel that obeying God and loving people are in conflict, the answer is not to drop one but to look again at what God actually commanded.

For worship. The Lord who reasoned so patiently about the eighth-day sign had received it himself: Luke tells us he was circumcised as a boy of eight days (Luke 2:21), marked with the covenant he had made with Abraham. And what the sign promised, he gives: a circumcision made without hands, the putting off of the body of the flesh by the circumcision of Christ (Colossians 2:11), so that people from every nation are marked as God’s own, not by a knife but by his death and rising.
verseByVerse.note: Circumcision on the eighth day went ahead even when that day was a Sabbath. It began with Abraham, before Moses.

verseByVerse.quote: "If on the Sabbath a man receives circumcision, so that the law of Moses may not be broken, are you angry with me because on the Sabbath I made a man's whole body well? Do not judge by appearances, but judge with right judgment."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Light and heavy. The argument goes from lesser to greater, a standard rabbinic method, which they called light and heavy. If it is right to perform circumcision, which affects one part of the body, on the Sabbath...

Are you angry with me because on the Sabbath I made a man’s whole body well? ...how much more right is it to make a whole man well? Some rabbis themselves argued that if circumcision, involving one member, overrides the Sabbath, saving a life overrides it too. Jesus takes the argument further: healing fits the very purpose of the Sabbath, a day of rest and restoration. The phrase he chooses is deliberate. One member against the whole man. If the part may be dealt with, how can healing the whole be a violation?

Right judgment. “Appearances” (opsis) means what is seen on the surface: they see only that he worked on the Sabbath. Right judgment looks at what was really done, and why, as God looks on the heart (1 Samuel 16:7). This verse is regularly quoted as if it said the opposite of what it says. It is a command to judge. Jesus is in the middle of telling a crowd that their verdict on him is wrong, and his complaint is not that they judged but that they judged badly.

So am I allowed to judge people or not? Yes and no, and Jesus’ two sayings fit together once you notice what each is about. Judge not, that you be not judged (Matthew 7:1) forbids the judgment that sets itself up as final, condemns the person, and applies to others a standard the speaker exempts himself from; it is followed at once by the log in one’s own eye. This verse requires the judgment that looks past the surface to the substance. The first forbids condemning. The second commands discerning. A Christian must tell right from wrong, truth from error, and a wolf from a sheep. What he must never do is sit in God’s seat over another person’s soul, or judge by rumour, appearance or prejudice.

Where Christians differ: the Sabbath today. Jesus never abolished the Sabbath in the Gospels, but showed its true purpose. Some Christians keep a strict Saturday or Sunday Sabbath; others see no special day at all. This commentary’s view: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our rest (Hebrews 4:9–10; Colossians 2:16–17). The Lord’s Day, the first day, when Christ rose, is a privilege for Christians, set apart gladly for worship, fellowship and rest, not as a binding law with rules about work, and with works of mercy always in place; no one may bind another’s conscience about it (Romans 14:5). The view of the Westminster and 1689 Baptist confessions, that the Lord’s Day is the Christian Sabbath under the fourth commandment, is held by many godly brothers and deserves respect.

What does keeping the Lord’s Day look like in practice? Begin with what it is for: meeting the risen Christ with his people. So put gathered worship at the centre and arrange the rest of the day around it, rather than fitting church into a busy Sunday. Rest from your ordinary work where you can, not as a rule to earn favour but as a gift that says your life does not depend on your labour. Make room for what refreshes the soul: the word, prayer, family, hospitality, visiting the lonely or the sick. Works of mercy and necessity are always in place: nurses, carers and parents of small children are not breaking anything. And do not make the day a burden for others; Jesus came to free the Sabbath from that.

parallels.desc: judge righteously

verseByVerse.quote: Some of the people of Jerusalem therefore said, "Is not this the man whom they seek to kill? And here he is, speaking openly, and they say nothing to him! Can it be that the authorities really know that this is the Christ?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people of Jerusalem. Not the pilgrims, but locals who know the plot the crowd denied (v. 20), watching a man under sentence teach in the temple courts unmolested.

Speaking openly. “Openly” is parrhēsia, saying everything without holding back, the word used of the crowd in verse 13: no one spoke openly of him. The people who admire him whisper; the man with a price on his head speaks freely in the temple.

Can it be that the authorities really know that this is the Christ? The Greek form expects the answer no. They are half joking, half wondering. “The Christ” (ho Christos), the Messiah, the anointed king. Their reasoning is not stupid. If the authorities wanted him, and he is standing in public, and nothing is happening, then something must have changed, and the only explanation they can think of is that the rulers have quietly come round.

The restraint nobody can see. They are wrong, and John will supply the reason four verses later: no one laid a hand on him, because his hour had not yet come (v. 30). The inaction they are trying to explain is a restraint nobody in the story can see. That is the shape of a great deal of providence, God’s unseen hand governing great events and small, so that not even a sparrow falls apart from your Father (Matthew 10:29). Things do not happen, and everyone constructs a reason; the real reason is not available to the people looking for it.

verseByVerse.quote: "But we know where this man comes from, and when the Christ appears, no one will know where he comes from."
verseByVerse.commentary:
We know. They know he is from Nazareth in Galilee. And the verb carries the deepest irony in the chapter: the whole of this Gospel is the answer to that sentence. John’s readers have known since the first verse that he comes from the Father’s side, and that the true answer to where he is from is a place none of them has considered.

No one will know. Some expected the Messiah to appear suddenly from hiding. Jewish writings speak of the Messiah being hidden until God revealed him. Others knew he would come from Bethlehem (v. 42). The crowd uses both traditions against him within fifteen verses. Here he is disqualified because his origin is known. There he is disqualified because it is the wrong one. Any candidate who satisfied the second would fail the first.

The irony. They know neither his birthplace, Bethlehem, nor his true origin, the Father. It is a recognisable human habit, not a peculiarly Jewish one. When a conclusion has been reached in advance, the reasons arrive afterwards and do not need to be consistent with each other, since their job is not to establish the conclusion but to protect it.

So where did Jesus come from? Three answers, all true. As a man, he was born in Bethlehem, the town of David, as Micah foretold (Matthew 2:1–6), and grew up in Nazareth, which is why he was called a Nazarene. As the Son, he came from the Father, with whom he was before the world began (1:1; 17:5). And he came into the world by the Holy Spirit, conceived in the womb of the virgin Mary (Luke 1:35). His enemies knew only the town where he grew up. Faith knows all of them: the eternal Son, born of a woman, raised in a despised village, so that no one could say God had come too high for them to reach.

For worship. The one whose goings forth are from of old, from ancient days (Micah 5:2), consented to have a hometown that people could sneer at. He came from the Father’s side to a carpenter’s house, and let men think they had him summed up. They did not know that the man in front of them had made the hills that Nazareth stood on.
verseByVerse.note: Some expected the Messiah to appear suddenly from hiding.

verseByVerse.quote: "So Jesus proclaimed, as he taught in the temple, 'You know me, and you know where I come from. But I have not come of my own accord. He who sent me is true, and him you do not know. I know him, for I come from him, and he sent me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Jesus proclaimed. “Proclaimed” (ekraxen, cried out): a loud, public, solemn declaration (v. 37; 12:44). He raises his voice in the temple courts.

You know me. It can be read as a concession, yes, you know the human facts and they are correct as far as they go, or with an edge, as near to sarcasm as he comes: so you know me, do you? The sentence that follows tips it toward the second. Whatever they know, it has left them ignorant of the one thing that would explain him: he has not come of his own accord, but was sent.

Him you do not know. “True” (alēthinos): genuine, real. To reject the Son is to show you do not know the Father (8:19; 15:21). He tells a courtyard of devout people, at their own feast, that they do not know God, not imperfectly but at all, and that he does. A man may say a great deal about God in that building and survive it; this is the charge they will not forgive.

I know him. Jesus knows the Father because he came from the Father’s presence. The ground he gives is not experience but origin: he started with God, as God (1:1, 18).

In the flow. The crowd has just said they know where he comes from (v. 27). Jesus says they know only the half that matters least: he comes from the Father who sent him. Everything else in John 7 and 8 rests on this claim, and the attempt to arrest him in the next verse shows they understood how much he was claiming.

Can someone be sincerely religious and still not know God? Yes, and this verse is the proof. These men prayed, fasted, studied Scripture and kept the feasts, and Jesus says they did not know the one they worshipped. Knowing God is not the same as being religious. Eternal life is to know the only true God and Jesus Christ whom he has sent (17:3), and no one comes to the Father except through the Son (14:6). That is not a reason to sneer at sincere people of other faiths or none, but it is a reason not to leave them where they are. And it is a question to ask ourselves, gently and honestly: do I know God through Christ, or do I only know the religion?

On a Tuesday. Knowing God comes through knowing the Son. If God feels distant or unreal to you, look at Jesus: read a Gospel, slowly, and ask at each page, so this is what God is like. Then talk to him about what you see.

verseByVerse.quote: So they were seeking to arrest him, but no one laid a hand on him, because his hour had not yet come. Yet many of the people believed in him. They said, "When the Christ appears, will he do more signs than this man has done?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
His hour had not yet come. Now the word John has been holding back returns: not kairos, the right moment of verse 6, but hōra, the appointment of his death, resurrection and return to the Father (2:4; 8:20; 12:23; 13:1; 17:1). That hour is the cross, and it will not come until chapter 12. What protects him here is not a bodyguard but an appointment with his own execution that has not yet fallen due. He is safe because his death is fixed for another day.

Does this mean nothing bad can happen to me until my work is done? Not quite, and it is worth being honest about what the verse promises. It does not say God’s servants are always preserved until they have done everything we think they should do; Stephen was stoned early in his ministry, and John the Baptist was beheaded on a whim at a party. What it says is narrower, harder and more solid: nothing whatever happens outside the Father’s timing, including the things that look like defeat. The same providence that kept hands off Jesus in this verse will hand him over in chapter 18, and it is the same providence doing the same loving work. Your days are written in his book (Psalm 139:16). No accident, no enemy and no illness can shorten them by an hour.

Many believed. In John, belief can be shallow (2:23–25; 8:30–31), but here it is a start. In a chapter of hostility and arrest warrants, faith is quietly spreading.

When the Christ appears, will he do more signs than this man has done? They reason from the signs. This is not the deepest faith, but signs are meant to lead to faith (20:30–31). Their reasoning is modest and mostly right: could anyone do more than this? It is not a complete confession. It is not nothing.

Is faith that starts from miracles real faith? It can be the beginning of real faith, and Jesus does not despise it. He does not break a bruised reed (Matthew 12:20). John himself wrote down the signs so that we may believe (20:31). But faith that only wants more signs, and stops at what Jesus can do, has not yet reached who he is. The crowd in chapter 6 wanted more bread and walked away when he offered himself. True faith moves from the works to the person: from what he did, to trusting him, loving him and following him when there are no signs at all. Whatever first drew you to Christ, the question is whether you have come to rest in him.

parallels.desc: his hour had come

verseByVerse.quote: The Pharisees heard the crowd muttering these things about him, and the chief priests and Pharisees sent officers to arrest him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd muttering. What actually triggers the warrant is telling. Not the teaching, not the Sabbath argument, not the claim in verse 29 to have come from God. It is verse 31: the muttering of the crowd, the fact that people are starting to believe. They move when the numbers move. What got reported was not a sermon but the mood of ordinary people, which tells you what they feared to lose: their grip on the people. When religion becomes a position to protect, the coming of God himself feels like a threat, and the people who should have been first to welcome him are the first to send for the police.

The chief priests and Pharisees. Two groups who normally disagreed. The chief priests were mostly Sadducees, the priestly aristocracy who controlled the temple and denied the resurrection (Acts 23:8); the Pharisees were the lay party of strict law-keeping. Together they made up much of the Sanhedrin, and in this Gospel they act together only to deal with him (11:47, 57; 18:3). Opposition to Christ unites people who cannot stand each other, as it will unite Herod and Pilate (Luke 23:12).

Officers to arrest him. The officers were the temple police, Levites who kept order in the temple under the chief priests. They set out with a straightforward job, and they will come back empty-handed, saying that no one ever spoke like this man (v. 46).
verseByVerse.note: The officers were the temple police.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus then said, "I will be with you a little longer, and then I am going to him who sent me. You will seek me and you will not find me. Where I am you cannot come."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will be with you a little longer. About six months remained before the cross. He answers a warrant for his arrest by announcing his travel plans, and the effect is to take the whole confrontation out of their hands. They think they are deciding whether he stays. He tells them he is leaving anyway, shortly, and for somewhere they cannot follow.

Going to him who sent me. Jesus speaks of his death, resurrection and ascension as a going home to the Father (13:1, 3; 16:5, 28). He is not driven out; he goes.

You will not find me. A solemn warning: there will come a time when it is too late. Compare Proverbs 1:28 and Isaiah 55:6: seek the Lord while he may be found. It is addressed to men holding an arrest warrant, who will one day want what he offered and find the offer withdrawn. That is not a threat aimed at the worried. It is a fact aimed at the comfortable.

Where I am you cannot come. Not “where I will be” but “where I am”: he speaks as the one who already belongs to the Father’s presence. Unbelievers cannot follow him there (8:21). He says something similar to the disciples later (13:33), but with a promise: you will follow afterwards (13:36; 14:3).

I am frightened that it may be too late for me. Is this verse about me? If you are troubled by it, that trouble is itself the evidence that it is not describing you. The seeking that fails in this verse is not the seeking of the frightened; it is the seeking of men who refused him to his face, and who would one day want rescue without wanting him. Scripture never shows a penitent sinner coming to God and finding the door shut. The whole burden of this Gospel is the opposite: whoever comes to me I will never cast out (6:37), said to a crowd that mostly walked away. While you are alive and can call on him, the door is open. Call on him now.

On a Tuesday. If there is something you have been meaning to settle with God, a sin to confess, a step of obedience, a first prayer, do not leave it for a better week.

For worship. He went home to the Father by way of the cross, and he did not go alone. The place where his enemies could not come is the place he has gone to prepare for his friends (14:2–3). To unbelief he says, where I am you cannot come; to faith he says, I will come again and take you to myself, that where I am you may be also. The same words that warn the proud are the hope of every believer.

verseByVerse.quote: The Jews said to one another, "Where does this man intend to go that we will not find him? Does he intend to go to the Dispersion among the Greeks and teach the Greeks? What does he mean by saying, 'You will seek me and you will not find me,' and, 'Where I am you cannot come'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Where does this man intend to go that we will not find him? They misunderstand again, thinking only of earthly places.

Does he intend to go to the Dispersion among the Greeks and teach the Greeks? The Dispersion (diaspora) means the Jews living scattered outside the land of Israel, in the cities of the Greek-speaking world. Probably more Jews lived outside the land than in it. They mockingly suggest he will go and teach Gentiles, something no respectable Jerusalem teacher would do. They are making his words sound absurd: either the man is talking nonsense, or he means something ridiculous, like going off to the scattered communities in foreign cities and teaching foreigners.

The irony. Their mocking guess was prophetic. Through his apostles, Jesus did go to the Dispersion and teach the Greeks. The gospel went from Jerusalem to the synagogues of the Dispersion and then to the Gentiles (Acts 11:20; 13:46), carried by a Pharisee trained in Jerusalem, and the letters of James and 1 Peter are addressed to the Dispersion. John was probably writing for readers who lived in those cities. When they reached this sentence, they were reading a mocking question that had turned into their own address.

Enemies who say more than they know. It is not the only time opponents of Jesus say more than they know. It will happen again at 11:50, when Caiaphas remarks that it is better for one man to die for the people, and John stops the story to point out that he was prophesying without the least idea of it. The people most determined to stop this are being used, and their own sentences are being taken up and made true in a sense they would have found intolerable.

What does he mean by saying...? They cannot understand, because they are thinking on the wrong level. And look at what they do with his words. They quote them back, both halves, in full: you will seek me and you will not find me, and where I am you cannot come. Men who are dismissing something do not usually repeat it that carefully. It is the behaviour of people worrying at a sentence they cannot get out of their heads. They have no idea what it means, they are certain it is nonsense, and they cannot leave it alone.
verseByVerse.note: The Dispersion means the Jews living scattered outside the land among the nations.

verseByVerse.quote: On the last day of the feast, the great day, Jesus stood up and cried out, "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, 'Out of his heart will flow rivers of living water.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the last day of the feast, the great day. Probably the seventh day, the climax of the water ceremony, though some think the eighth day of solemn assembly. Later Jewish writings describe water carried from Siloam in a golden pitcher each morning and poured out beside the altar, while the people sang the Hallel psalms (Psalms 113–118) and prayed for rain; on the seventh day the priests circled the altar seven times. The ceremony looked back to the water from the rock in the wilderness (Exodus 17:6) and forward to the promised day when living waters would flow out from Jerusalem (Zechariah 14:8, read at this feast) and from the temple (Ezekiel 47:1–12). The rabbis said that whoever had not seen the joy of the water-drawing had never seen joy in his life.

Jesus stood up and cried out. Teachers usually sat. He stands and calls out loudly, just as the water ceremony is ending for another year. The ceremony had been remembering water from a rock for a nation that would otherwise have died in the desert, and he offers, to anybody at all, what the ceremony had only ever pointed at.

If anyone thirsts. It echoes Isaiah 55:1: come, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters. He is the rock from which the water flows (1 Corinthians 10:4). To come and drink is to believe (6:35). And the terms are as wide as language permits: not if anyone is worthy, or prepared, or knows enough. The only qualification is an appetite, the one thing nobody can manufacture or fake. Nobody in that courtyard needed to be told that things run out.

As the Scripture has said. “Heart” is literally “belly” (koilia), the innermost being. No single Old Testament verse says exactly this; Jesus is summing up a theme: Isaiah 58:11 (a spring whose waters do not fail), Ezekiel 47 (the river from the temple), Zechariah 14:8, and the rock in the wilderness. He is gathering a theme rather than citing a line. Ezekiel saw the river from under the temple threshold deepening as it ran, until everything it touched lived. He is telling a crowd at that feast that the whole river of promise they had been singing about has arrived, and is standing in front of them.

Rivers. Not a cup, not a well: rivers, plural, more than any single person could ever use. He is thirty-odd years old, has no house, is under an arrest warrant, and will be dead by spring, and in the middle of the greatest festival of his people he offers to be the river. Living water was the everyday phrase for running water, from a spring or a stream, as against still water standing in a cistern, and God calls himself the fountain of living waters (Jeremiah 2:13). Jesus means life that keeps flowing from God himself and never goes stale.

Whose heart? The Greek can be punctuated two ways. Most take it as the believer’s heart: the one who drinks becomes a source of blessing to others (4:14). Others punctuate: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me, and let him drink who believes in me. As Scripture says, out of his heart...” so that the rivers flow from Christ’s heart. Both are true: the water flows from Christ (19:34 shows water flowing from his side), and through the believer to others. The ESV’s reading is natural, and most scholars think it likely. The second reading has real attractions: it fits a ceremony in which water flows from the temple, and Jesus is the new temple (2:19–21). But the difference is smaller than it first appears, since John explains in the next verse that he is speaking of the Spirit, and the Spirit comes from Christ to the believer and then out through him. The spring is Christ either way; the question is only how far downstream the sentence is looking.

In the flow. The chapter reaches its climax. Everything so far has been argument about Jesus; now he stops answering questions and issues an invitation. In 8:12 he takes up the feast’s other great image, the light.

I do not feel thirsty for God. Is this invitation for me? Thirst does not always feel like longing for God. Often it feels like restlessness, boredom, the sense that nothing quite satisfies, or the dull ache after the thing you hoped would fill you has not. Augustine confessed that God made us for himself, so that we find no rest anywhere else, and most restlessness is that thirst in disguise. If you have ever wanted more than this life gives, the invitation is for you. And if you feel nothing at all, come anyway, and ask him to make you thirsty. The invitation is to anyone.

So how do I actually come and drink? To come and drink is to believe: to trust Jesus himself, and to keep trusting him, for what only he can give. In practice it means turning to him in prayer, plainly, as someone who needs him; listening to him in his word, where he speaks; and receiving him in the means he has given, the preaching of the gospel, the fellowship of his people and the Lord’s Supper. Drinking is not a single gulp at conversion. It is a daily return to the spring. When you are dry, do not first try harder. Go back to him and drink again.

On a Tuesday. Think where you go when you are dry: the screen, the fridge, the shop, the bottle, the approval of others. None of them is the river. When you feel that thirst, pray a single sentence: Lord Jesus, I am thirsty; give me yourself. Then let it flow on to others. Rivers are for giving away.

For worship. The rock was struck in the wilderness and water gushed out for a rebellious people. The true Rock was struck on a hill outside Jerusalem, and from his pierced side came blood and water. The feast poured out one golden pitcher a morning; the river from him has run for two thousand years and never run low. And the offer has not been narrowed since the day it was shouted across the temple courts: if anyone thirsts, let him come.
verseByVerse.note: Later Jewish writings describe water being carried from the pool of Siloam and poured out at the altar each day of the feast. No single verse says these exact words; Jesus draws on several prophecies. The ESV notes a different punctuation that makes Jesus himself the source of the water.

parallels.desc: come to the waters
water flowing from the temple
living waters from Jerusalem

verseByVerse.quote: Now this he said about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive, for as yet the Spirit had not been given, because Jesus was not yet glorified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now this he said about the Spirit. The Old Testament often pictures the Spirit as water poured out (Isaiah 44:3; Ezekiel 36:25–27; Joel 2:28). John stops the story to explain, as he does when a saying would otherwise be misread (2:21; 12:33). The rivers are the Spirit: not an influence but a person. John writes as a man on the other side of Pentecost, describing something that had since happened to him and to everyone reading. Those who believed means every believer, not some special class (Romans 8:9; Galatians 3:2).

For as yet the Spirit had not been given. Literally “for the Spirit was not yet.” Of course the Spirit existed and was active in the Old Testament (Psalm 51:11) and in Jesus’ ministry (1:32). The meaning is that the Spirit had not yet been given in the new covenant way, poured out on all God’s people to dwell in them for ever (14:16–17). Before Pentecost the Spirit came mostly upon prophets, kings and craftsmen for particular tasks. After it he made his home in fishermen, slaves, widows and children, all who believe.

Because Jesus was not yet glorified. In John, Jesus is glorified in his death, resurrection and ascension (12:23; 13:31; 17:1). The Spirit could not come until Jesus had finished his work and returned to the Father (16:7). The cross opened the way; the exalted Christ poured out the Spirit at Pentecost (Acts 2:33). The river could not flow until the rock had been struck, which is why the invitation of verse 37 was made by a man on his way to a cross. To glorify is to show someone’s true greatness; in John that showing begins, astonishingly, at the cross, where the Son’s love and obedience are displayed most fully (12:23–24), and is completed when the Father welcomes him back to the glory he had before the world existed (17:5).

Where Christians differ: receiving the Spirit. Pentecostal and charismatic teaching often holds that the baptism of the Spirit is a second experience after conversion, marked by speaking in tongues. This commentary’s view: this verse says all who believe receive the Spirit. Every Christian has the Spirit from the moment of faith (1 Corinthians 12:13). There may be many fresh fillings and deeper experiences of the Spirit, but no second class of Christians. The sign gifts of the apostolic age, such as tongues and prophecy, served to confirm the founding of the church and have ceased, while the Spirit himself remains with every believer for ever. Scripture ties those gifts to the apostles and the founding of the church (Ephesians 2:20; Hebrews 2:3–4). Many faithful brothers and sisters in Pentecostal and charismatic churches read the evidence differently; they love the same Lord and seek the same Spirit, and they deserve to be heard with respect.

How do I know I have the Spirit? Not first by a feeling, but by what the Spirit does. He brings you to confess that Jesus is Lord and to mean it (1 Corinthians 12:3). He makes Christ precious to you (16:14). He teaches you to call God Father and to trust him as his child (Romans 8:15–16). He makes you hate sin and fight it, and he grows his fruit in you, slowly: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness (Galatians 5:22–23). If you trust Christ, the Spirit lives in you, whether or not you have had any dramatic experience. Weak faith is still Spirit-given faith.

What does it mean to be filled with the Spirit? It means to be more and more under his influence, as a sail is filled by the wind. Paul commands it as a continuing thing, be filled (Ephesians 5:18), and he shows its marks in the next verses: worship, thankfulness and humble service in home and church. It is not a second level of Christian, and it is not measured by how dramatic your experiences are. You seek it by keeping in step with him: reading the word he inspired, praying, confessing sin quickly, obeying what he shows you, and asking. Jesus promised that the Father gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask him (Luke 11:13).

On a Tuesday. If you believe in Christ, the Spirit lives in you. You are not waiting for him; ask him to fill you and flow through you. Before the hard conversation, the temptation or the task beyond you, pray simply: Holy Spirit, you live in me; help me now.

verseByVerse.quote: When they heard these words, some of the people said, "This really is the Prophet." Others said, "This is the Christ." But some said, "Is the Christ to come from Galilee?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
This really is the Prophet. “The Prophet” is the prophet like Moses whom Moses promised (Deuteronomy 18:15–18; compare 1:21; 6:14). Some Jews thought of the Prophet as distinct from the Messiah; Jesus is both (Acts 3:22).

Is the Christ to come from Galilee? The Greek expects the answer no. John knows the answer and does not stop to give it; he lets the objection stand. All through this Gospel people reject Jesus on grounds that would have collapsed under one honest question, and as far as John tells us, nobody asks it.

Why did people expect different figures: a prophet, a Christ? Because the Old Testament promises came in many strands, and few saw how they fitted together. Some looked for the prophet like Moses; some for a king of David’s line; some for a priestly figure; some for all of them, arriving separately. Jesus is all of them in one person: the Prophet who speaks God’s word, the Priest who offers himself, the King who reigns. The Reformers spoke of his threefold office for this reason. The categories built to receive him turned out to be too small one by one, and too confusing all together, until he came and filled them all.

For worship. Moses struck the rock and the people drank, and then he died outside the land, promising another prophet. The crowd saw Moses in Jesus, and they were right, and still short of the truth. Moses gave water; Jesus gives the Spirit. Moses spoke God’s words; Jesus is God’s Word. Moses was faithful in God’s house as a servant, and Christ is faithful over it as a Son (Hebrews 3:5–6).
verseByVerse.note: “The Prophet” is the prophet like Moses whom Moses promised.

verseByVerse.quote: "Has not the Scripture said that the Christ comes from the offspring of David, and comes from Bethlehem, the village where David was?" So there was a division among the people over him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The offspring of David. They were right that the Messiah would be a son of David (2 Samuel 7:12–16; Isaiah 11:1; Jeremiah 23:5).

And comes from Bethlehem, the village where David was? And right that he would come from Bethlehem (Micah 5:2; compare Matthew 2:5–6). These are not men twisting the text. They know it well, they are using it correctly, and they reach a false conclusion, because they have a fact wrong and have not thought to test it.

The irony. They did not know that Jesus had been born in Bethlehem, and was descended from David. John expects his readers to know the story (Matthew 1–2; Luke 2) and to see the irony: they reject him for not meeting the very prophecies he fulfils. It is possible to be a careful reader of Scripture, to quote it accurately, to apply it validly, and still to end up on the wrong side of God: not through bad interpretation but through an unexamined assumption smuggled in underneath it. He is from Galilee was never checked, because it felt like common knowledge.

A division. “Division” (schisma): Jesus divides people (9:16; 10:19). No one can stay neutral about him. The tear runs through crowds, through the council, and in this chapter through his own family. Jesus said himself that he had not come to bring peace but a sword, and that a man’s enemies would be those of his own household (Matthew 10:34–36). The division is not the goal and it is not the good. It is what happens when a claim this large meets people who are free to refuse it, and the alternative, a Christ small enough that nobody need decide about him, was never on offer.

What if following Christ is dividing my family? It hurts, and Jesus does not pretend otherwise. He knew it from the inside: his own brothers did not believe. First, make sure that the division is over Christ, not over your harshness, pride or a quarrel dressed up as faith. Then stay loving, patient and honest; do not withdraw, retaliate or preach at every meal. Honour your parents and keep your promises where you can do so without denying him (Ephesians 6:2). Keep bringing each of them to God in prayer. And take comfort that the division need not be the last word: the brothers who did not believe in John 7 were praying with the disciples in Acts 1.

For worship. The one they said could not be the Christ was born in the very town they named, of the very line they demanded. God kept his word to David to the letter, in a manger, while the scholars of Jerusalem went on arguing, and the division over his Son is the sign that the Son has come.
verseByVerse.note: They did not know that Jesus had been born in Bethlehem.

parallels.desc: from Bethlehem shall come a ruler

verseByVerse.quote: Some of them wanted to arrest him, but no one laid hands on him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one laid hands on him. Again, as in v. 30. John has told us why: his hour had not yet come. Three attempts (vv. 30, 44, 45), three failures, and John gives the reason only once.

What providence looks like from inside. What is striking is how little there is to see. No lightning, no escape, no crowd parting. Some men in a courtyard felt like seizing a teacher and somehow did not, and if asked they would probably have said the moment passed. The ordinary reasons why a thing did not happen are the means God uses, not an alternative to him. This time the restraint worked at the level of a private impulse, which rose in a man’s mind and did not become an action.

If God restrains evil, why does he not restrain all of it? Scripture does not give us the whole answer, but it gives us enough to trust him. God restrains a great deal of evil we never see, and he permits some evil for purposes we cannot yet see, never approving it, and always turning it to good for those who love him (Genesis 50:20; Romans 8:28). The clearest example is this very story. God held back these hands in the autumn, and in the spring he let wicked hands crucify his Son, because through that greatest evil he was accomplishing the greatest good. If he can do that with the cross, he can be trusted with what he permits in your life.

For worship. No hand could close on him that autumn, because the Father had not yet given him up. In the spring the Son of Man was delivered into the hands of men, as he had said he would be (Mark 9:31), and he went into them willingly, so that his people might be kept in his own. No one will snatch them out of my hand, he said (10:28), and the hand that holds them is the one he let men seize.

verseByVerse.quote: The officers then came to the chief priests and Pharisees, who said to them, "Why did you not bring him?" The officers answered, "No one ever spoke like this man!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The officers. The temple police sent in v. 32 return empty-handed, perhaps several days later. Long enough to hear the invitation of verse 37.

No one ever spoke like this man! An extraordinary admission from men trained to obey orders. They were sent to arrest him, and were arrested by his words. They had heard many teachers in the temple, but never anyone like this (Matthew 7:28–29). An excuse would have been easy: the crowd was too thick, there would have been a riot. Instead they give open admiration to the men who ordered the arrest. They make no confession of faith; they simply could not do it, and said why.

The truest sentence in the chapter. The most honest testimony in the chapter comes from men who were not believers and had everything to lose by giving it. No name is preserved; they say the truest sentence in the chapter, are sneered at, and disappear. That is its own small comfort for anyone who has said the right thing once, at cost, and seen nothing come of it. It went into the record. John was still writing it down decades later, and the men who said it had no idea it would outlast the council that mocked them.

What was it about how he spoke? It was not technique. Other teachers quoted authorities; he spoke with his own authority (Matthew 7:29). Other teachers explained God; he spoke as one who had come from him, and his words were spirit and life (6:63). He spoke with perfect truth and perfect love at once, which no one else has managed. He knew what was in a man (2:25), so his words went straight to the heart. And he spoke the Father’s own words (v. 16). When you read the Gospels and find a saying of his lodging in you and refusing to leave, you are feeling what the officers felt.

For worship. The voice that said let there be light spoke in the temple courts in the accent of Galilee, and hardened men sent to bind him went back unable to do it. It called Lazarus out of a tomb; it will call all the dead from their graves (5:28–29); and in between it calls, through the plain reading of his word, sheep who know it and follow (10:27).

verseByVerse.quote: The Pharisees answered them, "Have you also been deceived? Have any of the authorities or the Pharisees believed in him?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Have you also been deceived? “Deceived” (planaō): led astray, the same word as v. 12. This is not a request for reasons. It is a warning shot, and its purpose is to make the officers feel foolish, not to answer what they said. Nobody so much as answers what the officers said, that no one ever spoke like this man.

Have any of the authorities or the Pharisees believed in him? The argument from authority: none of the experts believe, so it must be false. A familiar argument to this day. The irony: one of them is about to speak up (v. 50), and later Joseph of Arimathea, a member of the council, will be revealed as a secret disciple (19:38), and many priests will believe (Acts 6:7). It is the oldest move there is. The claim is not that Jesus is wrong. It is that no one who matters thinks he is right. And it is aimed at policemen, who are being asked whether they propose to set their judgment against that of the learned. It is designed to remind them of their place, and it works: nothing more is heard from the officers. Meanwhile Nicodemus is sitting in that chamber while the question is put as though it answered itself, and both he and Joseph will carry the body of Jesus the following spring.

Consensus is evidence about people. Consensus is not nothing, and a wise reader does not despise it; the church has generally been right to be suspicious of the man who alone sees the truth. But consensus is evidence about people, not about the matter, and its worth depends entirely on whether the people are free to say what they think. In this room they were not, and the proof is that the one sympathiser present could manage only a question about procedure.

Should I ignore scholars and experts when they reject Christianity? No. Listen to them, learn from them, and take their arguments seriously; many scholars are believers, and honest scholarship has served the church well. But look at what kind of claim is being made. A sentence that begins, most educated people do not believe, is a statement about people, not an argument about the evidence. Ask what the actual reasons are, and weigh them. Remember too that every generation has its consensus, and the consensus of one century is often the embarrassment of the next. The question is not who believes, but whether it is true. Look at Christ yourself, and read the evidence for the resurrection with your own eyes.

parallels.desc: many even of the authorities believed

verseByVerse.quote: "But this crowd that does not know the law is accursed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This crowd that does not know the law. Religious leaders despised ordinary people who did not know the details of the law and its oral traditions. They called them the “people of the land” (am ha’aretz), and some rabbinic sayings warn against eating with them or marrying their daughters. The phrase hardened into something like a caste: people who could not be relied on to tithe or keep the purity rules.

Is accursed. The law did pronounce a curse on those who did not keep it (Deuteronomy 27:26). The irony again: the very leaders who know the law are breaking it, as Nicodemus will point out in the next verse. This is the class judgment of the educated on the uneducated, delivered as a theological verdict.

The people who got closest. And it is aimed at the people who had got closest to the truth in this chapter. The crowd is confused, divided and working from bad information. They are also the ones asking whether this might be the Christ. It is the pattern of the whole Gospel: a Samaritan woman hears one of the plainest statements of his identity (4:26), fishermen stay when the theologians leave, a blind beggar will out-argue the council. And the men who know most about God’s law say, in the same breath, that nobody who matters believes in him and everybody else is cursed.

Does this mean knowledge is dangerous and I should not study? No. Knowledge of God’s word is a great gift, and Scripture urges us to grow in it (2 Peter 3:18). The problem in this verse is not knowledge but pride: knowledge without love puffs up (1 Corinthians 8:1). The test is what your learning does to the way you see other believers. If it makes you more patient, more humble and more delighted when an untrained Christian sees something true, it is doing its proper work. If it makes you contemptuous, it has become the thing in this verse. Study hard, and stay low.

For worship. The rulers called the crowd accursed. Christ became a curse for them, and for us, hanging on a tree, so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the people of the land and the Gentiles alike (Galatians 3:13–14). He did not curse the ignorant; he taught them, healed them and died for them. The despised people of the land turned out to be the people of his heart.
verseByVerse.note: Religious leaders despised ordinary people who did not know the finer points of the law.

parallels.desc: cursed be anyone who does not confirm the words of this law

verseByVerse.quote: Nicodemus, who had gone to him before, and who was one of them, said to them, "Does our law judge a man without first giving him a hearing and learning what he does?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nicodemus, who had gone to him before. Nicodemus was a member of the council, the man who came to Jesus by night (3:1–2), and his presence answers their question (v. 48): here is one of the rulers at least open to Jesus.

Does our law judge a man without first giving him a hearing and learning what he does? He doesn’t defend Jesus outright, but appeals to justice. The law required a fair hearing (Deuteronomy 1:16–17; 17:4). The men who boast of knowing the law are condemning a man without trial. Nicodemus exposes them with their own law. It is easy to be disappointed that he says so little, but be accurate about the risk he was taking. He has just heard the room agree that no authority believes in Jesus and that anyone who does is deceived. Speaking at all marks him as a possible sympathiser, and the sneering reply he gets shows he was heard exactly that way. It names the price of going further. And on the merits he is entirely right. It is the only legally correct sentence spoken in the chamber, and it comes from the one man there who has actually met him.

The shape of his story. Three appearances: by night with a question (3:1–2); here, with a cautious objection about procedure; and finally at the cross, in daylight, in public, carrying about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes to bury a condemned man (19:39), a quantity fit for a king, at the moment when being associated with him could not possibly have looked worse. The journey took perhaps two years, and nobody in that room would have picked him out as a future disciple. Grace was not in a hurry, and it did not let go.

Is it all right to be a secret or cautious believer? A cautious beginning is not the same as settled secrecy. Nicodemus’ first steps were small, and Jesus did not despise them; many true believers begin quietly. But John does not leave him there, and neither should we stay there. Jesus warns that whoever is ashamed of him, he will be ashamed of (Mark 8:38), and John says sadly of some rulers that they believed but did not confess him, because they loved human praise (12:42–43). If you are a quiet believer, ask what the next honest step is: telling one friend, joining a church, being baptised. Faith that is real grows towards the light.

On a Tuesday. Nicodemus said little here, but he said something. In the meeting where someone is being talked about unfairly, the one sentence may be simply: should we not hear his side first? It costs something to say it, and the Lord who bore so patiently with Nicodemus will strengthen you for it.
verseByVerse.note: Nicodemus was a member of the council.

parallels.desc: inquire diligently

verseByVerse.quote: They replied, "Are you from Galilee too? Search and see that no prophet arises from Galilee." They went each to his own house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are you from Galilee too? They don’t answer his point. They mock him: are you one of these northern peasants too? Nicodemus asked a question about legal procedure. Nobody answers it. This is not a rebuttal but a way of putting a man in a category so that nothing he says needs weighing.

Search and see. “Search” means search the Scriptures. They were wrong: the prophet Jonah came from Gath-hepher in Galilee (2 Kings 14:25), and Isaiah had promised that a great light would shine in Galilee of the nations (Isaiah 9:1–2; Matthew 4:15–16). Gath-hepher is only a few miles from Nazareth. The men who dismissed the crowd as ignorant of the law (v. 49) get a fact about the prophets wrong, because they are angry, and never notice.

Textual note. One early papyrus reads “the Prophet” here, meaning the prophet like Moses would not arise from Galilee, which would make their claim less obviously false. The ESV follows the majority of manuscripts.

They went each to his own house. The council breaks up without decision. This sentence (v. 53) begins the passage about the woman caught in adultery (7:53–8:11), which the ESV places in brackets. The earliest and most reliable manuscripts do not contain it, and some place it elsewhere (after Luke 21:38, for example). Its style is unlike John’s, and the KJV prints it because it follows later manuscripts. It is very likely a true story about Jesus preserved in the church, but not originally part of John’s Gospel. The ESV keeps it with a note, and we comment on it in chapter 8 with that caution.

The flattest sentence in the chapter. No verdict, no arrest, no resolution, while the man they were discussing, as the bracketed story goes on to say, went out to the Mount of Olives. They went each to his own house. He had no house to go to. The Son of Man had nowhere to lay his head (Luke 9:58).

Why does my Bible put brackets here, in the middle of a scene? Because the passage that begins with this sentence and runs to 8:11 is the one the brackets surround, and it opens at the last verse of a chapter. That is why the bracket in your Bible seems to start in an odd place. The brackets are not a sign that the translators are hiding anything; they are telling you honestly what the manuscripts show. The story itself is very probably a true memory of Jesus, and it may be read and treasured as one, provided no doctrine is made to rest on it alone.

On a Tuesday. When you notice yourself answering a point by attacking the person who made it, stop. Ask whether what they said is true. Anger made these scholars forget their own Bibles; wait until you are calm before you answer.
verseByVerse.note: They were wrong: the prophet Jonah came from Gath-hepher in Galilee. The ESV notes that the earliest manuscripts do not include 7:53–8:11 and brackets the passage.

parallels.desc: Jonah son of Amittai, of Gath-hepher
Galilee of the nations

7.title: Rivers of Living Water
7.text: <sup>1</sup>After this Jesus went about in Galilee. He would not go about in Judea, because the Jews were seeking to kill him.<sup>2</sup>Now the Jews’ Feast of Booths was at hand.<sup>3</sup>So his brothers said to him, “Leave here and go to Judea, that your disciples also may see the works you are doing.<sup>4</sup>For no one works in secret if he seeks to be known openly. If you do these things, show yourself to the world.”<sup>5</sup>For not even his brothers believed in him.<sup>6</sup>Jesus said to them, “My time has not yet come, but your time is always here.<sup>7</sup>The world cannot hate you, but it hates me because I testify about it that its works are evil.<sup>8</sup>You go up to the feast. I am not going up to this feast, for my time has not yet fully come.”<sup>9</sup>After saying this, he remained in Galilee.<sup>10</sup>But after his brothers had gone up to the feast, then he also went up, not publicly but in private.<sup>11</sup>The Jews were looking for him at the feast, and saying, “Where is he?”<sup>12</sup>And there was much muttering about him among the people. While some said, “He is a good man,” others said, “No, he is leading the people astray.”<sup>13</sup>Yet for fear of the Jews no one spoke openly of him.<sup>14</sup>About the middle of the feast Jesus went up into the temple and began teaching.<sup>15</sup>The Jews therefore marveled, saying, “How is it that this man has learning, when he has never studied?”<sup>16</sup>So Jesus answered them, “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me.<sup>17</sup>If anyone’s will is to do God’s will, he will know whether the teaching is from God or whether I am speaking on my own authority.<sup>18</sup>The one who speaks on his own authority seeks his own glory; but the one who seeks the glory of him who sent him is true, and in him there is no falsehood.<sup>19</sup>Has not Moses given you the law? Yet none of you keeps the law. Why do you seek to kill me?”<sup>20</sup>The crowd answered, “You have a demon! Who is seeking to kill you?”<sup>21</sup>Jesus answered them, “I did one work, and you all marvel at it.<sup>22</sup>Moses gave you circumcision (not that it is from Moses, but from the fathers), and you circumcise a man on the Sabbath.<sup>23</sup>If on the Sabbath a man receives circumcision, so that the law of Moses may not be broken, are you angry with me because on the Sabbath I made a man’s whole body well?<sup>24</sup>Do not judge by appearances, but judge with right judgment.”<sup>25</sup>Some of the people of Jerusalem therefore said, “Is not this the man whom they seek to kill?<sup>26</sup>And here he is, speaking openly, and they say nothing to him! Can it be that the authorities really know that this is the Christ?<sup>27</sup>But we know where this man comes from, and when the Christ appears, no one will know where he comes from.”<sup>28</sup>So Jesus proclaimed, as he taught in the temple, “You know me, and you know where I come from. But I have not come of my own accord. He who sent me is true, and him you do not know.<sup>29</sup>I know him, for I come from him, and he sent me.”<sup>30</sup>So they were seeking to arrest him, but no one laid a hand on him, because his hour had not yet come.<sup>31</sup>Yet many of the people believed in him. They said, “When the Christ appears, will he do more signs than this man has done?”<sup>32</sup>The Pharisees heard the crowd muttering these things about him, and the chief priests and Pharisees sent officers to arrest him.<sup>33</sup>Jesus then said, “I will be with you a little longer, and then I am going to him who sent me.<sup>34</sup>You will seek me and you will not find me. Where I am you cannot come.”<sup>35</sup>The Jews said to one another, “Where does this man intend to go that we will not find him? Does he intend to go to the Dispersion among the Greeks and teach the Greeks?<sup>36</sup>What does he mean by saying, ’You will seek me and you will not find me,’ and, ’Where I am you cannot come’?”<sup>37</sup>On the last day of the feast, the great day, Jesus stood up and cried out, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.<sup>38</sup>Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, ’Out of his heart will flow rivers of living water.’”<sup>39</sup>Now this he said about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive, for as yet the Spirit had not been given, because Jesus was not yet glorified.<sup>40</sup>When they heard these words, some of the people said, “This really is the Prophet.”<sup>41</sup>Others said, “This is the Christ.” But some said, “Is the Christ to come from Galilee?<sup>42</sup>Has not the Scripture said that the Christ comes from the offspring of David, and comes from Bethlehem, the village where David was?”<sup>43</sup>So there was a division among the people over him.<sup>44</sup>Some of them wanted to arrest him, but no one laid hands on him.<sup>45</sup>The officers then came to the chief priests and Pharisees, who said to them, “Why did you not bring him?”<sup>46</sup>The officers answered, “No one ever spoke like this man!”<sup>47</sup>The Pharisees answered them, “Have you also been deceived?<sup>48</sup>Have any of the authorities or the Pharisees believed in him?<sup>49</sup>But this crowd that does not know the law is accursed.”<sup>50</sup>Nicodemus, who had gone to him before, and who was one of them, said to them,<sup>51</sup>“Does our law judge a man without first giving him a hearing and learning what he does?”<sup>52</sup>They replied, “Are you from Galilee too? Search and see that no prophet arises from Galilee.”<sup>53</sup>[[They went each to his own house,
7.overview:
Six months after the feeding of the five thousand, the Feast of Booths (Tabernacles) arrives: the joyful autumn festival when Israel lived in shelters of branches to remember the wilderness, and prayed for rain. Jesus’ unbelieving brothers urge him to go to Jerusalem and show himself; he refuses to move on their timetable, then goes up privately. Halfway through the feast he teaches in the temple, and the crowd cannot agree about him: a good man, a deceiver, mad, the Prophet, the Christ. The authorities send officers to arrest him.

On the last great day of the water ceremony, Jesus stands and invites anyone who thirsts to come to him and drink. John explains that he meant the Spirit, who would be given once Jesus was glorified. The officers come back without him, and when Nicodemus asks for a fair hearing he is mocked. Through the whole chapter runs one question: where does Jesus come from?

8.title: The Light of the World

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–30 — Light in the Darkness: The Second I AM
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: This first section has two parts: the bracketed story of the woman brought to Jesus in the temple at dawn (7:53–8:11), and Jesus’ claim to be the light of the world, the dispute over his testimony, and his warning that unless they believe that he is who he says, they will die in their sins (vv. 12–30).
verseByVerse.theology: The chapter is full of courtroom language and the bare words I am, the name of the God who spoke to Moses. Jesus says that he judges no one (v. 15), and also that his judgment is true (v. 16). The two belong to different times: he came first to save, and he will come again to judge, and those who trust him now will face no condemnation then, because he bore it at the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: She goes free not because the law is set aside, but because the one who alone had the right to condemn her would shortly bear the penalty himself. Every Christian stands where she stood.

verseByVerse.quote: but Jesus went to the Mount of Olives. Early in the morning he came again to the temple. All the people came to him, and he sat down and taught them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. John 8 continues the confrontation at the Feast of Booths and climbs higher than anything Jesus has yet said. It opens with the bracketed story of a woman caught in adultery, whom Jesus neither condemns nor excuses. Then comes the second great I am, I am the light of the world, and an argument about witness, freedom and true parentage. Three times Jesus uses the bare words I am, the name God gave himself at the burning bush, and the third time his hearers pick up stones. The chapter begins with a sinner who deserved stoning and was spared, and ends with the sinless one nearly stoned himself: the whole gospel in miniature.

A textual note first. The story of the woman caught in adultery (7:53–8:11) is printed in brackets in the ESV. The earliest and best Greek manuscripts do not have it; the early church fathers who commented on John verse by verse pass straight from 7:52 to 8:12; and where the story does appear in later manuscripts, it wanders: after 7:36, after 7:44, at the end of John, or after Luke 21:38. Its style is more like Luke’s than John’s, and most scholars, conservative evangelicals included, conclude that it was not part of John’s original Gospel; the KJV, following later manuscripts, prints it without brackets. Yet many believe it records a true event from Jesus’ life, preserved in the church’s memory. Because Scripture is God’s word as originally given, the church should not build doctrine on this passage alone; but what it shows of Jesus is taught elsewhere in Scripture too.

How could such a thing happen? A reader who has been told a passage may not be original usually wants to know. The evidence is not evenly balanced. The great fourth-century manuscripts do not have these verses, and neither do the earliest papyrus copies of John. Where later manuscripts do carry the passage, they cannot agree where to put it, and a floating passage is a strong sign of one that was added rather than removed. Many of the manuscripts that include it also mark it with the little symbols scribes used for doubtful material. They knew. And yet almost nobody thinks the story was invented. It was known very early in the Latin-speaking churches, and Jerome says he found it in many manuscripts. Augustine suggested that some men of little faith had removed it, fearing it would give their wives licence. Whether or not that is the reason, it is the kind of story that would be uncomfortable to keep and hard to imagine anyone making up. It is very probably a true memory of Jesus that circulated on its own and was written into John’s Gospel at a point where it fitted.

Should I be shaken by the brackets in my Bible? No. The brackets are the church showing its working, in public, about twelve verses out of some eight thousand in the New Testament. Nothing in them is a hidden embarrassment; it is printed in your Bible with an honest note precisely so that you can see it. And nothing is lost either way.
