The passage teaches nothing that the rest of Scripture does not teach plainly: the same Lord who says neither do I condemn you here says it in substance on every page of the Gospels, and calls sinners to leave their sin everywhere. So it may be read, treasured and preached as a faithful record of Jesus, with the caution that no doctrine should rest on it alone.

The Mount of Olives. Jesus spent nights on the Mount of Olives during his time in Jerusalem (Luke 21:37), across the Kidron Valley, on the hillside where, months later, he would pray in agony and be arrested. The council had gone each to his own house (7:53).

All the people came to him. While the leaders plot, ordinary people come, and the temple becomes again at daybreak a house of teaching.

He sat down. Sitting was the posture of a teacher, and of authority. He is not a guest in the temple but its Lord, teaching in his Father’s house.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus spent nights on the Mount of Olives during his time in Jerusalem. Teachers sat to teach.

verseByVerse.quote: The scribes and the Pharisees brought a woman who had been caught in adultery, and placing her in the midst they said to him, "Teacher, this woman has been caught in the act of adultery."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The scribes and the Pharisees. The scribes were the experts in the law; John never uses the word elsewhere, another sign of the passage’s different origin.

Caught in adultery. Where is the man? Adultery is not committed alone. The law required both to die (Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 22:22). His absence suggests a set-up: the men about to quote Moses have already broken the commandment they cite by leaving half the guilty party at home. That missing man tells you what this really is: they have chosen the defendant who is easier to drag and cheaper to spend. It is also, in the oldest and most familiar way, a woman made to carry in public a shame that a man is quietly allowed to walk away from.

In the midst. In a ring of men, in the temple courts at dawn, she is not brought to a court but to a lesson, and made the visual aid. And this is the human condition before the court of divine justice: no cover, no defence, fully seen.

Teacher. There is no doubt of her guilt. They open with the title of respect, spoken by men who have arranged the one situation in which they think any answer will destroy him.

Why does Jesus never mention the missing man? He does not need to. Everyone present could count. By refusing to play the part they had written for him, he declines to complete a sentence that was never being passed honestly, and he refuses to let the law of God be used as a stone in somebody else’s fight. The missing man stands as a silent witness against the accusers. And it is a warning for every age: when a community is fierce about one person’s sin and silent about another’s, according to who is more convenient to blame, it is not defending holiness. It is using it.

On a Tuesday. You stand only because Christ refused to use your sin against you. So watch for the moment in a conversation when someone else’s failure becomes useful to you: to win an argument, to look better, to settle a score. Put it down.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now in the Law, Moses commanded us to stone such women. So what do you say?" This they said to test him, that they might have some charge to bring against him. Jesus bent down and wrote with his finger on the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses commanded us. Stoning was specified for a betrothed woman (Deuteronomy 22:23–24), and the man was to die with her (Leviticus 20:10). They quote half the law. Men this careless about the letter are not the guardians of it they claim to be.

So what do you say? The trap. If Jesus says, “Let her go,” he contradicts Moses and loses his standing as a teacher of the law. If he says, “Stone her,” he loses his reputation as the friend of sinners, and he defies Rome, which did not allow the Jews to carry out death sentences (18:31). Either way, they have a charge.

To test him. The woman is not a person to them but a prop, and that is exploitation of a cruel kind.

He wrote on the ground. What did he write? We are not told, and guesses abound: the sins of the accusers, the law requiring both parties, a line from the prophets. Perhaps the point is simply that he refuses to be rushed.

The one guess worth knowing. One suggestion depends on where this scene sits rather than on imagination. Jeremiah says that those who turn away from the LORD shall be written in the earth, for they have forsaken the LORD, the fountain of living water (Jeremiah 17:13). The fountain of living water is the very thing Jesus had stood up and shouted about on the last day of the feast (7:37–38). If that is what his finger traced in the dust, the accusers were watching their own verdict being written while they waited for his. It cannot be proved and should not be preached as certain.

The posture. What can be said with confidence is the posture. He is asked to pronounce a death sentence, and his first act is to go down: to stoop into the dirt of the courtyard while a woman stands in the middle of a circle of men. Whatever he wrote, he had put himself lower than everyone present, including her.

On a Tuesday. When you are pushed for an instant answer by someone who has already decided what they want you to say, you are allowed to pause. Stoop before you speak: pray, think, and let the heat go out of the moment.

For worship. The Lawgiver himself was crouched in the dust of his own temple, and the men quoting his law at him did not know it. He had come down to the ground to keep that law in every point for people who had broken it, and in the end he would be lifted up from the ground to bear its curse (Galatians 3:13).
verseByVerse.note: The law required both the man and the woman caught in adultery to be put to death; the man is missing. Rome did not allow the Jewish authorities to carry out executions, so the question was a trap either way.

parallels.desc: both of them shall die

verseByVerse.quote: And as they continued to ask him, he stood up and said to them, "Let him who is without sin among you be the first to throw a stone at her." And once more he bent down and wrote on the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Without sin among you. Under the law the witnesses were to throw the first stones (Deuteronomy 17:7). They had to be honest witnesses, for the law gave a false witness the very penalty he had sought for another (Deuteronomy 19:16–19). Jesus turns the light on the accusers: are they fit to carry out God’s judgment? What he does not do matters as much. He does not deny the law, dispute the facts, or make a speech about mercy. He hands them the stones and attaches the condition the law already contained. It is the most conservative possible answer, and it empties the courtyard. In a group that had arrived with a woman and without the man, it would have landed like a hand on the shoulder.

Once more he bent down. He leaves them with their consciences. Having said the one sentence, he goes back to the ground and gives them the freedom to leave without being stared at. The genius of grace is that it does not humiliate even the accusers; it invites them to look at themselves.

So does a church or a court have to be sinless to deal with sin? No. If that were the rule, no human court could ever sit and no church could ever discipline anyone, and Scripture commands both. Judges and elders act as servants of God’s justice, not as people claiming to be better than the accused (Romans 13:4; Galatians 6:1). What this verse demands is honesty: that those who judge are not guilty of the same thing, are not using the process for their own ends, and come to it knowing their own need of mercy. A pastor confronting a sin, a parent correcting a child, a court sentencing a crime, can all do right, provided they do it with clean hands and a humble heart.

On a Tuesday. The last time you were quite certain somebody else was in the wrong, would your certainty have survived being asked, in front of witnesses, whether you were clear of the same thing? Remember the one who had every right to throw a stone at you and did not.
verseByVerse.note: Under the law the witnesses were to throw the first stones.

parallels.desc: the hand of the witnesses first against him

verseByVerse.quote: But when they heard it, they went away one by one, beginning with the older ones, and Jesus was left alone with the woman standing before him. Jesus stood up and said to her, "Woman, where are they? Has no one condemned you?" She said, "No one, Lord." And Jesus said, "Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beginning with the older ones. The oldest have the longest memories of their own sins, or simply the wisdom to know they are guilty. Stones are put down, one by one. Every one of them had come in sure that he stood on the right side of the law, and every one left knowing, at least for a moment, that he stood where she stood. That is the hardest discovery a religious person can make: that his record has not made him safe, and that he needs the same mercy as the sinner he came to accuse.

Left alone with the woman. Augustine’s famous phrase: two were left, misery and mercy. The only one without sin, the only one with the right to throw the stone, remains.

Woman, where are they? Has no one condemned you? “Woman” is a respectful address (2:4). The question is gentle, almost wondering. The trap has collapsed, and what remains is a woman, a silence, and mercy.

Neither do I condemn you. Jesus, who is without sin, does not condemn her. Not because her sin doesn’t matter, but because he came not to condemn the world but to save it (3:17). And how can the holy one release the guilty? Because he himself would bear her condemnation on the cross (Romans 8:1–3). This is not leniency: he does not say the charge was false or the law harsh. Everyone else had merely lost the right to throw; he had the right and declined to use it. This is mercy from the bench, and it costs. Within months the man who said neither do I condemn you was under condemnation himself, outside the city, with the sentence being carried out on him. She walked out of that courtyard alive because somebody else did not.

Sin no more. Grace and holiness together: he calls it sin, and tells her to leave it. He does not say, “Sin no more, and then I won’t condemn you.” He says, “I don’t condemn you; now go and sin no more.” Grace is the root of obedience, not its reward. The change of life follows an acquittal; it does not purchase one. And grace does not leave people where it finds them. The instruction is real, and it is addressed to a real situation she has to go home to.

Was she forgiven if she had not repented? The story does not tell us what was in her heart, and we should not invent it. What it shows is the order of grace: Jesus speaks mercy and then calls for a changed life, and that call is itself a call to repent. Elsewhere Scripture is plain that forgiveness is received through repentance and faith (Luke 24:47; Acts 3:19). The point here is not that repentance is unnecessary, but that it is not the price. No one earns the verdict by changing first. We come to Christ as we are, receive his mercy, and his mercy sends us out to live differently.

What if I keep falling into the same sin after being forgiven? Then come back, as often as you need to. Go and sin no more is a real command, and Christ means it to be obeyed. But it is the command of the one who has already said, I do not condemn you, and that verdict is not withdrawn when you stumble (1 John 1:9–2:1). Fight the sin, seriously: cut off what feeds it, tell a trusted believer, ask for help. And when you fall, do not hide from him, which is what shame always urges. Run to him. The freedom to obey grows out of being forgiven; it never grows out of the fear that he might stop forgiving you.

For worship. She had been marched in by a ring of men and stood in the middle; she walked out alone, through an open court, with no one holding her arm. That is how the Lord releases sinners: not on probation, not under watch, but sent home with a verdict that will never be reopened, because the one who spoke it was going to answer for it himself.

parallels.desc: no condemnation

verseByVerse.quote: Again Jesus spoke to them, saying, "I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life." So the Pharisees said to him, "You are bearing witness about yourself; your testimony is not true." Jesus answered, "Even if I do bear witness about myself, my testimony is true, for I know where I came from and where I am going, but you do not know where I come from or where I am going.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Again Jesus spoke to them. John’s original narrative picks up from 7:52: still the Feast of Booths, still in the temple.

In the flow. Verse 12 follows straight on from the last day of the feast: there Jesus offered living water (7:37–38); here he offers light. The rest of the chapter tests the claim, and chapter 9 acts it out, as he gives sight to a man born blind while the men who claim to see remain in the dark (9:41).

I am the light of the world. The second great “I am” saying (after 6:35). The lamps of the feast recalled the pillar of fire that led Israel through the wilderness (Exodus 13:21). Jesus is the true light, not just for Israel but for the world (1:4–9; Isaiah 42:6; 49:6). Light in Scripture means God’s presence, truth, holiness, salvation (Psalm 27:1).

Beside the cold lamps. John tells us where he was standing eight verses later: in the treasury (v. 20), in the Court of the Women, which is where the great lampstands of the feast had been lit every night. The sources describe four enormous golden lampstands, so tall that young priests climbed ladders to fill them, while men danced with torches through the night. Now the feast is probably over, and the lamps are out and cold. A man stands in that court, beside the extinguished stands, and says, I am the light of the world. As with the water, he waits until the ceremony has finished and says that the thing it pointed at is standing in front of them, and does not go out.

Will not walk in darkness. As Israel followed the pillar of fire. Darkness in John means sin, ignorance and death (1:5; 3:19; 12:35). And the promise is not first illumination but company. The verb is about walking, not seeing. Israel did not get a map in the wilderness; they got a pillar of fire that moved, and followed it one night at a time. And the one who follows will have the light of life, the light that gives life (1:4).

Your testimony is not true. They object on legal grounds: self-testimony was not accepted. Jesus himself had granted the principle (5:31). The objection is not stupid, and readers notice the apparent clash with chapter 5.

My testimony is true. The principle is meant for ordinary witnesses. Jesus is unique. He alone knows the truth about himself. And he is not withdrawing what he said in chapter 5 but denying that he is alone, which is exactly what he says next: it is not I alone who judge, but I and the Father (v. 16).

Where I came from and where I am going. He knows his origin and his destiny; they do not. No human can verify his testimony from outside; only God can, and he does (v. 18).

What does it mean in practice to follow the light? It means trusting Jesus and going where he leads, one step at a time, by his word. It does not mean you will always see far ahead, or understand why things happen. It means you will not be left in the darkness of sin, confusion about God, or hopelessness about death. Practically: read his words and do what they say; when you face a choice, ask what honours him and obeys him; when you sin, bring it into the light quickly rather than hiding it (1 John 1:7). Following the light is less like being given a floodlight and more like being given a lamp for your feet (Psalm 119:105).

On a Tuesday. Name the area of your life that feels darkest at the moment: a decision, a grief, a secret. Bring it to him in prayer today, and take one step of obedience in it, however small. The light comes to the one who follows.

For worship. The lamps of the feast burned for a week and were put away for a year. The light who spoke in the treasury that morning has never been put away. The darkness tried to put him out on a cross and could not; the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it (1:5). And at the end the city of God will need no sun or moon, for the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb (Revelation 21:23).
verseByVerse.note: At the Feast of Booths great lamps were lit in the temple courts. This is the second of Jesus’ “I am” sayings in John.

parallels.desc: a pillar of fire to give them light
a light for the nations

verseByVerse.quote: "You judge according to the flesh; I judge no one. Yet even if I do judge, my judgment is true, for it is not I alone who judge, but I and the Father who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You judge according to the flesh. By human standards, by appearances (7:24), from a merely human point of view. They looked at a Galilean with no credentials and drew the obvious conclusion, which was wrong.

I judge no one. Not that Jesus never judges (5:22, 27), but that he did not come to judge as they do, nor was judging the purpose of his first coming (3:17; 12:47). The resolution is in the timing: in his first coming anyone who meets him meets him as Saviour. The judging is real, it is his, and it is deferred.

My judgment is true. His judgment is God’s judgment, for the Father and the Son act together (5:30).

If Jesus will judge everyone, why does God seem to let things go now? Because the court has not yet sat, and the delay is grace. The reason a person is not being judged today is not that God has grown relaxed about sin. It is that he is patient, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance (2 Peter 3:9). The interval is given to be used: for the unbeliever to turn, and for the believer to call others to turn. It is also a comfort to anyone who has been wronged and has seen no justice. Nothing has been forgotten. The judge is Christ, and his judgment is true.

verseByVerse.quote: "In your Law it is written that the testimony of two people is true. I am the one who bears witness about myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness about me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In your Law. The law required two or three witnesses to establish a matter (Deuteronomy 17:6; 19:15). “Your Law” does not distance Jesus from the law; it emphasises that they are the ones who claim to live by it. There is a quiet authority in it: very well, let us proceed by your own procedure. A prophet says, thus says the LORD. This is the Lord of the law himself, agreeing to be tried by its rules.

The Father who sent me. On any ordinary reading it is an outrageous answer: the two-witness rule exists so that no man’s account of himself need be taken on trust, and he satisfies it by calling a witness nobody else can call and nobody present can cross-examine. But the second witness had already testified, publicly, three ways: in the works he gave Jesus to do (5:36), in the Scriptures (5:39), and at the Jordan (1:32–34). All of them had the Scriptures, and many had seen the works.

But how can I believe a witness I cannot see? In the same way these men were meant to: through the testimony he has given. The Father’s witness is not hidden. It is in the works of Jesus, recorded so that you may believe (20:31); in the Scriptures, which from Moses onwards point to him (5:39, 46); and supremely in the resurrection, by which God declared him to be his Son (Romans 1:4). And the Spirit himself bears witness, opening our eyes to see what is there (15:26; 1 John 5:6–10). You are not asked to believe without evidence. You are asked to receive the evidence God has given, rather than demanding a different kind on your own terms.

For worship. Two witnesses, and both of them God. At the Jordan the Father’s voice owned him as his beloved Son (Matthew 3:17); at the empty tomb the Father spoke again, louder, by raising him from the dead. The God who cannot lie has told us who Jesus is, and in telling us he has shown us what he is himself: a Father who delights in his Son, and gives him to the world.

parallels.desc: two or three witnesses

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him therefore, "Where is your Father?" Jesus answered, "You know neither me nor my Father. If you knew me, you would know my Father also." These words he spoke in the treasury, as he taught in the temple; but no one arrested him, because his hour had not yet come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Where is your Father? They want to see this second witness. Perhaps it is also a sneer at the rumours about his birth (v. 41). On its face the question is fair: he has named a second witness, and in any human court the next step is to ask to see him.

You know neither me nor my Father. They cannot see the Father because they don’t know the Son. He does not produce the Father, offer a sign, or argue. The witness they want to examine is not someone who can be summoned into the courtyard, and the only access to him is through the man they are cross-examining.

You would know my Father also. To know Jesus is to know the Father (14:7–9). This is one of John’s plainest statements that Jesus is the revelation of God, and that every other road to the Father is closed (14:6). It should be stated without softening: there is no way to know God that goes around Jesus: not through sincerity, not through the law these men administered, not through the temple they were standing in.

In the treasury. The treasury was probably in the Court of the Women, where thirteen trumpet-shaped offering boxes stood. It was among the busiest places in the temple, and where he would later sit and watch a widow put in two small coins (Mark 12:41–44). He is standing beside the giving of Israel when he says that they do not know God.

No one arrested him. The boldest claims are made in the busiest place, to the men who wanted him dead, and still no one could touch him.

What about people who love God but do not believe in Jesus? Jesus’ words are hard and clear: to know the Father you must know the Son, and to reject the Son is to show that you do not know the Father (5:23; 1 John 2:23). Many people are sincere, devout and morally serious without Christ, and we should respect their seriousness and treat them with love. But sincerity is not the same as knowing God, and Scripture says there is salvation in no other name (Acts 4:12). That is not a reason for pride; it is a reason for urgency and tenderness, because the God they are looking for has come in Jesus, and they need to hear of him.

On a Tuesday. When you catch yourself picturing God as harsh, distant or indifferent, set that picture beside the Jesus of the Gospels: crying out to the thirsty, touching the leper, weeping at a grave. Whoever has seen him has seen the Father (14:9), so let the Son correct the picture.
verseByVerse.note: The treasury was probably in the Court of the Women, where the offering chests stood.

verseByVerse.quote: So he said to them again, "I am going away, and you will seek me, and you will die in your sin. Where I am going, you cannot come." So the Jews said, "Will he kill himself, since he says, 'Where I am going, you cannot come'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am going away. As in 7:33–34, he is going to the Father, and where he is going they cannot come: heaven is closed to those who reject the one who opens it.

You will die in your sin. The most frightening sentence in the chapter. To die in your sin is to die unforgiven, still carrying your guilt, and so to face God’s judgment with it. Isaiah saw the holy God and cried out that he was lost (Isaiah 6:5); to come before that holiness with every sin still on your account is the most fearful thing that can happen to a human being (Hebrews 10:31). The warning of 7:34 comes back with a clause added: it is not repeated but completed.

One root, many fruits. “Sin” is singular here, the root sin of unbelief (16:9), and plural in verse 24, the sins that flow from it. The sin, singular, is named at verse 24: not believing that he is who he says. There is one thing fundamentally wrong with these men, and everything else follows from it. Every sin will be brought into the light at the judgment, and none will be overlooked. But the decisive matter is a person’s relation to Christ, because he is the only one who can take sins away. To refuse him is to keep every sin one has ever committed.

Will he kill himself? A worse misunderstanding than in 7:35. Suicide was thought to send a person to the lowest depths of Hades, so they mean, perhaps, that he is going where they would never go. The irony is deep: Jesus will lay down his life, of his own will (10:17–18), but not as they imagine, and it will be they who put him to death. They have guessed, in mockery, that he intends to die by his own decision. They are wrong about the manner and the motive, and right about the fact. Once again his enemies prophesy without knowing it.

Can a believer die in his sin? No. A believer dies in the Lord (Revelation 14:13), with every sin forgiven, because Christ has borne them. Dying in your sin means dying without Christ, still carrying your guilt. If you trust him, even weakly, even with sins you are still fighting, you will not die in your sin; you will die forgiven, and wake in his presence. The warning is for those who refuse him. For those who come to him, the promise of 6:37 stands: he will never cast them out.

On a Tuesday. Do not carry your sin to the grave. If there is anything you have never brought to Christ, bring it today.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, "You are from below; I am from above. You are of this world; I am not of this world. I told you that you would die in your sins, for unless you believe that I am he you will die in your sins."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are from below; I am from above. Two realms, two origins (3:31). He is not insulting them. He is explaining why the conversation keeps failing: two parties are using the same words, and one of them came from somewhere else.

That I am he. “That I am he” is literally “that I am” (egō eimi), with nothing added. This is the divine name. In Exodus 3:14 God revealed himself as “I am who I am,” and in Isaiah the Lord says again and again, “I am he” (Isaiah 41:4; 43:10, 13, 25; 46:4; 48:12), using in the Greek Old Testament the same words Jesus uses here. Jesus is claiming to be the God of Israel, come in the flesh. To be saved, one must believe that he is who he says he is. Salvation is not faith in faith, or vague faith in God, but faith in Jesus as Lord and God (20:28).

The bare name. Translators rightly supply the pronoun, but the bare form is what the hearers got, the form God used at the bush. It comes back at verse 28, and at verse 58 it will get him stoned. And the condition is as narrow as anything he ever said: not, unless you live well, or keep the law, which these men did with great rigour, but unless you believe that I am. There is no version of this in which the identity of Jesus is an optional extra on top of a decent life. He has made it the hinge, in the temple, in public, and the men listening understood him perfectly.

Where Christians differ: is Jesus God? Jehovah’s Witnesses, Unitarians and others teach that Jesus is a created being, a lesser god or a great prophet. This commentary’s view: Jesus here claims the divine name, and makes faith in it necessary for salvation. With 1:1, 5:18, 8:58, 10:30 and 20:28, John teaches plainly that Jesus is God the Son, one with the Father. This is not a secondary doctrine: unless you believe, you die in your sins.

Does this warning fall on people who have never heard of Jesus? This verse is spoken to men who had heard the claim plainly and were rejecting it, so its first force falls on everyone who has heard. Their danger was not ignorance but refusal: the one they rejected was standing in front of them. But Scripture as a whole is clear that salvation comes only through conscious faith in Christ: there is no other name under heaven by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12), and people cannot believe in one of whom they have never heard (Romans 10:14). That is why the church is sent to the nations. God is just, and no one will be condemned for rejecting a Christ they never heard of, but for real sins against the light they had (Romans 1:20; 2:12). And the Reformed churches have held that elect infants who die in infancy are saved by Christ through the Spirit. The right response is not to speculate but to go, and send, and pray.

On a Tuesday. When you say the creed, or sing that Jesus is Lord, do not let the words slide past. Jesus is God: the one who loves you is the I AM.

For worship. The fire that burned and was not consumed, the voice that sent Moses to Pharaoh, the God who said through Isaiah that before him no god was formed (Isaiah 43:10), stood in the temple in a human body and spoke the same name. The name that made Moses hide his face now has a face of its own, and it is turned towards sinners.
verseByVerse.note: “That I am he” is literally “that I am” — the divine name.

parallels.desc: that you may know and believe me, that I am he

verseByVerse.quote: So they said to him, "Who are you?" Jesus said to them, "Just what I have been telling you from the beginning. I have much to say about you and much to judge, but he who sent me is true, and I declare to the world what I have heard from him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who are you? The central question of the chapter, and of the Gospel. It may be a sneer: who do you think you are? After everything, the bread, the water, the light, the claim laid down twice already in this conversation, they still ask it. And they will go on asking it: Pilate will ask where he is from and get no answer at all (19:9). It is the question this Gospel exists to answer.

From the beginning. The Greek here is notoriously difficult. The ESV reads it as an answer: I am what I have said all along. Others take it as an exclamation: why do I speak to you at all? The ESV’s reading suits the context: Jesus has been telling them who he is from the start. Either way he offers them nothing new: he has said it, and the failure is not in the phrasing.

Much to judge. He knows a great deal about the men in front of him and says almost none of it: the restraint of one who could expose every heart and chooses not to, yet.

Why do some people hear the gospel many times and never seem to understand? Because the problem is rarely the explanation. These men had heard Jesus himself, the clearest teacher who ever lived, and still asked who he was. Understanding the gospel is not only a matter of information but of a heart opened by God (6:44; 2 Corinthians 4:4–6). That should keep us from two mistakes: thinking that if only we found cleverer words, everyone would believe; and giving up on people who do not understand yet. Keep saying it plainly and lovingly, and pray that God will open their eyes.

On a Tuesday. If you are waiting for God to say something new before you obey what he has already said, start with what he has said.

verseByVerse.quote: They did not understand that he had been speaking to them about the Father. So Jesus said to them, "When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he, and that I do nothing on my own authority, but speak just as the Father taught me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When you have lifted up the Son of Man. In John, “lifted up” (hypsoō) means both the cross and his exaltation (3:14; 12:32–33). It is the language of Isaiah 52:13 about the Servant who will be “lifted up.” They will lift him up on the cross, and that very act will be his exaltation. “You” will do it: they are responsible for his death. This is the second of three such sayings (3:14; 12:32–33), and John never lets the two meanings come apart: the enthronement and the execution are one event. So the hour when Jesus looked most defeated, nailed up where everyone could see him, was the hour he won the victory and was shown to be King. Pilate’s sign over the cross said so, in three languages (19:19–20).

Then you will know. Again “I am” (egō eimi). The cross will reveal who he is. Some will know it to their salvation (the centurion, Mark 15:39; the thousands at Pentecost, Acts 2:36–41); others to their judgment. Their understanding will come too late to stop the cross, and it will be the cross that brings it.

As the Father taught me. The cross will also show his perfect obedience to the Father. Taught is a domestic word: a son in a workshop, learning the trade by watching his father (5:19–20). The authority these men keep demanding an account of is not seized but received, as a trade is handed from father to son.

Does this make the Son less than the Father? No. The Son is equal with the Father in being (10:30; 8:58), but he is sent and the Father sends; he obeys and the Father commands. That order is a matter of their relation, not of their nature. Scripture shows it above all in the work of salvation, where the Son gladly takes the servant’s part for our sake (Philippians 2:6–8). The Son does nothing on his own because he and the Father act as one. A son who does exactly what his father does is not less than his father; he is his father’s likeness. And the Son’s obedience is not a sign of inferiority but the glory of his love: he delights to do the Father’s will.

How is the cross a glory, when it looks like defeat? Because at the cross we see most clearly who God is. There his justice is satisfied, his love poured out, his wisdom displayed and his power at work, all at once, in one man dying for others (Romans 3:25–26; 5:8). What looked like the end of Jesus’ influence became the start of his worldwide reign. What his enemies meant as his shame, God made his throne. That is why Christians speak of the glory of the cross, and why Paul would boast in nothing else (Galatians 6:14).

On a Tuesday. When you want to know whether God loves you, do not look first at your circumstances. Look at the cross. It is where the I AM was lifted up for you, and what it says does not change with the weather.
verseByVerse.note: In John, “lifted up” means both the cross and his exaltation.

parallels.desc: he shall be high and lifted up

verseByVerse.quote: "And he who sent me is with me. He has not left me alone, for I always do the things that are pleasing to him." As he was saying these things, many believed in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He has not left me alone. The Father is always with the Son, even when the world rejects him (16:32). He is surrounded and entirely unaccompanied: the crowd is hostile, the disciples are nowhere said to be present, and his brothers do not believe him. The ground of his calm is a person: the one who sent him has not gone away.

Always. “Always”: no one else could say this. It is a claim to sinlessness (v. 46; Hebrews 4:15). On the cross he would cry, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Mark 15:34): not because he had displeased the Father, but because he bore our sin, and in that very act was most pleasing to him. From anyone else always would be the remark of a man with no self-knowledge; nothing in the record suggests that of him.

Does this mean that when God feels absent, I must have displeased him? No, and it is important not to turn this verse into a formula that crushes people. Gethsemane and the cry from the cross forbid that reading. The one who always pleased the Father went into the dark anyway, and he did it so that those who have not always pleased him need not be abandoned. Believers may feel God’s absence for many reasons: grief, illness, exhaustion, or a trial God has sent to deepen their faith (Psalm 88; Isaiah 50:10). Sometimes sin is the cause, and then the remedy is confession. But your feelings are not the measure of his presence. His promise is: I will never leave you nor forsake you (Hebrews 13:5).

Many believed in him. In the middle of the most hostile exchange so far, faith is being born, and the next verses will test what it was worth: not all who believe in some way are true disciples.

On a Tuesday. When you stand alone for what is right, at work, in the family, in a room where everyone else has gone along, remember that the Father is with you as he was with the Son.

For worship. The Son always did what pleased the Father. That perfect obedience, which we could never offer, he offered for us, and it is counted as ours (Romans 5:19). On the cross he was forsaken so that we never will be. Because he always pleased the Father, the Father is pleased with all who are in him.

parallels.desc: I am not alone, for the Father is with me

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31–59 — The Children of Abraham and the Great I AM
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus now tests those who had believed him. The conversation moves from freedom and slavery (vv. 31–36), to whose children his hearers really are, Abraham’s, God’s, or the devil’s (vv. 37–47), to the charge that he has a demon and his claim to be greater than Abraham (vv. 48–58).
verseByVerse.theology: The passage sets two families side by side: Abraham’s children and the devil’s. The mark of each is not ancestry but likeness: Abraham’s children believe God, and the devil’s children lie and want to kill. This is a diagnosis of every unconverted heart, whatever its ancestry, not a charge against one people. The truth that sets free (v. 32) is not an idea but the Son himself (v. 36), and the freedom he gives is release from slavery to sin.
verseByVerse.examples: The stones at the end of the chapter are the authorities’ answer to his claim that before Abraham was, he is. They understood that he was claiming to be the eternal God, the I am of Exodus 3. They were right about what he claimed, and wrong to reject it.

verseByVerse.quote: So Jesus said to the Jews who had believed him, "If you abide in my word, you are truly my disciples, and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. The rest of the chapter is a hard conversation with people who had, in some sense, believed. Jesus tests their faith, and by v. 59 they are picking up stones: the section teaches what true discipleship, real freedom and a person’s true father are.

To the Jews who had believed him. Believed “him,” what he said, rather than believed “in him” (v. 30). John may intend no difference, but the conversation shows that their faith had not reached the root. That answers the question every reader asks: how can believers be told a few verses later that their father is the devil? They had accepted his claims; they had not given themselves to him.

If you abide in my word. “Abide” (menō): remain, continue, make your home in. The mark of a true disciple is not an initial response but continuing in Jesus’ word. Real faith lasts (15:4–10; Colossians 1:23; Hebrews 3:14). Those who leave were never truly his (1 John 2:19).

The truth will set you free. “The truth” is not just correct ideas, but the reality of God revealed in Jesus, who is the truth (14:6). Knowing him sets you free from sin (v. 34). The sentence is carved over government buildings and university gates to mean that information liberates. It cannot bear that meaning: it comes with a condition, if you abide in my word, and it speaks not of truth in general but of the truth, and the truth is a person.

Does abiding mean I can lose my salvation if I fail? No. Jesus is not describing a test you must pass to stay saved, but the mark that shows who is truly saved. Those whom the Father gives to the Son are kept by him, and no one can snatch them out of his hand (10:28–29). The same grace that brings a person to Christ keeps him continuing in Christ (Philippians 1:6). So abiding is both a command and a gift: we are told to remain, and God works in us so that we do. A true believer may stumble badly, like Peter, but he is brought back. What this verse warns against is a faith that never put down roots and so falls away when the word becomes hard.

So what does abiding in his word look like day to day? It means living in the Bible rather than visiting it. Read it regularly, not to tick a box but to hear his voice; let it shape what you think about God, yourself, money, sex, work and death. Sit under faithful preaching with his people. When the word says something you do not like, stay with it and ask for grace to obey, instead of drifting off. Memorise a verse and turn it over through the day. Abiding is less a technique than a home: the place you keep coming back to and living from.

verseByVerse.quote: They answered him, "We are offspring of Abraham and have never been enslaved to anyone. How is it that you say, 'You will become free'?" Jesus answered them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Never been enslaved. A remarkable claim. Israel had been in bondage to Egypt, Babylon and now Rome; the Roman garrison stood beside the temple as they spoke. They were fresh from a festival remembering the exodus, members of a nation whose Passover makes children ask why they were once slaves. They meant something narrower and prouder: that as Abraham’s offspring they had never lost their standing before God, whatever the politics. This is what a person will say when the alternative is admitting bondage.

A slave to sin. “Practices” (poiōn, present tense, keeps doing): habitual sin. “Slave” (doulos). Sin is not just something we do; it is a master that owns us (Romans 6:16–20). The worst slavery is spiritual, and this slave has nothing to buy his freedom with. Jesus does not argue about the history; he names a bondage they cannot check by looking out of the window, with the one word that would offend them most.

Is a Christian who still struggles with a habitual sin a slave of sin? Not in the sense Jesus means. If the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed (v. 36): a believer’s standing has changed, and sin will have no dominion over him (Romans 6:14). He may still fight, and lose battles, and must keep fighting. But the slave in this verse is the one who serves sin as his master without wanting to be free; the believer hates the sin he struggles with and runs to Christ for help. The struggle itself is a sign that a new master has come.

But is freedom not simply being free to run my own life? That is what most people mean by it, and it is exactly what these men thought they had. But everyone serves something. The person who lives for approval is ruled by other people’s opinions; the one who lives for success is driven by the next target; the one who lives for comfort cannot bear to lose it. Each of these masters promises freedom and then demands more. Jesus does not offer independence, which no creature has ever had. He offers a new master who gave himself for his servants, and whose yoke is easy and whose burden is light (Matthew 11:28–30).

On a Tuesday. Take the thing you would stop if you could: the temper, the drink, the screen, the way you talk about a particular person. You have decided to stop it before, and meant it. Paul spent a chapter on that condition, willing a thing and not doing it (Romans 7:14–25), and he ended it with thanks to God through Jesus Christ. So stop trying to free yourself, and ask the one who can.
verseByVerse.note: Israel had been in bondage to Egypt, Babylon and now Rome; they meant they had never inwardly accepted slavery.

parallels.desc: slaves of sin

verseByVerse.quote: "The slave does not remain in the house forever; the son remains forever. So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The son remains forever. A slave had no permanent place in a household; he could be sold or sent away at any time. A son belonged there for good. Perhaps there is an echo of Ishmael, son of the slave woman, who was sent away, while Isaac, the son of promise, remained (Genesis 21:10; Galatians 4:30). Being physically descended from Abraham does not secure a place in God’s house.

Free indeed. “Indeed” (ontōs) means really, truly: the freedom he gives is real and permanent, freedom from sin’s guilt and power. The Son, the one who is permanently in the house, has the authority to change a slave’s status, and what he gives is not parole but adoption into God’s family for ever (1:12; Romans 8:15). In adoption God brings outsiders into his household with the full standing of sons: his name, his care, his Spirit in their hearts and a share in the inheritance (Galatians 4:4–7).

Freedom that cannot be lost. Political freedom can be lost by a change of government, financial freedom in a market, and health goes. The freedom described here rests on the standing of someone who cannot be evicted from the house, and it is given, not earned, which means it cannot be forfeited by a failure, since it was never bought by success. And the condition lies with the Son, not the slave: not whether the slave improves, but whether the Son acts.

What does it feel like to be free indeed? It may not feel dramatic. Often it begins quietly: a conscience no longer crushed by guilt, because you know you are forgiven; the first real ability to say no to a sin that used to rule you; the strange new desire to please God rather than merely avoid punishment; the settled sense that you belong in the Father’s house and will not be thrown out. It grows over a lifetime. And its full flowering is still to come, when the children of God are finally set free from all decay and sin (Romans 8:21). Freedom is not doing whatever you want. It is wanting, more and more, what you were made for.

On a Tuesday. Live like a son, not a slave. If you find yourself serving God anxiously, as though one more failure would get you evicted, tell yourself the truth: in Christ you are a son, and the son remains for ever.
verseByVerse.note: A slave had no permanent place in a household; a son did.

parallels.desc: cast out this slave woman and her son

verseByVerse.quote: "I know that you are offspring of Abraham; yet you seek to kill me because my word finds no place in you. I speak of what I have seen with my Father, and you do what you have heard from your father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I know that you are offspring of Abraham. Physically, yes. The concession is generous: the descent is real, but it is not doing the work they think it does.

My word finds no place in you. “Finds no place” (ou chōrei): makes no progress, has no room in you. It is not that they have not heard him; they have heard him for days and can quote him back. It is that there is nowhere in them for it to go. We picture rejection as a verdict reached after consideration; this is closer to a house with every room occupied: the word arrives, finds no space, and stands in the doorway. And the evidence he gives is not their arguments but their intention. Whatever a man says about God, what he plans to do to God’s messenger tells the truth about him.

Two fathers. Jesus speaks from his Father; they act from theirs. Who their father is, he will soon say (v. 44). The verbs are unmatched: he speaks from sight of the Father; they act on report, received at second hand from a source they have never examined. That is a fair description of how most evil actually spreads. Very few people have consciously met the father of lies. They have simply heard something, about a neighbour, a race, a rival, and acted on it without asking where it came from.

What fills the room where Christ’s word should be? Usually not one great rebellion, but many ordinary things: busyness, entertainment, worry, the opinions of the people we most want to please, a settled idea of who God is that we do not want disturbed. Jesus’ parable of the sower names them: the cares of the world, the deceitfulness of riches and the desire for other things choke the word (Mark 4:19). Making room is practical. Turn off what crowds out silence. Bring your fixed ideas to Scripture and let it correct them. Ask God to clear space in you, and he will.

verseByVerse.quote: They answered him, "Abraham is our father." Jesus said to them, "If you were Abraham's children, you would be doing the works Abraham did, but now you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth that I heard from God. This is not what Abraham did."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham is our father. They repeat it, sensing the insult.

The works Abraham did. True children resemble their father. Abraham believed God (Genesis 15:6). The true children of Abraham are those who share his faith (Romans 4:11–12; Galatians 3:7). Abraham welcomed strangers who came from God with a message, and set food before them under a tree (Genesis 18:1–8). These men are planning to kill one. You would be doing implies that they are not.

A man who has told you the truth. The phrase he uses of himself is deliberately small. Not the Son of God, not the light of the world, though he has said both this week. He takes the least contestable description, and asks whether killing such a person is something Abraham would have done.

This is not what Abraham did. The whole argument in a sentence, and they answer it by changing the subject. Yet there is mercy in it. What is required is not a different ancestry, which nobody can acquire, but a different faith and life, which God can give.

Can I rely on my Christian family or background? No more than they could rely on Abraham. A Christian upbringing is a great gift, and God often works through families (Acts 16:31; 2 Timothy 1:5). But nobody is a child of God because his parents were. God has children, not grandchildren. Each person must come to Christ himself, by faith, and the evidence will be a family likeness: trusting God’s word, welcoming his Son, and doing the works of faith. If you grew up in the church, thank God for it, and make sure the faith you were taught has become your own.

For worship. Abraham set food before three strangers under the oaks of Mamre and found that the LORD had come to his tent (Genesis 18). His sons in the temple were planning the death of God’s messenger. Yet Abraham’s greatest Son did not disown the family. He died for it, and widened it, so that the promise of descendants as many as the stars is kept not by bloodline but by grace, in people from every nation who believe God as Abraham did.

parallels.desc: Abraham welcomes the LORD’s messengers

verseByVerse.quote: "You are doing the works your father did." They said to him, "We were not born of sexual immorality. We have one Father — even God." Jesus said to them, "If God were your Father, you would love me, for I came from God and I am here. I came not of my own accord, but he sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are doing the works your father did. Their father, he implies, is someone other than Abraham.

We were not born of sexual immorality. “We” may be emphatic: we were not, implying, unlike you. They may be hinting at rumours about Jesus’ own birth; later Jewish writings spread a story that he was illegitimate. Or they may mean that they are not spiritually illegitimate, not idolaters, which the prophets called sexual unfaithfulness (Hosea 2:4). If the first, then cornered on Abraham they reach for a rumour about his mother, and he does not stoop to answer it.

We have one Father, even God. They move from Abraham to God himself, the highest claim available to a Jew.

You would love me. The test of being God’s child is love for his Son. You cannot love the Father and hate the Son (1 John 5:1). Not, you would agree with me, but you would love me: children recognise the family, often before they have worked out the theology. The test is about the heart, and it cannot be answered by argument, which is why the conversation is about to collapse into abuse.

I came from God. He came out from the Father’s side, and did not come of his own accord; he was sent by the very one they claim as Father.

How do I know whether I love Jesus? Love for Christ is not first a feeling, though it often includes feeling. Jesus gave its marks himself: if you love me, you will keep my commandments (14:15). Love wants to be with him, in prayer and in his word. It treasures what he has done, and is grieved when he is dishonoured. It loves the people he loves, his church (1 John 4:20). It is sorry for sin because sin wounds him. If you find even a small and struggling version of these in yourself, that is the family likeness, and it is God’s work. If you find none, ask him to show you his Son, and keep looking at him in the Gospels, for that is where love for him is born.

On a Tuesday. We love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). Tell him today, in your own words, why you love him, and if the words do not come easily, ask him to make you love him more.
verseByVerse.note: Their retort may hint at rumours about Jesus’ own birth.

parallels.desc: have we not all one Father?

verseByVerse.quote: "Why do you not understand what I say? It is because you cannot bear to hear my word. You are of your father the devil, and your will is to do your father's desires. He was a murderer from the beginning, and does not stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he lies, he speaks out of his own character, for he is a liar and the father of lies."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why do you not understand what I say? It is because you cannot bear to hear my word. “What I say” is his speech (lalia), the way he talks; “my word” (logos) is the message. The problem is not intellect but will. They are unable to hear, because they will not (6:44; 7:17).

You are of your father the devil. The hardest words Jesus says in John. Not all Jews, but these men, who want to kill him, show by their actions whose children they are. Spiritual parentage is shown by behaviour (1 John 3:8–10). Every unbeliever, Jew or Gentile, is by nature under the power of the evil one (Ephesians 2:1–3; 1 John 5:19). This is not an ethnic slur but a moral diagnosis, and it is not a permanent sentence. Nor is it a loss of temper. Love that wants a man free must first tell him he is bound (v. 34), and the Jesus who speaks this hard word to men planning murder is the same Jesus who lays down his life for his sheep (10:11).

He was a murderer from the beginning. They want what the devil wants, and what he has always wanted is death. The devil’s lie led to death in Eden (Genesis 3:1–5; Romans 5:12); the first murder followed soon after (Genesis 4:8; 1 John 3:12). The desire to kill Jesus is the devil’s family trait.

In the flow. Verse 44 completes an argument begun at verse 37: Abraham’s children would act like Abraham (v. 39), God’s children would love God’s Son (v. 42), and now he names the father whose likeness they do show. The answer to who Jesus is also exposes who we are.

The father of lies. Lying is his native language. The two marks of the family are murder and lying, and both were in the courtyard: they intend to kill the one who tells them the truth, and they refuse the truth itself.

A family quarrel, from inside the family. No verse in this Gospel has been put to worse use: these words have been read from pulpits before massacres and quoted by men who planned genocide. It is a straight inversion of the text. The speaker is a Jew, in the Jewish temple, at a Jewish feast, who has already said in this Gospel that salvation is from the Jews (4:22). The Evangelist is a Jew, and the audience is not a race but particular people in a particular courtyard (v. 31). A prophet of Israel rebuking the leaders of Israel is not an outsider attacking a people; it is the oldest and most Jewish thing in the Bible. Isaiah called them rulers of Sodom (Isaiah 1:10), and nobody thinks Isaiah anti-Jewish. The man who takes these words as a weapon against Jewish people sides against the Jewish Messiah, whose charge here is that his hearers intend murder, and then goes out to commit it himself. The verse condemns him. Paul, who felt the whole weight of this, said he could wish himself cut off from Christ for the sake of his brothers according to the flesh (Romans 9:3), and that God has not rejected his people (Romans 11:1). That is the settled Christian mind.

Is everyone who is not a Christian a child of the devil? Scripture says that apart from Christ all of us were by nature children of wrath, following the prince of the power of the air (Ephesians 2:2–3). That is a description of the human condition, not a special insult for some. It includes the person reading this, before grace found him. So it gives no room for pride or contempt: the believer is a former member of that family, rescued by mercy. And it gives great hope: the Son came to destroy the works of the devil (1 John 3:8) and to bring people out of that family into God’s. Treat unbelievers as people you once were, and whom God may yet adopt.

On a Tuesday. You have been brought out of the liar’s family into the house of the God who cannot lie, and his Spirit lives in you, so refuse the old family likeness. Think of the small lies: the exaggeration, the excuse, the half-story that leaves you looking better. Speak the truth in love, even when it costs you.
verseByVerse.note: The devil’s lie led to death in Eden; the first murder followed.

parallels.desc: “You will not surely die”

verseByVerse.quote: "But because I tell the truth, you do not believe me. Which one of you convicts me of sin? If I tell the truth, why do you not believe me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because I tell the truth. Not “although” but “because.” The children of the father of lies reject truth precisely because it is truth. To a heart shaped by lies, truth is not neutral. It is repellent.

Which one of you convicts me of sin? “Convicts” (elenchei): proves guilty. A challenge no other human being could make. Jesus invites his enemies to name a single sin. No one could. He is the sinless Son (2 Corinthians 5:21; Hebrews 4:15; 1 Peter 2:22). Think what it takes to ask that. He stands before men who have watched him for months, sent officers, looked for a charge: men with every motive to produce one. And he invites them to name a single thing. John records no answer. That silence is the loudest thing in the chapter.

The saints move the other way. Put the question in the mouth of the best person you have ever known and it becomes unbearable within a sentence: the closer anyone gets to real goodness, the more sharply he sees his own failure. Here is one man nearer to God than anyone has ever been who never once, in any record, confesses a sin. He teaches his disciples to pray, forgive us our debts (Matthew 6:12), and does not join in. That is either a serious defect of self-knowledge, which nothing else about him supports, or it is simply true.

If I tell the truth, why do you not believe me? If he is sinless, he is no liar. Their unbelief has no excuse.

Why does it matter so much that Jesus never sinned? Because our salvation depends on it. A sacrifice for sin had to be without blemish (Exodus 12:5; 1 Peter 1:19). If Jesus had had a single sin of his own, he would have had his own account to settle, and nothing left over for anyone else. Because he owed nothing, he could pay what we owed. Because he was perfectly righteous, his righteousness can be counted to us (2 Corinthians 5:21). His sinlessness also makes him the perfect high priest: tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin, and so able to help us when we are tempted (Hebrews 4:15–16).

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever is of God hears the words of God. The reason why you do not hear them is that you are not of God." The Jews answered him, "Are we not right in saying that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever is of God hears the words of God. Belonging to God comes first, and hearing follows (10:26–27; 18:37). When Christ’s words are preached, something in such a person answers that this is true and for him, and he keeps coming back.

You are not of God. It is not that they are of God but fail to hear; it is that they do not hear because they are not of God. Their failure to hear is the evidence of where they stand: chapter 6 seen from the other end.

Are we not right in saying that you are a Samaritan and have a demon? Calling a Jew a Samaritan was an insult. Samaritans were considered heretics, of mixed race and false worship (4:9). Perhaps they meant he was a traitor to Israel, or that, like the Samaritans, he rejected the true tradition. “Have a demon” means mad or possessed. Having lost the argument, they turn to name-calling. There is a nasty precision in choosing Samaritan: he has just questioned their true parentage, and they reply by questioning his. And it is richly ironic, because the Samaritans are the ones who called him the Saviour of the world after two days (4:42), which is more than Jerusalem has managed. The demon charge is the standard explanation for a man whose power is undeniable and whose claims are unacceptable: the works are real, so something is at work in him, so it must not be God. It requires no evidence, and it ends the conversation, which is its purpose.

If hearing depends on being of God, is it my fault if I do not believe? Yes, still. Scripture holds both truths together. No one comes to Christ unless the Father draws him (6:44), and yet those who refuse him are fully responsible, because they refuse what they could see is true and love the darkness (3:19). These men are not described as people longing to believe and prevented. They do not want to hear. And if you do want to hear, if you are reading this and something in you is drawn to Christ, that drawing is the Father at work. Do not wait to discover whether you are of God before you come. Come, and you will find that you are.

On a Tuesday. When people run out of arguments, they often reach for insults. Don’t be surprised when it happens to you, and don’t answer in kind. And when you are losing an argument, do you reach for a label to stop having to listen?
verseByVerse.note: Calling a Jew a Samaritan was an insult.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "I do not have a demon, but I honor my Father, and you dishonor me. Yet I do not seek my own glory; there is One who seeks it, and he is the judge."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I do not have a demon. He calmly denies the second insult. He doesn’t answer the first: he is not ashamed to be thought a Samaritan (4:40). He denies it once, without heat, and moves straight back to the subject.

You dishonor me. To dishonour the Son is to dishonour the Father (5:23). He puts himself in the sentence: his honour and the Father’s are the same currency, and slighting the Son is no lesser offence than slighting the Father.

There is One who seeks it. He does not defend his reputation. The Father will vindicate him. He entrusts his honour to God (1 Peter 2:23). Called a Samaritan and a demoniac in public, he says his reputation is somebody else’s business, and the judge’s case will keep. The man in this verse was executed on a false charge the following spring, was publicly vindicated on the third day after it, and did nothing whatever to arrange either.

Should I never defend myself when I am slandered? Not never, but rarely in the way we want to. Paul defended himself when the gospel was at stake (2 Corinthians 11), and it can be right to correct a falsehood calmly, or to seek justice when real harm is being done; abuse and lies that endanger others should be brought into the light. But much of our self-defence is not about truth. It is about our reputation, and it is exhausting, never finished, and turns every insult into an emergency. Jesus shows another way: state the truth once, without heat, and then entrust your name to God, who judges justly.

On a Tuesday. Think of the last time you were described unfairly, and count how much of the following week went on it: the conversations, the mental rehearsals, the replies you drafted and did not send. The injustice matters, enough that God has appointed himself to deal with it; it has been taken out of your hands and put into better ones.

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, truly, I say to you, if anyone keeps my word, he will never see death.' The Jews said to him, 'Now we know that you have a demon! Abraham died, as did the prophets, yet you say, 'If anyone keeps my word, he will never taste death.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He will never see death. “Keeps” (tērēsē): holds fast, obeys, treasures. The believer will die physically, but will never experience death as the wages of sin, separation from God (5:24; 11:25–26).

Not a promise that the heart will not stop. The verse has troubled people at gravesides, for every believer who heard him say it has died. To see death means to experience it as the thing it is; what he denies is not the event but the encounter. Paul says the same: O death, where is your sting? (1 Corinthians 15:55). The sting is drawn; the creature is still there, and Christians grieve at funerals like everyone else and are not asked to pretend otherwise. What has changed is what the bite does.

Now we know. At verse 48 they said he had a demon; now they are sure. The promise about death has settled it for them: no sane man says such a thing. Only a madman or God could make such a claim; they have named the alternatives correctly, and chosen.

Abraham died, as did the prophets. They think only of physical death. It is a serious objection: the greatest men in history are in graves. His answer comes in chapter 11, at the tomb of Lazarus, four days dead, and it is not an argument.

What happens to a believer at the moment of death? The body dies and is buried, but the soul does not sleep or wait in some intermediate place of punishment. It goes at once to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23; Luke 23:43; 2 Corinthians 5:8). There is no purgatory, because Christ’s death has paid in full; there is no soul sleep, because to be absent from the body is to be at home with the Lord. And that is not the end: at his return the body will be raised, glorious and imperishable, and body and soul will be together with the Lord for ever (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17). So the believer can face death as a defeated enemy, still to be endured but no longer to be feared.

On a Tuesday. If you are afraid of dying, take that fear to him by name; he has been through it, and come out the other side. And if you have lost a believer, grieve, but not as those who have no hope.

verseByVerse.quote: "Are you greater than our father Abraham, who died? And the prophets died! Who do you make yourself out to be?" Jesus answered, "If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing. It is my Father who glorifies me, of whom you say, 'He is our God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are you greater than our father Abraham, who died? The Greek expects the answer no. As the Samaritan woman asked about Jacob (4:12). The answer is, of course, yes. And they cannot stop mentioning that Abraham is dead (vv. 52–53). The whole exchange has been about descent from a man in a grave. The one they are arguing with is about to say that he was there before Abraham was born.

Who do you make yourself out to be? The question of the chapter again. It is asked with contempt: the assumption is that he is inflating himself.

If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing. He makes no claim of his own. He agrees entirely that self-declared greatness is worthless.

My Father who glorifies me. The God they claim to worship is the one honouring Jesus. If the God they profess is real, he is the one glorifying Jesus, and their quarrel is with him.

How is Jesus greater than Abraham? In every way. Abraham was a creature; Jesus is the Creator (1:3). Abraham received the promise; Jesus is the promise kept (Galatians 3:16). Abraham believed God; Jesus is God. Abraham was justified by faith; Jesus is the one in whom we are justified. Abraham died and was buried; Jesus died and rose, and lives for ever. Abraham is the father of the faithful; Jesus is the Lord of the faithful, Abraham included, who rejoiced to see his day (v. 56). To honour Abraham rightly is to bow before the one Abraham longed for.

verseByVerse.quote: "But you have not known him. I know him. If I were to say that I do not know him, I would be a liar like you. But I do know him and I keep his word. Your father Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day. He saw it and was glad."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You have not known him. Jesus knows him, perfectly, and to say otherwise would make him a liar like them: false modesty would be a lie.

Abraham rejoiced. “My day”: the time of Messiah’s coming. Abraham received the promise that in his offspring all nations would be blessed (Genesis 12:3; 22:18). He looked forward to it with joy. Some rabbis taught that God showed Abraham the future ages (from Genesis 15). He rejoiced in the anticipation, and then he saw it: not a vague hope, but something shown to him.

He saw it and was glad. How? By faith, through the promise, and perhaps especially at Mount Moriah, when God provided the ram in Isaac’s place (Genesis 22:8, 13–14).

On the mountain of the LORD. Abraham walks up with his son, the wood on the boy’s back; the boy asks where the lamb is, and at the top a ram is caught in a thicket. The narrator adds: as it is said to this day, on the mount of the LORD it shall be provided (Genesis 22:14). A father, an only son, a substitute supplied at the last moment, and a name that points forward rather than back. And 2 Chronicles 3:1 says the temple was built on Mount Moriah; if, as Jewish tradition has long held, that is the place of Genesis 22, Abraham gave a prophetic name to the very ridge these men were standing on as they argued.

What did believers before Christ actually believe? Not something else. Not a different religion of law-keeping later replaced by grace. The same Christ, seen at a distance, through promise and shadow. These all died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar (Hebrews 11:13). Old Testament believers were saved exactly as we are: by grace, through faith in God’s promise of a Saviour, whose work they saw dimly and we see plainly (Romans 4:3, 23–25). Abraham is here described as a man who looked down the centuries and was glad about a particular day. There has only ever been one way of salvation, and one Saviour.

For worship. Abraham came down the mountain with his son alive, because God provided a substitute. Two thousand years later, near that ridge, God did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32). There was no ram in the thicket for Jesus. He was the Lamb, and the name Abraham gave the place has been true ever since: the LORD has provided.

parallels.desc: having seen them and greeted them from afar

verseByVerse.quote: So the Jews said to him, "You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?" Jesus said to them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, before Abraham was, I am."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham? They twist his words: he said Abraham saw his day, they ask whether he has seen Abraham. Fifty was a round number for the end of a man’s working life (Numbers 4:3); Jesus was in his early thirties (Luke 3:23). Abraham had lived some two thousand years earlier. They have reversed what he said, which is what people do when they are no longer really listening. And there is dismissiveness in it: you are not even at the end of a working life, and you are talking about the patriarchs.

Before Abraham was, I am. The climax of the chapter. Everything turns on the two verbs. “Was” (genesthai) means came into being: Abraham was born, had a beginning. “I am” (egō eimi) is present tense, timeless. Not “I was,” which would mean only that he existed earlier, but “I am,” claiming eternal, uncreated existence and the divine name of verse 24 (Exodus 3:14). Abraham had a first day, and the Son never did; there was never a time when he did not exist (1:1–2).

The grammar broken on purpose. Everything in the chapter has been built to hold this sentence, and the breakage is the meaning: he has no beginning, and he bears the Name, laid down at verses 24 and 28 with nothing after it. Here he sets it beside Abraham, and the crowd finally understands.

Where Christians differ: what does “I am” mean here? Some, especially Jehovah’s Witnesses, translate “before Abraham was, I have been,” to make it a claim only to pre-existence, not deity. This commentary’s view: the Greek present tense, set against the past tense of Abraham’s coming to be, marks a contrast between created and eternal being. And the hearers’ reaction settles it: they pick up stones, the penalty for blasphemy (v. 59; 10:33). They understood that he was claiming to be God.

His enemies are the best witnesses. Nobody picks up a stone because a man has claimed to be wise, or even a prophet; the penalty for blasphemy was stoning (Leviticus 24:16), and they went straight for it. His enemies are among the best witnesses in the New Testament to what he was claiming, because they had no motive to exaggerate it and every motive to wish he had not said it. A sceptic may reply that John wrote decades later and sharpened the words. But the earliest Gospel, Mark, already has Jesus answer the high priest with I am, and the council condemn him for blasphemy on the spot (Mark 14:62–64), so the charge John records is not his invention.

If Jesus is eternal, how could he be born, grow and die? Because the eternal Son took a true human nature without ceasing to be God. As God he has no beginning; as man he was conceived in Mary’s womb, grew, learned, hungered, wept and died. One person, two natures, without mixture and without division. The Word who is from eternity became flesh (1:14). So when we say that Jesus was born at Bethlehem, we mean that the eternal I AM entered time as a baby. He did not stop being who he always was; he added to himself what we are, so that he could save us.

On a Tuesday. The one who says I am has no yesterday that has slipped away from him and no tomorrow he is anxious about. Bring him the regret from your past and the fear about your future. He was there before both, and he is there now.

For worship. Before the mountains were brought forth, from everlasting to everlasting, he is God (Psalm 90:2). The I AM, without beginning, consented to have a birthday, a hometown and a grave, and came near enough to be stoned, so that creatures who began could live with him for ever.
verseByVerse.note: “I am” without anything added echoes the name God gave himself at the burning bush.

parallels.desc: “I AM WHO I AM”
from everlasting to everlasting

verseByVerse.quote: So they picked up stones to throw at him, but Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They picked up stones. They are about to lynch him. The same people who had “believed” (v. 31) now want to kill him. That is what shallow faith becomes when confronted with the full truth of Jesus. Building stones lay around in the courts, and the men who had come to worship picked up the building material of the house of God to kill the one it was built for.

Jesus hid himself. How? Perhaps simply slipping away in the crowd; perhaps by a miraculous hiding. In any case, his hour had not come. There may be a deeper sign: the glory of God leaving the temple, as in Ezekiel 10, as the one in whom God dwells walks out of the house that has rejected him. John describes no miracle: the Word who made the stone walks out of the temple through a crowd holding pieces of it, and nobody notices the glory has gone.

In the flow. With the stones the argument that began in chapter 7 ends; they understood verse 58 exactly. Chapter 9 follows straight on: the one who has left the temple opens a blind man’s eyes, and the man thrown out by the same leaders (9:34) is found by Jesus (9:35). The light the temple drove out goes on shining outside it.

Can people who once seemed to believe turn so completely against Christ? Sadly, yes, and the New Testament warns of it (Hebrews 6:4–6; 1 John 2:19). Those who were truly born of God are kept by him, but interest in Jesus can stop short of the heart, and when his full claims are pressed, it can turn into hostility. That is why Jesus tested these hearers so hard. It should not make true believers anxious, because the very fact that you are troubled by the possibility shows a heart that wants Christ. But it should make all of us honest: not resting in a past moment of interest, but abiding in his word, which is the mark of the real thing (v. 31).

On a Tuesday. The same Jesus who walked out of their temple is willing to dwell in the humblest heart that receives him. When his word presses on something in your life that you would rather keep, that is the moment the stones come out. Put them down. Let him stay.
verseByVerse.note: Stoning was the penalty for blasphemy.
