Later tradition merged the three, but the Gospels keep them distinct, and it is worth keeping them distinct, because each of them is a separate testimony to his grace.

Did Jesus really need friends? He did not need them as God, who is complete in himself. But he was truly man, and a true man is made for friendship. He chose to have a home where he was welcome, people he loved by name, a table where he could rest. That is no weakness. It is a picture of what he is: the Son of God who has come near enough to be your friend (15:15). And it is a dignity he gives to ordinary Christian hospitality. A house where Christ is loved and his people are welcome is doing something he himself valued.
verseByVerse.note: Bethany was a village on the Mount of Olives, about two miles east of Jerusalem. John mentions Mary’s anointing ahead of time; it comes in chapter 12.

parallels.desc: Martha and Mary

verseByVerse.quote: So the sisters sent to him, saying, "Lord, he whom you love is ill." But when Jesus heard it he said, "This illness does not lead to death. It is for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He whom you love is ill. The message is short, and it is a model of how to pray. There is no request in it. They state the situation and the relationship and stop. Their confidence is not in having framed the request correctly. It is in the fact that he loves their brother, and that he will know what to do with that information. “Love” here is phileō, the love of friendship; two verses later John uses agapaō, with no clear difference of weight.

This illness does not lead to death. A bereaved reader will stop at this sentence, because Lazarus dies. The Greek is pros thanaton: toward death, in the direction of death. He is not predicting whether the man’s heart will stop. He is saying where the illness is aimed and what it ends in. Its final outcome is not death but resurrection.

For the glory of God. As with the man born blind (9:3), the purpose is God’s glory. And the glory of God is the glory of the Son: the Father is honoured when the Son is honoured (5:23). The Son will be glorified by the miracle, and also by the death it will bring him to (v. 53; 12:23). The sign that shows his glory is the sign that sends him to it.

If I pray for healing and the person dies, did God fail? No, and this verse should not be used to promise what it does not promise. Christians die of their illnesses, and this text has been quoted over sickbeds in a way that later looked like a broken promise. What it actually says is stranger and better: that for those who belong to him, an illness can pass straight through death and still not have death as its destination. God may heal, and we should ask him to. But his answer is never limited to the two choices of healing or failure. For a believer, death is not God’s defeat but the doorway to his presence and the road to resurrection. Pray boldly, and leave the shape of the answer to his love.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus. So, when he heard that Lazarus was ill, he stayed two days longer in the place where he was.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus. John is careful to say it before he tells us of the delay, so that we cannot misread the delay as indifference.

So he stayed two days longer. The little word “so” is the hinge of the chapter, and it should be felt as a shock. The delay is the consequence of the love, not a suspension of it. He meant to give them something far greater than a healing: a resurrection, and a deeper knowledge of who he is.

The arithmetic. When Jesus arrives, Lazarus has been in the tomb four days (v. 17). The journey from Bethany beyond the Jordan to Bethany near Jerusalem probably took about a day. Before that, he waited two days. Before that, the messenger had to travel the same road, probably another day. Lazarus may well have died soon after the messenger set out, before the message ever reached Jesus. The two days did not cause the death, but they ensured that no one could doubt he was truly dead.

The comfort for if only. There is a form of bereavement that spends years on the timing: if the appointment had been a week earlier, if we had gone straight to the hospital, if the prayer had started sooner. This passage puts a family in exactly that position, lets them say the sentence twice (vv. 21, 32), and quietly shows that the arithmetic never worked. He allowed a death he could have prevented, in a family he loved, in order to give them and everybody watching something a healing could not have given. John does not make the four days pleasant, and records no attempt to.

Why does God delay answering my prayers? Scripture does not give a single reason for every case, but this chapter gives us the deepest one: his delays are governed by love, not neglect. Sometimes he waits because he intends to give something greater than what we asked. Sometimes the waiting itself is shaping us, teaching us to trust him rather than our timetable. Often we will not know why until later, and some things not until we see his face. What you can know now is the sentence John put first: Jesus loved them. Read every delay in your life with that sentence in front of it, and keep praying.

verseByVerse.quote: Then after this he said to the disciples, "Let us go to Judea again." The disciples said to him, "Rabbi, the Jews were just now seeking to stone you, and are you going there again?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let us go to Judea again. Not let us go to Lazarus, which is what the errand is, but Judea, where the stones are. And he does not go alone or send them: they are going into it together.

Seeking to stone you. The disciples are not being cowardly. The authorities had tried, twice, in a matter of months (8:59; 10:31, 39), the last time at the Feast of Dedication not long before.

And are you going there again? The word “again” appears twice, once in Jesus’ mouth and once in theirs. For him it is a return to unfinished business. For them it is the second time into a place that nearly killed him. That is generally how a call sounds from the two sides. The one giving it has the whole picture; the ones receiving it can only see the last time.

The shape of costly obedience. It rarely announces itself as heroism. Much faithfulness looks exactly like that: a hospital visit that may be awkward, a conversation that may be costly, a return to a place where you were once hurt.

Should I take risks for Christ, or be prudent? Both, in their place. Prudence is not sin; Jesus himself withdrew when his hour had not come (10:40; 11:54), and he told his disciples to flee from one town to the next under persecution (Matthew 10:23). But prudence becomes sin when it is used to excuse disobedience. The question is not, is this safe? but, is this where he is going? If Christ calls you to a costly duty, to love someone difficult, to speak truth, to serve in a hard place, the danger is not a reason to refuse. And if he has not called you, there is no virtue in seeking danger for its own sake.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "Are there not twelve hours in the day? If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world. But if anyone walks in the night, he stumbles, because the light is not in him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are there not twelve hours in the day? The picture depends on a fact of life before street lighting. The daylight hours were counted as twelve, from sunrise to sunset, whatever the season, so the hours were longer in summer and shorter in winter. When the light went, work stopped, and a man walking a stony Judean track after dark would fall. So the claim is about allotted time. Jesus’ day is the appointed time of his ministry (9:4), and it cannot be cut short until it is finished. He is not saying the danger is imaginary. He is saying the clock is not kept by the men holding the stones.

He does not stumble. The one who walks in God’s will walks safely. The disciples’ safety on this road is not a matter of the route but of whom they are following.

The light is not in him. The picture slips from the sun outside to something carried inside, which is where this Gospel has been going since chapter 1. The one without the light stumbles (12:35).

The hard edge of the picture. Twelve hours is a fixed allowance. It cannot be shortened by enemies, and it cannot be extended by carefulness either. He is telling them that safety cannot be manufactured by choosing a different road, and that the only truly dangerous position is to be walking somewhere he is not going.

Does this mean nothing bad can happen to me if I obey God? No. It is not a promise of long life or freedom from harm. This man’s own twelve hours had only weeks left in them, and, by early tradition, many of the men listening would die violently for him. It is a promise that the ending is not in the hands of whoever is throwing the stones. Your days are written in God’s book (Psalm 139:16), and nothing can cut them short before he says. That frees you from two fears: the fear that your enemies control your life, and the fear that you must control it yourself by endless caution.
verseByVerse.note: The daylight hours were counted as twelve, from sunrise to sunset.

verseByVerse.quote: After saying these things, he said to them, "Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I go to awaken him." The disciples said to him, "Lord, if he has fallen asleep, he will recover."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Our friend Lazarus. Not my friend, which he might have said about a man the disciples barely knew. He includes them in the friendship before he tells them the man is dead.

Fallen asleep. Sleep was a common picture of death for believers (Matthew 9:24; Acts 7:60; 1 Thessalonians 4:13–14). The noun built from it is koimētērion, a sleeping place, and that is where our word cemetery comes from. Sleep is not a nicer word for extinction; it is a claim about what death now is for those who belong to him. Sleep is temporary, and it ends in the ordinary way: somebody says your name, as is about to happen at the mouth of a cave.

I go to awaken him. The language is domestic, the ordinary language of rousing someone in the morning: to him a resurrection is going in to wake somebody up.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the soul sleeps unconscious between death and resurrection, as some teach. Sleep describes the body’s rest and the certainty of waking. The believer’s spirit goes at once to be with Christ (Luke 23:43; Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8). The dead in Christ are conscious and at rest with him, waiting for the resurrection of the body (the Westminster Confession 32.1).

He will recover. They take it literally: sleep is a good sign in illness. They are sensible and slightly relieved: if he is sleeping, he is turning the corner, and there is no need to walk into Judea. Their literalism has a motive. It usually does.

What actually happens when a Christian dies? The body is buried and returns to dust, but the person, the soul, is immediately with Christ, made perfect in holiness, in conscious joy, awaiting the redemption of the body (Westminster 32.1; 1689 31.1). There is no purgatory and no unconscious waiting. Then, when Christ returns, the body will be raised, transformed and reunited with the soul, never to die again (1 Corinthians 15:42–44, 51–53). So when a believer dies, we may say truly that he has fallen asleep, and truly that he is with the Lord. Both are true, of the body and of the soul.
verseByVerse.note: Sleep was a common picture of death for believers.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Jesus had spoken of his death, but they thought that he meant taking rest in sleep. Then Jesus told them plainly, "Lazarus has died,
verseByVerse.commentary:
They thought he meant sleep. Another of John’s misunderstandings, and John records it in full, writing decades later, with no attempt to make the twelve look better. That is one of the small marks of an honest witness: an inventor of a founding story would have little reason to write his leaders like that.

Lazarus has died. The word is parrēsia: plainly, openly, without veiling. But sleep had been heard as getting better, and rather than let them travel to Bethany with a comfortable misunderstanding, he takes the comfort away and gives them the fact.

How should I speak about death, especially to children? Plainly first, then with hope. Do not let the tenderest words become an anaesthetic that leaves people confused. Children especially can be frightened by vague phrases: gone away, lost, gone to sleep, said without explanation. Say that the person has died, that their body has stopped working and will not work again in this life. Then give the hope, clearly: if they trusted Jesus, they are with him now, and he will raise their body one day. Jesus himself did it in that order. First the fact, then the promise. The sleep could be explained afterwards, and would mean something then.

verseByVerse.quote: "and for your sake I am glad that I was not there, so that you may believe. But let us go to him." So Thomas, called the Twin, said to his fellow disciples, "Let us also go, that we may die with him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Glad that I was not there. He does not say he is glad Lazarus died. He says he is glad he was absent, because his presence would have produced a healing, and a healing would have produced a smaller faith than what is now possible. The disciples already believed (2:11), but faith grows, and they will need more than they have for what is coming in Jerusalem.

In the flow. So that you may believe is the aim of the whole Gospel in miniature (20:31). Within days these men will watch him arrested and killed, and they will need to have seen him empty a grave before they see him laid in one.

Let us go to him. To him, though dead. Jesus speaks of a dead man as someone you can still go to, because to him the dead are not beyond reach.

Thomas, called the Twin. Thomas’s name means twin in Aramaic; Didymus is the Greek equivalent. But there is something twinned in the man himself all through this Gospel. He is the one who says the brave thing and the doubting thing, and both come from the same place: he will not pretend to a confidence he does not have.

That we may die with him. He is remembered for one sentence spoken in a locked room after the resurrection (20:24–25), and it has cost him his name in English. But this is the first time he speaks in the Gospel. He has concluded, reasonably, that going to Judea means execution, and he proposes that they go. That is not doubt. It is loyalty without hope, which is a rarer and harder thing than loyalty with it. He proposes the journey in a flat voice, expecting the worst, because he would rather die with Jesus than live without him.

Is it all right to follow Christ while I am full of doubts and fears? Yes. Jesus did not wait for Thomas to become cheerful before he let him come, and he did not wait for perfect faith before accepting it. He works with what is offered and refines it along the way, as he did with Thomas a few weeks later (20:27–28). What matters is not how confident you feel but where you are walking. Bring your doubts with you, tell him about them honestly, and keep going in the direction he is going. Many of the best saints have followed in a flat voice for long stretches.
verseByVerse.note: Thomas’s name means “twin” in Aramaic; Didymus is the Greek equivalent.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus came, he found that Lazarus had already been in the tomb four days. Bethany was near Jerusalem, about two miles off.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four days. Burial in that world was usually on the day of death; the body was washed, wrapped with spices and laid in a rock tomb within hours, because the climate allowed nothing else. So four days in the tomb is four days from death, and decay would have been well under way. There was also a popular Jewish belief, preserved in later rabbinic writings, that the soul lingered near the body for three days hoping to return, and departed on the fourth when the face became unrecognisable. That is probably why John gives the number twice, here and again in Martha’s objection at the tomb (v. 39). He is establishing that Lazarus was beyond any hope of revival.

About two miles off. Literally about fifteen stadia, well under an hour’s walk: close enough for mourners to come out from the city, and for whatever happened to be in the temple courts by evening. This sign will not be deniable or quiet, and for exactly those reasons it is the one that gets him killed.

Everything in public. Everything in this chapter happens in the open, on a road, before a crowd, at the mouth of a cave. Jesus stops outside the village (v. 30), because the sign was never only for them.

Could Lazarus simply have been in a coma? Not after four days in a sealed tomb, wrapped in linen, with spices, in that climate, without water. Everyone present had seen death and buried their dead with their own hands; Martha expected the smell of decay (v. 39). Nothing in the record suggests that the authorities, who had every reason to explain the event away, tried to; they plotted to kill Lazarus too (12:10–11). John tells the details precisely so that we will know what kind of event this was. It was not a recovery. It was a dead man called back to life.

On a Tuesday. Is there something in your life you have written off as four days dead: a relationship, a habit you cannot break, a person you have stopped praying for? Bring it back to him. Nothing is beyond his reach.
verseByVerse.note: After four days there could be no doubt that he was dead. The ESV notes that the distance is literally fifteen stadia.

verseByVerse.quote: and many of the Jews had come to Martha and Mary to console them concerning their brother. So when Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went and met him, but Mary remained seated in the house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To console them. Mourning for a close relative lasted seven days, with friends and neighbours coming to sit with the family, weep, and bring food. These visitors came from Jerusalem, an hour’s walk, and they are still there on the fourth day, which suggests the family was well known. The sisters are not grieving in private. Every word either of them says to Jesus in this chapter is said in front of an audience, and so is everything he says back.

What the mourners were doing. Jewish consolation was a duty, not a social call. The mourners sat with the bereaved, said little, and stayed. Later Jewish custom was not to speak until the grieving person spoke first, a discipline the friends of Job kept for seven days (Job 2:13); it was when they began to answer him with explanations that everything went wrong. They came, they stayed four days, and when Mary got up they followed her so that she would not cry alone.

Martha went and met him. Martha, the active one, goes out; Mary, perhaps more crushed, stays seated, as mourners did. One of them needed to move and one of them could not, and both receive everything. Martha meets him first and receives the greatest sentence in the chapter. Mary meets him second and receives his tears. He does not have one way of dealing with grieving people.

What should I say to someone who is grieving? Often very little, at first. Your presence matters more than your words; the friends of Job did best when they were silent. Say that you are sorry, use the name of the person who has died, and do not hurry to explain the loss or rush to the hope. Avoid clichés that make the grief smaller. Offer practical help: meals, errands, company on the hard evenings. And keep coming after the funeral, when most people stop. When the time is right, and especially if the one who died was a believer, the hope of the resurrection is the greatest comfort there is. But let it be given as a gift, not as a reason to stop crying.

On a Tuesday. Christ came to grieving Bethany in person, and he has come to you; go in his name and sit with those who grieve. Find someone who lost a loved one months ago and whom everyone else has stopped visiting, and go this week.

For worship. Many came from Jerusalem to console, but none of them could do anything about the cave. He is the God of all comfort (2 Corinthians 1:3) walking in a body toward a grave, who does not sit beside death and sympathise with it but has come to overturn it.
verseByVerse.note: Mourning for a close relative lasted seven days, with friends coming to console the family.

verseByVerse.quote: Martha said to Jesus, "Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. But even now I know that whatever you ask from God, God will give you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you had been here. Grief, and perhaps a note of complaint. Mary will say exactly the same sentence in verse 32, word for word, which probably tells you what had been said in that house for four days, in the kitchen and in the night and to every new visitor, until it had worn a groove.

What Jesus does with it. He does not point out, though it was probably true, that he could not have arrived in time. He lets both of them say it, twice, and answers neither with the arithmetic. He answers them with himself.

Even now. She does not quite dare to ask for resurrection; verse 39 shows she did not expect it, when she objects to the stone being moved. What she has is something less specific and more lasting: a conviction that this man’s access to God is not affected by the fact that it is too late. That is a good place to pray from, and it is available to people who have run out of requests. Her faith is real, but not yet complete. She thinks of Jesus as one who asks God, not yet as the one who is himself the life.

Is it wrong to say to God, if you had been here? No. It is honest, and God would rather have your honest grief than polite silence. The psalms are full of it: why have you forsaken me? how long, O LORD? (Psalm 13:1; 22:1). Martha said it to Jesus’ face, and he did not rebuke her. What matters is where you say it. Martha brought her complaint to him, not away from him, and then she added but even now. Lament that is spoken to God is a form of faith. The danger is not in asking why, but in turning your back and refusing to wait for his answer.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "Your brother will rise again." Martha said to him, "I know that he will rise again in the resurrection on the last day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your brother will rise again. The words are deliberately open: now, or at the end. It was the standard consolation at a Jewish funeral, and Martha takes it so. He lets her, and waits to see what she does with it.

On the last day. Martha’s answer is entirely correct; she is often treated as having missed the point, and she has not. Pharisees and most Jews believed in a resurrection at the end of the age, based on texts like Daniel 12:2, many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, and Isaiah 26:19. Martha holds the orthodox hope, and Jesus never suggests she is wrong.

The gap the doctrine does not cross. The doctrine is intact, but it is scheduled for the end of the world, and her brother is in a cave a short walk away. That is exactly the gap Jesus is about to close, and the way he closes it is not by moving the last day nearer. It is by telling her that the thing she is waiting for is a person, and he is standing in front of her.

What exactly is the resurrection on the last day? When Christ returns, all the dead will be raised bodily: those who have done good to the resurrection of life, those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment (5:28–29). Believers will be raised with bodies that are real, recognisable and their own, yet transformed: imperishable, glorious, powerful, fitted for the new creation (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). It is not the soul escaping the body but the whole person, body and soul, made new. The body you bury is not discarded. It is sown like a seed, and what rises will be more fully you than you have ever been.
verseByVerse.note: Pharisees and most Jews believed in a resurrection at the end of the age.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live, and everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die. Do you believe this?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am the resurrection and the life. This is the fifth I am saying, and the one most often read aloud at funerals. Martha has just placed resurrection at the end of history. Jesus takes the whole doctrine and places it in himself. The thing she is waiting for on the last day is not an event he attends. It is who he is. The power that will raise the dead at the end is present in him now.

In the flow. Jesus has said this before: the dead will hear his voice and live, now and on the last day (5:21, 25, 28–29). What Martha hears in the road is the sermon of chapter 5, spoken to one grieving woman by name.

Though he die. The two halves are not saying the same thing twice. This first half is for the dead. Though he die concedes physical death flatly, but it is not the end of the sentence: believers who die will live, raised by him (5:28–29). This is the resurrection.

Shall never die. This second half is for the living, and it is the life. “Never die” means never die the true death, separation from God (8:51). A believer has that knowing already, and death cannot interrupt it: the friendship with God begun on earth carries straight on through the grave. Both halves are needed, because a mourner is standing between them: one brother dead, one sister alive, and a promise that covers each of them.

What it does not mean. This verse is quoted badly in both directions. It does not promise that Christians will not die physically; Lazarus dies again, and so does everyone in the story. And it does not shrink to a metaphor about living on in memory or influence. The man saying it is about to show what he means by shouting into a cave.

Do you believe this? The question is put to Martha, and to every reader. Not, do you believe in a resurrection? but, do you believe this, about me? Four words, put to a woman whose brother has been dead four days, before anything has been fixed. He does not raise Lazarus and then ask. He asks first, with the stone still in place and the smell still expected, and requires her to answer on nothing but his word. The question is not whether the doctrine is believed in general. Martha believed it in general, and said so, correctly, one verse earlier. The question is whether it is believed of a particular person on a particular day when it has already seemed to fail. That is a different question, and it is the only one he asks.

Is this not just wishful thinking, the kind of thing people say at funerals? Graveside words cost nothing, and if this were only a sentence the charge might stand. But Jesus does not leave it as a comforting idea. He stakes it on a public event, a named man four days dead, in front of a crowd that included his enemies, and soon afterwards on his own body, in a tomb the authorities had every reason to keep sealed. Wishful thinking does not usually volunteer for that kind of test. A sceptic may answer that the story itself was invented; that is a fair question about whether the Gospels are reliable, and worth weighing on its own ground, but the claim was at least made in public, while people who could check it were alive. Paul put it bluntly: if Christ has not been raised, our faith is futile and we are still in our sins (1 Corinthians 15:17). The Christian hope has always been willing to stand or fall on whether a grave was empty.

What about those who die without believing in him? The promise is to whoever believes in me, and Scripture does not offer it to anyone else. Those who die outside Christ will also be raised, but to the resurrection of judgment (5:29), and they will face conscious, eternal punishment, separated from the life that is in him (Matthew 25:46). That is a solemn truth, and it should make us earnest, not cold. It is why Jesus asked Martha the question, and why we must ask it of others while there is time. And it is why we can leave the dead, whom we cannot judge, in the hands of the God who always does right (Genesis 18:25), while we plead with the living.

For worship. He said I am before the stone was moved. Every grave of a believer now lies inside this sentence, and on the last day every one of them will open at his word.
verseByVerse.note: This is the fifth of Jesus’ “I am” sayings in John.

verseByVerse.quote: She said to him, "Yes, Lord; I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who is coming into the world." When she had said this, she went and called her sister Mary, saying in private, "The Teacher is here and is calling for you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yes, Lord; I believe. This confession is larger than it looks. John tells us at the end of his book exactly why he wrote it: these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name (20:31). Martha says it almost word for word. In Matthew it is Peter who says it and is called blessed (Matthew 16:16); here it is Martha, and her confession is as great as Peter’s (6:69).

The words of her confession. “I believe” is in the perfect tense: I have come to believe, and I still believe. She believes who he is before she sees what he will do. That is the order of grace: confession of Christ comes before the experience of his full power.

Who makes the great confessions in John. They are not made by the men who run the temple. They are made by a Samaritan woman with five husbands behind her, an excommunicated beggar who had been blind, and now a woman at the edge of a village who has just told him he arrived too late.

She called her sister. Privately, perhaps to avoid alerting the mourners, some of whom may have been hostile to Jesus. Martha gives her sister the chance to go to him without an audience.

The Teacher is calling for you. She knows her sister is sitting in a dark house and will not come for an invitation but will come for a summons. He calls each one personally, and Martha, who has just met him, does the first thing a believer does: she brings someone else to him.

Is it enough to believe the right things about Jesus? Martha’s confession is right in every word, and it is more than a list of facts. To believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, in the sense John means, is to trust yourself to him, as Martha did with her brother in a tomb. The devils believe facts and tremble (James 2:19). Faith says yes, Lord, and leans its whole weight on him. So hold the truth about Christ carefully, because it matters; and make sure it is not just in your head but is the ground you stand on when everything else has given way.

On a Tuesday. Who do you know who is sitting in a dark house, too weighed down to come out on their own? Go and tell them, gently and in private if need be, that the Teacher is here and is calling for them.

verseByVerse.quote: And when she heard it, she rose quickly and went to him. Now Jesus had not yet come into the village, but was still in the place where Martha had met him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She rose quickly. Mary has been in that house for four days receiving visitors, and she has not gone out to meet him. What he does say is that the moment she is told he is asking for her, she is on her feet. At his call, she goes at once.

In the place where Martha had met him. He had not moved. He waits outside, perhaps to meet the sisters away from the crowd, or near the tomb, which would be outside the village. He stands in a road outside a village where a family is grieving, sends for one of them, and stays put until she comes.

Inside the sound of it. What he will do there next is weep. Professional mourners, flute players and wailing women, would have been audible from some distance. He is waiting at the edge of the village inside the sound of grief.

verseByVerse.quote: When the Jews who were with her in the house, consoling her, saw Mary rise quickly and go out, they followed her, supposing that she was going to the tomb to weep there. Now when Mary came to where Jesus was and saw him, she fell at his feet, saying to him, "Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They followed her. The mourners follow Mary on a wrong assumption, made out of ordinary kindness, and it puts the entire crowd of Jerusalem witnesses at the graveside for what happens next. They are wrong about her destination and right about the direction, and they arrive as witnesses to something none of them came for. And that is how the raising of Lazarus acquired the witness list that will, within days, get Jesus condemned.

She fell at his feet. The difference from her sister is in the body rather than the words. Martha met him standing and talked theology with him in the road. Mary fell at his feet. And it is where she always is. Mary is at Jesus’ feet listening (Luke 10:39), grieving here, worshipping (12:3).

The same words. Mary says no more; she cannot say it upright. Martha gets a dialogue, a question and one of the great sayings of the Gospel. Mary gets one sentence, on the ground. What she receives in return is not an argument. It is his tears, which is what she needed and what an argument would not have been.

Is one way of grieving more spiritual than another? No. Martha talked and Mary wept, and Jesus received both with the same love, and neither is treated as having grieved wrongly. Some believers grieve with questions and activity; others grieve in silence and tears; most of us do both at different times. Do not measure your faith by how composed you are, and do not measure anyone else’s by how they cope. What matters is that both sisters brought their grief to his feet, or to his face. He meets each in the way each needs.

For worship. He did not ask Mary for a confession before he wept with her. The Lord who receives the speechless was himself led like a lamb that is silent before its shearers (Isaiah 53:7), and in Gethsemane he too fell on the ground (Mark 14:35). He knows from the inside the grief that cannot stand upright.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus saw her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her also weeping, he was deeply moved in his spirit and greatly troubled. And he said, "Where have you laid him?" They said to him, "Lord, come and see."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Deeply moved in his spirit. “Weeping” (klaiō) is loud wailing, the public lament a Jewish funeral expected. The word behind “deeply moved” (embrimaomai) carries a sense of anger or indignation; the ESV’s margin gives it as he was indignant in his spirit (also v. 38). Jesus is angry. “Greatly troubled” (etaraxen heauton) is literally he troubled himself: a deep inner agitation, which he does not merely suffer but takes up.

Angry at what? Not at Mary, who has done nothing but fall at his feet. Not at the mourners, who are behaving exactly as neighbours should. Some have suggested he is angry at their unbelief, but the text gives no sign of it, and the reading requires importing a rebuke that never comes. The answer that fits is death itself, the last enemy (1 Corinthians 15:26), and the devil who brought it, and the ruin sin has caused in God’s world. He is standing in front of a family destroyed by the thing he came to destroy, and he is about to walk to a cave and be shown what four days does to somebody who was loved. As he faces his friend’s grave, he faces the power he came to break.

God is not serene about death. The one who made the world is standing in a village road, indignant at what has been done to it. Death is not natural, not friendly, not simply part of the circle of life. It is an intruder, and the Son of God is angry at it.

Where have you laid him? Then he asks the last thing anybody expects from one who knows all things. He is not asking for directions. He is doing what a man does when he arrives at a house of mourning: he asks to be taken to the grave.

Lord, come and see. Almost the words Jesus used to the first disciples (1:39), and exactly those of Philip to Nathanael (1:46). He goes.

Is it right to be angry at death, or even at God, when someone dies? It is right to be angry at death, because Jesus was. Death is an enemy, and you do not have to pretend otherwise. Anger at God is different, and must be handled honestly. Bring it to him rather than nursing it, as the psalmists did. He can bear your raw words, and he will not despise them. But do not let it settle into a grudge that accuses him of evil, because the one who stood at Lazarus’s grave was not the author of death but its enemy, and he has already gone to war against it on your behalf.
verseByVerse.note: The words behind “deeply moved” carry a sense of anger or indignation — at death itself and the grief it brings.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus wept. So the Jews said, "See how he loved him!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus wept. The shortest verse in most English Bibles hides a distinction. The mourners in verse 33 are weeping with klaiō, the word for loud lamentation, the public noise of a funeral. What Jesus does is a different verb, found nowhere else in the New Testament. Dakryō means to shed tears. So the picture is probably not a man joining a wail, but a man in a road, surrounded by noise, with tears running down his face.

When it happens. Not at the news; he received that a day’s journey away and stayed where he was two more days. Not at the tomb. Here, at the sight of Mary on the ground and the crowd behind her. What breaks him is not the fact of the death but the sight of what it had done to people he loved.

He weeps anyway. He knows what is going to happen; very soon the man will walk out of that cave, and Jesus is the one who is going to do it. Why weep? Because he truly loves, and truly grieves with those who grieve (Romans 12:15). Because death is a real evil. Because he is truly man. That disposes of the idea, common and quietly cruel, that grief is a failure of faith, that a Christian who really believed in the resurrection would not be undone by a funeral. Here is the resurrection and the life, in person, minutes from proving it, in tears. If knowing the outcome were enough to stop the crying, his would have stopped.

See how he loved him! Some of the mourners read the tears correctly.

Two natures in one chapter. He could have raised the man from across the Jordan with a word, as he had healed the official’s son at a distance (4:50). Instead he walked a day’s journey to stand in the middle of it, let it reach him, and wept in front of a crowd. This short verse answers the oldest suspicion about God, that he is untouched by grief.

If Jesus is God, how could he weep? Because he is also truly man. The eternal Son took a full human nature, body and soul, and in that human nature he felt real sorrow, real tears, real grief. God in his own divine being is not overwhelmed by emotion or changed by what happens to him; he is unchanging and perfect. But that does not make him cold. The tears of Jesus show us the heart of God in a form we can see, a love that is moved toward us. When you are grieving, you do not pray to a God who has never felt grief. You pray to a High Priest who can sympathise with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15), because he wept at a grave.

How long is it right to grieve? There is no fixed limit. Grief for someone you loved can return in waves for years, and that is not a failure. Christians grieve, but not as others do who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). The difference is not that our grief is shorter but that it is held inside a larger hope. If grief has become despair, so that you cannot function, cannot pray, or no longer want to live, please tell someone: a pastor, a trusted friend, a doctor. That is not weakness of faith. It is the kind of burden God gives his people to bear together.
verseByVerse.note: This is the shortest verse in the English Bible.

verseByVerse.quote: But some of them said, "Could not he who opened the eyes of the blind man also have kept this man from dying?" Then Jesus, deeply moved again, came to the tomb. It was a cave, and a stone lay against it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But some of them said, Could not he who opened the eyes of the blind man also have kept this man from dying? Their question deserves to be taken at full strength. Look at what they concede in order to ask it. They accept the miracle of chapter 9, a couple of miles away, without argument. Their difficulty is not whether he can. It is why he did not. John does not tell us the tone. It could be a cynical taunt, and it could be bewilderment, and the words allow both. And that is exactly where a great many people are, and it is a more painful place than unbelief. Doubting God’s power is one kind of trouble. Believing in it completely and standing at a graveside is another.

Deeply moved again. He does not answer the question. Nobody at the tomb is told why the two days happened; only the disciples had been told (vv. 4, 15). What he does instead is grow indignant again, the same word as verse 33, perhaps at their unbelief too, and walk to the tomb. Here the answer is a man walking toward a cave with tears still on his face and anger in his heart, about to do something about it.

A cave, and a stone. Tombs were caves or rock chambers, with a large stone across the entrance to keep out animals and robbers. The stone will turn up again within weeks, at a different tomb, rolled away.

Why does God not explain my suffering? Often he does not, and Scripture is honest about it. He did not explain to Job, or to the crowd at Bethany. But he did something better than explain: he came. The answer to the question why is often not a reason but a presence, God coming to where the grief is and acting in a way that transforms the question. You may not know in this life why it happened. You can know who is with you in it, and you can know the end of the story: resurrection, and every tear wiped away. Faith is not having every answer. It is trusting the one who walks to the tomb.
verseByVerse.note: Tombs were caves or rock chambers, with a large stone across the entrance.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said, "Take away the stone." Martha, the sister of the dead man, said to him, "Lord, by this time there will be an odor, for he has been dead four days." Jesus said to her, "Did I not tell you that if you believed you would see the glory of God?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Take away the stone. Jesus could move it with a word; he tells them to do it. God often uses human obedience in his works, and what he asks here is not faith to raise the dead but strength to move a stone. That division of labour holds everywhere: obedience is generally something quite ordinary, done before there is any evidence it will matter.

The sister of the dead man. A quiet, painful touch. The man has been Lazarus all chapter. Here, at the mouth of the cave, he becomes the dead man.

By this time there will be an odor. Martha’s objection is among the most human sentences in the chapter, and it should not be treated as a lapse. Anyone who has believed something on Sunday and not managed it on Tuesday has the whole of Christian experience in Martha. And she is right. Bodies were not embalmed; spices were used, but did not stop decay, and after four days in that climate it was well under way. She is protecting her brother’s body, the last thing left to protect. Her faith of verse 27 is real, but she cannot imagine what Jesus will do.

Did I not tell you that if you believed you would see the glory of God? His reply is a reminder rather than a rebuke. He does not argue with the chemistry. He recalls a promise: the glory of God of verse 4, which the messenger had presumably carried back, and the do you believe this? of verses 25–26. Believe, and you will see. In this Gospel, faith comes before sight. And in this Gospel the glory of God has a face: we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father (1:14). What Martha is about to see at the mouth of the cave is not a general display of divine power. It is the glory of God shining in the man standing beside her, who has just told her to open the grave.

Does God need my faith before he can act? Does my weak faith stop him? God is not limited by our faith; he raised Lazarus, who had no faith at all, being dead. Faith is not a power that makes God able. It is the empty hand that receives what he gives, and the eye that sees his glory when he shows it. Martha’s faith was weak at that moment, and Jesus did not cancel the miracle. He called her back to his word. So do not try to manufacture enough faith to earn an answer. Look at his promise, take the next step of obedience, roll the stone, and leave the power to him.

On a Tuesday. What stone is Christ telling you to move? Perhaps a confession you have put off, a reconciliation you think is hopeless, a habit of prayer you abandoned because nothing seemed to happen. Your obedience will be as mixed as Martha’s, but it was never meant to carry you: Christ obeyed perfectly in your place, his obedience is counted as yours, and his Spirit now in you gives the strength for the next stone.
verseByVerse.note: Bodies were not embalmed; after four days decay was well under way.

verseByVerse.quote: So they took away the stone. And Jesus lifted up his eyes and said, "Father, I thank you that you have heard me. I knew that you always hear me, but I said this on account of the people standing around, that they may believe that you sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He lifted up his eyes. Jews commonly prayed looking upward (17:1; Psalm 123:1). The stone is gone, the smell is expected, the crowd is waiting, and the first thing he does is look to his Father.

Father, I thank you that you have heard me. The tense is past: he gives thanks before the miracle, for a prayer already answered, which means the asking happened earlier, unrecorded, perhaps when he first heard of Lazarus’s illness. The two days beyond the Jordan were not idle.

I knew that you always hear me. No one else in Scripture could make this claim. Elijah on Carmel prayed, answer me, O LORD, answer me (1 Kings 18:37): a man hoping. This is a Son stating a fact about his home.

On account of the people. He tells the crowd, out loud, in the middle of a prayer, that the prayer is partly for their benefit. He is saying openly that he does not need to speak in order to be heard, and is speaking so that they will know where the power is about to come from. Without the prayer, the raising would prove the wrong thing. A man who shouts into a tomb and gets a result looks like a wonder-worker, and the district had seen those. The prayer establishes what the sign is for: that the miracle comes from the Father, and that the Father sent him.

Should I thank God before I see the answer? What if the answer is no? Yes, give thanks, but be clear what you are thanking him for. Jesus knew the Father’s will; we often do not. So we thank God not for an outcome we have decided on, but for the certainty that he hears us, that he is good, and that he will do what is best (Philippians 4:6–7; Romans 8:28). That kind of thanks is never misplaced, because even when the answer is no or not yet, he has heard, and his answer is love. Thanking God in advance is not a technique to secure results. It is trust speaking before it sees.
verseByVerse.note: Jews commonly prayed looking upward.

verseByVerse.quote: When he had said these things, he cried out with a loud voice, "Lazarus, come out." The man who had died came out, his hands and feet bound with linen strips, and his face wrapped with a cloth. Jesus said to them, "Unbind him, and let him go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lazarus, come out. The word is kraugazō, a shout, used of a crowd bellowing (19:6). He has just prayed quietly to his Father; to the dead man he shouts a command. An old saying, often credited to Augustine, has it that if Jesus had not named Lazarus, all the dead would have come out. And the name is the whole of it. This is the shepherd of the previous chapter who calls his own sheep by name (10:3), doing exactly that, into a cave. It anticipates the last day: an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out (5:28–29). One tomb, one name, on a Judean afternoon, as a demonstration of what he will do to every grave.

The man who had died came out. John does not dramatise it.

Bound with linen strips. Bodies were wrapped in strips of linen, with a separate cloth for the face, and spices between the strips. Compare Jesus’ own grave clothes, left neatly behind (20:6–7). Lazarus comes out still wrapped; Jesus will rise leaving his behind. Lazarus will die again; Jesus will never die again (Romans 6:9). This is a resuscitation, a return to mortal life; Jesus’ resurrection will be the first of the new creation.

Unbind him, and let him go. Again, others help: Christ alone gives life, and his people help the newly living out of their grave clothes.

A picture of salvation. We were dead in sins (Ephesians 2:1–5), no more able to respond than Lazarus. This is regeneration, God’s effectual call: the dead hear and live (5:25). Regeneration means being born again (3:3–8): God giving new life to a heart that was spiritually dead, so that it begins to love and trust him. The effectual call means a call that does what it says. The gospel invitation goes out to everyone, but when God calls his own by name, as Jesus called Lazarus, the call itself creates the answer. Lazarus did not decide to live and then hear. He heard because the voice made him alive.

Why do Matthew, Mark and Luke say nothing about it? It is a fair question, and it deserves a straight answer, because it is the objection most often raised against this chapter. If a man four days dead walked out of a tomb outside Jerusalem, and it decided the authorities to kill Jesus (v. 53), why do the other Gospels not mention it? Part of the answer is how the four books are shaped. The first three concentrate on Galilee and bring Jesus to Jerusalem once, at the end; John is the one who fills in the Judean ministry, the feasts and the repeated visits to the city. And none of them is trying to be complete; John says so twice (20:30–31; 21:25). Nor were they shy of raisings: Mark and Luke both record the raising of Jairus’s daughter, and Luke tells of the widow’s son at Nain. There is a further suggestion worth weighing. The next chapter tells us that the chief priests planned to kill Lazarus too, because on account of him many were believing (12:10–11). A man in that position, living a short walk from the temple, would not be helped by having his name published across the empire. The earlier Gospels leave several people anonymous whom John alone names: it is John who tells us that the disciple with the sword was Peter and the servant who lost an ear was Malchus (18:10). John writes last, a generation on, when those who might have suffered for being named were beyond harm. That may be the whole explanation or part of it; either way it is a better answer than the assumption that a story this size was invented late.

What did Lazarus experience in those four days? Scripture does not say, and that silence is deliberate. Lazarus is given no story to tell. What we know of death, we know from Christ’s word, not from those who claim to have returned: if they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead (Luke 16:31). And for the believer, what we are told is enough: to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). So be wary of books and testimonies that claim to describe heaven or hell from a near-death experience. They may be sincere, but they are not Scripture, and they often contradict it. We do not need them. We have the word of the one who has the keys of death and Hades (Revelation 1:18).

What does unbinding look like in a church? Nobody in that crowd could have called Lazarus out. Every one of them could pick at a knot. The first thing the community is asked to do, in the presence of resurrection, is to get the grave clothes off somebody who is already alive. New believers often come out of the tomb still wrapped in old habits, fears, addictions, shame and confused ideas. The church’s work is patient: teaching them the word, welcoming them to the Lord’s Table after baptism, walking with them, praying, bearing burdens, and refusing to be shocked by the smell of the grave on them. We cannot give life. We can help someone who has been given it to walk freely.

For worship. The voice that called Lazarus called you from spiritual death, and one day it will call your body from the grave. On the last day the same voice will sound over every grave of every believer, and the whole sleeping church will rise.
verseByVerse.note: Bodies were wrapped in strips of linen, with a separate cloth over the face.

parallels.desc: all who are in the tombs will hear his voice

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 45–57 — The Decision to Kill Jesus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The council meets in alarm, Caiaphas urges that one man die for the people, and John explains what God meant by his words. From then on they plot Jesus’ death; he withdraws to Ephraim, and as Passover nears the crowds wonder whether he will come, while the authorities order his arrest.
verseByVerse.theology: Caiaphas’ calculation, sacrifice one man to save the nation, is both cynical politics and unconscious prophecy. The high priest spoke better than he knew (v. 51). The death he plots to keep the council’s power is the death that will save God’s people, not only in Israel but the scattered children of God throughout the world (v. 52). The cross is always more than its perpetrators intend, and exactly what God intends.
verseByVerse.examples: The council’s decision carries out what God had planned beforehand (Acts 4:27–28). The leaders plot what God has purposed, and the victim goes willingly to what they intend as murder and he intends as sacrifice. God works through human wickedness without being stained by it, and nowhere is that plainer than at the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: Many of the Jews therefore, who had come with Mary and had seen what he did, believed in him, but some of them went to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many believed in him. The sign leads to faith, as it was meant to (20:31).

Some went to the Pharisees. The same event, the same crowd, and two responses that could not be further apart. That is a plain answer to the idea that a sufficiently impressive miracle would settle the question of faith for everybody. This was the climax of the signs, done before witnesses, on a man they had buried themselves, and the reporters did not deny it. The evidence was accepted, and acted against. Why would anyone do that? Because believing would have cost them something they loved more, as the council is about to say aloud: their place and their nation (v. 48). The heart often has a say in what the mind will accept, in believers and sceptics alike, though that is not to say every honest doubt is a hidden refusal. It is also why, in the end, the remedy is not more evidence but a new heart.

Neither will they be convinced. Abraham said it in the parable: if they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead (Luke 16:31). And then a man named Lazarus did rise from the dead, and they were not convinced, and within days they were planning to kill him too (12:10). John also says simply that some of them went to the Pharisees, without saying why. It is possible some went in genuine excitement, thinking the authorities would want to know. What the authorities did with the news was not necessarily what the messengers intended, and that is its own small warning about how the machinery of a great wrong is often fed by people who thought they were being helpful.

If miracles do not convince people, what will convince my unbelieving friend? Only God himself, by his Spirit opening the eyes of the heart (2 Corinthians 4:6). That is not a reason for despair but for prayer. The Spirit uses means: the word of the gospel, the testimony of what Christ has done, the love of his people, honest answers to honest questions. So keep telling your friend what Christ has done, as the believing mourners did, live in a way that adorns it, and pray specifically that God will give new life. Arguments do not raise the dead. The voice of Christ does, and it is heard through the gospel you speak.

verseByVerse.quote: So the chief priests and the Pharisees gathered the council and said, "What are we to do? For this man performs many signs. If we let him go on like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The council. The council (synedrion), the Sanhedrin: the supreme Jewish court, traditionally of seventy-one members, led by the high priest.

And said, What are we to do? For this man performs many signs. There is exasperation in their question. The council has been convened because something has got out of hand. And they do not deny the miracles. They cannot. In closed session, among themselves, with no crowd to satisfy, the highest court in Israel states as a fact that the miracles are real. Everything they do from here is done with that on the record. The problem was never the evidence.

Everyone will believe in him. They are describing, as the disaster to be prevented, the exact outcome the Gospel was written to produce. John’s stated purpose is that his readers may believe (20:31). The council’s stated fear is that everyone will.

Our place and our nation. “Our place” means the temple, and perhaps their own positions. The Romans allowed Jewish self-rule as long as there was order, and a popular messianic uprising could end it. And the terrible irony is that they were right about the outcome and wrong about the cause. They killed Jesus to save the temple and the nation, and in AD 70 the Romans came and destroyed both. John has already told us what they could not see. When Jesus spoke of the temple being destroyed and raised in three days, he was speaking about the temple of his body (2:19–21). The council moved to save a building by destroying the true temple, the place where God now dwells with men, and on the third day God raised it up.

Can churches fall into the same trap? Yes, and often. Whenever a church or ministry protects its reputation, its building, its income or its leaders at the cost of truth, it is speaking the council’s language. The worst form is when abuse is hidden to protect the institution. That is never acceptable: victims must be heard and protected, wrongdoing reported to the proper authorities, and the truth told, whatever it costs the church’s name. The church belongs to Christ, not to us, and he does not need us to protect his reputation by sin. A church that loses its place for the sake of righteousness has lost nothing.

For worship. The council feared that everyone would believe in him, and the Lord has been granting their fear for two thousand years, in every tongue under heaven. He who sits in the heavens laughs at such counsels (Psalm 2:4), and makes the very council called against his Anointed serve his Anointed’s glory.
verseByVerse.note: “Our place” means the temple. The leaders feared a messianic movement would bring Roman retaliation — as happened in AD 70.

verseByVerse.quote: But one of them, Caiaphas, who was high priest that year, said to them, "You know nothing at all. Nor do you understand that it is better for you that one man should die for the people, not that the whole nation should perish."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Caiaphas, high priest that year. Caiaphas was high priest from about AD 18 to 36, an unusually long term, kept in office by the Romans, which tells you he was good at exactly this. His father-in-law Annas had been high priest before him and was still powerful (18:13). And John’s phrase “that year” has puzzled readers, since the office was not annual. John says it three times (here, v. 51, and 18:13), and the sense is almost certainly not that it rotated but that it was that year, the year everything turned on.

You know nothing at all. Nor do you understand that it is better for you that one man should die for the people, not that the whole nation should perish. Caiaphas opens with contempt for his own council, rude and arrogant in a style an ancient historian thought typical of Sadducees. Then comes political calculation: sacrifice one to save many. He means: kill Jesus before the Romans kill us all. Nobody at that table asks whether the man is guilty of anything. It is the oldest political arithmetic there is: an acceptable cost, a regrettable necessity, one life against many. It is always framed as responsibility, and it is always somebody else who pays.

For the people. One man should die hyper, on behalf of, in place of, the people. It is the exact word Jesus used of himself in chapter 10, of the shepherd laying down his life for the sheep (10:11), and a word Paul often uses of the atonement. The high priest of Israel, arguing for a judicial murder, reaches instinctively for the vocabulary of substitutionary sacrifice. He is a priest. It is the language he has.
verseByVerse.note: Caiaphas was high priest from about AD 18 to 36; “that year” means that fateful year.

verseByVerse.quote: He did not say this of his own accord, but being high priest that year he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the children of God who are scattered abroad.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He prophesied. John is claiming that God spoke through a man who was at that moment arranging a murder, and not despite his office but through it. God spoke through Caiaphas without his knowing it, as he spoke through Balaam (Numbers 23–24). His function was to speak for God to the people and for the people to God, and on the one occasion in the Gospels when Caiaphas exercises it, he does so accurately and without the faintest idea what he is saying. That does not make Caiaphas a good man or excuse anything. It says that God’s purposes are not hostage to the character of the people through whom they run. God can speak even through wicked men, and overrule their evil for good (Genesis 50:20; Acts 4:27–28).

That Jesus would die for the nation. Caiaphas meant a political substitute. God meant a saving substitute: on the cross Christ took the punishment sin deserves himself, in the place of his people, so that they will never bear it (Isaiah 53:5–6; 2 Corinthians 5:21).

To gather into one. John finishes the sentence Caiaphas started. Caiaphas meant saving the Jewish nation from Rome; John says not the nation only, and not from Rome, and the gathering runs to the ends of the earth. “The children of God scattered abroad” are most naturally the elect among the Gentiles, the other sheep of 10:16. The very next chapter shows the first of them arriving, when Greeks come asking to see Jesus (12:20–21) and he answers that, lifted up, he will draw all people to himself (12:32). His death is not a general provision but a purposeful gathering, and the verb is gather into one. The scattering is what sin did at Babel and what exile did to Israel; the gathering is what the cross undoes. The high priest of the old covenant pronounced the terms of the new one, out loud, in council, and voted for it.

Does God still speak through people like this today? God is sovereign over every word spoken by every human being, and he can overrule even the words of unbelievers for his purposes. But this was a unique moment, tied to the office of high priest at the climax of redemption. It does not mean we should look for new revelations from God in the words of the people around us. God’s revelation is complete in his Son and his written word (Hebrews 1:1–2; the Westminster Confession 1.1, 1.6; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 1.1, 1.6). What this verse teaches us is not to seek new messages, but to trust that no plot, no wicked decision and no cynical politician is outside his control.

parallels.desc: I will gather yet others

verseByVerse.quote: So from that day on they made plans to put him to death. Jesus therefore no longer walked openly among the Jews, but went from there to the region near the wilderness, to a town called Ephraim, and there he stayed with the disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From that day on. John dates it. There had been hostility for a long time and stones twice, but the decision is taken here, as a formal resolution of the council, and everything from this point is the working out of it. And what turned them was not a blasphemy but a resurrection: the last straw was an act of pure kindness to a family in Bethany.

In the flow. With verse 53 the Gospel turns a corner. Now the seventh sign produces the formal decision to kill him, and from here everything moves toward that hour: the anointing for burial, the entry into Jerusalem, and the Greeks whose request makes him say the hour has come (12:23).

No longer openly. His hour is close, but not yet, and the phrase reverses everything so far. From here to the entry into Jerusalem, he moves quietly. It is the first time in the Gospel that his public ministry has an after. And this is not fear. He has walked into Judea twice knowing what was waiting, and he will walk in again soon and let them take him. What he will not do is let them set the date. There is a Passover coming, and he intends to die at it, and not before.

A town called Ephraim. The town of Ephraim was probably north-east of Jerusalem, on the edge of the wilderness that drops toward the Jordan valley. John notes the wilderness deliberately. It is where the Baptist worked, and where Israel was formed before the great crossing.

He stayed with the disciples. Not preaching, not travelling, not doing anything John thinks worth recording: before the last week, a stretch of quiet, in a small town on the edge of the desert, with twelve men who did not know what was coming, and a Master who knew all of it.
verseByVerse.note: The town of Ephraim was probably north-east of Jerusalem, on the edge of the wilderness.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Passover of the Jews was at hand, and many went up from the country to Jerusalem before the Passover to purify themselves. They were looking for Jesus and saying to one another as they stood in the temple, "What do you think? That he will not come to the feast at all?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the Passover of the Jews was at hand. The third Passover in John (2:13; 6:4), the one at which Jesus will die as the true Passover Lamb (1:29; 19:36).

To purify themselves. The purification John mentions was a real and demanding business. Pilgrims came up early, a week or more, because anyone who had become ceremonially unclean needed time to be cleansed before he could eat the Passover (Numbers 9:6–12; 2 Chronicles 30:17–18). Contact with a corpse was a common cause, and the ritual took seven days (Numbers 19:11–12). Those laws were not fussiness. They taught Israel that God is holy, that death and sin are the opposite of his life, and that no one may come near him carelessly (Leviticus 10:3). And John, having just told of a man four days dead who walked out of a tomb, shows us a city preoccupied with the defilement that comes from touching a corpse. They purify themselves for a feast at which they will kill the Lamb who alone can make them clean.

They were looking for Jesus and saying to one another as they stood in the temple, What do you think? That he will not come to the feast at all? The Greek expects that he will not. Surely he will not dare? They are speculating about a celebrity: will he risk it, now there is a warrant out? It is the talk of a crowd with time to fill while they wait for the festival. They are not asking whether he is the Christ. They are asking whether he will turn up. He will come, within the week, on a donkey, with people shouting, and he will come precisely in order to be arrested, which is the one possibility hardly anyone standing in that temple seems to have considered. Days later they will be cutting branches and shouting Hosanna, and five days after that a crowd in the same city will shout for his death. The distance between those two noises is very short.

How am I made clean to come to God? Not by rituals, effort or a week of religious preparation. The pilgrims’ washings could only deal with outward defilement, and only for a time. The uncleanness that keeps us from God is sin, and only one thing removes it: the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin (1 John 1:7). You come to God clean not because you have prepared yourself well, but because Christ the Lamb was sacrificed for you. So come now, as you are, trusting him. Then, as one already washed, you will want to put away whatever defiles, out of love and not to earn your place.
verseByVerse.note: Pilgrims came early to undergo purification rites so they would be ritually clean for the feast.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the chief priests and the Pharisees had given orders that if anyone knew where he was, he should let them know, so that they might arrest him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Given orders. The chapter that began with a private message from two sisters ends with a public order for an arrest. Jesus is now a wanted man, and the authorities enlist the city. They did not need the general public in the end; they needed one man who already knew where he would be, and he was inside the twelve. This sets the scene for Judas (12:4; 18:2–3). John has laid the warrant on the table seven chapters before he collects it.

So that they might arrest him. The net is closing, but the one they plan to arrest has authority to lay down his life (10:18). The attempt has been made four times already in this Gospel and failed every time (7:30, 44; 8:20; 10:39). The next attempt will succeed, and when it comes it will be because he walks out of a garden and asks the soldiers whom they are looking for (18:4–8).

The cost of Bethany. The one who called Lazarus by name and gave him back to his sisters is now a wanted man because he did it. The whole journey was made on those terms: he raised his friend from the dead, and it cost him his life.

For worship. They issued a warrant for the arrest of the resurrection and the life, as though life itself could be taken into custody. When the one man who knew the place led them to it, the hunted one stepped forward into the torchlight, and his only request was that his friends be let go (18:8). He was bound so that his own could go free, as Lazarus was unbound and let go.

11.text: <sup>1</sup>Now a certain man was ill, Lazarus of Bethany, the village of Mary and her sister Martha.<sup>2</sup>It was Mary who anointed the Lord with ointment and wiped his feet with her hair, whose brother Lazarus was ill.<sup>3</sup>So the sisters sent to him, saying, “Lord, he whom you love is ill.”<sup>4</sup>But when Jesus heard it he said, “This illness does not lead to death. It is for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it.”<sup>5</sup>Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus.<sup>6</sup>So, when he heard that Lazarus was ill, he stayed two days longer in the place where he was.<sup>7</sup>Then after this he said to the disciples, “Let us go to Judea again.”<sup>8</sup>The disciples said to him, “Rabbi, the Jews were just now seeking to stone you, and are you going there again?”<sup>9</sup>Jesus answered, “Are there not twelve hours in the day? If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world.<sup>10</sup>But if anyone walks in the night, he stumbles, because the light is not in him.”<sup>11</sup>After saying these things, he said to them, “Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I go to awaken him.”<sup>12</sup>The disciples said to him, “Lord, if he has fallen asleep, he will recover.”<sup>13</sup>Now Jesus had spoken of his death, but they thought that he meant taking rest in sleep.<sup>14</sup>Then Jesus told them plainly, “Lazarus has died,<sup>15</sup>and for your sake I am glad that I was not there, so that you may believe. But let us go to him.”<sup>16</sup>So Thomas, called the Twin, said to his fellow disciples, “Let us also go, that we may die with him.”<sup>17</sup>Now when Jesus came, he found that Lazarus had already been in the tomb four days.<sup>18</sup>Bethany was near Jerusalem, about two miles off,<sup>19</sup>and many of the Jews had come to Martha and Mary to console them concerning their brother.<sup>20</sup>So when Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went and met him, but Mary remained seated in the house.<sup>21</sup>Martha said to Jesus, “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.<sup>22</sup>But even now I know that whatever you ask from God, God will give you.”<sup>23</sup>Jesus said to her, “Your brother will rise again.”<sup>24</sup>Martha said to him, “I know that he will rise again in the resurrection on the last day.”<sup>25</sup>Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live,<sup>26</sup>and everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die. Do you believe this?”<sup>27</sup>She said to him, “Yes, Lord; I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who is coming into the world.”<sup>28</sup>When she had said this, she went and called her sister Mary, saying in private, “The Teacher is here and is calling for you.”<sup>29</sup>And when she heard it, she rose quickly and went to him.<sup>30</sup>Now Jesus had not yet come into the village, but was still in the place where Martha had met him.<sup>31</sup>When the Jews who were with her in the house, consoling her, saw Mary rise quickly and go out, they followed her, supposing that she was going to the tomb to weep there.<sup>32</sup>Now when Mary came to where Jesus was and saw him, she fell at his feet, saying to him, “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.”<sup>33</sup>When Jesus saw her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her also weeping, he was deeply moved in his spirit and greatly troubled.<sup>34</sup>And he said, “Where have you laid him?” They said to him, “Lord, come and see.”<sup>35</sup>Jesus wept.<sup>36</sup>So the Jews said, “See how he loved him!”<sup>37</sup>But some of them said, “Could not he who opened the eyes of the blind man also have kept this man from dying?”<sup>38</sup>Then Jesus, deeply moved again, came to the tomb. It was a cave, and a stone lay against it.<sup>39</sup>Jesus said, “Take away the stone.” Martha, the sister of the dead man, said to him, “Lord, by this time there will be an odor, for he has been dead four days.”<sup>40</sup>Jesus said to her, “Did I not tell you that if you believed you would see the glory of God?”<sup>41</sup>So they took away the stone. And Jesus lifted up his eyes and said, “Father, I thank you that you have heard me.<sup>42</sup>I knew that you always hear me, but I said this on account of the people standing around, that they may believe that you sent me.”<sup>43</sup>When he had said these things, he cried out with a loud voice, “Lazarus, come out.”<sup>44</sup>The man who had died came out, his hands and feet bound with linen strips, and his face wrapped with a cloth. Jesus said to them, “Unbind him, and let him go.”<sup>45</sup>Many of the Jews therefore, who had come with Mary and had seen what he did, believed in him,<sup>46</sup>but some of them went to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done.<sup>47</sup>So the chief priests and the Pharisees gathered the council and said, “What are we to do? For this man performs many signs.<sup>48</sup>If we let him go on like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation.”<sup>49</sup>But one of them, Caiaphas, who was high priest that year, said to them, “You know nothing at all.<sup>50</sup>Nor do you understand that it is better for you that one man should die for the people, not that the whole nation should perish.”<sup>51</sup>He did not say this of his own accord, but being high priest that year he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation,<sup>52</sup>and not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the children of God who are scattered abroad.<sup>53</sup>So from that day on they made plans to put him to death.<sup>54</sup>Jesus therefore no longer walked openly among the Jews, but went from there to the region near the wilderness, to a town called Ephraim, and there he stayed with the disciples.<sup>55</sup>Now the Passover of the Jews was at hand, and many went up from the country to Jerusalem before the Passover to purify themselves.<sup>56</sup>They were looking for Jesus and saying to one another as they stood in the temple, “What do you think? That he will not come to the feast at all?”<sup>57</sup>Now the chief priests and the Pharisees had given orders that if anyone knew where he was, he should let them know, so that they might arrest him.
11.overview:
The raising of Lazarus is the seventh and greatest sign in John, and the event that leads directly to the cross. Jesus delays, returns to Judea despite the danger, tells Martha that he is the resurrection and the life, weeps with Mary, and calls a man four days dead out of his tomb.

Many believe, but the council meets in alarm, and Caiaphas argues that one man should die for the people. John hears in it a prophecy of the cross. From that day they plan to kill him. The one who gives life will give his own.

12.title: The Hour Has Come

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–19 — The Anointing and the Entry
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Six days before Passover, at a dinner in Bethany with Lazarus at the table, Mary anoints Jesus’ feet with costly nard, and Jesus defends her against Judas. The next day the festival crowds go out with palm branches to meet Jesus as he rides into the city on a young donkey, and the Pharisees despair that the world has gone after him.
verseByVerse.theology: Mary’s extravagance is the fitting response to Jesus: Matthew records him calling it a beautiful thing (Matthew 26:10). Judas’ objection sounds pious and is calculated: he uses the language of charity to cover his own greed. The contrast between Mary’s love and Judas’ arithmetic is the contrast between true discipleship and a discipleship that has never left the world’s way of counting.
verseByVerse.examples: The crowd hails Jesus as king, right about the title and wrong about its meaning. Jesus comes on a donkey, fulfilling Zechariah 9:9, the humble king of peace. The disciples understand it only after he is glorified (v. 16), as so often in John: the events become clear in the light of the cross and resurrection, through the Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: Six days before the Passover, Jesus therefore came to Bethany, where Lazarus was, whom Jesus had raised from the dead. So they gave a dinner for him there. Martha served, and Lazarus was one of those reclining with him at table.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. John 12 closes the first half of the Gospel, the Book of Signs.
