12.overview:
Chapter 12 closes the first half of John’s Gospel, the book of signs, and opens the way to the cross. At Bethany Mary anoints Jesus for his burial; the next day crowds hail him as King of Israel as he rides into Jerusalem on a young donkey.

When some Greeks ask to see him, Jesus announces that his hour has come: like a grain of wheat he must die to bear much fruit, and lifted up from the earth he will draw all people to himself. John explains from Isaiah why so many did not believe, and Jesus makes his last public appeal.

13.title: The Foot Washing and the New Commandment

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — The Foot Washing: Love to the End
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At supper, knowing his hour has come and that all things are in his hands, Jesus washes the disciples’ feet. Peter’s protests draw out what the washing means: no one has a share in Christ unless he cleanses him, and the one already bathed needs only his feet washed. Then Jesus explains it as an example for them to follow, and warns that one at his table will turn against him.
verseByVerse.theology: The footwashing is both a moral example (do as I have done) and a picture of the cleansing only Christ gives (if I do not wash you, you have no share with me). The one already bathed needs only his feet washed: the believer is justified once for all, and needs the daily cleansing of confession, not to be justified again.
verseByVerse.examples: Jesus does not wash feet because he has forgotten who he is; he washes feet because he knows exactly who he is (vv. 3–4, 13). Those anxious about their position never serve freely; those who know they are secure in the Father’s love can take the towel without self-protection.

verseByVerse.quote: Now before the Feast of the Passover, when Jesus knew that his hour had come to depart out of this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end. During supper, when the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon's son, to betray him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. The second half of John’s Gospel begins here. John’s account of the last evening fills five chapters (13–17), far more than the other Gospels give it. And at the centre of the evening John sets something the other Gospels leave out: the Lord of glory on the floor with a towel round his waist, and the love that put him there.

The setting. It is Thursday evening in an upper room in Jerusalem, at Passover, and before the sun sets again the true Passover Lamb will be dead and buried. Everything John records from here to the end of chapter 17 is said in a few hours, to men who will all run away before morning.

Before the Feast. John says this happened before the Feast, later says the authorities avoided the governor’s headquarters so that they might eat the Passover (18:28), and calls the day of the crucifixion the day of Preparation of the Passover (19:14). Matthew, Mark and Luke present the Last Supper plainly as the Passover meal itself.

Is there a contradiction about the date? The tension is real, but it is smaller than it looks, and most of it dissolves in the wording. The word rendered Preparation is the ordinary Greek term for Friday; it is still the word for Friday in Greek today. So the day of Preparation of the Passover most naturally means the Friday of Passover week, not the day before the meal. And Passover was used loosely for the whole seven-day festival, so to eat the Passover at 18:28 can easily mean the festival meals that followed. Read that way, John and the others agree: the supper was the Passover meal, and Jesus was crucified on the Friday of the feast. A second solution has long been offered, that different groups reckoned the feast a day apart. Either resolution serves; neither can be proved, and careful believing scholars still weigh them, but both show that the accounts can honestly be read together. What should not be said is that John invented a date to make a point. He did not need to. Jesus really did die at Passover, and John’s great theme, behold the Lamb of God, was handed to him by the calendar, not the other way round.

Where is the bread and the cup? All three of the other Gospels record the institution of the Lord’s Supper at this table, and Paul had already written it down for the Corinthians. John gives us a basin and a towel instead. The most likely reason is the one that explains much else in this Gospel: John probably writes last, with the other accounts long in circulation and the church keeping the Supper for some sixty years. He does not repeat what everyone has; he supplies what is missing. And he had already given the meaning of that meal at length in chapter 6: the bread that came down from heaven, the flesh given for the life of the world. Having taught what the Supper means, he gives us here what the Supper requires.

His hour had come. All through the Gospel the hour has not yet come (2:4; 7:30; 8:20). Now it has, and John’s word for his death is gentle: a departure (metabē), out of this world to the Father, at the feast when the LORD passed over. For Jesus the cross is not the end of a road but a doorway home, and he walks toward it knowing exactly where it leads.

His own. The word for his own is idios, and John used it twice in one of the saddest verses of the prologue: he came to his own, and his own people did not receive him (1:11). Here, twelve chapters later, on the last night, he has his own again, eleven men in a room and one who is leaving, and this time the sentence ends differently. His own are those the Father gave him (10:3–4; 17:6), the sheep he calls by name.

He loved them to the end. The Greek eis telos can mean to the end of his life, and to the uttermost, completely. Everything in chapters 13–17 is an expression of this love, and so is the cross that follows them.

Into the heart of Judas. The money is already agreed (Mark 14:10–11), so the man whose feet are about to be washed has an arrangement in place. The devil planted the idea, and Judas welcomed it. And John tells us this not afterwards, as an explanation, but at the top, before the basin comes out, so that the reader watches the whole washing knowing. Love and treachery sit side by side at one table, and Jesus knows it all and washes Judas’s feet anyway.

Does to the end mean Jesus’ love for me could still run out? No; it means the opposite. To the end is the measure of a love that has already been tested at its worst point and held. It held when one of the Twelve was selling him, when Peter was about to deny him, when all of them were about to run. If it did not fail them that night, it will not fail you on yours. Jesus himself says that no one will snatch his sheep out of his hand (10:28), and Paul that nothing in all creation can separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:38–39). The question to ask is not whether his love will last, but whether you are one of his own, and the mark of his own is that they hear his voice and follow him. If you want to follow him, however falteringly, that wanting is itself his voice at work in you.

On a Tuesday. Most of us have a quiet stopping point in our love: the colleague who let us down once, the relative privately written off, the friend whose need comes at a bad time. Love one of them past that point, not with a feeling but with an act that costs something. But you can love one step further than you did, because you have been loved all the way.
verseByVerse.note: John’s account of the last evening fills five chapters (13–17). “Simon’s son” is a different Simon from Peter.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come from God and was going back to God, rose from supper. He laid aside his outer garments, and taking a towel, tied it around his waist.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All things into his hands. John gives him the largest possible credentials: everything handed over (3:35), come from God, going to God. And the next thing those hands do is pick up a towel. Jesus does not stoop because he has forgotten who he is. He stoops because he knows exactly who he is.

Rose from supper. In the middle of the meal, not before it at the door, where a servant would have done it. Apparently nobody had, and the meal had gone on with dirty feet. Luke tells us that at this same supper the Twelve argued about which of them was the greatest (Luke 22:24); Jesus may well have got up in the middle of it.

He laid aside his outer garments. He laid aside (tithēmi) is the word he used repeatedly in chapter 10 about his life: the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (10:11, 15, 17, 18). And in verse 12 he will take his garments again, with the verb of taking his life up again: the crucifixion in miniature, hours before it happens. And behind it lies the whole movement of the incarnation: he who was in the form of God emptied himself, took the form of a servant, and humbled himself to the point of death (Philippians 2:6–8).

A towel. He is dressing as a slave, visibly the lowest person in the household, the one whose task it was to wash the guests’ feet.

Where does the freedom to serve come from? Not from thinking little of yourself. The man in this verse knows exactly who he is; John has just told us in the most extravagant terms available, and that is given as the reason he can kneel. Nobody who is still trying to establish his position can afford to take the towel. Only someone whose position is beyond question has nothing to lose by it. That is why the Christian’s freedom to serve grows out of knowing who he is in Christ: a child of God, forgiven, loved, with his future secure. A man who knows he is accepted by the Father no longer needs the best seat to prove anything.

For worship. The hands that hold all things together tied a towel round his waist. He had come from God and was going to God, and between the two he went down to the floor, not because he lost sight of his glory, but because this is what his glory is like.
verseByVerse.note: Washing guests’ feet was the job of the lowest household slave; roads were dusty and people wore sandals.

parallels.desc: I am among you as the one who serves

verseByVerse.quote: Then he poured water into a basin and began to wash the disciples' feet and to wipe them with the towel that was wrapped around him. He came to Simon Peter, who said to him, "Lord, do you wash my feet?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A basin. Footwashing was no quaint courtesy. Feet arriving at a house were genuinely filthy, and washing them was the job at the bottom of the household list. Later rabbinic writings say that a Jewish slave could not be required to do it, and record a rabbi teaching that a disciple should do anything for his teacher except loosen his sandal. There had been a basin in that room all evening, and nobody had touched it. Then the Lord of glory kneels at each pair of feet in turn.

He came to Simon Peter. Peter’s objection seems to come partway through. Whatever the sequence, at some point in that circuit he knelt in front of Judas, and Judas put his feet in the water, and neither of them said anything that John thought worth recording.

Lord, do you wash my feet? In Greek the words you and my stand side by side for emphasis: Lord, you, my feet? Peter is shocked, and his objection is not false modesty. He is registering that the universe is the wrong way up. And he is right, which is what makes him wrong. Everything Peter’s instinct is protecting is true: this is the Lord, and lords do not wash feet. What he cannot yet accommodate is a Lord who does, and within a day he will have to accommodate a Lord who is executed, which is the same problem at full scale. Peter’s difficulty at the basin and his difficulty at the cross are one difficulty. The one who should be served serves; the one whose feet should be washed washes. The incarnation and the atonement are both versions of the same reversal.

Why did Jesus wash Judas’s feet if he knew? Because his love is not a reward for loyalty. He washed the feet of a man he knew had already sold him, and the knowledge did not change the service by one degree. It was a real kindness and, as the morsel will be in verse 26, a real appeal, though it was refused. It also shows the disciples, and us, that the command to wash one another’s feet reaches even those who will wrong us (Luke 6:27–28). It does not mean Judas was cleansed; verse 10 says plainly he was not. Outward kindness from Christ is not the same as inward cleansing by Christ.

On a Tuesday. Think of the person in your life whose feet you would least like to wash: the one who has used you, or criticised you, or simply wearies you. Do that person one hidden kindness this week, as he did for Judas without a word.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered him, "What I am doing you do not understand now, but afterward you will understand." Peter said to him, "You shall never wash my feet." Jesus answered him, "If I do not wash you, you have no share with me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Afterward you will understand. He does not explain, though he could have; the explanation comes a few verses later. The understanding is promised, and it is promised for later: after the cross and resurrection, when the Spirit would bring these things to mind (12:16; 14:26), Peter would see that this washing pointed to Jesus’ death for him.

Living in the not yet. That is the position a good deal of the Christian life is lived from. Something is being done that does not make sense while it is happening, and the assurance offered is not an account of it but a person’s word that it will make sense in retrospect. John himself is the proof: he is writing this some sixty years afterwards, and the afterward arrived.

You shall never. He is not hesitating; he is forbidding. It is Peter’s pride dressed up as humility, and refusing grace is not humility.

No share with me. The word is meros: an allotted share. The washing now clearly means more than feet. Unless Christ cleanses us from sin, we have no part in him or his kingdom. Which turns the whole exchange: Peter thinks he is defending his master’s dignity, and he is in fact refusing his own salvation, and the two look identical from inside.

The refusal that looks like reverence. There is a refusal of grace that presents as humility: I could not ask that, others need it more, I will manage. The way to tell them apart is to ask what it protects. Reverence protects God’s honour. This protects a self-image in which one does not need to be carried, and it will keep a man out of the kingdom while he is being admired for it. I am not worthy can be a deeper refusal than I do not need it.

What if I feel too dirty or too unworthy to come to Christ? Then you are exactly the person he washes. The basin is for dirty feet; clean ones do not need it. Feeling unworthy is not the obstacle. The obstacle is refusing to let him do what only he can do. You do not clean yourself up first and then present yourself. You come as you are, put your feet in the water, so to speak, and let him wash you: that is what faith is. His word to Peter is his word to you: unless he washes you, you have no part with him, and if he washes you, you are completely clean (v. 10).

verseByVerse.quote: Simon Peter said to him, "Lord, not my feet only but also my hands and my head!" Jesus said to him, "The one who has bathed does not need to wash, except for his feet, but is completely clean. And you are clean, but not every one of you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not my feet only. Peter swings to the opposite extreme, entirely in character: if this is the condition, wash all of me. He is wrong twice in ninety seconds, in opposite directions, and both times because he is trying to control the terms. First he will have none of it; then he will have more than is offered. What he never does is simply put his feet in the water.

Bathed and completely clean. The one who has bathed (louō, to wash the whole body) does not need to wash (niptō, to wash a part). Guests would bathe at home before a banquet and then walked to the house through the streets, and by the time they arrived only their feet needed attention. Nobody had a second bath at the door. So: one bath, many footwashings.

Justification once, cleansing daily. That is the whole of the Christian doctrine of assurance and confession in a household image. The one who has been cleansed by Christ once for all, in justification and regeneration (Titus 3:5), does not need to be saved again. Justification is God’s verdict that a sinner is right with him because Christ’s righteousness is counted as his (Romans 4:5). It is not lost when a believer stumbles and then won back, because it never rested on his walking. And yet the walking does soil, daily and genuinely, and the feet do need washing (1 John 1:7–9), and pretending otherwise is not faith but grubbiness. Justification happens once; confession and forgiveness go on.

A textual note. One important early manuscript and some early Christian writers lack the words except for his feet, and a footnote may appear in a modern Bible. The shorter reading gives essentially the same sense, that the bathed man does not need washing, and the distinction between the bath and the feet is carried by the two verbs regardless.

But not every one of you. The disciples are clean by the word he has spoken to them (15:3), but not all. Twelve pairs of feet were washed; eleven men are clean.

When I sin as a Christian, do I need to be saved all over again? No. If you have truly trusted Christ, you have had the bath, and you are completely clean in God’s sight; your standing as his child does not lapse every time you fall. What you need is the footwashing: to bring that sin to him in honest confession, trust that he forgives it (1 John 1:9), and get up and walk on. A believer who keeps asking to be saved again is like Peter asking for his head to be washed, and the answer is the same: you are clean. But a believer who never confesses is walking about with dirty feet. Both the once-for-all and the daily belong to the Christian life.
verseByVerse.note: Guests bathed before a banquet and needed only their feet washed on arrival.

parallels.desc: you are already clean

verseByVerse.quote: For he knew who was to betray him; that was why he said, "Not all of you are clean." When he had washed their feet and put on his outer garments and resumed his place, he said to them, "Do you understand what I have done to you?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For he knew. The reader is told twice, at verse 2 and again at verse 11, that nothing about Judas was hidden. This is not a story about a man who was fooled.

The warning of the means of grace. Judas received the footwashing along with the eleven, but without the cleansing it signified. External participation in the means of grace, baptism, the Lord’s Supper, the ministry of the word, does not by itself produce inward cleansing. They are genuine means by which God blesses his people, but they bless through faith, not apart from it. God uses them to feed the faith of those who trust his Son, and to the one who does not trust him they bring only greater accountability (1 Corinthians 11:27–29).

Resumed his place. He took (elaben) his garments, the verb of taking up his life again (10:17–18), closing the loop verse 4 opened: the descent, and the return.

Do you understand what I have done to you? Having done it, he asks a question rather than delivering a lesson. Note the order, because it is his method throughout this Gospel and it is the reverse of ours. The sign comes first and the explanation second. He turned water into wine before anyone knew what to make of it, fed five thousand before the discourse about bread, healed the blind man and only afterwards spoke of who is truly blind (9:39–41). Here he washes twelve pairs of feet in silence, dresses, sits down, and then asks what they made of it. And the answer at that moment was almost certainly no; verse 7 has already said so. He asks anyway, not to expose them but to begin the explanation, which is the next thing he does: a second meaning, an example.

Can a person go to church, be baptised and take communion, and still not be saved? Sadly, yes, and Judas is the warning. He was chosen as an apostle, lived with Jesus for about three years, preached, saw miracles, and had his feet washed by the Son of God, and he was not clean. This is not said to make sincere believers anxious, but to stop anyone resting on outward things. The question is not whether you have been near Jesus but whether you have trusted him. If you have come to him as a sinner and rest on him alone, the outward signs are real blessings to you. If you have not, no amount of religious contact will substitute. Come to him today.

verseByVerse.quote: "You call me Teacher and Lord, and you are right, for so I am. If I then, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another's feet."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Teacher and Lord. Jesus does not modestly disclaim the titles. His service does not lessen his authority; it shows what kind of Lord he is.

You also ought. If the Lord serves, how much more should the servants. Ought (opheilete) is a word of obligation, the language of a debt owed. The way Jesus loves is the way his people are to love: the voluntary downward movement of serving those who cannot repay.

Where Christians differ: is footwashing an ordinance? Some churches practise footwashing as a regular ordinance alongside baptism and the Lord’s Supper, and they are not being silly: the sentence says you also ought to wash one another’s feet. This commentary’s view: Jesus calls it an example (v. 15), not a sacrament. There is no record that the apostles practised or commanded it as a church rite; in 1 Timothy 5:10 it appears as an act of humble hospitality. The command is to do the humble, menial, loving service that meets real needs, whatever form that takes today. A literal footwashing can be a moving act, but the point is the lowly love behind it.

The harder obedience. Where a church does not wash feet, it is under exactly the same obligation and has a harder time discharging it, because the substance is not a ritual with a towel but the willingness to do, for one another, the job nobody wants. A footwashing service can be got through in twenty minutes once a year. What he is describing has no fixed occasion and no end.

What does washing one another’s feet look like today? It looks like doing the needed thing nobody notices or wants. Cleaning up after the church meal. Visiting the elderly member who repeats herself. Changing the nappy, sitting with the dying, driving the person without a car, doing the paperwork for the widow, listening to the same trouble for the fifth time. It includes the humbler work of forgiving, of bearing with someone’s faults, and of gently helping a brother with his sin (Galatians 6:1–2). The mark of footwashing is that it is beneath your dignity and meets a real need.

verseByVerse.quote: "For I have given you an example, that you also should do just as I have done to you. Truly, truly, I say to you, a servant is not greater than his master, nor is a messenger greater than the one who sent him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I have given you an example. The word is hypodeigma: a pattern, a specimen, a model laid down to be copied (1 Peter 2:21).

Just as I have done. The measure of the imitation is the original act, and the original act was performed by somebody with all things in his hands, for people who were arguing about rank, including one who was selling him. The pattern has specifications: it is voluntary, it is downward, it is done for people who will not repay it, and at least one of the recipients does not deserve it.

A servant is not greater than his master. If the master is not too proud to wash feet, the servant cannot be. And this proverb comes back later in the farewell discourse with the comfort taken out of it. In chapter 15 the same sentence will mean that if they persecuted me, they will also persecute you (15:20). The proverb cuts twice: it puts a limit on how high a disciple may hold himself, and it warns him not to expect gentler treatment than his master received.

Nor is a messenger greater. The word for messenger is apostolos, apostle, and this is the only time the word occurs in John’s Gospel: in a sentence about not being above the job. It cuts against a particular danger in Christian service: the servant who begins to think the work is his. Everything an apostle has, the message, the authority, the commission, arrived from somewhere else.

Am I meant to copy everything Jesus did? Not everything. Some of what he did belongs to him alone: he alone died for sins, rose from the dead, and is Lord. We follow him as servants, not as substitutes. But in his humility, his love and his patience toward the undeserving, he is meant to be copied, and the footwashing is given precisely as that kind of example. Peter says Christ left us an example so that we might follow in his steps, and in the same breath says he bore our sins in his body on the tree (1 Peter 2:21–24). He is first our Saviour, and then our pattern.

On a Tuesday. If you serve in church in any visible way, watch for the sign that you have begun to think of the work as yours: the sting when someone else gets the credit, or when your role is changed without your being consulted.

verseByVerse.quote: "If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them. I am not speaking of all of you; I know whom I have chosen. But the Scripture will be fulfilled, 'He who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed are you if you do them. Two conditions, and the blessing hangs on the second. Knowing is assumed; he has just explained it. The blessing is attached to the doing (James 1:22–25), on the far side of the gap. Yet it is spoken to men already washed and clean (v. 10): the blessing is the joy of children doing their Father’s will, not the price of becoming his, and the Helper he is about to promise (14:16–17) is the power that carries them across the gap.

Whom I have chosen. Jesus chose the Twelve, including Judas (6:70). But here whom I have chosen probably means chosen for salvation: he knows his own, and he knows Judas is not among them. When he chose Judas he was not deceived about him. He chose with open eyes, within God’s sovereign purpose, so that the Scripture might be fulfilled.

Lifted his heel. From Psalm 41:9, where David laments a close friend’s betrayal. To eat someone’s bread was to bind yourself in friendship. Lifting the heel is a picture of treachery: what a horse does before it kicks, or showing someone the sole of one’s foot, a deep insult in the East. Judas would betray the friend who had just fed him and washed his feet.

What he leaves out. The psalm says my close friend in whom I trusted, and Jesus drops that clause. He could not say it. He had known from the beginning who would betray him (6:64). He was betrayed by someone he had not trusted, and had kept beside him anyway for about three years, and had just washed.

Was Judas, then, chosen to be lost and so less guilty? Jesus chose him to be an apostle (6:70), not to be saved. Judas acted willingly, for money, and was fully responsible; Scripture foretold his act but did not force it (Acts 1:16). Jesus said it would have been better for that man not to have been born (Matthew 26:24). God’s sovereignty and Judas’s guilt stand side by side, as they do at the cross itself (Acts 2:23).

Could I turn out to be a Judas? If you are asking that question with fear and longing to be true to Christ, it is very unlikely you are. Judas was not a tender believer who fell; he was a thief all along (12:6), and he never showed grief over his sin before Christ, only remorse that ended in despair. The warning is for those who are comfortable near Jesus without loving him. If you hate your sin, run to Christ with it, and want him more than what he gives, those are the marks of the Spirit’s work, and the one who began that work will finish it (Philippians 1:6).
verseByVerse.note: Lifting the heel against someone is a picture of treachery.

parallels.desc: my close friend, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me

verseByVerse.quote: "I am telling you this now, before it takes place, that when it does take place you may believe that I am he. Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever receives the one I send receives me, and whoever receives me receives the one who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before it takes place. The reason is pastoral rather than merely predictive. If one of the hand-picked Twelve had sold him without warning, the obvious conclusion is that Jesus had been taken in. So he gives them the true reading before the event, so that the thing which looks most like a failure of his judgement becomes evidence of the opposite.

That I am he. Again I am (egō eimi), the words of 8:24 and 8:28. The God of Isaiah declares the end from the beginning (Isaiah 46:10; 48:5), and Isaiah 43:10 is closely echoed: “that you may know and believe me and understand that I am he.” Jesus is not claiming to be a prophet who happens to know what is coming; he is claiming to be the God who planned it. This is the function of prophecy in John’s Gospel: not to satisfy curiosity about the future but to strengthen faith when the future arrives.

Whoever receives the one I send. He has been talking about a man who was sent and went wrong; now he tells the other eleven what it will mean when they are sent. The chain runs unbroken from the Father through the Son to them (Matthew 10:40), and even after Judas’s betrayal, their mission stands. He does not wait until they have proved reliable.

How do I receive the ones Jesus sends today? The apostles were sent once, and their message now stands written in the New Testament; to receive their word is to receive Christ, and to reject it is to reject him. So the first application is to receive the apostolic Scriptures as the very word of the Lord. The principle reaches further, in a secondary way: those who faithfully bring that word to you, your pastor, a missionary, a friend who shares the gospel, are to be welcomed for the sake of the one whose message they carry, not for their eloquence (1 Thessalonians 2:13).

parallels.desc: that you may know and believe that I am he

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–38 — The Betrayer Exposed and the New Commandment
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus identifies the betrayer by the morsel, and Judas goes out into the night. Then Jesus speaks of his glory, gives the new commandment, and foretells that Peter, for all his brave promise, will deny him three times before the rooster crows.
verseByVerse.theology: The new commandment is not new because love was absent from the law (Leviticus 19:18), but because the measure is new: as I have loved you, the costly, foot-washing, cross-bearing love Jesus has just shown and is about to complete.
verseByVerse.examples: The prediction of Peter’s denial answers Peter’s most confident declaration. Jesus does not shame him but tells him the truth he needs: his fidelity rests on a foundation he has not yet tested. The failure will come, and the restoration that follows (chapter 21) will rest on a more honest foundation than confidence ever was: Christ’s hold on Peter, not Peter’s on Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: After saying these things, Jesus was troubled in his spirit, and testified, "Truly, truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me." The disciples looked at one another, uncertain of whom he spoke.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus was troubled in his spirit. This is the third time John uses this verb of him, and the three occurrences map the whole approach of the cross. At the tomb of Lazarus he was greatly troubled (11:33). In the temple courts, when the Greeks came: now is my soul troubled (12:27). And now, at the table, troubled in his spirit. The Son of God was not serene in the sense of untouched; he felt it.

One of you will betray me. He testified: a solemn declaration, the language of a witness on oath, not a guess or a mood.

Uncertain of whom he spoke. Judas had been helping himself from the bag (12:6); he had gone to the chief priests, taken money, and come back to supper. And not one of the men who had lived on the road with him had the faintest suspicion. He had hidden his heart perfectly.

Is it I? Matthew and Mark record that they each asked, Is it I? (Mark 14:19), which is the other half of the same fact. Nobody could point at Judas, and every one of them was uncertain enough about himself to ask. That is worth having in both directions. A man can be indistinguishable from a disciple for years, not by clever acting but by doing the same things and going to the same places, and be nothing of the kind. And the disciples’ instinct, when told there was a traitor at the table, was to look inward rather than around the room. It is the healthier reflex, a healthy self-suspicion, and the one Judas never had.

Is it wrong for Jesus to be troubled, if he is God? No. He is truly God and truly man, and as man he had a real human soul that could be grieved, shaken and pained, without any sin (Hebrews 4:15). His trouble was not doubt or panic; it was the holy grief of a pure heart facing treachery and death. That is a great comfort. When you are troubled by betrayal or loss, you are not praying to a Saviour who cannot understand. He has been there, at a table with a friend who had sold him.

verseByVerse.quote: One of his disciples, whom Jesus loved, was reclining at table at Jesus' side, so Simon Peter motioned to him to ask Jesus of whom he was speaking.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of his disciples, whom Jesus loved. The first appearance of the disciple whom Jesus loved, a title that will recur and never be attached to a name. He is at the supper, at the cross (19:26), at the empty tomb (20:2), on the beach (21:7, 20), and named at the end as the one who wrote these things (21:24): most probably John, son of Zebedee, as early tradition says. He never uses his own name. He describes himself not by his love for Jesus but by Jesus’ love for him.

At Jesus’ side. Guests at a formal meal reclined on couches around a low table, leaning on the left elbow, so the man to the host’s right had his head near the host’s chest and could lean back to speak privately. The Greek is in the bosom of Jesus, the words the prologue used of the Son at the Father’s side (1:18). So the Gospel’s opening picture of the Son against the Father’s heart is reproduced at the supper table, with a man in the Son’s place, and the man is the one who will write it all down. He tells us who Jesus is because he was lying against him when he found out.

Peter motioned to him. Peter was apparently further away and could not ask quietly, so he signals to the man who can. Peter acts; John sees. Peter, who will soon fail most visibly, organises the inquiry; John, who will stand at the cross, is already in the place of intimate witness.

Did Jesus have favourites? Not in any sense that slights the others. He loved all his own to the end (v. 1), and he died for each. John’s title is not a claim that he was loved more but a confession of wonder that he was loved at all, and every believer may say the same of himself: the Son of God loved me and gave himself for me (Galatians 2:20). Jesus did have friendships of different closeness, as any true man does: the Twelve, then Peter, James and John, then John. Closeness in friendship is not partiality in salvation.
verseByVerse.note: Guests reclined on couches, leaning on the left elbow; the one on the host’s right lay with his head near the host’s chest. The disciple “whom Jesus loved” is traditionally identified as John, the Gospel’s author.

verseByVerse.quote: So that disciple, leaning back against Jesus, said to him, "Lord, who is it?" Jesus answered, "It is he to whom I will give this morsel of bread when I have dipped it." So when he had dipped the morsel, he gave it to Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This morsel of bread. The answer to the whispered question is a gesture of honour. Bread seems to have been dipped into a common dish, perhaps of bitter herbs or sauce, and handed to a particular guest: a host singling somebody out for favour, the equivalent of serving him first. So the morsel itself is not a mark of guilt.

The seating plan. The place of highest honour at such a meal was immediately beside the host, close enough that he could reach it without effort. The beloved disciple is on Jesus’ right, since he leans back against his chest to ask. And Jesus hands the morsel to Judas without any indication of getting up or passing it along. That puts Judas within arm’s reach on the other side, perhaps in the place of honour. Whether or not the seating was deliberate, it means the two men closest to Jesus at that supper may well have been the disciple he loved and the man who had already sold him, one on each side.

He gave it to Judas. A final offer of love. The betrayer is identified by an act of hospitality, and only John knew the meaning of the gesture; the others saw a kindness, which is why they do not understand when Judas leaves. Jesus knew everything, the arrangement, the money, the hour, and what he does with the knowledge is offer the man the best piece of bread. It is the last thing he ever gives him.

Was Judas present for the Lord’s Supper? Luke places the warning about the betrayer after the cup (Luke 22:21), while Matthew and Mark place it before, and John has Judas leave right after the morsel. Luke sometimes arranges events by topic rather than strict order, and the more likely reading is that Judas left before the bread and cup were shared. Christians have read the order differently since early times, and nothing in the faith hangs on it.

Grace offered and refused. Judas receives the morsel that names him, and it seals him instead. Grace offered and refused becomes the occasion of judgement.
verseByVerse.note: Handing a guest a dipped morsel was a mark of honour.

verseByVerse.quote: Then after he had taken the morsel, Satan entered into him. Jesus said to him, "What you are going to do, do quickly." Now no one at the table knew why he said this to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Satan entered into him. It is the only time John uses the name Satan in the whole Gospel, and the timing is exact: after the morsel. The last kindness offered was the point at which the door closed. Grace refused does not leave a man where it found him. Verse 2 said the devil had already put the idea into his heart; verse 27 says he entered; Luke speaks of Satan entering him earlier still, when he went to strike the bargain (Luke 22:3). Refused love hardens. Judas is not a puppet; he chose, and his choice gave Satan entry.

Do quickly. Jesus sets the timing of his own betrayal. Judas thinks he is running an operation, and has fooled eleven men; but the man he is selling tells him to get on with it, he goes when he is told, and the arrest happens on the night Jesus intends to die.

Not permission, but enough. It is the last word Jesus ever speaks to Judas, and it is a dismissal from the room: the point at which a man who has decided is allowed to go and do it. God does not compel anybody’s betrayal. But there comes a moment when he stops restraining it, and this verse is what that sounds like.

No one at the table knew. The most decisive moment of the evening passes in front of eleven witnesses and registers as nothing. The cross is not understood until the Spirit interprets it in the light of the resurrection.

Can a Christian be possessed by Satan like Judas? No. A true believer belongs to Christ and is indwelt by the Holy Spirit, and he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world (1 John 4:4). Satan can tempt, accuse and harass a Christian, and a Christian can give him a foothold by sin (Ephesians 4:27), but he cannot own one whom Christ has bought. Judas was never a believer (6:64, 70); he was a man who had kept company with Jesus while his heart belonged elsewhere. The way to resist the devil is to submit to God and to keep near to Christ (James 4:7–8), not to live in fear.

On a Tuesday. If there is a sin you keep hearing warnings about and keep putting off, remember that every refusal of grace makes the next refusal easier. Confess it today, tell a trusted friend, and remove what feeds it. And if this warning frightens you, take heart: a heart that is hardening seldom worries about it, and your concern is a sign that grace is still at work.

verseByVerse.quote: Some thought that, because Judas had the moneybag, Jesus was telling him, "Buy what we need for the feast," or that he should give something to the poor. So, after receiving the morsel of bread, he immediately went out. And it was night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Buy for the feast. The disciples’ two guesses show how completely normal Judas seemed. Buying for the festival was an ordinary errand for the man with the bag, and giving to the poor at Passover was a custom, the very cause Judas had championed so publicly over Mary’s ointment (12:5). That is how betrayal generally leaves a room: not with a slammed door but with a plausible explanation that everybody accepts because they have no reason not to.

And it was night. He gets up from a table where the Light of the world is sitting and goes out. It is a statement of fact: it was after sundown, and the meal was a night meal. But John does not write about darkness by accident. He opened the book with it: the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it (1:5). Jesus had said on the way to Bethany that if anyone walks in the night, he stumbles, because the light is not in him (11:10; compare 12:35). He left the Light, and the night outside the door was already inside the man.

Is it ever too late to come back? For anyone who wants to come back, no. Judas did not go out because the door was locked against him; he went out because he chose the dark, and he never came back to Christ even when remorse came (Matthew 27:3–5). Peter fell that same night and wept and was restored. The difference is not the size of the sin but where each man went with it. If you feel the pull to return to Christ, that pull is grace, and he has promised that whoever comes to him he will never cast out (6:37).

For worship. The Light of the world sat at the table, and the darkness could not overcome it, though a man walked out into the night to bring it down. For all his own, the night is not the last word: the Lamb is the lamp of the city where there is no night (Revelation 21:23–25).
verseByVerse.note: Giving to the poor at Passover was a custom.

parallels.desc: send portions to anyone who has nothing ready
the power of darkness

verseByVerse.quote: When he had gone out, Jesus said, "Now is the Son of Man glorified, and God is glorified in him. If God is glorified in him, God will also glorify him in himself, and glorify him at once."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he had gone out. With the betrayer gone, the events are set in motion. The great discourse of chapters 14 to 17, the vine, the Spirit, the peace, the prayer, begins the moment the door shuts behind Judas.

Now is the Son of Man glorified. What Jesus says is astonishing, because the situation has just become irreversible: the betrayer is on his way to the chief priests. Not on the third day: now, with the trial and the nails still ahead. He greets the beginning of the darkest night of his life by announcing that his glory has started.

Glorified, five times. The verb appears five times in two verses, and the movement in it is mutual: the Son is glorified, God is glorified in him, God will glorify the Son in himself, and at once. The cross is the glory of the Son: there his love, obedience and holiness shine most brightly. And it is the glory of the Father: there God’s justice and mercy are both displayed, so that he is both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:25–26).

The dying itself is the glory. The claim is not only that God brought good out of the cross afterwards, but that the dying itself is the glory, that if you want to know what the weight and beauty of God look like, the answer is a man on a Roman cross taking what he did not owe. Anywhere else, glory means the absence of humiliation. Here it is the same event.

How can a death be glorious? Glory in the Bible is the shining out of what God is. At the cross more of God is seen than anywhere else: his holiness, which will not overlook sin; his justice, which punishes it fully; his love, which bears that punishment himself in his Son; his wisdom, which saves sinners without compromising his righteousness; and his power, which turns the devil’s victory into his defeat. The cross is ugly as a human deed and glorious as a divine one. That is why Christians sing about it and Paul would boast in nothing else (Galatians 6:14).

For worship. The light of the knowledge of the glory of God shines in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6), and it shines most brightly from the face that was spat on, crowned with thorns, and lifted up for sinners.

verseByVerse.quote: "Little children, yet a little while I am with you. You will seek me, and just as I said to the Jews, so now I also say to you, 'Where I am going you cannot come.' A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another: just as I have loved you, you also are to love one another."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Little children. A tender word (teknia), like a father about to leave his children. It is the sort of word an old man uses, and John himself will use it seven times in his first letter, decades later, evidently having kept it.

Where I am going you cannot come. He said it before to the men who wanted him dead (7:34; 8:21). The same sentence, now turned to his friends, with the difference that for them it is temporary: not yet (v. 36).

A new commandment. The obvious question is what is new about it. Loving one another is not an innovation; Leviticus 19:18 had said you shall love your neighbour as yourself, and Jesus had already called it the second greatest commandment (Matthew 22:39). What is new? The new standard: as I have loved you, the love that washes feet and lays down its life. The new community: a family of disciples bound to one another in Christ. And the new covenant, of which this is the law written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:33). Under the old covenant the law stood outside a man, on tablets of stone, telling him what to do. In the new covenant God puts his own Spirit within his people and changes what they want, so that they begin to love what he commands (Ezekiel 36:26–27). The Latin for commandment, mandatum, is the likely source of the name Maundy Thursday.

As I have loved you. Leviticus gave a measure that everybody carries with them: as yourself. What replaces it here is a measure outside the self altogether, one that has just been demonstrated on the floor with a basin, and will be demonstrated again tomorrow afternoon.

Impossible on purpose. As yourself can be attempted. As I have loved you cannot be attempted at all in the ordinary sense; it can only be received first and then passed on, which is why the Spirit is promised in chapter 14, the Spirit who raised Jesus now living in his people (Romans 8:11), and the vine follows in chapter 15. His love is both the pattern and the power for ours: we love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). And where our loving falls short, as it does every day, his own perfect love, kept to the end, is counted as ours (Romans 5:19), so failure sends us back to him, not out of his love. The commandment is impossible on purpose, and the rest of the discourse is the provision for it.

Does one another mean only Christians? In this verse, yes: Jesus is speaking of the love of his disciples for each other, the family love of the church. Elsewhere he commands love for neighbours and even enemies (Luke 6:27–36; 10:25–37), so this is not permission to love Christians only. But there is a particular, covenant love owed within the household of faith (Galatians 6:10), and it is this love that the world is meant to see (v. 35). In practice that means the hardest test is often not the stranger but the fellow member you find difficult.

On a Tuesday. Pick one believer you find hard to love and ask what the love that washes feet would look like toward him this week. Pray for him first, asking the Lord who loved you for more of his love, and then do one thing.
verseByVerse.note: Love of neighbour was old; the new standard is “as I have loved you.”

verseByVerse.quote: "By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another." Simon Peter said to him, "Lord, where are you going?" Jesus answered him, "Where I am going you cannot follow me now, but you will follow afterward."
verseByVerse.commentary:
By this all people will know. He names the badge, and it is not what we might expect. Not doctrine, though he cared enormously about truth. Not miracles, numbers, buildings, learning or zeal. The mark of a Christian community before the watching world is its love. He is handing the world a criterion and inviting it to use it.

Vindication and humiliation. The second-century writer Tertullian reported pagans saying of Christians, see how they love one another, and the early church’s care for its poor and its plague victims was noticed across the empire and is often thought to be one reason it grew. The same church has produced schisms, wars, and cold congregations. The sentence hands unbelievers a fair objection whenever the love is not there, and he said it anyway. The world can argue with theology; it finds it far harder to argue with a community that loves the unlovable, forgives the unforgivable, and serves the unworthy.

Does this mean doctrine matters less than love? No. The same Lord who said this prays in chapter 17 that his people be sanctified in the truth, and John’s letters insist that love and truth belong together (2 John 1–6). Love without truth is not Christ’s love, because he loved us by telling us the truth and dying for it. But truth without love fails the very test he gives the world. The answer is not to choose but to hold both: to be as careful with one another’s souls as with one another’s doctrine.

Lord, where are you going? Peter, it seems, has hardly taken it in. Jesus has just given the new commandment, and Peter skips over it to ask about Jesus’ departure. He is still back at verse 33.

You will follow afterward. Not a refusal; a postponement, and a promise. What Peter cannot do tonight he will do later: in death, as a martyr (21:18–19), and into glory. The cross that separates them now will be the path Peter himself eventually walks.

parallels.desc: the death by which Peter would glorify God

verseByVerse.quote: Peter said to him, "Lord, why can I not follow you now? I will lay down my life for you." Jesus answered, "Will you lay down your life for me? Truly, truly, I say to you, the rooster will not crow till you have denied me three times."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lord, why can I not follow you now? I will lay down my life for you. Peter’s promise uses the exact words Jesus has used of himself: lay down (tithēmi), the verb from the good shepherd (10:11, 15), the verb from laying aside the garments at the start of this evening. He has been listening to the shepherd language and has taken it on himself. And he means it. Peter is usually treated as a braggart here, and he is not. Within a few hours he will draw a sword against an armed band in the dark (18:10), which is not the act of a coward. He was willing to die. What he was not able to do was survive a servant girl’s question by a fire. He does not know his own weakness, and that is a real thing about human courage. Often we fail not at the point we had braced for. Peter had prepared himself for a fight and was undone by a conversation. And there is a quiet idol in his promise: he is trusting his own devotion. The religious heart is always tempted to rest on the strength of its love for Christ, when the only safe resting place is the strength of Christ’s love for it.

Will you lay down your life for me? Gently, Jesus echoes his words back to him as a question. The irony: Peter says he will lay down his life for Jesus; in fact, Jesus will lay down his life for Peter (10:11).

Before the rooster crows. Peter’s denials follow in 18:15–27, and the specificity is the mercy. A general warning that he would fail would have been forgotten or argued with. What he gives Peter is a marker so precise that when it happens there can be no doubt it was foreseen. Luke records the moment it lands, when the rooster crows and the Lord turns and looks at Peter, and Peter goes out and weeps bitterly (Luke 22:61–62).

Two failures, two endings. Judas also failed that night, and the warnings he had been given did not bring him back; he went out and hanged himself (Matthew 27:5). The difference between the two men is not the size of the sin. It is that one of them had been prayed for (Luke 22:32), and had been told in advance, and therefore knew at the worst moment of his life that he had not surprised the Lord who had washed his feet. Jesus does not give up on him. He restores him with three questions by the lake (21:15–17).

What if I have failed Christ badly, after promising him much? Then Peter is your brother. He made the boldest promise in the room and broke it three times within hours, with curses. Jesus knew it would happen, loved him through it, prayed that his faith would not fail, and went looking for him after the resurrection. Your failure does not surprise Christ, and it does not cancel his love. Do what Peter did: weep over it honestly, do not run from him as Judas did, and let him restore you. Then, like Peter, strengthen your brothers out of what you have learned (Luke 22:32).

For worship. He knew exactly what every one of them was about to do, Judas going out into the night, Peter by the fire, the rest scattering, and he had already knelt down and washed all twenty-four feet. Our hold on Christ fails within hours. His hold on us does not fail at all.

But the Scripture will be fulfilled, ’He who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me.’<sup>19</sup>I am telling you this now, before it takes place, that when it does take place you may believe that I am he.<sup>20</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever receives the one I send receives me, and whoever receives me receives the one who sent me.”<sup>21</sup>After saying these things, Jesus was troubled in his spirit, and testified, “Truly, truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me.”<sup>22</sup>The disciples looked at one another, uncertain of whom he spoke.<sup>23</sup>One of his disciples, whom Jesus loved, was reclining at table at Jesus’ side,<sup>24</sup>so Simon Peter motioned to him to ask Jesus of whom he was speaking.<sup>25</sup>So that disciple, leaning back against Jesus, said to him, “Lord, who is it?”<sup>26</sup>Jesus answered, “It is he to whom I will give this morsel of bread when I have dipped it.” So when he had dipped the morsel, he gave it to Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot.<sup>27</sup>Then after he had taken the morsel, Satan entered into him.
