You will seek me, and just as I said to the Jews, so now I also say to you, ’Where I am going you cannot come.’<sup>34</sup>A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another: just as I have loved you, you also are to love one another.<sup>35</sup>By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.”<sup>36</sup>Simon Peter said to him, “Lord, where are you going?” Jesus answered him, “Where I am going you cannot follow me now, but you will follow afterward.”<sup>37</sup>Peter said to him, “Lord, why can I not follow you now? I will lay down my life for you.”<sup>38</sup>Jesus answered, “Will you lay down your life for me? Truly, truly, I say to you, the rooster will not crow till you have denied me three times.
13.overview:
With chapter 13 the “book of glory” begins. The public ministry is over, and for five chapters (13–17) Jesus is alone with his disciples on the night before he dies. John opens with a sentence that sums up the cross: having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end. Jesus washes his disciples’ feet, the task of a slave.

Then, troubled, he exposes the betrayer with a morsel of bread, and Judas goes out: “and it was night.” With the betrayer gone, Jesus speaks of his glorification, gives the new commandment to love one another as he has loved them, and foretells Peter’s denial.

14.title: I Am the Way, the Truth, and the Life

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — The Way to the Father
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus calls his troubled disciples to trust him as they trust God. He goes to prepare a place and will return for them; he is the one way to the Father, and in him the Father is seen. Because he goes to the Father, they will do greater works, and he will answer what they ask in his name.
verseByVerse.theology: I am the way, and the truth, and the life is both comfort and exclusivity. Comfort: there is a real way to the Father, and it is Jesus. Exclusivity: it is the only way. This is not arrogance but follows from the incarnation: if God has come in one person, for one purpose, then there is one way home, and that offence cannot be removed without removing the gospel.
verseByVerse.examples: Whatever you ask in my name (v. 13). Prayer in Jesus’ name is not a formula attached to the end of requests but asking as he would ask, for what he would ask, to the Father’s glory. Such prayer brings our desires into line with God’s will, and his will always accomplishes its purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: "Let not your hearts be troubled. Believe in God; believe also in me. In my Father's house are many rooms. If it were not so, would I have told you that I go to prepare a place for you?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. John 14 is Jesus’ comfort to frightened disciples. He has just told them he is leaving, that one of them will betray him, and that Peter will deny him. Now he tells them why they need not be troubled: he is going to prepare a place for them, he is the way to the Father, he will send the Spirit, and he gives them his peace. It is read at countless funerals, and it was first spoken by a man on the last night of his life to the friends he was about to die for.

The setting. The meal is over, Judas has gone out into the night, and eleven men remain in the upper room. Peter has just been told he will deny his Lord three times before dawn. There is no break between 13:38 and 14:1; the comfort comes straight after the warning, to the man who will fail and to the others who will scatter.

Let not your hearts be troubled. Troubled (tarassesthō) means stirred up, agitated, churned, and John has used it of Jesus himself three times already: at the tomb of Lazarus (11:33), in the temple (12:27), and at this table an hour ago (13:21). So this is not a man telling frightened people to pull themselves together. It is the only person in the room who has been visibly shaken three times in three chapters, and he knows precisely what he is asking. He was troubled so that they need not be.

Hearts, and one heart. In Greek the word your is plural, spoken to all of them, but the word heart is singular. That is ordinary Greek idiom, yet it fits the scene: one shared fear in eleven men. The command does not forbid the feeling. It forbids letting it settle in and take charge.

Believe also in me. The remedy is not an explanation but two imperatives with an astonishing claim in the second. The Greek can be read as commands or statements; most likely, keep trusting God, and keep trusting me. Either way the structure is the same: whatever trust they place in God, place the identical trust in the man sitting opposite them. Nobody in Israel could have said that sentence and remained a faithful Jew, unless it was true.

Many rooms. The rooms are monai, dwelling places, and the noun comes straight from menō, the abiding word that will run through the whole of chapter 15. A monē is a staying place, somewhere one remains. The old translation mansions is not a mistranslation so much as a word that has drifted; it came from the Latin mansiones, which meant dwellings or stopping places. What the text promises is not grand apartments but room to stay, permanently, in a great family house, and the emphasis falls on many. There is room for all the Father has given the Son.

If it were not so, would I have told you that I go to prepare a place for you? The ESV notes an alternative reading of verse 2: if it were not so, I would have told you; for I go to prepare a place for you. Something like that reading is familiar from the KJV. Either way, the point is that Jesus would never mislead them. He is going ahead to make ready. The cross is the preparation; the resurrection and ascension complete it.

How can I stop my heart being troubled? Not by pretending the trouble is not there. Jesus does not tell the disciples that nothing bad is coming; the darkest night of their lives is a few hours away. He gives them something to do with the trouble: trust God, and trust him. In practice that means taking the specific thing that troubles you and placing it, in prayer, in the hands of the God who has shown his heart in Jesus. It means reminding yourself of what he has promised, a room, his return, his presence, his peace, and saying them back to him. The feelings may not go at once. But a troubled heart that keeps turning to Christ is already obeying this verse.

On a Tuesday. When anxiety rises today, the bill, the test result, the child who will not speak to you, say this verse aloud, slowly, name what is troubling you, and say: I trust you with this, Lord Jesus. Do it as many times as the trouble returns.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes an alternative reading of verse 2: “if it were not so, I would have told you, for I go to prepare a place for you.” Family houses were often extended with rooms as the family grew.

parallels.desc: I shall dwell in the house of the LORD forever

verseByVerse.quote: "And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and will take you to myself, that where I am you may be also. And you know the way to where I am going."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Prepare a place. How does he prepare it? By his death, resurrection and ascension he opens the way into the Father’s presence, entering as our forerunner behind the curtain (Hebrews 6:19–20; 9:24). In the temple a curtain shut off the Most Holy Place, where God’s presence dwelt, and only the high priest went in, once a year, with blood (Hebrews 9:7). Jesus has gone into God’s very presence ahead of us, by his own blood (Hebrews 9:12), and because he is there, the way is open for us. The place is prepared by the cross.

I will come again. The promise has been read four ways. Some have taken it of the resurrection, which is three days off; some of Pentecost; some of his coming to each believer at death; and most, rightly, of his visible return at the end of the age (Acts 1:11; 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17). The reason the last is best is the second half of the sentence: that where I am you may be also. The resurrection appearances did not accomplish that; he left again. Pentecost did not, in the sense meant here. What is being described is a fetching, and a permanent one.

Take you to myself. The verb is domestic rather than judicial: paralambanō, to take somebody along with you, to receive them to yourself. It is the word for collecting a person, not summoning him. The trumpet and the judgement seat are genuinely biblical, but they are not what Jesus reaches for at a supper table with frightened men. What he says is: I am going to get a room ready, and then I am coming back for you personally.

Where I am. The purpose clause is the whole point. Not that you may be in a good place or comfortable at last, but with him. Heaven is defined here entirely by a location relative to a person. Whatever else is true of it, and Scripture says a great deal elsewhere about a body, a city and a new earth, the reason given for the whole operation is that he wants them where he is (17:24; Philippians 1:23). The heart of heaven is not the place but the person.

Where Christians differ: the coming again and the rapture. Dispensationalists (Christians who read God’s dealings with Israel and with the church as distinct stages) see this as a secret rapture before a seven-year tribulation, distinct from Christ’s visible return. They long for his coming as much as anyone; the question is how many comings Scripture describes, and the passage most used for a secret rapture speaks of a shout, an archangel’s voice and the trumpet of God (1 Thessalonians 4:16). This commentary’s view: Scripture speaks of one return of Christ, visible, glorious, and final, at which the dead are raised, believers caught up to meet him, and the world judged (Matthew 24:30–31; 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–10). There is no secret rapture. The Lord comes once, and takes his people to be with him for ever.

You know the way. Jesus says they know it; Thomas is about to say flatly that they do not. Both are true, which is the point of the exchange: they had been walking the way for years without ever having heard it named. They know him, and he is the way (v. 6).

What happens to a Christian who dies before Jesus comes back? He goes at once to be with Christ. Paul says that to depart is to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23), and that to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). There is no sleep of the soul in between and no purgatory; the believer’s soul, made perfect in holiness, is received into heaven at death, while the body rests in the grave until the resurrection (the Westminster Confession 32.1; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 31.1). Then, when Christ returns, the dead in Christ will be raised with glorified bodies, and all his people together will be with him for ever. So this promise holds for those who have already died: he will come for them too.

For worship. The Lord of glory has gone ahead to make ready, and he will not send for us; he will come himself. He will take us to himself, as a bridegroom takes his bride home, and where he is we will be. All the comfort of heaven is gathered up in that one promise: with him, for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: Thomas said to him, "Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?" Jesus said to him, "I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thomas’s question. Give Thomas (11:16; 20:25) his due: he is the one man in the room willing to say he is lost, and his question produces one of the most quoted sentences in the Gospel. Bewildered people who admit it out loud have done the church more good than confident people who do not.

I am the way, and the truth, and the life. This is the sixth of Jesus’ great I am sayings in John, and perhaps the most comprehensive. Three definite articles: not a way, not one truth among others. And not I show the way, but I am the way; he does not point to a road, he is the road. The truth: he is the reality of God revealed (1:14, 17), not merely accurate information but God as he is. The life: he is the source of eternal life (1:4; 11:25), the life of God shared with humanity, beginning now and continuing for ever.

The way is the main idea. The three are not a list of separate titles. The second two explain the first: he is the way because he is the truth about God and the life of God. A road that does not correspond to reality leads nowhere, and a road that cannot carry you alive is no use either.

No one comes to the Father. Now the hard half, and it should be met directly, because it is the sentence that makes Christianity intolerable to many decent people: there are not many ways to God, but one (Acts 4:12; 1 Timothy 2:5). Three things need saying. The first is that the offence is not removable. Every attempt to soften this into Jesus is the way for Christians founders on the grammar. If it is not true it is monstrous, and if it is true it is the best news there has ever been, and it is hard to find a third position.

Not a boast. The second is that the exclusivity is not a boast about the people who hold it. Christians have used this verse to feel superior, and that is an abuse of it. The sentence says there is one bridge; it says nothing about the merit of the people crossing it, and this Gospel has been at pains to establish that they have none. Nor is the Christian alone in making an exclusive claim. The person who says that all religions lead to God is also saying that every religion which denies it is wrong; the only question is whose exclusive claim is true, and this one was made by a man who backed it by rising from the dead.

Where Christians differ: are there other ways to God? Many today hold that all religions lead to God (pluralism), or that people may be saved through Christ without knowing him, by following the light they have (inclusivism). This commentary’s view: no one comes to the Father except through me leaves no exceptions, and Acts 4:12 says there is no other name under heaven by which we must be saved. Salvation is through conscious faith in Christ (Romans 10:13–17). This is why the church must send missionaries. It is not arrogance to say this; it is what Jesus himself said. And the way is open to anyone, from any background, who comes through him.

What about those who never heard? This is the question everybody actually wants answered. No one is saved except through Christ, and no one comes to the Father but through him. Those who never hear are not condemned for rejecting a message they never received, but for their sins against the light of creation and conscience they did have (Romans 1:18–20; 2:12–16). Some Christians hope that God may save people who respond to that light without knowing Christ; but Scripture never promises it, and Paul’s argument is that faith comes from hearing the word of Christ (Romans 10:14–17). Infants dying in infancy, and those unable to understand, are a different case: the elect among them are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where he pleases, and there we may rest in the mercy of the Judge of all the earth who will do what is just (Genesis 18:25). Parents who have lost a little one may hold on to that: David, grieving his infant son, expected to go to him (2 Samuel 12:23), and many Reformed pastors have taught that God’s mercy to such little ones is large. The right response to this question is not speculation but sending.

An answer to a frightened man. The third thing to say is what the sentence is doing where it stands. It is not a boundary marker put up against outsiders. It is an answer to a frightened disciple asking how to get home, and the answer is that the way is not a map or a technique or a standard, but the man who is talking to him.

On a Tuesday. Think of someone trying to reach God by another road: good works, another religion, spirituality without Christ, or simply hoping it will be all right. Bring them to the Father in prayer today. And if the opportunity comes, tell them gently and plainly that Jesus said he is the way, and that the way is open to them.
verseByVerse.note: This is the sixth of Jesus’ “I am” sayings in John.

parallels.desc: no other name
the Way

verseByVerse.quote: "If you had known me, you would have known my Father also. From now on you do know him and have seen him." Philip said to him, "Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
From now on you do know him. To know Jesus is to know the Father (8:19). And the promise, easy to miss under Philip’s interruption, is that from the coming hour of the cross and resurrection something changes, not in what is available to be seen, which has stood in front of them since Cana, but in their capacity to see it. The Spirit is promised nine verses later. That is worth having for anyone who has read the Gospels a long time and found them flat. The problem is not usually the light but our eyes, and opening them is the Spirit’s work.

Show us the Father. Philip’s request is one of the oldest in the Bible. Moses had asked it: please show me your glory (Exodus 33:18). He was told he could not see God’s face and live, hidden in a cleft of rock while the glory passed, and permitted to see only the back. Now a man from Bethsaida asks the same thing, and adds that it would be enough. He is right about that. And the answer he gets is not a refusal. It is that the request has been granted all along and he has not noticed.

What Philip assumes. His request assumes that the Father is somewhere else, and that Jesus might be able to arrange an introduction. That is the natural religious instinct: the visible teacher is a means of access to the invisible God behind him. Everything in this Gospel has been dismantling it, and here it is again, sincerely meant, from a man who has been present for all of it.

In the flow. This whole conversation is carried forward by interruptions. Peter asked where he was going (13:36), Thomas how to know the way (v. 5), Philip to be shown the Father (v. 8), and Judas, not Iscariot, will ask why he shows himself to them and not to the world (v. 22). Each question is a misunderstanding, and each answer goes deeper. It is the promise of the prologue being kept: no one has ever seen God, and the only Son has made him known (1:18).

Will I ever see God? Yes. Scripture promises that the pure in heart will see God (Matthew 5:8), and that his servants will see his face (Revelation 22:4). That sight will come in glory, when we see Christ as he is and are made like him (1 John 3:2). Now we see by faith, through the Son whom the Scriptures show us. But the God you will one day see face to face is not a stranger behind Jesus; he is the Father whose heart you have already seen in the Son. Seeing God in glory will not be meeting someone new, but seeing fully the One you have known.

For worship. Moses was hidden in the rock while the glory passed by. Philip was sitting at the table with it, and the glory had just washed his feet. The God who could not be looked on and lived has come close enough to be looked at, touched and misunderstood, and to have him is to have enough.

parallels.desc: please show me your glory

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to him, "Have I been with you so long, and you still do not know me, Philip? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father. How can you say, 'Show us the Father'? Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? The words that I say to you I do not speak on my own authority, but the Father who dwells in me does his works."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Have I been with you so long, and you still do not know me, Philip? A gentle rebuke, with sadness in it rather than anger: three years together, and Philip still asks. It is one of the very few places where we are allowed to hear what it cost him to be misunderstood by his friends.

Whoever has seen me has seen the Father. It does not say Jesus is the Father; since the first verse of the book the Word was with God and was God, a distinct person. Nor does it say Jesus merely resembles the Father or teaches accurately about him. It says that looking at the one is seeing the other. Jesus is the image of the invisible God, the exact imprint of his nature (Colossians 1:15; Hebrews 1:3). The Father is fully revealed in the Son.

No God behind Jesus. That settles something that would otherwise remain permanently open. There is a suspicion, very old and still current, that behind the kindness of Jesus stands a different sort of God: sterner, more remote, harder to please. It survives in people who are perfectly orthodox on paper. They trust Christ and are afraid of God, and they would not put it that way, but it governs how they pray. This verse forbids it. There is no God behind Jesus who is unlike him. Look at Jesus: his compassion, his holiness, his tears at the tomb, his anger in the temple, his hands washing feet, his body on the cross. The face that wept at a grave, and knelt with a towel, and did not break a bruised reed, is the face.

Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? The mutual indwelling (10:38), later called by the church the perichoresis of the persons, is not offered as a speculation but as the reason his words and works are what they are. In other words, the Father and the Son are two persons, not one person wearing two masks, and yet they are not two Gods side by side: each is wholly in the other, sharing the one divine life (10:30).

Not on my own authority. His words and works are the Father’s, done through him. He claims almost nothing for himself in a sentence that claims everything.

But is the God of the Old Testament not harsher than Jesus? No; he is the same God, and Jesus himself said so. The God who thundered at Sinai is the God who proclaimed his name as merciful and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love (Exodus 34:6), and Jesus is the full showing of that name. And the Jesus of the Gospels is not soft: he drove traders from the temple, pronounced woes on hypocrites, and, it is often said, spoke more about hell than anyone else in Scripture. Holiness and love meet in both Testaments, and they meet perfectly in Christ, and supremely at the cross. Read the Old Testament through him, and the one God comes into focus.

On a Tuesday. Consider the picture of God that comes up unbidden when you pray badly, or when you have failed. If what appears is a face that is disappointed, or cold, or busy elsewhere, then something other than this verse is furnishing the image, and it needs correcting from a Gospel rather than from experience. Read one Gospel scene today and let it redraw the picture.

verseByVerse.quote: "Believe me that I am in the Father and the Father is in me, or else believe on account of the works themselves. Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do; and greater works than these will he do, because I am going to the Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believe me. His own testimony is the first and best ground of faith; or else the works, for he meets weak faith where it is and gives it something to hold. And whoever believes means not the apostles only, not the specially gifted.

Greater works than these. This promise is claimed far too much and believed far too little. It cannot mean more impressive miracles: nobody in Acts or since has fed five thousand from a boy’s lunch or called a man four days dead out of a cave. Jesus supplies the reason in the clause attached: because I am going to the Father. So it is not a promise about the disciples’ capacities but about what becomes possible once the ascension has happened and the Spirit has come (16:7).

Greater in scope. Jesus in his earthly ministry was one man, in one province, speaking to whatever village his feet reached. Within thirty years of that supper the message was in Rome. He is describing a work that would go where he did not go in the flesh, through people who could be in a hundred places at once because there were a hundred of them.

Greater in effect. On the day of Pentecost Peter preached one sermon and about three thousand people were converted (Acts 2:41), far more than the hundred and twenty believers who had gathered after the ascension (Acts 1:15), and the gospel went to the nations. Nothing like that happened in his ministry, because the cross had not happened yet. Peter could preach a finished atonement (Christ’s death fully paying for sin) and a risen Lord; Jesus in the days of his flesh preached a coming one. The disciples’ sermons were greater in the only sense that finally matters: they could tell people the thing had been done.

Where Christians differ: greater works and miracles. Some take this as a promise that every believer can do greater miracles than Jesus. Others, including many Pentecostal and charismatic brothers and sisters, do not claim that, but do believe the miraculous gifts continue today, and they should be heard with charity. This commentary’s view: no believer has ever done greater miracles than Jesus; the promise must mean something else. The greater works are the saving works of the Spirit through the gospel, bringing people from death to life. Miraculous sign gifts accompanied the apostles to confirm their message (Hebrews 2:3–4; 2 Corinthians 12:12), and ceased with the apostolic age (the generation of the apostles). The reason for that conclusion is that the message these signs confirmed now stands complete in the New Testament; it does not limit God, who still heals in answer to prayer when he pleases. But the greatest work, new birth, goes on wherever the gospel is preached.

Both guards. Against the overreach: this verse does not license a Christian to expect more remarkable deeds than Jesus did, and preachers who have promised such things have left disappointed and ashamed people behind them. Against the deflation: it is a promise, not a metaphor, fulfilled in public. The ordinary Christian who says something true about Christ to somebody who then believes it has taken part in a work that Jesus, in the days of his flesh, did not do in that way. And the work is still his: it is the risen Christ, working by his Spirit through his people, who saves.

Can I do greater works if I am not a preacher? Yes, because the greater works are not about platform but about the gospel reaching people. The mother teaching her children the faith, the friend who invites a colleague to church, the believer who gives so a missionary can go, the church member who prays for the lost by name: all of these share in the work of bringing people from death to life. The power is not in you but in the Spirit Christ sends, and in the word. You are not asked to be impressive; you are asked to be a faithful witness.
verseByVerse.note: “Greater works” refers to the worldwide spread of the gospel after the Spirit came.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whatever you ask in my name, this I will do, that the Father may be glorified in the Son. If you ask me anything in my name, I will do it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whatever you ask. This is one of the most quoted and most quietly resented promises in the New Testament, and it needs to be met head-on, because someone reading it prayed for something enormous and did not get it. Read as a blank cheque, the sentence is falsified by the life of every Christian who has ever lived, including the men it was spoken to. Paul asked three times for the thorn to be taken away and was refused (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). Jesus himself asked that, if it were possible, the cup might pass, and drank it. Every one of the eleven at that table prayed for things they did not receive, and, as early tradition records, most of them died violently. So either the promise is false, or it means something other than the flat reading. And the qualification is not hidden in the small print; it is in the middle of the sentence.

In my name. In the ancient world a person’s name stood for his character and authority; to act in someone’s name was to act as his representative, within his commission. An ambassador can commit his government to anything the government would want and nothing it would not. So praying in Jesus’ name means praying as his representatives, according to his will and for his glory (1 John 5:14). It is not a magic formula added to the end of a prayer. To pray in Jesus’ name is to come to the Father on the basis of who Jesus is and what he has done, and to ask what he would ask.

That the Father may be glorified. The purpose of prayer stands openly in the sentence as its boundary. The promise is unlimited within it and does not exist outside it.

Ask me. The words mean prayer to Jesus himself, as well as to the Father. A modern Bible may footnote it, since some manuscripts omit the word me, and the KJV follows them. If it stands, it is remarkable: prayer directed to Jesus, said by Jesus, at a table with Jews who prayed only to God. Prayer to Christ is right, because he is God (Acts 7:59).

What it does not mean. It does not mean we can get anything we want by saying in Jesus’ name. Prayer in his name is prayer shaped by his will and aimed at the Father’s glory. Underneath the blank-cheque reading lies an old idol: a god who signs whatever we write. Prayer in Jesus’ name hands our plans back to a Father wiser than we are, and that is a relief, not a loss.

What about the good prayer that was refused? Something must be said to the person for whom all that is cold comfort, because the honest difficulty is not the greedy prayer. It is the prayer that was plainly good, healing for a child, a marriage saved, a friend brought to faith, that was refused, when the sufferer knows perfectly well it was the kind of thing the Father is glorified by. Two things are true. The first is that Scripture never explains each case. There is no verse that accounts for why one good prayer is answered and another is not, and any commentary that produces a formula is selling something. The second is that the New Testament everywhere assumes the refusals are not indifference. The same Gospel has a man deliberately waiting two days while his friend died (11:6), and the family got more than they asked for and nothing like what they wanted at the time. A refused prayer is heard by a Father who is working a greater good than we can see (Romans 8:28), and who will one day show us why.

On a Tuesday. Take one thing you are praying for and ask whether Jesus would ask for it and how it would glorify the Father. The prayer may change shape, or you may find you can pray it with new boldness. Then pray it in Jesus’ name, and leave the answer with him.
verseByVerse.note: Praying “in my name” means praying as his representatives, according to his will.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–31 — The Promise of the Spirit and the Peace of Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Love for Jesus shows itself in keeping his word, and he will not leave his people orphaned: the Spirit of truth will be with them for ever, and through him Jesus and the Father come and make their home with them. The Spirit will remind them of all he said. He leaves them his peace, tells them that his going to the Father is cause for gladness, and rises to go out and meet the ruler of this world, who has no claim on him.
verseByVerse.theology: The Helper (*paraklētos*, one called alongside) is described four ways in the farewell discourse: the Spirit of truth (14:17), who teaches and reminds (14:26), who bears witness about Jesus (15:26), and who convicts the world (16:8). Each is part of one mission: to apply what Jesus accomplished. He brings no new revelation beyond Jesus, but makes what Jesus said and did present to each generation.
verseByVerse.examples: Not as the world gives. The world’s peace is the absence of conflict and the management of anxiety. Jesus’ peace holds in the middle of trouble, because it is the wholeness of being right with God and secure in his love. The disciples will need it before the night is over.

verseByVerse.quote: "If you love me, you will keep my commandments. And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper, to be with you forever,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you love me, you will keep my commandments. This sets love and obedience in an order worth getting right, because reversed it becomes a machine for producing anxiety. He does not say keep my commandments and that will prove you love me. It is a plain future, a statement about what love does, not a test love must pass. Love shows itself in obedience (vv. 21, 23; 1 John 5:3). Keep (tērēsete) means guard, treasure, obey. The Spirit who is given writes the law on the heart, creating the desire to obey that the law alone could not create.

Another Helper. The word has no good English equivalent, which is why translations disagree: Helper, Comforter, Advocate, Counsellor; some simply transliterate it, Paraclete (the ESV margin gives Advocate or Counselor). Paraklētos means, literally, one called alongside. In ordinary Greek it was a legal term: the friend you brought to court with you, not so much a hired advocate as somebody of standing who stood at your side and spoke for you. Comforter is Wycliffe’s word and it has weakened badly; in his day it still carried the sense of strengthening (the Latin fortis means strong), not only of soothing.

Another. The word is allon: another, and the context makes it another of the same kind. Jesus has been their Helper; the Spirit will be another like him. John will call Jesus himself a paraklētos in his first letter, using the same word (1 John 2:1), so the promise is not a substitute of a lesser order: you are losing me, and you are getting one exactly like me. This also shows that the Spirit is a person, not a force: Jesus would not compare himself to a power. And the Trinity is here: the Son asks, the Father gives, the Spirit comes.

To be with you forever. They have had Jesus in the flesh for a few short years and are losing him tonight. What is coming has no term on it at all.

In the flow. Since 13:33 the disciples’ unspoken question has been how they can go on once he has gone. Verses 15–24 are the answer, with two threads: love for Jesus that keeps his word (vv. 15, 21, 23), and the coming of the Spirit, through whom Jesus himself comes back to them (vv. 16–18).

What if I do not feel that I love Jesus enough to obey him? Then start where the love starts: not with your love for him, but his for you. We love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). Love for Christ grows as you look at what he has done, so read the Gospels, sit at the cross, and remember your forgiveness. Then obey in the small thing in front of you, even without strong feeling. Obedience is often how love is learned, as a child learns love for a parent partly by trusting and doing what he says. And the Helper is given precisely because you cannot do this alone. Ask him for love, and he gives it (Romans 5:5).

On a Tuesday. Before a hard conversation, a difficult task, or a temptation you know is coming, pause and ask the Spirit to stand with you and give you words and strength. Then go in, not alone.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “Helper” can also be rendered “Advocate” or “Counselor.” “Another” implies one like Jesus himself.

parallels.desc: an advocate with the Father

verseByVerse.quote: "even the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him. You know him, for he dwells with you and will be in you. I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit of truth. He is the Spirit who brings and teaches the truth, and the truth is Christ (15:26; 16:13). The unbelieving world, which neither sees him nor knows him, has no capacity to receive him (1 Corinthians 2:14), because spiritual sight requires the new birth he creates.

With you and in you. Two prepositions mark the change of an age: with you now, in the person of Jesus; in you after Pentecost. The Spirit had always been at work: he came upon judges and prophets and kings, and rested on Jesus without measure. But in the old covenant he came and went, and came on particular people for particular tasks. What is promised here is permanent residence in ordinary believers, which is precisely what Ezekiel and Joel had said would mark the last days (Ezekiel 36:27; Joel 2:28–29). The ESV notes that some manuscripts read and is in you. The difference is small; the future reading fits the context of Jesus’ promise better.

Not as orphans. Orphans (orphanous) means bereaved children, and disciples whose teacher had died were sometimes called orphans. So he is naming exactly what they are about to be, and denying it. By tomorrow evening they will look, to anybody watching, precisely like a school whose master has been executed: leaderless, frightened, with nothing to do but go home. He tells them in advance that the appearance will be false.

I will come to you. Not I will send help, but I will come: in the resurrection appearances (v. 19), and by the Spirit, who brings Christ’s own presence (v. 23). The coming of the Spirit is the coming of Christ himself to his people, by another route.

For the one who has lost the person who explained things. There is a particular loneliness that belongs to people who have lost the one who made the world make sense: a parent, a mentor, a pastor. This verse was spoken to eleven men about to be exactly that, by the man they were about to lose, and what he promised was not a replacement but his own return.

How do I know the Spirit is in me? Not chiefly by unusual feelings, but by what he does. The Spirit makes you confess that Jesus is Lord (1 Corinthians 12:3), makes you cry out to God as Father (Romans 8:15–16), makes you love Christ and his people, gives you a hatred of your sin and a desire to be holy, and opens the Scriptures to you so that they speak. If you have trusted Christ, the Spirit dwells in you, for anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him (Romans 8:9). You do not have to earn a second gift; you have been given the Helper.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “and is in you.”

verseByVerse.quote: "Yet a little while and the world will see me no more, but you will see me. Because I live, you also will live. In that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The world will see me no more. After his death the world will not see him again until he returns; the disciples will see him in the resurrection appearances, and by faith.

Because I live. The ground is stated as a fact, and the consequence follows from it and not from anything about the disciples. I live is present tense: he is the living one, even facing death. His resurrection life is the source and guarantee of theirs, both now in the new birth and at the last in the resurrection of their bodies. Paul says the same thing in a sentence that is unanswerable if this one is true: if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile (1 Corinthians 15:17).

Where assurance rests. That is where a Christian’s assurance finally rests. The question is not whether my faith is strong enough to survive, or whether my grip will hold. It is whether he is alive. If the answer to that is yes, the rest follows by the logic of this verse, and the strength of my grip is not what holds me.

In that day. That day is the day of resurrection and Pentecost. Three circles of union run from the life of God outward: the Father and the Son, the believer in the Son, the Son in the believer. It is not merely a comparison but a series of nested indwellings, and the outermost is God’s own; we are drawn into the fellowship of the Trinity (17:21–23). And it will be known only in that day, not by argument, when the Spirit comes and the whole evening becomes clear.

What does it mean to be in Christ? It means that by faith, through the Spirit, you are joined to him so closely that what is true of him becomes true of you. His death counts as your death to sin, his righteousness as your righteousness, his life as your life, his Father as your Father (Romans 6:4–11; 2 Corinthians 5:21). It is not a feeling, though it brings feelings; it is a fact God has made. Every blessing of salvation comes to you in him (Ephesians 1:3). And because it is his work, it does not come undone. The branch does not hold the vine; the vine holds the branch.

For worship. He said I live on the night before he died, and it was true even then, because death could hold his body only until the third day and could never take hold of him. The life he has is the life of God, and he has opened it to people who could only have died. Glory to the living one, who died and is alive for evermore and holds the keys of Death and Hades (Revelation 1:18), so that the grave of every believer is a locked room whose key is in the Saviour’s hand.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever has my commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves me. And he who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him." Judas (not Iscariot) said to him, "Lord, how is it that you will manifest yourself to us, and not to the world?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Has my commandments and keeps them. To have his commandments is to know them; to keep them is to do them. Love for Christ is not sentiment but allegiance expressed in the pattern of a life.

Loved by my Father. The chain of love here does not run the way religion expects. Read carelessly it is a transaction: love him, and God will love you back. It cannot be, because the same Gospel has already said the Father loved the world first (3:16), and John’s letter will make it explicit: we love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). What is described is not the beginning of the Father’s love but its answering movement. Somebody who has come to love Christ finds himself inside a love that was there before he arrived, and now comes toward him in a particular and personal way.

Manifest myself. Manifest (emphanisō) means make visible, show plainly. It is a promise of something experienced rather than merely believed, and it is the reason Judas asks his question.

Judas (not Iscariot). This Judas is Judas the son of James, probably the Thaddaeus of Matthew and Mark’s lists (Luke 6:16; Matthew 10:3). John’s parenthesis is one of the small human touches in this Gospel. By the time John is writing, the name has become a byword for treachery, and he will not let it stand without the note: a small mercy toward a man who did nothing wrong and had his name ruined by somebody else.

Lord, how is it that you will manifest yourself to us, and not to the world? He is not being slow. He expects the Messiah to show himself publicly to the world. If the Messiah is going to make himself plainly visible, surely that is a public event; the whole point of the messianic hope was a disclosure the nations could not miss. Why only to them?

Why does Jesus seem more real to some Christians than to me? Part of the answer is in this verse: he shows himself to those who love him and keep his word. Closeness to Christ grows along the path of obedience and his word, not by waiting for a special experience. Where there is unconfessed sin, neglect of Scripture, or a divided heart, the sense of his presence often fades. But not every dry season is caused by sin; godly believers have walked through long stretches of darkness while trusting him (Isaiah 50:10). Keep reading, keep praying, keep obeying, and keep company with his people. He has promised to make himself known, and he keeps his promises.

On a Tuesday. Choose one command of Christ you know you have been slow to keep: forgiving someone, speaking truthfully, being generous, guarding your eyes. Keep it today, as an act of love for the one who loved you first, leaning on the Helper he has given; he delights to make himself known to those who walk with him.
verseByVerse.note: This Judas is Judas the son of James, probably the Thaddaeus of Matthew and Mark.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered him, "If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him. Whoever does not love me does not keep my words. And the word that you hear is not mine but the Father's who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If anyone loves me. Jesus answers Judas indirectly, and the condition is repeated for the third time in this chapter. Whatever else this indwelling is, it is not available to mere admiration.

Make our home with him. One word turns the whole chapter round, and it is invisible in English. Home is monē, the singular of the rooms of verse 2. So the chapter has two dwelling places pointing in opposite directions: Jesus goes to prepare a dwelling for us in the Father’s house, and meanwhile the Father and the Son come to make their dwelling in us.

The answer to Judas. How will he manifest himself to us and not to the world? By moving in. The disclosure is not a display the nations could photograph; it is the Father and the Son taking up residence in a person, which is a thing only that person and God can know.

We. Father and Son together, by the Spirit: in the same discourse the Spirit is given to be with them for ever (v. 16) and to be in them (v. 17), so all three are described in one chapter as taking up residence in ordinary people. The whole Trinity dwells in the believer. Every believer is a temple of God (1 Corinthians 3:16; 6:19). And where God dwells, the place is holy. The tabernacle was hedged with curtains and sacrifices; now the holy God lives in sinners he has cleansed, which is both the deepest comfort and the most searching call to holiness (2 Corinthians 6:16–7:1).

The dwelling moves into people. This is the fulfilment of the promise that ran through the whole Old Testament. God dwelt in a tent, and then in a temple, and the glory departed from it in Ezekiel’s vision (Ezekiel 10). John said at the start of this Gospel that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (1:14). Now the dwelling moves again, into people.

Not mine but the Father’s. The other side. To reject Christ’s word is to reject the Father’s. The stakes of hearing the gospel are as high as its source.

If God lives in me, why do I still sin so much? Because the house is being renovated while he lives in it. God does not wait for a believer to be perfect before he moves in; he moves in to make him holy. His presence is the reason you now hate your sin and fight it, which you did not before. Your body is his temple (1 Corinthians 6:19), so sin is now a grief to him (Ephesians 4:30), and that should make you serious. But it is not a reason to doubt that he dwells in you. He has not moved in to move out again: the work he began in you he will finish (Philippians 1:6).

On a Tuesday. Ask what in your life you would be ashamed for the Father and the Son to see: the screen, the grudge, the habit. Clear one room today, not to earn his presence but because he is already there.

For worship. Solomon asked whether God would indeed dwell on the earth, when even the highest heaven cannot contain him (1 Kings 8:27). The answer is given in every believer: the Father and the Son come, not to a house of cedar and gold, but to sinners whom the blood of the Son has made clean, and they come to stay. The high and lofty One who inhabits eternity dwells with the contrite and lowly in spirit (Isaiah 57:15), and calls the place home.

parallels.desc: my dwelling place shall be with them

verseByVerse.quote: "These things I have spoken to you while I am still with you. But the Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
While I am still with you. They have heard much they do not yet understand. But the Helper, the Holy Spirit, will be sent by the Father in the Son’s name: as the Son’s representative, to continue his work. This is the first time in the Gospel that the full title the Holy Spirit appears in Jesus’ own teaching.

Teach and remind. The second verb is the more remarkable: a promise about memory, made to men who had misunderstood much of what they were told. As far as we know, nothing had been written down. The teaching of Jesus existed inside the heads of eleven frightened men, who within a few decades would need to hand it on accurately to churches all round the Mediterranean, and eventually into books.

The promise that grounds the New Testament. This is a promise especially to the apostles. The Spirit would remind them of all Jesus said, and teach them its meaning. This is the basis of the New Testament: the Gospels rest on the memory of men whom the Spirit helped to remember, by his work of inspiration (2 Peter 1:21), and the letters come from men whom he taught. We have the apostles’ testimony in Scripture because of this promise. And John, writing decades later, reproduces long discourses, exact phrases, the fragrance of the ointment, the number of the water jars, the seating at a supper. Detail alone does not prove an eyewitness, and some scholars take the discourses as the church’s later reflection; John’s own claim is that the Spirit reminded rather than invented, and the church received his Gospel as the testimony of one who was there (21:24).

In the flow. Verse 25 opens the last paragraph of the chapter, where Jesus gathers up his threads: the Helper of verse 16 is named in full and given his first task, peace is bequeathed, and the opening words return (v. 27).

Where Christians differ: the Spirit’s teaching today. Some claim the Spirit gives new revelation today, beyond Scripture. Most who speak of such words do not mean to add to the Bible, and many test what they hear by it; the real question is whether such words carry God’s authority. This commentary’s view: the promise is first to the apostles, and was fulfilled in the New Testament, which is complete and sufficient (Jude 3; 2 Timothy 3:16–17). The Spirit still teaches every believer, not by new revelation, but by illuminating the Scripture he inspired. The canon is closed; the Spirit opens our eyes to it.

The boundary. The Spirit does not bring new material. Everything in the two verbs is tethered to what Jesus said: teaching all things, and reminding of all that I have said to you. Every claim to fresh revelation that adds to or contradicts what is in these books has this verse standing against it. That cuts against a particular kind of enthusiasm, and also against dryness. The Spirit is not a source of information beyond Christ, nor is he an idea; his work is to make what Christ said land in a person who has read it many times without it moving anything.

Does the Spirit still guide me personally? Yes, but through his word, not beside it. He gives wisdom as you study Scripture, pray and take counsel (James 1:5); he brings to mind what you have read when you need it; he convicts, comforts and directs your heart along the lines Scripture has drawn. What you should not do is treat impressions, dreams or inner nudges as new words from God that bind you or others. Test every impression by Scripture, and where Scripture leaves a choice open, choose wisely and in faith, trusting God’s providence. A feeling may be from the Spirit, but only the Bible is certainly from him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. Not as the world gives do I give to you. Let not your hearts be troubled, neither let them be afraid. You heard me say to you, 'I am going away, and I will come to you.' If you loved me, you would have rejoiced, because I am going to the Father, for the Father is greater than I."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. Peace (shalom) was simply how a Jew said goodbye: the everyday greeting and farewell, what you said at a door, and it still is. So the sentence begins as the most ordinary farewell in the language. And leave is what a man does in a will. He is dying tomorrow and disposing of his estate, and this is what is in it. His peace is wholeness, right relationship with God, the calm that comes from reconciliation (Romans 5:1; Philippians 4:7), bought at the cross by the one who bequeaths it.

Not as the world gives. The world’s peace is the absence of trouble, sought in control: money, health, the children settled, our reputation safe. It lasts only as long as the circumstances do, which is why it leaves us anxious even while we have it. The world’s shalom at a doorway is a wish that commits the speaker to nothing; he is distinguishing a bequest from a pleasantry. What he bequeaths is not a quiet life. Within hours the men receiving it will scatter into the dark. It means that the thing which makes a person whole, being right with God, has been settled elsewhere and cannot be reached by circumstances. Christ’s peace holds in the middle of trouble (16:33).

Neither let them be afraid. The chapter returns to its start. He has been talking for a whole chapter and the fear is still in the room, so he says it again, and adds the word for what they are actually feeling.

You would have rejoiced. His going is gain for him: return to glory.

For the Father is greater than I. How can this be, if the Son is equal with God (5:18; 10:30)? Not greater in nature or being, but greater in position: in his incarnation and earthly mission, the Son took the role of a servant, and the Father sent him. Now he returns to the glory he had with the Father (17:5). The Son is equal with the Father in being, power and glory. In the work of salvation he willingly came as the one the Father sent and obeyed him, even to death (5:19, 30; Philippians 2:6–8). That submission belongs to his mission, not to any inferiority of nature, and it shows that order and equality are not rivals.

Where Christians differ. Arians in the fourth century (followers of Arius, who taught that the Son was the first and highest created being), and Jehovah’s Witnesses today, cite this verse to show that the Son is a lesser being. This commentary’s view: the same Gospel calls him God (1:1; 20:28). This verse speaks of his incarnate state, as the one sent; greater refers to role and position, not essence. A son can be equal to his father in nature and still honour his father as the head of the house. Athanasius and the Nicene Creed held both truths together.

Four answers to the Arian reading. This was an anchor text of Arius, whose teaching the Council of Nicaea was called to answer, and it is the verse a Jehovah’s Witness is most likely to open at your door. Four things answer it. First, look at what the sentence is for. It is not a concession wrung out of him in debate; it is a reason he gives his friends to be glad. Nobody offers a confession of inferiority as consolation. Second, the word is greater, not better. Greater is the language of position: a king is greater than his son without being more human than he is. Third, and this is decisive, consider who wrote it down. The same man in the same book tells us the Word was God (1:1), that Jesus said I and the Father are one (10:30) and before Abraham was, I am (8:58), and closes with Thomas saying to him, my Lord and my God, uncorrected (20:28). A sentence must be read inside the book it belongs to. Fourth, remember where he is standing. He is hours from the cross, having taken the form of a servant, the one whom Paul describes as being in the form of God and not counting equality with God a thing to be grasped (Philippians 2:6–7). A man on his way to be crucified saying the Father is greater is telling you where he has placed himself, not what he is: greater in office, equal in nature. And there is tenderness in it. He is not lecturing them about the Trinity but telling frightened men that where he is going is better, and that if they loved him they would be glad for him.

How do I keep Christ’s peace when life is falling apart? By remembering where it is kept. His peace does not live in your circumstances, so circumstances cannot take it; it lives in your standing with God, which he has settled by his blood. When fear rises, bring it to him in prayer with thanksgiving, and the peace of God will guard your heart (Philippians 4:6–7). Fill your mind with what is true. Keep company with believers. And do not mistake feeling shaken for having lost his peace: Jesus himself was troubled in spirit while perfectly at peace with the Father. The storm may be loud; the anchor still holds.
verseByVerse.note: “Peace” (shalom) was the everyday greeting and farewell. “The Father is greater” speaks of the Son in his humble human state, not a lesser divine nature.

parallels.desc: the LORD give you peace

verseByVerse.quote: "And now I have told you before it takes place, so that when it does take place you may believe. I will no longer talk much with you, for the ruler of this world is coming. He has no claim on me,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before it takes place. He did the same with the betrayal (13:19): he foretells the event so that, when it comes, it confirms their faith instead of destroying it. The disciples will endure the passion with greater faith because they remember these words.

The ruler of this world is coming. Satan comes through Judas and the soldiers (13:27; 18:3), through the temple police and the cohort with lanterns.

He has no claim on me. Literally, in me he has nothing. It can be pictured as a search: the enemy will go over this man and find nothing belonging to him, no handhold, no debt, no compromise. That is the claim of sinlessness stated in its most practical form, and it is what makes the next three days work.

The sting with nothing to inject. Everyone else who has ever died had something in them that death could rightly claim. Hebrews describes the devil as the one who has the power of death (Hebrews 2:14), and Paul puts the mechanism plainly: the sting of death is sin (1 Corinthians 15:56). The devil has a claim on every sinner, for the wages of sin is death (Romans 6:23). On Jesus he has none. So Jesus does not die because Satan has power over him, but freely, for love of the Father. When they come for him in the garden, they are arresting a man over whom they have no rights whatever, and he goes anyway.

Does the devil have a claim on me? If you are in Christ, no. His accusations are real, and some of them are true, but they have no legal force, because Christ has paid the debt in full and cancelled the record that stood against you, nailing it to the cross (Colossians 2:14). Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies (Romans 8:33). When the accuser reminds you of your sins, agree that they were real, and then point him to the cross where they were punished. He has nothing in Christ, and you are in Christ.

On a Tuesday. When guilt over a forgiven sin comes back at you today, answer it with Scripture, not feelings: there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). Say it aloud if you need to.

verseByVerse.quote: "but I do as the Father has commanded me, so that the world may know that I love the Father. Rise, let us go from here."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the Father has commanded me. The voluntary obedience of the Son is the world’s lesson in what love for the Father looks like.

That I love the Father. The only place in the Gospels where Jesus says in so many words that he loves the Father, and it is a startling reason to give for a crucifixion. The cross is a ransom, a substitution, a victory, and here he names it as a demonstration of his love for his Father, put on where the world can see it.

Rise, let us go from here. There is a real puzzle here, better faced than ignored: three more chapters of discourse follow before anybody actually leaves. Chapter 18:1 says that when Jesus had spoken these words, he went out with his disciples across the brook Kidron. Some think they left the upper room here, with chapters 15–17 spoken on the way to the garden, perhaps passing the vines on the slopes or the golden vine on the temple gate (15:1). Others think they rose but lingered, which is exactly what happens when people are about to part. Either is possible. Many scholars think instead that the words mark a seam, where the discourse once ended before chapters 15–17 were placed after it. That cannot be ruled out, and it would not make the words any less his; but the author could easily have removed a few words if they jarred, and he left them.

Not the words of a victim. Not they are coming for me, not it is time to hide. He is the one who ends the meal, opens the door, and sets off toward the garden where he knows Judas will bring the soldiers, because he told him to go and do it quickly. Nobody fetches him from the room; he goes out to meet them, in love, not under compulsion.

Why did Jesus have to obey the Father, if he is equal with him? Because in the plan of salvation the Son freely took the place of the servant, as the second Adam who would obey where the first disobeyed (Romans 5:19). His obedience is not the obedience of an inferior being but the willing obedience of a Son who shares the Father’s will and delights in it. And it was for us: his perfect obedience in life and death is counted to everyone who trusts him. When you obey God, you are not earning his favour; you are walking in the steps of the Son whose obedience has already won it for you.
verseByVerse.note: Some think they left the upper room here, with chapters 15–17 spoken on the way; others that they rose but stayed.

And the word that you hear is not mine but the Father’s who sent me.<sup>25</sup>“These things I have spoken to you while I am still with you.<sup>26</sup>But the Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you.<sup>27</sup>Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. He has no claim on me,<sup>31</sup>but I do as the Father has commanded me, so that the world may know that I love the Father. Rise, let us go from here.
14.overview:
Jesus has just told his friends that he is leaving, that one of them will betray him and that Peter will deny him. Into their fear he says: “Let not your hearts be troubled.” He is going to prepare a place for them in his Father’s house and will come again for them. Thomas’s question draws out that he is himself the way to the Father, and Philip’s that whoever has seen him has seen the Father.

The second half promises the Holy Spirit as “another Helper”, through whom Jesus himself comes to them, and in whom the Father and the Son make their home with those who love him. He leaves them his peace, and goes out to the cross so that the world may know that he loves the Father. The Trinity is not argued here but lived: the Father sends, the Son goes and prays, the Spirit comes, and all three make their home with the believer.

15.title: The True Vine

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — Abide in Me: The Vine and the Branches
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus is the true vine and his Father the vinedresser, who removes fruitless branches and prunes fruitful ones. The disciples must stay joined to him, his words in them, and so live in his love, share his joy, and love one another. He calls them friends, chosen and appointed to bear fruit that lasts.
verseByVerse.theology: Israel was the vine God planted, and repeatedly failed (Psalm 80:8; Isaiah 5:1–7). Jesus is the vine Israel was always meant to be: the true Israel, the faithful Son, who bears fruit that lasts. The branches’ fruitfulness depends entirely on their union with him. A branch does not manufacture fruit; it bears what the life of the vine produces in it.
verseByVerse.examples: You did not choose me, but I chose you (v. 16). The disciples’ following of Jesus is traced back to his choosing, not their decision. This does not make them passive; they are appointed to go and bear fruit. But the initiative and the guarantee of their fruitfulness rest with the one who chose them.

verseByVerse.quote: "I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser. Every branch in me that does not bear fruit he takes away, and every branch that does bear fruit he prunes, that it may bear more fruit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. John 15 teaches what life in Christ looks like after he has gone. First, the vine and the branches: union with Christ, from which all fruit flows (vv. 1–17). Then the world’s hatred, which his people must expect (vv. 18–27). Abiding in Christ, loving one another, and bearing witness in a hostile world: that is the Christian life. And underneath all of it is the vine himself, the true Israel, through whom the life of God flows into ordinary people and makes them fruitful.

The setting. Jesus has just said, Rise, let us go from here (14:31). He may be speaking these words in the upper room as they gather themselves to leave, or on the walk through the city and down toward the Kidron valley, past vineyards and perhaps past the temple. It is the last hours before his arrest, and Judas has gone out to fetch the soldiers.

I am the true vine. The seventh and last of the great I am sayings in John. The force of true lands only once you know what the vine had always meant: a familiar picture of Israel, planted by God but fruitless (Psalm 80:8–16; Isaiah 5:1–7; Jeremiah 2:21; Ezekiel 15; Hosea 10:1). In Isaiah’s song the owner planted his vineyard with choice vines, looked for it to yield grapes, and it yielded wild grapes (Isaiah 5:2). So when a Jew heard vine, he heard a story that had gone wrong: a people planted with every advantage who produced nothing worth picking.

True, not derivative. The word alēthinē does not mean truthful. Here it means real as against derivative: the genuine article of which the others were copies, the same word John used of the true light (1:9) and the true bread (6:32). So the claim is: everything that vine was meant to be and never was, I am. Jesus is the real Israel, the faithful Son, who bears the fruit Israel did not. So a place among God’s people no longer comes by birth, nation or ceremony, but by being united to Jesus through faith, so that a Gentile who trusts him is as much a branch as any son of Abraham (Galatians 3:29).

The golden vine. They may even have been able to see one. Josephus describes a vine of gold above the entrance to the temple sanctuary, with clusters as tall as a man, and the Mishnah adds that worshippers gave golden leaves and grapes to hang on it as offerings. If chapter 14 ended with them leaving the room, the road to the Kidron may have run within sight of the temple. It cannot be proved, and it does not need to be; but a man saying I am the true vine under a golden one worth a fortune would not have needed to explain himself.

My Father is the vinedresser. Vinedresser (geōrgos) means farmer, gardener. The Father tends the vine. Nothing happens to the branches by accident; every cut is made by the Father’s hand.

He takes away. In context, Judas is the clearest example: outwardly attached to Christ, a disciple, but never truly united to him by faith. Some take takes away (airei) as lifts up, as a vinedresser lifts trailing branches off the ground. It is an attractive reading, and it is probably wrong: verse 6 describes the same kind of branch being thrown out, withering, gathered and burned, which is not what happens to a branch that has been tied up.

Can a believer be cut off? The branch taken away is one that bears no fruit at all, and v. 6 shows what becomes of it. It was attached to the vine outwardly, but never drew life from it; it is a professing, not a living, branch (compare 1 John 2:19). If you are anxious that this describes you, the anxiety is itself a sign of life: a branch with no sap in it does not care whether it bears fruit.

He prunes. Pruning hurts, but it makes a vine more fruitful. The Father uses trials, discipline and his word to cut away what hinders fruit (Hebrews 12:5–11). And this second knife is the important one, because it falls on the healthy branch. Both branches feel a blade; the difference is what it is for. The pruning is not punishment but cultivation. God sometimes cuts away what is good to produce what is better, and removes what is comfortable to make room for what is fruitful.

How do I know whether I am being pruned or punished? If you belong to Christ, the Father’s knife on your life is never punishment in the sense of paying for your sins, because Christ has borne that punishment in full (Romans 8:1). What you experience is a Father’s discipline, which is always for your good, that you may share his holiness (Hebrews 12:10). Sometimes he removes a sin; sometimes he removes a comfort, a plan, a reputation, or even a good thing that had become too large in your heart. You may not know the precise reason for each cut. You can know the purpose: more fruit, more likeness to Christ, more joy in him. Ask him what he is teaching you, and trust the hand that holds the knife.

On a Tuesday. Take the loss or difficulty that has hurt most this year, and ask the Father, not why, but what fruit he means to grow from it. Then tell him you trust his hands.
verseByVerse.note: The vine was a familiar picture of Israel, planted by God but often fruitless; Jesus is the true vine. This is the seventh of his “I am” sayings in John. Vinedressers cut away dead wood and pruned living branches hard.

parallels.desc: a vine brought out of Egypt
the vineyard that yielded wild grapes
discipline yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness

verseByVerse.quote: "Already you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you. Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you, unless you abide in me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Already you are clean. The eleven have been cleansed by receiving his word in faith (13:10); Judas has gone. And there is wordplay between verses 2 and 3 that no English version can carry: he prunes, kathairei; you are clean, katharoi. Same root. So the pruning is not primarily about productivity, as a modern reader assumes. It is cleansing. The blade takes off what is diseased or dead or simply in the way, and what is left is clean.

The knife is the word. The knife is what he says. That locates the pruning somewhere unexpected: not only in circumstances, though God certainly uses those, but in the word landing on a person and taking something off him (Hebrews 4:12).

Abide in me. Now the command, and the keyword of the chapter: abide (menō), remain, stay, live in. It is both a command and a promise: abide in me is the command, and I in you is the promise that Christ lives in the one who stays.

What abide means. Abide in Christ is a phrase that can be preached warmly and leave people with nothing to do on Monday. It is not a mystical exercise. Menō is the ordinary word for staying: the disciples asked where he was staying and then stayed with him (1:38–39); he stayed two days in Samaria (4:40); he remained beyond the Jordan (10:40). It means to go on being where you already are, which is a relief. The command is not get in; the branches are already in the vine. The command is: do not go anywhere.

How do we abide? The chapter supplies the content rather than leaving it vague. By keeping his word in us (v. 7): Scripture staying resident rather than visited. By resting in his love (v. 9): staying inside his love rather than trying to earn it. By keeping his commandments (v. 10): doing what he said. And by prayer, which runs through all three. So abiding turns out to consist of ordinary things done continuously. Nothing there requires a special temperament or technique. It is the difference between a branch attached to a vine and a branch lying on the ground, and the branch does not achieve it. It simply does not detach.

Unless it abides in the vine. A branch does not produce fruit by effort but by staying connected to the life of the vine. This is the dependence that pride always resists and grace always establishes.

What does abiding look like on a busy day with no time for long devotions? It looks like staying turned toward Christ in the ordinary hours. Begin the day with even a few verses, read with attention, and carry one with you. Speak to him briefly and often: before the meeting, in the queue, when you are tempted, when you are glad. Obey him in the small next thing. Remember, when guilt or worry rises, that you are loved and forgiven in him. Abiding is not measured by the length of your quiet time but by whether you are depending on him or on yourself. Longer times with the Scriptures and prayer feed it, and you should make room for them, but a branch abides all day, not only in the morning.

parallels.desc: the washing of water with the word

verseByVerse.quote: "I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing. If anyone does not abide in me he is thrown away like a branch and withers; and the branches are gathered, thrown into the fire, and burned."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are the branches. He says it again, plainly, and promises much fruit. What is the fruit? Christlike character, the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23); obedience (v. 10); love (v. 12); joy (v. 11); answered prayer (v. 7); and people brought to Christ (4:36; Romans 1:13).

Apart from me you can do nothing. The most absolute statement of dependence in the Gospel: nothing of spiritual value. The separated branch does not produce diminished fruit; it produces none. A humbling truth: all our gifts, efforts and plans produce nothing that lasts without him. And an encouraging one: with him, by the Spirit through whom his life flows into us, everything he calls us to is possible (Philippians 4:13). Apart from me you can do nothing means, from the other side, with me, everything.

Thrown away like a branch. Vine wood is useless for building, and pruned branches were burned because they were good for nothing else (Ezekiel 15:2–5). The gathering into the fire is a picture of final judgement (Matthew 13:40–42), and it is not casual language. It describes the branch that seemed to be in the vine but had no living connection, finally revealed and removed.

Can a branch in Christ be cut off and burned? That answer should not be given quickly, because the words are severe and a reader may be frightened by them, and the difficulty is real. Verse 2 says every branch in me that does not bear fruit he takes away. In me. How can a branch be in Christ and be cut off and burned, when the same Lord said five chapters earlier that no one is able to snatch them out of his Father’s hand (10:29)?

The vine was always mixed. The picture itself supplies the answer. In the Old Testament the vine is Israel, full of people who belonged to the covenant community outwardly, carried its sign in their bodies, kept its feasts, and were not the true people of God at all. To be a branch on that vine never guaranteed life in it. And one of the Twelve has just gone out into the night to sell him (13:30). Judas was a branch in every visible sense, called, trusted with the common purse, and he bore nothing, because there was nothing in him to bear with. John gives us the category plainly in his letter: they went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have continued with us (1 John 2:19).

No sheep prised from his hand. So the two sayings stand together without strain. The fruitless branch is not a sheep prised out of the Shepherd’s hand; it is a branch tied on to the vine that never drew a drop of sap from it. Union with Christ that is real produces fruit, always, however slowly and however little: that is what the passage means by fruit, not a level of achievement but evidence of life.

Where Christians differ: can a true believer be cut off? Some take this to teach that genuine Christians can lose their salvation if they stop abiding. This commentary’s view: the branches that are burned are those who “do not abide,” like Judas: outwardly attached, never inwardly united. True abiding is the mark of true disciples (8:31), and Jesus has promised that his sheep will never perish (10:28). The warning is real, and it is one of the means God uses to keep his people abiding. It calls us to examine whether our union with Christ is real, not to fear that the Father will drop his own.

The Arminian reading. Arminian Christians (those who hold that God’s saving grace can be resisted and that a true believer can finally fall away) read this verse as a warning that a true believer can fail to abide and be cut off and lost (compare Hebrews 6:4–6; Galatians 5:4). They are right that the warning is real and must be heeded. But the passage itself does not set the warning against the Shepherd’s promise. It shows the warning to be one of the means by which Christ keeps the true branches abiding, while the branches that are burned are those who seemed to belong to him and never did.

If this frightens you. To the person genuinely alarmed by this verse: the very desire to abide is sap moving. Christ did not tell his friends this to leave them measuring themselves for the fire; the command in the passage is not examine yourself but abide in me, and abiding is not an achievement to be pulled off. It is a staying put. Stay where you are, in him, and the fruit is his business, not yours.

How much fruit must I see to be sure I am a true branch? There is no quota. Jesus speaks of fruit, more fruit and much fruit (vv. 2, 5), which means growth, not a fixed measure. Look for the kind of thing the chapter names, not for impressive results: a real love for Christ and his word, a hatred of your sin and a willingness to fight it, love for his people, and some desire that others know him. Those may be small and mixed with much weakness, but they are signs of sap. And do not base your assurance chiefly on your fruit. Base it on Christ’s promise to keep his sheep, and on the Spirit’s witness that you are God’s child (Romans 8:16); then let the fruit confirm what the promise declares.

On a Tuesday. Before each significant task today, the email, the meeting, the meal with your family, pray in one sentence: Lord, I can do nothing of value here without you; work through me.

For worship. The words are severe, and they are spoken in love by the one who within hours would bear the judgement his people deserved, so that no branch truly joined to him would ever be gathered for the fire. The warning that sobers us is the very voice that keeps us, calling us to stay where we are, in him. In him the weakest branch bears fruit that lasts, and of all whom the Father has given him he will lose not one (6:39).
verseByVerse.note: Vine wood is useless for building; pruned branches were burned.

parallels.desc: the wood of the vine

verseByVerse.quote: "If you abide in me, and my words abide in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you. By this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit and so prove to be my disciples."
verseByVerse.commentary:
My words abide in you. You cannot abide in Christ while ignoring his word; Scripture filling the mind and heart is how he dwells richly in us (Colossians 3:16).

Ask whatever you wish.
