This is the second of three prayer promises in chapters 14 and 15, and the conditions accumulate: in my name (14:13–14); here, abiding and his words abiding; at verse 16, being chosen and sent. The boundary here is the most searching: not a formula appended to a request but a condition about where the person praying is living.

The prayers change before the answers do. A person saturated in what Christ said begins, over time, to want different things, so that the wishing itself has been under instruction. Nor is the promise empty, as if God grants only what he was going to do anyway; it describes what happens to desire when somebody lives close to Christ for a long time. The wishes are genuinely the person’s own. They have simply stopped being arbitrary.

By this my Father is glorified. The vine’s purpose is the vinedresser’s glory. What does it mean to glorify God? Not to add anything to him, for nothing can be added, but to make his worth visible, as a heavy crop shows the skill of the gardener. When a harsh man grows gentle or a fearful woman grows brave, people see what kind of God has been at work (Matthew 5:16).

Prove to be my disciples. More literally, and become my disciples: discipleship is something one grows into, not only a status secured at the start. Fruit does not earn the title; it is how the title becomes visible.

How can I let Christ’s words abide in me, if I struggle to read the Bible? Start small and steady rather than large and occasional. Read a short passage, perhaps a few verses of a Gospel, at the same time each day. Read it twice, slowly, and ask: what does this show me of Christ, and what does it ask of me? Choose one sentence to carry with you, and say it to yourself during the day. Listen carefully to the preaching on Sunday and talk about it afterwards. Learn a verse by heart each week. If reading is hard for you, listen to Scripture read aloud. The aim is not to finish a plan but to let his words take up residence.

verseByVerse.quote: "As the Father has loved me, so have I loved you. Abide in my love. If you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love, just as I have kept my Father's commandments and abide in his love."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the Father has loved me. The comparison is the largest in the chapter, and easy to read past as a pleasantry. The measure of Christ’s love for us is not a great deal, or more than you know, but the love the Father has had for the Son from before the foundation of the world (17:24).

In the flow. In verses 1–8 Jesus spoke in a picture; here he says plainly what flows through the vine: his love. So the passage runs downhill like a river: from the Father’s love for the Son, to the Son’s love for his disciples, to their love for each other.

Abide in my love. The phrase can be heard as a threat: stay in it or you will fall out of it. Read it against the picture. A branch does not generate the sap; it lives in a supply that is already flowing. Abiding in his love is not maintaining his affection at a certain level, which is impossible and was never asked; it is remaining inside something that is there whether one feels it or not.

If you keep my commandments. Obedience is how we stay in his love, not to earn it but to enjoy it. The sentence does not say obedience purchases the love, and the clause that follows settles it.

As I have kept my Father’s commandments. Nobody supposes the Son earns the Father’s love by good behaviour. His obedience is the form of a love that was never in question, and the disciples’ obedience is being described in the same way. Obedience is love’s response, not love’s price. And his keeping was perfect where ours never is (1 John 1:8). That perfect obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19), so a branch that keeps his commands only haltingly still abides in a love that rests on his record, not its own.

Does God love me less when I disobey? No. His love for his children rests on Christ, not on their performance, and it does not rise and fall with your week (Romans 8:38–39). But your enjoyment of his love can be clouded by sin, as a child who has disobeyed may avoid his father’s eyes even while his father loves him as much as ever. The way back is not to make up for it first, but to come home: confess, receive his forgiveness, and walk with him again. You do not obey to get into his love; you obey because you are in it, and obedience keeps you in the warmth of it.

On a Tuesday. If after a bad week you approach God expecting the temperature to have dropped, something is being treated as a wage that this verse treats as a home. Christ loves you as the Father loves him. Live there today.

parallels.desc: keep yourselves in the love of God

verseByVerse.quote: "These things I have spoken to you, that my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be full. This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
That my joy may be in you. Not joy in general but a joy that belongs to him, the joy of the Son in the Father’s love and in doing his will, and the man handing it over will be dead by tomorrow afternoon. That means the joy he proposes to hand over is not a mood produced by favourable circumstances, because his circumstances at that moment were as dark as any man’s have ever been. Hebrews describes the same thing from the far side: for the joy that was set before him he endured the cross, despising the shame (Hebrews 12:2).

Full. Filled up, brought to the brim (compare 1 John 1:4). The Christian life is not grim duty; obedience and joy go together.

For the believer who does not feel joyful. There is a reader for whom this verse is an accusation. Christians are frequently told they ought to be joyful, and the ones who are not conclude that something is defective in them, which is often untrue and always unhelpful, particularly for people whose flatness is a matter of temperament, exhaustion or illness rather than of the soul. Look at where the joy is located. It is his, and it arrives by abiding. It is not summoned up, and it has nothing to do with being naturally cheerful. Some of the most joyful Christians in history, Charles Spurgeon among them, fought long battles with depression. And the location of the sentence tells against the sunny reading. This is not said at a wedding. It is said in a room somebody has just walked out of to fetch soldiers.

How can I have joy and sorrow at the same time? Because Christian joy is deeper than mood. Paul describes himself as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing (2 Corinthians 6:10). Joy in this sense is the settled gladness of knowing that you are loved by God, forgiven in Christ, and kept for glory, and it can sit underneath real grief like the deep water under a stormy surface. You do not have to pretend to be happy at a graveside or in a hospital ward. You can weep, and still know that the One who loves you is risen and that the end of the story is good. That is his joy in you.

This is my commandment. The new commandment of 13:34, repeated, now on the ground of the vine: branches in the same vine are branches in relationship with each other.

On a Tuesday. Make a list of five things that are true of you in Christ, whatever your feelings today: forgiven, loved, adopted, kept, heading home. Read it slowly and thank him for each. Then do one loving act for another believer, because joy and love grow on the same branch.

verseByVerse.quote: "Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends. You are my friends if you do what I command you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Greater love has no one than this. This sentence is carved on many war memorials, and it belongs there. A man who dies to bring his friends out is doing what Christ himself calls the greatest love there is, and no Christian should be grudging about it.

Greater than the greatest. But the verse says something the memorials cannot. He is defining the ceiling of human love and then going beyond it the following afternoon. Paul makes the point explicitly: one will scarcely die for a righteous person, but God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Romans 5:7–8), and a few lines later, while we were enemies (5:10). So the soldier’s love is the highest thing on the human scale, and Christ exceeds it, because his friends at that moment were not behaving like friends. One had sold him, one would deny him three times before dawn, and the rest would run. He calls them friends anyway, and the word is not sentimental: philoi, from the affectionate verb, the same root as the word the sisters used of Lazarus, he whom you love (11:3). His love is greater than the greatest love.

If you do what I command. The condition sounds like a friendship on probation, and the next verse forbids that reading: he has already called them friends (v. 15). What the conditional does is describe the shape of the friendship rather than set its price: friends of this particular friend are people who do what he says, because of who he is. Not that obedience makes us his friends, but that it shows we are. And the command is given by somebody who is about to obey a harder one: he asks nothing of them that he is unwilling to do first.

Can I really call Jesus my friend? Yes, and with wonder, because he calls you that first. Friendship with Christ does not make him less than Lord; you are friends of the King, not his equals. So the friendship is full of reverence as well as warmth. But it is real: he has laid down his life for you, he has told you the Father’s plans, he hears you, he is for you. You may speak to him with the openness of a friend, bring him your troubles without performance, and trust his loyalty when you feel least loyal yourself. What a friend we have in Jesus is sentimental only if it forgets the cross; remembered there, it is the plain truth.

On a Tuesday. Think of someone in your church who needs a friend who will lay something down for them, time, comfort, convenience, money, and lay one thing down for that person this week, quietly, for Christ’s sake.

For worship. Every other love that has died for a friend died for someone worth dying for. This one died for men who would run before morning, and he did not wait for them to become friends before he called them by the name. The highest love on the human scale is where his love begins. And the friendship he bought is not on loan: the one who laid down his life for it took that life up again, and he will never let his friends go.

parallels.desc: he laid down his life for us

verseByVerse.quote: "No longer do I call you servants, for the servant does not know what his master is doing; but I have called you friends, for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you. You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you that you should go and bear fruit and that your fruit should abide, so that whatever you ask the Father in my name, he may give it to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
No longer servants. Every great figure of the Old Testament is a servant. It is the title of honour: Moses my servant, David my servant, Israel my servant, and the prophets my servants. To be called the servant of the LORD was the highest thing a Jew could aspire to, and he takes it off them, for a precise reason: a slave is told what to do and not why.

I have called you friends. In the whole Old Testament only Abraham is called the friend of God (2 Chronicles 20:7; Isaiah 41:8; taken up in James 2:23), and of Moses alone it is said that the LORD spoke to him face to face, as a man speaks to his friend (Exodus 33:11). Two men, in all of Israel’s history, with whom God shared his plans (Genesis 18:17). Now Jesus calls all his disciples friends. The promotion is in disclosure: not easier commands, but the reasons, as he has been doing all evening. They are still his servants (v. 20; Romans 1:1), but more than servants: trusted friends.

All, and yet more to come. Jesus says he has made known all that he has heard from his Father, yet soon says he still has many things to say to them, but they cannot bear them now (16:12). He has told them all they need as his friends; the rest the Spirit will bring out after his glory, through the apostles (16:13).

You did not choose me. In that culture, as far as we can tell, disciples usually chose their rabbi, and at least two of these men had first followed John the Baptist (1:35–40). Jesus reverses it. That is a blow to pride and a relief to the anxious: nobody at that table could boast of having picked the right teacher, and nobody needed to fear being found out later, because the one who chose them knew exactly whom he was choosing. The Bible’s word for this is election: God choosing people for himself before they had done anything good or bad, out of his own love and not for their worth (Ephesians 1:4; Romans 9:11).

Is I chose you about salvation, or about the apostles’ office? In the first place it is the choosing of the Eleven for their mission, that you should go and bear fruit; Judas, too, was chosen as an apostle (6:70). But it rests on the same truth that runs through John, that those who come to Christ come because the Father gave them and drew them (6:37, 44). So it is rightly applied to every believer: our faith began with his choice. It reflects the deeper truth of election to salvation (13:18; 17:6; Ephesians 1:4). Our salvation starts with his choice, not ours. We chose him only because he first chose us.

Does election make my choice meaningless? No. You really did repent and believe; no one did it for you, and it was truly your act. Election explains why you did. Left to ourselves we would never have chosen him (6:44), so behind your choosing lies his, which made it possible and certain. That does not make you a puppet; it makes you a rescued sinner. And it brings two great gifts: humility, because you cannot boast about having chosen well, and security, because what began with his choice does not depend on the strength of yours.

Appointed to bear fruit. Chosen for a purpose, not a privilege but a calling. Election in this verse runs straight out into mission, and the last word about the fruit is the chapter’s keyword, abide. Fruit that stays.

Whatever you ask the Father. Prayer is connected with fruitful mission. Those whom he has chosen and sent pray in his name, and the Father answers them.

On a Tuesday. He chose and appointed you for this, so ask: what fruit that lasts could I invest in today? A conversation about Christ, time with a younger believer, prayer for a missionary, teaching your children. Do one of them.
verseByVerse.note: Abraham and Moses were each called the friend of God.

parallels.desc: Abraham, my friend
as a man speaks to his friend

verseByVerse.quote: "These things I command you, so that you will love one another."
verseByVerse.commentary:
These things I command you. The sentence closes the first half of the chapter by naming what all of it was for: the vine, the pruning, the abiding, the joy, the friendship, the choosing were all aimed at love among his people. The world will hate them (v. 18); they must love one another.

Not where we would have put the emphasis. Given a discourse on union with Christ, we might land on the upward direction: know him better, depend on him more, pray with confidence. Those are all in the passage, but he says the point of the whole thing is that they should love each other. Good doctrine always runs out into love: election produces humility, grace produces gratitude, and both produce the servant-hearted love of the community of the chosen.

Love that flows from the vine. The love is put as the purpose and expected result of the teaching taking hold, which fits the vine, because fruit is not extracted from a branch by exhortation; it comes from the life flowing into it. The love these men are to have for one another is Christ’s own love passing through them. He loved them first, he is about to lay down his life for them, and the sap of that love is what will turn eleven quarrelling men into a family.

To these men, that night. There is a reason this needed saying to these particular men. Luke tells us that at this supper they had argued about which of them was the greatest (Luke 22:24), and within hours they would all abandon him and then spend the weekend locked in a room together, with Peter’s failure in the middle of it. The community he is commanding to love one another was not good at it. He gives the command anyway, for the third time that evening (13:34; 15:12): whatever else they carried out of that room, this needed saying repeatedly.

What if the Christian I find hardest to love has really wronged me? Then love will look like forgiveness, and forgiveness is not pretending the wrong did not happen. It means you do not hold it against him or seek to pay him back, because Christ has not held your sins against you (Ephesians 4:32). It may mean a hard conversation (Matthew 18:15), and where there is abuse or danger it means protection and, where needed, the involvement of church leaders and the authorities; love never requires you to stay in harm’s way. But it does mean praying for him, refusing bitterness, and being ready for reconciliation when there is repentance. Ask Christ for his love, because yours will run out.

On a Tuesday. If anything is still unresolved from your last disagreement with a fellow believer, take a step toward peace this week: a message, a call, an apology for your part, a prayer for his good.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–27 — The World's Hatred and the Spirit's Witness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The world will hate the disciples because it hated Jesus first and because he chose them out of it. Its hatred is without excuse, since he spoke and did works no one else did. But the Spirit of truth, whom Jesus will send from the Father, will bear witness about him, and so will they.
verseByVerse.theology: The world’s hostility to the church is not an accident to be explained away but follows from the conflict between the kingdom of God and a world in rebellion against him. Jesus does not promise that clever strategy will remove it; he promises the Spirit, who bears witness about Jesus alongside the disciples who were with him from the beginning.
verseByVerse.examples: If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you (v. 20). This is both warning and honour: to suffer for Christ is to share in his sufferings. The disciple should not manufacture hostility, but when it comes for Christ’s sake he may take it as confirmation, not contradiction, that he belongs to Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you. If you were of the world, the world would love you as its own; but because you are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If the world hates you. The change of subject is abrupt and deliberate: from love (vv. 9–17), without a pause, to hatred (vv. 18–25). The community that has just been commanded to love one another is going to need to, because nobody outside it will. The world in John is humanity in rebellion against God. That does not mean the planet, or people as such, for God so loved the world (3:16). It means human life arranged without God: its approval, its values and its loyalties, wherever they are found, including in religion. And the word (miseō) is not dislike but hatred. He is not warning them about awkwardness at parties.

It has hated me before. The world’s hatred is first directed at Christ, and the disciples share in what he suffered because they share his name (1 Peter 4:12–14).

The world would love its own. The logic is oddly comforting once it is seen. The hostility is not evidence that something has gone wrong with the disciples; it is evidence that they no longer belong to the system that is doing the hating. Belonging elsewhere is the whole cause.

I chose you out of the world. They now belong to another kingdom (17:14–16), with different loyalties and a different love, and the world resents it. Their chosenness is the source of both their dignity and their danger.

Two guards. This passage is misused in both directions. The first guard is against manufacturing persecution: treating any friction as proof of faithfulness, when much of what Christians suffer in comfortable countries is the ordinary consequence of being rude, ill-informed or needlessly provocative. Peter drew the line himself: let none of you suffer as a murderer or a thief or an evildoer or as a meddler (1 Peter 4:15). Being disliked for being disagreeable is not sharing in the sufferings of Christ. The second guard is against the opposite error. This passage is not history. Many Christians are imprisoned, dispossessed and killed today, and a church that reads verse 18 as a metaphor for social awkwardness has quietly excluded much of its own family. The honest position for a comfortable believer is neither to invent a persecution nor to conclude the verse is spent, but to pray for the persecuted church.

Should I try to be liked by unbelievers, or expect to be hated? Neither as a goal. Aim to be faithful to Christ and kind to people, and leave the reaction to God. Scripture tells us to live such good lives among unbelievers that they may see our good deeds (1 Peter 2:12), to be wise toward outsiders and gracious in speech (Colossians 4:5–6), and to live peaceably with all as far as it depends on us (Romans 12:18). Many unbelievers will respect, even love, a gentle and honest Christian. But when faithfulness to Christ costs you their approval, do not trade him for it. Being hated is not a mark of holiness in itself; being hated for his name is.

On a Tuesday. Pray today, by name if you can, for a persecuted believer or church somewhere in the world. And ask whether any of the friction you feel is your fault rather than his name; if so, put it right.

verseByVerse.quote: "Remember the word that I said to you: 'A servant is not greater than his master.' If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you. If they kept my word, they will also keep yours. But all these things they will do to you on account of my name, because they do not know him who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A servant is not greater than his master. The word he tells them to remember is one he said earlier that evening, at the basin (13:16), where it was an argument for washing feet. Here the other edge is out: if the master is hunted, no servant should expect to be exempt. The same proverb produces humility in one direction and realism in the other, and John is the only evangelist who records both uses.

If they persecuted me. The church shares her Lord’s experience (Acts 9:4; 2 Timothy 3:12), because the world sees in her something of him.

They will also keep yours. The parallel runs both ways. The verse is not a prediction of universal hostility but that the disciples’ reception will mirror his, and his was mixed. A Samaritan village believed; some of the authorities believed and would not say so. The church should not expect nothing but rejection: his reception included Nicodemus and Nathanael and a beggar who worshipped him (9:38).

On account of my name. Persecution of the church is ultimately aimed at Christ himself, and its root is ignorance of the true God (16:3). The hostility is not fundamentally about the disciples, their manner or their politics; they are being hit by something aimed past them. And the ignorance is not innocent: they have had the opportunity to know and refused.

How should I respond when I am treated badly for being a Christian? Remember that you are sharing your Master’s lot, and that it is an honour (Acts 5:41; Matthew 5:11–12). Do not repay evil for evil or insult for insult, but bless (1 Peter 3:9). Pray for those who mistreat you, as Jesus did on the cross. Speak the truth gently and stand firm without bitterness. Use lawful protections where you have them, as Paul did (Acts 22:25). And keep on with the work: some who now oppose you may later keep the word, as Saul of Tarsus did.

verseByVerse.quote: "If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have been guilty of sin, but now they have no excuse for their sin. Whoever hates me hates my Father also."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They would not have been guilty. Read flatly, it says something Scripture denies everywhere else. He cannot mean they would have been innocent. Paul spends three chapters establishing that the whole world is guilty before God (Romans 1–3), and John himself has already had Jesus say that people loved the darkness rather than the light (3:19). What is meant is the specific sin the chapter is about: rejecting God’s Son with the evidence in front of them. That sin was not available before he arrived. A man cannot refuse a person he has never met.

Responsibility tracks light. The principle underneath runs right through the Bible: privilege increases responsibility (9:41; Luke 12:47–48). The servant who knew his master’s will and did not do it receives the heavier beating, so the position of the well-informed is more dangerous, not safer. A person who has grown up hearing the gospel and can predict the sermon is in this verse’s territory.

No excuse. Excuse (prophasin) means pretext, a cloak: the plausible cover story. What his coming did was not to create the guilt but to remove the covering that had made it deniable.

Whoever hates me hates my Father also. There is no loving the Father while hating the Son (5:23; 1 John 2:23). It is 14:9 turned round: if seeing him is seeing the Father, then hating him is hating the Father. And it closes off a common position, held sincerely by many: that one may honour God and set Jesus to one side as a good man about whom the church has exaggerated. This verse says the arrangement does not exist. There is no God available behind Christ to be respected while Christ is declined.

What about religious people who worship God but reject Jesus? This verse speaks to them with great seriousness and great love. Many sincerely believe they honour God while rejecting Jesus as the Son. But Jesus says that the Father and the Son cannot be separated: to refuse the Son is to refuse the Father who sent him (5:23). That is why Christians must lovingly and humbly tell their Jewish, Muslim and other religious neighbours about Christ, not to win an argument but because there is no other way to the God they seek. We should honour their sincerity and their questions, and never despise them, while still saying plainly who Jesus is.

On a Tuesday. If you have grown up in church, ask honestly whether you have ever personally come to Christ, or only been near him. If not, come today; he casts out no one who comes (6:37). If you have, thank God for the light you were given, and ask what he wants you to do with it this week.

verseByVerse.quote: "If I had not done among them the works that no one else did, they would not be guilty of sin, but now they have seen and hated both me and my Father. But the word that is written in their Law must be fulfilled: 'They hated me without a cause.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The works that no one else did. His works were unique (9:32), a category of evidence the council itself conceded in closed session (11:47).

Seen and hated. Seeing and hating: the clearest evidence of the depth of sin. When perfect goodness came among them, the world’s enmity against God became fully visible.

Written in their Law. Their Law here means the Scriptures as a whole, including the Psalms. He has used the phrase before (8:17; 10:34), and it is not a repudiation of Scripture: he quotes it as authoritative, so that the court’s own law testifies against the verdict. The words come from Psalm 35:19 and 69:4, laments of David hated by enemies without reason. Psalm 69 is one of the most quoted psalms in the New Testament: it supplies the zeal for the house that consumed him (2:17), the sour wine offered on the cross (19:28–29), the reproaches that fell on him (Romans 15:3), and this line. Even their hatred fulfilled Scripture.

Without a cause, and as a gift. Without a cause is dōrean. It means gratuitously, as a free gift, for nothing. The same word appears in Romans 3:24: we are justified by his grace as a gift, dōrean, freely, for nothing. So the two great gratuitous acts in the story are described with the identical word. The world’s hatred of Christ was unearned, and the sinner’s acquittal is unearned, and they meet at the same cross. He received hatred he had done nothing to deserve; the people who hated him receive a righteousness they have done nothing to deserve.

Why would anyone hate Jesus? Because his light exposes what we love in the dark (3:19–20). He was kind, but he was also holy, and his holiness told people the truth about themselves. He claimed authority over their lives, their religion and their future. He would not be used. People who wanted a different kind of God found in him the real one, and resisted. The same thing happens in every heart before the Spirit changes it: we may admire Jesus at a distance, but when he comes close and claims us, the natural heart pushes him away. That is why new birth is necessary (3:3).

On a Tuesday. When you are treated unfairly today, remember that the Lord was hated without cause, and was silent like a lamb. Then remember that you were loved without cause, and let that shape how you answer.

For worship. The Holy One was hated for nothing, and he did not answer hatred with hatred. David sang his lament out of the dark and did not know whose voice he was singing in. The Son of David has sung it to the end, and turned the song of the friendless into the gospel of grace for every enemy who comes to him.
verseByVerse.note: “Their Law” here means the Scriptures as a whole, including the Psalms.

parallels.desc: those who hate me without cause

verseByVerse.quote: "But when the Helper comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me. And you also will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the flow. The promise of the Spirit arrives in the middle of a warning about hatred, and belongs exactly there. The case against Christ looks lost, so Jesus names his witnesses. The trial of Jesus does not end in Pilate’s court; it goes on in the world, and the defence is given the last word.

When the Helper comes. Here paraklētos has its courtroom sense most clearly, for the Helper is also the Advocate: in a hostile world, the Spirit stands alongside the persecuted church and speaks for Christ. And in this verse the Son sends him, where earlier that evening the Father was said to send him (14:16, 26). Both send.

Who proceeds from the Father. Proceeds (ekporeuetai) means goes out from, comes forth. Most take this to describe the Spirit’s mission, his being sent out into the world. Theologians have also seen in it his eternal relationship to the Father.

The phrase that divided the church. The Nicene Creed, as agreed in the fourth century, said the Spirit proceeds from the Father, in the words of this verse. And the same verse holds the other half of the later argument: whom I will send to you from the Father. The East protects the Father as the single source within the Godhead; the West protects the Son’s full involvement. Both are defending something the verse says. And on Easter evening the risen Son will breathe on the disciples and say, receive the Holy Spirit (20:22).

Where Christians differ: does the Spirit proceed from the Son? The Western church added to the Nicene Creed that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son (filioque). The Eastern Orthodox church rejected the addition, and it was a major cause of the split of 1054. This commentary’s view: the Western confession, held by the Reformed churches (the Westminster Confession 2.3; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 2.3), is right in substance: the Spirit is the Spirit of the Son as well as of the Father (Galatians 4:6; Romans 8:9), and the Son sends him, as here. Yet the matter is subtle, and should be held humbly, with respect for Eastern brothers and sisters who confess the same Trinity.

He will bear witness about me. The Spirit’s great work is to point to Christ (16:14). He does not draw attention to himself; he is the floodlight that shines on the Son.

You also will bear witness. Two witnesses, the requirement of the law that runs through this Gospel (8:17). And the qualification for the human half is purely factual: not eloquence or bravery, neither of which they were about to prove, but that they were there. The apostles were eyewitnesses from the beginning of his ministry (Acts 1:21–22). Their witness, preserved in Scripture, is the foundation of the church (Ephesians 2:20). And the Spirit still bears witness through every believer who speaks of Christ.

The pressure taken off. The Spirit’s witness is the one that convinces; the disciples’ job is to say what they saw. Nobody is asked to produce faith in anybody. And you have been with me from the beginning was said to eleven men who would, before the night was over, all be somewhere else. He sent them anyway.

I was not an eyewitness, so how can I bear witness? By passing on faithfully what the eyewitnesses saw, and by telling what Christ has done for you. The apostles’ testimony is written down for you (20:31; 1 John 1:1–3), so you do not need to invent anything; you point people to it. And you can say, as the healed blind man did, what you know: I was blind, now I see (9:25). The Spirit uses that ordinary testimony. You are not responsible for convincing anyone. You are responsible for being honest and clear about Jesus, and leaving the convincing to the Spirit who loves to glorify him.

For worship. The Spirit of truth has one subject, and it is the Son. He came forth from the Father to shine on Christ, and he has never once turned the light on himself, so that from Pentecost until now every heart that has seen the glory of Jesus has seen it by his light. The world has never silenced the witness of eleven frightened men, because behind their weak words stood the Spirit who will not let Christ be forgotten. Glory to the Father who sends, the Son who is shown, and the Spirit who shows him.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “Helper” can also be rendered “Advocate” or “Counselor.”

parallels.desc: we are witnesses, and so is the Holy Spirit

15.text: <sup>1</sup>“I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser.<sup>2</sup>Every branch in me that does not bear fruit he takes away, and every branch that does bear fruit he prunes, that it may bear more fruit.<sup>3</sup>Already you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you.<sup>4</sup>Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you, unless you abide in me.<sup>5</sup>I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.<sup>6</sup>If anyone does not abide in me, he is thrown away like a branch and withers; and the branches are gathered, thrown into the fire, and burned.<sup>7</sup>If you abide in me, and my words abide in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you.<sup>8</sup>By this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit and so prove to be my disciples.<sup>9</sup>As the Father has loved me, so have I loved you. Abide in my love.<sup>10</sup>If you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love, just as I have kept my Father’s commandments and abide in his love.<sup>11</sup>These things I have spoken to you, that my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be full.<sup>12</sup>“This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you.<sup>13</sup>Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends.<sup>14</sup>You are my friends if you do what I command you.<sup>15</sup>No longer do I call you servants, for the servant does not know what his master is doing; but I have called you friends, for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you.<sup>16</sup>You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you that you should go and bear fruit and that your fruit should abide, so that whatever you ask the Father in my name, he may give it to you.<sup>17</sup>These things I command you, so that you will love one another.<sup>18</sup>“If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you.<sup>19</sup>If you were of the world, the world would love you as its own; but because you are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you.<sup>20</sup>Remember the word that I said to you: ’A servant is not greater than his master.’ If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you. If they kept my word, they will also keep yours.<sup>21</sup>But all these things they will do to you on account of my name, because they do not know him who sent me.<sup>22</sup>If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have been guilty of sin, but now they have no excuse for their sin.<sup>23</sup>Whoever hates me hates my Father also.<sup>24</sup>If I had not done among them the works that no one else did, they would not be guilty of sin, but now they have seen and hated both me and my Father.<sup>25</sup>But the word that is written in their Law must be fulfilled: ’They hated me without a cause.’<sup>26</sup>“But when the Helper comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me.<sup>27</sup>And you also will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning.
15.overview:
In the Old Testament Israel was God’s vine, planted and tended by him but so often fruitless (Psalm 80:8–16; Isaiah 5:1–7). Jesus now says, “I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser.” His disciples are the branches, and all their fruit comes from abiding in him: apart from him they can do nothing. Abiding means living in his love, keeping his word, and loving one another as he has loved them. He calls them friends, and reminds them that he chose them and sent them to bear lasting fruit.

The second half turns from love within the church to hatred from the world. The world hated him first, without a cause, and his servants should expect the same. Yet they will not be alone: the Spirit of truth will bear witness about Jesus, and they too will bear witness, because they have been with him from the beginning.

16.title: The Spirit and the Joy of the Disciples

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — The Spirit Convicts the World
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus forewarns the disciples of persecution so that it will not trip them. His going, which grieves them, is for their good, because then he will send the Helper, who will convict the world and lead the apostles into all the truth about Christ.
verseByVerse.theology: The Spirit convicts the world on three counts: sin (its refusal to believe in Jesus), righteousness (Jesus vindicated by his return to the Father), and judgment (the ruler of this world condemned at the cross). This conviction is not coercion but illumination: the Spirit opens eyes to what is actually true about our condition, about Jesus, and about the verdict already given at Calvary. The gospel is not an optional improvement but rescue from real condemnation.
verseByVerse.examples: He will guide you into all the truth (v. 13). The promise was first to the apostles, and was fulfilled in the New Testament. The Spirit does not add to it, but still opens believers’ eyes to the word he inspired (1 Corinthians 2:10–13). This does not make every interpretation equally valid; it means the church, reading the Spirit’s word with prayer and humility, can come to the truth Jesus promised.

verseByVerse.quote: "I have said all these things to you to keep you from falling away. They will put you out of the synagogues. Indeed, the hour is coming when whoever kills you will think he is offering service to God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. John 16 completes Jesus’ farewell teaching. He warns of persecution, explains why his going is good for them, describes the Spirit’s work in the world and in the church, and promises that their sorrow will turn to joy. It ends with one of the great promises of Scripture: I have overcome the world. Spoken to men about to scatter, it is the voice of a Victor who has not yet fought and has never doubted the outcome.

The setting. The words follow straight on from the end of chapter 15, where Jesus warned that the world would hate his disciples. It is late on Thursday night, and he is either still in the upper room or on the way to the Kidron valley. Within hours he will be arrested, and these men will be asked whether they know him.

To keep you from falling away. Falling away (skandalisthēte) is to be tripped, to stumble over something in the road, not formally to renounce the faith: a man catching his foot on an obstacle he did not see, and the obstacle Jesus has in mind is persecution arriving without warning.

The stumbling-block placed in view. He is removing a stumbling-block by putting it in the road ahead of them where they can see it. Suffering that has been predicted by the one you are following is a different experience from suffering that seems to prove he was not in control. Jesus’ warnings are one of the means by which he keeps his people.

They will put you out of the synagogues. As had already happened to the man born blind (9:22, 34). For a Jew of that day, it meant being cut off from community, worship, family and livelihood.

Offering service to God. The English softens the word, and it is chilling. Service (latreia) is worship, the technical term for what went on in the temple (Romans 12:1). So what is predicted is not that religious people will do something violent and afterwards justify it, but that the killing will be performed as an act of worship, offered up like a sacrifice, by men who go home afterwards believing they have pleased God. Religious zeal without the knowledge of God can become murderous. Stephen was the first recorded to die this way (Acts 7:58–60).

The case study who became an apostle. Paul had been such a man. He says of himself that he was convinced he ought to do many things in opposing the name of Jesus of Nazareth (Acts 26:9–11), that he had been extremely zealous for the traditions of his fathers (Galatians 1:13–14), and he hunted Christians sincerely. That is the hope buried inside the warning: the first man to fulfil this prophecy on a large scale ended up writing a large part of the New Testament. Nothing in verse 2 puts a person beyond the reach of grace.

Why does God let his people be persecuted at all? Scripture does not give a complete explanation, but it gives enough to trust him. Suffering for Christ joins us to him and makes us share his path (Philippians 3:10; 1 Peter 4:13). It purifies faith like fire refining gold (1 Peter 1:6–7). It bears witness to the world, as the blood of martyrs has so often been seed for the church. And it is temporary, while the glory to come is eternal and far outweighs it (Romans 8:18; 2 Corinthians 4:17). None of this makes persecution good in itself. But God never wastes the sufferings of his people, and he holds the persecutors, too, in his hand.

On a Tuesday. Do not be shaken when opposition comes in religious dress; Jesus told us it would. And pray today for someone who opposes the gospel fiercely. Saul of Tarsus was such a man, and God made him an apostle.
verseByVerse.note: Paul had been such a man, persecuting believers as a service to God.

parallels.desc: Paul’s zeal as a persecutor

verseByVerse.quote: "And they will do these things because they have not known the Father, nor me. But I have said these things to you, that when their hour comes you may remember that I told them to you. I did not say these things to you from the beginning, because I was with you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They have not known the Father. The diagnosis is the most important sentence in the passage: religious violence is not caused by too much God but by not knowing him. The root of persecution is ignorance of God (15:21). That cuts against a common modern account, which holds that strong religious conviction is itself the danger and that the cure is holding beliefs more loosely. Jesus says the opposite. The men who will kill his followers as an act of worship are not people who know God too well. They do not know him at all, and their zeal is the evidence of it.

A usable test. Any conviction that makes a person willing to destroy someone in God’s name has, by that fact, revealed itself as ignorance of the God who sent his Son to be destroyed rather than to destroy. Those who truly know the Father, who loves the world and gave his Son, cannot persecute those who bear the Son’s name. And the test reaches the respectable as well as the violent. Contempt offered as zeal, the cold shoulder and the cutting remark made in God’s name, grow from the same root: religion used to prove oneself right, instead of knowledge of the God who justifies the ungodly (Romans 4:5).

When their hour comes. The hour of the persecutors. When it comes, the memory of these words will produce not despair but confirming faith: this is what he said would happen, and it is happening, therefore he is true.

Not from the beginning. While he was with them, the hostility was aimed at him. Matthew records earlier warnings (Matthew 10:17–22), but what is new tonight is that he is leaving, and the blows will now land on them. He had held this back because there had been no need while he was there to absorb it. There is information God holds back, and the holding back is not deception. It is timing.

Does this mean every religious person who opposes Christians does not know God? It means that no one who truly knows the Father will persecute those who belong to his Son. People may disagree with Christians, even sharply, for many reasons, and many in other religions are sincere and morally serious. But Jesus says the deepest reason for hostility toward him and his people is not knowing the Father as he has revealed himself in the Son. That is a reason for compassion, not contempt: they need what we have been given, the knowledge of God in the face of Jesus Christ. And Christians must apply the test to themselves first: the church has sometimes persecuted in God’s name, and every time it did, it was failing to know him.

parallels.desc: I had acted ignorantly in unbelief

verseByVerse.quote: "But now I am going to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, 'Where are you going?' But because I have said these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But now I am going to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, Where are you going? The apparent contradiction should be dealt with directly, because a careful reader trips on it. Peter had asked precisely that three chapters earlier: Lord, where are you going? (13:36). Thomas had asked something very close (14:5). The resolution is in what is happening in the room: none of you asks me, now, at this moment. Peter asked earlier and did not want the answer; he immediately turned the conversation to his own loyalty. They had asked only about the separation, not about where he was going and why it would be good. Nobody is asking now, and the rest of the sentence says why. They are thinking only of their loss.

Sorrow has filled your heart. That is a real observation about grief. Sorrow closes questions down. These men have absorbed only the one fact, that he is going, and it has filled the heart like a vessel with nothing left over.

What Jesus does not do with it. He does not tell them to stop being sad, or hurry past it. He names it, and takes responsibility for having caused it. Then he begins, slowly, to give them the one thing that will eventually turn it round, which is not an argument but a fact about the Spirit.

Is it wrong for a Christian to grieve deeply? No. Jesus did not rebuke these men for their sorrow, and he himself wept at a grave (11:35). Paul did not tell the Thessalonians to stop grieving, only not to grieve like those who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Grief is love feeling the weight of loss, and the Psalms give us words for it. What faith adds is not the removal of sorrow but a window in it: the knowledge that God is doing something we cannot yet see, and that the story does not end here. So grieve honestly, bring your grief to the Lord, and let others carry it with you. In time, ask him to show you what he is doing.

On a Tuesday. In a season of grief, notice which questions have gone quiet: the curiosity about what God is doing, the interest in anything beyond the loss. Their silence is not sin. But do not wait for your own heart to reopen them. Read one of Jesus’ promises aloud today and let the answer come to you from outside, as it came to them.

verseByVerse.quote: "Nevertheless, I tell you the truth: it is to your advantage that I go away, for if I do not go away, the Helper will not come to you. But if I go, I will send him to you. And when he comes, he will convict the world concerning sin and righteousness and judgment:"
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is to your advantage that I go away. The most counterintuitive sentence of the farewell discourse. The verb, sympherei, is the word Caiaphas used: it is better for you that one man should die for the people (11:50), cold political arithmetic in a council chamber. Here it is one of the tenderest things ever said to frightened friends. Caiaphas meant: better for us that he dies. Jesus means: better for you that I go. The same calculation, and the difference is everything.

The Helper will not come. Why could the Spirit not come while Jesus was here? The passage gives one reason directly and implies another. Directly: the Spirit is sent by the glorified Son, and John has already told us that the Spirit was not yet given because Jesus was not yet glorified (7:39). The cross, resurrection and ascension come first, then Pentecost (Acts 2:33): the Spirit applies the finished work, and there was nothing to apply until the work was done.

A distribution of his presence. Implied, and this is the part that touches the disciples’ grief: a body is in one place. Through his ministry, being near Jesus meant being in the same room as Jesus. The Spirit is with every believer everywhere, always, and within them. What is coming is not a replacement for his presence but a distribution of it. He is not saying you will manage, but the arrangement they are grieving the loss of was the inferior one.

Did Old Testament believers not have the Spirit? They did: David prayed take not your Holy Spirit from me (Psalm 51:11), and they too were born of God, as Jesus implies when he rebukes Nicodemus, Israel’s teacher, for not understanding the new birth (3:10). What came at Pentecost was the Spirit poured out on all God’s people, dwelling in them permanently, on the ground of Christ’s finished work. That is what Jesus means: the Spirit as the promised gift of the new covenant could not come until he had gone.

He will convict the world. Convict (elenxei) is a courtroom word: to cross-examine, to bring to light, to prove a case. The Spirit acts like a prosecutor, proving the world wrong on three counts. The world thinks it has judged Jesus; the Spirit turns the case around.

Would it not be better to have Jesus here in person? It feels that way, and Jesus says plainly that it is not. If he were here in the flesh, he could be in only one place; you might live your whole life without getting near him. By the Spirit he is with every believer, in every place, at every hour, and not beside you only but within you. The disciples who walked with him in Galilee often misunderstood him; after Pentecost the same men understood and preached with boldness. You are not a second-class Christian for living after the ascension. You live in the age Jesus called better.

For worship. The Son went away by the road Caiaphas planned for him, and the high priest’s cold arithmetic became the Father’s kindest gift. What Caiaphas meant as murder God meant as salvation, and what the disciples felt as loss God meant as gain. His leaving was itself a gift: he went away in order to come nearer than he had ever been.

parallels.desc: they were cut to the heart

verseByVerse.quote: "concerning sin, because they do not believe in me; concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father, and you will see me no longer;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not making people feel bad. Convict does not mean to make somebody feel bad, and to confuse the two does real harm. What the Spirit does is show a person what is true. What the accuser does is press a person about what he is. The one produces clarity and moves toward a remedy; the other produces a fog of general unworthiness and moves nowhere at all.

Concerning sin. Not sins, plural, catalogued, but the root: the world’s great sin is not first its immorality but unbelief (3:18–19), and every other sin is fruit of this tree. The Spirit’s first move is not to make the world ashamed of its behaviour but to expose what is underneath it. This is how conviction began at Pentecost: “cut to the heart” over the one they crucified (Acts 2:36–37).

Concerning righteousness. This is the difficult clause. Jesus was tried, convicted and executed as a blasphemer and a criminal. On the world’s verdict he was a sinner, rightly put to death. The ascension is the appeal court: the Father receives him, which is a public overturning of the sentence. His return to the Father, in resurrection and ascension, proves that he was righteous (Acts 2:24, 32–36; 1 Timothy 3:16). So the Spirit convinces people that Jesus was in the right, that the standard of righteousness the world applied was itself the thing on trial, and that their own righteousness is worthless. And the righteousness of Christ, now accepted in heaven, is the righteousness God gives to all who believe (Romans 3:21–22). For the believer this changes everything: God does not weigh our better days against our worse ones and hope they balance. He counts Christ’s perfect record as ours the moment we trust him, so that we stand before him accepted as Christ is accepted (2 Corinthians 5:21). That is what justification means: God declaring the guilty righteous because of Christ.

And you will see me no longer. The phrase belongs to the argument: the vindication is invisible. Nobody watched the Father receive him. The Spirit’s work is to convince the world of a verdict handed down out of sight.

How can I tell the Spirit’s conviction from false guilt? The difference is practical. Conviction from the Spirit is specific: it names a thing, and it can be dealt with, and there is a door out of it marked with the name of Christ. The other kind is vague, cumulative, and always about the whole self rather than an act, and it never once suggests anything to do. If what you are hearing has no exit, it is not this verse. When the Spirit convicts, he leads you to confess and to trust Christ’s blood (1 John 1:9), and then he lifts the burden. When the accuser speaks, he tells you that you are beyond help. Answer him with the cross.

On a Tuesday. Pray for the Spirit to convict your friends of the sin of unbelief; only he can. And if you are carrying a vague guilt today, ask the Spirit to show you specifically what is wrong, confess it, and receive Christ’s forgiveness. If he shows you nothing specific, refuse the fog and rest in Christ’s righteousness.

parallels.desc: raised for our justification

verseByVerse.quote: "concerning judgment, because the ruler of this world is judged. I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Concerning judgment. The tense is what matters: the ruler of this world is judged, already, said before the cross, about the cross. The world judged Jesus at the cross, but in fact it was Satan who was judged there (12:31). The Spirit is not prosecuting an open case. He is publishing a verdict already entered. When the world looks as though the enemy is winning, the question of who governs was settled on a Friday afternoon and nothing since has reopened it. The Spirit convinces people that the world’s verdicts are wrong and God’s judgement is certain (Acts 17:31).

You cannot bear them now. One of the kindest sentences in the Gospel. Bear is to carry a weight: not only would they fail to understand, they could not hold it. He has more to say, and he stops, because he can see the limit of what they can carry tonight. This is why the New Testament contains more than the Gospels: the apostles’ letters unfold what Jesus began to teach.

Measured to our strength. The God who deals with us is not indifferent to capacity. If you suspect that God is expecting more of you than you can manage, this verse has him doing the arithmetic in the other direction: measuring what he says against what they can carry, and stopping short. And he does not say they will never hear it. The Spirit will bring it, later, when the weight can be borne. Nothing is being permanently withheld; it is being postponed to a point where it will help rather than crush.

If Satan is already judged, why is there still so much evil? Because his sentence has been passed but not yet fully carried out. At the cross Christ disarmed him and broke his claim on God’s people (Colossians 2:15; Hebrews 2:14–15), and the gospel now goes out to the nations, freeing his captives. He still prowls like a lion (1 Peter 5:8), but on a chain, and his time is short. At Christ’s return the sentence will be executed in full, and he will be cast out for ever (Revelation 20:10). We live between the verdict and the execution. That is why we fight, and why we fight without fear.

For worship. The prince of this world came to the cross to finish the Son, and was condemned there by the Son he meant to finish. And the same Lord, strong enough to break the devil’s claim, looked at eleven exhausted men and stopped speaking, because they could carry no more that night. The arm that cast out the enemy weighs every word it lays on the weak. Mighty against Satan, gentle toward his own: there is no other Lord like ours.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth, for he will not speak on his own authority, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will declare to you the things that are to come. He will glorify me, for he will take what is mine and declare it to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Into all the truth. A promise first to the apostles. Guide (hodēgēsei) comes from the word for a road: what a guide does for a traveller who does not know the country. All the truth means everything they need about Christ and the gospel: not all truth about everything, chemistry or astronomy, but the truth about God, salvation and the meaning of Jesus. This was fulfilled in the writing of the New Testament.

No new country. This verse needs a boundary, because it has been claimed by every movement that ever wanted to add something to Scripture. A guide does not invent the terrain. He takes people over ground that is already there. So the church tests every claim to a fresh word from the Spirit by the word the Spirit has already given, and finds in it everything needed to make us wise for salvation and equipped for every good work (2 Timothy 3:15–17). Christians who expect the Spirit to speak today usually agree that nothing he says can contradict Scripture; the question between us is whether such words carry Scripture’s authority, and this verse ties the truth the Spirit brings to what Christ gave his apostles.

Not on his own authority. Jesus states the limit himself. The Spirit does not bring a different message from the Son, any more than the Son brought a different message from the Father. He is not a second source. He reports.

The things that are to come. These words should not be inflated into a promise of prediction to individual believers about their own futures. Read alongside the rest of the New Testament they most naturally mean the things the apostles would be given to understand and write: the meaning of the cross, the shape of the age, the end.

He will glorify me. The Spirit shines the spotlight on Jesus, not on himself, and this is one of the surest tests of any spiritual claim. So the question to ask of any teaching, experience, movement or manifestation that claims the Spirit is not whether it is impressive, or emotional, or accompanied by power. It is simpler and much harder to fake: does it make much of Christ? Does it end up with people thinking more of Jesus Christ?

The Spirit who stands out of the light. A great deal that has gone under the Spirit’s name over the centuries fails that test on its own terms, because the attention settles on the phenomenon, or on the man producing it, or on the Spirit himself as the object of interest. The Spirit does not seek his own glory, which is a striking thing to notice about the third person of the Trinity: he is the one who habitually stands slightly out of the light and points.

Is this a promise to every believer, or to the apostles? In the first place it is to the apostles, who received the Spirit’s guidance into all truth and wrote it down in the New Testament. Believers today share in the promise through their word, as the Spirit opens our eyes to it (1 Corinthians 2:12–13). It is not a promise of new revelation beyond Scripture.

If the Spirit guides into truth, why do Christians disagree? Because the Spirit’s guidance into all the truth was given infallibly to the apostles, and what he gave them is in Scripture without error. Our reading of it is not infallible. We are sinners, limited in knowledge, shaped by our backgrounds, and sometimes stubborn. Where Scripture is clear, on Christ, the gospel and the way of salvation, true believers broadly agree, and that agreement is itself the Spirit’s work. Where we differ, the remedy is to go back humbly to the text, to pray, to listen to the church’s wiser teachers, and to love those with whom we disagree. The Bible is the judge, not our impressions.

verseByVerse.quote: "All that the Father has is mine; therefore I said that he will take what is mine and declare it to you. A little while, and you will see me no longer; and again a little while, and you will see me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
All that the Father has is mine. One of the largest claims in the Gospel, dropped in almost casually. Not all that the Father has given me, the language of a servant entrusted with an estate, but all that the Father has. No creature could say it. The Father, the Son and the Spirit share all things (17:10).

He will take what is mine. The Spirit takes from the Son, and everything the Father has belongs to the Son, so what the Spirit brings to the church is drawn from the whole wealth of God. There is no smaller supply reserved for people at this end of the chain.

In the flow. Jesus’ teaching on the Spirit (vv. 7–15) reaches its summit in verse 15, and verse 16 opens the last movement, sorrow turned into joy (vv. 16–24). It is not a change of subject: the same departure, now seen from the side of the friends who must live through it.

A little while. His death, in a few hours.

And again a little while. His resurrection, on the third day. Some also see a reference to his second coming. The two little whiles are not the same length. The first is less than a day. The second runs to the third day, and behind it, arguably, the whole age of the church, since the seeing that began on Easter has not ended. That elasticity is not a trick. It is how the New Testament always speaks about the interval: yet a little while, and the coming one will come and will not delay (Hebrews 10:37), written nearly two thousand years ago.

What does it mean for me that all the Father has belongs to Christ? It means that in Christ you lack nothing that you truly need. Every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places is yours in him (Ephesians 1:3); his righteousness, his sonship, his inheritance, his access to the Father are shared with you. Paul could say that all things are yours, and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s (1 Corinthians 3:21–23). When you feel spiritually poor, the remedy is not to look for some other source, a technique or an experience, but to look to Christ, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden (Colossians 2:3). The Spirit’s work is to show you what is already yours.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–33 — Sorrow Turned to Joy: I Have Overcome the World
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The disciples are puzzled by the little while. Jesus tells them their grief will turn to joy, as a woman’s labour gives way to the joy of a child, and that they will pray to a Father who himself loves them. When they declare that now they believe, he warns that they will scatter, and ends with peace in him and victory over the world.
verseByVerse.theology:
The second half of the chapter turns on time. Jesus speaks of what is coming as already settled: the ruler of this world is judged, and I have overcome the world, in the perfect tense, before the arrest. The disciples are taught to live inside an outcome that is settled but not yet visible, which is the permanent situation of the church.

That is why the childbirth image governs the section: not pain compensated afterwards by an unrelated good, but pain that turns out to have been the way the joy came. And prayer in Jesus’ name belongs here, not as a technique for extracting outcomes, but as the asking of people whose end is secured. Its stated goal in verse 24 is fullness of joy.
verseByVerse.examples:
In the world you will have tribulation (v. 33) stands against every version of Christianity that promises exemption. And it sits beside in me you may have peace without contradiction: two locations, and a believer is in both at once.

No one will take your joy from you (v. 22) is not a promise of cheerfulness. The joy is grounded in his seeing them, not in their managing to feel anything, which is why no one can confiscate it.

verseByVerse.quote: So some of his disciples said to one another, "What is this that he says to us, 'A little while, and you will not see me, and again a little while, and you will see me'; and, 'because I am going to the Father'?" So they were saying, "What does he mean by 'a little while'? We do not know what he is talking about."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What is this that he says to us? The disciples are puzzled, and whisper among themselves. John has recorded something almost comic and entirely human. They repeat the riddle back to each other, word for word, as though saying it again might help. They add the other thing he said, about going to the Father, in case it is a clue.

What does he mean by a little while? We do not know what he is talking about. And then they give up. An honest admission of confusion. The repetition of the phrase shows how much it bothered them. They could not imagine death and resurrection. And notice that they do not ask him. He is sitting there. They discuss it among themselves in what was probably an audible mutter, and John says he knew they wanted to ask, which means nobody did. Why not? Probably the same reason anybody sits on a question in a room where the mood has turned: it has been a long evening, they have already been told one of them is a traitor and that Peter will deny him, and asking would mean admitting in front of the others that they had not followed.

They had understood very little. After years of the best teaching ever given, on the final evening they cannot make out what he means: not the footwashing, not the vine, not the going away. That puts the ordinary Christian experience of not understanding into a more forgiving light. Whatever is required to follow him, comprehension on the night is evidently not it.

The riddle answered by his own body. The puzzle they could not solve was not a puzzle of words. A little while, and you will see me no longer, was Friday’s tomb; again a little while, and you will see me, was Sunday’s garden. The answer was sitting at the table with them, and within three days he gave it, not by explaining himself better but by dying and rising. What changed these men was not a clearer sentence but Easter, and then the Spirit. Christ is himself the meaning of what he says, and those who cannot follow the words are carried through by the deed.

John’s own voice inside it. John was at the table that night (13:23), perhaps among the men muttering, and decades later he could have made the disciples look wiser. Instead he preserves the flat admission in the first person plural: we do not know what he is talking about.

Is it wrong to have doubts and questions about the faith? Questions are not the same as unbelief. These men loved Jesus and were confused, and he did not reject them for it. Thomas doubted, and Jesus came to meet him (20:27). The Psalms are full of honest questions put to God. What matters is where you take them. Bring them to Christ in prayer, to his word, and to mature believers, rather than nursing them in private or letting them harden into a reason to walk away. Some questions will be answered as you grow; some will wait for glory. Faith is not the absence of questions but trust in the Lord while you ask them.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus knew that they wanted to ask him, so he said to them, "Is this what you are asking yourselves, what I meant by saying, 'A little while and you will not see me, and again a little while and you will see me'? Truly, truly, I say to you, you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice. You will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will turn into joy."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus knew. He answers the question they did not put, but not with the explanation they were after. They wanted the timetable decoded; he tells them instead what it is going to feel like, which is the thing they will actually need.

You will weep and lament. Weep is the ordinary word for shedding tears; lament is formal mourning, the wailing at a funeral. And at the cross the disciples will mourn while his enemies celebrate. That was the hardest thing about the cross for the people who loved him: not only grief, but grief while other people were pleased.

Your sorrow will turn into joy. Not followed by joy, not replaced by joy, but turned into joy. The thing they wept over on the Friday is the thing the church has sung about ever since (Galatians 6:14). Nothing was deleted; the same event changed meaning.

A better promise. It does not say the bad thing will be compensated for later by a good thing, but that the bad thing will turn out to have been the good thing, seen from the wrong end. He does not tell them the sorrow will be short, only that it will change. The disciples on the Saturday did not need a timetable. They needed to have been told, by somebody who knew it would happen, that what they were feeling was not the end of the story.

Does this mean every sorrow of mine will become joy? For the believer, yes, in God’s time, though not always in the way or on the timetable we would choose. God works all things together for good for those who love him (Romans 8:28), and the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory to be revealed (8:18). Some sorrows are turned within this life: a loss that later bears fruit, a trial that deepens faith. Others will be turned only when Christ returns and wipes away every tear (Revelation 21:4). But nothing a Christian suffers is wasted or final. The cross is the proof: if God could turn that into joy, he can turn yours.

For worship. The Man who made this promise walked into the sorrow first, and on the third day his own anguish was turned, not erased: the risen Lord still bore his wounds, and he showed his friends his hands and his side, and then they were glad (20:20). The scars that were the world’s triumph became the sight that filled them with joy. Every grief of his people is held by the One whose wounds prove that sorrow can become glory. He does not ask us to forget the Friday. He shows us his hands.

parallels.desc: weeping may tarry for the night, but joy comes with the morning

verseByVerse.quote: "When a woman is giving birth, she has sorrow because her hour has come, but when she has delivered the baby, she no longer remembers the anguish, for joy that a human being has been born into the world. So also you have sorrow now, but I will see you again, and your hearts will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Her hour has come. That is his word, running through this Gospel since Cana and meaning, almost throughout, the cross. He now lends it to a woman in labour. It is an Old Testament picture for the pains that come before God’s new age (Isaiah 26:17–19; 66:7–14).

The pain is the way the joy arrives. He could have said the sorrow passes, as weather passes, or that it is worth it, as a price is worth paying. Childbirth says something neither of those says: that the pain is not incidental to the joy but is the way the joy arrives. Nobody gets the child by another route. The cross is the birth pang of the new creation.

She no longer remembers the anguish. The clause can be overstated: no mother forgets that labour hurt. What is meant is that the pain stops being the thing the day is about. It is still in the account, and it has ceased to be the headline, displaced by something in the room that was not there before.

I will see you again. He will come to them in the resurrection (20:20), and the direction matters: not you will see me, as in verse 16, but he will see them. The joy is grounded in his looking at them, not in their managing to catch sight of him.

No one will take your joy. Not nothing: no one, and in a chapter that has just said the ruler of this world stands judged, that includes him. Joy grounded in the risen Christ cannot be taken away by persecution, loss or death; the apostles rejoiced after being flogged (Acts 5:41).

But I have lost my joy; was it taken? The joy itself, rooted in the risen Christ, cannot be taken, but your sense of it can be clouded: by sin, by sorrow, by exhaustion, by illness, by spiritual attack. David prayed, restore to me the joy of your salvation (Psalm 51:12), which shows that a true believer can lose the feeling and still have the salvation. Go back to the source. Confess any known sin. Rest your body if it is worn out. Get help if you are ill. Look again at the risen Christ in the Gospels, and keep company with his people. The joy has not been stolen; it is waiting where it always was, in him.

verseByVerse.quote: "In that day you will ask nothing of me. Truly, truly, I say to you, whatever you ask of the Father in my name, he will give it to you. Until now you have asked nothing in my name. Ask, and you will receive, that your joy may be full."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You will ask nothing of me. That day is after the resurrection, and English uses one word for two things. Ask here is erōtaō, which here means to ask a question, as in v. 19 (it can also mean to request, as in 14:16). It is what the disciples have been doing all evening, from Peter’s question to the muttering about a little while. They will no longer be confused, because the Spirit will teach them.

Whatever you ask of the Father. This ask is aiteō, to petition. So the sentence is not saying that prayer to Jesus will cease, but that the questions will stop. The interrogation ends; the asking begins. There is little record after Easter of the disciples asking Jesus what he meant. They ask about the timing of the kingdom once, are told it is not for them to know, and then they go and preach (Acts 1:6–8). A new way of prayer opens: directly to the Father, in the name of the Son.

Until now you have asked nothing in my name. Prayer in Jesus’ name is new, made possible by his death and exaltation as our mediator (Hebrews 4:14–16). The disciples had prayed, but not yet on the ground of the Son’s completed work.

That your joy may be full. Prayer is presented not as a duty but as the pathway to the full joy Jesus has been promising throughout this discourse.

At full stretch. The promise stands here at full stretch, and must be handled honestly, because every Christian who has prayed for long has asked and not received. A parent prays for a dying child. A wife prays for twenty years for a husband who never turns. To leave the sentence unqualified is to hand such people either a false hope or a private verdict on their own faith, and neither is what Jesus is doing on the last night of his life.

Not a formula. Two things keep the promise from becoming a formula. The first is that in my name means asking as his representative, for what he himself would ask (see 14:13–14). John states it plainly in his letter: this is the confidence that we have toward him, that if we ask anything according to his will he hears us (1 John 5:14). The promise is not that God will do our will if we invoke the right name, but that he will not refuse his own.

The prayer he did not press. The second is that Jesus had prayed such a prayer himself. Facing the cross he said, now is my soul troubled. And what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour? And then he answered his own question: but for this purpose I have come to this hour (12:27). He raises the request and declines to press it, because there was something he wanted more. That is what praying in his name looks like from the inside, and it is why the promise is safe. The Father did not save him from that hour, and the whole world was saved through it.

The stated end is joy. The verse is easy to misread as a guarantee of acquisition, but the stated end is joy, not delivery of goods. Some prayers God grants outright; some he answers with something better than we had the wit to ask for; and some he answers with himself, which is why saints who received almost nothing they asked for have so often been the gladdest people in the room. The prayer that goes unanswered in the form we wanted has not fallen to the ground. It has been taken up by a Father who is committed to the fullness of our joy and not merely to the shortening of our discomfort.

How do I pray in Jesus’ name in practice? Come to the Father as his child because of Christ, not because of your own record. Bring what is on your heart honestly; you do not have to tidy it first. Ask yourself whether what you are asking fits what Jesus loves and what Scripture promises, and let that shape your request. Pray for his kingdom and his glory first, as he taught in the Lord’s Prayer, and then for your daily needs without embarrassment. End with in Jesus’ name, not as a password but as a confession: I come only through him. Then trust the Father with the answer.

On a Tuesday. Take the prayer you have prayed longest without an answer. Bring it to the Father again today, in Jesus’ name, and add: but above all, Father, glorify your name, and fill my joy in you. Then leave it with him.
