verseByVerse.quote: "I have said these things to you in figures of speech. The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures of speech but will tell you plainly about the Father. In that day you will ask in my name, and I do not say to you that I will ask the Father on your behalf;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have said these things to you in figures of speech. Figures of speech (paroimiai) are veiled sayings, pictures: the same word John used of the shepherd discourse that nobody followed (10:6). The vine, the woman in labour, the house with many rooms, the shepherd, the bread, the water: figures that point beyond themselves.

Plainly about the Father. After the resurrection, through the Spirit, the meaning of every figure will be plain, and the questions of the last night will stop.

I do not say that I will ask. The delicate clause sounds at first like a withdrawal of the intercession, and it is not. Hebrews says he always lives to make intercession (Hebrews 7:25), Paul that he is at the right hand of God interceding for us (Romans 8:34), and John’s own letter calls him our advocate with the Father (1 John 2:1). What he is dismantling is a picture: a Son who has to work on a reluctant Father, prayer as something extracted by a sympathetic mediator from a reluctant judge. The Son’s mediation is not distance but access; the name of Jesus opens the door, and does not stand between the one praying and the Father. He says at once why that picture is wrong: the Father himself loves them (v. 27).

If the Father loves me, why do I need Jesus as mediator at all? Because the Father’s love for sinners is holy love. He loves us, and he will not pretend our sin is nothing. In Christ, love found a way to be just and to justify (Romans 3:26): the Father gave the Son, and the Son bore our sins, so that we could come near. Christ’s mediation is not the cause of the Father’s love but its gift. The Son did not die to make the Father love us; the Father sent the Son because he already loved us (3:16). So we need Jesus, and we need not fear the Father. Through the one we come confidently to the other.

On a Tuesday. If you tend to pray to Jesus but avoid addressing the Father, as though he were sterner, begin your prayer today with Father, and speak to him as a loved child.

verseByVerse.quote: "for the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and have believed that I came from God. I came from the Father and have come into the world, and now I am leaving the world and going to the Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Father himself loves you. The emphatic himself is doing deliberate work: not because Jesus asks him to, but directly, without anything having to be arranged. Loves here is phileō, a word of warm affection, though John uses it and the other common verb for love almost interchangeably; the weight falls on himself. The Father sent the Son because he loved the world (3:16).

A common distortion. The picture of a severe Father and a merciful Son standing between us and him has no basis in this Gospel (14:9), and it makes prayer a kind of legal manoeuvre. There is nobody to be got round.

Because you have loved me and have believed that I came from God. Their love and faith are the evidence that they belong to the Father’s family, and themselves the fruit of his love.

Does the Father’s love, then, depend on ours? No. We love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). Jesus is speaking of the Father’s fatherly delight and fellowship with those who love his Son (compare 14:21, 23), not of the love that chose them before they loved. Their love for Jesus is itself the fruit of God’s love, and the Father rejoices in it.

I came from the Father. The whole of Jesus’ mission in one sentence, in four movements: his pre-existence with the Father, the incarnation, the cross, and the resurrection and ascension. It is a creed before there were creeds, said conversationally at a supper table, and the disciples’ response is the first sign all evening that something has got through.

How can I believe the Father loves me when I feel so far from him? Look not first at your feelings but at what he has done. The Father sent his Son into the world for you; that is how you know the love of God (1 John 4:9–10). He has given you his Spirit, who cries Abba, Father, in your heart (Galatians 4:6), even when your own voice is weak. He has adopted you, and a father does not disown his child on a bad day. Feelings of distance are real and painful, and the Psalms are full of them, but they are not the measure of his love. The cross is. Speak to him as Father even when it feels hollow, and let his word, not your mood, tell you who you are.

verseByVerse.quote: His disciples said, "Ah, now you are speaking plainly and not using figurative speech! Now we know that you know all things and do not need anyone to question you; this is why we believe that you came from God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now you are speaking plainly. There is something touching and slightly absurd about this. They say it after a sentence arguably no plainer than anything else he has said that evening. They have not solved the riddle; something has simply landed, and the relief in their voices is audible.

You know all things. What has convinced them is not the vine or the Spirit but that he answered the question they had not asked aloud (v. 19). It is a real thing to have noticed, and it is a very small basis for what is coming.

This is why we believe. A real confession, but their confidence is ahead of their understanding. The faith they express is genuine but not yet refined by the fire of the passion.

Lighter than it feels. Faith attaches itself to the evidence that happens to be in front of it: an answered prayer, a coincidence too neat to dismiss, a sermon that seemed addressed to one person in the room. None of that is false. It is simply lighter than it feels, and the weight it will have to carry is not known in advance. Jesus does not disparage their confession. He asks one question about it, and then tells them what will happen before dawn.

Is my faith real if it is weak and untested? Yes. These men truly believed, and Jesus prayed for them as those the Father had given him (17:6–8). Weak faith in a strong Saviour saves, because it is the Saviour who saves, not the strength of the faith. But faith grows by being tested, and God will test it, not to break it but to deepen it (1 Peter 1:6–7; James 1:2–4). So do not despise your faith for being small, and do not trust it for being fervent. Trust Christ, and let him strengthen it through the trials he sends.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered them, "Do you now believe? Behold, the hour is coming, indeed it has come, when you will be scattered, each to his own home, and will leave me alone. Yet I am not alone, for the Father is with me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you now believe? The Greek can be read as a question or a flat statement, so now you believe, and either way there is no mockery in it. Not doubting their faith, but warning them of its weakness. He does not say they are wrong. He says what their believing is about to do.

You will be scattered. The language is Zechariah’s: strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered (Zechariah 13:7), which Matthew and Mark record him quoting that same night (Matthew 26:31; Mark 14:27, 50). And the detail is what makes it hurt: each to his own home. Not a heroic collapse. They will simply go back to where they came from, individually, the way people do when something ends.

And will leave me alone. All of them would run. The specificity of the prediction is its own kind of mercy: Jesus is not surprised by their failure; he has accounted for it in advance.

Yet I am not alone. The Father never leaves him (8:29). This sentence has to be handled with great care, because it stands a few hours from a cry that appears to contradict it. What then of his cry from the cross that God had forsaken him (Mark 15:34)? Both are true, and the church has generally held them together rather than choosing. There the Son bore the Father’s judgement against our sin, and experienced the loss of the Father’s comforting presence. The abandonment at Golgotha is real: it is the sin-bearing, the cup, the thing he asked to be spared. Yet even there the Father’s love for the Son never ceased, and the unity of the Trinity was never broken. It is the Son experiencing, in our place, the one thing he had never known. Jesus could still say my God and, at the end, Father, into your hands (Luke 23:46).

Why the words here are not made false. What happens on the Friday is the specific, temporary, substitutionary exception, and it fell on him precisely so that it would never fall on them.

What if I feel completely alone? Then you are in the place where Jesus has been, and where he has promised to meet you. He knows what it is to have every friend go home. And he knows, in a way nobody else ever will, what it is to bear the Father’s turning away, which means that the promise I will never leave you nor forsake you (Hebrews 13:5) is not a slogan. It cost something to be able to say it. If you are in Christ, the Father is with you as he was with his Son, and he will never forsake you, because the forsaking was borne for you. Tell him how alone you feel. Then reach out to his people; loneliness often lies to us about who would gladly come.

On a Tuesday. Contact one person in your church this week who may feel alone: a widow, a single parent, a student far from home, a member who has stopped coming. You may be the way the Father says, I am with you.

For worship. The Shepherd did not stop loving the sheep he knew would scatter. He went on alone to bear the stroke Zechariah foretold, and to drink a cup no friend could share. Then he came back, and found them behind locked doors, and stood among them and said, Peace be with you (20:19). The flock that ran from him was gathered round him again, and it has been gathering ever since, around the Shepherd who was left alone so that none of his own ever will be.

parallels.desc: strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered

verseByVerse.quote: "I have said these things to you, that in me you may have peace. In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
That in me you may have peace. The purpose of the whole farewell discourse is peace, and the location comes first: not in circumstances, but in me, the preposition of the vine chapter. The peace does not depend on the world outside, because it is not stored there.

In the world you will have tribulation. Tribulation (thlipsis) is pressure, distress, affliction: the same word used of the woman in labour in verse 21. And the verb is not might, but will (Acts 14:22). It is one of the most useful sentences in the New Testament for correcting expectations.

Two locations. The two prepositions stand side by side. In me, peace. In the world, tribulation. Both are true at the same time and of the same people, which is why a Christian life so often feels like two contradictory reports about the same afternoon. It is not a contradiction. It is two locations, and a believer is in both at once.

I have overcome the world. Take heart (tharseite) means be courageous. And the tense is the thing: I have overcome (nenikēka) is a completed victory with lasting effect, said before the arrest, the trial and the nails. By the cross and resurrection he has defeated sin, death and Satan. The verb is the ordinary word for winning, and John will use its noun in his letter: this is the victory that has overcome the world, our faith (1 John 5:4). His people share in his victory (Revelation 3:21).

The order of the verse. The trouble is guaranteed, the peace is available, and the outcome was settled before the fight started. He does not promise to remove the tribulation; he tells them where the peace is kept and who has already won. Anxiety often demands a life it can control and keep free of trouble, and Jesus never offers that. He offers himself, and a victory that does not depend on our keeping anything under control.

Before the prayer. This is the closing sentence of four chapters of farewell, and the next words out of his mouth are a prayer to his Father. By any measure available that evening he had overcome nothing yet: the traitor was out arranging the arrest, the eleven were about to scatter. And he says it in the perfect tense, finished and standing, with the whole of it still in front of him, because he had never once been in any doubt about how it ends.

If Jesus has overcome the world, why do I keep losing? Because the victory is his before it is yours, and you are living in the time between the decisive battle and the final peace. The world still presses, sin still wounds, and you will sometimes fall. But the outcome is not in doubt, because it does not rest on your strength but on what he has already done. Your faith joins you to the Victor (1 John 5:4–5), and he will finish the work he began. So fight, but fight from victory, not for it. When you fall, get up in his strength, not yours. The last chapter is already written, and in it the Lamb has conquered.

On a Tuesday. When trouble comes today, say both halves of the verse: in the world I have tribulation; in him I have peace. Then do the next right thing with the courage his Spirit gives.

parallels.desc: the victory that has overcome the world

16.text: <sup>1</sup>“I have said all these things to you to keep you from falling away.<sup>2</sup>They will put you out of the synagogues. Indeed, the hour is coming when whoever kills you will think he is offering service to God.<sup>3</sup>And they will do these things because they have not known the Father, nor me.<sup>4</sup>But I have said these things to you, that when their hour comes you may remember that I told them to you. “I did not say these things to you from the beginning, because I was with you.<sup>5</sup>But now I am going to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, ’Where are you going?’<sup>6</sup>But because I have said these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart.<sup>7</sup>Nevertheless, I tell you the truth: it is to your advantage that I go away, for if I do not go away, the Helper will not come to you. But if I go, I will send him to you.<sup>8</sup>And when he comes, he will convict the world concerning sin and righteousness and judgment:<sup>9</sup>concerning sin, because they do not believe in me;<sup>10</sup>concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father, and you will see me no longer;<sup>11</sup>concerning judgment, because the ruler of this world is judged.<sup>12</sup>“I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now.<sup>13</sup>When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth, for he will not speak on his own authority, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will declare to you the things that are to come.<sup>14</sup>He will glorify me, for he will take what is mine and declare it to you.<sup>15</sup>All that the Father has is mine; therefore I said that he will take what is mine and declare it to you.<sup>16</sup>“A little while, and you will see me no longer; and again a little while, and you will see me.”<sup>17</sup>So some of his disciples said to one another, “What is this that he says to us, ’A little while, and you will not see me, and again a little while, and you will see me’; and, ’because I am going to the Father’?”<sup>18</sup>So they were saying, “What does he mean by ’a little while’? We do not know what he is talking about.”<sup>19</sup>Jesus knew that they wanted to ask him, so he said to them, “Is this what you are asking yourselves, what I meant by saying, ’A little while and you will not see me, and again a little while and you will see me’?<sup>20</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice. You will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will turn into joy.<sup>21</sup>When a woman is giving birth, she has sorrow because her hour has come, but when she has delivered the baby, she no longer remembers the anguish, for joy that a human being has been born into the world.<sup>22</sup>So also you have sorrow now, but I will see you again, and your hearts will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you.<sup>23</sup>In that day you will ask nothing of me. Truly, truly, I say to you, whatever you ask of the Father in my name, he will give it to you.<sup>24</sup>Until now you have asked nothing in my name. Ask, and you will receive, that your joy may be full.<sup>25</sup>“I have said these things to you in figures of speech. The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures of speech but will tell you plainly about the Father.<sup>26</sup>In that day you will ask in my name, and I do not say to you that I will ask the Father on your behalf;<sup>27</sup>for the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and have believed that I came from God.<sup>28</sup>I came from the Father and have come into the world, and now I am leaving the world and going to the Father.”<sup>29</sup>His disciples said, “Ah, now you are speaking plainly and not using figurative speech!<sup>30</sup>Now we know that you know all things and do not need anyone to question you; this is why we believe that you came from God.”<sup>31</sup>Jesus answered them, “Do you now believe?<sup>32</sup>Behold, the hour is coming, indeed it has come, when you will be scattered, each to his own home, and will leave me alone. Yet I am not alone, for the Father is with me.<sup>33</sup>I have said these things to you, that in me you may have peace. In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world.”
16.overview:
Jesus warns his disciples plainly so that persecution, even persecution in God’s name, will not make them fall away. His going fills them with sorrow, but it is for their good, for unless he goes the Helper will not come. The Spirit will convict the world concerning sin, righteousness and judgment, and will guide the apostles into all the truth, glorifying Christ.

Then Jesus speaks of “a little while”, and with the picture of a woman in labour promises that their grief will be turned into a joy no one can take. They will pray to the Father in his name, for the Father himself loves them. He foretells that they will scatter and leave him alone, yet he is not alone. His last words before his prayer are a promise for every age: “In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world.”

17.title: The High-Priestly Prayer

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–26 — Jesus Prays for Himself, the Disciples, and All Believers
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prayer moves outward in three circles. Jesus asks to be glorified in the hour that has come, and defines eternal life as knowing the Father and the Son he sent. He asks that the disciples be kept, made holy by the word, and sent into a hostile world as he was sent. Then he prays for every later believer: that they may be one, so that the world may believe, and that they may be with him to see his glory. It ends with the Father’s love, and the Son himself, dwelling in his people.
verseByVerse.theology: The prayer is called the High-Priestly Prayer because it recalls the high priest on the Day of Atonement, the one day in the year when he entered the Most Holy Place to intercede for the people. Jesus is both priest and sacrifice: he intercedes for his people while preparing himself for the offering that will accomplish what he asks. What he asks for them, protection (v. 11), joy (v. 13), holiness (v. 17) and unity (vv. 21–23), is what the church still lives on.
verseByVerse.examples: That they may be one, as we are one (v. 22): the unity Jesus prays for is patterned on, and drawn from, the unity of the Father and the Son. It is not one organisation or a merger of churches but a shared life of love and purpose. It is also how the world is meant to see the truth (vv. 21, 23), so a church at war with itself undercuts its own witness. In Jesus’ prayer, unity and mission belong together.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus had spoken these words, he lifted up his eyes to heaven, and said, "Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son that the Son may glorify you, since you have given him authority over all flesh, to give eternal life to all whom you have given him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. John 17 is often called Jesus’ high priestly prayer: he prays as the great High Priest for his people before offering himself as their sacrifice. Like the high priest who carried the names of the tribes on his heart into the holy place (Exodus 28:29), Jesus carries his people before the Father. He prays for himself (vv. 1–5), for his disciples (vv. 6–19), and for all who will believe through them (vv. 20–26). It is his longest recorded prayer, and it lets us overhear the conversation within the Trinity. The farewell teaching of chapters 13 to 16 has ended; within the hour he will cross the Kidron and be arrested. He spends his last quiet praying aloud, in the hearing of his friends.

He lifted up his eyes to heaven. John records the posture, and it is not what most readers picture. Eyes open, head up, looking. That was a common Jewish posture in prayer, standing, face raised, hands often spread; the bowed head and closed eyes many of us default to are a later Christian habit, good in its place but not a biblical instruction. He did the same at the tomb of Lazarus (11:41). It changes the scene. This is not a man with his face in his hands. It is a man looking his Father in the face on the last evening of his life.

The Son who looks up and the sinner who cannot. Set beside him the one man in the Gospels who could not do it: the tax collector in the parable, who would not even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast (Luke 18:13). Both were heard. There is no single correct posture in Scripture. There is a Son who looks up because he has every right to, and a sinner who cannot because he has none, and the Father receives them both, the second because of the first.

Father. Six times in this prayer he says it, and twice with an adjective: Holy Father at verse 11 and righteous Father at verse 25, forms of address found nowhere else in the Bible. He is not reaching for formality. He is using the family word, the one he taught his disciples to use, and qualifying it only where the petition needs it.

The hour has come. The hour so long awaited closes a thread that has run the whole length of the book. Three times it was not yet: at Cana to his mother (2:4), and twice when men tried to seize him and could not (7:30; 8:20). Then, from the arrival of the Greeks onward, it has come (12:23, 27; 13:1; and here). For three years the not-yet was a protection; no hand could touch him before his Father’s time. It has now expired, by his own announcement, and the first thing he does with the news is pray.

Glorify your Son. Not a selfish prayer. The Son asks to be glorified in his death, resurrection and exaltation, so that he can glorify the Father. Their glory is one. And he expects the glorifying to begin not on a throne but on a cross. In this Gospel the lifting up on the cross is the beginning of the lifting up to glory (3:14; 12:32–33). The Father’s glory is the shining out of who he is, and nowhere does he show what he is more fully than in the hour when he gives his Son for sinners. The Son is asking to be the place where that is seen.

Authority over all flesh. All humanity answers to the Son (Matthew 28:18). The man about to be bound and led from court to court is the one to whom every human being in those courts already answers.

All whom you have given him. The Father’s giving of a people to the Son runs right through this prayer (vv. 2, 6 twice, 9, 24; and, in the manuscripts behind older translations, vv. 11 and 12 as well). His authority is universal; his saving gift is particular. This is what is called the covenant of redemption (v. 24; Ephesians 1:4): before anything was made, the Father and the Son agreed together on the rescue of a particular people, the Father giving them and the Son undertaking to save them, so that every believer’s salvation was planned in love before he existed. Some read given as those the Father foresaw would believe. But Jesus will say, I am not praying for the world but for those whom you have given me (v. 9), which shows that the giving is the Father’s choice, not merely his foresight. And none of those given will fail to receive what the Son was given authority to give (6:37–39).

If some are given, can I know whether I am one of them? You do not find out by looking into the secret counsel of God; you find out by coming to Christ. The same Jesus who spoke of those the Father gives him said in the same breath, whoever comes to me I will never cast out (6:37). The giving is the hidden root; the coming is the visible fruit. Nobody has ever come to Christ and been turned away because his name was missing from a list. If you are coming to him, trusting him, wanting him, that is how the Father’s gift shows itself in a human life. Election is not a wall to keep anyone out. It is the reason anyone comes in at all.

On a Tuesday. Pray with your eyes on the Father, not on yourself. Before you bring him a list, say his name the way a child does, and remember who taught you to say it. Then, when the hour you have been dreading arrives, a diagnosis, a hard conversation, a day you cannot avoid, do what Jesus did with his: speak to your Father first, and ask that he be glorified in it.
verseByVerse.note: John 17 is often called Jesus’ high priestly prayer: he prays for himself, his disciples and all future believers.

verseByVerse.quote: "And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent. I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do."
verseByVerse.commentary:
That they know you. Verse 3 is the nearest thing to a definition of eternal life anywhere in Scripture, and it is not the definition most people carry. Not: eternal life is living for ever. Not: eternal life is going to heaven when you die. Both of those are true, and neither is what he says. Eternal life is knowing, and the verb (ginōskō) here means the knowledge of a person rather than of a subject (Jeremiah 31:34; Hosea 6:6). It is the word for a husband knowing his wife, for God knowing his people, for the new covenant promise that they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest.

Eternal life has already begun. That has two consequences, and both matter. The first is that eternal life has already started for anyone who has it. If it were duration, it would begin at death. Because it is a relationship, it begins when the relationship does, the moment we come to know God, and dying does not interrupt it. That is precisely what he told Martha at the tomb: everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die (11:25–26). It grows for ever, but it does not wait.

What makes eternal life eternal. The second consequence is more searching. Endless existence without God would not be eternal life at all. Suppose a person were granted unlimited time, health restored, every faculty intact, and God were simply absent. That is not the offer being described here, and on this verse’s terms it would not be life. What makes eternal life eternal is not the length of it but who is in it. Heaven without God would be a long exile; a cell with God in it is already the beginning of heaven.

The only true God. This verse is sometimes used against the deity of Christ, as though the only true God excluded Jesus, and the argument deserves an answer rather than a dismissal. Look at what the sentence actually does. It makes knowing Jesus Christ part of the definition of eternal life, standing in the same clause and joined by and to knowing the only true God. No monotheist would put a creature there. He does not deny his own deity by calling the Father the only true God; he denies the idols. The Son is included within the one true God (1:1). And John, who wrote this sentence, wrote in his letter of the Son: “He is the true God and eternal life” (1 John 5:20), using the same two words. The verse distinguishes the Father from the Son, which orthodoxy has always done. It does not divide them.

Jesus Christ. One curiosity worth flagging honestly: this is the only place in the Gospels where Jesus uses the full name Jesus Christ of himself. Some think John has phrased his Lord’s words for readers a generation later, which would be in keeping with how he writes. Nothing turns on it either way; the words are the true Word of God as John was moved to record them.

Having accomplished the work. The verb means completed, finished, from the same family as the cry “It is finished” (19:30). He speaks from the threshold of the cross as though it were behind him, because his obedience was already settled: there was no part of the Father’s will he would leave undone. And look at what he claims. Every word, every sign, every hour of thirty-odd years, offered to the Father without a single failure. No other human being has ever been able to say, I glorified you on earth, without needing to add a confession.

How do I actually get to know God better? The same way you come to know anyone: by listening to him, speaking with him, and spending time in his company. He speaks in Scripture, so read it not only to learn facts but to meet him; ask as you read, what does this show me of God and of Christ? Speak to him in prayer, honestly, as a child does. Meet him with his people at his table and under his preached word. And obey what you learn, because Jesus said the one who keeps his commands is the one to whom he shows himself (14:21). Knowledge of God grows slowly, like a friendship, and it grows most in the hard seasons when he is all you have.

Is it not narrow to say eternal life comes only by knowing Jesus Christ? It is narrow in the way any true answer is narrow. If eternal life is a relationship with God, the question is not which religion is most sincere but whether God can be known at all, and Jesus says he is known in the one he sent (14:6). Every other road asks us to climb up to God by devotion or goodness, which favours the disciplined and the respectable and leaves everyone else without hope. This road is open to the worst sinner, and closed only to the person who insists on coming as anything other than a receiver. A door that only God could open, held open to anyone who will come, is not arrogance. It is mercy.

On a Tuesday. Give him ten unhurried minutes today with a Gospel open, and ask, Lord, show me yourself. And when you are tempted to measure your life by its achievements, remember that the one thing that will last for ever is the friendship God has begun with you.

For worship. The God who made the galaxies has made himself knowable, and the knowing of him is life itself. He did not leave us to guess at him. He sent his Son, the only man who could tell the Father that he had glorified him on earth with nothing left undone, and that finished obedience is credited to people whose obedience is full of holes. To know the only true God in the face of Jesus Christ is to have begun a life that will outlast the stars, because the One we know has no end.
verseByVerse.note: “Know” in the Bible means a personal relationship, not mere information.

parallels.desc: that he understands and knows me
“It is finished”

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, Father, glorify me in your own presence with the glory that I had with you before the world existed. I have manifested your name to the people whom you gave me out of the world. Yours they were, and you gave them to me, and they have kept your word."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The glory that I had with you. Verse 5 is said as a request. No prophet ever prayed anything remotely like it. Moses asked to see God’s glory; this is a man asking for his own back. And the claim inside the request is the whole of the Prologue in a single clause: he had glory, with the Father, before there was a world to have it in. It is one of the clearest statements of Christ’s eternal pre-existence. God says he will not give his glory to another (Isaiah 42:8). So the Son is not another; he is God.

With you. It is the same thought as 1:1, the Word was with God: not glory given him at some point, but glory possessed alongside the Father when nothing else existed. The Son did not begin at Bethlehem. He came from somewhere, and he is about to go back.

The glory set down. In the incarnation he veiled that glory: he did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself (Philippians 2:6–7). This prayer is the same fact from the inside: a man asking to be given back what he had before, having spent some thirty years without its outward splendour. And he asks to return to it now in his human nature as well. The one who goes back to the Father’s presence goes back with hands that were pierced and a body that was raised. Our flesh has entered that glory in him.

Did Jesus stop being God when he laid his glory aside? No. He did not lay aside his deity; he laid aside the open display of it. He remained what he always was while becoming what he was not, a man. The emptying of Philippians 2 is explained by the next words, taking the form of a servant: he emptied himself by adding, not by subtracting. So even in the manger and on the cross he was the eternal Son, upholding all things (Hebrews 1:3). The glory was hidden, as the sun is hidden behind cloud. At times it broke through, at Cana, on the mountain, at the tomb of Lazarus. Here he asks for the cloud to be taken away.

Your name. The name is God’s character, all that he is (1:18). The whole ministry of Jesus, teaching, signs, foot-washing and finally the cross, is the disclosure of the Father’s name. No one needs to guess at the Father any more: he has been shown, in full, in the Son.

Yours they were, and you gave them to me. They belonged to the Father before they belonged to the Son. Chosen before they came (6:37; Ephesians 1:4), they are not first the Son’s and then the Father’s; they are first the Father’s and then, by gift, the Son’s. Election is the Father’s prior claim on the people the Son will redeem.

They have kept your word. This is startlingly generous. Look at who he is talking about: eleven men who have understood very little all evening, who, Luke tells us, argued that same night about which of them was the greatest (Luke 22:24), who will soon run into the dark, and one of whom will deny knowing him three times before the cock crows. And this is his report to his Father about them. Not they are trying. Not they will improve. They have kept your word.

How he measures his people. He is not blind, and he is not flattering. He is describing them as what they had become by receiving his word, which is a different measurement from the one we habitually run on ourselves.

Does this mean my sin does not matter to him? No. He grieves over it and he will deal with it; after the resurrection, beside the Sea of Galilee, he will restore Peter by name, and it will hurt (21:15–17). But he does not define his people by their failures. He defines them by what grace has made them: people who have received his word and are his. That should make you more serious about sin, not less, because you are being treated as something better than your worst nights. And it should silence the voice that tells you that your stumbles prove you were never his.

On a Tuesday. When you pray about your failures, confess them plainly; and then listen to how your High Priest speaks of you to the Father. When you speak to other believers about their failures, ask whether you sound like him. A church in which people describe each other as Jesus described the eleven is a church in which the weak grow strong.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now they know that everything that you have given me is from you. For I have given them the words that you gave me, and they have received them and have come to know in truth that I came from you; and they have believed that you sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything is from you. The teaching, the signs, the authority, the men themselves. Nothing in the ministry of Jesus came from him acting on his own, apart from the Father (5:19), and the disciples have finally grasped it, on the last night, not long before their nerve fails them.

Given, received, known, believed. The chain of revelation runs Father to Son, Son to disciples, and through them to us, and these two verses lay out four verbs in sequence. Faith begins by receiving: not by inventing God’s word or improving it, but by taking what is handed over. That is the whole mechanism of Christian faith in one sentence. Only the first is God’s action in the grammar, though the whole prayer has been saying that the rest are his doing too.

Knowing before believing. The order is instructive. Knowing comes before believing here, which is not how we usually put it. But look at what is known and what is believed. They came to know that I came from you: his origin. They believed that you sent me: his commission. The recognition of who he is precedes the trust in what he was sent to do, and both rest on words that were handed over rather than worked out.

Two errors corrected at once. Faith is not a leap made in the absence of content; there are words here, given and received, and a person to be known. And it is not a conclusion reached by unaided reasoning either, since the words came from outside, from the Father through the Son. Christian faith is neither blind nor self-made. It is the open-eyed reception of what God has said.

My faith feels nothing like as solid as that. Does it count? Yes. The disciples’ faith that night was real, and within an hour it was shaking badly. Jesus called it faith anyway, because faith is measured by its object, not by its strength. A trembling hand that grasps a strong rope is as safe as a steady one. If you have received his words as true, if you believe that Jesus came from God and that the Father sent him to save sinners, you have the faith this verse describes, however weak it feels. Feed it with the same words that created it, and ask him, as a father once did, to help your unbelief (Mark 9:24).

verseByVerse.quote: "I am praying for them. I am not praying for the world but for those whom you have given me, for they are yours. All mine are yours, and yours are mine, and I am glorified in them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am praying for them. I am not praying for the world. It is the coldest-sounding sentence in the warmest chapter in the Bible, and people are genuinely troubled by it, so it should not be hurried past. Jesus’ high priestly intercession here is particular: for those the Father has given him. That does not mean he never prayed for unbelievers (Luke 23:34), or that we should not (1 Timothy 2:1). But his intercession as High Priest, which secures salvation, is for his own (Hebrews 7:25; Romans 8:34). His sacrifice and his intercession have the same scope. He prays for those for whom he dies, and he dies for those for whom he prays. Reformed readers see here one of the strongest supports for definite atonement. Definite atonement means that when Christ died he intended actually to save a particular people, those the Father had given him, and not merely to make salvation possible for everyone and then wait to see who would take it. His death and his prayers aim at the same people, and they do not miss (10:11, 15). Many faithful Christians read the matter differently, holding that Christ died for every person alike and pointing to verses such as 1 John 2:2; they are brothers in the same gospel, and the question is how to hold those verses together with this prayer, where the High Priest’s pleading has a definite people in view.

What the sentence is. Three things help. The first is simply what the sentence is: a statement about the scope of this petition, not about the heart of the one praying. He is asking for something specific, that these men be kept, and that what he is about to do for them be applied to them, and the world that is rejecting him cannot be the subject of that request. To ask that someone be protected from a danger is not, in the same breath, to ask a blessing on the danger.

The world in the same prayer. The second is that the same prayer turns to the world twice, a few verses on: so that the world may believe that you have sent me (v. 21); so that the world may know (v. 23). The unity he asks for is asked for the world’s sake. A man indifferent to the world does not make its persuasion the goal of his petition for the church. He prays for his church in order to reach the world.

Father, forgive them. The third is the plainest. Within hours the man who said I am not praying for the world would be praying, out loud, from a cross, for the men driving the nails: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34). (These words are missing from some early manuscripts of Luke, but many scholars judge them original and most Bibles print them.) That is not indifference. So what the verse does say, and it does say it, is that there is a particular intercession which has a particular object, and the object is the people the Father gave him. This is the High Priest with the names on his breastplate. He is not praying generically. He is praying for named individuals, and the naming is the comfort rather than the offence.

For they are yours. He pleads for them on the ground that they belong to the Father. The argument is the argument of a son to a father: these are yours; take care of what is yours.

All mine are yours, and yours are mine. Then the clause that sounds like accounting and is not. Any of us could say the first half. Everything I have is God’s: that is ordinary piety, and it is true. Nobody else can say the second half. Yours are mine is a claim to hold the Father’s property as one’s own (16:15). Luther is said to have observed that no creature could utter it. It is the language of perfect equality, spoken quietly as a matter of course.

I am glorified in them. Their existence is his ongoing glory: an exhibition of what grace produces in those who receive it. The eleven are not much to look at tonight, and he says he is glorified in them anyway, as a craftsman is honoured by the work still on his bench.

Is Jesus praying for me now? Yes, if you are his. He always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25), and Paul names it as one of the reasons no one can condemn us: Christ Jesus is the one who died, was raised, is at the right hand of God, and indeed is interceding for us (Romans 8:34). His intercession is not a nervous pleading with a reluctant Father; it is the risen Son presenting his finished sacrifice for the people it was offered for, and asking for what it purchased. It is never refused. On the days you cannot pray, he is not silent.

Then should I pray only for Christians? No. The Son’s high priestly intercession is unique to him, and it is not our pattern for every prayer. We are told to pray for all people, kings and those in authority included (1 Timothy 2:1–4), to pray for our enemies (Matthew 5:44), and to plead for the lost as Paul did for Israel (Romans 10:1). We do not know who the Father has given to the Son, so we pray for everyone and preach to everyone, trusting that he will call his own through those prayers and that preaching.

On a Tuesday. Think of the believers you know who are struggling, and picture your High Priest carrying their names before the Father. Then bring them by name yourself, and add one person who does not yet know him. You will be imitating your Lord in both: his intercession for his own, and his prayer from the cross for those who did not know what they were doing.

verseByVerse.quote: "And I am no longer in the world, but they are in the world, and I am coming to you. Holy Father, keep them in your name, which you have given me, that they may be one, even as we are one. While I was with them, I kept them in your name, which you have given me. I have guarded them, and not one of them has been lost except the son of destruction, that the Scripture might be fulfilled."
verseByVerse.commentary:
No longer in the world. He speaks as if already gone, and he knows exactly what a hostile world will cost them. Everything he now asks for them is asked with that picture before him: his friends left behind, in enemy country.

Holy Father. He has been saying Father all evening. Here he adds holy, and the reason is in the petition attached: he is asking that these men be kept in a world that is unholy, and that they be made one. Holiness and fatherhood together: the God who is utterly set apart from all evil is the God who holds his children close. Holy is the word for the God whose presence on Sinai could not be approached without washing and warning (Exodus 19:10–13): a purity so bright that sinners cannot stand before it. That this God should be Father to men like the eleven is not something to take for granted. It is grace. Keep means guard, protect, preserve. (Where the ESV reads your name, which you have given me, the KJV, following later manuscripts, reads those whom thou hast given me; the earliest manuscripts speak of the name given to the Son.) In your name means by the power of who you are, and in loyalty to your revealed character. This is the basis of their perseverance: those whom God has given to Christ will be kept in faith to the end. They may stumble badly, as Peter did that very night, but they will not finally fall away, because the one who began a good work in them will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6).

Which you have given me. The Father has given the Son his name: the divine name (Philippians 2:9–11). The Son keeps his people by the same name in which he reveals the Father, the name above every name.

That they may be one. The goal of their preservation is unity modelled on the Trinity: not organisational sameness, but the unity of shared life, love and purpose that the Father and Son have always had.

The son of destruction. There is a wordplay here that no English version can show: apōleto and apōleias, the same root twice in one clause. Not one was lost except the son of lostness. The man is named by the very thing that did not happen to anybody else. “Son of destruction” is a Hebrew way of describing one who belongs to destruction and is destined for it; the phrase turns up once more in the New Testament, for the man of lawlessness (2 Thessalonians 2:3). It is Judas. He was never one of those truly given; he was lost because he never truly belonged (6:64, 70).

That the Scripture might be fulfilled. The Scripture Jesus means is probably the psalm he quoted of Judas earlier that same evening: “Even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me” (Psalm 41:9). Peter later applies another psalm to him: “Let another take his office” (Acts 1:20; Psalm 109:8). Jesus did not fail to keep him; Judas’s end shows his own guilt and God’s sovereign purpose, both together.

Was Judas free? The hard question must not be dodged. Two things have to be held, and the New Testament holds them both without visible strain. Judas is never once described as a victim. He is called a thief who helped himself to the money bag (12:6), Satan enters him after he takes the morsel (13:27), and Peter says he turned aside to go to his own place (Acts 1:25): his own, chosen, fitting. Nothing in any account treats him as a man who wanted otherwise. And equally, Scripture had said it would happen, and Peter at Pentecost says the whole event went forward according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, in the same breath as you crucified and killed him by the hands of lawless men (Acts 2:23). What Scripture never does is derive one from the other. It does not say Judas betrayed him because it was written; it says it was written, and he did it, and both are true. Anyone who claims to have resolved that has almost certainly done so by quietly dropping one half.

Could I be the one exception, like Judas? The verse is not given to help us classify anybody, still less to frighten the trembling. It is given to explain why the keeping did not fail: I have guarded them, and not one of them has been lost. The exception is the man who was never inside the guarding in the first place. Judas loved money, kept his heart closed, and never came to Jesus in sorrow; even his remorse took him away from Christ rather than to him (Matthew 27:3–5). If you fear that you might be a hypocrite and run to Christ with that fear, you are doing the one thing Judas never did. The sheep who worry that they are goats are seldom goats. Bring your fear to the Shepherd, and let his keeping be your confidence.
verseByVerse.note: “Son of destruction” describes one destined for destruction — Judas.

verseByVerse.quote: "But now I am coming to you, and these things I speak in the world, that they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves. I have given them your word, and the world has hated them because they are not of the world, just as I am not of the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
My joy fulfilled. He is praying, they are listening, and he says he prays aloud for their sake (15:11). That is a strange and moving thing to realise about this chapter. It is a genuine prayer, addressed to the Father throughout, and it is also being said where eleven frightened men can hear every word. He wanted them to overhear it.

Overheard love. Consider the difference between somebody telling you that they value you, and overhearing them say it to a third party when they did not know you were listening. The second is the one that lands. This prayer was spoken so that it would land that way. Everything in it about their being given to him, kept, guarded, loved and sent, they heard him say to his Father, and they were meant to spend the rest of their lives remembering what he said about them when he was talking to God. John did remember, and wrote it down, so that we could overhear it too.

My joy. Joy has come up again and again in the last hour (15:11; 16:20–24; and here). He keeps returning to it on the worst night of his life, which tells you what he thought his friends were going to need. And it is his joy he gives: not a mood they must manufacture, but the joy of the Son in the Father’s love and in doing the Father’s will. That joy did not leave him in the garden. It was the joy set before him for which he endured the cross (Hebrews 12:2).

The world has hated them. The sober half. The word they received sets them apart, and draws the world’s hatred. He does not pray it away. He states it as the present condition, has hated, already, before the arrest, and moves straight on to what he will ask instead.

Not of the world. Their origin is now from above, like his (3:3). The new birth has made them citizens of another country, and the world can sense it. They are hated not because they are odd but because they belong to the one the world rejected.

In the flow. Verse 14 names what they are being kept in: a world that hates them. That sets up the two requests that follow, not removal but protection (v. 15), and holiness for the mission on which he is sending them (vv. 17–18). And for the book, it gathers up the promise of 16:22, that their sorrow would turn into a joy no one could take from them.

Why does the world hate Christians, and what if I am not hated? The world’s hatred is first a hatred of Christ, and it falls on his people because they carry his word (15:18–20). It does not always look like persecution; often it is scorn, exclusion, or simply being left out. And many Christians in many places live quietly with kind neighbours, which is a mercy to be thankful for, not a sign of failure. But if your faith never costs you anything, it is worth asking whether anyone can see it. Do not court hostility by being unpleasant; Peter says we should suffer as Christians, not as wrongdoers or meddlers (1 Peter 4:15–16). Simply be faithful, and let the response be his business.

On a Tuesday. Take the joy he gives into the place where you are least welcome as a Christian: the office where your faith is mocked, the family gathering where it is ignored. Joy is not denial of the hostility; it is a deeper possession that the hostility cannot reach.

For worship. On the night of his betrayal, with the cross before him, the Son of God was thinking about his friends’ joy. The gladness he gave them was his own, the joy he has had in the Father from all eternity. The world can take a great deal from the people of God, but it cannot reach the joy that lives in the heart of the Son, and that is the joy he has given.

verseByVerse.quote: "I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the evil one. They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not out of the world. This verse settles what a Christian is to do with the world by refusing both of the available shortcuts, for his people must stay in the world for their mission (v. 18). The first shortcut is withdrawal: the compound, the Christian bubble, the instinct to arrange a life in which one need never deal with anybody who does not already agree. It is an ancient instinct and it is not wicked; it is usually driven by a genuine desire not to be defiled. He declines to ask for it, and he had the strongest possible reason to want it for men he loved who were about to be hunted.

From the evil one. The evil one is Satan (1 John 5:18–19), and the danger is not the world itself but the one who works in it. The Greek form is genuinely ambiguous; it could equally be rendered from evil, and translators differ, which is the identical ambiguity in the last line of the Lord’s Prayer (Matthew 6:13). Either way, behind the evil stands the evil one, and the Father’s keeping is the answer to his strategy.

Protection, not exemption. Not that nothing will happen to them: a great deal did, and, as early tradition tells it, most of them died for it. But that the one who wants them will not get them. Satan may sift them like wheat (Luke 22:31); he will not keep them. A Christian can lose his job, his health, his life for Christ, and lose nothing that the evil one was after.

The prayer he taught them. This prayer keeps brushing against the one he gave them: a Father addressed, a name made known and honoured, a will done, a keeping from evil. He taught them to pray it, and here he is doing something very like it himself, on the last night, with the petitions turned toward them.

In, not of. The second shortcut is assimilation, and this verse blocks it. Staying in the world is not the same as belonging to it. So the position he prays for is the uncomfortable middle, and it is the only one on offer. Its practical shape is not withdrawal from the neighbours but a difference in what one is loyal to, which is much harder to arrange and impossible to fake. They are citizens of heaven on embassy in the world.

Where Christians differ: separation from the world. Some Christians have sought holiness by withdrawing from society; others have so blended in that no difference remains. This commentary’s view: Jesus prays for neither. His people are to live in the world, engaged in its life, but distinct in character and loyalty, kept by God from evil. Not monasteries, nor conformity, but holy presence.

So is it wrong to protect my children or avoid certain places? No. Wisdom is not withdrawal. Parents rightly guard young children from what would harm them, and every Christian should flee situations that feed his own particular temptations (2 Timothy 2:22). The question is direction and purpose. Are you sheltering in order to grow strong enough to go out, or hiding so that you never have to? Christian schooling, careful choices about entertainment, a decision not to take a job that would compromise you: none of these is the error Jesus refuses. The error is a life that has no unbelieving friends, no presence among the lost, and no intention of having any. He sends his people in, and he keeps them while they are there.

On a Tuesday. Picture the place where you feel most out of step as a Christian, and instead of planning your exit, ask what it would look like to be there this week as one Christ has sent: honest when others cut corners, kind where others are cruel, unashamed when the subject comes up. Then ask the Father to keep you from the particular evil that place presents.

For worship. The Son who had every reason to ask that his friends be taken out of danger asked instead that they be kept in it. And the Father has kept them: through arenas and exiles, through two thousand years of hostility, his church has never been taken out of the world and never been swallowed by it. The evil one is strong, but he has never yet taken from the Father one whom the Father was asked to keep. Our safety is not distance from danger. It is the hand of God.

parallels.desc: deliver us from evil

verseByVerse.quote: "Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth. As you sent me into the world, so I have sent them into the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sanctify them. Two things in verse 17 are sharper than the English suggests. The first is that sanctify is not first a moral word. Hagiazō means to set apart for a purpose: it is what was done to vessels, to a day, to a priest. The moral content follows from the setting apart rather than the other way round: a thing devoted to God must then be fit for him. So to sanctify is both a status (set apart, 1 Corinthians 6:11) and a process (made holy, 1 Thessalonians 5:23). The petition is not first make them better but make them yours, for this work, which is exactly why the next verse is about being sent.

Your word is truth. The second is the grammar of the last clause. Not your word is true, which would be a claim about accuracy, though it is accurate. Your word is truth: a noun, not an adjective. It does not merely correspond to reality; it is the thing reality is measured by: not contains truth or becomes truth, but is truth. We grow in holiness as we are shaped by God’s word (Psalm 119:9, 11; Ephesians 5:26; 2 Timothy 3:16–17). What does that mean in practice? When your feelings, your culture or your own reasoning disagree with what God has said, it is not his word that must give way. It is the fixed point, and everything else is checked against it (Isaiah 40:8).

The answer is a book. The instrument named for the sanctifying is that word: not an experience, not a technique, not a decision. The most common Christian instinct when growth has stalled is to look for a new method or a stronger resolution. This verse points somewhere quieter and more effective, the same place the pruning came from in chapter 15: you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you (15:3). The Spirit sanctifies, and the sword he uses is the word of God (Ephesians 6:17).

As you sent me. The Son’s mission is the pattern for the church’s (20:21). This is the Gospel of John’s version of the Great Commission, often overlooked because it sits inside a prayer, and he will say it to their faces on Easter evening. The comparison is not modest. The pattern for how the church is sent is how the Son was sent, which meant coming all the way in, living among people at their level, and being at their disposal. Of course the church does not atone; that work is his alone. But it goes as he went: humbly, truthfully, and at cost.

What if reading the Bible feels dry? It sometimes will, and the word works anyway. Much of what nourishes us does so without our feeling it; nobody remembers last month’s meals, but they are why you are alive. Keep reading, and read more of it at a time so that you see its shape. Read it with others, ask questions of it, hear it preached, and pray before you open it: open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law (Psalm 119:18). Read it to meet Christ, not only to tick a box. And remember that sanctification is the Father’s work in answer to the Son’s prayer. You are not making yourself holy by effort; you are putting yourself where he has promised to work.

On a Tuesday. Choose one verse from your reading this morning and carry it into the day: write it on a card, say it at the moments you are tempted, let it shape one decision.
verseByVerse.note: To sanctify is to set apart for God and make holy.

parallels.desc: your law is true

verseByVerse.quote: "And for their sake I consecrate myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth. I do not ask for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
I consecrate myself. Verse 19 has the priest and the sacrifice in one sentence. Consecrate is the same word as sanctify in verse 17, and Jesus was already holy. Here he means he sets himself apart for the sacrifice, as a priest was consecrated and as an offering was consecrated (Exodus 28:41; Deuteronomy 15:19). He dedicates himself to death for their sake (hyper, on their behalf and in their place). In the Old Testament ritual those were different operations performed by different parties. The priest was consecrated; the animal was consecrated; the priest offered the animal. Here one person does all of it to himself, for other people, the night before it takes effect.

That they also may be sanctified. Their being set apart depends on his: he goes first, and what he does to himself is the reason the thing can be done to them at all. We are sanctified by the will of God through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all; by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified (Hebrews 10:10, 14).

How can my holiness depend on his? Because holiness is first a belonging and only then a likeness. By his death Christ has set you apart for God once and for all; you were washed, you were sanctified (1 Corinthians 6:11). That is finished, and it cannot be undone by a bad week. Out of that settled status comes the daily growth in holiness, as the Spirit uses the word to make you in practice what Christ’s sacrifice has already made you in standing. So you do not fight sin in order to become God’s; you fight it because you already are his, and you fight it with the confidence of someone whose victory was bought before the battle started.

Those who will believe. Now Jesus prays for us. The prayer has been about eleven men in a room, and in one sentence it opens out to the whole church, in every century, including whoever is reading this page. If you believe, Jesus prayed for you that night.

Through their word. The chain is specified. The eleven spoke, and people believed, and those people spoke, and it has not stopped. Anybody who believes in Christ today believes because that word arrived, by however long a route, and this verse says such a person was in view on the Thursday night. And the word is still theirs: the apostolic word we have in the New Testament, which is why the church has always measured its preaching by Scripture. So everything that follows, the unity, the glory given, being loved as the Son is loved, being with him where he is, is not asked for the apostles alone. It is asked for the ordinary Christian who has never seen a miracle and finds prayer difficult.

How can he have prayed for me if I did not exist yet? Because he is the eternal Son, and he knew the people the Father had given him before the foundation of the world (v. 24; Ephesians 1:4). He named you in the only way a person can be named who does not yet exist, those who will believe in me, and the Father, who knows every one of them, heard the request as a request for each. And he did not merely foresee you. He prayed for you, and then he went out and made it possible.

On a Tuesday. Trace the chain that brought the word to you: the person who first told you, the person who told them, the church that sent them. Thank God for them by name. Then ask who is the next link. Somebody will one day believe in Christ through your word, spoken over a kitchen table or written in a message, and that person too is in this prayer.

For worship. Nobody has ever been prayed for like that. With the arrest drawing near, the Son of God spent his last quiet on strangers who had not been born, people twenty centuries later who would come to him because a handful of fishermen eventually told somebody. And the One who prayed for them set himself apart, priest and lamb in one, and walked out into the night to be the offering that would make them holy. Every believer since has been brought near to God on that prayer and that blood, and the High Priest who prayed it has never stopped praying.

parallels.desc: sanctified through the offering of his body

verseByVerse.quote: "that they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be in us, so that the world may believe that you have sent me. The glory that you have given me I have given to them, that they may be one even as we are one,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
That they may all be one. This is the verse on which the whole question of a divided church turns, and three answers have been given to it. Rome reads the prayer as asking for one visible institution under one visible head, and takes the existence of separated churches as the standing wound this prayer was meant to prevent. The ecumenical movement of the last century read it as a mandate to merge structures, and set about doing so. And a good many Protestants have read it as a prayer for an invisible unity only, on the comfortable assumption that since all true believers are already one in Christ, our visible divisions cost nothing.

As you, Father, are in me. The prayer itself rules out each of the three readings. Against the single-institution and merger readings, look at the pattern Jesus gives. The unity he asks for is modelled on the life of the Trinity, where the persons are genuinely distinct and the unity is one of love, life and will rather than of administration. Nothing in that picture requires a single earthly organisation, and the apostolic churches of the New Testament were plainly many congregations, not one structure.

That they also may be in us. Christian unity is rooted in union with the Father and the Son. It is not first something we build but something we are brought into. The unity of believers is a share in the life of God himself, and that is why it is precious and why breaking it is serious.

So that the world may believe. Unity is a witness. And here is the answer to the invisible-only reading: a unity the world cannot see cannot persuade the world of anything. Whatever this unity is, it must show. Which leaves the harder and better answer. It is not a summons to dissolve our confessions into one institution, and it is not permission to be comfortable about our divisions. It asks for a love between Christians that outsiders can actually observe and cannot account for: believers who honour one another across the lines, refuse to caricature, and are visibly glad of grace wherever it appears (13:35).

Unity and truth in one prayer. One thing more must be said, because it is in the same prayer. Four verses earlier Jesus asked, sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth (v. 17). Unity and truth are petitions of one prayer and cannot be traded against each other. A unity bought by agreeing to say less than the gospel says is not the answer to this prayer but a counterfeit of it, and the Reformers, who did not leave lightly, understood that. Neither does unity in the truth excuse needless division among true believers. What is asked here is not that we stop caring what is true. It is that those who hold the truth should stop treating each other as enemies. And it searches the heart: much division among believers is not a stand for truth at all, but the old idol of being right, and being seen to be right, dressed up as zeal.

The glory that you have given me. The glory of the Son, revealed in his life and above all in the cross, he shares with his people. Given is past tense, before the cross, to eleven men who were about to run. Whatever this glory is, it was already theirs while they were behaving at their worst, which rules out reading it as a reward for anything. And the prayer says what it is for in the same breath: that they may be one even as we are one. The glory given is the shared life that produces the unity. Not radiance, not status, not visible splendour, but a share in what the Father and the Son have between them.

When should I leave a church, and when should I stay? Stay through disagreements over secondary matters, through disappointing preaching, through personalities that grate; those are the very places where the unity Jesus prayed for is proved. Leave, peaceably and without slander, when a church abandons the gospel itself, denies the authority of Scripture, or will not deal with serious sin or abuse, and only after you have raised your concern honestly with its leaders. Even then, do not burn the bridge; you may be leaving brothers and sisters you will spend eternity with. And never leave a church simply to escape a person you have refused to forgive.

Can I be united with Christians whose baptism or church order differs from mine? Yes, in the deepest sense, and in more practical ways than many think. A Baptist and a Presbyterian who both trust Christ alone are already one in the Father and the Son. They may not be able to form one congregation, because each must act on his convictions about baptism with a clean conscience. But they can pray together, honour each other’s ministers, share platforms for the gospel, help each other’s churches in need, and speak of each other with warmth. This commentary holds believer’s baptism, and holds it alongside a glad affection for paedobaptist brothers (those who baptise the infants of believers) who love the same Lord.

On a Tuesday. Most of us have one believer we are quietly at odds with, and that is the place where this prayer comes closest. A message written, a call made, a forgiveness asked or offered: Christ has already made you one in himself, and he prayed for the world to see it.

verseByVerse.quote: "I in them and you in me, that they may become perfectly one, so that the world may know that you sent me and loved them even as you loved me. Father, I desire that they also, whom you have given me, may be with me where I am, to see my glory that you have given me because you loved me before the foundation of the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Perfectly one. Perfectly means brought to completion; unity grows towards its goal. The word belongs to the same family of words as accomplished in verse 4 and as the cry from the cross, It is finished (19:30). What his finished work secured, his people grow into.

Loved them even as you loved me. Two clauses in these verses are among the hardest things in the Bible to believe about oneself, and they should be stated as plainly as possible. The first is this one. Not loved them. Not loved them very much. Even as you loved me: the same comparison he used at 15:9, now made to the Father in prayer, which means it is not a figure of speech aimed at encouraging anybody. He is telling the Father what is the case. The Father loves believers as he loves the Son. Not that we are equal to the Son, but that we are loved with the same love, because we are in him.

The measure of the Father’s love. This is uncomfortable. Most Christians will affirm that God loves them, and most, if pressed, would describe that love as something a good deal cooler than the love of the Father for the Son: a settled goodwill, perhaps a determination to put up with them. This verse forbids it. The measure is not a lot; the measure is the love that has existed between the Father and the Son from before the world was made, and the sentence has no qualifier in it anywhere.

How can God love me like that when I am so sinful? Because he does not love you on the strength of what you are in yourself. He loves you in his Son. You have been united to Christ by faith, clothed in his righteousness, adopted into his sonship (Galatians 4:4–7). When the Father looks at you he sees you in the Beloved (Ephesians 1:6), and the love that rests on the Son rests on you there. Your sin is real, and it grieves him; but it was laid on Christ and punished in him, so it cannot shut you out of the love that Christ enjoys. You will not feel this every day. It is true every day.

I desire. The second is verse 24, and the verb changes. Everything up to now has been asking. Here it is thelō, I will: not a request but the confident will of the Son, in perfect agreement with the Father. It is the language of a son who knows exactly where he stands, exercising a right. And what he uses it for is not deliverance, or vindication, or a shorter road. He uses it to ask that the people he is leaving should end up where he is (14:3).

To see my glory. Heaven is seeing Christ’s glory. This is the second time in this prayer he has looked back before the world existed: first to ask for his glory back (v. 5), now to say why the Father gave it. God did not need to create to have someone to love. He is love, from all eternity (1 John 4:8). Before light, before time, before there was anything to be glorified in front of, there was a Father loving a Son, and this prayer asks that a crowd of latecomers be brought in to watch.

What will heaven actually be? Before it is a place of rest or reunion, it is being with Christ and seeing him. Everything else follows from that. The reunions are real, the end of pain is real (Revelation 21:4), the renewed creation is real; but the centre is the face of the Lamb (Revelation 22:4). Paul said to depart and be with Christ is far better (Philippians 1:23), and John said that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). If heaven seems vague or dull to you, it is usually because Christ seems vague to you now. Get to know him here, and you will long to see him there.

On a Tuesday. Say it to yourself before you get out of bed: the Father loves me as he loves his Son. Then let that settle how you face the day’s small humiliations and fears. A person who knows he is loved like that does not need to win every argument or be noticed in every room.

verseByVerse.quote: "O righteous Father, even though the world does not know you, I know you, and these know that you have sent me. I made known to them your name, and I will continue to make it known, that the love with which you have loved me may be in them, and I in them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
O righteous Father. This is the second and last of the qualified addresses (v. 11). He reaches for righteous at the point where he is contrasting the world’s ignorance with his own knowledge and the disciples’ recognition. It is the word for a judge who gets the verdict right, and it is used at the moment when a right verdict is about to be spectacularly withheld by every human court he will stand in before morning. The courts of men will condemn him; the righteous Father will raise him.

I know you. Three groups: the world that does not know God, the Son who knows him perfectly, and the disciples who know that the Son came from him. The only way out of the first group into the third is through the second. Nobody comes to know the Father except through the Son who knows him (Matthew 11:27).

I will continue to make it known. Two tenses, and the future is the striking one. He is close to arrest and speaks of a work of disclosure that will go on. He said at verse 4 that he had accomplished the work he was given, and here he says the making known continues. Both are true: the accomplishing is the cross, and the disclosing does not stop at the cross. It goes on through the Spirit, through the word, through the preaching of the church, and it is going on now, wherever the gospel is read.

That the love may be in them. The prayer ends where all the purposes of God end: the love of the Father for the Son dwelling in believers, and Christ himself dwelling in them. These are the last words he speaks before the garden. Not that they may know about the love. That the love itself, the actual love of the Father for the Son, should be located inside them.

And I in them. The prayer ends without a petition. He does not close with a request or a summary; he ends by naming a destination, and the destination is not a place. Four chapters of farewell, a discourse about a vine, a promise of the Spirit, an intercession for the whole church across every century, and the final word is a preposition and a pronoun. In them. That is where all of it was going. Not to a system, not to an institution, not even to heaven considered as a location, but to the Son of God taking up residence in ordinary people.

In the flow. These verses close the whole farewell of chapters 13 to 17. The prayer opened with the hour and the glory (v. 1); it ends with love and indwelling, because the glory he asked to show is seen above all in the Father’s love given to sinners. And the next sentence of the book has him crossing the Kidron (18:1). Everything he has just asked, keeping, holiness, unity, glory, the Father’s love in his people, he goes out to secure by being arrested, condemned and lifted up.

What does it mean in practice that Christ is in me? It means you are never alone and never left to your own resources. By his Spirit the risen Christ lives in every believer (Romans 8:9–10; Galatians 2:20; Colossians 1:27). That is why you can love people you could not love by nature, endure what would otherwise crush you, and keep praying when prayer feels empty: the life of Christ is working in you. You will not usually feel it as a sensation. You will see it, over years, in a growing likeness to him and a love for him that was not there before. It is also why you can face death calmly: what is in you cannot die.

17.text: <sup>1</sup>When Jesus had spoken these words, he lifted up his eyes to heaven, and said, “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son that the Son may glorify you,<sup>2</sup>since you have given him authority over all flesh, to give eternal life to all whom you have given him.<sup>3</sup>And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.<sup>4</sup>I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do.<sup>5</sup>And now, Father, glorify me in your own presence with the glory that I had with you before the world existed.<sup>6</sup>“I have manifested your name to the people whom you gave me out of the world. Yours they were, and you gave them to me, and they have kept your word.<sup>7</sup>Now they know that everything that you have given me is from you.<sup>8</sup>For I have given them the words that you gave me, and they have received them and have come to know in truth that I came from you; and they have believed that you sent me.<sup>9</sup>I am praying for them. I am not praying for the world but for those whom you have given me, for they are yours.<sup>10</sup>All mine are yours, and yours are mine, and I am glorified in them.<sup>11</sup>And I am no longer in the world, but they are in the world, and I am coming to you.
