Holy Father, keep them in your name, which you have given me, that they may be one, even as we are one.<sup>12</sup>While I was with them, I kept them in your name, which you have given me. I have guarded them, and not one of them has been lost except the son of destruction, that the Scripture might be fulfilled.<sup>13</sup>But now I am coming to you, and these things I speak in the world, that they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves.<sup>14</sup>I have given them your word, and the world has hated them because they are not of the world, just as I am not of the world.<sup>15</sup>I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the evil one.<sup>16</sup>They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world.<sup>17</sup>Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth.<sup>18</sup>As you sent me into the world, so I have sent them into the world.<sup>19</sup>And for their sake I consecrate myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth.<sup>20</sup>“I do not ask for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word,<sup>21</sup>that they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be in us, so that the world may believe that you have sent me.<sup>22</sup>The glory that you have given me I have given to them, that they may be one even as we are one,<sup>23</sup>I in them and you in me, that they may become perfectly one, so that the world may know that you sent me and loved them even as you loved me.<sup>24</sup>Father, I desire that they also, whom you have given me, may be with me where I am, to see my glory that you have given me because you loved me before the foundation of the world.<sup>25</sup>O righteous Father, even though the world does not know you, I know you, and these know that you have sent me.<sup>26</sup>I made known to them your name, and I will continue to make it known, that the love with which you have loved me may be in them, and I in them.”
17.overview:
Before going out to Gethsemane, Jesus lifts his eyes to heaven and prays aloud. Since the sixteenth century this has been called his “high-priestly prayer”: like the high priest on the Day of Atonement, he prays for himself, for his priests (the apostles), and for the people. It is the longest prayer of Jesus recorded, and lets us hear the Son speaking to the Father on the night before the cross.

Every Christian is in view in this prayer, and Christ’s intercession continues for them in heaven (Hebrews 7:25).

18.title: The Arrest, the Denial, and the Trial Before Pilate

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–27 — Gethsemane, the Arrest, and Peter's Denial
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The arrest in the garden across the Kidron, the hearing before Annas, and Peter’s three denials, which John sets side by side with Jesus’ own questioning, so that we watch the disciple fail outside while his Lord stands firm inside.
verseByVerse.theology: I am he, in Greek *egō eimi*, is the divine name Jesus has been claiming throughout this Gospel (8:58). When he says it in the garden, armed men fall to the ground. He gives himself up not because he is overpowered but because he chooses to: the Shepherd lays down his own life for the sheep (10:11, 18). The arrest is at once his most vulnerable moment and his most sovereign act.
verseByVerse.examples: Peter’s denials come at a charcoal fire among the servants and officers: to a servant girl, to a group at the fire, and to a relative of the man whose ear he had cut off, three times as Jesus had said, and then the rooster crows. What fails here is self-confident discipleship, faith leaning on its own courage rather than on Christ. His restoration in chapter 21 will be built on a different foundation: the love and prayer of his Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus had spoken these words, he went out with his disciples across the brook Kidron, where there was a garden, which he and his disciples entered. Now Judas, who betrayed him, also knew the place, for Jesus often met there with his disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. John’s account of the arrest and trials shows Jesus in complete control. He goes out to meet his captors, they fall before him, he protects his disciples, and before Pilate he is the one who judges. Meanwhile Peter denies him three times. The King goes to the cross as the Lord who lays down his life of his own accord (10:18). Every power in Jerusalem will take its turn with him, the temple guard, the high priests, the Roman governor, the soldiers, the crowd, and each will think it is deciding his fate. John wants us to see from the first verse that none of them is.

Across the brook Kidron. The Kidron Valley lies between Jerusalem and the Mount of Olives, on the east side of the city. It was dry most of the year: John calls it a cheimarros, a winter torrent, a stream bed that runs only after rain. There is a tradition, impossible to verify, that the blood of the temple sacrifices was channelled down into it, which at Passover would have been the blood of thousands of lambs. Whether or not that is so, the Lamb of God now crosses it on his way to his own death.

The king who crossed the Kidron weeping. There is an Old Testament scene underneath this crossing, and once it is seen the whole night changes shape. A thousand years earlier another king went out of Jerusalem, betrayed: “And all the land wept aloud as all the people passed by, and the king crossed the brook Kidron” (2 Samuel 15:23). David is fleeing Absalom, going up the Mount of Olives weeping, head covered and feet bare. The man who had betrayed him was Ahithophel, his own counsellor, the friend whose advice had been “as if one consulted the word of God” (2 Samuel 16:23). David prayed that his counsel would be turned to foolishness (2 Samuel 15:31), and when Ahithophel saw that his counsel had not been followed, he set his house in order and hanged himself (2 Samuel 17:23). It has all happened before, and the Son of David now walks the same ground with the opposite purpose. David went over it to save his life. This King goes over it to lay his down.

A garden. Matthew and Mark call it Gethsemane, “oil press” (Mark 14:32), an olive grove across the valley on the Mount of Olives. John plainly knows the place, but he alone calls it a garden (kēpos), and he will use the word again: in the place where he was crucified there was a garden (19:41). John does not spell out an echo of Eden, but many readers have heard one: a garden, where Adam fell; a garden, where the second Adam is arrested; and a garden, where he will be buried and rise. The story that went wrong in a garden is being put right in one, and John has quietly bracketed the passion between two of them.

Judas also knew the place. The place was not discovered. It was known, because it was theirs, and the only reason Judas could find him in the dark is that he had been welcome there. That is the pattern of all intimate betrayal: the enemy uses knowledge gained in trust. And Jesus did not hide. He did not change his habits that night or choose a safer olive grove. He went where Judas would find him.

Was it right for Jesus to walk into danger like that? Yes, because his hour had come and his Father had sent him to this. For three years he had withdrawn when men tried to seize him early (7:30; 10:39), because his time was not yet. Now it was, and to avoid the garden would have been to refuse the cup. That is very different from courting danger or despising one’s life. Jesus is not teaching us to put ourselves in harm’s way for the sake of it; ordinary prudence is right for us, as it was for him in the years before. He is showing us a Saviour who laid down his life when it was required, and not one moment before or after.

On a Tuesday. If one of the places where you have known Christ’s company has become the place of a wound, a betrayal in the fellowship, a hurt in the church, remember that your Lord knew that too. He did not stop going to the garden because Judas knew it. Do not abandon the places of fellowship because one person abused them.
verseByVerse.note: The Kidron Valley lies between Jerusalem and the Mount of Olives; it is usually dry except in the rainy season. Matthew and Mark name the garden Gethsemane.

parallels.desc: David, betrayed, crosses the Kidron weeping

verseByVerse.quote: So Judas, having procured a band of soldiers and some officers from the chief priests and the Pharisees, went there with lanterns and torches and weapons. Then Jesus, knowing all that would happen to him, came forward and said to them, "Whom do you seek?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A band of soldiers. Two things about the arresting party are absurd, and the absurdity is the point. The first is the size. The band was a cohort (speira), a tenth of a Roman legion, nominally six hundred men, though probably only a detachment was sent. Their presence shows the Romans were involved from the start, which suggests that Pilate had already been approached. With them came the temple police (“officers”). All this, at night, for a man who had taught openly in the temple every day and could have been taken there at noon (18:20).

With lanterns and torches. The second is the equipment. It is Passover, which falls at full moon. They have come out on the brightest night of the month, carrying fire, to look for the light of the world, and they will not find him until he steps out and tells them where he is. They come with their little lights to arrest the Light.

Knowing all that would happen. Not was found, not was seized: he went out to them. Everything that follows in this Gospel’s account of the passion is governed by that verb. And John pauses to tell us what he knew as he did it. Not the general shape of it. All of it: the ropes, the courtyard, the slap, the flogging, the nails, the cross. Some courage depends on not knowing quite how bad it will be. This is the other kind, and it is much rarer. He walked out of the trees toward the torches with the whole of the following day already in view.

Whom do you seek? It is the first thing he says in the passion narrative, and it echoes the first words Jesus speaks in this Gospel, what are you seeking?, asked of two men following him (1:38). He will ask it again of Mary at the tomb (20:15). The book opens with him asking what people want, the arrest opens with the same question put to men with weapons, and the resurrection morning opens with it put to a weeping woman. The hunters are asked to name their quarry, as though he were in charge of the proceedings, which he is.

Did Jesus really know everything that would happen? Yes. As the eternal Son he knows all things, and in his human mind he had been given to know his path in detail; he had predicted his betrayal, his handing over to the Gentiles, the mocking, the flogging and the cross (Mark 10:33–34). That is what makes his going forward so astonishing. Nothing took him by surprise. And it is a comfort for us: the Christ who goes before you into your sufferings is not improvising. He knows the road you are on, and he walked a harder one with his eyes open.

On a Tuesday. When you know a hard thing is coming, the operation next week, the conversation you have been putting off, the consequence of an old sin, do not hide among the trees and wait to be found. Go forward to meet it, as he did, praying.

For worship. The hunted one is the great Seeker. Men came with torches to find him, and he let himself be found, because he had come into the world to look for people who were not looking for him. He asked the soldiers whom they sought, and the true answer lay behind their swords: he was seeking them, and Judas, and the scattered eleven, and every lost sinner since. The Lamb went to the altar on his own feet, and his searching love found us in our darkness long before we lifted a lantern toward him.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the “band of soldiers” was a cohort, a tenth of a Roman legion — Roman troops joined with the temple police.

verseByVerse.quote: They answered him, "Jesus of Nazareth." Jesus said to them, "I am he." Judas, who betrayed him, was standing with them. When Jesus said to them, "I am he," they drew back and fell to the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am he. Jesus of Nazareth is a man from a despised village (1:46), the name that will be nailed above his head in three languages (19:19). His reply is barer in Greek than the English can be: two words, egō eimi, with no he. The ESV notes that “I am he” is literally “I am” here and in verses 6 and 8. On one level, it simply means I am the one. But John’s readers have heard Jesus use these words as the divine name (8:24, 28, 58). The two words he speaks in the dark are the same two words that made them pick up stones at 8:58, before Abraham was, I am, and they echo what God said out of the bush (Exodus 3:14).

Judas was standing with them. John will not let it pass. In the middle of the sentence about the divine name, he records where the man was standing: among the soldiers.

They fell to the ground. They could not take him unless he let them (10:18). And when they went down, Judas, standing among them, presumably went down too.

What the falling is and is not. It is not a rescue: nobody is prevented from anything, and within moments he is being tied up. It is not a threat; he does not follow it up. The soldiers get up and do their job. What it is, is a demonstration placed at exactly the point where the reader most needs it. From here to the end of the book, everything done to him is done by other people: he is bound, struck, tried, flogged, sentenced, nailed. John puts one moment at the front of that sequence in which an armed cohort goes over backwards at two words, so that nobody afterwards can say he was overpowered.

Why did they fall? Was it a miracle? John does not explain the mechanism, and we should not invent one. He simply records that when the Son of God spoke his name, armed men could not stand. Some have suggested shock or confusion, but that would not explain why soldiers who had come for this very purpose went down together. The plain sense is that for a moment the majesty of who he is broke through, as it did on the mountain of transfiguration, and creatures fell before their Creator. The day is coming when every knee will bow at that name (Philippians 2:10). In the garden, a company of armed men bowed early.

On a Tuesday. When Christ seems weak in your world, mocked at work, ignored in the news, outvoted in the culture, remember the garden. He has never been overpowered. He has only ever been patient. Let that steady you when you speak of him, and let it humble you when you are tempted to think his cause depends on your cleverness.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “I am he” is literally “I am” here and in verse 8 — the words of the divine name.

parallels.desc: my adversaries stumble and fall

verseByVerse.quote: So he asked them again, "Whom do you seek?" And they said, "Jesus of Nazareth." Jesus answered, "I told you that I am he. So, if you seek me, let these men go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So he asked them again. He is directing his own arrest, identifying himself a second time to men who have just been knocked down by the first.

Let these men go. It is a condition. He is negotiating, at the moment of his arrest, with a cohort that has just been knocked off its feet, and the only thing he asks for is that his friends be allowed to walk away. Consider what he does not ask for. Not a hearing. Not fair treatment. Not time. Not that the disciples be permitted to come with him, which is what they had all sworn they wanted a few hours earlier. He uses the one piece of leverage he has to get them out of the garden (10:11–12).

And it worked. Every one of the eleven survived that night, which is not what usually happened to the followers of an executed insurrectionist. The Romans had every reason to take the lot of them. He had prayed earlier that night, out loud where they could hear, that the Father would keep them (17:12). Here he is making it true himself, with soldiers in front of him. The prayer and the answer to the prayer are the same person. He asked the Father to keep them, and then kept them, and the keeping cost him the thing he was keeping them from.

Is this really a picture of the cross? Yes, and John means it to be. The arrest is not the atonement; that happens on the cross, where Jesus bears God’s wrath for sin. But the garden shows its shape in advance: the Shepherd stepping between his sheep and the danger, accepting what was coming for them so that they can go free. At the cross he does the same thing before a far greater judgment. The law’s sentence against his people falls on him, and they are released. Whenever you feel the accusation of your sins, hear him say to it: if you seek me, let these go.

On a Tuesday. When you have the chance to shield someone weaker, a colleague being blamed, a child being mocked, a believer being slandered, step forward as he did, even at cost to yourself. Those who have been released by a substitute should be quick to stand in the gap for others.

verseByVerse.quote: This was to fulfill the word that he had spoken: "Of those whom you gave me I have lost not one." Then Simon Peter, having a sword, drew it and struck the high priest's servant and cut off his right ear. (The servant's name was Malchus.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
To fulfil the word. Jesus’ words are fulfilled like Scripture, because they are Scripture. The word is from 17:12 (and 6:39). John applies a saying about eternal security to a matter of physical safety on one particular night. That is not a misapplication; it is a window. The man who will not let them be arrested in a garden is the same man who will not let them be lost at the end, and the second promise is made credible by watching him keep the first.

Simon Peter, having a sword. Only John names Peter as the swordsman. Peter acts as he promised (13:37), bravely and foolishly, against a cohort. But be fair to him. He was hopelessly outnumbered. He had been told at supper that he would deny his master before dawn and had flatly contradicted it. He drew anyway. Whatever else this is, it is not cowardice, and the same man will be denying everything before morning, which tells you something uncomfortable about how little courage in one form predicts courage in another.

The servant’s name was Malchus. An eyewitness detail: if, as many think, John is the other disciple who was known to the high priest (18:15), he knew the household, and the other Gospels say only that someone struck the servant of the high priest. Perhaps Peter aimed for the head. John gives the wounded man a name, and he will mention him again when a relative of his recognises Peter at the fire (18:26). To the soldiers he was one of the party; to Peter he was a target. To Jesus, as Luke the doctor tells us, he was a man to be healed (Luke 22:51), and so the last healing before the cross was done for an enemy, mending what a disciple had broken. The Lord whose own body was about to be torn spent one of his last free moments repairing the body of a man sent to bind him.

What Peter got wrong. Peter’s fault was not his courage but his reading of the situation. He had heard about the cup and the hour and the Good Shepherd laying down his life, and he arrived at the garden believing his job was to stop it. This is uncomfortable for zealous people, but ask what you are currently defending God from. If the answer involves preventing something he has already said he intends to do, a loss, a humbling, a door closing, then the sword is out, and the most likely outcome is somebody else’s ear.

How can I tell whether my zeal is Peter’s sword? Ask three questions. Is it in line with what Christ has actually said, or with what I assume he must want? Am I using the weapons he gave, truth spoken in love, prayer, patient witness, or the world’s weapons of force, manipulation and contempt? And who is getting hurt? Zeal that wounds the people Christ came to save, or that would have kept him from the cross, is zeal without knowledge (Romans 10:2). Real zeal for Christ looks like his own: it is willing to suffer, quick to heal, and never needs to win by cutting someone down.
verseByVerse.note: Only John names Peter as the swordsman and Malchus as the servant.

verseByVerse.quote: So Jesus said to Peter, "Put your sword into its sheath; shall I not drink the cup that the Father has given me?" So the band of soldiers and their captain and the officers of the Jews arrested Jesus and bound him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Put your sword into its sheath. His kingdom does not advance by the sword (v. 36; Matthew 26:52), and he has to rescue his disciples not only from the soldiers but from themselves.

Shall I not drink the cup that the Father has given me? The “cup” pictures the suffering and judgment the Father had appointed for him. In the Old Testament the cup is often the cup of God’s wrath (Psalm 75:8; Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15). That wrath is no sudden flare of irritation. It is the holy resistance of a pure God to evil, his just response to sin (Romans 1:18), and it would be a lesser God who looked at the world’s cruelty and felt nothing. Jesus will drink the cup of God’s anger against sin, so that his people never have to. The other Gospels record his prayer in the garden, “remove this cup” (Mark 14:36); John gives us his resolve: shall I not drink it? And notice whose cup it is: the cup the Father has given. Not Judas’s cup, not Caiaphas’s, not Pilate’s. Behind every human hand that night stands the Father’s purpose, and the Son receives it from him.

Where is Gethsemane? The word cup prompts a question about what John has not told us. All three of the other Gospels place at this spot the most famous prayer ever prayed in a garden: Jesus falling on his face, in anguish (Luke’s detail of sweat like drops of blood is missing from some early manuscripts), asking that the cup might pass, and the disciples asleep a stone’s throw away. John gives us none of it. He brings Jesus across the Kidron, and the next thing that happens is that Judas arrives with lanterns. He is not concealing the anguish, and the proof is that he assumes it here. Jesus speaks of the cup the Father has given him as of something already settled between them; you cannot resolve a struggle you never had, and the sentence only makes sense if there was one. John has written the agony in his own place and his own way. He put it in chapter 12, in daylight, in public, before a crowd: now is my soul troubled, and shall I ask to be saved from this hour? No, for this purpose I have come to this hour (12:27). That is much the same prayer, the same request raised and the same refusal to press it, only moved out of the dark and into the open where everyone could hear.

Both pictures are needed. That is the shape of the whole passion in this Gospel. The others show us a man overtaken by horror and holding on; John shows us a man walking into it with his eyes open, going out to meet the soldiers rather than waiting to be found, asking whom they seek, knocking them off their feet with a word, and then holding out his hands. Both are true and the church has always needed both. Take John without the others and you may forget what it cost him. Take the others without John and you may forget that nobody took his life from him.

Did Jesus resist the Father’s will in the garden? No. In Gethsemane his human soul shrank from the cup with all the horror of a holy man facing the wrath of God against sin, and he said so honestly. But every time he said it he added, not my will, but yours, be done (Luke 22:42). To feel the full weight of something terrible and still embrace God’s will is not resistance; it is the deepest obedience there is. And it means that when you pray in agony, asking God to take something away while longing to do his will, you are not sinning. You are praying the way your Lord prayed.

And bound him. The captain is a chiliarchos, commander of a thousand, a senior Roman officer. They bind the one who had just floored them. He lets them. There was a man in Israel’s memory who had been bound by his father and laid on wood on a mountain, and who, Jewish tradition said, was old enough to have resisted and did not (Genesis 22:9). Jewish tradition called it the Akedah, the Binding, and some Jewish writings of the period linked it with the Passover season. Isaac was released and a ram was found. This time the ropes stay on.

On a Tuesday. When suffering comes, ask not first who caused it but who gave it, and whether you can receive it from your Father’s hand. That is not passivity: Jesus objected to injustice within the hour. It is trust.

For worship. The cup was ours. We filled it with every sin we ever committed, and the Father put it into the hands of his Son, and the Son did not set it down. Shall I not drink it? he asked, and on the next afternoon he drank it to the bottom, so that not one drop of wrath is left for those who are his. What remains for us is another cup altogether, the cup of blessing at his table (1 Corinthians 10:16), filled not with anger but with the new covenant in his blood.
verseByVerse.note: The “cup” pictures the suffering and judgment the Father had given him to bear.

verseByVerse.quote: First they led him to Annas, for he was the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was high priest that year. It was Caiaphas who had advised the Jews that it would be expedient that one man should die for the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
First they led him to Annas. Annas had been high priest from AD 6 to 15, until the Romans removed him, but five of his sons and his son-in-law Caiaphas held the office after him, so for roughly half a century the high priesthood was a family business run out of one house. Many Jews still regarded him as the true high priest, since the office was meant to be for life, and Luke can write of the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas (Luke 3:2), naming two men for an office that had one holder. Only John records this preliminary hearing.

Father-in-law of Caiaphas. The family dominated the temple, and it is often thought that they profited from its trade, the very trade Jesus had disrupted (2:13–16). So Jesus is taken first not to a court but to the house of the man whose family had the most to lose. It is not a legal step. Annas holds no office. It is a private call before anything official begins.

Expedient that one man should die. The verdict was decided before the trial (11:49–52), and John told us then that Caiaphas spoke a prophecy he did not know he was uttering. Now the prophet is the presiding judge, accomplishing his own prophecy without understanding it.

A night of irregularities. Jewish law as later written down forbade capital trials at night, forbade them on the eve of a festival, required a day to elapse before a death sentence, and required the court to sit in its own chamber. Every one of those appears to be broken in the next few hours. How much of that later law was in force in the AD 30s is genuinely disputed, and the point should not be pressed further than the evidence allows. But the men conducting this are the guardians of the law, and they are working in the middle of the night in a private house.

Why did God let such corrupt men hold the high priesthood? Because he was bringing the old priesthood to its end and replacing it with a better one. The very men who should have recognised the Lamb of God handed him over, and in doing so fulfilled the purpose of the priesthood without knowing it: a sacrifice was offered for the people. God often lets human corruption run its course in order to show that salvation comes from him and not from human institutions. The true High Priest stood bound before the false ones, and within days the temple curtain would be torn in two (Matthew 27:51).

On a Tuesday. If you are caught in a process that has already decided against you, at work, in a family dispute, in a court, tell him plainly. Do what is right within it, speak the truth, and leave the final verdict with the Judge who cannot be bribed.
verseByVerse.note: Annas had been high priest from AD 6 to 15; five of his sons and his son-in-law Caiaphas held the office after him, and he remained the power behind it. Only John records this first hearing.

parallels.desc: the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas

verseByVerse.quote: Simon Peter followed Jesus, and so did another disciple. Since that disciple was known to the high priest, he entered with Jesus into the courtyard of the high priest, but Peter stood outside at the door. So the other disciple, who was known to the high priest, went out and spoke to the servant girl who kept watch at the door, and brought Peter in.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simon Peter followed. Brave, after the others had fled (Mark 14:50). Peter had not taken the option of distance, and whatever is about to happen, he fails in a place most of the others never went.

And so did another disciple. He is often thought to be the beloved disciple, John himself (20:2), which fits the way this Gospel refers to its author in the third person and never by name. The difficulty is the next clause: he was known to the high priest, and a Galilean fisherman’s acquaintance with the household of Annas is not obvious. How he was known is uncertain: perhaps through business (supplying fish), or family connections (some traditions say John was of priestly descent). Some think he is someone else entirely. The Gospel does not say, and neither should a commentary.

Into the courtyard. A large house with a central courtyard, which Annas and Caiaphas may have shared. Whoever the other disciple was, what is not in doubt is what he did with his access: he brought Peter in.

A door opened in kindness. That is one of the small ironies of the passion. The man with the connections uses them to bring his friend inside, and inside is precisely where Peter will fail. The kindness was real; left in the street, Peter might have gone home. That is not a reason to be careful about kindness. It is a reason to be honest about how failure arrives: seldom through malice, often through a door somebody opened for us out of love. And the door is kept by a servant girl, whose idle question will bring down the most famous denial in history.

Two men through one gate. John sets Master and disciple in the same courtyard on purpose. Jesus goes in bound, under guard, knowing exactly what is about to happen at the fire; Peter goes in free, confident and unaware. Inside, one will be questioned and tell the truth; outside, the other will be questioned and lie, and John will cut between them so that we watch both at once. The Lord did not go in to keep Peter from falling that night. He went in to be condemned in Peter’s place, and he had already prayed, as Luke records, that Peter’s faith would not fail (Luke 22:32).

Should I avoid places where I might be tempted? Often, yes, and with no shame in it. Scripture tells us to flee youthful passions (2 Timothy 2:22) and to make no provision for the flesh (Romans 13:14). But Peter’s problem was not that he went into the courtyard; following his Lord into danger was right. His problem was that he went in sure of his own strength, having brushed aside the warning (13:37–38). Go where Christ calls you, even into hard places. But go praying, aware of your weakness, and leaning on him, not on your record of loyalty.
verseByVerse.note: The “other disciple” is often thought to be the beloved disciple, John.

verseByVerse.quote: The servant girl at the door said to Peter, "You also are not one of this man's disciples, are you?" He said, "I am not." Now the servants and officers had made a charcoal fire, because it was cold, and they were standing and warming themselves. Peter also was with them, standing and warming himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You also are not one of this man’s disciples, are you? She frames the question so that it invites a no. She is not accusing him; she is a girl at a door, making conversation, probably without much interest either way. “Also” means like the other disciple, whom she knows to be one of them and who has come to no harm.

I am not. No threat has been made, and no soldier is looking at him. And Peter, who a few hours ago swung a sword at an armed man’s head in the dark, says ouk eimi, I am not. The contrast with the garden is deliberate (vv. 5, 6, 8). The Lord named himself and a cohort went over backwards; the disciple denies who he is to a girl minding a gate.

A charcoal fire, because it was cold. Jerusalem, high in the hills, can be cold on spring nights, and John’s eye for it is the eye of a man who was there. The word (anthrakia) appears only here and in 21:9, where the risen Jesus cooks breakfast and restores Peter beside another charcoal fire. John does not explain the connection. The smell of that second fire may well have taken Peter back to this night, and the risen Lord lit it to heal what the first had witnessed. For now Peter stands with the enemies of Jesus, among the officers who arrested his master, at their fire, getting warm.

How denial usually happens. Denial is rarely dramatic. It is much more often what Peter does here: taking the answer somebody has already assumed, because correcting them would be awkward and nothing much seems to be at stake. It costs nothing at the time, which is exactly why it is so easy, and Peter’s began the same way. Underneath it is the fear of man, the wish to be accepted by the people round the fire, and Scripture calls that fear a snare (Proverbs 29:25). The cure is not a stronger will but a greater fear: the fear of the Lord, whose opinion matters more than any circle we want to belong to.

Is keeping quiet about my faith the same as denying Christ? Not always. There is a time to keep silence and a time to speak (Ecclesiastes 3:7), and not every conversation calls for a testimony. Wisdom, tact and timing are not cowardice. But silence becomes denial when someone asks you directly, or assumes something false about you, and you let it stand to protect yourself. The test is the motive. Am I silent because this is not the moment, or because I am ashamed of him? If it is shame, Jesus’ words apply: whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him will the Son of Man be ashamed (Mark 8:38). Ask him for courage before the question comes. And if you have already failed in exactly this way, remember that the man who stood at this fire was restored by the same Lord and sent out to preach.
verseByVerse.note: Jerusalem, high in the hills, can be cold on spring nights. John mentions a charcoal fire again when Peter is restored.

verseByVerse.quote: The high priest then questioned Jesus about his disciples and his teaching. Jesus answered him, "I have spoken openly to the world. I have always taught in synagogues and in the temple, where all Jews come together. I have said nothing in secret."
verseByVerse.commentary:
About his disciples and his teaching. Annas, called high priest by courtesy, fishes for evidence. It is what a security official asks, perhaps looking for a charge of sedition or false teaching.

Which high priest is this? John calls both Annas and Caiaphas high priest. Annas had held the office and still bore the title, and many read v. 19 as his questioning, with Jesus then sent to Caiaphas (v. 24). Others read vv. 19–23 as Caiaphas. The first is the more likely.

Why John leaves out the trial before the council. A reader comparing the Gospels will see what John does not give us here. Matthew and Mark record a full session of the Sanhedrin with witnesses, the charge about destroying the temple, the high priest’s question under oath, and the verdict of blasphemy. John has none of it, and sends Jesus on to Caiaphas in a single sentence (v. 24). The likeliest reason is the one that explains most of John’s omissions: the other accounts were long in circulation and he supplies what they lacked. Nobody else records the Annas hearing at all, and the other disciple, perhaps John himself, was inside the courtyard that night.

He would not name them. Jesus answers only the question about his teaching. Not one word about the disciples. He has just got them out of the garden; he is not going to name them in a courtyard. Meanwhile, a few yards away, one of those disciples is refusing to name him.

Openly to the world. The word for openly (parrhēsia) is the one John uses of speaking with boldness, in public, without concealment, and it is a claim that can be checked, because everything he taught was taught in the two most crowded buildings available.

Nothing in secret. This does not deny that Jesus taught the Twelve privately (chapters 13–17). His private teaching explained the same message he preached openly (Mark 4:34); there was no secret doctrine for insiders.

The God who did not speak in secret. Jesus is using the language of the God of Israel. Through Isaiah the Lord had said, I did not speak in secret, in a land of darkness (Isaiah 45:19), setting himself against the idols and oracles with their hidden whispers. Now the prisoner in Annas’s house says the same of his own ministry, and it fits, because he is the Word made flesh (1:14), God’s speech in person. The God who spoke openly by the prophets has spoken openly in his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2). Annas wants secrets. He is standing before the one in whom God has hidden nothing he means his people to know.

The contrast not stated. He is standing in a private house, in the middle of the night, before a man who holds no office, and he replies that he has said everything in daylight. The contrast is not stated. It does not need to be.

Is there any hidden teaching for advanced Christians? No. Christianity has no secret inner doctrine reserved for an elite. Every generation has had teachers claiming special knowledge beyond the Bible, from the Gnostics of the second century to modern movements promising a deeper revelation, and every one is answered by this verse. What Jesus taught he taught openly, and what the apostles received they wrote down for the whole church (1 John 1:3). The deepest things of God are in the same Scriptures that a child can read. Growth in Christ is not access to hidden knowledge; it is going further into what has been openly given.

On a Tuesday. When you are asked about other believers by someone who means them harm, gossip, an employer’s probing, a hostile questioner, follow your Lord and protect them.

parallels.desc: I did not speak in secret

verseByVerse.quote: "Why do you ask me? Ask those who have heard me what I said to them; they know what I said." When he had said these things, one of the officers standing by struck Jesus with his hand, saying, "Is that how you answer the high priest?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why do you ask me? Ask those who have heard me. Under Jewish law, a case should be established by witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15), and later Jewish tradition would not let the accused be made to testify against himself. Jesus calls for a proper trial. The hearing is already procedurally compromised, and he says so.

Struck with his hand. The slap should be allowed its full weight. The word (rhapisma) can mean a blow with a rod, but probably means an open-handed blow across the face, illegal and humiliating. It is not mainly a way of causing pain. It is the standard gesture for putting an inferior back in his place.

Is that how you answer the high priest? Showing off to his master. The officer explains himself in exactly those terms. So the first violence done to Jesus is not judicial and not even angry. It is an act of etiquette enforcement by a junior official who thought the prisoner’s tone was wrong. This is the man through whom all things were made, standing bound in a courtyard, being corrected on his manners by a member of the temple staff.

I gave my back. Isaiah had described it, and the wording is worth having beside the scene: “I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard; I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting” (Isaiah 50:6). The verbs are active. I gave. I hid not. The Servant in that passage is not overwhelmed; he presents himself.

Why did God allow his Son to be humiliated like this? Because our sin is not only guilt but shame, and he came to bear both. We dishonoured God; the Son received dishonour. We exalted ourselves; he was struck and put in his place. Hebrews says he endured the cross, despising the shame (Hebrews 12:2), and the shame began here, with a slap from a servant. And in John’s account the first blow does not come from Roman soldiers but from a servant of the temple, in the high priest’s own house: he came to his own, and his own people did not receive him (1:11). If you carry shame, for what you have done or for what was done to you, look at this courtyard. Your Lord has stood in it. He knows what it is to be treated as worthless by those who should have honoured him, and he bore it so that you could be clothed with honour as a child of God.

On a Tuesday. Notice whether you ever do the officer’s work: the cutting word to a junior, the public correction meant to impress someone above you. Repent of it, and bring it to the one who took that blow for sins like it.

parallels.desc: you shall not revile God, nor curse a ruler

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered him, "If what I said is wrong, bear witness about the wrong; but if what I said is right, why do you strike me?" Annas then sent him bound to Caiaphas the high priest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If what I said is wrong, bear witness about the wrong; but if what I said is right, why do you strike me? Calm and dignified. The reply shows what to do with an injustice, and most of us have only two settings. He does not absorb it silently, and he does not retaliate. He states the principle: there are two possibilities, and the blow is wrong under both. If what he said was wrong, produce the evidence; that is what a court is for. If it was right, the blow has no justification at all. Either way the officer has skipped the only step that mattered. And he does not appeal to who he is. He could have. The argument he uses is one that would protect any prisoner in any courtyard.

Turning the other cheek. Jesus does not literally turn the other cheek here (Matthew 5:39), but neither does he retaliate. Turning the other cheek means refusing revenge, and it evidently permits a man to say plainly that what has just been done to him was unjust.

Entrusting himself to him who judges justly. Peter, who was near enough that night, wrote about it afterwards, and his summary is hard to better: “when he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23). The last clause is the mechanism. It is possible to say plainly that a thing is unjust and still not fight it, provided one genuinely believes there is a court that will sit later.

Sent bound to Caiaphas. The formal trial before the council is described by the other Gospels (Mark 14:53–65). He has been questioned by a man who holds no office, struck by a member of that man’s staff, and is now passed on with the ropes still on him to the next stage of a process whose outcome had been decided long before (11:53). Nothing has been established. Nobody has produced a charge. He is simply being moved.

When should I speak up against wrong done to me, and when should I stay silent? Speak when truth or justice needs it, calmly, without insult or threat, as Jesus did here and as Paul did when he appealed to his rights as a Roman citizen (Acts 16:37; 22:25). Use the proper channels: a complaint, a court, the elders of the church; and if you are being abused, tell someone and get safe, because Scripture never asks you to stay under harm. Stay silent when speaking would only be revenge, self-display, or a fight for your pride. In both cases, the heart beneath is the same: you entrust yourself to God, who judges justly, and you refuse to repay evil for evil (Romans 12:17–19).

verseByVerse.quote: Now Simon Peter was standing and warming himself. So they said to him, "You also are not one of his disciples, are you?" He denied it and said, "I am not." One of the servants of the high priest, a relative of the man whose ear Peter had cut off, asked, "Did I not see you in the garden with him?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Warming himself. John has interleaved the scenes deliberately: Peter denies (vv. 15–18), Jesus is questioned and struck (vv. 19–24), Peter denies twice more (vv. 25–27). Both men are being asked who they are. One says no; the other will not name a single one of his disciples.

The second denial. The pressure rises: not a servant girl at a gate but several men at the fire at once (they said to him), with the same expected-no form of question.

A relative of Malchus. Another eyewitness detail, and the danger is real: this man saw him with the sword.

Did I not see you in the garden with him? The Greek expects the answer yes. That is a different order of danger. This man was there. He has a family grievance and an eyewitness identification, and Peter is standing in the household of the injured party warming his hands.

Before we feel superior to Peter. The escalation is real, and the honest thing to say is that by the third question Peter had something to be afraid of. The first denial cost him nothing and was therefore inexcusable. The third might have cost him his life. Nothing in the account suggests that any of us, standing where he stood, would have done better, and the others, apart from the unnamed disciple who got him in, are not in the courtyard at all.

Courage in the wrong form. Look also at what the questioner’s memory contains. The ear. Peter’s one act of courage that night has become the evidence against him, and the thing he did to prove his loyalty is what makes him identifiable when he wants to deny it. Bravery in the wrong form does not bank anything for later.

On a Tuesday. Peter’s first lie made the second necessary, and the second made the third almost automatic. If you have told a small untruth to avoid embarrassment this week, go back and correct it before it grows. You can do it without dread: the Lord who told the truth inside while Peter lied outside kept the law perfectly in your place, and his record, not yours, is your standing before God.

For worship. Peter swore he had not been with Jesus, and only hours earlier Jesus had asked the Father that those given to him might be with him where he is, to see his glory (17:24). The denial lasted a night. The prayer has outlasted every night since. The Son’s asking is stronger than our disowning: he would not hand Peter’s name to Annas, he will not hand it to death, and he will have his denier with him for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: Peter again denied it, and at once a rooster crowed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter again denied it. Matthew and Mark say he swore and called down curses (Mark 14:71). John says nothing else. No weeping, no look, no comment. The worst night of Peter’s life is reported in a handful of words, and then the narrative simply moves to Pilate.

A rooster crowed. Exactly as Jesus said (13:38). Luke is the one who supplies what happened next, and it is almost unbearable: “And the Lord turned and looked at Peter” (Luke 22:61). Perhaps he was being moved from Annas to Caiaphas at that moment. He turned his head. Then Luke’s next clause: Peter remembered the saying of the Lord, and he went out and wept bitterly (Luke 22:61–62). The crow did not condemn him. It reminded him that the worst moment of his life had been foreseen by the man he had just disowned, and had not stopped him being at that supper, or having his feet washed, or being prayed for by name.

The mercy hidden in the prediction. That is why Jesus made it. A failure nobody warned you about seems to say that everything has come apart. A failure your Lord described to your face beforehand is inside the story rather than the end of it. If you carry a particular memory, ask whether Christ knew about it before it happened. He did. Then ask what he did with that knowledge in Peter’s case. He announced it, washed the man’s feet anyway, prayed for him by name, arranged his escape from the garden, and on the third day sent word specifically to him through the messenger at the tomb: “go, tell his disciples and Peter” (Mark 16:7).

The four accounts. The Gospels name different questioners, a servant girl, another girl, the bystanders, and in John alone a relative of Malchus, and they place Peter differently in the courtyard. They agree on three denials and the rooster. Questions were flying round a crowded fire; John, who knew the household, remembered the kinsman of the wounded servant. Mark adds that the rooster crowed twice (Mark 14:72).

The fire still to come. John, who leaves the weeping out here, has not forgotten. He will tell of Peter’s restoration (21:15–19): three questions of love to match the three denials, and a man given his work back.

Judas and Peter. Both failed Jesus that night, and John has shown us both at close range. Judas went out into the night (13:30); Peter wept and would be brought back. What separated them was not that one sin was large and the other small. It was Christ. Jesus had prayed for Peter (Luke 22:32), and Peter was among those the Father had given the Son, of whom he had just told the Father that not one had been lost except the son of destruction (17:12).

Can a Christian who has denied Christ be forgiven? Yes. Peter is the proof, and he became the preacher of Pentecost. Jesus’ warning that he will deny before the Father whoever denies him (Matthew 10:33) speaks of a settled, final rejection of Christ, the life that disowns him and never returns. It does not speak of a believer who falls in weakness and comes back weeping. The warnings of Hebrews 6 describe those who fall away for good, not those who are grieved by their fall; if you are troubled that you have denied him, that very trouble shows the Spirit is still at work in you. Confess it, as plainly as Peter wept over it, and believe that the blood of Jesus cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7–9).

On a Tuesday. If someone you know has fallen badly, do not write them off. The Lord who sent a message to Peter by name on Easter morning may be asking you to carry one to them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–40 — The Trial Before Pilate: What Is Truth?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Roman trial begins. John moves Pilate back and forth between the accusers outside and the prisoner inside, and at its centre puts the conversation the accusers never heard: about a kingdom not of this world, and about truth.
verseByVerse.theology: Are you the King of the Jews? is the question of this trial, and the title Pilate later fixes over the cross (19:19) will turn out to be the truest sentence anyone writes that day. Jesus’ kingdom is not from this world: it does not advance by the sword, as Peter learned, or by political force. It advances by truth, by the witness of the one who is the truth, heard by those who are of the truth. Pilate asks what truth is while standing in front of the answer.
verseByVerse.examples: The Barabbas exchange is the gospel in miniature: the guilty goes free and the innocent is condemned. Barabbas was a bandit and insurrectionist, exactly what Jesus’ accusers had claimed Jesus was. In choosing him the crowd chose the liberation it wanted, political and violent, and rejected the one it needed, which only a substitute could win.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they led Jesus from the house of Caiaphas to the governor's headquarters. It was early morning. They themselves did not enter the governor's headquarters, so that they would not be defiled, but could eat the Passover. So Pilate went outside to them and said, "What accusation do you bring against this man?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
To the governor’s headquarters. The governor’s headquarters is the praetorium: either Herod’s old palace near the city’s western wall or the Antonia Fortress at the corner of the temple. Pilate, governor of Judea from AD 26 to 36, normally lived in Caesarea, but came to Jerusalem at feasts to keep order. John’s account of what happens there is built like a drama in seven scenes, with Pilate going out to the accusers and in to the prisoner and out again. Keep that picture in mind: a man forever going in and out, never settling, is Pilate all over.

It was early morning. Roman officials began work at dawn. The night’s proceedings have produced a prisoner and no case, and the leaders want the matter finished before the festival crowds wake.

So that they would not be defiled. Entering a Gentile house was thought to make a Jew ritually unclean, barred from the festival meals of that day. So they stand in the street and make Pilate come out. The irony is crushing: men who will not step over a threshold because of a ceremonial rule are arranging a judicial killing on the other side of it (Matthew 23:24).

A conscience pointed at the wrong object. The mechanism is not hypocrisy in the crude sense of knowing better and pretending. These men were, as far as we can tell, sincere about the purity rule. That is what makes it frightening. A real conscience about small things can stay in perfect working order while the large thing goes past unnoticed.

Eat the Passover. This raises a famous question. The other Gospels present the Last Supper as a Passover meal (Mark 14:12–16); here, the Passover seems still to come. It is a real difficulty: the answer below is the most likely harmonisation rather than a certainty, and believers hold the Gospels true while scholars still debate the details of the calendar.

Where Christians differ: the date of the Passover. Some say John has moved the date for theological reasons, so that Jesus dies as the lambs are slaughtered; others that different groups followed different calendars. This commentary’s view: “eat the Passover” can refer to the whole seven-day feast of Unleavened Bread, which was also called Passover (Luke 22:1), including the festal offering eaten on the next day (2 Chronicles 30:22). The Last Supper was a Passover meal, and the leaders here wished to stay clean for the feast’s continuing meals. The Gospels do not contradict one another.

What accusation do you bring against this man? Pilate starts a formal Roman trial. And Pilate goes out to them, which is the first move of the trial and sets its direction. A Roman governor was not obliged to conduct business in the street to accommodate the religious sensibilities of a subject people. He does it anyway, and by the end of the morning he will have conceded everything. When authority loses the will to be just, it becomes the instrument of injustice, however correct its procedures appear.

Clean for the feast, outside the Lamb’s door. John has called Jesus the Lamb of God from his first chapter (1:29, 36). He will tell us that Jesus was handed over to be crucified on the day of Preparation (19:14), and that not a bone of his was broken (19:36), which was the rule for the Passover lamb (Exodus 12:46). So the scene at the door is no accident. The men guarding their purity for the Passover meal are delivering up the Passover Lamb himself, and Paul’s sentence is being acted out in a Jerusalem street: Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed (1 Corinthians 5:7). They would not cross a Gentile threshold to stay clean. He would cross from heaven to earth, and into death, to make the unclean clean.

How do I know if I am straining gnats and swallowing camels? Look at where your conscience is loudest. If you are troubled about small matters of practice, the right wording, the right music, the right habits, while untroubled by bitterness, greed, a harsh tongue or an unreconciled brother, the scale is wrong. Jesus did not say the small things do not matter; he said these you ought to have done, without neglecting the others (Matthew 23:23). Ask God to recalibrate you by his word, especially by the weightier matters of justice, mercy and faithfulness, and ask a trusted friend where they think your blind spot lies.

On a Tuesday. Before your next communion service, examine not only your small observances but the large things: whom you have not forgiven, what you have done to someone this week that you would rather not name. Bring them to the Lamb whose table it is, who makes the unclean clean, and come clean in heart, not merely tidy in practice.

For worship. The Lamb was handed across the threshold the priests would not cross, into Gentile hands, and so the Lamb of Israel was slain by Jew and Gentile together, for Jew and Gentile together. The wall they guarded so carefully that morning he broke down in his flesh (Ephesians 2:14), and now the unclean of every nation are made clean and welcomed to his feast.
verseByVerse.note: The governor’s headquarters is the praetorium. Entering a Gentile’s house would make them ritually unclean for the festival.

verseByVerse.quote: They answered him, "If this man were not doing evil, we would not have delivered him over to you." Pilate said to them, "Take him yourselves and judge him by your own law." The Jews said to him, "It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If this man were not doing evil. Their first answer is not an answer, and Pilate notices. They do not name a charge; they are asking a Roman court to ratify a verdict already reached without hearing the grounds for it.

Judge him by your own law. Pilate does not want to be involved in a religious quarrel. His reply is procedurally correct and also an attempt to get rid of the case. Rome generally left internal religious matters to local courts.

Not lawful for us. Now they show their real goal: in Judea Rome kept the power of capital punishment for itself. Historians have debated this, since Stephen is stoned in Acts 7 and the woman in chapter 8 was nearly stoned in the temple (an account missing from the earliest manuscripts of John, though it is widely thought to be a true story). The distinction is between mob action, which happened and which Rome punished when it noticed, and a formal judicial execution, which in a Roman province was reserved to the governor. What they are saying is not that killing him is impossible but that killing him legally requires Pilate.

Why does John keep saying the Jews handed Jesus over? He uses the phrase for the Jerusalem leaders and those who followed them, not for the whole people; Jesus, his disciples and the first believers were all Jews. Pilate himself says Your own nation and the chief priests (18:35). The guilt for the cross belongs to those who planned it, to Pilate who allowed it, and, in the deepest sense, to all of us whose sins put him there. Peter says the Jerusalem crowd and their rulers acted in ignorance (Acts 3:17), and the gospel was preached to them first. The charge of collective Jewish guilt, used to justify persecution, has no ground in John or anywhere in Scripture.

A prisoner with no charge. They cannot name a crime because there is none to name. Jesus had asked them openly, Which one of you convicts me of sin? (8:46), and no one had answered. Now, with a night of questioning behind them, they have nothing better to bring the governor. The sinless one stands at the door of the praetorium, and the emptiness of their case is the first testimony of the morning to what Pilate will say three times: I find no guilt in him. The Passover lamb had to be without blemish (Exodus 12:5), and the men handing him over are proving, without meaning to, that he is.
verseByVerse.note: Rome kept the power of capital punishment for itself in Judea.

parallels.desc: Stephen stoned by a mob

verseByVerse.quote: This was to fulfill the word that Jesus had spoken to show by what kind of death he was going to die. So Pilate entered his headquarters again and called Jesus and said to him, "Are you the King of the Jews?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
By what kind of death. John’s note turns the whole exchange. Stoning was the Jewish penalty for blasphemy; being “lifted up” meant crucifixion, the Roman penalty (3:14; 8:28; 12:32–33). If the council had been able to act alone, he would have been stoned. The jurisdictional technicality that looks like an accident of Roman administration is the means by which the manner of his death was secured.

Hanged on a tree. And there is more in it than the shape of the execution. Being hanged on a tree meant being under God’s curse (Deuteronomy 21:23; Galatians 3:13). Paul builds on that very verse: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). He had to die that way, under that sentence, and the men insisting on the correct paperwork were arranging it.

What does it mean that Christ became a curse? It means he stood where the law’s judgment falls. The law pronounced a curse on everyone who does not keep it (Galatians 3:10), and that is all of us. On the cross the Father treated his Son as the bearer of that curse, not because Jesus had sinned, but because our sin was laid on him (2 Corinthians 5:21). The tree was the outward sign of the inward reality: the Holy One under God’s judgment in our place. So the curse is not merely lessened for the believer. It has been exhausted on Christ, and the blessing of Abraham comes to us instead (Galatians 3:14).

Are you the King of the Jews? The charge is now political. Luke says they accused him of forbidding tribute to Caesar and claiming to be Christ a king (Luke 23:2). In Greek, Pilate’s “you” is emphatic, placed first: su, you? This beaten, bound man? A king? It is contemptuous, and understandably so. In front of him is a man in his thirties, unarmed, tied up, handed over by his own nation’s leadership, with no supporters visible anywhere in the building. Pilate has spent years managing real insurgencies in this province, and he has seen what a claimant to a throne looks like. This does not.

The only charge that could interest Rome. That is why the question sits at the centre of the trial. It is the only charge that could interest a Roman court, treason, a rival king, and everything the priests want depends on making it stick. They have not led with the charge of blasphemy, because Pilate would have thrown it out; it surfaces only later, when they are desperate (19:7). They were right that he was a king, and wrong about what kind, and Pilate is about to be right for the wrong reasons and write it on a board (19:19).

In the room they would not enter. The heart of the trial, the one conversation in which Jesus explains himself, happens in a room the accusers refused to walk into. They arranged the whole thing and were not present for the only part of it that mattered. Pilate meanwhile goes out (v. 29), comes in (v. 33), goes out again (v. 38), and never settles anywhere, not even with his own verdict.

On a Tuesday. When events in your life seem to turn on technicalities, a missed form, a rule applied against you, a decision made by someone who did not care, remember that the death that saved the world turned on one. God is not limited to dramatic interventions. He governs the paperwork too.
verseByVerse.note: Stoning was the Jewish penalty for blasphemy; being “lifted up” pointed to Roman crucifixion.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "Do you say this of your own accord, or did others say it to you about me?" Pilate answered, "Am I a Jew? Your own nation and the chief priests have delivered you over to me. What have you done?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you say this of your own accord, or did others say it to you about me? The prisoner starts interrogating the judge. If Pilate means a political rebel king, the answer is no. If he means the Messiah, the answer is yes. That is not evasion. It is the question that separates two entirely different conversations, and in effect it is an offer: the offer he made to Nicodemus and the woman at the well and the man born blind, extended to the Roman prefect of Judea in the early morning.

Am I a Jew? Contempt. Why would a Roman care about Jewish religious ideas? And it is a self-revealing sentence. He is declining to be personally involved. Whatever this is about, it is not his world and he does not intend to enter it. The effect is to shut the door on the only conversation in the room that could have done him any good.

Your own nation. Immediately after refusing to be interested, Pilate does still want to know. That is the tragedy of Pilate throughout this narrative: he is not a monster and he is not stupid. He asks good questions and repeatedly declines to stay for the answers. His words also concede something: he has worked out that this is an internal matter being routed through him, which is why he keeps trying to hand it back. He knows he is being used, and he says so out loud. And he goes through with it anyway, which is the difference between seeing a thing clearly and being willing to pay for acting on it. What he would not pay was his standing with Caesar, and when the crowd later cries that releasing this man would make him no friend of Caesar, that settles it (19:12). Many who see clearly enough who Jesus is are held back by the same thing: not a lack of evidence, but the fear of what following him would cost.

Can I keep Jesus at arm’s length, like Pilate? You can try, and many do: interested in him as a historical figure, a moral teacher, a subject for discussion, but unwilling to let the question become personal. Jesus will not leave it there. He asked Pilate, in effect, are you asking this for yourself? and he asks every reader the same. Neutrality about Christ is not available, because he claims to be the King to whom every person will answer (Acts 17:31). Pilate tried to be a spectator at his own trial of Jesus, and ended as the man whose name is spoken in every recitation of the Creed: suffered under Pontius Pilate.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting, that I might not be delivered over to the Jews. But my kingdom is not from the world." Then Pilate said to him, "So you are a king?" Jesus answered, "You say that I am a king. For this purpose I was born and for this purpose I have come into the world — to bear witness to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth listens to my voice."
verseByVerse.commentary:
My kingdom is not of this world. One preposition in this answer carries more weight than anything else in the trial. The Greek is ek, out of, from. It is a statement about origin, not about location. His kingdom does not come from this world or work the way the world’s kingdoms do: its source is heaven, and its power is truth, not swords. He is not saying it is somewhere else, purely spiritual. Its territory is very much this world, which is why he is standing in a Roman courtroom.

Why the preposition matters. Read as a statement about location, the sentence becomes a charter for a Christianity that concedes the actual world to other powers and retreats into private religion, the arrangement every tyranny has been happy to grant the church. Read as a statement about origin, it says something far more disturbing to Pilate: there is a kingdom operating in his province whose authority did not come from Rome, does not depend on Rome, and will outlast Rome.

My servants would have been fighting. Jesus gives evidence Pilate can check: exactly one sword had been drawn in the garden, and its owner had been told to put it away. The absence of a fight is the proof of the kingdom’s origin. Every time the church has reached for the sword to advance the faith, and it has, repeatedly, and worse than Peter did, it has contradicted the sentence its Lord spoke at his own trial.

So you are a king? Pilate seizes on the word, and Jesus answers, You say that I am a king: a cautious yes. He is a king, though not in Pilate’s sense, and his kingdom’s origin is God.

Born, and came. A man born, and one who came from elsewhere: incarnation in a phrase. It is the only time in this Gospel he speaks of his birth. Everything else has been I came, I was sent, I came down. To a Roman he says it the ordinary way as well: I was born for this.

To bear witness to the truth. He conquers by testimony. The purpose named is not to reign, or to conquer, or even to die. He describes himself to the Roman governor as a witness, which is the humblest possible job description, and it is the one that gets him killed.

Listens to my voice. His subjects are those who hear him, as the sheep hear the shepherd (10:27), and the sentence is an invitation even to Pilate.

In the flow. At the centre of the Roman trial John gathers up a thread that runs through the whole book. Nathanael hailed him as King of Israel (1:49); the crowd tried to make him king by force and he withdrew (6:15); he rode into Jerusalem as the king Zechariah promised (12:13–15). Now he tells a Roman what kind of king he is, and within hours Pilate will write the title over the cross in three languages (19:19–20). John wants us to see that this King is never more truly enthroned than when he is lifted up.

Where Christians differ: the kingdom and the state. Some have sought to establish Christ’s kingdom by political power or force; others have concluded that faith has nothing to say to public life. This commentary’s view: Christ’s kingdom advances by the word and Spirit, not by the sword. The church must not use the state’s weapons to spread the gospel. Yet Christ is king over all, and his truth addresses rulers too, as here.

Does this mean Christians may never fight? Some Christians, pacifists, read it so, and their earnest witness against violence deserves respect. But Jesus is speaking of his kingdom: it will never be advanced by force. That does not abolish the state’s God-given sword (Romans 13:4), nor forbid a Christian to serve as a soldier or police officer (Luke 3:14), nor to defend life. The church must never use force to spread the gospel; a Christian citizen may share in the just defence of others.

What does it mean to be of the truth? It means to belong to the truth rather than merely to hold opinions about it: to have been born of God, so that his voice is recognised as the voice of home. Jesus is not saying that some people are naturally better at truth than others. He is saying that those whom God has drawn will hear the Shepherd when he speaks (6:44–45; 10:26–27). In practice it shows in a willingness to be corrected by Christ, to come to the light even when it exposes you (3:21), and to keep listening to his word when it is unwelcome. If his voice is the one you want to hear above all others, you are of the truth.

On a Tuesday. In your workplace, your vote, your conversations about public life, refuse the weapons of slander, manipulation and contempt even when your cause is right. The King you serve won without them.

For worship. Bound and on trial, the King told the representative of the greatest empire on earth that he too was a king, that he had been born for it and had come from beyond the world for it, and that his throne needed no soldiers. Rome has fallen. His kingdom has spread to every nation by nothing but the word of the cross and the power of the Spirit, and it will stand when every throne on earth is dust.

parallels.desc: the good confession before Pontius Pilate

verseByVerse.quote: Pilate said to him, "What is truth?" After he had said this, he went back outside to the Jews and told them, "I find no guilt in him. But you have a custom that I should release one man for you at the Passover. So do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
What is truth? There are two ways to say it. It can be a sneer: the tired cynicism of a career official who has watched every faction in a difficult province dress up its interests as principle, and who has concluded that truth is a word people use when they want something. That is the usual reading and it fits the man. It can also be genuine, and something in the scene allows it. He has just been told by a bound prisoner that there is such a thing as truth and that men can be of it. Pilate may be, for one moment, actually asking. Either way, the Truth is standing in front of him (14:6).

He did not stay. What settles it is not the tone but the timing: whatever he meant by it, he did not wait. Francis Bacon wrote: “What is truth? said jesting Pilate, and would not stay for an answer.” The distance between Pilate and the answer was a few feet, and he had the authority to keep the man there as long as he liked. He asked the largest question a person can ask, in the presence of the only one who could have answered it, and left the room. Many still ask the question without wanting the answer.

How do I answer a friend who says there is no such thing as truth? Gently, and with a question of your own. Is that statement true? If it is, there is at least one truth; if it is not, there is no reason to believe it. Then move from argument to a person. Christianity does not claim merely to have found some true ideas; it claims that the Truth became a man, lived, died and rose, and that his resurrection is a public fact that can be examined (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). Invite your friend to read one of the Gospels with you. Pilate’s problem was not lack of evidence; it was that he would not stay for it. Ask your friend to stay.

I find no guilt in him. This is the first of three times (19:4, 6). Three times the Roman court, in the person of its highest local representative, returns a verdict of not guilty, and three times it proceeds anyway. The innocent will die for the guilty.

A custom. Look at what he does immediately after acquitting him. He does not release him, which is what an acquittal requires. He offers a deal, which means that from this moment Jesus is no longer being tried. He is being negotiated over. An honest note: no source outside the Gospels attests this amnesty, though it is consistent with Roman practice of clemency at festivals, provincial governors are known to have released prisoners to please a crowd, and Pilate would hardly be the first official to invent a precedent when he needed one. Offering them the King of the Jews, he is trying to wriggle out and mocking the leaders with the title.

verseByVerse.quote: They cried out again, "Not this man, but Barabbas!" Now Barabbas was a robber.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not this man, but Barabbas! Mark says Barabbas had committed murder in an insurrection (Mark 15:7). So the man the crowd asks for is a real one: an armed nationalist with blood on his hands, of exactly the kind Rome crucified in batches, and of exactly the kind Jesus had been accused of being.

Son of the father. His name means “son of the father” (bar abba). Some early manuscripts of Matthew call him Jesus Barabbas (Matthew 27:16–17), which, if it stood, would mean Pilate asked the crowd to choose between Jesus son of the father and Jesus who is called Christ. The evidence is divided, and it should not be leaned on. John does not press the name either. But the scene makes the point the name suggests: a guilty son of a father goes free, and the innocent Son of the Father dies.

Barabbas was a robber. The word (lēstēs) means bandit, insurrectionist, the word used of the thieves and robbers in 10:1, 8, who climb into the sheepfold by another way. It is the violent kind of intruder, as opposed to the sneak-thief, and it is what the historian Josephus calls the insurgents of the period. They chose the robber over the Good Shepherd, the kind of liberation, violent and political, that Rome could crush, and refused the liberation no power can overcome.

The exchange acted out. What happens next is the doctrine of substitution acted out in a courtyard, once, in front of witnesses, before anybody had a word for it. One man guilty of insurrection and murder, one declared innocent by the judge: the guilty man walks out of a Roman prison free while the innocent one is taken away to the cross that had been prepared. Barabbas is the first person whose life was saved by Jesus’ death in a literal sense. That morning he was a condemned man, and somebody else was nailed up in his place, and he went home. Every believer can read his own case into that morning.

What became of him. Nothing is recorded of what became of Barabbas. He walks out of the story and out of history: no conversion, no repentance recorded, nothing asked of him and nothing given. He did not choose it, did not deserve it, and as far as we know never thanked anybody. That is the exchange: not a bargain, not a reward, not a transaction anybody entered into, but a guilty man’s sentence served by an innocent one, arranged by people who were trying to do something else entirely, on the morning of the Passover.

In the flow. Verse 40 closes the first round of the Roman trial, and the crowd’s choice shuts the door on release, so that the next verse turns to the scourging (19:1). In the argument of the book it is one more witness to what Caiaphas prophesied without knowing it: one man dying for the people (11:50), and here a guilty man walking free because of it.

Was Barabbas saved? Scripture does not tell us, and we should not guess. His release was physical; he was spared a Roman cross, which is not the same as being forgiven by God. To be saved from the judgment of God a person must trust in the one who took his place (3:16, 36). Barabbas is a picture of substitution, not proof that everyone it pictures receives it. That is why the picture ends with a question for us rather than for him: you have heard that Christ died in the place of sinners; have you received him as dying in yours?

Is it just for an innocent man to be punished in place of the guilty? It would be unjust if the substitute were unwilling, or a third party dragged in against his will, or if the judge simply waved the guilt away. None of those is true at the cross. The Son came willingly (10:18); the Judge whose law was broken is the same God who provides the substitute (Romans 3:25–26); and the Son is united to his people as their head, so that what he does, he does as one of us and for us. Barabbas’s release was an injustice by Pilate. Our release is the justice of God satisfied by the love of God, so that he is both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus. To justify means to declare a person righteous in God’s court: not to make him better by degrees, but to pronounce the verdict in his favour, because his penalty has been borne and Christ’s righteousness is counted as his (Romans 4:5; 2 Corinthians 5:21).

On a Tuesday. You are Barabbas. When someone wrongs you, remember how much you were released from, and let that make you quick to forgive.

For worship. Barabbas walked out of the prison into the morning light, and the Lord of glory walked out of the praetorium toward the cross Rome kept for men like Barabbas. The trade the crowd made in folly, God had purposed in wisdom before the world began, and every rebel who trusts in Christ goes out through that same door. The prison stands open because the cross was occupied, and the one who hung there was the King of the Jews, our substitute.
verseByVerse.note: Mark says Barabbas had committed murder in an insurrection; “robber” was often used for violent rebels.
