So, if you seek me, let these men go.”<sup>9</sup>This was to fulfill the word that he had spoken: “Of those whom you gave me I have lost not one.”<sup>10</sup>Then Simon Peter, having a sword, drew it and struck the high priest’s servant and cut off his right ear. (The servant’s name was Malchus.)<sup>11</sup>So Jesus said to Peter, “Put your sword into its sheath; shall I not drink the cup that the Father has given me?”<sup>12</sup>So the band of soldiers and their captain and the officers of the Jews arrested Jesus and bound him.<sup>13</sup>First they led him to Annas, for he was the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was high priest that year.<sup>14</sup>It was Caiaphas who had advised the Jews that it would be expedient that one man should die for the people.<sup>15</sup>Simon Peter followed Jesus, and so did another disciple. Since that disciple was known to the high priest, he entered with Jesus into the courtyard of the high priest,<sup>16</sup>but Peter stood outside at the door. So the other disciple, who was known to the high priest, went out and spoke to the servant girl who kept watch at the door, and brought Peter in.<sup>17</sup>The servant girl at the door said to Peter, “You also are not one of this man’s disciples, are you?” He said, “I am not.”<sup>18</sup>Now the servants and officers had made a charcoal fire, because it was cold, and they were standing and warming themselves. Peter also was with them, standing and warming himself.<sup>19</sup>The high priest then questioned Jesus about his disciples and his teaching.<sup>20</sup>Jesus answered him, “I have spoken openly to the world. I have always taught in synagogues and in the temple, where all Jews come together. I have said nothing in secret.<sup>21</sup>Why do you ask me? Ask those who have heard me what I said to them; they know what I said.”<sup>22</sup>When he had said these things, one of the officers standing by struck Jesus with his hand, saying, “Is that how you answer the high priest?”<sup>23</sup>Jesus answered him, “If what I said is wrong, bear witness about the wrong; but if what I said is right, why do you strike me?”<sup>24</sup>Annas then sent him bound to Caiaphas the high priest.<sup>25</sup>Now Simon Peter was standing and warming himself. So they said to him, “You also are not one of his disciples, are you?” He denied it and said, “I am not.”<sup>26</sup>One of the servants of the high priest, a relative of the man whose ear Peter had cut off, asked, “Did I not see you in the garden with him?”<sup>27</sup>Peter again denied it, and at once a rooster crowed.<sup>28</sup>Then they led Jesus from the house of Caiaphas to the governor’s headquarters. It was early morning. They themselves did not enter the governor’s headquarters, so that they would not be defiled, but could eat the Passover.<sup>29</sup>So Pilate went outside to them and said, “What accusation do you bring against this man?”<sup>30</sup>They answered him, “If this man were not doing evil, we would not have delivered him over to you.”<sup>31</sup>Pilate said to them, “Take him yourselves and judge him by your own law.” The Jews said to him, “It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death.”<sup>32</sup>This was to fulfill the word that Jesus had spoken to show by what kind of death he was going to die.<sup>33</sup>So Pilate entered his headquarters again and called Jesus and said to him, “Are you the King of the Jews?”<sup>34</sup>Jesus answered, “Do you say this of your own accord, or did others say it to you about me?”<sup>35</sup>Pilate answered, “Am I a Jew? Your own nation and the chief priests have delivered you over to me. What have you done?”<sup>36</sup>Jesus answered, “My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting, that I might not be delivered over to the Jews. But my kingdom is not from the world.”<sup>37</sup>Then Pilate said to him, “So you are a king?” Jesus answered, “You say that I am a king. Everyone who is of the truth listens to my voice.”<sup>38</sup>Pilate said to him, “What is truth?” After he had said this, he went back outside to the Jews and told them, “I find no guilt in him.<sup>39</sup>But you have a custom that I should release one man for you at the Passover. So do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews?”<sup>40</sup>They cried out again, “Not this man, but Barabbas!” Now Barabbas was a robber.
18.overview:
John’s account of the arrest and trials shows Jesus not as a victim but as the one in control. In the garden he steps forward to meet his captors, and they fall at his word; he secures his disciples’ release and goes willingly to drink the cup his Father has given him. Bound, he is questioned by Annas, while in the courtyard outside Peter denies him three times.

At dawn he is brought to Pilate. The leaders who will not enter a Gentile house before the feast are handing over the true Passover Lamb. Before the governor Jesus speaks of a kingdom not of this world and of the truth he came to bear witness to. Pilate finds no guilt in him and still bargains him away, and the crowd asks for Barabbas. The judge is on trial before the truth, and fails.

19.title: The Crucifixion and Burial of Jesus

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — The Crown of Thorns and the Cross
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The sentence and the crucifixion. Pilate’s attempts to release Jesus fail one by one, through the flogging, the presentation of the man, and the fear stirred by the claim that he is the Son of God, until the threat about Caesar settles it. Jesus carries his own cross to Golgotha, and Pilate refuses to change the title over it.
verseByVerse.theology: Behold the man (v. 5) and Behold your King (v. 14) are Pilate’s two presentations of Jesus, each truer than Pilate knows. Here is humanity’s representative, the man who is also the King. Pilate intends mockery; God intends revelation. The crown of thorns (the curse of Genesis 3:18 placed on the head of the one who came to bear it) and the purple robe are parodies of kingship that are at the same time true of the King who reigns from the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: Crucified between two others (v. 18): the innocent numbered among the guilty. The title in Aramaic, Latin and Greek, the languages of home, of law and of trade, makes the proclamation universal, posted beside a road outside the city at the busiest time of the year. The chief priests want it turned into a mere claim; Pilate refuses: What I have written, I have written.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pilate took Jesus and flogged him. And the soldiers twisted together a crown of thorns and put it on his head and arrayed him in a purple robe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. John 19 tells of Jesus’ sentence, crucifixion, death and burial. John presents the cross as the King’s enthronement: crowned, robed, proclaimed king in three languages, lifted up. And it is the Passover sacrifice: he dies on the day of Preparation in Passover week, no bone broken, offered sour wine on hyssop. At the centre stands his cry: It is finished. Everything in this Gospel has been moving here: the Lamb of God (1:29), the serpent lifted up (3:14), the Shepherd laying down his life (10:11), the grain of wheat falling into the ground (12:24). John tells it with a restraint that makes every detail weigh.

Flogged him. Roman flogging used a whip weighted with bone or metal. It tore the flesh to ribbons, and sometimes killed the prisoner before crucifixion. Roman practice knew several grades of beating, and the severest was the standard prelude to crucifixion. This one comes in the middle of the trial, before any sentence, and Luke supplies Pilate’s reasoning in his own words: I will therefore punish and release him (Luke 23:16, 22).

A compromise worse than a miscarriage. Pilate has found no guilt, and he is trying to give the crowd something short of a death. It is the classic manoeuvre of an official who knows what justice requires and is looking for a cheaper alternative. It did not work, and the attempt is in some ways worse than a straightforward miscarriage. Pilate has inflicted a savage punishment on a man he has publicly declared innocent, not as a sentence but as a bargaining position.

A crown of thorns. The Greek word is not diadēma, the usual word for a king’s crown. What they twist together is a stephanos, a word used above all for the victor’s wreath, given to the winner of the games or to a general on his return. They meant it as part of the joke. It is the wrong joke. Within days the man wearing it will be seen to have won, and the word they chose is the one the New Testament uses for the crown he will give away: the crown of life, of righteousness, of glory that does not fade (James 1:12; 2 Timothy 4:8; 1 Peter 5:4).

The thorns of the curse. Thorns were part of the curse on the ground after Adam’s sin (Genesis 3:18): one of the first named consequences of the fall, the thing every farmer since has fought. A handful of it is pressed onto his head by men who are laughing. The King bears on his head the sign of God’s just sentence on a world gone wrong through sin, so that those who trust him receive blessing instead: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13).

A purple robe. Purple was the colour of royalty, made from costly dye; this was perhaps an old soldier’s cloak. The soldiers are doing theology without knowing it: robing the King, crowning him, dressing him for his throne. They are adorning what they intend to destroy.

Why did Jesus have to suffer so much? Would his death alone not have been enough? Scripture does not treat his sufferings as a mere preliminary to the real work. His whole humiliation, the flogging, the mockery and the pain as well as the death, was part of his obedience and his bearing of our sin. Isaiah links the wounds themselves to our healing (Isaiah 53:5), and Peter says he bore our sins in his body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24). The suffering also shows us what sin is: not a small fault but a thing that, when it fell on the holy Son, looked like this. And it means that there is no pain you can suffer that he has not entered. He is a High Priest who can sympathise with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15).

On a Tuesday. When you suffer in your body, tell the Lord who was flogged. You do not have to explain pain to him.

For worship. The King’s first crown was made of thorns. Soldiers twisted it, pressed it down and laughed, and he wore it without complaint for people who had brought thorns into the world. The head they mocked is crowned now with many diadems (Revelation 19:12), the royal crowns they would never have given him, and he wears them still bearing the marks of the first. There is no crown in heaven that was not won under that one.
verseByVerse.note: Roman flogging used a whip weighted with bone or metal. Purple was the colour of royalty.

verseByVerse.quote: They came up to him, saying, "Hail, King of the Jews!" and struck him with their hands. Pilate went out again and said to them, "See, I am bringing him out to you that you may know that I find no guilt in him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hail, King of the Jews! A parody of “Hail, Caesar!” These are probably auxiliary troops in Roman service, and they mock him with the truth. What the mockery does, without anybody intending it, is stage a coronation. There is a robe, a crown, an acclamation, and a court paying homage. Every element of an accession is present and every one is inverted.

Struck him. Repeatedly, in the Greek. This is happening between the flogging and the crucifixion, to a man who has been awake all night. The King receives blows rather than inflicting them.

I find no guilt in him. The second declaration of innocence (18:38). The horror is quiet and official: the verdict is innocent, and the prisoner has just been flogged. The same man reports both in the same breath and sees no contradiction, because to him the beating is not a sentence. It is an offer. And he wants credit for the verdict. He is asking the crowd to notice his fairness, in the very sentence in which he produces a man he has had beaten half to death for no offence.

Why does God let people mock Christ, then and now? Because he is patient, and because he is not threatened. The mockery of the soldiers was not a defeat for God; it was the means by which the King was led to his throne. The mockery of today, the jokes, the contempt, the casual blasphemy, is no more a threat to his reign than theirs was. God is giving time for repentance (2 Peter 3:9), and some of the mockers will be his. Mark tells us that a Roman centurion, watching him die, confessed him as the Son of God (Mark 15:39). When you hear Christ mocked, grieve, speak up where you can with grace, and pray for the mocker. He may yet kneel.

On a Tuesday. Watch for the Pilate in yourself: the wish to be seen as fair while doing the unjust thing. If you have harmed someone and are now asking others to admire your reasonableness, stop, and put it right; the King who took those blows has borne that sin too, so you can own it without fear.

verseByVerse.quote: So Jesus came out, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple robe. Pilate said to them, "Behold the man!" When the chief priests and the officers saw him, they cried out, "Crucify him, crucify him!" Pilate said to them, "Take him yourselves and crucify him, for I find no guilt in him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold the man! In Latin, Ecce homo, and few scenes in the Gospels have been painted more often. What Pilate means by it is entirely cynical: look at the state of him; this is your dangerous insurgent. He is inviting the crowd to be embarrassed by their own charge.

Pity that did not come. Pilate is betting that if they see the man they will stop wanting him dead. He has miscalculated, and the miscalculation is instructive: the sight of suffering does not reliably produce pity. It can produce the opposite, and here it produces a howl.

The true man. But John hears more. Here is the man: the true human being, the second Adam, the Son of Man (Daniel 7:13), suffering for all. There is a line in Zechariah that might be heard behind the words: behold, the man whose name is the Branch (Zechariah 6:12), a man who will be crowned, who will build the temple, and who will be a priest on his throne. Whether anyone in that courtyard caught it cannot be known; John has recorded the phrase that makes it audible. What is being pointed at is not a specimen of suffering but the human race’s representative, who stands in for others, so that what he does counts for them: as by Adam’s disobedience the many were made sinners, so by Christ’s obedience the many will be made righteous (Romans 5:19). The old Adam was made in a garden and lost everything; this is the new one, and the curse that fell on the first is sitting on his head in the form of thorns. God’s verdict on humanity and his answer to it stand in one figure.

Crucify him, crucify him! The chief priests and officers lead the shout. The response is the only honest thing in the scene, and we should resist the instinct to distance ourselves from it too quickly. This is what happened when God became visible and stood in front of a crowd at close range without power: not indifference, not confusion, but a demand that he be removed. Anyone who has wondered why God does not simply show himself finds at least part of an answer in this verse, and it is not a comfortable one. Pilate’s reply is his third declaration of innocence, and a taunt: he knows they cannot legally crucify.

Would I have shouted with the crowd? In one sense, yes. Not because you would have been in Jerusalem that morning, but because the same heart that shouted is in every one of us by nature: the heart that wants God out of the way when he comes too close (Romans 8:7). That is why the cross is not only something done by them; it was done for our sins, and in that sense by us. But the gospel does not leave you in the crowd. The man they rejected prayed for those who crucified him (Luke 23:34, words missing from some early manuscripts but printed in most Bibles), and about three thousand people in that same city were baptised seven weeks later (Acts 2:23, 36–41). The shout of crucify him is answered by the cry of it is finished.

On a Tuesday. Take five minutes today and simply look at him: read this passage slowly and imagine the scene. Do not hurry to the lesson. Then ask what it would mean for you to receive him, rather than to want him removed, in the area of your life where he is most inconvenient.

parallels.desc: no beauty that we should desire him

verseByVerse.quote: The Jews answered him, "We have a law, and according to that law he ought to die because he has made himself the Son of God." When Pilate heard this statement, he was even more afraid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We have a law. The law against blasphemy (Leviticus 24:16): their law, which a Roman court had no business enforcing. They had spent the morning translating a religious conviction into a political one because that was the only version Rome would hear. Now, frustrated, they revert to the real one, and hand Pilate a problem he has no competence to judge.

The Son of God. The real charge comes out (5:18; 10:33). All morning it has been the charge of kingship. Now, cornered by Pilate’s refusal, they say what the council had actually condemned him for. They are right that he had claimed it. Chapters 5, 8 and 10 are a record of them understanding him exactly and seeking to kill him for it, in the last two with stones in their hands. The only question is whether it is true.

Even more afraid. He was already uneasy, and John has not said so until now. Something about this prisoner has been unsettling him since the first interview. Matthew says his wife had warned him of a dream: have nothing to do with that righteous man (Matthew 27:19). Romans believed in sons of gods, divine men who walked among mortals. Augustus was officially called son of the deified Julius; the category existed and the emperors used it. And every Roman knew stories of gods walking about in disguise and of what happened to men who mistreated them without recognising them. What if this man really was one?

Fear that does the wrong thing. So the governor is now frightened, superstitious, out of his depth, and holding a verdict he cannot enforce. It is exactly the condition in which men do the thing they know to be wrong, because the wrong thing is the one that makes the fear stop soonest.

Did Jesus really claim to be God? Yes, and his enemies understood it better than many modern readers. He claimed God as his own Father in a way that made himself equal with God (5:18). He said, before Abraham was, I am (8:58). He said, I and the Father are one, and they took up stones because, as they said, you, being a man, make yourself God (10:30–33). He accepted Thomas’s confession, my Lord and my God (20:28). He did not die for claiming to be a good teacher; he died for claiming to be the Son of God. As C. S. Lewis argued, a man who said these things would be deluded, a deceiver, or the Lord he claimed to be. The resurrection settled which.

On a Tuesday. If he is the Son of God, then everything he says has the authority of God, including what he says about your money, your marriage, your fears and your sins. Ask which of his words you have been treating as optional, and bring that area under his claim today, trusting the Spirit he has given you to work in you both the will and the doing (Philippians 2:13).

parallels.desc: whoever blasphemes the name of the LORD shall surely be put to death

verseByVerse.quote: He entered his headquarters again and said to Jesus, "Where are you from?" But Jesus gave him no answer. So Pilate said to him, "You will not speak to me? Do you not know that I have authority to release you and authority to crucify you?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Where are you from? Not his hometown; Pilate knows that (Luke 23:6–7). He means: who are you, really? It is the great question of John’s Gospel, asked before by the crowd who said they knew where he came from and therefore he could not be the Christ (7:27), and by the Pharisees who said they did not know where he came from (9:29). Now a Roman asks it, frightened, in a private room, and it is the right question at last.

No answer. After a night of speaking, the one question that goes to the centre is met with silence. Not sullenness, and not the silence of a man with nothing to say, but the Servant of Isaiah: he was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth (Isaiah 53:7). And something more specific: Pilate had already heard the truth (18:37) and brushed it aside. He had asked what truth is and walked out before the answer. A man who leaves before the answer to one question does not get an answer to the next.

The answer John has already given. The reader has had the answer since the first verse of the book. He is the Word who was in the beginning with God and was God (1:1). He said of himself, I came from the Father and have come into the world (16:28), and, I am from above (8:23). The prisoner in the purple robe is the one through whom Pilate, Rome and the stone pavement under their feet were made (1:3). The question where he is from is the question of who he is, and the answer is that he is from the Father’s side, and he has come to take sinners back there with him (14:3).

What if God is silent when I ask him something? There are people who have asked God something real, not idly, not to score a point, and received nothing. Not a refusal. Silence. The temptation is to conclude either that nobody is there, or that the asking was somehow disqualified. This verse establishes that the silence of God is not always what it appears. Jesus’ silence was not indifference; the man in front of Pilate was at that moment on his way to dying for sinners. The nearest thing to an answer Pilate was ever going to get was standing there in a purple robe with his hands tied. That does not explain any particular silence, and it is not offered as an explanation. It establishes something narrower and worth having: a silent Christ and an absent Christ are not the same thing. Keep praying, keep reading his word, and remember that he has already given his clearest answer at the cross.

Do you not know that I have authority to release you and authority to crucify you? Pilate falls back on his power. He thinks he holds Jesus’ life in his hands. It is the response of small authority everywhere to being ignored. He has just been frightened. Now he reaches for rank. Power has seldom been so mistaken about itself.

For worship. Christ was silent before his judge, so that we might have something to say before ours: he died for me. The Word stood wordless before a frightened governor, keeping silence on the road to bearing the sins of the world. He held his peace so that we could have peace. And the one who would not answer Pilate answers every sinner who comes to him: whoever comes to me I will never cast out.

parallels.desc: he opened not his mouth

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered him, "You would have no authority over me at all unless it had been given you from above. Therefore he who delivered me over to you has the greater sin." From then on Pilate sought to release him, but the Jews cried out, "If you release this man, you are not Caesar's friend. Everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar."
verseByVerse.commentary:
From above. The word for from above is one this Gospel has used before, and it is not the obvious one. It is anōthen, the very word that baffled Nicodemus in chapter 3, where being born anōthen could mean again or from above. Here there is no ambiguity, and the claim is enormous. All human authority is delegated by God (Romans 13:1). The authority by which a Roman prefect is about to have the Son of God executed is authority that was issued to him, from above. God has ordained this hour (Acts 2:23; 4:27–28). Pilate thinks he is in charge; Jesus tells him he holds real power, and that it is on loan.

The greater sin. It is singular, he who delivered me, most probably Caiaphas (some think Judas, or the leaders as a group), who had the Scriptures, the office, and full knowledge of what he was doing, as against a Gentile administrator out of his depth. Pilate is guilty, but less so. There are degrees of sin (Luke 12:47–48). Scripture consistently weighs guilt by the light received, which is uncomfortable for the well-taught and merciful toward the ignorant.

Comfort under bad authority. There is a great deal of comfort here for anyone under an authority that is behaving badly, and it needs stating carefully so as not to become a defence of tyranny. It does not say that what Pilate is about to do is right. The next clause says the opposite: somebody in this affair has the greater sin, which means sin is being committed and measured. What it says is that the power being abused is derivative, borrowed and bounded, and that the man wielding it will answer for how he used what he was lent.

Not Caesar’s friend. This is the sentence that ends the trial. Friend of Caesar was an honorary title for loyal officials. Pilate’s record was poor, and the emperor Tiberius was suspicious and quick to punish disloyalty. He had provoked riots by bringing military standards bearing the emperor’s image into Jerusalem, and had been forced to remove them. He had put up shields in Herod’s palace and, probably about this time, been overruled by Tiberius after the Jewish leaders complained over his head. Within a few years he would be removed from office and sent to Rome to answer for a massacre in Samaria. A report to Rome could end his career, or his life. The men making the threat know his file. They are telling a governor with two black marks against him that there will be a third.

The threat works. Everything before this, the acquittals, the fear, the attempts to release him, collapses the moment his career is named.

If God is in control, was Pilate really to blame? Yes. God’s sovereignty never excuses human sin. Pilate’s authority came from above, but his decision to condemn an innocent man to save his own position came from his own heart, and Jesus calls it sin. Peter holds both together in one sentence: Jesus was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, and you crucified and killed him by the hands of lawless men (Acts 2:23). God ordained the end; the men who did it did what they wanted, and they are answerable. That is not a puzzle to be solved by dropping one half. It is the comfort of the believer: even the worst human choices cannot escape God’s purpose.

Must I obey authorities who act unjustly? In general, yes, in everything lawful, because their authority is from God (Romans 13:1–7; 1 Peter 2:13–17), and that includes respecting rulers we did not vote for and employers we do not admire. But obedience has a limit: when a ruler commands what God forbids, or forbids what God commands, we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). Christians may also use lawful means to resist injustice: appeal, protest, the ballot, the courts. And abuse in a home or a church is never to be submitted to; get help and get safe. Above all, remember that every ruler is lent his power and will answer for it.
verseByVerse.note: “Friend of Caesar” was an honorary title for loyal officials; the threat was that Pilate would be reported to the emperor.

parallels.desc: there is no authority except from God

verseByVerse.quote: So when Pilate heard these words, he brought Jesus out and sat down on the judgment seat at a place called The Stone Pavement, and in Aramaic Gabbatha. Now it was the day of Preparation of the Passover. It was about the sixth hour. He said to the Jews, "Behold your king!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The judgment seat. The bēma was the raised platform from which a Roman official gave formal sentence. It stood at the Stone Pavement, in Aramaic Gabbatha, perhaps meaning a raised place: an eyewitness detail. The Greek could even mean that Pilate sat Jesus on the judgment seat, in mockery. Either way, the irony is that Jesus is the true Judge (5:22, 27). Pilate sits on the seat of judgment over the one before whose judgment seat Pilate himself will one day stand (2 Corinthians 5:10).

The day of Preparation. This was the regular term for Friday (v. 31; Mark 15:42), so here it means the Friday of Passover week, and John wants us to see that Jesus is the Passover Lamb (1:29).

But was the Last Supper a Passover meal? Matthew, Mark and Luke say it was (Mark 14:12–16), while John seems to put the Passover a day later (13:1; 18:28). Some think different groups followed different calendars that year, or that Jesus held the meal early. The more likely answer is that the day of Preparation of the Passover means the Friday of Passover week, the day of preparation for the Sabbath (compare 19:31; Mark 15:42), and that in 18:28 the Passover means the meals of the festival week. On that reading the Supper was a Passover meal, and Jesus died on the Friday of Passover. It is not the only careful answer, and believers who hold every word of the Gospels true still weigh these options.

It was about the sixth hour. About noon by Jewish reckoning. This is one of the most frequently cited discrepancies in the Gospels. Mark says he was crucified at the third hour, about 9 a.m. (Mark 15:25). Reckoned from sunrise, that is noon against nine in the morning, and the trial cannot be running three hours after the crucifixion. Two answers are offered and both are reasonable. The first is that John is counting hours the Roman civil way, from midnight, so that his sixth hour is about six in the morning. The second may be truer to how anyone told the time before clocks: the day was divided into rough quarters, and a writer named the marker nearest the event, Mark the third hour and John the sixth, for a morning that ran somewhere between the two. John writes about the sixth hour; he is not claiming precision, and nobody in that courtyard had a watch.

The day, not the clock. One honest consequence follows. If John is using Roman hours, then a neat correspondence with the midday slaughter of the lambs is not available, and that point should be held lightly. What does not depend on the hour is the thing that matters: Jesus was condemned and killed on the day of Preparation, in the week when the Passover lambs of that feast were sacrificed. John says so twice, and the symbolism he is pressing rests on the day, not on the clock.

Behold your king! Pilate mocks the Jews, and speaks the truth. The King he presents is still thorn-crowned and purple-robed. That is exactly what the King of the new covenant looks like: enthroned in suffering, crowned with the curse.

In the flow. The trial has been about one question since Pilate first asked, Are you the King of the Jews? (18:33), and here it reaches its climax. The next verse makes Israel’s leaders choose between this King and Caesar, and John has told us the day, so the reader now sees both threads at once: the King is about to be enthroned on a cross, and the Lamb is about to be sacrificed in Passover week. Everything that follows in the chapter, the title over the cross, the hyssop, the unbroken bones, carries those two threads to their end.
verseByVerse.note: The judgment seat was the raised platform from which a Roman official gave judgment. The ESV notes that the sixth hour was about noon; Mark gives the third hour for the crucifixion — times were approximate and may be reckoned differently.

verseByVerse.quote: They cried out, "Away with him, away with him, crucify him!" Pilate said to them, "Shall I crucify your King?" The chief priests answered, "We have no king but Caesar." So he delivered him over to them to be crucified. So they took Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Away with him! Total rejection, and Pilate twists the knife.

We have no king but Caesar. This sentence is easy to walk past because it sounds like ordinary political talk. It is said by the chief priests: not the crowd, not a hothead, but the men whose office existed to represent Israel before God. Israel longed for the Messiah, the son of David, to rule under God its King. Now, to get rid of Jesus, they renounce both.

What Israel was. Israel was a nation founded on the conviction that its true King was God. When the people first asked Samuel for a king, the LORD’s verdict was that they had rejected him from being king over them (1 Samuel 8:7). Gideon refused a crown on exactly that ground: the LORD will rule over you (Judges 8:23). The psalms are full of it; the LORD reigns is the shortest summary of the religion. And this is said at Passover, which celebrated deliverance from a pagan king, in Jerusalem, a few hundred yards from the temple, by the priesthood, about the emperor of the occupying army, in order to secure the execution of their own Messiah. In rejecting Jesus they reject God. Some forty years later Caesar’s soldiers burned the temple to the ground.

Does this mean God has rejected the Jewish people? No. This verse has been used badly, and the guard must be stated. It is a sentence spoken by a group of officials in a particular courtyard on a particular morning, and it is not a verdict on a people. The Gospel’s author, its subject, Jesus’ mother and every one of his apostles were Jews, and Paul says plainly that God has not rejected his people (Romans 11:1–2). Christians hold different views on what Romans 11 promises for Israel’s future, but none of them gives any ground for contempt. What this verse is, is a warning about religious leadership, and it lands nearest those who most resemble the men who said it: people who know the Scriptures, hold religious office, and find the real King inconvenient.

There is always a Caesar. Something can always be appealed to as the real authority when the true King is inconvenient. Career, safety, respectability, the approval of a group whose good opinion is load-bearing. The chief priests did not stop believing in God that morning. They simply, under pressure, named somebody else as the one whose displeasure they could not risk.

Delivered him over. To them means to their will; Roman soldiers carried it out (v. 23). The verb is weighted. Judas delivered him to the priests, the priests delivered him to Pilate, Pilate delivers him to be crucified. And behind them all stands another delivering: he who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32). Human justice fails; divine love triumphs through the same event.

On a Tuesday. Finish this sentence honestly: the thing I could not bear to lose, even for Christ, is.... Whatever fills the gap is the Caesar you are tempted to bow to. Bring it to him today, and say aloud that he is your King.

For worship. His own priests disowned the King, and he did not disown them. They chose Caesar to be rid of him. Within weeks his apostles stood in the same city proclaiming that God had made this Jesus, whom they crucified, both Lord and Christ (Acts 2:36), and thousands bowed to him, and before long a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith (Acts 6:7). Caesar’s throne is dust. His stands, and its gates are still open to those who once cried, Away with him.

parallels.desc: they have rejected me from being king over them

verseByVerse.quote: And he went out, bearing his own cross, to the place called The Place of a Skull, which in Aramaic is called Golgotha. There they crucified him, and with him two others, one on either side, and Jesus between them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bearing his own cross. Condemned men carried their own crossbeam to the place of execution. The upright post usually stood there already. The other Gospels tell us Simon of Cyrene was made to carry it, perhaps after Jesus faltered (Mark 15:21). Nobody need be wrong. Jesus started out carrying the beam, after a night of blows and a Roman flogging, and men in that condition often could not finish the walk. Luke’s wording is that they laid the cross on Simon to carry it behind Jesus (Luke 23:26), which fits a man who has faltered part of the way. The others record the stranger pressed into service. John, whose whole passion narrative insists that nothing was taken from Jesus and everything was given, records that he went out carrying it himself.

Isaac and the wood. John may be recalling Isaac carrying the wood up Mount Moriah for his own sacrifice (Genesis 22:6). The son carried the wood up the mountain, and the father said God would provide the lamb. Here the Father provides the Lamb, and the Lamb carries the wood.

Outside the camp. He went outside the city, as the sin offering was burned outside the camp (Leviticus 16:27; Hebrews 13:12). The letter to the Hebrews makes a doctrine of it: Jesus suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood, so let us go to him outside the camp and bear the reproach he endured (Hebrews 13:12–13). The place of rejection is where the sin offering went, and where his people go to meet him. To sanctify means to make holy: to cleanse sinners and set them apart as God’s own, fit to come into his presence.

Golgotha. Perhaps a rocky hill shaped like a skull, or a place of execution. “Calvary” comes from the Latin calvaria, skull. The Church of the Holy Sepulchre probably marks the site, just outside the city wall of that time, and beside a road, because public execution was meant to be seen.

There they crucified him. It is the shortest sentence about the most important event in history. Not one of the four Gospels describes the physical process; every first-century reader knew what the words covered. Crucifixion was the most cruel and shameful death Rome could inflict, reserved for slaves and rebels. Nails were driven through his hands and, it seems, his feet (20:25; Luke 24:39; the word for hand can include the wrist); the victim died slowly, of exhaustion, shock and laboured breathing, often over days. Cicero said the very word “cross” should be far from a Roman citizen’s thoughts. The evangelists show great restraint, though much Christian art and film has since supplied what they withheld. They want us to see not the gore but the meaning.

Jesus between them. Numbered with the transgressors (Isaiah 53:12). The other Gospels call them robbers or criminals. The arrangement of the three crosses is Isaiah’s sentence carried out by a Roman work detail with no idea what they were doing.

What does it mean for me to take up my cross? Not to carry his cross; that was his alone, and no one can share the work of atonement. But Jesus said that anyone who would follow him must deny himself, take up his cross daily and follow (Luke 9:23). To carry your cross is to accept, for his sake, the cost of belonging to him: the loss of approval, the death of your own way, the hardships that come from obedience. It is not every misfortune, a bad back or a difficult neighbour, though he helps with those too. It is the shame and loss that come because you are his. And it is always carried following him, which means it leads, as his did, through death to resurrection.
verseByVerse.note: Condemned men carried their own crossbeam to the place of execution; Simon of Cyrene was later made to carry it. Golgotha is Aramaic for “skull.”

parallels.desc: Isaac carries the wood

verseByVerse.quote: Pilate also wrote an inscription and put it on the cross. It read, "Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews." Many of the Jews read this inscription, for the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city, and it was written in Aramaic, in Latin, and in Greek.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An inscription. The charge was usually written on a board (titulus) and carried before the condemned man or hung around his neck, then nailed to the cross. It was part of the deterrent: the crowd would know what the state was punishing. Which makes this one remarkable. Matthew calls it the charge against him (Matthew 27:37), yet it names no deed, only a person and a title. The only crime it can point to is being who he is, and Pilate had three times said he found no guilt in him.

The King of the Jews. The charge was meant to mock and warn: this is what happens to would-be kings. But it proclaims the truth: on the cross, Jesus is enthroned as King. The Latin initials INRI (Iesus Nazarenus Rex Iudaeorum) appear on many crucifixes. Pilate meant ironic humiliation; he wrote the gospel.

In Aramaic, in Latin, and in Greek. The King is announced to the whole world. Aramaic, which the people of that land actually spoke, the language of home and street. (The Greek word is literally Hebrew, as older translations have it, but it usually means the Aramaic spoken in Judea.) Latin, the language of the army and the law, in which the empire issued its orders. Greek, the common language of trade and learning across the Roman world. So the first public proclamation of the kingship of Jesus was in three languages, official, posted over his head beside a main road at the busiest time of the Jewish year, and paid for by the Roman government.

Many read it. Golgotha was close enough to the wall and the gate that a crowd going in and out for the feast would pass it.

Is Jesus King now, or only when he returns? Now. He was enthroned at the cross and the resurrection, and he is seated at the Father’s right hand, reigning until all his enemies are put under his feet (1 Corinthians 15:25; Ephesians 1:20–22). Matthew records the risen Lord’s own claim to all authority in heaven and on earth (Matthew 28:18). His reign is hidden now, exercised through his word and Spirit as he gathers his people from every nation, and it will be visible to all when he returns. That is why the church can be confident in every age and every place. The board over the cross was not a joke that came true later. It was true when it was nailed up.

On a Tuesday. Pray today for the gospel to go out in a language other than your own: for Bible translators, for missionaries learning a hard tongue, for a church in a country whose language you do not speak. The cross was first proclaimed in three languages. It will finally be praised in all of them.
verseByVerse.note: Aramaic was the local language, Latin the language of Roman government, Greek the common language of the eastern empire.

verseByVerse.quote: So the chief priests of the Jews said to Pilate, "Do not write, 'The King of the Jews,' but rather, 'This man said, I am King of the Jews.'" Pilate answered, "What I have written, I have written."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not write The King of the Jews. The chief priests are humiliated: the sign says that the Jews’ king has been crucified. Their objection is precise and grammatical. They want the statement turned into a reported claim by a dead pretender. They are asking for the sentence to be turned into a quotation. It is an old way of disposing of a truth without denying it outright.

What I have written. Pilate, who has spent the morning conceding everything, refuses. The perfect tense, twice: it stands written and it will go on standing. It is the flattest, most immovable sentence anybody speaks in the chapter, and it comes from the man who has just handed over somebody he knew to be innocent. It is probably not conscience. It reads like a man who has been pushed around all morning and finds one thing he can refuse: a small, safe, spiteful assertion of the authority he failed to use when it mattered.

God served by a governor’s irritation. The truth stays on the cross. Like Caiaphas (11:51), Pilate testified to the truth without meaning to. God’s purposes at Calvary were served by a governor’s petty irritation, as they were served by soldiers gambling and by a priest’s political calculation. Nobody in the chapter is trying to accomplish anything for God, and every one of them accomplishes it. The result is that the only official document we know the crucifixion of Jesus Christ produced, the one legal text, in three languages, over his head, unretracted, says that he is the King. God’s word stands written.

The proverb. The sentence has had a long life. Quod scripsi, scripsi passed into proverb, and it is usually quoted admiringly, as the mark of a man who will not be moved. It was said by somebody who had been moved on every question that mattered, about a notice, after the nails were in.

How do people today turn the truth into a quotation? Every time Jesus’ claims are reported as merely what he said, or what his followers believed, so that nobody has to reckon with whether they are true. It is the way of much modern talk about religion: Christians believe that Jesus is Lord, rather than Jesus is Lord. That can be honest description, and in the right setting it is fair. But watch for it in your own heart: the habit of holding Christ’s words at arm’s length, as interesting claims, rather than receiving them as the truth about the world. Scripture does not say he said he was King. It says he is.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–42 — The Death and Burial of Jesus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the cross: the soldiers and the seamless tunic, the women who stayed and the mother given a home, the thirst and the last word, then the spear, the eyewitness’s testimony, and the burial. Four times in a few verses John notes that Scripture was fulfilled.
verseByVerse.theology: It is finished stands at the centre of John’s account. It announces a completed action whose effects remain: the work of redemption is done and needs no addition. No later act of piety, effort or moral striving adds to what was finished on the cross. Salvation is received, not achieved.
verseByVerse.examples: The beloved disciple who stood at the cross with the women is a model of discipleship under pressure: present where the cost was highest, faithful where the others had fled. He saw the blood and water from the soldier’s spear, the sign that Jesus truly died, and testifies that what he saw is true, so that we also may believe.

verseByVerse.quote: When the soldiers had crucified Jesus, they took his garments and divided them into four parts, one part for each soldier; also his tunic. But the tunic was seamless, woven in one piece from top to bottom, so they said to one another, "Let us not tear it, but cast lots for it to see whose it shall be." This was to fulfill the Scripture which says, "They divided my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots." So the soldiers did these things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four parts. The four shares suggest a squad of four soldiers; the clothes of the condemned were the executioners’ perk, and the number is a routine detail recorded by somebody who was watching. The items were perhaps the outer cloak, the belt, the sandals, the head covering. One item is left over. Jesus was probably crucified naked, as the condemned usually were, the final humiliation.

The tunic was seamless. This was the inner garment. Some note that, according to Josephus, the high priest’s robe was woven in one piece (compare Exodus 28:32). The coincidence has struck readers since the early centuries: the garment of the priest, on the body of the priest, preserved whole while everything else is divided. Jesus dies as our High Priest. Others have seen the unity of the church. It should be offered as an echo rather than an argument. John does not explain; he points to the fulfilment of Scripture.

To fulfil the Scripture. The verse is Psalm 22:18. (In verse 16 of that psalm, the Hebrew of the line about hands and feet is uncertain: most Hebrew manuscripts read like a lion, while the ancient Greek translation and some Hebrew evidence point to pierced, which the ESV follows.) Written about a thousand years earlier, centuries before crucifixion is known to have been practised, the psalm contains a line that had no obvious application to anything: they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots. Two different actions, dividing and gambling. It reads like ordinary Hebrew poetry, saying one thing twice. At Golgotha it turns out to be two things. They divided the garments and they cast lots for the tunic, and the reason they did both is a technical accident of weaving.

In the flow. Here John begins a run of four fulfilments of Scripture in a few verses: the garments here, the thirst (v. 28), the unbroken bones (v. 36) and the pierced side (v. 37). Nowhere else in the Gospel do they come so thick. The trial has shown human beings doing what they chose; the cross shows God doing what he had said.

Psalm 22 read whole. It opens with the cry Jesus quotes from the cross. It has men mocking and wagging their heads; it has hands and feet pierced; it has bones out of joint and a tongue sticking to the jaw; and it ends, unaccountably, in worldwide praise, with all the families of the nations worshipping and a people yet unborn told that he has done it. A sceptic may say the story was shaped to fit the psalm, and that objection deserves the answer given below; but Christians from the first have found it very hard to read as coincidence.

Did the Gospel writers simply make the story fit the psalm? It is a fair question, and the answer lies in what they could not have invented. Dividing a prisoner’s clothes was routine for Roman execution squads, done in public in front of a crowd, and John says he stood at the cross himself (19:26, 35). More than that, nobody inventing a Messiah would have given him a cross. A crucified Christ was a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles (1 Corinthians 1:23); the first Christians did not choose the story because it suited them. They told it because it happened, and then found, to their astonishment, that God had written it down a thousand years before.

So the soldiers did these things. The soldiers noticed none of it. They were solving a practical problem about a garment that would be ruined if cut. Four men gambling at the foot of a cross, entirely at liberty, fulfilling to the letter a poem they had never read.

Was Psalm 22 really about Jesus, or about David? Both, in their proper order. David wrote out of his own suffering, and the psalm makes sense in his life. But it goes far beyond anything David endured: the piercing, the stripping, the casting of lots, and above all the ending, where the sufferer’s deliverance brings the ends of the earth to worship God. David was a prophet and knew that God had promised a greater Son (Acts 2:30–31). The Spirit who moved him to write was speaking of the sufferings of Christ and the glories to follow (1 Peter 1:11). So Jesus could take its first line on his lips as his own, and John could see its details fulfilled at the foot of the cross. The psalm was always his.

On a Tuesday. Read Psalm 22 today from beginning to end, slowly, and at each verse ask what it shows you of the cross. Then pray its last verses for the world: that the families of the nations would turn to the Lord. The psalm of the cross ends in mission.
verseByVerse.note: The four shares suggest a squad of four soldiers; the clothes of the condemned went to them.

parallels.desc: they divide my garments among them

verseByVerse.quote: but standing by the cross of Jesus were his mother and his mother's sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene. When Jesus saw his mother and the disciple whom he loved standing nearby, he said to his mother, "Woman, behold, your son!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Standing by the cross. Count the women, and see who is missing. Probably four: his mother; her sister (perhaps Salome, mother of James and John, Mark 15:40; Matthew 27:56, which would make John Jesus’ cousin); Mary the wife of Clopas; and Mary Magdalene, from whom Jesus had cast seven demons (Luke 8:2). The Greek also permits three, if the sister and Mary of Clopas are the same person. Peter is somewhere in the city. The men who had sworn the night before to die with him are absent, except one, and the ones standing near enough for him to see are women with no power to do anything at all.

Being there. That is worth saying to anybody who has ever stood beside a suffering they could not fix. These women could not stop it. They had no standing, no legal voice, no ability to intervene, and if they had tried they would have been moved on by soldiers. What they could do was be there, in full view, close enough for him to see them. It was not nothing. In those hours it was the one thing anybody could do for him, and John records their names.

A sword through her soul. Simeon’s prophecy to Mary is fulfilled: a sword will pierce through your own soul also (Luke 2:35). She was told it when the baby was forty days old. She has had some thirty years to wonder what he meant, and she is finding out. And the son she watches die is dying for her too. She had rejoiced in God her Saviour when she first carried him (Luke 1:47); now she stands beneath the cross as one of those he is saving, and in the hour he bears her sins he also provides for her body. If you have stood beside a child’s suffering or buried a son or daughter, you are not alone at that place: the mother of the Lord stood there, and her Son saw her.

Woman, behold, your son! The disciple whom he loved is the only one of his male followers John places at the cross. “Woman” is not cold but respectful, and he has used it to her once before, at Cana, when she wanted him to do something about the wine and he told her his hour had not yet come (2:4). John has bracketed the ministry with the word: Cana, where the hour had not come; Golgotha, where it has. In his agony, he provides for his mother, as the eldest son should; his brothers did not yet believe (7:5). Even on the cross, he keeps the fifth commandment.

Where Christians differ: Mary at the cross. Roman Catholic teaching sees here Mary made the spiritual mother of all believers, and sometimes speaks of her as co-redemptrix, sharing in Christ’s saving work. This commentary’s view: the plain meaning is that a loving son provides a home for his widowed mother. Christ alone is the Redeemer, and his sacrifice needs no human partner (1 Timothy 2:5; Hebrews 10:14). Mary is honoured as a believer and the mother of our Lord, but she is not a mediator. This also suggests that Mary had no other sons who believed at that time, but it does not prove she had no other sons at all (Mark 6:3).

Does this make Mary the spiritual mother of all believers, as Roman Catholic teaching holds? The text shows a son providing for his widowed mother, and the disciple taking her to his own home (v. 27). Nothing gives her a role in the church’s salvation or prayers. Mary is honoured as the mother of the Lord and a believer among believers (Acts 1:14), but Christ alone is our mediator. Many Roman Catholic friends honour Mary out of real love for her Son, and that love deserves respect even where we must differ.

What if my own family does not believe? Jesus knows what that is like; his brothers did not believe in him at the time (7:5), and he still loved and provided for his own. Keep loving them, honour your parents, and pray for them patiently. Do not make them feel they are a project. The brothers who doubted came to faith after the resurrection: James became a leader of the Jerusalem church, and both he and Jude wrote letters in the New Testament (Acts 1:14; 15:13). And in the meantime, the church becomes family to you, as the beloved disciple became a son to Mary.

On a Tuesday. Even in agony, Jesus kept the fifth commandment, and he kept it perfectly in your place, where your own honouring has fallen short. So look after your parents gladly, especially in their need. And when someone you love is suffering and you can do nothing to fix it, do not stay away for fear of being useless. Be there. It was what his mother and her friends could do for him.

parallels.desc: a sword will pierce your own soul

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to the disciple, "Behold, your mother!" And from that hour the disciple took her to his own home. After this, Jesus, knowing that all was now finished, said (to fulfill the Scripture), "I thirst."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, your mother! A new family is formed at the cross. He had brothers; under any ordinary reckoning the eldest son’s responsibility passes to the next son. He passes it instead to a disciple. That is not a slight on the family. It is a statement about what the new family is founded on. The tie that binds this household together is not blood. So the believers in your church are your family in Christ, bound to you by his blood rather than by birth, and that bond will outlast every earthly one. Jesus had said it plainly: whoever does the will of God is his brother and sister and mother (Mark 3:35).

To his own home. Tradition says she later lived with him in Ephesus. It is the first act of the church, performed while its Lord was still dying, and it consists of somebody taking a widow in (James 1:27).

Knowing that all was now finished. The word is the same as in v. 30: everything the Father gave him to do was complete, except his final words and death. He is being executed, and on a cross every breath was probably a labour of its own. And what he does with that breath is domestic: settling who will look after his mother.

I thirst. The Scriptures are Psalm 69:21 and Psalm 22:15. A reader may stumble here, as though the thirst were staged for the sake of a quotation. It was not. The man had been flogged, had lost blood for hours, and had been hanging on the cross for hours; dehydration is one of the ways crucifixion kills. The thirst is as real as thirst gets. What John means is that he knew what he was doing when he said it aloud. He is not manufacturing a fulfilment; he is naming, in the last minutes, the one thing left on the list.

The fountain thirsts. The giver of living water (4:14; 7:37), who promised a woman at a well that she would never thirst again, died thirsty.

Did Jesus suffer as God or as man? He suffered as the one person who is both. God in his divine nature cannot suffer or die; the eternal Son did not cease to uphold the universe on the cross. But the Son took a true human nature, body and soul, and in that nature he truly thirsted, bled and died. Because it was the Son of God who suffered in that nature, Scripture can say God purchased the church with his own blood (Acts 20:28). So the thirst on the cross was not play-acting by a divine being in a costume. It was the real thirst of a real man, who was also God.

On a Tuesday. Take someone in. Is there an elderly believer, a single parent, a lonely student in your church who needs a family? Invite them to your table this week.

For worship. The Lamb died thirsty, so that a multitude no one can number will never thirst again. He spent his last breaths making a new family and fulfilling the Scripture, with his tongue stuck to his jaw. And because he thirsted there, the Lamb in the midst of the throne will be the shepherd of his people, guiding them to springs of living water, while God wipes away every tear from their eyes (Revelation 7:16–17).

parallels.desc: my tongue sticks to my jaws

verseByVerse.quote: A jar full of sour wine stood there, so they put a sponge full of the sour wine on a hyssop branch and held it to his mouth. When Jesus had received the sour wine, he said, "It is finished," and he bowed his head and gave up his spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sour wine. Cheap, vinegary wine (oxos), the soldiers’ drink. Not the drugged wine he refused earlier (Mark 15:23).

On a hyssop branch. Hyssop was the plant used to sprinkle the blood of the Passover lamb on the doorposts (Exodus 12:22), and in purification (Psalm 51:7). A small, bushy plant with a weak stem; it is not an obvious thing to hold a soaked sponge up with, and some think a long stalk is meant. But John wrote hyssop, and the reason is very likely that he knew what hyssop was for. Hyssop is the applicator of the Passover blood, and at the moment the true Passover Lamb is dying, a stalk of it is lifted to his mouth. John records it and says nothing, which is his habit.

It is finished. One word in Greek: tetelestai. Perfect tense: finished, and remaining finished, a thing completed with results that stand. The verb turns up in business papyri for a tax or debt paid, and it is often said that receipts were marked with it to mean “paid in full”; however that may be, the New Testament uses the same verb for paying a tax (Matthew 17:24; Romans 13:6). Not “I am finished,” which is what a dying man says, but “It is finished”: the subject is the work the Father gave him (4:34; 17:4), not the man. The sacrifice for sin is complete, the debt is paid, the prophecies are fulfilled.

In the flow. This is the word the whole Gospel has been moving toward. John opened the upper room by saying he loved his own to the end (13:1), and the word for end belongs to the same family as finished. The hour that had not yet come at Cana (2:4) has come and is now complete. What follows in the chapter, the spear, the witness and the burial, establishes that he truly died, and chapter 20 will show that the finished work has been accepted.

The guard this word sets. This word puts a guard on everything afterwards. If the work is finished, nothing can be added to it: not by penance, not by devotion, not by a lifetime of good behaviour, not by anything a person does on their worst day or their best. The commonest form of Christian misery is the suspicion that something is still outstanding. This word was cried from a cross to settle it.

He bowed his head. John’s word order is deliberate, and it is backwards. A dying man’s head falls when he dies. John has him bow it first, as one lying down to rest, and then give up his spirit; the verb is one of handing over, of giving something into someone’s keeping. Two thousand years of art have him hanging with his head fallen. John says he laid it down. The Good Shepherd had said, no one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord (10:18), and this is the sentence where he does it. Luke records his last words, “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” (Luke 23:46).

Nothing was taken. Nothing was taken from him that afternoon that he did not give. The clothes were taken, and the freedom, and the reputation, and the blood. His life he handed over, at a moment of his choosing, having first said that the account was settled.

Where Christians differ: what happened at the cross? Some say Christ’s death was mainly an example of love, or a victory over evil powers, and reject the idea that he bore God’s punishment for our sin. This commentary’s view: Christ’s death was a victory and an example, but at its heart it was penal substitution: he bore the penalty of our sins in our place (Isaiah 53:5–6; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Galatians 3:13; 1 Peter 2:24). That is why “It is finished” can mean “paid in full.” Nor does the Mass repeat or re-present the sacrifice; it was offered once for all, finished (Hebrews 9:25–28; 10:10–14).

Was Jesus really forsaken by the Father? Yes, in the sense Scripture means, and it was the deepest part of his suffering. On the cross he cried, My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? (Mark 15:34). The Father did not stop loving his Son; the Son was never more pleasing to him than in this obedience. But as the sin-bearer, Christ endured the Father’s judgment on sin and the withdrawal of the felt comfort of his presence, the experience of the condemned. The union of the Trinity was not broken. What he bore was the forsakenness that our sins deserved, so that we would never be forsaken (Hebrews 13:5). John records the end of it: when the wrath was exhausted, he cried, it is finished, and committed his spirit to his Father.

If it is finished, why do I still struggle with sin and suffering? Because what was finished is the payment, not yet the whole renewal. The work that saves you is complete: your guilt is paid, your standing with God secure, your future certain. Nothing you suffer is punishment for sins Christ has paid for; it is a Father’s training (Hebrews 12:5–11). But the application of that finished work goes on: the Spirit is making you holy, and the creation still groans until Christ returns (Romans 8:18–23). You fight sin not to finish what he left undone, but because he has finished it, and the victory he won guarantees yours.

On a Tuesday. Most of us have something we keep trying to add to the cross: the extra effort to feel forgiven, the penance of self-punishment after a sin, the private sense that God is still waiting for you to make it up to him. Name it, and say the word aloud. Confess the sin, receive the forgiveness, and get up and serve him out of gratitude, not to pay a debt that has been cancelled.

For worship. Glory to the Lamb who did not die defeated. Every altar in Israel had been waiting for a word no priest had ever spoken, because no priest’s work was ever done: they stood day after day offering the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins (Hebrews 10:11). He offered one sacrifice for sins for all time, and said so, with hyssop at his lips. Then he bowed his head and gave his spirit into his Father’s hands, and he lives to make sure that not one of those he paid for is ever charged again.
verseByVerse.note: Hyssop was the plant used to sprinkle the blood of the Passover lamb. “It is finished” is a cry of completion, not defeat.

parallels.desc: a bunch of hyssop

verseByVerse.quote: Since it was the day of Preparation, and so that the bodies would not remain on the cross on the Sabbath (for that Sabbath was a high day), the Jews asked Pilate that their legs might be broken and that they might be taken away. So the soldiers came and broke the legs of the first, and of the other who had been crucified with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not on the Sabbath. The law forbade leaving a hanged body overnight (Deuteronomy 21:22–23), and the coming Sabbath made it urgent. The Romans often left bodies on crosses for days as a warning, but in Judea they seem generally to have respected Jewish custom. And look at who does the asking: the same officials, going back to the same governor, a second time in one day. The first request was for a death. The second is to have it hurried up so as not to spoil the evening.

The curse taken down before nightfall. The law they invoke says why the body must come down: a hanged man is cursed by God, and the land must not be defiled (Deuteronomy 21:23). The leaders are anxious about a corpse on a pole at sunset. They do not know that the man on the middle cross is bearing that very curse, not for any crime of his own but for the sins of his people, as Paul would write, becoming a curse for us so as to redeem us from the curse of the law (Galatians 3:13). The law wanted the curse over by nightfall, and his was: It is finished had already been spoken (2 Corinthians 5:21).

A high day. This was the weekly Sabbath falling within the festival, especially solemn, which is why the pressure to have the bodies down was unusually strong, and why the burial that follows is done at such speed.

That their legs might be broken. Breaking the legs (crurifragium) with a heavy mallet sped death. It is commonly thought that a man could breathe only by pushing himself up on his feet, so that with his legs broken he could no longer push up and died quickly. Brutal mercy. It is the same irony as the governor’s doorstep that morning (18:28): men who would not enter a Gentile house in case it barred them from a meal are, that afternoon, arranging for the legs of living men to be shattered so that the evening’s observance is not spoiled.

Along the row. Both criminals still lived, and the soldiers work along the row to the middle cross.

What about the thief who believed? Luke tells us that one of these two men turned to Jesus and asked to be remembered when he came into his kingdom, and Jesus answered, truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:42–43). So one of the men whose legs were broken that afternoon died soon after and went straight into the presence of Christ. He had no baptism, no record of good works, no time to make amends. He was saved by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, and his broken legs could not keep him from paradise. There is no purgatory in that promise, only today, and with me.

For worship. The Lord of the Sabbath died on the eve of the Sabbath. In the beginning God worked six days and on the seventh rested, his work finished. In that week the Son finished the work of redemption on the sixth day, rested in the grave on the seventh, and rose on the first day of the next to begin the new creation. The hurried afternoon, the mallets and the calendar all served a rest that he had planned, and that he shares with every weary sinner who trusts him.
verseByVerse.note: The law forbade leaving a hanged body overnight; the coming Sabbath made it more urgent. Breaking the legs stopped a crucified man pushing up to breathe and hastened death.

parallels.desc: his body shall not remain all night on the tree

verseByVerse.quote: But when they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs. But one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and at once there came out blood and water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Already dead. Jesus died quickly, after some hours on the cross (about six, on Mark’s timing), and Pilate was surprised (Mark 15:44). First the question on which everything else rests: was he actually dead? The suggestion that he merely fainted and revived in the cool of the tomb has been made repeatedly since the eighteenth century, and it founders on this verse. The men at the foot of the cross were a professional execution squad. Killing people was their trade, and a soldier who let a condemned man off a cross alive would have faced severe punishment. They looked at him and did not bother breaking his legs, which is the judgement of experts.

Blood and water. The soldier meant to make sure, and what came out settled it. Medical explanations vary, the separation of clot and serum after death, or fluid gathered round the heart or in the chest after the flogging and the strain, and no single account commands agreement. What matters for John is that the professionals were satisfied: this man was dead.

Why John insists on it. By the time this Gospel was written, teachers were already circulating who held that the Christ could not really have suffered: that the divine had departed before the death, or that the body was only an appearance (the error later called docetism, from the Greek for seem). John’s letters go after exactly that error: every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God, and every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God (1 John 4:2–3). The blood and water are his answer, and he saw them come out. He is not making a devotional point first. He is a witness giving evidence about a body.

The sign in the wound. But John also sees a sign. Blood and water: the blood of atonement and the water of cleansing and life (7:38–39; 1 John 5:6–8). (In 1 John 5:7–8 the KJV adds words about three that bear record in heaven; they appear only in late manuscripts, so modern Bibles leave them out.) Atonement means the dealing with sin that brings sinners back to God: their guilt removed by a sacrifice offered in their place, so that God and the sinner are at one. Many church fathers saw here the gospel’s two great gifts, forgiveness and the Spirit, and pictures of the Supper and baptism. That older reading is not to be dismissed, since John does write on more than one level; but the primary meaning is the plainer and harder one, the evidence of death. Zechariah 13:1 promised a fountain opened for sin and uncleanness. From the wounded side of the Lamb, it flows.

Does it matter whether Jesus really died? Everything depends on it. If he did not die, he did not bear the penalty of sin, which is death (Romans 6:23), and there was no resurrection, only a recovery. Paul says that if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins (1 Corinthians 15:17), and there is no resurrection without a death. The real death also means he has gone through what we will go through. He has tasted death for everyone who is his (Hebrews 2:9), and he knows the way out. When you stand at a deathbed, you are standing where he has been.

parallels.desc: the water and the blood
a fountain opened for sin

verseByVerse.quote: He who saw it has borne witness — his testimony is true, and he knows that he is telling the truth — that you also may believe. For these things took place that the Scripture might be fulfilled: "Not one of his bones will be broken."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He who saw it has borne witness. This verse is the author breaking cover. Apart from one phrase in the prologue (1:14), John has written eighteen chapters without once stopping to vouch for himself. Here he stops the story and swears a statement. The beloved disciple, who stood at the cross (19:26), insists he saw it (21:24). That is not how a devotional writer talks. It is how a witness talks under oath, and the Christian faith rests on historical events, seen and reported.

That you also may believe. This is the purpose of the whole Gospel (20:31). He is not recording the spear-thrust because it is moving. He is recording it because the reader’s faith depends on the man having actually died, and he was there.

Not one of his bones. This is the fulfilment the whole Gospel has been building toward since John the Baptist pointed at him in chapter 1. The Passover lamb was to be roasted whole, eaten within the house, and not a bone of it broken (Exodus 12:46; Numbers 9:12). Passover after Passover, in household after household, the lamb was handled under that rule. Psalm 34:20 says the same of the righteous sufferer. Jesus is the true Passover Lamb, whose blood shelters his people from judgment.

How the rule was kept. At the middle cross the soldiers stopped for the entirely practical reason that the man was already dead. That is how the rule was kept: not by anyone’s intention. A Roman work detail, hurrying to finish before sunset on the day of Preparation, left one body intact because there was nothing to be gained by damaging it, and in doing so handled the Lamb of God exactly as the law required.

Can I trust testimony written down decades later? Yes, for good reasons. John was there; he says so with unusual force, and he was writing while others who were there could still contradict him. The Gospels were written within the lifetime of eyewitnesses, as Luke says he consulted those who were eyewitnesses from the beginning (Luke 1:1–4), and Paul could appeal to more than five hundred who had seen the risen Christ, most of them still alive (1 Corinthians 15:6). Ancient people remembered and passed on testimony carefully, and these witnesses gained nothing by it except hardship and, for many, death. And the Spirit who inspired the writing bears witness in the heart of the reader that it is true (1 John 5:6).

On a Tuesday. Your faith rests on a witness, not on a feeling. On a day when belief feels thin, go back to the testimony: read a Gospel account of the cross and resurrection as evidence, given by men who saw it. Then pass the testimony on. Someone near you may believe because you told them what was seen.
verseByVerse.note: The Passover lamb’s bones were not to be broken.

parallels.desc: he keeps all his bones

verseByVerse.quote: And again another Scripture says, "They will look on him whom they have pierced." After these things Joseph of Arimathea, who was a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews, asked Pilate that he might take away the body of Jesus, and Pilate gave him permission. So he came and took away his body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Him whom they have pierced. In Zechariah 12:10 it is the Lord himself who speaks of being pierced, and the people mourn as for an only child. It is one of the strangest sentences in the prophets, and John quotes it over a body with a spear-wound in its side. At Golgotha God the Son was pierced in the flesh he had taken. Some looked in mockery; many will look in repentance and faith (Revelation 1:7).

From looking to mourning to a fountain. The Zechariah passage is not about condemnation. What follows the looking is mourning, a whole land weeping, family by family, and then, in the next verse, a fountain opened to cleanse them from sin and uncleanness (Zechariah 13:1). The looking leads to grief and the grief to a fountain. That is the way every sinner comes to Christ: he looks at the one he pierced, grieves, and is washed.

Will Israel one day look on him and mourn? Christians differ on this, and the views should be stated fairly. Some believe Zechariah and Romans 11:25–27 point to a great turning of the Jewish people to Christ before his return, in which they will look on the one they pierced and mourn. Others understand all Israel to mean the whole number of God’s elect from Jews and Gentiles together, gathered through the age, and see the mourning fulfilled whenever Jews and Gentiles come to faith, from Pentecost onward (Acts 2:37). Both agree that John sees the prophecy beginning at the cross, that its full completion comes when every eye sees him at his return (Revelation 1:7), and that there is one way of salvation for Jew and Gentile alike: looking in faith to the pierced Christ.

Joseph of Arimathea. Arimathea was a town of Judea. Joseph was a member of the council who had not agreed to its decision (Luke 23:50–51), and a rich man (Matthew 27:57). His secrecy came from the same fear that silenced the parents of the blind man and the authorities who believed and would not say so (9:22; 12:42).

He asked for the body. Mark says he took courage (Mark 15:43). Not during the trial, when a voice might have helped, but when the movement seemed finished, he goes to a Roman governor to ask for the body of an executed rebel. The fear of man lays a snare, says Proverbs (29:25), and Joseph had been caught in it, perhaps for years. Now, at the worst possible moment, he steps out of it.

Courage at the costliest moment. Joseph’s years of silence were real and this Gospel does not excuse them. But the moment he chose to break cover was the moment it cost most and profited least, and hardly anyone else in Jerusalem did it. Jesus had said that when he was lifted up from the earth he would draw all people to himself (12:32). The cross scattered the Twelve, and among the first people drawn to him after he died were two members of the council who had been too afraid to come while he lived.

I have kept my faith quiet for years. Is it too late? No. Joseph kept silent too long, and when he finally came out, Christ received his gift. The Lord does not shame the timid who come; he welcomed Nicodemus by night and accepted Joseph’s tomb by day. But do not wait for the moment that costs most. Tell one person this week that you belong to Christ: a friend, a colleague, a family member. Ask to be baptised if you have not been, and join a church. Secret discipleship may begin in fear; it is not meant to stay there, and the cross is what draws it into the open.
verseByVerse.note: Arimathea was a town of Judea. Joseph was a member of the council.

parallels.desc: they look on me, on him whom they have pierced
