verseByVerse.quote: Nicodemus also, who earlier had come to Jesus by night, came bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about seventy-five pounds in weight. So they took the body of Jesus and bound it in linen cloths with the spices, as is the burial custom of the Jews.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nicodemus also. The man who came in the dark (3:2) now comes in the light, and the whole arc is now visible. He came in the dark, cautiously, with a compliment and a question, and was told he must be born again and could not follow it. He turned up again in chapter 7, in a council meeting, making a careful procedural point, does our law judge a man without first giving him a hearing?, and was slapped down for it (7:50–51). And now he is here in daylight, in public, with a great weight of spices and his hands on a dead body.

A slow conversion. This is a comfort for the reader who has been waiting a long time for somebody. It took Nicodemus years, and the visible steps were a private conversation, one cautious question in a hostile room, and then everything at once at the worst possible moment.

What Nicodemus had been told. On that first night Jesus spoke of the Son of Man lifted up like the serpent in the wilderness (3:14–15), and Nicodemus could not follow it. This afternoon he has seen it: the Son of Man lifted up on a Roman cross outside the city. He had been the most religious man in the room on that first night, and he was told that his religion could not get him into the kingdom: he must be born from above, like anyone else (3:3). The teacher of Israel who stumbled over talk of new birth is now handling the body through which it comes, and the king’s burial he brings is his confession that the one lifted up is the King.

Myrrh and aloes. The ESV notes that the weight is literally a hundred Roman pounds, about 34 kilograms. An enormous amount, fit for a king’s burial (2 Chronicles 16:14): a load a man would struggle to carry, and worth a great deal of money. Ordinary burials used a fraction of it. Josephus records that five hundred servants carried spices at Herod the Great’s funeral, which is the register this belongs to. Nicodemus has brought a king’s burial to a criminal’s execution. Myrrh was a fragrant resin; aloes, a fragrant wood powder. They did not embalm the body, but covered and surrounded it with spices to honour it and mask the smell of decay.

Linen cloths with the spices. Strips of linen were wound around the body, with spices between, as with Lazarus (11:44): not Egyptian embalming, but Jewish burial. And it cost them more than spices. Handling a corpse made a Jew ritually unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:11). Both these men, on the eve of the feast’s high Sabbath, made themselves unclean in order to bury him. They would spend the rest of the festival week unclean. They had missed nothing. The Lamb was already dead.

Does it matter how Christians bury their dead? Scripture does not lay down a law about burial or cremation, and the resurrection does not depend on what happens to the body; God who made it from dust can raise it from ashes or the sea (Revelation 20:13). But burial has long been the Christian custom, following the burial of Christ and the patriarchs, because it treats the body with honour as something that belongs to the Lord and will be raised (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). Whatever your family chooses, do it with reverence and hope, not as disposal. The body you lay to rest is a seed, not rubbish.

On a Tuesday. Give him your best. Not your leftovers of time and money, but something costly, given when it looks as though it will gain you nothing. And if you are waiting for a slow-moving friend or relative, do not give up. Nicodemus took years.

For worship. A fortune was poured out on a corpse: Nicodemus thought he was honouring a dead king, and he was wrapping the body that would leave the linen behind on the third day and need none of it. No love spent on Christ is wasted, even when it seems to come too late, because the one it is spent on does not stay dead.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the weight is literally a hundred Roman pounds — a quantity fit for a royal burial. Myrrh and aloes were aromatic spices laid with the linen wrappings.

parallels.desc: King Asa laid on a bier filled with spices
myrrh at his birth

verseByVerse.quote: Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden, and in the garden a new tomb in which no one had yet been laid. So because of the Jewish day of Preparation, since the tomb was close at hand, they laid Jesus there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A garden. John now closes the bracket he opened at 18:1: a garden at the beginning, where he was taken, and a garden at the end, where he is laid. Eden was lost in a garden; the King is buried in one; and in this garden he will rise, and Mary will think him the gardener (20:15). John does not explain the echo of Eden; he simply lets the reader hear it. The new creation begins in a garden.

A new tomb. Matthew says it was Joseph’s own tomb, cut in the rock (Matthew 27:60). Two details matter and both are evidential. It was new, with no other body in it, which closes off any confusion about whose body was missing on Sunday. And it belonged to Joseph, which means a wealthy man gave away the grave he had probably cut for himself and his family.

With a rich man in his death. Isaiah, describing the Servant, had said something that made no sense as a prediction: they made his grave with the wicked and with a rich man in his death (Isaiah 53:9). Both halves came true within hours, and by opposite means: the state numbered him with criminals and meant him to lie with them, and a private citizen put him in a rich man’s tomb.

Close at hand. Time was short before the Sabbath began at sunset. The last clause is very flat: they chose it because it was near and the light was going. There is no ceremony in the sentence, no reflection, no farewell. Two men who had been afraid of being seen with him work quickly against a deadline, put a body in a borrowed grave, and go home. And that is where the chapter stops. John does not close it with a promise or a hint. He leaves the reader at a closed tomb on a Friday evening, which is exactly where everybody who loved him was left.

Why the burial matters. “He was buried” is part of the gospel (1 Corinthians 15:4). It proves he truly died. And his burial sanctifies the graves of his people: he has lain where we will lie, and has come out.

Where was Jesus between his death and resurrection? His body lay in Joseph’s tomb; his human soul went to his Father. He had said to the thief, today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43), and he committed his spirit into his Father’s hands (Luke 23:46). He did not sleep unconscious, and he did not go to a place of further suffering; his suffering was finished on the cross. When the Apostles’ Creed says he descended into hell, Reformed Christians have understood it of the hellish agonies he endured on the cross (Heidelberg Catechism, question 44) and of his remaining under the power of death until the third day (Westminster Larger Catechism, question 50). The same is true for believers: at death the body rests in the grave, while the soul goes at once to be with Christ, awaiting the resurrection (Philippians 1:23; Westminster Confession 32.1; 1689 London Baptist Confession 31.1).

On a Tuesday. On the days that feel like Friday evening, when everything you hoped for seems sealed behind a stone, remember that John left his readers there too, and that Sunday was already coming.

For worship. The one who had said, I am the resurrection and the life, was silent among the dead in a borrowed grave. But he had gone into the grave as a conqueror goes into an enemy’s fortress, and he had gone there for us. Every Christian grave since has been a garden plot, because his was first: the grain of wheat fell into the ground and died (12:24), and on the third day it came up as the firstfruits of all who sleep in him.

parallels.desc: with a rich man in his death

19.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Pilate took Jesus and flogged him.<sup>2</sup>And the soldiers twisted together a crown of thorns and put it on his head and arrayed him in a purple robe.<sup>3</sup>They came up to him, saying, “Hail, King of the Jews!” and struck him with their hands.<sup>4</sup>Pilate went out again and said to them, “See, I am bringing him out to you that you may know that I find no guilt in him.”<sup>5</sup>So Jesus came out, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple robe. Pilate said to them, “Behold the man!”<sup>6</sup>When the chief priests and the officers saw him, they cried out, “Crucify him, crucify him!” Pilate said to them, “Take him yourselves and crucify him, for I find no guilt in him.”<sup>7</sup>The Jews answered him, “We have a law, and according to that law he ought to die because he has made himself the Son of God.”<sup>8</sup>When Pilate heard this statement, he was even more afraid.<sup>9</sup>He entered his headquarters again and said to Jesus, “Where are you from?” But Jesus gave him no answer.<sup>10</sup>So Pilate said to him, “You will not speak to me? Do you not know that I have authority to release you and authority to crucify you?”<sup>11</sup>Jesus answered him, “You would have no authority over me at all unless it had been given you from above. Therefore he who delivered me over to you has the greater sin.”<sup>12</sup>From then on Pilate sought to release him, but the Jews cried out, “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend. Everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar.”<sup>13</sup>So when Pilate heard these words, he brought Jesus out and sat down on the judgment seat at a place called The Stone Pavement, and in Aramaic Gabbatha.<sup>14</sup>Now it was the day of Preparation of the Passover. It was about the sixth hour. He said to the Jews, “Behold your King!”<sup>15</sup>They cried out, “Away with him, away with him, crucify him!” Pilate said to them, “Shall I crucify your King?” The chief priests answered, “We have no king but Caesar.”<sup>16</sup>So he delivered him over to them to be crucified. So they took Jesus,<sup>17</sup>and he went out, bearing his own cross, to the place called The Place of a Skull, which in Aramaic is called Golgotha.<sup>18</sup>There they crucified him, and with him two others, one on either side, and Jesus between them.<sup>19</sup>Pilate also wrote an inscription and put it on the cross. It read, “Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews.”<sup>20</sup>Many of the Jews read this inscription, for the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city, and it was written in Aramaic, in Latin, and in Greek.<sup>21</sup>So the chief priests of the Jews said to Pilate, “Do not write, ’The King of the Jews,’ but rather, ’This man said, I am King of the Jews.’”<sup>22</sup>Pilate answered, “What I have written I have written.”<sup>23</sup>When the soldiers had crucified Jesus, they took his garments and divided them into four parts, one part for each soldier; also his tunic. But the tunic was seamless, woven in one piece from top to bottom,<sup>24</sup>so they said to one another, “Let us not tear it, but cast lots for it to see whose it shall be.” This was to fulfill the Scripture which says, “They divided my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots.” So the soldiers did these things,<sup>25</sup>but standing by the cross of Jesus were his mother and his mother’s sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene.<sup>26</sup>When Jesus saw his mother and the disciple whom he loved standing nearby, he said to his mother, “Woman, behold, your son!”<sup>27</sup>Then he said to the disciple, “Behold, your mother!” And from that hour the disciple took her to his own home.<sup>28</sup>After this, Jesus, knowing that all was now finished, said (to fulfill the Scripture), “I thirst.”<sup>29</sup>A jar full of sour wine stood there, so they put a sponge full of the sour wine on a hyssop branch and held it to his mouth.<sup>30</sup>When Jesus had received the sour wine, he said, “It is finished,” and he bowed his head and gave up his spirit.<sup>31</sup>Since it was the day of Preparation, and so that the bodies would not remain on the cross on the Sabbath (for that Sabbath was a high day), the Jews asked Pilate that their legs might be broken and that they might be taken away.<sup>32</sup>So the soldiers came and broke the legs of the first, and of the other who had been crucified with him.<sup>33</sup>But when they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs.<sup>34</sup>But one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and at once there came out blood and water.<sup>35</sup>He who saw it has borne witness— his testimony is true, and he knows that he is telling the truth— that you also may believe.<sup>36</sup>For these things took place that the Scripture might be fulfilled: “Not one of his bones will be broken.”<sup>37</sup>And again another Scripture says, “They will look on him whom they have pierced.”<sup>38</sup>After these things Joseph of Arimathea, who was a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews, asked Pilate that he might take away the body of Jesus, and Pilate gave him permission. So he came and took away his body.<sup>39</sup>Nicodemus also, who earlier had come to Jesus by night, came bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about seventy-five pounds in weight.<sup>40</sup>So they took the body of Jesus and bound it in linen cloths with the spices, as is the burial custom of the Jews.<sup>41</sup>Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden, and in the garden a new tomb in which no one had yet been laid.<sup>42</sup>So because of the Jewish day of Preparation, since the tomb was close at hand, they laid Jesus there.
19.overview:
John tells the crucifixion as the hour of Jesus’ glory and the fulfilment of Scripture. Pilate, though he declares Jesus innocent three times, has him flogged, presents him to the crowd, and gives way when his loyalty to Caesar is threatened; the chief priests disown every king but Caesar. Jesus is crucified under a title in three languages naming him King of the Jews.

From the cross he gives his mother a home, fulfils the Scriptures, and with “It is finished” lays down his life. John, an eyewitness, insists that he truly died: no bone broken, as with the Passover lamb, and his side pierced. Two secret disciples come into the open to give him a king’s burial in a new tomb in a garden.

20.title: The Resurrection

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — The Empty Tomb and Mary's Encounter with the Risen Lord
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The empty tomb and the first meeting: the two disciples at the grave clothes, and Mary in the garden, who knows the risen Lord when he calls her by name and is sent to tell his brothers.
verseByVerse.theology: The resurrection appearances in John turn on recognition. The beloved disciple believes from the linen cloths; Mary knows Jesus when he calls her name, as the sheep know the Good Shepherd’s voice (10:3); Thomas knows him when invited to touch the wounds. Each meeting is different, suited to each person, and in each it is the same Jesus, now risen, who comes to the disciple where he or she is.
verseByVerse.examples: Mary Magdalene, weeping at a tomb, heard her name from the one she thought was dead, and was sent with the first resurrection message: I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God. The news is both his and theirs: through the risen Son, his Father has become their Father.

verseByVerse.quote: Now on the first day of the week Mary Magdalene came to the tomb early, while it was still dark, and saw that the stone had been taken away from the tomb. So she ran and went to Simon Peter and the other disciple, the one whom Jesus loved, and said to them, "They have taken the Lord out of the tomb, and we do not know where they have laid him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. John 20 tells of the resurrection: the empty tomb, the risen Jesus meeting Mary, the disciples, and Thomas. Each meeting moves from grief, fear or doubt to faith and joy, and the chapter ends with the Gospel’s purpose: these things are written so that you may believe. The resurrection is not a myth or a feeling but a historical event, attested by witnesses, which changes everything. Chapter 19 left everyone who loved Jesus beside a sealed tomb on a Friday evening. Now the first day of the week dawns.

Now on the first day of the week. Sunday: in Greek, literally day one of the week. It is the ordinary idiom, but with an echo worth hearing. John opened this Gospel with in the beginning, deliberately echoing Genesis. Now, after a Friday on which Jesus said it is finished and a Sabbath on which his body lay at rest in the tomb, comes day one again. The Son who finished his work on the sixth day, as God finished the heavens and the earth, opens the new creation on its first morning, and the day he rose became the day his people gather. A new creation is not a figure of speech: Jesus’ risen body is the first piece of the world God will make new, the firstfruits of the harvest (1 Corinthians 15:20), and everyone joined to him by faith already belongs to that new world: if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17).

Does this mean Sunday is the Christian Sabbath? The day of resurrection became the church’s day of gathering (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2), and John calls it the Lord’s day (Revelation 1:10). Christians who love the Scriptures hold two main views. Many Reformed Christians, with the Westminster Confession (Westminster 21.7–8) and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, regard the Lord’s Day as the Christian Sabbath, the fourth commandment’s weekly day of rest and worship moved to the day of resurrection. Others read the Sabbath as fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 4:9–10), and see Sunday gathering as a glad privilege rather than a sabbath law. This commentary’s view: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our rest, and the first day is set apart gladly, out of joy and wisdom, not as the fourth commandment transferred to Sunday; no one may bind another believer’s conscience over it (Romans 14:5; Colossians 2:16–17). The Westminster and 1689 view (1689 22.7–8) is held by many godly brothers and deserves respect. Both agree that Christians should gather with the church each Lord’s Day, and should rest in Christ’s finished work.

Early, while it was still dark. Darkness outside, and in her heart. While it was still dark sits beside Mark’s when the sun had risen (Mark 16:2), and anyone who has set out early knows both are true of the same walk. She left in the dark and arrived as it was getting light.

The stone taken away. Not rolled away so that Jesus could get out: that same evening he will stand in a room with the doors locked (v. 19). It was moved so that the witnesses could get in. The stone is not the beginning of the resurrection but the announcement that it has already happened. Before anyone arrived, in the dark, the Son had taken up again the life he laid down, as he said he had authority to do (10:18), and nobody saw it. The greatest event in history had no human spectator. It had only evidence, left for those who loved him to find.

They have taken the Lord. Her first thought: grave robbers, or the authorities. Resurrection does not cross her mind. Her interpretation is wrong, and it is the sensible one: a tomb sealed on Friday is open on Sunday, so somebody has moved the body. The witnesses did not expect it, which makes their testimony more believable: they were not people who saw what they wanted to see.

The we that was left standing. John names only Mary Magdalene. Matthew has her with the other Mary; Mark adds Salome; Luke speaks of the women who had come from Galilee. A sceptical reader might call that a discrepancy. Then Mary opens her mouth: we do not know. John has written the scene around one woman and left the plural pronoun standing in her speech, which is the kind of thing that happens when somebody reports a conversation without tidying it. He tells it through Mary because she matters for what follows, and has not troubled to remove the evidence that she was not alone.

She ran to Peter. She goes to the man who denied him, whom the others might reasonably have written off, and to the beloved disciple, and treats them as the people to be told. Nobody in the account has excluded Peter from anything.

On a Tuesday. Every Sunday is a small Easter. Prepare for it on Saturday: get to bed, plan to arrive early, come expecting to meet the risen Lord with his people.

For worship. On the first day God said, let there be light, and on this first day the Light of the world had risen before anyone came looking, while it was still dark. Mary walked through the last of the old night toward a grave, and the new creation was waiting for her at the end of the path. The Lord of life needed no witness to rise and no hand to help with the stone. Every first day since has dawned in the light of his morning.
verseByVerse.note: The first day of the week is Sunday.

verseByVerse.quote: So Peter went out with the other disciple, and they were going toward the tomb. Both of them were running together, but the other disciple outran Peter and reached the tomb first.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter went out. Two grown men sprinting through Jerusalem at first light on the strength of a report neither of them believed, because Mary’s message was that the body had been stolen, and that is what they were running to investigate. Whatever they expected to find, it was not what they found.

Outran Peter. A vivid, almost humorous detail, mentioned twice (here and at verse 8); the usual guess is that the other disciple, traditionally John, was the younger man.

The pair. These two men appear together again and again in these chapters: at the supper (13:23–24), in the courtyard (18:15–16), at the tomb, and on the shore in the next chapter. John and Peter are consistently placed side by side, the one who sees and the one who acts, and the opening chapters of Acts have them still together, going up to the temple at the hour of prayer (Acts 3:1). Love arrives first; courage goes in first. The church has always needed both.

Of those you gave me I have lost not one. Why does Peter run at all? Only days earlier he had sworn beside a fire that he did not know the man. John has already given the answer. In the garden Jesus stepped forward to be arrested so that his disciples could go free, that the word he had spoken might be fulfilled: of those whom you gave me I have lost not one (18:8–9). Peter’s denial had not cancelled that word. The man running through the streets is held by a grip stronger than his own, and the race to the tomb is the first sign that the Shepherd who laid down his life has kept every sheep the Father gave him, including the one who disowned him.

Why would the Gospel record such small details? Because they are the kind of things eyewitnesses remember and inventors have little reason to include. Who ran faster, who stooped and who went in, how the cloths lay: none of these obviously serves a theological purpose, and some of them do the disciples no credit. Vivid detail cannot prove a report on its own, since a skilled storyteller can invent it too; but it fits what this Gospel claims to be, the testimony of a man who was there (21:24). A man constructing a legend would not have built it around the testimony of a woman and then had two men arrive, look, and go home. The story does nothing to make its witnesses impressive. These small, unpolished details are part of why many historians, not only believers, take the Gospels seriously as testimony.

On a Tuesday. Run to Christ, whatever your past failures. Peter did, held by a Shepherd who had not let him go. If you have been avoiding church, prayer or a Christian friend because of something you are ashamed of, go today; his welcome does not wait on your record.

parallels.desc: Peter runs to the tomb

verseByVerse.quote: And stooping to look in, he saw the linen cloths lying there, but he did not go in. Then Simon Peter came, following him, and went into the tomb. He saw the linen cloths lying there,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stooping to look in, he saw the linen cloths lying there. Tomb entrances were low; the beloved disciple has to stoop to look in, which fits the rock-cut tombs of the period. Lying (keimena): lying flat, in place. Not thrown, not scattered, not gathered up. But he did not go in, perhaps from awe, or reluctance to defile himself.

Peter went in. Peter, characteristically, goes straight in, past his friend and into a grave, though he had every reason to hang back. Neither is criticised, and John records the hesitation as his own.

He saw the linen cloths lying there. “Saw” (theōrei): looked carefully, studied. John describes the seeing in stages. At verse 5 the beloved disciple stoops and catches sight of the cloths. At verse 6 Peter goes in and takes stock. At verse 8 the other disciple goes in, and saw and believed. A glance, then a study, then an understanding, told by a man who was there.

What they were looking at. The position of the cloths is the thing. Grave robbers would hardly stop to undress a body; the linen and spices were valuable, and anyone stealing it would surely have carried the whole bundle out. These men are staring at grave clothes still lying where a body had been. John uses two words: the othonia, the linen strips that bound the body, and the soudarion of the next verse, the cloth that covered the face and was tied round the head. He distinguishes them because their positions were different, and their positions are the whole point.

Linen for a king. The cloths Peter is studying were not cheap. Nicodemus had brought about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes, and the body was bound in linen with the spices (19:39–40): a burial fit for a king, given to a man crucified under a notice that called him King of the Jews. Now the king’s burial clothes lie empty. The honour his friends gave him in death was real and loving, and he has no further use for it. No one took his life from him, and no one could keep his body: the grave clothes are what a king leaves behind when he has no more need of a burial.

On a Tuesday. Faith in Christ is not a refusal to look; it is a willingness to look carefully. If you have doubts, read a careful book on the resurrection, or simply read the four accounts side by side and ask what best explains them.

For worship. The hands of his friends wrapped the Son of God in linen and spices, and he let them. The Lord of glory submitted even to being carried and laid down like any dead man, so that no grave of his people would be a place he had not been. He went into the place we dread, and he left it empty for us.

verseByVerse.quote: and the face cloth, which had been on Jesus' head, not lying with the linen cloths but folded up in a place by itself. Then the other disciple, who had reached the tomb first, also went in, and he saw and believed;
verseByVerse.commentary:
The face cloth. Robbers would not have left the costly linen and spices, still less folded the face cloth. Some take folded (entetuligmenon) to mean rolled up, keeping its shape where the head had been. Either way, it looked as if the body had simply passed out of the wrappings.

Lazarus came out bound. Compare the other tomb in this Gospel. Lazarus came out with his hands and feet bound and his face wrapped in a cloth, and Jesus had to tell the bystanders to unbind him (11:44). He came back to a life that would end again, and needed others to untie him. Jesus came out of death for ever and left the wrappings behind, folded, because nothing of the grave clings to him any more. At Bethany he had said, I am the resurrection and the life (11:25). Lazarus received resurrection; Jesus is it. Lazarus needed a voice to call him out; the Son, who has life in himself (5:26), was raised by the Father and rose in his own power.

A story to set aside. A guard is needed here, because a sermon illustration about this verse circulates widely and it is not true. The story goes that a Jewish servant, clearing a master’s table, would leave the napkin crumpled if the meal was over and fold it neatly if he intended to return, so the folded face cloth is Jesus saying I am coming back. It is a lovely idea with one defect: there is no evidence for any such custom in any ancient source, and the word here is not about table linen at all. A face cloth is exactly that, used at burials. The story appears to be a modern invention, and the verse is strong enough not to need it.

He saw and believed. In John’s account he is the first to believe in the resurrection, and John writes the sentence about himself, in the third person, with no elaboration. No angel had spoken to him; he would not see the risen Lord until that evening; nobody had explained anything, and the next verse says outright that he still did not understand the Scripture about the resurrection. What he had was an empty tomb and the way the linen was lying. That was enough. Blessed are those who have not seen (v. 29).

What about the other explanations? Many alternatives have been tried, and each runs into a known difficulty. The disciples stole the body: then they suffered, and some died, for what they knew was a lie, and the grave clothes would hardly have been left. The authorities moved it: then they would have produced it when the apostles began preaching in Jerusalem weeks later. The women went to the wrong tomb: then the authorities would only have needed to show the right one. Jesus only fainted: Roman soldiers knew death, and a half-dead man could not have convinced anyone he had conquered it. The disciples hallucinated: hallucinations are normally private experiences, not something a whole group shares at once, again and again over weeks, and hallucinations do not empty tombs. The explanation that best fits the empty tomb, the appearances, and the transformation of frightened men into bold witnesses is the one they gave: he is risen. Thoughtful sceptics still propose other theories, and no argument can force faith; but believers are not choosing against the evidence when they say it.
verseByVerse.note: Grave robbers would not have unwrapped the body and left the cloths neatly behind.

verseByVerse.quote: for as yet they did not understand the Scripture, that he must rise from the dead. Then the disciples went back to their homes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They did not understand the Scripture. They believed because of what they saw, not yet because of Scripture. They had never grasped it, though Jesus had told them plainly and repeatedly that he would be killed and rise on the third day. Later they understood that the Old Testament foretold it (Luke 24:25–27, 44–46). Must (dei): it was necessary, part of God’s plan. The Son did not merely survive death; he rose because the Father had written his rising into the plan of salvation before the cross was raised.

Which Scriptures? The apostles later point to Psalm 16: you will not abandon my soul to Sheol, or let your holy one see corruption, and Peter builds his Pentecost sermon on it (Acts 2:25–31). Paul says Christ was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:4). Hosea has a third day (Hosea 6:2), Jonah has three days, and Isaiah 53 has a servant who is cut off and then shall see his offspring and prolong his days (Isaiah 53:10). It was all there. It had been there for centuries, and none of them had put it together, and one of them is writing this sentence about himself decades later without any attempt to look better.

Back to their homes. Probably where they were staying in Jerusalem. It is the flattest verse in the resurrection narrative: one of them has just believed, and there is no announcement, no gathering, no prayer meeting. That is so unlike how a legend would be written, and so exactly like people. And it means that the first person actually to meet the risen Christ is the one who stayed.

How should I read the Old Testament, then? With Christ at the centre, as Jesus himself taught. On the road to Emmaus he began with Moses and all the Prophets and interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself (Luke 24:27). That does not mean every verse is a hidden riddle about Jesus. It means the whole story is moving toward him: the promises to Abraham, the sacrifices, the kings, the psalms of suffering and vindication, the prophets’ hope. As you read, ask: what does this show me of the God who would send his Son? What problem is crying out for Christ to solve? Where does this promise land in him? Read it that way and the Old Testament will open to you as it opened to them.

For worship. The God who promised that his Holy One would not see corruption kept his word to the letter on the third day. He had been writing toward this morning since the first promise in Eden, that the woman’s offspring would crush the serpent’s head, and the Son walked out of the tomb as the Amen to every one of those promises (2 Corinthians 1:20). His slow, forgetful disciples were given the joy of discovering, too late to have helped and just in time to believe, that every word had been true.

parallels.desc: you will not let your holy one see corruption

verseByVerse.quote: But Mary stood weeping outside the tomb, and as she wept she stooped to look into the tomb. And she saw two angels in white, sitting where the body of Jesus had lain, one at the head and one at the feet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mary stood weeping. The but is doing all the work: the men have gone home; Mary stays. She had walked there in the dark, run to fetch them, walked back, and now stands outside a tomb that everyone else has finished with. She has no plan and is not waiting for anything, because as far as she knows the body has been stolen, and the last service left to her, anointing it properly, has been taken away too. She is simply unable to leave.

The one who could not go home. That is worth saying plainly to anyone whose grief has outlasted everybody else’s patience with it. This is the person the risen Christ appears to first. Not the one who reasoned correctly from the evidence, not the one who went in first, and not the eleven. The one who could not go home.

She stooped to look into the tomb. The same verb used of the beloved disciple in verse 5, a second look at a space two men have already searched. Grief does that too: it checks again. And this time there is something there.

Two angels in white. They are sitting quietly in an empty grave, not standing guard or blazing, and Mary does not seem to realise they are angels. She is not frightened and does not remark on them; she answers their question as though they were attendants, and turns away. Her grief is large enough that two angels do not register.

The mercy seat. One at the head and one at the feet, with an empty space between them where a body had lain, like the two cherubim of gold at either end of the mercy seat on the ark of the covenant (Exodus 25:18–22), where the blood of atonement was sprinkled and where God said he would meet with his people. John does not say so, but the picture is hard to miss. Jesus himself is the true mercy seat: Paul calls him a propitiation, using the Greek Bible’s word for the mercy seat (Romans 3:25). A propitiation is an offering that bears God’s holy anger against sin and so puts it away. The ark pictured that once a year; at the cross it happened once for all, and the empty place where his body lay is the proof. The Most Holy Place had been behind a curtain, entered once a year, with blood. This one has a woman crying at the entrance and, as Matthew records, the curtain torn (Matthew 27:51).

Is it wrong for a Christian to grieve so deeply? No. Mary wept at the tomb, Jesus wept at the tomb of Lazarus (11:35), and nobody in this scene tells her to stop. Paul does not forbid Christians to grieve; he says we do not grieve as others do who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Christian grief is real grief, sometimes long and heavy, held in the hands of a risen Lord. If your sorrow has outlasted other people’s patience, do not be ashamed of it. Bring it to him, stay near him, and keep coming back to the place where he has met you before. He came first to the one who could not stop weeping.

On a Tuesday. Look around your church for the one who is still grieving after everyone else has moved on: the widow a year later, the parents after a miscarriage, the friend whose loss nobody mentions now. Sit with them. Say the name of the one they lost.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to her, "Woman, why are you weeping?" She said to them, "They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him." Having said this, she turned around and saw Jesus standing, but she did not know that it was Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woman, why are you weeping? A gentle question. The angels ask her the same question Jesus will ask a moment later, and it is not an accusation in either mouth. It is the question that gets somebody to say aloud what is wrong. Nobody in this scene tells her to stop crying. Two angels and the risen Son of God, and not one of them says she should not be upset. They ask her why. And the next to ask it is the one who wept at the grave of Lazarus (11:35) and is himself the answer to her tears: she is weeping over the absence of a body that is standing behind her, alive.

They have taken away my Lord. At verse 2 she said they have taken the Lord; here she says my Lord. The public title has become a personal one. She still thinks of a dead body, and she is not making a theological statement; she is explaining, to someone who has asked, why she cannot stop crying.

She did not know that it was Jesus. He was behind her, for how long John does not say, while she was bent over an empty grave describing his disappearance to two angels. The risen Jesus was not always recognised at first (Luke 24:16; John 21:4). His resurrection body was the same body, with its wounds (v. 20), but transformed. And her eyes were full of tears, and she was not expecting him: grief had already settled the range of possibilities, and none of them was the man she had watched die. She was a few feet from the answer to her weeping and could not see it, and there was nothing blameworthy in that at all.

Will we recognise one another in the resurrection? Yes. The risen Jesus was recognised in the end by those who knew him: Mary knew his voice, the disciples knew his wounds, the Emmaus pair knew him at the breaking of bread. He was the same person in a glorified body. Paul expects to see his converts in the presence of Christ as his crown and joy (1 Thessalonians 2:19), and the comfort he gives the bereaved is that we shall be with them and with the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:17). We will not be strangers in the new creation. We will know as we are known (1 Corinthians 13:12), and the faces we loved will be there, made new.

On a Tuesday. When you are overwhelmed, it can be hard to see what God is doing. Ask him today: Lord, where are you standing in this? Look back over a hard season you have come through, and you may find he was nearer in it than you knew at the time.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you seeking?" Supposing him to be the gardener, she said to him, "Sir, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away." Jesus said to her, "Mary." She turned and said to him in Aramaic, "Rabboni!" (which means Teacher).
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whom are you seeking? The question of 1:38 and 18:4. In 1:38 it was what; here, as in the garden, it is whom. His first words to her are a question he has asked at the moments that matter in this book. He asked the first two disciples who followed him in chapter 1 what they were seeking, and he asked the arresting party in the garden, twice (18:4, 7). Now, in another garden, at the end, he asks it of a weeping woman. The whole Gospel is bracketed by that question, and it has always been aimed past the person answering it.

Supposing him to be the gardener. An understandable mistake, and a profound one. He is the gardener of the new creation, the second Adam in the garden (19:41). The first Adam was put in a garden to work it and keep it, and lost it. The last Adam stands in a garden at dawn on the first day of the new creation, and a woman mistakes him for the man who tends it. She is more right than she knows.

I will take him away. Love that does not calculate. She proposes to carry off a grown man’s body, wrapped in a load of spices, by herself, with no plan for where to put it, and she makes the offer to a stranger without embarrassment.

Mary. Then one word, her name. Not an explanation. Not it is I. Not a rebuke for failing to recognise him, and no reference to the resurrection at all. He says her name, and she is turned round in an instant. The Good Shepherd calls his own sheep by name, and they know his voice. He had said that in Jerusalem, after he gave sight to a man born blind (10:3–4). This is that sentence happening.

Rabboni. “Rabboni” is Aramaic for “my teacher,” a warm and respectful form of “rabbi.” John keeps the word rather than translating it away. She uses the name she always used, because the man in front of her is the same man, and there is not yet a vocabulary for what has happened. She does not yet grasp all that he now is.

Does the risen Jesus really know me personally? Yes. He knows his sheep by name (10:3, 14), and his knowledge of you is not general but particular: your history, your sins, your griefs, the things you have never told anyone. The Father gave you to him by name before the world began (17:6), and he laid down his life for you by name. He calls you now through his word, and the Spirit makes that call personal in your heart, so that you know the voice is for you (10:27). You may feel forgotten in a crowd of eight billion. You are not forgotten by him.

On a Tuesday. Read 10:1–5 and 10:27–29 aloud, and put your own name where it fits: he calls me by name; I know his voice; no one will snatch me out of his hand.

For worship. Death could not make the Shepherd forget one of his sheep. The Word through whom all things were made, who calls the stars by name, came out of the grave and spent his first words on a single woman’s name, and that one word was enough to turn a mourner into a witness. The same voice will sound over every grave of his people (5:28–29), and each of them will hear their own name, turn, and know him.
verseByVerse.note: “Rabboni” is Aramaic for “my teacher,” a warm and respectful address.

parallels.desc: he calls his own sheep by name

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "Do not cling to me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father; but go to my brothers and say to them, 'I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.'" Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, "I have seen the Lord" — and that he had said these things to her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not cling to me. Not “do not touch me” (the old translation), but stop holding on to me. The old Latin rendering, Noli me tangere, has produced a great many paintings of a recoiling Christ and a rebuked woman, and it misleads. The Greek is a present imperative, and in a prohibition like this it usually means: stop doing what you are already doing. She has hold of him, as if never to let go (Matthew records the other women taking hold of his feet, Matthew 28:9), and the instruction is to let go. Not do not come near me, but you cannot keep me here. He has not come back to the old life in Galilee. A new relationship is coming, by the Spirit, after he ascends.

Not yet ascended. He is on his way, and there is a task now. A week later Jesus invites Thomas to put his finger in the nail marks (v. 27), so this is no ban on touching. Mary must not hold him as though the days on the road in Galilee had come back unchanged. He is going to the Father, and from there he will be with all his people at once, nearer than an embrace, by the Spirit (16:7).

My brothers. For the first time in this Gospel, Jesus calls his disciples brothers. After the cross, they are members of his family, children of his Father (Hebrews 2:11–12). At supper, three nights earlier, he had raised them from servants to friends (15:15), and that was already extraordinary. Now, after every one of them has run away, and one has denied him three times to strangers, he calls them his brothers. The first thing he does with a resurrected body is raise the standing of the men who abandoned him.

My Father and your Father. Not our Father. His sonship is unique and eternal; theirs is by adoption, through him, and yet he shares his Father with them, because the cross has made it possible. It is often pointed out that nowhere in the Gospels does he include himself with the disciples in a single our Father; even when teaching them to pray it, he gives it to them to say. The two halves of the phrase keep both truths.

In the flow. Ever since 13:1, when Jesus knew that his hour had come to depart out of this world to the Father, this Gospel has spoken of his going to the Father (14:12, 28; 16:28). The cross was the first step of that journey, the resurrection the second, and the ascension, forty days later, will complete it (Acts 1:3, 9). Verse 17 tells Mary that the journey is not yet finished, and that its goal is not his glory alone: he goes so that his Father may be theirs, and so that the Spirit may come (16:7), the Spirit he will breathe on them in verse 22.

I have seen the Lord. The first witness to the risen Christ was a woman, at a time when women’s testimony was not readily accepted in Jewish courts. Nobody fabricating an account would have picked her as its first witness. She is sometimes called the apostle to the apostles, and her message is the simplest and fullest resurrection proclamation there is: personal, direct, certain.

Does Mary’s witness mean women should be pastors? Mary was the first to announce the resurrection, and her witness was honoured by Christ himself. Every Christian, man or woman, is called to say what she said: I have seen the Lord, and this is what he told me. Women prayed, prophesied and laboured in the gospel throughout the New Testament (Acts 1:14; Romans 16:1–7; Philippians 4:2–3). But Mary was sent with a message to the apostles, not appointed one of them, and the New Testament reserves the office of elder or pastor to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7; Titus 1:5–9). That is not a judgment on women’s gifts or worth; Christ entrusted the greatest news ever told to a woman first. It is the pattern of ordered service he gave his church. Paul grounds that pattern in creation, not in local custom (1 Timothy 2:13), which is why this commentary holds it (the view often called complementarian: equal worth, different callings). Many faithful Christians read these passages differently and recognise women as pastors, and they deserve to be heard as brothers and sisters who love the same Lord.

What does it mean that God is my Father because he is Christ’s Father? It means your standing with God is not a lesser copy of a relationship, but a share in the real one. By nature the Son alone is the Father’s child. But by adoption, through faith in Christ, the Father receives you as his son or daughter, with the Spirit in your heart crying Abba (Galatians 4:4–7). You approach him not as a servant hoping for wages but as a child at home. He knows what you need before you ask (Matthew 6:8), disciplines you because he loves you (Hebrews 12:6), and has given you an inheritance with his Son (Romans 8:17). The risen Christ came out of the tomb and called the Father yours.

On a Tuesday. When you pray today, begin with the word the risen Son himself put in your mouth: Father.
verseByVerse.note: “Do not cling to me” means the old relationship cannot simply resume; he is going to the Father.

parallels.desc: not ashamed to call them brothers

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–31 — Appearances to the Disciples and to Thomas
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two Sunday meetings behind locked doors: the risen Jesus gives the disciples peace, his commission and the Holy Spirit, and a week later brings Thomas to faith. The section ends with the purpose of the whole Gospel.
verseByVerse.theology: Peace be with you (vv. 19, 21, 26): Jesus says it three times. The peace he brings is not first the end of the disciples’ fear but his own presence among them. And he shows them his hands and his side: the wounds are carried into the resurrection body. The resurrection does not undo the cross; it vindicates it, and the scars remain as the lasting sign that the atonement is real and its benefits are for ever.
verseByVerse.examples: Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed (v. 29): this is the blessing on every Christian since the first generation, who believe on the word of those who were there, written in Scripture and made living by the Spirit. Thomas needed to see the wounds; we trust the testimony about them, and Jesus counts us blessed.

verseByVerse.quote: On the evening of that day, the first day of the week, the doors being locked where the disciples were for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood among them and said to them, "Peace be with you." When he had said this, he showed them his hands and his side. Then the disciples were glad when they saw the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That evening. Easter Sunday evening. It is the reunion, and John reports it in two verses.

The doors being locked. That is where the church is on Easter Sunday evening, expecting arrest: in a bolted room, with men who have heard from Mary that she has seen the Lord and have made no visible use of it. Luke says the women’s words seemed to them an idle tale (Luke 24:11). The contrast with the boldness of the coming months is the measure of what the risen Christ and his Spirit will do with them.

Jesus came and stood among them. Locked doors do not stop him. His resurrection body is real, physical, but not limited as ours are (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). John does not explain it and neither should anyone else. There is no suggestion of a door opening.

Peace be with you. This was the ordinary Jewish greeting, shalom, the thing anyone said on entering a house. But from the risen Lord, to the men who deserted him, it is far more. It is the peace he promised (14:27; 16:33), now won by the cross (Romans 5:1; Ephesians 2:14–17). He does not begin with a rebuke, or an explanation, or I told you so, all three of which were available and deserved. He greets them. Peace with God is more than a calm feeling. It means the war between a holy God and rebel sinners is over, because the Son took the hostility on himself (Romans 5:10), and the men who ran from him are welcome at his side.

He showed them his hands and his side. Proof: the same Jesus, the one who was crucified. Nothing required a resurrection body that can enter a locked room to be marked, and yet the wounds are there, and he displays them deliberately, and in eight days he will invite a man to put his hand into one. The marks were kept on purpose. The one piece of the old world carried out of the grave into the new creation is the evidence of what it cost. His wounds remain in his glorified body, the eternal marks of his love (Revelation 5:6).

They were glad. Three nights earlier he had promised it: you will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will turn into joy; I will see you again, and your hearts will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you (16:20–22). The sorrow arrived exactly as described and so did the joy, and the man who predicted both was standing in the room.

What will our resurrection bodies be like? Like his. Paul says Christ will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body (Philippians 3:21), and John says we shall be like him (1 John 3:2). His risen body was truly physical: he could be touched, he ate fish (Luke 24:42–43), he bore the marks of his history. Yet it was no longer subject to weakness, decay or death, and it was not hindered as ours are now. It is sown perishable and raised imperishable, sown in weakness and raised in power (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). The same you, made whole and glorious, with nothing lost that was truly yours and nothing left that sin had spoiled.

On a Tuesday. Behind which locked door are you hiding this week: fear of a diagnosis, of a person, of the future, of being found out? The risen Christ comes through locked doors with peace, and his wounds are the proof that you are safe with him. Tell a trusted friend what you are afraid of, and pray together.
verseByVerse.note: “Peace be with you” was the ordinary Hebrew greeting, shalom — now full of meaning.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them again, "Peace be with you. As the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you." And when he had said this, he breathed on them and said to them, "Receive the Holy Spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the Father has sent me. Peace again, and this time for their mission: this is John’s Great Commission. The Son’s mission becomes the church’s mission (17:18): to make the Father known, to serve, to suffer, and to bring people to God. And the comparison is a staggering one to make about the church’s work. Not in the same general spirit, but as. The Son was sent all the way in, to people’s level, at his own cost, and stayed within reach of those who did not want him; so are they. And he says it while showing them the marks.

He breathed on them. The verb (emphysaō) occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, and John has chosen it with care. Breathing on them recalls God breathing life into Adam (Genesis 2:7), the same Greek verb in the Greek Old Testament: the LORD God formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life. And it recalls Ezekiel’s vision of the Spirit breathing life into dry bones: come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe on these slain, that they may live (Ezekiel 37:9). Creation, and re-creation from a field of corpses: in a locked room, on the first day of the week, a new creation begins.

Receive the Holy Spirit. The word for spirit is the word for breath in both Hebrew and Greek, which is why the picture works and why English cannot reproduce it. He breathes, and says: receive the Breath.

Where Christians differ: this gift and Pentecost. Some see this as John’s version of Pentecost; others as a separate, partial gift. This commentary’s view: this is a real gift, but also an acted promise, preparing the disciples for the full outpouring at Pentecost about seven weeks later, when Jesus had ascended (7:39; 16:7; Acts 1:4–5, 8). The Spirit was given to them here, and poured out in power there. Both show that the Spirit comes from the risen Christ.

Not a mere symbol. What no reading should do is make this only a gesture. John has just described a creation act. Something was given. And the commission in the previous verse shows what for: they are being sent, and no one is sent on that errand without the Spirit.

In the flow. Verses 19–23 keep, one after another, the promises Jesus made in the upper room: peace (14:27), joy (16:22), the sending (17:18) and the Spirit (14:16–17; 16:7). The order matters. Peace comes first, because men who are not at peace with God cannot be sent; then the commission; then the Spirit, the power to carry it out; and in verse 23 the message itself, forgiveness of sins. The book of Acts is that commission being carried out.

Do I need a second experience of the Spirit after conversion? No. The apostles stood at a unique turning point in history, between the resurrection and Pentecost, and their experience of the Spirit came in stages because redemption itself was unfolding in stages. Since Pentecost, every believer receives the Spirit at conversion: anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him (Romans 8:9), and in one Spirit we were all baptised into one body (1 Corinthians 12:13). What you need is not a second blessing but a daily filling, to keep in step with the Spirit you already have (Galatians 5:25; Ephesians 5:18), through the word, prayer and obedience. Ask for more of his fruit and his strength. You do not need to ask for him to come, as though he were absent. Many Pentecostal and charismatic believers, often marked by deep love for Christ, teach a later baptism in the Spirit; we differ because the letters written to ordinary churches never tell believers to seek one, but we differ as brothers.

On a Tuesday. You are sent as Christ was sent. Pick the place this week where you are most like a missionary: the office, the school gate, the club, the family table. Ask the Spirit for courage there, and do one concrete thing for one person in his name.

For worship. The Son who received the Spirit without measure now breathes him out on his friends: the risen Christ is not only the one on whom the Spirit rests but the one who gives him, and that is the prerogative of God. In the first creation the breath of life came from the Lord God into the dust. On the first day of the new creation, it came from the mouth of a man with nail marks in his hands, and he is the Lord God.
verseByVerse.note: Breathing on them recalls God breathing life into Adam.

parallels.desc: the breath of life
come, O breath

verseByVerse.quote: "If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you withhold forgiveness from any, it is withheld." Now Thomas, one of the twelve, called the Twin, was not with them when Jesus came.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you forgive the sins of any. In the best-attested text both verbs are in the Greek perfect tense: they have already been forgiven, they have already been withheld. The disciples do not create forgiveness; they announce what God has already done. By preaching the gospel, they declare forgiveness to all who believe, and declare that those who refuse remain in their sins (Matthew 16:19; 18:18; Acts 2:38; 13:38–39).

Where Christians differ: who forgives sins? Roman Catholic teaching sees here the institution of the sacrament of penance, giving priests power to absolve sins in confession. This commentary’s view: only God forgives sins (Mark 2:7). The words are given to the disciples as a group, and their exercise in Acts is the preaching of the gospel: forgiveness is proclaimed to all who repent and believe. Every Christian who declares the gospel speaks with this authority. Church discipline also applies it (1 Corinthians 5:4–5; 2 Corinthians 2:7–10). There is no special priestly power to absolve.

The reading that deserves an answer. The reading set aside in that verdict should be named carefully, since it is held by a great many Christians. Rome takes this verse as the institution of penance: the apostles, and the bishops and priests who succeed them, are given the power to absolve sins, exercised in the confessional, where the priest says I absolve you. The Council of Trent (the sixteenth-century Roman Catholic council) cited this text for it directly. The words plainly commit something about sins to these men, so it deserves an answer rather than a dismissal.

The grammar. Three things answer it. The first is the grammar already noted, the perfect tense. Grammar alone cannot settle a doctrine, but it points one way. It is the same construction Jesus used about binding and loosing (Matthew 16:19; 18:18), where the sense is what shall have been bound in heaven. Heaven does not ratify the church’s verdict. The church announces heaven’s.

The rest of the New Testament. The second is the absence of any such practice in the rest of the New Testament: nowhere do we see an apostle hear a private confession and pronounce a man absolved. When Simon the magician needs forgiveness, Peter, who would have had this power if anyone did, does not absolve him but sends him to God: “Repent, therefore, of this wickedness of yours, and pray to the Lord that, if possible, the intent of your heart may be forgiven you” (Acts 8:22). And John, who wrote this verse down, tells us in his own letter where a sinner is to take his sins: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9). Confession there is to God, and the promise rests on his faithfulness, not on a mediator’s word.

What the verse does mean. The third is what the verse does mean, which is not nothing. Christ has entrusted his church with the announcement that decides where people stand: the keys, as Matthew calls them. When the gospel is preached, forgiveness is really offered and really withheld. To the man who repents and believes, the church may say with full authority, your sins are forgiven; to the one who will not, it must say with equal authority that they are not. The Reformers kept the substance of this and were right to. They kept the declaration of pardon in public worship, and Luther valued private confession to a pastor for a conscience too troubled to believe a general promise. What they refused was the idea that the forgiveness waits on the minister. He is a herald carrying a message, not a judge holding a power, and the best thing he can do for a frightened soul is tell him what God has already said.

Should I ever confess my sins to another Christian? Yes, sometimes, though not to receive absolution. James says, confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed (James 5:16). Confessing a secret sin to a mature believer or a pastor can break its power, bring accountability, and let you hear the promises of the gospel spoken to you by name. Where you have sinned against someone, confess to them and make it right (Matthew 5:23–24). But the forgiveness itself comes from God alone, through Christ alone, the moment you confess to him. A brother can remind you that you are forgiven; only God can forgive you. Every sin is first of all against God himself (Psalm 51:4), and only the one who has been wronged can release the debt.

Thomas was not with them. We are not told why. His absence will lead to the encounter that brings the Gospel’s climactic confession.

verseByVerse.quote: So the other disciples told him, "We have seen the Lord." But he said to them, "Unless I see in his hands the mark of the nails, and place my finger into the mark of the nails, and place my hand into his side, I will never believe." Eight days later, his disciples were inside again, and Thomas was with them. Although the doors were locked, Jesus came and stood among them and said, "Peace be with you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Unless I see. The ten give Thomas the testimony Mary gave them, we have seen the Lord, and he answers with a condition. The word for hand could include the wrist. Doubting Thomas has become a byword, and the text does not support the caricature. When Jesus appeared to the other ten, he showed them his hands and his side, and only then were they glad (v. 20); they had not believed Mary’s word either (Luke 24:11). Thomas is asking for exactly what the other ten were given. He is not demanding more evidence than his friends had; he is refusing to accept less.

I will never believe. Never is the strong negative (ou mē). Thomas wants physical proof. He is not a cynic, but a realist who will not accept something so great on hearsay. His doubt, recorded honestly, adds to the evidence: the disciples were not credulous. And this is the man who, when the others were arguing against going back to Judea, said, let us also go, that we may die with him (11:16). Whatever his faults, cowardice and half-heartedness were not among them. Yet his words carry a warning too. Unless I see, I will never believe: the heart loves to set God its terms and tell him what proof it will accept. Jesus met Thomas’s terms in mercy, but he is not bound to meet ours, and he has already given the evidence he means us to weigh (vv. 30–31).

The week he spent. Consider the eight days that followed. Ten men he had lived with for three years, all telling him the same impossible thing, all glad, and he alone outside it, unable to make himself believe them and unwilling to pretend. He stayed. He did not leave the group. He turned up on the following Sunday and was in the room.

The marks he insisted on. Thomas’s test is more theological than he knows. He does not ask to see a figure in glory or a sign in the sky; he asks for the nail marks and the spear wound. The only risen Lord he will believe in is the crucified one, and he is right. A Christ without wounds would be some other figure, a ghost or a hero, and could save no one. The resurrection is not the cross undone but the cross vindicated: the body that bore our sins is the body God raised, and the scars prove that the sacrifice and the victory belong to the same person.

Eight days later. The next Sunday, counting inclusively: the disciples gathered again on the first day of the week, and Thomas was with them.

What should I do when I struggle to believe? Do what Thomas did: stay where the others are, and keep turning up. Thomas did not reason his way out; he was in the room when Jesus came back. Do not withdraw from the church because you are struggling. Tell a trusted believer honestly what you are finding hard. Keep reading the testimony, especially the Gospels, and pray even if it feels like talking to the ceiling: I believe; help my unbelief (Mark 9:24). Distinguish doubt from unbelief. Doubt is a faith that is struggling; unbelief is a refusal. Jesus was patient with the first, and he came back for Thomas.

On a Tuesday. If someone in your church is going through a season of doubt, do not treat them as a problem or a threat; keep inviting them. Thomas was given a week among friends who did not throw him out, and that week ended with my Lord and my God.
verseByVerse.note: Nails were driven through the hands (or wrists) and feet.

parallels.desc: they have pierced my hands and feet

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to Thomas, "Put your finger here, and see my hands; and put out your hand, and place it in my side. Do not disbelieve, but believe." Thomas answered him, "My Lord and my God!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Put your finger here. Jesus gives Thomas his own words from eight days earlier, almost exactly, though he was not visibly there when they were said. And there is no rebuke in the offer. He does not say, you should not have needed this. He gives him precisely what he asked, which is what he had already given the other ten without being asked.

Do not disbelieve, but believe. Literally “do not become unbelieving, but believing.” It is addressed to the whole direction of Thomas’s heart, not only to the moment.

My Lord and my God! The climax of John’s Gospel. We are not told that Thomas touched him; John moves straight from the invitation to the confession, and the offer itself seems to have been enough. It is the highest confession in the Gospels. A devout Jew, whose creed was “the Lord our God, the Lord is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4), stands in front of a man he watched die and calls him God, and Jesus does not correct him, which is the point, because he had corrected people about far less. My: personal faith. Not the Lord, but my Lord. It is not a doctrinal formula; it is a man handing himself over.

The architecture of the book. The Gospel opened: in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was God. Twenty chapters later it arrives at my Lord and my God, three verses before the book’s first ending. John has framed the whole account between two statements of the deity of Christ: the first his own, about a Word nobody had yet seen; the last spoken by the most reluctant man in the group, to a face, in a locked room, with the wounds visible. It also answers the claim, often repeated, that the church made Jesus God centuries later, at the Council of Nicaea (AD 325): here the confession stands in a first-century Gospel, on the lips of an eyewitness, and Paul’s letters, earlier still, already worship him as Lord (Philippians 2:6–11).

Our lord and god. If this Gospel was written in the nineties, as many think, there is a further edge to it. The emperor Domitian is reported to have liked being styled our lord and god. Christians in Asia Minor may well have been pressed on exactly that point, and John hands them a sentence in which those words are addressed to somebody else.

Where Christians differ: what Thomas meant. Some, such as Jehovah’s Witnesses, suggest Thomas was exclaiming in surprise, like an oath, or addressing the Father. This commentary’s view: the Greek says Thomas answered “him,” Jesus; and a devout Jew would hardly use God’s name as an exclamation (the third commandment). It is a confession, addressed to Jesus, and Jesus commends it in the next verse. Jesus is God.

Why did Jesus not correct Thomas, when he refused worship elsewhere? Because the confession was true. When people tried to worship Paul and Barnabas, or when John fell at an angel’s feet, they were rebuked at once: worship God (Acts 14:14–15; Revelation 19:10). Jesus receives worship throughout the Gospels without protest (Matthew 14:33; 28:9, 17), and here he receives the highest title there is. If he were not God, accepting it would be the very blasphemy he was crucified for. He accepts it, and blesses those who will say it after Thomas.

On a Tuesday. Make Thomas’s confession your own, and ask what it means for this week. If he is your Lord, what instruction of his are you resisting? If he is your God, what are you trusting instead of him? Two possessive words hand over the whole of life, and none of us hands it over completely; but the wounded Lord obeyed the Father perfectly in our place, and his Spirit goes on making the confession true.

For worship. The wounds Thomas demanded to see are the wounds of God. The Lord of glory was crucified (1 Corinthians 2:8), and the hands held out to the doubter are the hands through which all things were made. Nothing in heaven or on earth stands higher than the one in that locked room, and nothing ever came lower to reach us. He is my Lord, because he bought me with those wounds. He is my God, because no one less could have paid that price.

parallels.desc: my God and my Lord

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to him, "Have you believed because you have seen me? Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed." Now Jesus did many other signs in the presence of the disciples, which are not written in this book;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Have you believed because you have seen me? Not a rebuke, but a statement. Thomas is not cursed; he is standing there having just confessed Jesus as his God.

Blessed are those who have not seen. The last beatitude of the Gospels, and it is for us. Every believer since the apostles has believed without seeing (1 Peter 1:8), resting on the testimony of those who saw (v. 31; 1 John 1:1–3), and Jesus calls us blessed, not second-class. At that moment there were only some hundreds of people alive who would ever see the risen Christ (more than five hundred at one time, Paul says, 1 Corinthians 15:6); everybody else, for two thousand years, would rely on testimony. He was looking past the room at people he had prayed for on the night before he died: I do not ask for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word (17:20). The beatitude is that prayer answered.

Not blind faith. This answers a common suspicion: that faith would be easier and better if only one could have been there. This verse says that not seeing is no disadvantage and carries a blessing of its own. And the beatitude is not blessed are those who believe without evidence. John has just spent twenty chapters supplying evidence, and says in the next verse that he selected it on purpose. Those who have not seen have the testimony of people who did.

Many other signs. John has been selective (21:25), the mark of an honest writer: seven signs, as they are usually counted, out of many; a handful of days, out of three years. That is worth having when somebody objects that the Gospels leave things out, or differ in what they include. Of course they do; the author says so, and then explains what his selection was for.

In the flow. The whole chapter has been a ladder of believing. The beloved disciple believed at the sight of folded linen (v. 8), Mary at the sound of her name (v. 16), the ten at the sight of his hands and side (v. 20), Thomas when the wounds were offered to him (v. 28). Verse 29 adds the last rung, and it is ours: believing through the word of those who saw. That is why verses 30–31 follow at once. The book in our hands is the testimony on which that blessed faith rests.

Why does Jesus not appear to people today to settle their doubts? Because he has already given what is needed, and more sight would not change hearts that will not believe. Abraham told the rich man that if people will not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead (Luke 16:31). The risen Christ appeared to chosen witnesses (Acts 10:40–41), whose testimony is written so that all may believe. Now he speaks through that word, and the Spirit opens blind eyes to see his glory in it (2 Corinthians 4:6). When he does appear again, it will not be to invite faith but to judge and to save (Hebrews 9:28). Today is the day of believing without seeing. None of this makes honest questions wrong: Jesus was patient with Thomas, and the witnesses wrote precisely so that questioners could weigh what they saw.

parallels.desc: though you do not now see him, you believe in him

verseByVerse.quote: but these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So that you may believe. The purpose statement of the whole Gospel, and the last sentence of the book as John first ended it; chapter 21 reads as an epilogue. Like Luke’s preface (Luke 1:1–4), it tells the reader plainly what it is for. John arranged twenty chapters around one outcome, and he states it in a single sentence and then stops.

Come to believe, or go on believing? The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “may continue to believe.” An honest note on the Greek: one reading suggests that you may come to believe, which makes the book evangelistic, addressed to outsiders; the other, that you may go on believing, which makes it a book for the church. The manuscripts are divided and the argument has never been settled. The difference matters little: John writes both to bring people to faith and to strengthen those who believe. It is a happy dispute, because the book plainly does both. It has brought people to Christ who began it as sceptics, and it has held Christians steady for twenty centuries, and nothing in the sentence has to be given up.

That Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God. The content of faith. Jesus, the man from Nazareth, is the Christ, the promised Messiah of Israel, and the Son of God, sharing the Father’s nature. Martha confessed it (11:27); Thomas confessed it in its fullest form (v. 28). Both titles have been fought over in this book. The Christ: the promised one of Israel, which is what the crowds argued about at the feast. The Son of God: which is what they picked up stones over, what the council condemned him for, and what Pilate was afraid of.

Life in his name. Eternal life, now and for ever (3:16; 17:3), through who he is and what he has done. This is where the book started: in him was life, and the life was the light of men (1:4). Everything in between, the water made wine, the bread on the hillside, the man who could see, the voice at the tomb of Lazarus, the towel and the basin, the cross, the empty grave, the name spoken in a garden, has been in service of that one word, and it is offered, at the end, to whoever is holding the book.

How do I know whether I have this life? Ask what you believe about Jesus and what you are trusting. Do you believe that he is the Christ, the Son of God, who died for sinners and rose again? Are you relying on him, and not on your record, for your acceptance with God? Then you have life, now, because he has said so: whoever believes in the Son has eternal life (3:36), and John wrote his letter so that those who believe in the name of the Son of God may know that they have eternal life (1 John 5:13). The evidence of that life will grow: love for God’s people, hatred of sin, a desire to obey him. But it rests on his promise, not on your feelings. If you are not sure, believe him now. That is what the book was written for.

On a Tuesday. Give a copy of John’s Gospel to someone this month, and offer to read it with them. That is what it was written for.

For worship. The Son of God did not leave his glory to rumour. He chose the witnesses, filled their memory with what he had done, and had it written down, so that people he would never meet in the flesh could hear his voice on a page and live. The faith the book asks for is his gift, and the life it promises is his own, shared with everyone who comes to him by it. Glory to Jesus, the Christ, the Son of God, the Life who would not keep his life to himself.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “may continue to believe.”

20.text: <sup>1</sup>Now on the first day of the week Mary Magdalene came to the tomb early, while it was still dark, and saw that the stone had been taken away from the tomb.<sup>2</sup>So she ran and went to Simon Peter and the other disciple, the one whom Jesus loved, and said to them, “They have taken the Lord out of the tomb, and we do not know where they have laid him.”<sup>3</sup>So Peter went out with the other disciple, and they were going toward the tomb.<sup>4</sup>Both of them were running together, but the other disciple outran Peter and reached the tomb first.<sup>5</sup>And stooping to look in, he saw the linen cloths lying there, but he did not go in.<sup>6</sup>Then Simon Peter came, following him, and went into the tomb. He saw the linen cloths lying there,<sup>7</sup>and the face cloth, which had been on Jesus’ head, not lying with the linen cloths but folded up in a place by itself.<sup>8</sup>Then the other disciple, who had reached the tomb first, also went in, and he saw and believed;<sup>9</sup>for as yet they did not understand the Scripture, that he must rise from the dead.<sup>10</sup>Then the disciples went back to their homes.<sup>11</sup>But Mary stood weeping outside the tomb, and as she wept she stooped to look into the tomb.<sup>12</sup>And she saw two angels in white, sitting where the body of Jesus had lain, one at the head and one at the feet.<sup>13</sup>They said to her, “Woman, why are you weeping?” She said to them, “They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him.”<sup>14</sup>Having said this, she turned around and saw Jesus standing, but she did not know that it was Jesus.<sup>15</sup>Jesus said to her, “Woman, why are you weeping?
