Whom are you seeking?” Supposing him to be the gardener, she said to him, “Sir, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away.”<sup>16</sup>Jesus said to her, “Mary.” She turned and said to him in Aramaic, “Rabboni!” (which means Teacher).<sup>17</sup>Jesus said to her, “Do not cling to me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father; but go to my brothers and say to them, ’I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.’”<sup>18</sup>Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, “I have seen the Lord”—and that he had said these things to her.<sup>19</sup>On the evening of that day, the first day of the week, the doors being locked where the disciples were for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood among them and said to them, “Peace be with you.”<sup>20</sup>When he had said this, he showed them his hands and his side. Then the disciples were glad when they saw the Lord.<sup>21</sup>Jesus said to them again, “Peace be with you. As the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you.”<sup>22</sup>And when he had said this, he breathed on them and said to them, “Receive the Holy Spirit.<sup>23</sup>If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you withhold forgiveness from any, it is withheld.”<sup>24</sup>Now Thomas, one of the twelve, called the Twin, was not with them when Jesus came.<sup>25</sup>So the other disciples told him, “We have seen the Lord.” But he said to them, “Unless I see in his hands the mark of the nails, and place my finger into the mark of the nails, and place my hand into his side, I will never believe.”<sup>26</sup>Eight days later, his disciples were inside again, and Thomas was with them. Although the doors were locked, Jesus came and stood among them and said, “Peace be with you.”<sup>27</sup>Then he said to Thomas, “Put your finger here, and see my hands; and put out your hand, and place it in my side. Do not disbelieve, but believe.”<sup>28</sup>Thomas answered him, “My Lord and my God!”<sup>29</sup>Jesus said to him, “Have you believed because you have seen me? Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.”<sup>30</sup>Now Jesus did many other signs in the presence of the disciples, which are not written in this book;<sup>31</sup>but these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name.
20.overview:
John 20 tells of the first Easter Sunday and the Sunday after it. Before dawn Mary Magdalene finds the tomb open; Peter and the beloved disciple run to it and find the grave clothes lying in place, and the beloved disciple believes. Mary stays weeping until the risen Jesus speaks her name, and she becomes the first witness of the resurrection.

That evening Jesus comes through locked doors with peace, shows his wounds, sends the disciples as the Father sent him, and breathes on them the Holy Spirit. A week later he meets the doubting Thomas, who confesses him as Lord and God. John then gives the purpose of his whole book: these things are written so that you may believe, and by believing have life in his name.

21.title: The Restoration of Peter and the Beloved Disciple

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–25 — The Breakfast on the Shore: Restoration and Commission
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The great catch and the breakfast on the shore; Peter’s threefold restoration and commission; the call to follow, whatever road each disciple is given; and the closing witness of the beloved disciple who wrote this book.
verseByVerse.theology: The restoration of Peter is one of the most pastoral scenes in the Gospels. Three questions match three denials, and three commissions answer three failures. The charcoal fire (the same word as 18:18) brings the scene of the denial back, and the same kind of fire becomes the place of restoration. Jesus does not ignore the failure or pretend it did not happen; he brings Peter back to it and heals it. His answer to failure is not silence but a renewed commission: the shepherd who fell is restored to shepherd the flock.
verseByVerse.examples: The beloved disciple is the witness who wrote these things (v. 24): the Gospel rests its authority on eyewitness testimony, the account of one who saw the water turned to wine, stood at the cross, ran to the empty tomb and ate breakfast on this shore. And it ends not with a doctrine but with a person, so great that the world itself could not contain the books that would be written about him.

verseByVerse.quote: After this Jesus revealed himself again to the disciples by the Sea of Tiberias, and he revealed himself in this way. Simon Peter, Thomas (called the Twin), Nathanael of Cana in Galilee, the sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples were together.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. John 21 is an epilogue. John 20 ended with the purpose of the book; now John adds a final scene in Galilee. It shows the risen Lord providing for his disciples, restoring Peter after his denials, commissioning him to shepherd the flock, foretelling his death, and correcting a rumour about John. It tells us that the risen Christ cares for failures, calls them to serve, and gives each his own path. Without this chapter, Peter’s denial would still be lying where chapter 18 left it, three times beside a charcoal fire, unhealed.

By the Sea of Tiberias. The Sea of Tiberias is the Sea of Galilee, named after the city Herod Antipas built on its shore in honour of the emperor Tiberius. It is where he fed the five thousand and walked on the water, and the setting is thick with memory. Jesus had told them he would meet them in Galilee (Mark 16:7). Revealed himself (ephanerōsen): made himself known. John uses the word twice in one verse, and the initiative is entirely on one side: these men did not go looking for him; they went to work, and he showed himself to them, as he so often does in this Gospel (1:43).

Seven disciples. Simon Peter is listed first: the denier who will be restored is the centre of this final scene. Thomas is here, the last we see of him, back at work on a lake with the others; whatever the caricature has made of him, John’s final picture is of a man who stayed. Nathanael is given a home town for the only time in the Gospel: Cana, where Jesus did his first sign (2:1–11). John has waited twenty chapters to mention that one of the men who had probably watched the water become wine lived in the village. The sons of Zebedee appear only here in this Gospel, and James and John are never named in it at all, John characteristically hiding himself. And two are left unnamed, an odd choice for a writer inventing a scene, who would more naturally supply names.

The book closing its circles. The book began by the water with men being called, and it ends by the water with the same men. Seven of them, in a Gospel that has given us seven signs and seven I am sayings. John is tying the ends of his story together.

Does Jesus still reveal himself today? Yes, though not by appearing in a body on the shore. Those appearances were given to chosen witnesses for a limited time (Acts 1:3; 1 Corinthians 15:5–8), and they ended with his ascension, apart from the unique appearance to Paul, last of all (1 Corinthians 15:8). Now he makes himself known through his word, preached and read, by his Spirit, who takes what is Christ’s and declares it to us (16:14). He is present when his people gather in his name (Matthew 18:20), and he meets us at his table. And, as here, he often makes himself known in the ordinary places, at work and at home, when we are not looking for anything in particular. Do not wait for a vision. Open the book where he has already revealed himself.
verseByVerse.note: The Sea of Tiberias is the Sea of Galilee. Nathanael came from Cana; the sons of Zebedee are James and John.

parallels.desc: he is going before you to Galilee

verseByVerse.quote: Simon Peter said to them, "I am going fishing." They said to him, "We will go with you." They went out and got into the boat, but that night they caught nothing. Just as day was breaking, Jesus stood on the shore; yet the disciples did not know that it was Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am going fishing. Some see Peter giving up and returning to his old trade, and the sentence is regularly preached as apostasy, Peter throwing in the towel and going back to his nets. The text will not carry it. The risen Jesus had sent word: tell my brothers to go to Galilee, and there they will see me (Matthew 28:10; Mark 16:7). Galilee is where these men are. They have obeyed an instruction and are waiting for him in the place they were told to wait, with no date given, and men who are waiting have to eat. Peter owned a boat and knew a trade, and nothing in the story suggests that using it was a betrayal. Six of them go with him without hesitation, including the disciple whom Jesus loved.

The flatness of it. What is true, and sadder, is the flatness of it. A man who has seen the risen Lord twice, and denied him three times, says I am going fishing, which is what people do when they do not know what else to do with themselves. It is not rebellion. It is the ordinary, unglamorous business of filling the hours while waiting for something you cannot arrange.

That night they caught nothing. Fishing on the lake was often done at night, when the fish came near the surface and could not see the nets. A wasted night for professional fishermen on their own lake, as at their first calling (Luke 5:5). It is the second time John has put them on that water in the dark with nothing going right (6:16–21), and both times the story ends with somebody standing where they did not expect him.

As day was breaking. As at the tomb, at dawn, and at exactly the moment the night’s failure is confirmed and there is nothing left to do but come in empty. He does not appear in the boat; he stands on the shore, already through his own night, watching theirs end. That is where the risen Christ is for his church: not absent from the dark, but ahead of it, on the far side of death, where the morning has already come.

What should I do while I wait for God to show me the way? Do the next ordinary, faithful thing. The disciples had been told to go to Galilee and wait, and they waited by working. Waiting on God is not idleness, and it is not anxious searching for signs. Keep doing what is right in front of you: your job, your family duties, your place in the church, your prayers. Obey what he has already made clear, and trust him for what he has not. Guidance usually comes as it did here, to people already at their nets, not to people standing on the shore refusing to move until the heavens open.

On a Tuesday. If you are in a season of empty nets, a job search going nowhere, a ministry with no visible fruit, prayers that seem unanswered, keep at the work and keep looking toward the shore. The night is not the end of the story.
verseByVerse.note: Fishing on the lake was done at night.

parallels.desc: we toiled all night and took nothing

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them, "Children, do you have any fish?" They answered him, "No." He said to them, "Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some." So they cast it, and now they were not able to haul it in, because of the quantity of fish.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Children, do you have any fish? “Children” was a friendly way of addressing men, like “lads.” It is paidia here, not the tender little children of the upper room but the everyday word a man uses hailing a boat. And what he asks for is not fish in general but the bit of fish you eat with your bread. It is the question a buyer shouts from the beach at dawn: caught anything? The Greek form expects the answer no. So the risen Son of God opens the conversation of Peter’s restoration by asking for breakfast. Their answer is one word. No. John records it bare, which is how a man says it after a whole night of nothing.

Cast the net on the right side. A strange instruction to experienced fishermen, from someone they do not yet recognise, and they obey. It is the risen Lord’s first command in Galilee, and it is about fish. The Word through whom all things were made (1:3) is Lord of the shoal under the boat as well, and he knows where it is.

Not able to haul it in. A miracle that recalls their first calling, when Jesus said they would be fishers of men (Luke 5:4–10). Then too he got into Peter’s boat after a night in which they had caught nothing, told him to let down the nets, and filled them so full that the nets began to break and a second boat nearly sank. And Peter fell down and said, depart from me, for I am a sinful man. That is where Peter’s discipleship began: a wasted night, a stranger’s instruction, an impossible catch, and a man on his knees saying he was not fit.

The same lake, at the end. The empty night, the instruction from the shore, the catch, and this time Peter does not ask him to go away. He goes into the water to get to him. John does not mention Luke’s story. He does not have to. The men in the boat had lived it, and when the nets went heavy for the second time in their lives, at least one of them worked out immediately who was on the beach. Their mission will be fruitful only by his word. Without him, they catch nothing (15:5); with him, more than they can haul.

If I obey God, will he always give me success? Not always success as we would measure it, but always fruit as he measures it. Obedience is not a technique for guaranteed results; plenty of faithful servants in Scripture saw little visible fruit, like Jeremiah, who preached for forty years and was rejected. The promise is that whoever abides in Christ bears much fruit (15:5), and that your labour in the Lord is not in vain (1 Corinthians 15:58). The size and timing of the catch are his. What this scene teaches is the source: without him nothing, with him more than we can manage. So work hard, obey his word, and leave the results in his hands.

On a Tuesday. Fruit in Christ’s work comes from his word, not our skill. Before you start the task you are most experienced at, the one you could do in your sleep, stop and pray over it. Experience is a gift, but it is not the reason the net fills.

For worship. He called them with a full net and he recalled them with a full net, and between the two he went to the cross. The Lord who filled Peter’s boat at the beginning, when Peter begged him to go away, filled it again at the end for a man who now wanted nothing more than to reach him. Everything between those two catches was his doing, and the harvest of the nations still comes up in nets that he fills.
verseByVerse.note: “Children” was a friendly way of addressing men.

parallels.desc: the first great catch

verseByVerse.quote: That disciple whom Jesus loved therefore said to Peter, "It is the Lord!" When Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he put on his outer garment, for he was stripped for work, and threw himself into the sea. The other disciples came in the boat, dragging the net full of fish, for they were not far from the land, but about a hundred yards off.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is the Lord! The beloved disciple, quick to perceive as at the tomb (20:8), works it out, and Peter moves. One sees; the other jumps. The two men behave exactly as they have all the way through, and John clearly enjoys recording it.

The Lord. Since the empty tomb this Gospel has given Jesus one title above all. Mary says I have seen the Lord, the ten say we have seen the Lord, Thomas says my Lord and my God, and now the beloved disciple, peering at a figure on a beach, says it is the Lord. Kyrios is the word the Greek Old Testament used to render the name of God himself. The man on the shore with a fire going is not merely a teacher recovered from death. He is the risen Lord, and recognising him behind a filled net is the confession the church has made ever since (Romans 10:9).

He put on his outer garment. Fishermen worked in a loincloth or a short tunic. It is a small comic detail that has puzzled readers for centuries: he dressed to swim. The likeliest explanation is that a Jew would not greet a person of standing improperly clothed; a greeting, it is often said, was something close to a religious act. Peter is about to meet his Lord, and he is not going to arrive stripped for work, so he tucks up his garment and goes over the side in it.

Threw himself into the sea. He was about a hundred yards out. He could have waited perhaps three minutes for the boat. That is the whole man. It is the same impulse that drew a sword in the garden and swore he would die first. Nothing about Peter’s temperament has been corrected by his failure, and Jesus is about to give him a job without asking him to become somebody else.

The others brought the boat in. They drag the net ashore, doing the necessary work while one of them swims. John does not rank them. Both arrive.

About a hundred yards off. The ESV notes that the distance is literally two hundred cubits, about 100 yards or 90 metres. Somebody looked at the distance and remembered it. These small measurements run all through this Gospel: six stone jars holding twenty or thirty gallons, twenty-five or thirty stadia rowed on a dark lake, seventy-five pounds of spices, a hundred yards to a beach. They do nothing for the theology. They are the kind of thing a man includes when he is describing something he watched; they cannot prove the account on their own, but they fit its claim to come from one who was there (v. 24).

Does Jesus want me to change my personality? He wants to sanctify it, not erase it. Peter was still impulsive after the resurrection, and John still quietly perceptive; Christ used both. Grace does not turn every Christian into the same kind of person. What it does is purge the sin that clings to our temperament: Peter’s rashness had to be humbled, and his boasting broken, but his eagerness was turned toward Christ. So do not envy another believer’s temperament or despise your own. Ask the Lord to cut away what is sinful in it and to use what is left for his glory. The church needs both those who see first and those who jump first, and those who quietly bring in the boat.

On a Tuesday. Thank God this week for a believer whose temperament is unlike yours, perhaps one who irritates you, and tell them something you value in them.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the distance is literally two hundred cubits.

verseByVerse.quote: When they got out on land, they saw a charcoal fire in place, with fish laid out on it, and bread. Jesus said to them, "Bring some of the fish that you have just caught."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A charcoal fire. The word for a charcoal fire occurs exactly twice in the New Testament: here, and in the courtyard on the night Peter said I am not (18:18). John used it once when Peter was warming his hands among the men who had arrested his master, and he uses it again now without explanation. It is deliberate. Few things call back a memory like the smell of a fire. Peter comes up the beach soaked to a fire like the one he last stood beside: he has been brought back to the scene of it. He denied his Lord beside one charcoal fire; he will be restored beside another.

Breakfast already cooking. Before there was a catch, before Peter had done anything at all, while seven men were still failing to fish, breakfast was already cooking. The risen Lord serves his disciples, as he did at the supper (13:4–5). And the fire is in place: already down to coals hot enough to cook on, which takes time. They had spent the night failing on the water, and he had spent part of it making a fire.

Bring some of the fish. He does not need their fish; he has his own. But he asks for theirs and puts them on the fire beside his own, which is a wonderfully gentle thing: the risen Lord, who has provided everything, arranging for the men to contribute to a meal they could not have produced. That is very close to the whole doctrine of Christian work. Nothing we bring is required. It is asked for anyway, and it goes on the fire with his.

What if the memory of my failure keeps coming back? Look at what Jesus did with Peter’s memory. He did not pretend the courtyard had not happened, and he did not leave Peter alone with it. He lit the same kind of fire and made breakfast beside it, so that the smell of failure would from then on be mixed with the smell of grace. When an old sin comes back to you, do not try to bury the memory or let it accuse you. Bring it to Christ and look at it in the light of the cross: it was real, it was forgiven, and he has given you work to do since. The Lord does not erase our history; he redeems it, until the worst memory becomes a place where we learned how much he loves us.

On a Tuesday. Bring what you have to Christ’s work this week, however small: an hour, a skill, a meal for someone, a few words of witness. He does not need it, and he asks for it anyway.

For worship. Peter had warmed himself at one charcoal fire while his Lord was being struck; now his Lord has lit another and waits at it with bread. Between the two fires stood the cross, where the Shepherd took the blows the sheep deserved. That is why this fire smells of grace and not of shame. The one who tends it has already dealt with the failure it recalls, and he has breakfast ready before the failure is even mentioned.
verseByVerse.note: John mentions a charcoal fire only here and at Peter’s denial.

verseByVerse.quote: So Simon Peter went aboard and hauled the net ashore, full of large fish, 153 of them. And although there were so many, the net was not torn. Jesus said to them, "Come and have breakfast." Now none of the disciples dared ask him, "Who are you?" They knew it was the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
153 of them. The number has attracted more ingenuity than any other detail in the Gospel. Jerome said there were 153 kinds of fish, standing for all nations, so that the catch would represent every kind of person gathered in. Augustine noticed that 153 is the sum of every number from 1 to 17, and built an elaborate structure on 10 (the commandments) plus 7 (the Spirit). Others have counted the numerical values of Hebrew letters. None of it commands agreement, and most of it could be done for almost any number.

Fishermen count the catch. The simplest explanation is much more likely and is not less interesting. Fishermen counted their catch to share it out. It was a remarkable haul, somebody sat on the beach and counted it, and decades later an old man still remembered the figure. That is worth more than any allegory. A precise number fits the memory of an eyewitness, though it cannot prove one by itself, and the great catch points to the worldwide mission.

The net was not torn. In Luke 5:6 the nets began to break; here they hold. Some see a picture of the church: gathering all kinds of people, and not torn apart.

None of the disciples dared ask him, Who are you? They knew it was the Lord. Something about him was different, and yet they knew. Awe and certainty together. It is perhaps the most awkward sentence in the chapter. They knew, and nobody said anything. Seven men stand round a fire in a silence too large to break: not doubt, and not fear exactly, but the strangeness of standing beside someone you abandoned, who died, and who is cooking your breakfast. And the words that hang over that silence are his own, spoken a moment before: come and have breakfast. It is as plain an invitation as there is, and the Lord of life speaks it. He does not explain himself or ease the awkwardness; he feeds them. The guest who supplied the wine at a wedding in Cana is the host now, and the first thing he does with men too awed to speak is give them a place at his fire.

In the flow. Chapter 20 ended with the disciples sent as the Father sent the Son (20:21). Chapter 21 shows what that sending will be like. Without him the nets are empty; at his word they overflow (vv. 3–11). Then, in verses 15–17, the fishermen are made shepherds: those who gather people in must also feed them. And the breakfast between the two scenes says that the one who sends them goes on feeding them himself.

What does the full net say about the church’s mission? That the gathering of people is Christ’s work, that it is great, and that his net holds. The disciples had been told they would be fishers of men, and their first attempt at fishing without him ended in an empty net. With him the net was full, and it did not break. The church today is gathered from every nation and kind, and it often looks as though the strain must tear it. It will not. Christ will bring in all whom the Father has given him (6:37), and not one will slip through. So pray for missionaries, support the work of the gospel, and cast your own net, knowing that the outcome is in his hands.

On a Tuesday. Come and have breakfast with Jesus. Start each day in fellowship with him. Before the phone, before the news, before the day’s demands, give the first minutes to him: a psalm, a Gospel passage, a prayer. He has already prepared the meal.
verseByVerse.note: Many symbolic meanings have been proposed for 153; the plainest point is that someone counted — a detail from an eyewitness.

parallels.desc: their nets were breaking

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and so with the fish. This was now the third time that Jesus was revealed to the disciples after he was raised from the dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He took the bread and gave it. Three verbs, and this Gospel has used them before, at the feeding of the five thousand by the same lake (6:11): on a hillside above this water he took the loaves, gave thanks, and distributed them to the crowd. The host serves his guests. Luke tells us the risen Jesus also ate (Luke 24:42–43): his body was real.

He serves them. The risen Lord of glory, not long out of a grave, with the marks still in his hands, stands at a fire on a beach handing bread to seven fishermen who have been up all night. He had told them, at the supper, that he was among them as the one who serves (Luke 22:27), and he had knelt with a towel to prove it. Nothing about the resurrection has changed that. The one who washed their feet before he died is cooking their breakfast after.

The third time. The third appearance to the group of disciples in John (20:19, 26). There were others (1 Corinthians 15:5–8). The first two were indoors, in a city, behind bolted doors, with fear in the room. This one is outdoors, at dawn, in their own country, over a meal, with the door of the world standing open.

The second meal of bread and fish. Bread and fish is the only meal this Gospel records him providing twice. The first time it was a sign, and the crowd wanted to make him king and then walked away when he explained what it meant. This time there is no crowd, no argument, and no discourse afterwards. Just seven men eating breakfast with him.

Is this a picture of the Lord’s Supper? Not directly; it is a real breakfast on a real beach, and John does not call it a sacrament. But it does echo the meals that point to his table: the feeding of the five thousand, where he spoke of himself as the bread of life, and the upper room, where he took bread and gave it to them. In all of them the same Lord feeds his people with his own hands. When you come to the Lord’s Supper, it is a memorial of his death and a means by which he nourishes your faith; you are not merely remembering an absent Christ. You are being fed by the risen one, spiritually present by his Spirit, who still takes bread and gives it to his disciples.

On a Tuesday. Serve someone a meal this week as he served his friends: a tired colleague, a new family at church, a neighbour living alone. The risen Lord of glory thought it worth his morning.

For worship. The bread of life (6:35) stood at a fire and handed bread to his friends. The risen Christ has not been promoted out of serving. Exalted to the right hand of God, he still feeds his people by his word and at his table, and he has promised that when he returns the master himself will dress for service, have his servants recline at table, and come and serve them (Luke 12:37). The fire on the beach was a foretaste of that table.

verseByVerse.quote: When they had finished breakfast, Jesus said to Simon Peter, "Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?" He said to him, "Yes, Lord; you know that I love you." He said to him, "Feed my lambs." He said to him a second time, "Simon, son of John, do you love me?" He said to him, "Yes, Lord; you know that I love you." He said to him, "Tend my sheep."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simon, son of John. Not Peter, the rock, but his old name, as at his first meeting with Jesus (1:42), when he was told, you shall be called Cephas. Peter has not been a rock. Now, after a courtyard and a fire and three denials, he is addressed by the name he had before the promise was made, three times. It is not cruelty. It is the honesty of a restoration that refuses to pretend. A man who has failed badly cannot be repaired by being told the failure did not matter. Jesus takes him back to Simon son of John, and starts again from there.

Do you love me more than these? “More than these” probably means more than the other disciples love me, since Peter had boasted that even if all fell away, he would not (Mark 14:29). Some take it as more than these things: the boats, nets and fish. The first is more likely. Jesus gently probes his pride. The comparison was Peter’s own. Jesus raises it once and then drops it, and never mentions it again.

The question nobody would predict. Not are you sorry. Not will you promise. Not do you understand what you did. Peter is never asked to explain himself, never asked to apologise, never once given the chance to make the vow he had made before and broken. Do you love me? That is the whole examination for restoration to apostolic ministry, put three times, and it is about love rather than performance. That is worth knowing for anyone who has failed and assumes that what is wanted is a better record. Religion left to itself tends to offer a way back by penance: prove you are sorry, earn your place again, and then perhaps you will be trusted. Jesus offers no such scheme, because Peter’s debt was paid at the cross; what he asks for is not repayment but love.

Yes, Lord; you know that I love you. Peter no longer compares himself with others. He appeals to Jesus’ knowledge.

Two words for love. Jesus asks with agapaō the first two times; Peter answers with phileō each time; the third time Jesus uses phileō. Some see great significance: Jesus asks for the highest love, Peter can only offer friendship love, and Jesus comes down to Peter’s level. But John uses the two words interchangeably elsewhere (both are used of the Father’s love for the Son, 3:35; 5:20), and he varies other words in this passage too (lambs and sheep, feed and tend). The main point is the threefold question, not the variation.

Four pairs of synonyms. The change of verbs does not stand alone. In these three exchanges John uses two words for love, two for feeding and tending, two for lambs and sheep, and two for knowing: four pairs in three verses, very likely varied for the ear. That does not settle it, and the older reading remains moving: Jesus meeting a chastened Peter where he is, no longer pressing him to claim the higher love he had once boasted of. Nothing in the passage’s meaning depends on the outcome: three questions answering three denials, and a full restoration to shepherd Christ’s flock.

Feed my lambs. Peter’s restoration is also his commission. The flock is my lambs: they belong to Christ, not to Peter. Not many days before, beside a charcoal fire, Peter would not own the Shepherd; now the Good Shepherd who laid down his life for the sheep (10:11) puts the sheep into his hands. The shepherd must feed them, with the word of God, and tend them (poimaine): shepherd, care for, guide, protect.

In the flow. Peter’s story in this Gospel runs in three scenes. At the supper he boasted that he would lay down his life for Jesus, and was told that before the rooster crowed he would deny him three times (13:37–38). In the courtyard he did, beside a charcoal fire (18:17, 25–27). Here, beside another fire, verses 15–17 answer the three denials with three questions, and verses 18–19 take up the old boast: Peter will indeed lay down his life, not by his own resolve this time, but because the Lord who restored him will keep him.

Does Feed my sheep make Peter the head of the church and the first pope? Roman Catholic teaching reads it so. But the threefold question answers the threefold denial: it restores a fallen apostle to his work. It speaks of no office above the other apostles and of no successors. Peter himself later tells the elders, as a fellow elder, to shepherd the flock of God that is among you (1 Peter 5:1–2). The commission is for every faithful pastor.

What if I do not feel much love for Jesus? Then do what Peter did: take your love, such as it is, to the one who knows everything. Love for Christ is not measured by the intensity of your feelings on a given day, but by whether you want him, trust him, grieve when you fail him, and want to obey him. Weak love is still love. And love grows by looking at his love for you: we love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). Read the passion narrative slowly, and this chapter, and see what he did for a man who had denied him. Then ask him to increase your love. It is a prayer he delights to answer.

On a Tuesday. Love for Christ shows itself in care for his people. Think of one lamb in your church, a new believer, a child, a struggling member, and do one thing to feed them this week: a word of Scripture, an invitation, a conversation over coffee. That is what love for Jesus looks like on an ordinary day.
verseByVerse.note: “More than these” probably means more than the other disciples love me — Peter had claimed he would never fall away.

parallels.desc: shepherd the flock of God

verseByVerse.quote: He said to him the third time, "Simon, son of John, do you love me?" Peter was grieved because he said to him the third time, "Do you love me?" and he said to him, "Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you." Jesus said to him, "Feed my sheep. Truly, truly, I say to you, when you were young, you used to dress yourself and walk wherever you wanted, but when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you and carry you where you do not want to go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to him the third time. Each denial is answered by a confession of love. Jesus does not pretend the denials did not happen; he heals them. The restoration is as precise as the failure: a charcoal fire for a charcoal fire, three questions for three denials.

Peter was grieved. The third time stung. The verb is strong: distressed, pained. And John tells us exactly what caused it: not the question, but the third one. He knew what the third meant. Nobody had to say it.

You know everything. Peter throws himself on Jesus’ knowledge; he cannot prove his love by his record. That is the appeal of a man who has run out of evidence about himself. His record is a courtyard and a fire and a rooster. Not I have been faithful, which he could not say; not I will do better, which he had said before and which had proved worthless. Just: you know everything. And Peter is saying something about Jesus as well as himself. Only God knows the human heart (1 Kings 8:39; John 2:24–25), and the disciples had already confessed, now we know that you know all things (16:30). Peter stakes everything on a knowledge that belongs to God alone. Jesus accepts it, requires no more, and at once hands over the sheep. Failure is not the end of service.

When you were young. A description of Peter’s life so far, impulsiveness included. Stretch out your hands was an ancient way of describing crucifixion, and the next verse says outright that it refers to his death. Early tradition says Peter was crucified in Rome under Nero, around AD 64–68, and a later tradition adds that he asked to be crucified upside down, feeling unworthy to die as his Lord did. Peter had said he would lay down his life for Jesus (13:37); now Jesus says he will. The restoration comes with the truth attached: he is told quietly, over breakfast, that he will die for his Lord when he is old, and will not want to go. The Lord does not pretend the road is easy, and he does not withhold the commission because the man will suffer for it.

Where Christians differ: Peter and the papacy. Roman Catholic teaching sees this passage, with Matthew 16:18, as Christ giving Peter primacy over the whole church, passed on to the bishops of Rome. This commentary’s view: this is the restoration of a fallen apostle, not the founding of an office. Peter calls himself a “fellow elder” (1 Peter 5:1) and tells all elders to shepherd the flock (1 Peter 5:2). Paul opposed him to his face (Galatians 2:11). The New Testament says nothing of Peter’s successors. All pastors are under-shepherds of the one Chief Shepherd (1 Peter 5:4).

Can a pastor who has fallen be restored to ministry? Every repentant sinner can be restored to Christ and to the fellowship of the church, fully and gladly. Restoration to the office of pastor is a different question. Peter was restored by the Lord himself, in person, to an apostleship that only Christ could give. Today the church must apply the qualifications Christ has set: an elder must be above reproach, faithful in marriage, self-controlled and well thought of (1 Timothy 3:1–7). Some sins, especially abuse of the flock, betray a trust so deeply that the person should never again hold the office, however real his repentance; protecting the sheep comes first. Other failures may allow a careful return after time, accountability and proven change. Forgiveness is always offered. Office is a trust, not a right.

On a Tuesday. Your past failure does not disqualify you from Christ’s service. He restores, and sends. If you have been sitting on the sidelines of the church because of something in your past that has been confessed and forgiven, ask your pastor this week how you can serve.

For worship. The Lord who knows everything chose to speak to Peter’s love rather than his denials, because the denials had already been carried to the cross and paid for in the wounds he bore. His own hands had been stretched out first, and Peter’s would be stretched out after him, not to pay for anything but to follow. The fisherman who once could not admit to a servant girl that he knew Jesus died owning him before the world, and the grace that did that has not grown weaker since.
verseByVerse.note: Three questions mirror Peter’s three denials. “Stretch out your hands” was an expression used of crucifixion; early Christian tradition says Peter was crucified in Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: This he said to show by what kind of death he was to glorify God. And after saying this he said to him, "Follow me." Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following them, the one who also had leaned back against him during the supper and had said, "Lord, who is it that is going to betray you?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
By what kind of death. A martyr’s death is not a defeat but a way of honouring God, and by the time John wrote, Peter had died. John has used this formula once before, almost word for word, about Jesus: he said this to show by what kind of death he was going to die (12:33). The same construction is applied to the Master and then to the disciple. In this Gospel, glorifying God through a death has had one reference for twenty chapters. Peter’s end will do what his Lord’s did: not atone, which is given to no one else, but glorify. What does it mean to glorify God by dying? It means showing, by the way one dies, how great and trustworthy God is. A man who goes to a cross rather than deny Christ tells the watching world, with the last thing he has, that Christ is worth more than life (Philippians 1:20–21).

Follow me. Where it began (1:43; Mark 1:17), it ends. The whole Christian life in two words. Follow, all the way, even to a cross. They are the words he said to Philip as he set out for Galilee three years earlier, and the words Matthew records him saying to Peter himself beside this very lake, with a net in his hands: follow me, and I will make you fishers of men (Matthew 4:19). Everything has happened in between, the walking on water and the sinking, the sword and the courtyard and the rooster, and the instruction has not changed by a syllable.

The same terms. There was no new arrangement for a man who had failed: no reduced role, no probation, no adjusted terms. The same two words he was given at the beginning, given back to him at the end, as though nothing needed altering. And it is not a single decision but a way of going on.

What does following Christ look like day by day? It means going where he leads, at his pace, by his word. In practice: beginning the day by listening to him in Scripture; taking his commands as your instructions for that day, at work, at home, in your thoughts; choosing his way when it costs you; confessing quickly when you stray and getting back behind him. It means being with his people, because he is leading a flock, not a set of individuals. And it means accepting the road he chooses, which for Peter included a cross and for John a long old age. Following is not admiring him from a distance. It is walking behind him, one step at a time, until the road ends where he is.

On a Tuesday. Follow me is not only a word for the great crossroads. It is spoken over the commute, the inbox and the hard conversation you would rather avoid, and it is answered there, one ordinary step behind him, in the strength of the Spirit he breathed on his friends. You will follow unevenly, as Peter did; the one ahead of you did the Father’s will without a misstep, in your place, and your standing rests on his obedience, not yours.

verseByVerse.quote: When Peter saw him, he said to Jesus, "Lord, what about this man?" Jesus said to him, "If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow me!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lord, what about this man? Very human. Having just heard of his own death, Peter wants to know about John’s. The timing is what makes this so useful. He has just been restored, commissioned, and told how he will die. And within about one sentence he has turned round, spotted John walking behind them, and asked what is going to happen to him. It is not malice. It is the instinct that arrives the moment a person is given something hard: to find out what the other man is getting. Peter has just been handed a cross, and his first move is to check whether it is being handed out evenly.

If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you? Jesus will not satisfy Peter’s curiosity. Each disciple has his own path, appointed by the Lord. Comparison is a trap. It is a blunt word. There is no explanation offered. He does not tell Peter what John’s road will be, or justify the difference, or soften it. He declines the question entirely.

You follow me! You is emphatic, the pronoun brought forward: mind your own call. Jesus’ will for John is not Peter’s business.

Until I come. Inside the hypothetical sits a certainty. Jesus does not say whether John will live to see it, but he speaks of his coming as fixed, the horizon against which every disciple’s road is measured. Peter’s cross and John’s old age are both lived before the return of the same Lord, who holds both lives in his hand and will close both roads at his appearing (14:3). The question for a disciple is never how long he has, but who is coming.

The comparison that corrodes. This sentence applies far past martyrdom. Every Christian eventually notices that the terms are not identical: another believer’s marriage, health, children, work or ease in prayer looks easier, and the comparison corrodes in both directions, breeding resentment when we come off worse and complacency when we come off better. Recall the last time a comparison with another Christian held your thoughts for more than a moment, and hear what Jesus said about that exact activity to the man he had just restored: what is that to you? The call is not comparative. By early tradition Peter’s road ended on a cross in Rome and John’s in extreme old age in Ephesus, and neither was owed the other’s.

Is it wrong to ask God why my life is harder than someone else’s? It is not wrong to bring your grief honestly to God; the psalmists did it constantly (Psalm 73). Asaph envied the prosperity of the wicked until he went into the sanctuary of God and saw their end. What is wrong is to keep the comparison as a grievance, as though God owed you another person’s road. Bring the question to him, and then let him answer as he answered Peter: your road is mine to choose; follow me on it. The comfort is that he chose it in love, that he walks it with you, and that every road his people walk ends in the same place, with him.

verseByVerse.quote: So the saying spread abroad among the brothers that this disciple was not to die; yet Jesus did not say to him that he was not to die, but, "If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you?" This is the disciple who is bearing witness about these things, and who has written these things, and we know that his testimony is true.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The saying spread abroad. The rumour may have spread because the beloved disciple lived to a great age; tradition says John lived in Ephesus until the reign of Trajan, around AD 98, the last of the apostles. It is exactly what happens to a remark: a hypothetical gets repeated, the if falls off in the retelling, and within a generation people treat it as a promise. Presumably, as John grew very old, the story hardened and was causing difficulty by the time this was written.

Jesus did not say. John corrects the rumour without indignation or embarrassment: he quotes the sentence back exactly as it was said, with the if restored, and points out the difference. That is a community handling misinformation about its own founder by returning to the words, as the church has had to do ever since.

The disciple who is bearing witness. The author identifies himself as the beloved disciple: the Gospel is eyewitness testimony. Witness is the thread John has run through the whole book. John the Baptist came to bear witness about the light (1:7); the Father and the works bore witness to the Son (5:36–37); and in the upper room Jesus promised that the Spirit would bear witness about him, and you also will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning (15:26–27). Here that promise is kept. The man who leaned against him at the supper has borne his witness, and it is all about one person. He never names himself; he names Jesus on every page.

We know. “We”: probably the elders of the church at Ephesus, or John’s circle, who knew him and endorsed his Gospel. They vouch for him.

Was chapter 21 added later? That shift to we know matters, since it sounds like the community’s voice and a reader may fairly wonder what that implies. Some scholars argue that this whole chapter was added after John’s death by the church that preserved his teaching. The case is not silly: 20:30–31 reads like the end of a book, this chapter opens after that ending, and here at the close someone other than the author appears to be vouching for him. Two things weigh heavily the other way. The first is weighty and simply stated: no surviving manuscript of this Gospel that preserves its ending lacks chapter 21. Not one, as far as is known, in any language. That is a completely different situation from the passage about the woman caught in adultery, or the long ending of Mark, where the copies genuinely divide and your Bible carries a footnote saying so. Whatever the history of how this book was put together, there is no evidence that it ever circulated without these verses. The second is that the we needs no editor to explain it. John writes this way elsewhere of the shared apostolic witness, we have seen his glory (1:14), and a document could carry the endorsement of the elders who published it without ceasing to be the author’s own, much as a preface signed by others does not make a book someone else’s.

No ascension scene. John never describes the ascension. Luke tells it twice because he is writing the sequel; John simply stops, on a beach in Galilee, with two words spoken to a man who had failed: follow me. He told us at 20:31 why he wrote, that you may believe and that believing you may have life, and once that is done he does not need a departure scene. He leaves you not watching the sky, but standing on the sand, with a command and an open road.

How do I guard against misreading Scripture as the rumour did? Do what John did: go back to the exact words. Read the whole sentence and its context, not a phrase lifted out of it. Notice the small words, the ifs and buts and therefores, because the rumour was born when an if fell off. Compare Scripture with Scripture, because the Bible is its own best interpreter. Be suspicious of any teaching that rests on a single verse read in isolation, especially one that promises something Jesus did not clearly say. And read with the church, past and present, whose careful reading has kept God’s people from many such rumours.
verseByVerse.note: The rumour may have spread because the beloved disciple lived to a great age. Verse 24 identifies him as the author of the Gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there are also many other things that Jesus did. Were every one of them to be written, I suppose that the world itself could not contain the books that would be written.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many other things. Twenty-one chapters can be read in an afternoon, and a person could close the book thinking he now has Jesus of Nazareth, complete, between two covers. John’s last act is to say: this is a selection, chosen for a stated purpose (20:31), and what is not here would swamp the world.

The world could not contain the books. A deliberate exaggeration, a common ancient way of saying countless. The writer flags it himself with I suppose. He is not making a claim about library space. He is doing what a man does when he has finished writing about someone he loves, looks at what he has produced, and finds it absurdly inadequate. But there is truth in it. The person and work of Jesus are inexhaustible. If the Word through whom all things were made (1:3) became flesh, then the world itself is too small to hold the full account of him. The book is finished. The subject is not.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that we need other sources, traditions or revelations to know Jesus truly. What is written is enough to believe and have life (20:31). The Scriptures are sufficient, though not exhaustive. Sufficient means that everything we need to know Christ, be saved and live for God is there (2 Timothy 3:15–17); not exhaustive means that they do not tell us everything there is to know about him.

The last picture. And so the Gospel ends: not with a doctrine, not with an ascension, but on a beach in Galilee, with a charcoal fire burning down and a man who had failed being told to keep walking. The Lord of glory, days out of a grave and about to go home to his Father, spent that morning cooking fish for seven tired men who had caught nothing, deserved nothing, and had run away from him not long before. This is the last picture the Gospel gives of him: not a throne or a cloud, but a meal cooking, a question that is not are you sorry but do you love me, and two words that never change.

Will we keep learning about Jesus in heaven? Yes, for ever. Knowing him is eternal life (17:3), and an infinite person cannot be exhausted by finite creatures in any number of ages. Paul prays that we may comprehend the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge (Ephesians 3:18–19), and the coming ages will show the immeasurable riches of his grace (Ephesians 2:7). We will know fully, in the sense of truly and without distortion (1 Corinthians 13:12), but never completely, because he is God. Heaven will not be the end of discovery. It will be its beginning, without sin to blur the view, and every new sight of him will be cause for fresh worship.

On a Tuesday. If you have read this Gospel through, do not put it away as finished. Begin it again, and ask for one new sight of Christ in every chapter.

For worship. The Lord whose deeds would overflow every library on earth stooped into a single human life, three years, one week, a cross and a garden, and then let an old disciple choose a handful of days to show us who he is. It is enough to believe and live. It is not enough to finish him. The book closes and its subject goes on, and the whole of eternity will be his people discovering that the half was not told them.

21.text: <sup>1</sup>After this Jesus revealed himself again to the disciples by the Sea of Tiberias, and he revealed himself in this way.<sup>2</sup>Simon Peter, Thomas (called the Twin), Nathanael of Cana in Galilee, the sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples were together.<sup>3</sup>Simon Peter said to them, “I am going fishing.” They said to him, “We will go with you.” They went out and got into the boat, but that night they caught nothing.<sup>4</sup>Just as day was breaking, Jesus stood on the shore; yet the disciples did not know that it was Jesus.<sup>5</sup>Jesus said to them, “Children, do you have any fish?” They answered him, “No.”<sup>6</sup>He said to them, “Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some.” So they cast it, and now they were not able to haul it in, because of the quantity of fish.<sup>7</sup>That disciple whom Jesus loved therefore said to Peter, “It is the Lord!” When Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he put on his outer garment, for he was stripped for work, and threw himself into the sea.<sup>8</sup>The other disciples came in the boat, dragging the net full of fish, for they were not far from the land, but about a hundred yards off.<sup>9</sup>When they got out on land, they saw a charcoal fire in place, with fish laid out on it, and bread.<sup>10</sup>Jesus said to them, “Bring some of the fish that you have just caught.”<sup>11</sup>So Simon Peter went aboard and hauled the net ashore, full of large fish, 153 of them. And although there were so many, the net was not torn.<sup>12</sup>Jesus said to them, “Come and have breakfast.” Now none of the disciples dared ask him, “Who are you?” They knew it was the Lord.<sup>13</sup>Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and so with the fish.<sup>14</sup>This was now the third time that Jesus was revealed to the disciples after he was raised from the dead.<sup>15</sup>When they had finished breakfast, Jesus said to Simon Peter, “Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.” He said to him, “Feed my lambs.”<sup>16</sup>He said to him a second time, “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.” He said to him, “Tend my sheep.”<sup>17</sup>He said to him the third time, “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” Peter was grieved because he said to him the third time, “Do you love me?” and he said to him, “Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you.” Jesus said to him, “Feed my sheep.<sup>18</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, when you were young, you used to dress yourself and walk wherever you wanted, but when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you and carry you where you do not want to go.”<sup>19</sup>(This he said to show by what kind of death he was to glorify God.) And after saying this he said to him, “Follow me.”<sup>20</sup>Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following them, the one who also had leaned back against him during the supper and had said, “Lord, who is it that is going to betray you?”<sup>21</sup>When Peter saw him, he said to Jesus, “Lord, what about this man?”<sup>22</sup>Jesus said to him, “If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow me!”<sup>23</sup>So the saying spread abroad among the brothers that this disciple was not to die; yet Jesus did not say to him that he was not to die, but, “If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you?”<sup>24</sup>This is the disciple who is bearing witness about these things, and who has written these things, and we know that his testimony is true.<sup>25</sup>Now there are also many other things that Jesus did. Were every one of them to be written, I suppose that the world itself could not contain the books that would be written.
21.overview:
John 21 is an epilogue, set by the Sea of Galilee. After a fruitless night’s fishing, seven disciples are given a great catch at the word of a stranger on the shore, and the beloved disciple knows him: it is the Lord. Jesus feeds them breakfast beside a charcoal fire.

Beside that fire, the same kind as the one where Peter denied him, Jesus asks Peter three times whether he loves him, and three times gives him the flock to shepherd. He tells Peter the death by which he will glorify God, and calls him to follow, and when Peter asks about the beloved disciple, tells him to mind his own call. John corrects a rumour, names the beloved disciple as the author whose testimony is true, and closes by saying the world could not hold the books needed to tell all that Jesus did. The Gospel ends with a forgiven disciple, a renewed calling and the command to follow.
